gR0Fmf.description: An imaging technique used to evaluate the intrahepatic bile duct, extrahepatic bile duct, and pancreatic duct. Typically does not require contrast agents. Unlike endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), MRCP is not used for interventions (e.g., stone removal).

SR0ymf.title: ICD
SR0ymf.description:
An abbreviation that can refer to:
1. Implantable cardioverter defibrillator
2. International classification of diseases
3. Irritant contact dermatitis
4. Intercostal drain
5. Impulse control disorder

hR0c5f.title: Pallanaesthesia
hR0c5f.description: Loss of the ability to sense vibration. Typically appears in polyneuropathies and/or diseases that affect the dorsal spinal column.

3R0S5f.title: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
3R0S5f.description: A cytokine that stimulates the production of granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) in the bone marrow. Recombinant G-CSF can be used to treat granulocytopenia.

destinations.label: Basics of hematology → Bone marrow and hematopoiesis

RR0l5f.title: Sudden cardiac death
RR0l5f.description: A sudden, unexpected death that occurs within 1 hour of symptom onset as a result of cardiac arrest (e.g., from ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, asystole, and/or pulseless electrical activity). The most common underlying cause of SCD in elderly individuals is acute coronary syndrome; causes of SCD in young patients include cardiomyopathies, prolonged QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and myocarditis. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are used as primary prevention in patients at high risk of SCD.

QR0u5f.title: Pinealoma
QR0u5f.description: A tumor that forms in or near the pineal gland and includes pineocytomas, pineoblastomas, and pineal germinomas. Can cause Parinaud syndrome (due to compression of the tectum), obstructive hydrocephalus (due to compression of the cerebral aqueduct), and precocious puberty (if it produces β-hCG).

jR0_5f.title: Friedlander pneumonia
jR0_5f.description: Atypical pneumonia that is caused by Klebsiella. The disease is named after Carl Friedlander, a German microbiologist, who discovered that pneumonia was caused by bacteria in 1883.

PR0WMf.title: Central venous pressure
PR0WMf.description: The blood pressure in the right atrium or in the superior vena cava. CVP is measured by introducing a central venous catheter into the SVC via the external or internal jugular vein. Normal range: 4–10 cm H₂0 (= 3–8 mm Hg). In a patient that is semireclined, the height of jugular venous pulsations can serve as a rough clinical estimate of CVP.

media.title: Jugular venous pressure waveforms in common cardiac conditions

kR0mMf.title: Cerclage
kR0mMf.description:
A surgical procedure in which an organ or a structure is encircled with a wire loop or ligatures in order to provide structural support.
1. Cervical cerclage: cerclage of the cervical os in order to treat cervical incompetence during pregnancy
2. Eyeball cerclage (scleral buckling): Cerclage of the eyeball in order to treat retinal detachment
3. In orthopedic surgery: cerclage of the ends of an oblique fracture

OR0IMf.title: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin
OR0IMf.description: A nonvirulent form of Mycobacterium bovis. Used as a live vaccine to provide active immunity against severe forms of tuberculosis (esp. tubercular meningitis) and as intravesical immunotherapy against early-stage bladder cancer.

lR0vMf.title: Mass vaccination
lR0vMf.description: Vaccination of a large number of people in the shortest possible time, after the outbreak of an epidemic. The goal of mass vaccination is to improve herd immunity and thus prevent further transmission of the pathogen.

NR0-Mf.title: Hepatitis B surface antigen
NR0-Mf.description: A surface protein in the viral envelope of the hepatitis B virus. HbsAg is the first marker to be elevated in a patient with hepatitis B infection. Higher levels of HbsAg also correlate with increased infectivity. The persistence of HBsAg in serum for more than 6 months indicates chronic hepatitis B infection.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

media.title: Serology time course of acute and resolved hepatitis B infection
Serology of active chronic hepatitis B infection

mR0Vnf.title: Anti-hepatitis B surface antigen antibody
mR0Vnf.description: A group of antibodies against the surface antigen of the hepatitis B virus (HbsAg). Increased anti-HBs antibodies in an individual with hepatitis B infection indicates elimination of the virus and recovery from infection. The presence of anti-HBs antibodies in a healthy individual indicates immunity against the hepatitis B virus either as a result of a past infection or as a result of vaccination.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

media.title: Serology time course of acute and resolved hepatitis B infection

5R0inf.title: Hepatitis B core antigen
5R0inf.description: A protein that is found in the nucleocapsid core of the hepatitis B virus. HBcAg does not circulate in blood and can only be detected in hepatocytes following a liver biopsy. The presence of HBcAg in hepatocytes indicates active viral replication.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

MR0Mnf.title: Anti-hepatitis B core antibody
MR0Mnf.description: A group of antibodies (IgM and IgG) produced against the core antigen of the hepatitis B virus (HBcAg). Increased IgM anti-HBc antibodies indicate acute hepatitis B infection; increased IgG anti-HBc antibodies indicate a chronic infection.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

media.title: Serology of active chronic hepatitis B infection

nR07nf.title: Hepatitis B e antigen
nR07nf.description: A modified form of hepatitis B virus core antigen (HBcAg) that is present between the lipid envelope and the nucleocapsid. Unlike HBcAg, HBeAg is present in blood. HBeAg is a prognostic marker in patients with chronic hepatitis B infection (i.e., ↑ HBsAg and ↑ IgG anti-HBc), with increased HBeAg levels indicating active viral replication and therefore a poor prognosis.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

LR0wnf.title: Anti-hepatitis B envelope antibody
LR0wnf.description: An antibody against the hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg). The presence of this antibody in a patient with chronic hepatitis B infection (i.e., ↑ HBsAg, ↑ IgG anti-HBc) indicates that viral replication is not taking place.

destinations.label: Hepatitis B → Overview of HBV serology

oR00Lf.title: Fraction of inspired oxygen
oR00Lf.description: The fraction of oxygen (by volume) in inspired air. Room air has an FiO₂ of 21%. Supplemental oxygen can be provided at varying levels of FiO₂ depending on the indication; e.g., an FiO₂ of 100% is often used in emergencies.

KR0ULf.title: Orchiectomy
KR0ULf.description: The surgical removal of one or both of the testes. Radical orchiectomy, the primary treatment of choice in patients with testicular cancer, is the removal of the entire spermatic cord and the testicle through an inguinal incision.

6R0jLf.title: Copremesis
6R0jLf.description: The presence of feces in vomitus. Common causes include intestinal obstruction in the ileum and gastrocolic fistulas.

pR0LLf.title: Papilla
pR0LLf.description:
A tiny nipple-like elevation. 
1. Lingual papillae: the various forms of papillae (e.g., circumvallate, filiform, fungiform, or conical papillae) that cover the the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
2. Optic papilla: the optic disc (blind spot)
3. Papilla of Vater (duodenal papilla): the common orifice of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct, which is located in the second part of the duodenum
4. Papillary dermis: the upper level of the dermis that is directly beneath the stratum basale; has papillae that extend into the epidermis

JR0sLf.title: Payr test
JR0sLf.description: Pain at or near the medial joint line when a physician performs the Payr test (applying downward pressure on the knee of a patient who is sitting cross-legged). This is a sign of a tear in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.

qR0CLf.title: Girdlestone procedure
qR0CLf.description: Complete resection of the head and neck of the femur with or without acetabular reaming. The procedure is named after the British surgeon Gathorne Girdlestone, who first developed it to treat tuberculosis of the hip at a time when antibiotics were not available. In contrast to hip arthroplasty (hip replacement), a hip prosthesis is not inserted in this procedure. Instead, the femur is allowed to fuse to the acetabulum (hip arthrodesis). The Girdlestone procedure is used to treat septic arthritis and painful hip diseases (e.g., avascular necrosis of the femoral head) when hip arthroplasty is contraindicated.

7R04of.title: N-acetylcysteine
7R04of.description: An antioxidant administered to restore depleted hepatic glutathione in patients with acetaminophen toxicity. Also used as a mucolytic (by reducing the disulfide bonds of mucoproteins) for some pulmonary conditions (e.g., cystic fibrosis, COPD) and as a nephroprotective agent to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.

GR0Bof.title: VACTERL association
GR0Bof.description: A group of associated birth defects consisting of Vertebral, Anal, and Cardiac abnormalities; Tracheoesophageal fistula; and Renal and Limb abnormalities.

8R0OKf.title: Psoriasiform
8R0OKf.description: A descriptor for skin lesions that resemble the scaly, plaque-like, erythematous lesions of psoriasis.

uR0pKf.title: Cheilitis
uR0pKf.description: A condition of inflammation of the lips that presents with dryness, scaling, and swelling. The surrounding skin and/or oral mucosa may also be involved. Etiologies include atopic dermatitis, contact irritants, nutritional deficiencies (e.g., iron deficiency), and autoimmune disorders (e.g., Crohn disease).

ER08Kf.title: Bacteremia
ER08Kf.description: The presence of bacteria in circulation. Can be harmless and transient or the result of serious infection, in which case it can lead to disseminated infection, sepsis, and septic shock.

vR0AKf.title: Brushfield spots
vR0AKf.description: An aggregation of connective tissue in the periphery of iris. Visible as white or grayish-brown spots. Can occur in otherwise healthy individuals but is commonly associated with Down syndrome.

DR016f.title: ACR
DR016f.description:
An abbreviation that can refer to:
1. American College of Rheumatology
2. American College of Radiology
3. Albumin-to-creatinine ratio

xR0E6f.title: Aortic sinus
xR0E6f.description: A space immediately above the aortic valve, between an aortic valve leaflet and the wall of the ascending aorta. There are three aortic sinuses (one above each aortic leaflet): the left, right, and posterior aortic sinuses. The left and right aortic sinus give rise to the left and right coronary artery. The three aortic sinuses together with the aortic valve leaflets form a dilation of the root of the aorta called the aortic bulb.

BR0z6f.title: Pseudopolyp
BR0z6f.description: A mass of colonic mucosa that forms from repeated mucosal ulceration and regeneration (e.g., from inflammatory conditions such as ulcerative colitis). Can resemble true intestinal polyps.

AR0Rpf.title: Vertigo
AR0Rpf.description: A sensation of rotating around in space (subjective vertigo), or of having objects rotate around the individual (objective vertigo). Etiologies include peripheral causes (e.g., vestibular neuritis, Ménière disease, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) and central causes (e.g., vertebrobasilar ischemia, cerebellar stroke).

_R05pf.title: Minimal erythema dose
_R05pf.description: The minimum amount of UV radiation that is required to produce an erythematous skin rash. Can be used to titrate doses for phototherapy and to identify causes of photodermatoses.

zR0rpf.title: Fecal impaction
zR0rpf.description: The presence of hardened fecal matter that has accumulated in the rectum and/or colon, which results in the inability to have a bowel movement. Occurs as a result of constipation (e.g., due to a low-fiber diet, decreased physical activity, use of opioids, and/or decreased fluid intake).

-R0Dpf.title: Debridement
-R0Dpf.description: The removal of dead, damaged or infected tissue to improve the efficiency of wound healing. Can be performed surgically (excisional debridement) or nonsurgically (e.g., hydrocolloid dressings that promote liquefaction and enzymatic autolysis of the necrotic tissue).

Zi0ZJf.title: Union for international cancer control
Zi0ZJf.description: An international organization with the main objective of promoting research in the field of oncology, as well as prevention, early diagnosis, and effective treatment of cancers. Based on the TNM classification, the UICC developed a cancer staging system, which is currently in its 7th edition. The staging system (which stages cancer from 0–IV) is used to guide therapy and determine prognoses.

0i0eJf.title: Barotrauma
0i0eJf.description: A mechanical injury caused by rapid and/or large pressure differentials across tissue planes. Pulmonary barotrauma (rupture of the alveoli) can occur as a complication of positive pressure ventilation. Barotrauma can also occur if air-filled structures such as the inner ear or sinuses are subjected to rapid pressure changes (e.g., diving, flying, or blast injury).

ai0QJf.title: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
ai0QJf.description: The partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood. Depends on the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli, the diffusion coefficient of the alveolar membrane, and the ventilation-perfusion ratio. A rough estimate of the expected PaO₂ in a normal individual is five times that of the concentration of oxygen in inhaled air (FiO₂).

destinations.label: Arterial blood gas analysis → Arterial blood gas analysis

bi0HJf.title: Seroprevalence
bi0HJf.description: The proportion of individuals in a population that are seropositive for a particular infectious disease (i.e., that produce antibodies against a specific pathogen). The level of endemic infection, or the extent of vaccination coverage, can be determined when seroprevalence is measured using IgG antibody levels.

ci0aqf.title: Scanning speech
ci0aqf.description: A type of speech characterized by slow speech with recurring pauses between syllables and undue emphasis on various syllables. Seen in disorders that affect the cerebellum and/or cerebellar tracts (e.g., cerebellar stroke, multiple sclerosis).

destinations.label: Cerebellum → Functional zones of the cerebellum

1i02qf.title: Synechia
1i02qf.description: An adhesion that connects two structures that are normally not connected: e.g., conjunctival synechiae between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, anterior synechiae between the iris and cornea, posterior synechiae between the iris and the crystalline lens, intrauterine synechiae that develop following uterine curettage (Asherman's syndrome), intranasal synechiae.

Wi0Pqf.title: Pallhypesthesia
Wi0Pqf.description: A decreased perception of vibration. Common cause includes lesions affecting the dorsal spinal tract and polyneuropathies.

di0oqf.title: Sialorrhea
di0oqf.description: An involuntary drooling of saliva from the mouth caused by excessive production of saliva (hypersalivation), and/or decreased clearance of saliva (e.g., due to dysphagia, due to facial nerve palsy).

Vi0Gqf.title: Vasoactive intestinal peptide
Vi0Gqf.description: A polypeptide hormone primarily produced by the duodenum, the pancreas, and parasympathetic neurons in sphincters. Relaxes sphincters and increases the secretion of water and electrolytes.

destinations.label: Gastrointestinal tract → Secretory and regulatory products of the gastrointestinal tract

ei0xqf.title: Orchiopexy
ei0xqf.description: A surgical procedure in which a testicle is mobilized and fixed to the scrotal wall. Typically indicated for cryptorchidism or to prevent recurrence of testicular torsion.

Ui0bIf.title: Echopraxia
Ui0bIf.description: The involuntary imitation of another person's movements. Common causes include schizophrenia, tic disorders (e.g., Tourette syndrome), and certain autistic disorders.

Ti06If.title: Epileptogenic
Ti06If.description: A descriptor for any agent (e.g., a drug, pathogen, or toxin) that increases the risk of seizures. Also used to describe areas of the brain responsible for seizures (e.g., an epileptogenic focus).

hi0crf.title: Vector
hi0crf.description:
1. An organism that transmits a pathogen from one organism to another. Invertebrates such as ticks, mites, lice, mosquitoes, and/or flies are important disease vectors.
2. A quantity with both a magnitude and a direction: e.g., an ECG is a recording against time of the sum of all electrical field vectors generated by the heart.
3. An agent that can introduce genetic material into the genome of another cell: e.g., modified bacteriophages, plasmids

3i0Srf.title: Nucleoside analogues
3i0Srf.description: A group of drugs with structures that resemble nucleosides (pentose sugar + nitrogenous base). Divided into purine analogues and pyrimidine analogues. Examples include certain chemotherapy agents and antiviral drugs such as NRTIs.

ii0Jrf.title: Incubation period
ii0Jrf.description: The interval between the entry of a pathogen into the body of an individual and the appearance of the first clinical symptom(s).

ji0_rf.title: Isoenzyme
ji0_rf.description: An enzyme that can be found in several organs but has the same function. Can vary in certain physical properties (e.g., electrophoretic motility).

4i037f.title: Tympanic resonance
4i037f.description: A loud, high-pitched, drum-like reverberation that is heard upon percussing a cavity full of air (esp. over the stomach and the bowel).

ki0m7f.title: Rapid urease test
ki0m7f.description: A test used to identify urease-producing bacteria based on the pH change that is associated with the production of ammonia (an alkali) from urea. Organisms that are urease-positive produce a pH change in urea agar within 24 hours (e.g., H. pylori, Cryptococcus, Proteus, Yersinia, Brucella, Corynebacterium).

Oi0I7f.title: Malnutrition
Oi0I7f.description: Malnutrition includes undernutrition (e.g., protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies) and overnutrition (e.g., obesity, hypervitaminosis). Often used interchangeably with the term "undernutrition," which is insufficient body nutrient stores relative to tissue growth and breakdown, leading to a loss of muscle and/or organ mass and to negative clinical outcomes.

li0v7f.title: Marasmus
li0v7f.description: A form of primary protein-energy malnutrition characterized by generalized wasting (cachexia) caused by a negative calorie balance (deficiency of energy intake).

Ni0-7f.title: Kwashiorkor
Ni0-7f.description: A primary protein-energy malnutrition form caused by severe protein deficiency. Primarily affects undernourished children in developing countries. Patients typically present after weaning has begun with lethargy, failure to thrive, muscle wasting, anemia, depigmentation of hair and skin, generalized edema, a pot belly (due to ascites and hepatomegaly), and increased susceptibility to infections.

mi0VHf.title: β2-transferrin
mi0VHf.description: A form of transferrin (an iron-transporting protein) that does not have sialic acid residues. β2-transferrin is found exclusively in CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) and in the perilymph of the inner ear. Therefore, evidence of β2-transferrin on electrophoresis is used as a specific marker of a CSF leak  (e.g., in CSF rhinorrhea following a fracture of the base of the skull).

5i0iHf.title: Cribriform
5i0iHf.description: A sieve-like appearance with many small perforations; e.g., cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, cribriform fascia of the thigh, cribriform hymen, cribriform apex of the renal papillae, cribriform histological pattern of an adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Mi0MHf.title: Opportunistic pathogen
Mi0MHf.description: An organism that typically only cause an infection in an immunocompromised host.

Li0wHf.title: C-peptide
Li0wHf.description: A peptide released during cleavage of insulin from proinsulin. Very low C-peptide levels indicate an absolute insulin deficiency and are seen in type 1 diabetes. Elevated C-peptide levels may indicate insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, and are seen in type 2 diabetes. Exogenous insulin use does not elevate C-peptide levels.

oi00sf.title: Transesophageal echocardiography
oi00sf.description: An ultrasound examination of the heart performed by placing a transducer into the esophagus to obtain a detailed assessment of cardiac structure and function. It allows for better visualization, especially of posterior cardiac structures, than transthoracic echocardiography. Used in the diagnosis of various cardiac conditions, including endocarditis, cardiac emboli, and aortic dissection.

Ki0Usf.title: Transthoracic echocardiography
Ki0Usf.description: A noninvasive ultrasound examination of the heart. Provides detailed images of the heart's chambers and valves, the ascending aorta, and pericardium, and can assess valvular function and myocardial contractility. Used in the diagnosis of various cardiac conditions, including valvular heart diseases, heart failure, aneurysms, and pericardial effusion.

6i0jsf.title: Hematopoiesis
6i0jsf.description: The formation of blood cells such as erythrocytes (erythropoiesis), leukocytes (leukopoiesis), and platelets (thrombopoiesis) from pluripotent stem cells. Normally, hematopoiesis takes place in the bone marrow. However, hematopoiesis occurs in sites other than the bone marrow  (extramedullary hematopoiesis) such as the liver and spleen during normal fetal development, in chronic, severe anemia, and in some hematological malignancies (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma).

destinations.label: Basics of hematology → Bone marrow and hematopoiesis

Ji0ssf.title: Affect (psychiatry)
Ji0ssf.description: The objective emotional expressiveness of a person as shown in the face, eyes, tone of speech, and bodily gestures. It may be characterized according to the type of emotion (e.g., happy, sad), the appropriateness (e.g., inappropriate if the patient appears happy while discussing a sad story), the consistency (e.g., considered labile if the patient rapidly shifts between happy and sad), and the range (e.g., considered blunt if the amount of emotional expression if very limited).

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Mood and affect

qi0Csf.title: Dead end host
qi0Csf.description: An intermediate host that is normally not involved in the life cycle of a parasite. If a parasite inadvertently infects a dead-end host, it cannot be transmitted to a definitive host. Since the parasite is not evolutionarily adapted to evade the immune system of a dead-host host, an infection can provoke a heightened immune response, resulting in severe immune-mediated damage to the dead-end host (e.g., Echinococcus infection).

7i04Gf.title: Enthesitis
7i04Gf.description: An inflammation of the enthesis (the point at which a tendon attaches to bone). Typically seen in patients with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, enthesitis-associated juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or reactive arthritis. Commonly affected sites include the spine, Achilles tendon, plantar fascia, and supraspinatus tendon.

si0tGf.title: Giant cell
si0tGf.description: A large, multinucleated cell formed by the fusion of many cells of the same type. Usually refer to giant cells formed from many mononuclear phagocytic cells (e.g., tissue macrophages). Found in some tumors (e.g., giant cell tumor of the bone, osteosarcomas), vasculitides (e.g., temporal arteritis), granulomatous diseases (e.g., tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), and viral infections (e.g., herpesviruses, paramyxoviruses).

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

media.title: Multinucleated giant cells in pulmonary sarcoidosis

ti0Xtf.title: Relative contraindication
ti0Xtf.description: A contraindication that applies in all but a few extenuating circumstances, such as when no other form of therapy is available, or when the benefits of a therapy significantly outweigh the associated risks (e.g., the postoperative continuation of aspirin therapy in a patient who has a history of acute coronary syndrome despite the increased risk of bleeding).

Fi0gtf.title: Endocytosis
Fi0gtf.description: A process in which the cell membrane invaginates to take in a foreign substance (e.g, protein, pathogen), which is then contained within an intracellular vacuole.

ui0ptf.title: Trench fever
ui0ptf.description: A type of relapsing fever in which the fever episodes last for five days. Five-day fever is caused by infection with Bartonella quintana, a gram-negative bacillus that is transmitted through the bite of an infected body louse.

destinations.label: Louse- and flea-borne diseases → Louse-borne diseases

Ei08tf.title: Generation time
Ei08tf.description: The time required by bacteria to double in number in a culture medium. The generation time depends on the species of bacterium (e.g., 20 minutes for E. coli and 12–18 hours for M. tuberculosis) and the type of culture medium (e.g., the generation time is shorter in specially enriched media).

vi0Atf.title: Piano key sign
vi0Atf.description:
1. A springy resistance that is felt when the physician presses on the distal end of the clavicle. A piano key sign is seen in patients with a severe acromioclavicular joint injury (Tossy type III or Rockwood type V injury).
2. The presence of pain or laxity at the distal radioulnar joint when the physician tries to distract the radius from the ulna in either the dorsal or ventral direction. A positive piano key sign in a patient with a wrist injury is a sign of a tear in the triangular fibrocartilage complex, a stabilizer of the distal radioulnar joint.
3. The keyboard-like appearance of a longitudinal section of the jejunal wall on abdominal ultrasonography. A positive keyboard sign, which may be seen in patients with ileus (mechanical or paralytic), is the result of edema of the valvulae conniventes (circular mucosal folds in the wall of the jejunum).

media.title: Piano key sign in dilated small bowel

Di01Ff.title: Mutism
Di01Ff.description: An inability or unwillingness to speak despite the faculties of speech being intact. Typically occurs as a result of a psychiatric disorder (e.g., selective mutism) and rarely as a result of organic lesions (e.g., akinetic mutism in patients with frontal lobe lesions and/or hydrocephalus).

wi0hFf.title: Glottis
wi0hFf.description:
1. The structures of the larynx that are responsible for phonation (vocal cords, vocal folds, vocalis muscle, and the arytenoid cartilages). 
2. The intervening space between the vocal cords and arytenoid cartilages (rima glottidis).

9i0NFf.title: Blood-brain barrier
9i0NFf.description: A barrier that separates the extracellular fluid of brain tissue from circulating blood. Composed of three layers: pedicles (foot processes of astrocytes), a basal membrane, and capillary endothelial cells bound by tight junctions. The BBB is selectively permeable to certain substances (e.g., glucose, metabolic waste, and gases) and prevents entry of other substances (e.g., bacteria, toxins, certain medications) into the brain parenchyma.

destinations.label: The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system → Microscopic anatomy

Ci0qFf.title: Blood-CSF barrier
Ci0qFf.description: A barrier that separates cerebrospinal fluid from circulating blood. The blood-CSF barrier, which is present in the choroid plexus (the main site of CSF secretion), is made up of three layers: modified ependymal cells (choroid epithelial cells) that are bound by tight junctions, a basal membrane, and fenestrated capillary endothelium cells. The blood-CSF barrier is selectively permeable to certain substances (e.g., glucose, electrolytes) but restricts the entry of cells, almost all proteins, and potential toxins (e.g., hydrophilic medications, bacteria) from plasma into the cerebrospinal fluid.

destinations.label: The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system → Microscopic anatomy

yi0d8f.title: Fibrosis
yi0d8f.description: A proliferation of fibroblasts and deposition of collagen in tissues as a result of a reparative process (e.g., following injury, inflammation, and/or necrosis) or as part of a reaction to chronic irritants (e.g., pneumoconiosis, chronic lymphedema).

Ai0R8f.title: Myeloablation
Ai0R8f.description: The therapeutic destruction of bone marrow by high-dose chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. Myeloablation followed by bone marrow transplantation is used to treat certain forms of hematologic malignancies.

_i058f.title: High-dose chemotherapy
_i058f.description: The administration of one or more chemotherapeutic drugs in higher than usual doses with the goal of destroying all malignant cells. Since high-dose chemotherapy often results in severe adverse effects such as bone marrow failure, a bone marrow and/or stem cell transplantation is often performed following high-dose chemotherapy. High-dose chemotherapy is potentially curative for certain hematological malignancies (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia).

zi0r8f.title: Infantile hypotonia
zi0r8f.description: A generalized decrease in muscle tone (hypotonia) in a neonate or an infant.

-i0D8f.title: Facultative pathogen
-i0D8f.description: A pathogen that is capable of surviving outside of a host and causes disease in susceptible hosts (e.g., opportunistic pathogens that cause disease in immunocompromised hosts).

0Q0euf.title: Contracture
0Q0euf.description: A deformity or a restriction of joint movement as a result of connective tissue fibrosis in the adjacent skin, fascia, muscles, and/or joint capsule.

destinations.label: Collection of orthopedic conditions → Joint contractures

XQ09uf.title: Pseudocyst
XQ09uf.description: A cystic collection of cell debris and fluid that is lined by granulation or fibrous tissue and not by epithelial or endothelial cells (hence “pseudocyst”). Usually formed by the necrosis of tissue; e.g., pancreatic pseudocysts (a complication of pancreatitis).

cQ0aEf.title: Pretest probability
cQ0aEf.description: The probability that a patient with a particular clinical manifestation (or a constellation of clinical manifestations) has a specific disease before the result of the diagnostic test is known.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

1Q02Ef.title: Codon
1Q02Ef.description: A sequence of three nucleotides that codes for a specific amino acid (except stop codons, which terminate peptide formation). Because the genetic code is redundant, there are 64 codons in total (most amino acids have more than one specific codon).

destinations.label: Translation and protein synthesis → Genetic code

media.title: Pairing of codon and anticodon in translation

WQ0PEf.title: Ischemia
WQ0PEf.description: A condition of decreased blood supply.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Ischemia

dQ0oEf.title: Sessile
dQ0oEf.description: A morphologic descriptor for a lesion that is attached by a broad base.

VQ0GEf.title: Volar flexion
VQ0GEf.description: Bending the hand toward the ventral surface of the forearm (flexion of the wrist).

destinations.label: Anatomical terms → Anatomical terms of motion

eQ0xEf.title: Adenoma
eQ0xEf.description: A benign tumor that arises from glandular epithelial cells.

UQ0bvf.title: Tissue factor
UQ0bvf.description: A protein that is found in the cytoplasm of vascular endothelial cells, on the surface of fibroblasts in the subendothelium of blood vessels, and within leukocytes. Tissue factor is involved in the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. Damage to blood vessels results in the release of tissue factor, which binds to circulating factor VII and allows its activation. The complex of activated factor VII (VIIa) and tissue factor can then activate factor X of the common pathway in the coagulation cascade.

2Q0Tvf.title: von Willebrand factor
2Q0Tvf.description: A circulating glycoprotein that is involved in the process of coagulation. It is produced in megakaryocytes, as well as in the endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue of blood vessels. It is stored in the Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells and α-granules of platelets. vWF mediates adhesion of platelets to exposed collagen fibrils of damaged blood vessels via the GP1b surface receptor. It assists aggregation by interlinking between the GpIIb/IIIa receptors of platelets (as fibrinogen also does). Lastly, it prevents the breakdown of factor VIII.

TQ06vf.title: Hyperthermia
TQ06vf.description: An elevated body temperature caused by an inability to maintain temperature at the normal hypothalamic setpoint, i.e., thermoregulatory failure. Common causes include increased ambient temperature (nonexertional heat stroke), heavy physical exertion (exertional heatstroke), malignant hyperthermia, and drugs (e.g., antipsychotics and amphetamines). Extreme hyperthermia can cause severe peripheral vasodilation, relative hypovolemia, and loss of consciousness.

gQ0Fvf.title: Lithotomy position
gQ0Fvf.description: A supine position with the buttocks at the end of the examination or operating table, the knees flexed, the hips flexed and rotated slightly externally, and the feet held in place by straps. This position is used for gynecological examination, vaginal delivery of a fetus, surgeries involving the perineal region, and, less commonly, for rectal examination.

SQ0yvf.title: Parosmia
SQ0yvf.description: A distorted perception of smell; e.g., pleasant odors are perceived as offensive (or vice versa) or odors are perceived when not actually present. Common causes include upper respiratory tract infections, intravenous fluid therapy in postoperative patients, olfactory nerve damage (e.g., due to diabetic neuropathy, or a fracture of the skull base), temporal lobe epilepsy, Parkinson disease, and certain psychiatric conditions.

hQ0cDf.title: Tonic
hQ0cDf.description: A descriptor for increased muscle tension due to prolonged muscle contraction (tonus).

RQ0lDf.title: Philtrum
RQ0lDf.description: The vertical groove between the middle of the upper lip and the nose. Hypoplasia of the philtrum can indicate an underlying condition (e.g., fetal alcohol syndrome).

media.title: Development of the face and palate

PQ0Wwf.title: Exenteration
PQ0Wwf.description: A radical surgical procedure in which all the contents of a surgical cavity are removed (e.g., exenteration of the pelvis in advanced uterine, bladder, and/or rectal carcinomas)

4Q03wf.title: Stent
4Q03wf.description: A hollow, tube-shaped frame that is placed intraluminally within a hollow viscus (e.g., esophagus, artery) in order to widen a stenosis of the lumen, support the walls of the viscus, and prevent or delay restenosis.

kQ0mwf.title: Double-contrast barium enema
kQ0mwf.description: A diagnostic procedure in which x-rays of the colon and rectum are taken after rectal administration of a contrast agent. Commonly used to diagnose Hirschsprung disease.

lQ0vwf.title: Anhedonia
lQ0vwf.description: An inability to enjoy acts or experiences that are normally pleasurable. Anhedonia is a typical symptom of a major depressive episode but may also occur in schizophrenia.

NQ0-wf.title: Choanae
NQ0-wf.description: A pair of funnel-shaped openings at the posterior end of the nasal cavity. The choanae connect the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx.

mQ0V9f.title: Coprolalia
mQ0V9f.description: The uncontrollable and/or obsessive utterance of obscenities. Coprolalia occurs in certain tic disorders such as Tourette syndrome.

5Q0i9f.title: Torticollis
5Q0i9f.description: A postural deformity characterized by head tilt and/or neck rotation. May be congenital (e.g., due to muscular or bony abnormalities), acquired (e.g., due to muscular, bony, or neurologic conditions), or idiopathic.

MQ0M9f.title: Inotropy
MQ0M9f.description: The ability to influence the force of cardiac muscle contraction. Positively inotropic drugs (e.g., catecholamines) increase the force of contraction, while negatively inotropic drugs (e.g., beta blockers) decrease the force of contraction.

destinations.label: Cardiac physiology → Regulation of cardiac activity

nQ079f.title: Dromotropic
nQ079f.description: The ability to influence the conductivity of cardiac tissue. Positively dromotropic drugs (e.g., catecholamines) increase the rate of conduction of an electrical impulse through cardiac tissue, while negatively dromotropic drugs (e.g., digoxin) decrease the rate of conduction of an electrical impulse through cardiac tissue.

destinations.label: Cardiac physiology → Regulation of cardiac activity

LQ0w9f.title: Chronotropic
LQ0w9f.description: The ability to influence heart rate. Positively chronotropic drugs (e.g., adrenaline) increase heart rate, while negatively chronotropic drugs (e.g., beta blockers) decrease heart rate.

destinations.label: Cardiac physiology → Regulation of cardiac activity

oQ00Cf.title: Bathmotropic
oQ00Cf.description: The ability to influence the stimulation threshold of cardiac muscle and thereby cardiac excitability. Positively bathmotropic drugs (e.g., adrenaline, digoxin) increase the excitability of cardiac tissue (or decrease the stimulation threshold), while negatively bathmotropic drugs (e.g., amiodarone) decrease cardiac excitability (or increase the stimulation threshold).

KQ0UCf.title: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition
KQ0UCf.description: The fifth iteration of a system that provides nomenclature for and classifies psychiatric disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association.

6Q0jCf.title: Dermatome
6Q0jCf.description: An area of the skin that receives sensory innervation from a specific spinal root.

destinations.label: Spinal cord tracts and reflexes → Dermatomes

JQ0sCf.title: Kyphosis
JQ0sCf.description: A dorsal convexity of the spine. The thoracic and sacral spine are physiologically kyphotic. Increased kyphosis (hyperkyphosis) in the thoracic spine occurs with Scheuermann disease (juvenile kyphosis), vertebral fractures, osteoporosis, degenerative disc disease, spondylolisthesis, ankylosing spondylitis, and connective tissue disorders.

qQ0CCf.title: Hernia
qQ0CCf.description: A protrusion of a structure (e.g., a vertebral disc, a loop of bowel, fat, brain tissue) through a weakness or opening in the wall of a surrounding cavity. Examples include inguinal hernia, diaphragmatic hernia, and cerebral hernia.

IQ0Yxf.title: Dysphagia
IQ0Yxf.description: A symptom characterized by inability to swallow or difficulty swallowing. Can result from a disorder of peristalsis or from obstructive lesions in the oropharynx or esophagus.

rQ0fxf.title: Galactorrhea
rQ0fxf.description: A milky, multiductal physiological nipple discharge unrelated to childbirth and nursing that can be unilateral or bilateral. Most commonly caused by hyperprolactinemia and affects women and men.

HQ0Kxf.title: Fibrin
HQ0Kxf.description: A filamentous, insoluble protein that stabilizes a thrombus by forming a mesh in which platelets, erythrocytes, and leukocytes become entangled. The end product of the coagulation cascade. Produced from fibrinogen (factor I) through the action of thrombin (factor IIa).

sQ0txf.title: Prothrombin
sQ0txf.description: A protein that is converted to thrombin (factor IIa) in the common pathway of the coagulation cascade by the action of factor Va, factor Xa, and calcium ions.

GQ0Bxf.title: Analeptic
GQ0Bxf.description: A drug that stimulates the central nervous system (especially the centers of the brain responsible for breathing and/or circulatory reflexes). Caffeine, e.g., is an analeptic that is used to stimulate respiration in the case of primary neonatal apnea.

tQ0XBf.title: Multiparous
tQ0XBf.description: A woman who has carried more than one fetus to the point of viability (≥ 20 weeks of gestation), regardless of whether the infants were alive at birth or born dead. A grand multiparous woman is one who has carried five or more fetuses to the point of viability (≥ 20 weeks of gestation), regardless of whether the infants were alive at birth or born dead.

FQ0gBf.title: Holosystolic murmur
FQ0gBf.description: A cardiac murmur that can be heard throughout systole.

uQ0pBf.title: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide
uQ0pBf.description: The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood. May refer to venous (PvCO₂) or, more commonly, arterial blood (PaCO₂). PaCO₂ is dependent on the ventilation-perfusion ratio, the amount of CO₂ produced by cellular respiration, and the acid-base balance of the body. The normal range for arterial blood is usually 35–45 mm Hg.

vQ0ABf.title: Anticoagulant
vQ0ABf.description: A drug or a substance that prevents coagulation. Used to treat and/or prevent conditions associated with thrombus formation (e.g., deep vein thrombosis). Examples include heparin and low molecular weight heparin, vitamin K antagonists (e.g., warfarin), pentasaccharide molecules (e.g., fondaparinux), direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g., dabigatran), and factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban).

media.title: Mechanism of action: anticoagulants that prevent secondary hemostasis

DQ01yf.title: Osteolysis
DQ01yf.description: The softening, resorption, and destruction of bone tissue. A function of osteoclasts caused by neoplastic or inflammatory processes (e.g., osteomyelitis, bone metastases, multiple myeloma) that stimulate osteoclast activation.

wQ0hyf.title: Hematometra
wQ0hyf.description: The collection of blood in the uterus, usually as a result of cervical atresia or stenosis.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the vulva and vagina

9Q0Nyf.title: Pouch of Douglas
9Q0Nyf.description: An intraperitoneal space that lies between the uterus and the rectum in women (rectouterine pouch) and between the bladder and rectum in men (rectovesical pouch). The pouch of Douglas is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity and is therefore a common site of fluid collection and/or intraperitoneal metastases.

destinations.label: Pelvis and hip joint → Pelvic cavity and pelvic spaces

CQ0qyf.title: Vesicouterine pouch
CQ0qyf.description: A small intraperitoneal recess between the bladder and the uterus. The vesicouterine pouch is a common site for pelvic endometriosis.

destinations.label: Pelvis and hip joint → Pelvic cavity and pelvic spaces

xQ0Eyf.title: Functio laesa
xQ0Eyf.description: A loss of function in a tissue, an organ, and/or a part of the body.

BQ0zyf.title: Acetabulum
BQ0zyf.description: The socket of the hip joint. The acetabulum is formed by the ileum, ischium, and the pubis. The acetabulum forms a ball and socket joint with the femoral head.

destinations.label: Pelvis and hip joint → Hip joint

yQ0dAf.title: Liquorrhea
yQ0dAf.description: The leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space through an external opening. Most cases occur following trauma as a result of fractures in the base of the skull.

AQ0RAf.title: Lanugo
AQ0RAf.description: The short, fine, soft, nonpigmented hair that covers the face and body of a fetus during the second trimester. Replaced by vellus hair during the third trimester. Included as part of the physical criteria in the Ballard score for assessing fetal maturity. Can also develop postnatally due to malnourishment (e.g., in patients with anorexia nervosa).

destinations.label: Prenatal and postnatal physiology →  The fetal period

zQ0rAf.title: Monro-Richter line
zQ0rAf.description: An imaginary line that runs between the umbilicus and the left anterior superior iliac spine. The Monro point, which lies approximately at the midpoint of this line, corresponds to the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle. The Monro point is a site of trochar insertion for laparoscopic surgery and the site of needle insertion for abdominal paracentesis (ascitic tap).

-Q0DAf.title: Pneumoperitoneum
-Q0DAf.description: The presence of air in the peritoneal cavity. An abdominal or chest x-ray showing a radiolucent area under the diaphragm and/or the delineation of the bowel wall by a radiolucency is diagnostic. Pneumoperitoneum can occur after perforation of a hollow abdominal viscus (e.g., perforated peptic ulcer) or after surgery in which air is introduced into the abdominal cavity.

Zj0Z_f.title: Allograft
Zj0Z_f.description: A tissue or organ from a donor who is not genetically identical to the recipient but belongs to the same species. Most transplanted organs are allografts.

0j0e_f.title: Xenograft
0j0e_f.description: A tissue or organ from a donor that does not belong to the same species as the recipient: e.g., bovine heart valves for valve replacement surgery.

aj0Q_f.title: Definitive host
aj0Q_f.description: An organism in which a parasite attains sexual maturity.

bj0H_f.title: Reservoir host
bj0H_f.description: A host that can carry the pathogen indefinitely without any ill effects (i.e., asymptomatic/latent infection). This host provides an ecological niche for the pathogen when active transmission to a definite or intermediate host is not possible.

Xj09_f.title: Autograft
Xj09_f.description: A tissue or organ that is transplanted from one part of the body to another part of the same individual: e.g., skin grafts from the medial aspect of the thigh to treat burns or wounds, saphenous vein grafts for vessel anastomosis, or bone grafts from the iliac crest to fill bony defects.

cj0azf.title: Fetor hepaticus
cj0azf.description: A characteristic breath odor similar to that of fresh loam, seen in patients with severe hepatic failure. Fetor hepaticus occurs because sulfur-containing compounds produced by colonic bacteria (e.g., methyl mercaptan, dimethyl sulfide) bypass hepatic metabolism and reach the lung via portocaval shunts.

Wj0Pzf.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
Wj0Pzf.description: A group of conditions characterized by recurrent inflammation of the intestine. Can also have extraintestinal manifestations (e.g., pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, eye inflammation, oral ulcerations, arthritis). Associated with malnutrition and increased risk of colorectal cancer. The two most common forms are Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

media.title: Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease

dj0ozf.title: Nucleotide analogue
dj0ozf.description: A group of drugs comprised of structures that resemble nucleotides (pentose sugar + nitrogenous base + phosphate group), the building blocks of DNA. Used as antiviral drugs (e.g., tenofovir in patients with HIV or hepatitis B).

destinations.label: Human immunodeficiency virus infection → Antiretroviral therapy
Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

ej0xzf.title: Rhinorrhea
ej0xzf.description: The production of mucoid, watery, nasal discharge.

Uj0b-f.title: Thoracic spine
Uj0b-f.description: A portion of the spine located inferior to the cervical spine and superior to the lumbar spine. Consists of 12 vertebrae (T1–T12).

media.title: Range of motion of the spine

2j0T-f.title: Cervical spine
2j0T-f.description: The most superior portion of the spine. Consists of 7 vertebrae (C1-C7), which includes the atlas (C1) and axis (C2).

Tj06-f.title: Centripetal
Tj06-f.description:
1. Any phenomenon (e.g., contrast enhancement) or disease manifestation (e.g., skin lesion, nerve palsy) that begins peripherally and progresses toward the center (or midline).
2. A force that is directed toward the central axis in a rotating or revolving system.

gj0F-f.title: Centrifugal
gj0F-f.description:
1. A phenomenon (e.g., contrast enhancement) or a disease manifestation (e.g., skin lesion, nerve palsy) that begins centrally (or in the midline) and progresses toward the periphery.
2.  A force that is directed away from the central axis in a rotating or revolving system.

hj0cZT.title: Carpopedal spasm
hj0cZT.description: A spasmodic contraction of the hands and feet with flexion of the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of the fingers, dorsiflexion of the ankles, and plantarflexion of the toes. Can be caused by hypocalcemia, which increases neuronal excitability (tetany).

3j0SZT.title: Palmar
3j0SZT.description: An anatomic descriptor indicating the direction of the palm (palmar surface) or the sole (plantar surface).

ij0JZT.title: Anal gland
ij0JZT.description: A mucin-secreting gland that lies between the external and internal anal sphincter and opens into anal crypts, which are located at the level of the dentate line. Thought to be vestigial scent glands without a clear function in humans. Infection of the anal glands can lead to anal abscesses and fistulas.

Qj0uZT.title: Chyme
Qj0uZT.description: A semifluid mixture of digested food and digestive enzymes that is present in the stomach and small intestine.

jj0_ZT.title: Isthmus
jj0_ZT.description: A narrow structure or a narrow passageway that connects two larger structures or cavities (e.g., aortic isthmus, thyroid isthmus, uterine isthmus).

Pj0W0T.title: Acantholysis
Pj0W0T.description: The dissolution of intercellular bridges (e.g., desmosomes) that connect keratinocytes in the stratum spinosum. Causes separation of epidermal cells and formation of intraepidermal (suprabasal) blisters. Seen in many blistering disorders, including pemphigus vulgaris.

4j030T.title: Nuclear pleomorphism
4j030T.description: The presence of nuclei of various shapes and sizes in cells of the same tissue. Nuclear pleomorphism, which is a sign of rapid mitosis, is seen in neoplasms.

kj0m0T.title: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy
kj0m0T.description: A procedure in which a flexible fiber-optic endoscope is passed through the mouth and oropharynx to visualize the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and, sometimes, the duodenum. Commonly used to diagnose and manage upper gastrointestinal disorders, monitor precancerous syndromes, and guide endoscopic percutaneous feeding tube placement.

lj0v0T.title: Idiopathic
lj0v0T.description: A descriptor for a condition with an unknown cause or pathophysiology.

Nj0-0T.title: Macroglossia
Nj0-0T.description: An enlargement of the tongue. Etiologies include trisomy 21, myxedema, acromegaly, amyloidosis, angioedema, certain glycogen storage diseases, and vascular/solid tumors.

mj0VaT.title: Seborrhea
mj0VaT.description: A condition of abnormally increased production of sebum (an oily secretion) by the sebaceous glands of the face and/or scalp, resulting in oily skin with greasy scales. Etiologies include genetic predisposition, diseases such as Parkinson syndrome, and as an adverse effect of certain medications (e.g., methyldopa, cimetidine). Can lead to seborrheic dermatitis and acne vulgaris.

5j0iaT.title: Tumor doubling time
5j0iaT.description: The time taken by a tumor to double in volume. Tumors that grow rapidly have a short doubling time.

Mj0MaT.title: Telomere
Mj0MaT.description: The distal end of a chromosome that contains a non-coding, repetitive base sequence (TTAGGG in humans). A chromosome is shortened with every successive cycle of DNA replication because the enzymes that replicate DNA cannot proceed all the way to the end of a DNA sequence. The presence of expendable, non-coding telomeres at the end of a chromosome ensures that important genetic information is not lost with every cycle of cell division.

nj07aT.title: Alien limb syndrome
nj07aT.description: Involuntary but purposeful limb movements in which the affected limb feels foreign to the individual. May be associated with hemineglect. Caused by damage to the contralateral supplementary motor cortex or other frontal lobe regions. Commonly occurs in corticobasal degeneration but may also occur in aura preceding epileptic seizures.

Lj0waT.title: Trepanation
Lj0waT.description: A surgical procedure in which access to a cavity is gained by boring through the wall that encloses the cavity: e.g., cranial trepanation for neurosurgical procedures (burr hole surgery), corneal trepanation.

oj00YT.title: Asthenia
oj00YT.description:
A term that can refer to:
1. An abnormal loss of strength.
2. A slender, tall body type.

Kj0UYT.title: Galea aponeurotica
Kj0UYT.description: A sheet of connective tissue that lies over the cranium and connects the occipital and frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle. The galea aponeurotica, which is the third layer of the scalp (after skin and subcutaneous tissue), is connected to the cranial periosteum by loose connective tissue.

6j0jYT.title: Synchondrosis
6j0jYT.description: The fusion of two bones or two parts of a bone by hyaline cartilage. Synchondroses occur between the two halves of the mandible, between certain bones at the base of the skull, between the manubrium and the body of the sternum, and at the first sternocostal joint. Epiphyseal plates are examples of specialized synchondroses. Synchondroses may be permanent or ossify at a later point (in which case they are called synostoses).

pj0LYT.title: Asthenopia
pj0LYT.description: A collection of symptoms of eye strain, such as eye pain, headache, lacrimation, and/or blurred vision caused by fatigue of the intraocular muscles (accommodative asthenopia) or extraocular muscles (muscular asthenopia).

Jj0sYT.title: Tachypnea
Jj0sYT.description: An increased rate of breathing. For adults: > 20/min. For children 1–5 years of age: > 40/min; for children 2–12 months of age: > 50/min; for children less than 2 months of age: > 60/min).

qj0CYT.title: Colony-forming unit
qj0CYT.description:
1. A hematopoietic stem cell that is committed to forming a particular line of cells; e.g., CFU-E → erythrocytes, CFU-L → lymphocytes, CFU-GM → granulocytes and macrophages, CFU-Meg → megakaryocytes (platelet precursor)
2. A viable bacterium or fungal element that can independently give rise to a colony in a culture medium. The bacterial or fungal load in a specimen (e.g., urine) can be indirectly calculated based on the number of colony-forming units that grow in a culture medium, after inoculating the medium with a specific dilution of the specimen.

Ij0YbT.title: Diphtheria
Ij0YbT.description: An infectious disease caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae that is usually transmitted via respiratory droplets. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, and development of a grayish-white pseudomembrane on the posterior pharyngeal wall. Since the development of the DTaP vaccine, the incidence of diphtheria has decreased dramatically.

rj0fbT.title: Legionellosis
rj0fbT.description: A group of infections caused by Legionella bacteria. Includes Legionnaires' disease and Pontiac fever.

7j04bT.title: Tetanus
7j04bT.description: An acute disease caused by neurotoxins from the bacterium Clostridium tetani. Patients classically present with a triad of trismus, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonus, due to inhibition of release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (e.g., GABA, Glycine).

Hj0KbT.title: Gas gangrene
Hj0KbT.description: A life-threatening, necrotizing soft tissue infection typically caused by the rapid proliferation and spread of Clostridium perfringens from a contaminated wound.

tj0XXT.title: Food poisoning
tj0XXT.description: A type of foodborne illness caused by the ingestion of food or drink contaminated with preformed toxins, such as those produced by bacteria (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium botulinum) and marine toxins (e.g., histamine fish poisoning).

Fj0gXT.title: Lyme disease
Fj0gXT.description: A tick-borne infection caused by certain species of the Borrelia genus (B. burgdorferi in the US). The disease has three stages, beginning with localized rash and ultimately causing systemic infection involving the joints, skin, and central nervous system.

8j0OXT.title: Leptospirosis
8j0OXT.description: The most common zoonotic disease worldwide. Caused by gram-negative Leptospira bacteria. Direct transmission to humans occurs when broken skin and mucous membranes come into contact with the urine of infected animals, such as rodents. Usually self-limited but can progress to a severe form (Weil disease).

uj0pXT.title: Anthrax
uj0pXT.description: Uncommon illness caused by Bacillus anthracis, a rod-shaped, gram-positive aerobic bacteria. Can cause either cutaneous (most common), inhalational (rapidly fatal), or gastrointestinal disease. Can occur naturally via exposure to spores in soil, but is also considered a form of bioterrorism.

Ej08XT.title: Brucellosis
Ej08XT.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species. Transmitted through ingestion of infected animal products, contact with infected animals, and inhalation of Brucella. Typically manifests with flu‑like symptoms and can cause undulant fever.

vj0AXT.title: Listeriosis
vj0AXT.description: An infectious disease caused by the gram-positive bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. Transmission is usually via contaminated food (especially raw milk). Infection in immunocompetent hosts is often asymptomatic, but a mild flu-like illness or febrile gastroenteritis is possible. In immunocompromised and elderly patients, invasive disease can lead to sepsis and meningitis.

Dj01cT.title: Human immunodeficiency virus
Dj01cT.description: A virus that causes a complex disease pattern that can result in chronic immunodeficiency (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, AIDS). Can be transmitted sexually, parenterally, or vertically (peripartum from mother to child). The virus infects CD4+ leukocytes (especially T cells) and thus impairs one of the key mechanisms of cellular immune defense.

media.title: HIV fact sheet and prevalence map

Cj0qcT.title: Infectious mononucleosis
Cj0qcT.description: A highly contagious, acute condition most commonly caused by the Epstein-Barr virus and spread via bodily secretions, especially saliva. Symptomatic cases typically last for 2–4 weeks and manifest with fever, malaise, fatigue, acute pharyngitis, tonsillitis, lymphadenopathy, and/or splenomegaly.

media.title: Lymphadenopathy in a patient with mononucleosis

xj0EcT.title: Malaria
xj0EcT.description: A potentially life‑threatening tropical disease caused by Plasmodium parasites. It may present with relatively unspecific symptoms like fever, nausea, and vomiting 1 to 6 weeks after infection. Clinically suspected cases are confirmed by direct parasite detection in a blood smear. Patients are treated with antimalarial drugs (e.g., mefloquine, chloroquine, quinine), some of which can also be used as a prophylaxis against the disease.

Bj0zcT.title: Amebiasis
Bj0zcT.description: An infectious disease caused by amoebas. Most commonly refers to infections caused by the anaerobic protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, which can cause intestinal disease (blood diarrhea) or extraintestinal disease (e.g., liver abscess). Can also refer to infections caused by free-living amoebas (e.g., Naegleria fowleri).

yj0d1T.title: Toxoplasmosis
yj0d1T.description: A disease caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Typically asymptomatic in immunocompetent patients but can cause cerebral toxoplasmosis (which manifests with headache, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits) and toxoplasmic chorioretinitis in patients who are immunocompromised.

Aj0R1T.title: Leishmaniasis
Aj0R1T.description: A disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Leishmania, which is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected phlebotomine sandfly. The parasite subtype and the patient's immune factors influence disease progression to a cutaneous, mucosal, or visceral form of the disease.

_j051T.title: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
_j051T.description: An opportunistic interstitial pneumonia caused by the yeast-like fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. Occurs almost exclusively in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV infection, in whom it is considered an AIDS-defining condition. Symptoms include progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, low-grade fever, weight loss, and malaise.

media.title: Perihilar opacities in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
Ground glass opacification in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia

zj0r1T.title: Candidiasis
zj0r1T.description: An infection caused by Candida species that can occur in multiple parts of the body. Manifestations in immunocompetent individuals include thrush, vaginal yeast infections, and infections of intertriginous areas. More widespread and systemic infections can occur in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., neonates, diabetics, and HIV patients).

-j0D1T.title: Aspergillosis
-j0D1T.description: A fungal infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus or Aspergillus flavus. Contracted primarily by inhaling mold spores. Most commonly affects the lungs. May present with asthmatic symptoms, fever, chest pain, and hemoptysis depending on disease severity.

media.title: Aspergilloma (fungus ball) within right upper lobe cavity

0P0eWT.title: Norovirus infection
0P0eWT.description: A condition of acute, viral gastroenteritis caused by the highly contagious Norovirus. Elderly and immunocompromised patients are most commonly affected. After an incubation period of 12–48 hours, nausea, acute-onset vomiting, abdominal cramping, and watery, nonbloody diarrhea occur. Symptoms usually resolve after 48–72 hours.

aP0QWT.title: Helminth infections
aP0QWT.description: An infection caused by worms of various species, such as nematodes (or roundworms, e.g., Toxocara, Enterobius, Ascaris, Trichinella, Strongyloides, Ancylostoma, Necator), cestodes (or tapeworms, e.g., Taenia, Diphyllobothrium, Echinococcus), or trematodes (or flukes, e.g., Schistosoma). Typically transmitted via ingestion of parasitic eggs or larvae, penetration of worms through the skin, or entry via the bite of a vector species. Common gastrointestinal complaints include abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea, but extraintestinal manifestations are also possible.

YP0nWT.title: Echinococcosis
YP0nWT.description: A helminthic infection caused by cestodes of the genus Echinococcus (e.g., E. granulosus, E. multilocularis). Infection is typically acquired by accidental ingestion of Echinococcus eggs, which are shed in the feces of infected dogs. Infection results in cystic lesions in the liver (75% of cases), lung (15% of cases), and, rarely, other organs.

cP0adT.title: Poisoning
cP0adT.description: The harmful effects of exposure to a substance through inhalation, ingestion, or cutaneous absorption. Common causes of poisoning include organophosphates, cyanide, certain mushrooms, and carbon monoxide.

1P02dT.title: Nosocomial infections
1P02dT.description: An infection acquired during hospitalization that was not present or incubating at the time of admission. More likely to be caused by multidrug-resistant organisms (e.g., methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing bacteria, vancomycin-resistant enterococci) than community-acquired infections.

WP0PdT.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
WP0PdT.description: A chronic inflammatory autoimmune disorder of unknown etiology. Characterized by pain, swelling, stiffness, and destruction of synovial joints. Can also cause various extraarticular manifestations, such as rheumatoid nodules and interstitial lung disease.

dP0odT.title: Ankylosing spondylitis
dP0odT.description: A chronic inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton that leads to partial or complete vertebral fusion and spine rigidity. It mainly affects male individuals and > 90% of patients are positive for HLA-B27. Clinical features include pain and stiffness in the neck and lower back that improves with exercise.

media.title: Bamboo spine and dagger sign in ankylosing spondylitis

VP0GdT.title: Reactive arthritis
VP0GdT.description: An immune-mediated condition that typically occurs 1-4 weeks after a bacterial infection of the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract. Particularly common after infection with Shigella, Yersinia, Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Chlamydia. The characteristic triad of symptoms consists of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis.

UP0bVT.title: Osteoarthritis
UP0bVT.description: A condition characterized by degeneration of the articular cartilage and the underlying bone as a result of chronic wear and tear. Usually occurs in the elderly but can be accelerated in patients with an underlying joint pathology and increased or abnormal biomechanical forces on the joint, including elevated BMI.

media.title: Illustration of right hip radiograph in osteoarthritis

fP0kVT.title: Osteoporosis
fP0kVT.description: A skeletal condition that usually affects postmenopausal women and the elderly population, in which the loss of bone mineral density leads to decreased bone strength and an increased susceptibility to fractures.

gP0FVT.title: Connective tissue diseases
gP0FVT.description: A broad group of disorders that affect connective tissue. Due to the variety and abundance of connective tissue in the body, manifestations of connective tissue diseases are diverse and can affect cartilage, blood vessels, bones, tendons, and organs. Includes autoimmune disorders (e.g., scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) and inherited disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome).

hP0ceT.title: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
hP0ceT.description: A group of rare systemic diseases characterized by progressive weakness due to chronic skeletal muscle inflammation, as well as various extramuscular features. They are classified based on clinicopathological findings and include dermatomyositis (DM), overlap myositis (OM), immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), inclusion-body myositis (IBM), and polymyositis (PM). Patients typically have difficulties reaching overhead, climbing the stairs, and/or standing up due to proximal muscle weakness.

3P0SeT.title: Systemic sclerosis
3P0SeT.description: A systemic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy and fibrosis of the skin and other organs. Typical manifestations include cutaneous thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, and esophageal dysmotility. Classified as limited or diffuse depending on the extent of cutaneous thickening.

RP0leT.title: Fibromyalgia
RP0leT.description: A chronic neurosensory disorder characterized by diffuse chronic musculoskeletal pain of unknown etiology. The pain is typically accompanied by other distressing functional symptoms (e.g., fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive dysfunction).

iP0JeT.title: Vasculitides
iP0JeT.description: A heterogeneous group of autoimmune diseases, all characterized by inflammation of blood vessels, potential ischemia and damage to the organs supplied by these vessels.

QP0ueT.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
QP0ueT.description: An immune-mediated necrotizing vasculitis that most commonly affects small and medium-sized vessels in the upper and lower respiratory tract, eyes, and kidneys. Associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and the formation of noncaseating granulomas. Manifestations include rhinosinusitis, lung disease, glomerulonephritis, and skin lesions.

PP0WUT.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome
PP0WUT.description: A group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell neoplasms characterized by impaired proliferation and differentiation of myeloid stem cells within the bone marrow. Most commonly idiopathic, but may also be caused by exposure to chemotherapy or radiation. Classic findings include one or more cytopenias (e.g., anemia, thrombocytopenia) and dysplasias in the myeloid cell lines. May progress to acute myeloid leukemia or bone marrow failure.

kP0mUT.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
kP0mUT.description: A low-grade, non-Hodgkin, B-cell lymphoma that presents with lymphocytosis. The most common leukemia in adults, especially in advanced age.

media.title: Gumprecht shadows in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

OP0IUT.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia
OP0IUT.description: A neoplasm characterized by excessive proliferation of the myeloid lineage, particularly granulocytes. Caused by a mutation in the Philadelphia chromosome 22 that results in the formation of a BCR-ABL fusion gene.

media.title: Left shift to promyelocyte stage in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)

lP0vUT.title: Polycythemia vera
lP0vUT.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an irreversible increase in erythrocyte, granulocyte, and platelet counts due to a mutation in the JAK2 gene. The increased blood cell mass leads to hyperviscosity, increasing the risk of thrombosis and poor oxygenation.

NP0-UT.title: Myeloproliferative neoplasms
NP0-UT.description: A group of disorders characterized by a proliferation of malignant hematopoietic stem cells of the myeloid cell lineage. The most common are chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), polycythemia vera (PV), primary myelofibrosis (PMF), and essential thrombocythemia (ET).

mP0V2T.title: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas
mP0V2T.description: A group of hematologic cancers arising from lymphocytes and the most common hematopoietic neoplasm. In contrast to Hodgkin lymphomas, non-Hodgkin lymphomas lack Reed-Sternberg cells. Examples include diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, and MALT lymphoma.

5P0i2T.title: Hodgkin lymphoma
5P0i2T.description: A malignant lymphoma that typically arises from B-cells. Associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV infection). Typically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and involuntary weight loss.

MP0M2T.title: Multiple myeloma
MP0M2T.description: A malignancy of white blood cells characterized by overproduction of either one or multiple lineages of B lymphocytes. The proliferation of B lymphocytes and their associated proteins (antibodies) causes decreased kidney function, hypercalcemia, anemia, and disruption in bone metabolism that manifests as bone pain. Patients also report foamy urine due to Bence Jones proteinuria.

media.title: Lytic calvarial lesions in multiple myeloma
Clusters of plasma cells in multiple myeloma

nP072T.title: MALT lymphoma
nP072T.description: A low-grade, B-cell, non-Hodgkin lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) that arises from the marginal zone of extranodal lymphoid follicles. The most common sites of origin are the stomach and small intestine. Associated with H. pylori infection.

media.title: MALT lymphoma of the small intestine

LP0w2T.title: Mycosis fungoides
LP0w2T.description: The most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Characterized by pruritic plaques and patches, which can progress to nodular tumors and/or systemic involvement in advanced disease.

oP00fT.title: Splenomegaly
oP00fT.description: An enlargement of the spleen. Can be caused by various conditions, including malignancy, infection, and venous congestion. Often seen in conjunction with hepatomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly).

KP0UfT.title: Anemia
KP0UfT.description: A decrease in the number of circulating red blood cells (RBC), represented by a reduction in hemoglobin concentration (Hb), hematocrit (Hct), or RBC count. May be due either to inadequate RBC production, excessive RBC destruction, or blood loss.

pP0LfT.title: Hemolytic anemia
pP0LfT.description: A condition characterized by the excess breakdown of RBCs, caused by either abnormalities of the RBCs themselves (defective hemoglobin, RBC membrane, or intracellular enzymes), called corpuscular hemolytic anemia, or by external causes (immune-mediated or mechanical damage), referred to as extracorpuscular hemolytic anemia. Characteristic lab findings include ↓ haptoglobin, ↑ LDH, ↑ indirect/unconjugated bilirubin, ↑ reticulocytes.

JP0sfT.title: Hereditary spherocytosis
JP0sfT.description: The most common congenital hemolytic disorder among northern Europeans. Typically an autosomal dominant disease caused by red blood cell membrane protein defects, which render the red blood cells more vulnerable to osmotic stress and hemolysis.

qP0CfT.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
qP0CfT.description: An enzyme deficiency that results in the decreased ability to regenerate glutathione, an antioxidant, which in turn increases the susceptibility of RBCs to oxidative stress, resulting in periodic hemolytic anemia with exposure to oxidative conditions.

media.title: Reduction and oxidation reactions of glutathione
Bite cells in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency

IP0YTT.title: Sickle cell anemia
IP0YTT.description: The most severe clinical presentation of sickle cell disease. Genotypes that cause sickle cell anemia include homozygous HbSS and compound heterozygous HbSβ0thal (a form of sickle beta thalassemia).

media.title: Sickle cell disease with drepanocytes and target cells

7P04TT.title: Hemostasis and bleeding disorders
7P04TT.description: A group of disorders characterized by defects in hemostasis, which leads to an increased susceptibility to bleeding. Caused either by platelet disorders (primary hemostasis defect), coagulation defects (secondary hemostasis defect), or a combination of both. Coagulation defects may be further divided into intrinsic or extrinsic defects according to the pathway of the coagulation cascade affected.

sP0tTT.title: Thrombocytopenia
sP0tTT.description: Decreased thrombocytes (< 150,000/mm³). Usually asymptomatic but can manifest with mucosal bleeding (e.g., nosebleeds, gum bleeding), bruising, and petechiae if < 30,000/mm³. Causes include reduced production (e.g., leukemia, sepsis, hereditary conditions), increased destruction (e.g., idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hypersplenism), and medications (e.g., valproic acid).

tP0XgT.title: IgA vasculitis
tP0XgT.description: An acute immune complex-mediated small vessel vasculitis that most commonly occurs in children. It is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection and typically manifests with a tetrad of symptoms: palpable purpura, arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease.

8P0OgT.title: Arginine vasopressin disorders
8P0OgT.description: A group of conditions characterized by inappropriately dilute urine due to either arginine vasopressin deficiency (previously known as central diabetes insipidus) or arginine vasopressin resistance (previously known as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus). Individuals with excessive thirst (polydipsia) in response to fluid loss typically maintain euvolemia, but those with adipsia or low fluid intake are at risk of dehydration and hypernatremia.

uP0pgT.title: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
uP0pgT.description: An endocrine disorder caused by increased ADH secretion in the pituitary gland (e.g., due to infection, drugs), ectopic production of ADH (e.g., in small cell lung carcinoma), or increased renal sensitivity to ADH as a result of a genetic mutation (nephrogenic SIADH). Hyponatremia develops due to increased water retention in the kidneys (not sodium deficiency) and systemic fluid overload.

destinations.label: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

EP08gT.title: Hypopituitarism
EP08gT.description: The inadequate production of one or more anterior pituitary hormones as a result of damage to the pituitary gland and/or hypothalamus.

vP0AgT.title: Hyperprolactinemia
vP0AgT.description: A condition of elevated serum prolactin, which commonly manifests with galactorrhea in women, gynecomastia in men, and symptoms of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (due to ↓ FSH and LH secretion) in both sexes.

DP01ST.title: Acromegaly
DP01ST.description: A condition characterized by enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, and pathological growth of internal organs due to excess growth hormone (GH) in adults. Most commonly caused by a GH-secreting anterior pituitary adenoma. In children, abnormal growth due to excess GH is called gigantism.

9P0NST.title: Hyperthyroidism
9P0NST.description: Elevated circulating thyroid hormones. Etiologies include a hyperfunctioning thyroid gland (e.g., Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, thyroid nodule), thyroid gland destruction (e.g., thyroiditis), and ingestion of exogenous thyroid hormone. Manifestations include heat intolerance, weight loss or inappropriate weight gain, diarrhea, tachycardia, fine tremor, and muscle weakness.

CP0qST.title: Hypothyroidism
CP0qST.description: A condition in which the thyroid gland is underactive, resulting in a deficiency of the thyroid hormones triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4). Clinical features include fatigue, bradycardia, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight gain.

yP0dhT.title: Thyroid cancer
yP0dhT.description: A malignancy that originates from the thyroid tissue. The majority are well-differentiated (papillary or follicular) carcinomas and have a much better prognosis than poorly differentiated (medullary or anaplastic) carcinomas.

AP0RhT.title: Adrenal insufficiency
AP0RhT.description: A state of decreased production of adrenocortical hormones (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and adrenal androgens). Categorized as primary (adrenal dysfunction), secondary (pituitary dysfunction), or from chronic exogenous steroid use. Symptoms may include postural hypotension, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, anorexia, lethargy, depression, and/or hyponatremia.

_P05hT.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism
_P05hT.description: An excess of aldosterone caused by autonomous overproduction. Typically due to adrenal hyperplasia or adrenal adenoma.

zP0rhT.title: Cushing syndrome
zP0rhT.description: A metabolic disorder characterized by hypercortisolism from exogenous (administration of corticosteroids) or endogenous causes (overproduction of corticosteroids).

-P0DhT.title: Pheochromocytoma
-P0DhT.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor originating in chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (i.e., an intra-adrenal paraganglioma). Causes sustained or paroxysmal hypertension with episodic blood pressure crises, paroxysmal headaches, diaphoresis, palpitations, and pallor due to excess epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine secretion.

040e3T.title: Multiple endocrine neoplasia
040e3T.description: A term used to describe three autosomal dominant syndromes that are associated with certain hormone-producing neoplasias. MEN 1 presents with primary hyperparathyroidism, often in association with endocrine pancreatic tumors and/or pituitary adenomas. MEN 2A and MEN 2B both present with medullary thyroid carcinoma and sometimes pheochromocytoma. MEN 2A is further associated with primary hyperparathyroidism as well, while MEN 2B causes a marfanoid habitus and sometimes neurinomas.

a40Q3T.title: Diabetes mellitus
a40Q3T.description: A group of metabolic diseases characterized by chronic hyperglycemia. The two most common forms are type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 1 is the result of an autoimmune response that triggers the destruction of insulin-producing β cells in the pancreas and results in an absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2, which is much more common, has a strong genetic component and a significant association with obesity and sedentary lifestyles.

Y40n3T.title: Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state
Y40n3T.description: A life-threatening condition characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolarity, and absence of ketosis and acidosis, predominantly seen in older adults with type 2 diabetes. Manifests with profound dehydration and altered mental status, ranging from lethargy to coma.

b40H3T.title: Hypoglycemia
