b40H3T.description: An abnormally low level of glucose in the blood resulting from an endogenous (e.g., insulinoma, sepsis) or exogenous cause (e.g., insulin use). Thresholds for symptomatic hypoglycemia depend on individual factors (e.g., diabetic status) and range from 55–70 mg/dL (3.0-3.9 mmol/L). Neurogenic (autonomic) symptoms are mediated by catecholamine release and include tremors, sweating, and palpitations. Neuroglycopenic symptoms are the result of brain glucose deprivation and include drowsiness, confusion, seizure, and coma.

X4093T.title: Metabolic syndrome
X4093T.description: The co-occurrence of medical conditions that increase the risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and type 2 diabetes: elevated blood glucose, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and/or abdominal obesity.

1402RT.title: Acute kidney injury
1402RT.description: A sudden loss of renal function with a consecutive rise in creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Most frequently caused by decreased renal perfusion (prerenal), but may also be due to direct damage to the kidneys (intrinsic) or inadequate urine drainage (postrenal).

W40PRT.title: Chronic kidney disease
W40PRT.description: An abnormality of kidney function or structure that persists for > 3 months and affects health. The most common causes in the US are diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and glomerulonephritis.

V40GRT.title: Nephrotic syndrome
V40GRT.description: A syndrome characterized by massive renal loss of protein (> 3.5 g/24 hours) resulting in edema and hypoalbuminemia. Occurs due to damage to the glomerular filtration barrier (e.g., in diabetic nephropathy, membranous nephropathy). Often causes hyperlipidemia, hypercoagulability, and an increased risk of infection.

media.title: Serum protein electrophoresis in nephrotic syndrome

U40biT.title: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
U40biT.description: An acute glomerular inflammation that results from a preceding infection with nephritogenic strains of group A (beta-hemolytic) Streptococcus pyogenes. Most commonly seen in children approximately 1–6 weeks following group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis or possibly skin infections such as impetigo.

240TiT.title: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
240TiT.description: Glomerulonephritis that manifests as nephritic syndrome with rapid decline in renal function in days to weeks. Causes include anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (e.g., Goodpasture syndrome), immune complex deposition (e.g., in lupus nephritis), and vasculitis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis). Can cause flank pain, edema, decreased urine output, increased serum BUN and creatinine, and red blood cell casts on urinalysis.

f40kiT.title: Tubulointerstitial diseases
f40kiT.description: A group of diseases characterized by acute or chronic inflammation of the renal tubules and interstitium. Etiologies include drug toxicity, metabolic disease, and hematologic malignancies.

T406iT.title: Nephrolithiasis
T406iT.description: The formation of urinary calculi, including renal, ureteral, and bladder calculi. The most common types are calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. Others types include uric acid, struvite, and cystine stones.

g40FiT.title: Dehydration
g40FiT.description: A state of decreased total body water (usually in excess of sodium), which typically results in a hypertonic and hypernatremic state. Can be caused by insufficient water intake in combination with increased free water loss.

h40cQT.title: Disorders of potassium balance
h40cQT.description:
An imbalance of potassium homeostasis. Can refer to:
1. Hyperkalemia 
2. Hypokalemia

R40lQT.title: Malignant hyperthermia
R40lQT.description: A condition characterized by uncontrollable contraction of skeletal muscle that leads to a life-threatening hypercatabolic state and an increase in body temperature in genetically susceptible individuals, typically triggered by volatile anesthetics or the muscle relaxant succinylcholine.

media.title: Pathomechanisms and therapeutic approach in malignant hyperthermia

i40JQT.title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
i40JQT.description: A severe inflammatory reaction characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and injury to alveolar capillaries and endothelial cells. Etiologies include systemic inflammatory response syndrome, trauma, inhalation injury, aspiration pneumonitis, pulmonary infarction, and transfusion-related acute injury.

media.title: Pathophysiology of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
Management of acute respiratory distress syndrome

Q40uQT.title: Achalasia
Q40uQT.description: A condition characterized by impaired lower esophageal sphincter relaxation due to degeneration of inhibitory neurons within the esophageal wall. Symptoms include dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, retrosternal pain, and weight loss.

j40_QT.title: Esophageal diverticula
j40_QT.description: A collection of abnormal pouches that arise from the wall of the esophagus. There are two types, true diverticula in which all the layers of the esophageal wall protrude, and false diverticula in which only mucosa and submucosa bulge through weak points in the muscularis propria.

P40WjT.title: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
P40WjT.description: A condition in which gastroesophageal reflux (i.e., movement of stomach contents into the esophagus) causes troublesome symptoms (e.g., retrosternal burning pain, dysphagia) and/or complications (e.g., erosive esophagitis, Barrett esophagus).

k40mjT.title: Boerhaave syndrome
k40mjT.description: A transmural rupture of the distal esophagus as a result of a sudden increase in intraesophageal pressure. Usually caused by severe retching or vomiting (e.g., due to excessive alcohol consumption). Manifestations include severe, retrosternal chest pain and mediastinal and/or subcutaneous emphysema.

l40vjT.title: Esophageal cancer
l40vjT.description: Cancer arising from the esophagus. There are two main subtypes: Esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma (eSCC), which affects upper two-thirds of the esophagus and is more common worldwide; and esophageal adenocarcinoma, which affects the lower one-third of the esophagus and which is more common in industrialized nations like the USA.

media.title: Mediastinal mass with narrowed tracheal lumen

N40-jT.title: Atrophic gastritis
N40-jT.description: A condition characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa with atrophy, gland loss, and metaplastic changes. Caused by autoimmune disease and Helicobacter pylori infection. Symptoms vary in severity but include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and hematemesis.

m40VPT.title: Peptic ulcer disease
m40VPT.description: A break in the continuity of the mucosal lining of the stomach or duodenum. Most commonly due to an infection with Helicobacter pylori or the use of NSAIDs.

540iPT.title: Gastric cancer
540iPT.description: A neoplasm of the stomach or the esophagogastric junction. Most common type is adenocarcinoma; additional types include lymphoma, GI stromal tumor, and carcinoid. Typically has early, aggressive, local growth and metastases. Patients often present late. Associated with acanthosis nigricans and Leser-Trélat sign.

M40MPT.title: Gastrointestinal bleeding
M40MPT.description: Bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract. Can originate from the upper or lower gastrointestinal tract, or from the small bowel.

n407PT.title: Malabsorption
n407PT.description: The impaired absorption of nutrients. Features depend on the cause and may include diarrhea, steatorrhea, abdominal distention, flatulence, weight loss, and signs of nutritional deficiencies, e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency, iron deficiency anemia. Commonly used as an umbrella term for both malabsorption (impaired absorption due to functional or structural alterations of the intestinal mucosa) and maldigestion (impaired breakdown of food in the intestinal lumen).

L40wPT.title: Celiac disease
L40wPT.description: An autoimmune disorder characterized by intestinal hypersensitivity to gluten, a protein found in grains (e.g., wheat, rye, and barley). Gluten triggers an autoimmune reaction and the production of autoantibodies that target tissue transglutaminase within the small intestine. Manifestations include symptoms of malabsorption such as vitamin deficiencies, anemia, fatigue, weight loss, and diarrhea.

o4004T.title: Lactose intolerance
o4004T.description: A clinical syndrome resulting from the presence of lactose in the large intestine. Caused by an inability to absorb lactose in the small intestine due to lactase deficiency (genetic or acquired). Symptoms include pain, diarrhea, and bloating.

K40U4T.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
K40U4T.description: A common GI condition manifesting with recurrent, nonspecific changes in bowel movements and abdominal symptoms (diffuse pain, bloating, diarrhea, constipation) in the absence of a specific organic pathology.

p40L4T.title: Diverticular disease
p40L4T.description: An umbrella term for various intestinal conditions characterized by abnormal outpouching of the colonic mucosa (diverticula), including diverticulosis and diverticulitis.

q40C4T.title: Clostridioides difficile infection
q40C4T.description: An infection caused by toxigenic Clostridioides difficile in the lower gastrointestinal tract. Bacterial toxins cause colonic inflammation and profuse diarrhea. Severe cases are characterized by the formation of pseudomembranous colitis due to necrosis of the colonic mucosa and exudation of fibrin.

I40YkT.title: Crohn disease
I40YkT.description: An inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural inflammation that involves any region of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the perianal area.

r40fkT.title: Ulcerative colitis
r40fkT.description: An inflammatory bowel disease with chronic mucosal and submucosal inflammation of the colon, typically starting in the rectum, and may extend to the distal colon or to the cecum. Most commonly occurs in individuals 20–30 years of age. Manifests with bloody diarrhea with mucus, fecal urgency, abdominal pain, and tenesmus. Extraintestinal manifestations are common and include uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, arthritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum.

7404kT.title: Colon polyps
7404kT.description: A collection of slow-growing overgrowths on the inner lining of the intestinal mucosa that protrude into the lumen. Can become malignant. Common in individuals > 50 years of age.

H40KkT.title: Lynch syndrome
H40KkT.description: A hereditary cancer syndrome caused by a mutation in mismatch repair genes. Individuals have a significantly higher risk of developing colorectal, gastric, ovarian, and endometrial cancer.

s40tkT.title: Colorectal carcinoma
s40tkT.description: A malignancy (typically adenocarcinoma) arising from the colon or rectum. Cancers located within 15 cm from the anal verge are considered rectal cancers and those located further proximally are classified as colon cancers. Clinical signs are often nonspecific and can include a change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, and weight loss.

G40BkT.title: Anal cancer
G40BkT.description: A rare malignancy that most frequently arises from the squamous cells of the anal canal or the anal verge. Risk factors include infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), immunosuppression, tobacco use, and receptive anal intercourse. Most commonly manifests with rectal bleeding, anal pruritus, and tenderness or pain in the anal area.

t40XOT.title: Acute pancreatitis
t40XOT.description: A sudden-onset inflammation of the pancreas that is usually associated with a history of alcohol use disorder or gallstones. Other etiologies include hypertriglyceridemia, trauma, and infection. Causes constant, severe epigastric pain that classically radiates toward the back.

media.title: Hypoechoic pancreas in acute pancreatitis (interstitial edematous pancreatitis)

F40gOT.title: Chronic pancreatitis
F40gOT.description: A disease caused by progressive inflammation and irreversible damage to the pancreas. Common etiologies include alcohol abuse and pancreatic ductal obstruction. Patients can be asymptomatic or present with abdominal pain and features of pancreatic enzyme insufficiency (e.g., steatorrhea, weight loss, impaired glucose tolerance).

840OOT.title: Pancreatic cancer
840OOT.description: A malignancy of the pancreas. Most common type is ductal adenocarcinoma, often located in the pancreatic head. Usually asymptomatic in early stages, then presents with belt-like epigastric pain that radiates to the back, jaundice, weight loss, and a painless, enlarged gallbladder. Risk factors include smoking, high alcohol consumption, and chronic pancreatitis.

u40pOT.title: Insulinoma
u40pOT.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor arising from beta cells. Characterized by an overproduction of insulin that can cause hypoglycemic episodes. Insulinomas have low potential for malignant spread.

E408OT.title: Gastrinoma
E408OT.description: A gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor that is most often localized to the duodenum and pancreas. May occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome. Malignant in more than half of patients. Typically presents with recurrent, therapy-resistant peptic ulcer disease and diarrhea due to elevated serum gastrin and low gastric pH.

D401lT.title: Cirrhosis
D401lT.description: The final stage of chronic liver disease. Characterized by regenerative nodules and fibrous septae (usually irreversible) in liver parenchyma in response to hepatic injury. Etiologies include alcohol use, viral infections, diabetes, hypertension, and hemochromatosis. Clinical findings include jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, skin changes (spider angiomata, palmar erythema, caput medusae), and hormonal changes (gynecomastia, hypogonadism, sexual dysfunction).

w40hlT.title: Hepatitis A
w40hlT.description: A viral infection that causes liver disease. Usually results in acute hepatitis with a clinical course characterized by prodromal symptoms of fever and malaise, followed by jaundice. Unlike hepatitis B and C, does not cause chronic liver disease. Transmission is fecal-oral, usually from contaminated water or food, and often acquired during visits to countries in which hepatitis A virus is endemic.

media.title: Serology of hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection

940NlT.title: Hepatitis B infection
940NlT.description: A viral infection that causes acute or chronic inflammation of the liver after an incubation period of 1–6 months. Transmitted sexually, parenterally, or perinatally. Inflammation is usually mild or asymptomatic and resolves within a few weeks or months. However, it can rarely cause acute liver failure, and 5% of all adult patients and 90% of infants develop chronic hepatitis.

media.title: Serology time course of acute and resolved hepatitis B infection

C40qlT.title: Hepatitis C
C40qlT.description: A viral infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), which attacks liver cells and causes liver inflammation. HCV is a bloodborne pathogen commonly transmitted through needlestick injuries in health care settings or shared drug-injecting needles; it can also be transmitted sexually or perinatally. If untreated, acute infection most commonly leads to chronic hepatitis.

media.title: Serology of chronic hepatitis C infection

x40ElT.title: Alcohol-associated liver disease
x40ElT.description: A spectrum of progressive liver conditions caused by chronic harmful alcohol use. Early ALD manifests with potentially reversible alcohol-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis. Continued alcohol consumption can lead to alcohol-associated hepatitis. Patients with advanced ALD may develop alcohol-associated cirrhosis.

B40zlT.title: Primary biliary cholangitis
B40zlT.description: A chronic, progressive liver disease of autoimmune origin characterized by destruction of the intralobular bile ducts and hypercholesterolemia due to altered lipoprotein metabolism. Primarily affects middle-aged women and is frequently associated with other autoimmune conditions (e.g., sicca syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease).

media.title: Overview of PSC, PBC, and autoimmune hepatitis

y40dNT.title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
y40dNT.description: A progressive chronic inflammation of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. The exact etiology is unknown but there is a strong association with autoimmune diseases, particularly ulcerative colitis.

media.title: Overview of PSC, PBC, and autoimmune hepatitis

A40RNT.title: Portal hypertension
A40RNT.description: A condition of increased portal venous pressure (normal pressure is 5–10 mm Hg) resulting from prehepatic (e.g., portal vein thrombosis), hepatic (e.g., liver cirrhosis), or posthepatic (e.g., right-sided heart failure) obstruction in portal blood flow. Can be complicated by portosystemic anastomoses (e.g., esophageal varices), splenomegaly, and/or ascites.

_405NT.title: Ascites
_405NT.description: The abnormal accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity and a common complication of diseases presenting with portal hypertension (e.g., liver cirrhosis, acute liver failure) and/or hypoalbuminemia (e.g., nephrotic syndrome).

z40rNT.title: Hepatocellular carcinoma
z40rNT.description: The most common type of liver cancer. Usually develops in patients with preexisting liver cirrhosis (e.g., due to viral hepatitis, alcohol use, aflatoxin, or hemochromatosis).

Zk0ZmT.title: Hemochromatosis
Zk0ZmT.description: A group of conditions characterized by excess iron deposition in the body. Includes hereditary hemochromatosis and secondary iron overload.

0k0emT.title: Wilson disease
0k0emT.description: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder of copper (due to ATP7B gene mutation) in which both impaired binding to its transporter protein (ceruloplasmin) and biliary excretion increase free serum copper, leading to accumulation in the body. Leads to copper deposits in the liver (early stages) and other organs (later stages), most importantly in the brain and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Presentation involves hepatitis (or even cirrhosis), dementia, and parkinsonism.

media.title: Copper metabolism in normal hepatocyte and hepatocyte affected by Wilson disease

ak0QmT.title: Heart failure
ak0QmT.description: A complex clinical syndrome in which there is structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling and/or ejection of blood to meet the metabolic needs of the body.

Yk0nmT.title: Cardiac arrhythmias
Yk0nmT.description: A group of abnormalities in the generation or transmission of electrical impulses in the myocardium, causing an accelerated, slowed, or irregular heart rate.

bk0HmT.title: Sinus node dysfunction
bk0HmT.description: A dysfunction of the sinoatrial node that can cause bradyarrhythmias (e.g., sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial pauses, blocks, and arrest) and/or tachyarrhythmias (e.g., Afib, SVT). Depending on the extent of bradycardia or tachycardia, the condition can be asymptomatic or manifest with symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnea, lightheadedness, and syncope.

media.title: Sinus bradycardia with sinus pause and junctional escape rhythm

Xk09mT.title: Supraventricular premature beats
Xk09mT.description: Atrial contractions triggered by ectopic foci rather than the sinoatrial node. Arise within the atria (atrial premature beats) or, through retrograde conduction, in the atrioventricular node (junctional premature beats).

ck0a5T.title: Atrial fibrillation
ck0a5T.description: A common supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, caused by uncoordinated atrial activation resulting in an irregular ventricular response. Patients are often asymptomatic but have an irregular pulse on physical examination. When present, symptoms usually include palpitations and lightheadedness. Patients with atrial fibrillation are at an increased risk of stroke and other thromboembolic complications.

media.title: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

1k025T.title: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia
1k025T.description: The most common cause of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Caused by two alternative electrical conduction pathways, one fast and one slow, within the AV node. The fast accessory pathway occasionally leads to a nonextinguishable circulating electrical impulse, or reentrant circuit, within the AV node that activates the atria and ventricles simultaneously and at a rapid rate. Causes episodic symptoms of palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness and/or syncope.

destinations.label: Supraventricular tachycardia → Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia

media.title: Pathophysiology of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)

Wk0P5T.title: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
Wk0P5T.description: A group of arrhythmias that have a sudden, abrupt onset and sudden termination. Includes atrioventricular re-entrant tachyarrhythmia (AVRT), AV nodal re-entrant tachyarrhythmia (AVNRT), junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET), and unifocal/multifocal atrial tachycardia. Most PSVTs result in tachycardia with a narrow QRS complex and regular rhythm. Clinical findings include dizziness, dyspnea, chest pain, and/or syncope.

dk0o5T.title: Premature ventricular complex
dk0o5T.description: An abnormal early electrical firing caused by an ectopic focus in the ventricles, often leading to a premature contraction. Usually asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally; can be idiopathic or secondary to cardiovascular disease, electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia), or use of certain drugs and substances (e.g., digoxin or alcohol). ECG findings include broad QRS complexes and compensatory pauses.

media.title: ECG rhythm strip with frequent premature ventricular complexes (PVCs)

Vk0G5T.title: Ventricular tachycardia
Vk0G5T.description: A potentially life-threatening arrhythmia that originates in the ventricles. Characterized by broad QRS complexes (> 120 ms) and tachycardia (> 120 bpm) on ECG. Can cause palpitations, syncope, cardiogenic shock, and sudden cardiac death.

media.title: QRS morphology criteria for ventricular tachycardia

ek0x5T.title: Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular flutter
ek0x5T.description: A life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia characterized by disorganized, high-frequency (usually > 300 bpm) ventricular contractions that result in diminished cardiac output and hemodynamic collapse. Characterized by a very irregular rhythm with indiscernible P waves or QRS complexes on ECG.

2k0TMT.title: Acute coronary syndrome
2k0TMT.description: A set of three clinical entities with similar pathophysiology: unstable angina pectoris, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). ACS is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic coronary artery disease associated with unstable plaques and, in the case of myocardial infarction, plaque rupture.

media.title: Acute inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

Tk06MT.title: Infective endocarditis
Tk06MT.description: An infectious inflammation of the endocardium that typically affects the heart valves but can affect the mural endocardium and septal defects. Typically caused by bacteremia (especially from gram-positive cocci). Divided into acute and subacute forms. Signs and symptoms include constitutional symptoms (e.g., fevers, chills, tachycardia, weight loss), cough, pleuritic chest pain, new heart murmur or arrhythmia, and extracardiac manifestations (e.g., cutaneous changes, renal injury).

gk0FMT.title: Myocarditis
gk0FMT.description:
Inflammation of the myocardium, which can impair cardiac output and the cardiac conduction system.
Commonly caused by viral infections (e.g., coxsackievirus B, parvovirus B19), acute rheumatic fever, and systemic conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and vasculitic syndromes.

Sk0yMT.title: Cardiomyopathy
Sk0yMT.description: A disease of the muscle tissue of the heart. There are four major morphological types: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.

3k0SnT.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
3k0SnT.description: A genetic heart disease characterized by unexplained hypertrophy and fibrosis of the left ventricular wall, which leads to diastolic dysfunction. It is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. While many patients are asymptomatic, symptoms may include exertional dyspnea and syncope, which are often exacerbated by exercise.

Qk0unT.title: Aortic regurgitation
Qk0unT.description: A valvular disease characterized by incomplete closure of the aortic valve, causing reflux of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole. On auscultation, characterized by S₃ and a high-pitched, decrescendo, early diastolic murmur.

media.title: Changes to pressure-volume loop in aortic regurgitation

jk0_nT.title: Mitral stenosis
jk0_nT.description: A valvular disease characterized by obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle during diastole.

Pk0WLT.title: Hypertension
Pk0WLT.description: A condition defined by a systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mm Hg and/or a diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90 mm Hg based on Joint National Commission (JNC) 8 guidelines. The 2017 guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) defined hypertension as a systolic blood pressure ≥ 130 mm Hg and/or a diastolic blood pressure ≥ 80 mm Hg. Classified as either primary (essential) or secondary (e.g., from renal, endocrine or vascular diseases).

4k03LT.title: Peripheral arterial disease
4k03LT.description: A chronic condition characterized by the luminal narrowing of the peripheral arteries due to atherosclerotic plaques. Typically used to describe lower extremity PAD, but arteries of the neck, bowel, or kidneys can also be involved. Limb PAD can be asymptomatic or cause intermittent claudication, rest pain, or ischemic ulcers.

media.title: Localization of arterial occlusion in PAD

kk0mLT.title: Acute limb ischemia
kk0mLT.description: A vascular emergency with a critically reduced arterial blood supply of one or more extremities. May be caused by an arterial embolism originating in the heart, arterial thrombosis, or arterial dissection. Typically manifests with the 6 Ps: limb pain (almost all cases), pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, paresthesia, and poikilothermia in the affected extremity.

Nk0-LT.title: Raynaud phenomenon
Nk0-LT.description: A phenomenon characterized by recurrent vasospasm of the fingers and toes, which usually occurs in response to stress or cold exposure. It can occur as a primary condition (Raynaud disease) or secondary to another condition (usually autoimmune). The vasospasm is paroxysmal, bilateral, and associated with normal capillaroscopy findings. Management primarily consists of avoiding triggers, including cold temperatures, nicotine use, and certain medications (e.g., CCBs, iloprost).

mk0VoT.title: Thromboangiitis obliterans
mk0VoT.description: An inflammatory, nonatherosclerotic, vasoocclusive disease of small and medium-sized vessels in the extremities that is strongly associated with tobacco consumption. Clinical features include ischemic ulcerations in the toes and fingers, intermittent claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and superficial thrombophlebitis.

media.title: Corkscrew collaterals in thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)

5k0ioT.title: Deep vein thrombosis
5k0ioT.description: A thrombosis of the deep veins of the extremities that can lead to pulmonary embolism. Clinical signs of DVT include swelling, tenderness, and redness or discoloration. Risk factors include the Virchow triad: endothelial damage (surgery/intravascular instrumentation), venous stasis (immobilization, obesity), hypercoagulable state (undetected malignancy, thrombophilia).

Mk0MoT.title: Chronic venous disease
Mk0MoT.description: A spectrum of disorders caused by venous dysfunction. Mild forms include telangiectasia and varicose veins. In advanced stages, chronic venous insufficiency can develop, causing edema, skin changes, and ulceration.

media.title: Venous ulcer in chronic venous insufficiency
Skin changes in chronic venous disease (1/2)

nk07oT.title: Acute bronchitis
nk07oT.description: A lower respiratory tract infection that causes inflammation of the bronchi. Most frequently caused by a viral infection. Typically manifests with a self-limited cough.

Lk0woT.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Lk0woT.description: A lung disease caused by airflow obstruction and alveolar gas exchange abnormalities. COPD is characterized by chronic respiratory symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, cough, sputum production), which are often progressive.

ok00KT.title: Bronchiectasis
ok00KT.description: An irreversible and abnormal dilation of the bronchial tree that may be caused by chronic pulmonary infections, obstructive pulmonary diseases (e.g., COPD), or disorders of secretion clearance and mucous plugging (e.g., cystic fibrosis). Typically manifests with chronic productive cough with copious mucopurulent sputum.

Kk0UKT.title: Asthma
Kk0UKT.description: A respiratory disease that is characterized by chronic airway inflammation. Manifests with respiratory symptoms (e.g., cough, dyspnea) and variable expiratory airflow.

media.title: Mechanisms of endobronchial obstruction in asthma

6k0jKT.title: Carbon monoxide intoxication
6k0jKT.description: An intoxication with the gas carbon monoxide (CO), which has a strong affinity to hemoglobin. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, nausea, chest pain, respiratory failure, seizures, and coma. Findings include high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (from lactic acidosis), normal SpO2 on pulse oximetry, and carboxyhemoglobinemia.

pk0LKT.title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
pk0LKT.description: A hypersensitivity reaction caused by inhalation of environmental and/or occupational antigens, manifesting in interstitial lung disease.

media.title: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis with mosaic attenuation

Jk0sKT.title: Silicosis
Jk0sKT.description: A type of lung disease caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica dust, usually as a result of occupational exposure. Most commonly seen in workers involved in sandblasting, mining, or glass production.

qk0CKT.title: Asbestosis
qk0CKT.description: A type of pneumoconiosis caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. Often manifests with progressive exertional dyspnea, lung fibrosis, and impaired respiratory function 20–30 years after exposure. Primarily caused by occupational exposure.

Ik0Y6T.title: Interstitial lung disease
Ik0Y6T.description: A heterogeneous group of lung disorders marked by inflammatory changes in the alveoli. ILDs can be idiopathic or due to secondary causes such as autoimmune disease, or exposure to drugs or toxic substances.

rk0f6T.title: Pneumonia
rk0f6T.description: A respiratory infection characterized by inflammation of the alveolar space and/or the interstitial tissue of the lungs.

7k046T.title: Tuberculosis
7k046T.description: A bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that typically affects the lungs. Primary infection is often initially asymptomatic, and bacteria remain dormant in the body until reactivation occurs in the case of immunodeficiency. Active disease classically manifests with fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a productive cough.

media.title: Bilateral upper lobe cavitary lung disease

Hk0K6T.title: Sarcoidosis
Hk0K6T.description: An idiopathic, chronic inflammatory disease characterized by the formation of noncaseating granulomas, typically in the lung and, less commonly, in the liver, eyes, and skin. Predominantly occurs in young, African American women. Chest x-ray often reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. First-line treatment is corticosteroids.

media.title: Multinucleated giant cells in pulmonary sarcoidosis

sk0t6T.title: Lung cancer
sk0t6T.description: A malignancy that originates within the airway or pulmonary parenchyma.

tk0XpT.title: Pulmonary embolism
tk0XpT.description: An obstruction of the pulmonary artery and/or one of its branches by a thrombus that most commonly originates from the deep vein system in the legs or pelvis and embolizes to the lungs via the inferior vena cava. Less commonly, the cause of obstruction is a fat or air embolus. Risk factors include stasis (e.g., immobility, surgery), hypercoagulable states (e.g., pregnancy and the puerperium), and endothelial dysfunction (e.g., trauma).

media.title: Pulmonary embolism: thrombus formation and embolization
Pulmonary embolism: pathophysiologic response of the lung

Ek08pT.title: Erysipelas
Ek08pT.description: A superficial skin infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics usually caused by group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes). Most commonly affects the lower limbs. Presents with sudden-onset, tender, sharply demarcated, erythematous, edematous, warm patches and plaques. When lymphangitis is present, red streaks can radiate from erythematous areas.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Nonpurulent SSTIs

Dk01JT.title: Actinomycosis
Dk01JT.description: An infection caused by Actinomyces bacteria (especially Actinomyces israelii). The most frequent form of infection is cervicofacial actinomycosis, which occurs after injury to the oral cavity, face, or neck, although other parts of the body may be affected. Initial disease manifests as coarse, inflammatory nodules, which frequently develop into purulent, draining fistulae.

wk0hJT.title: Rabies
wk0hJT.description: A viral disease usually contracted from the saliva of an infected animal. Manifests with a prodrome of nonspecific flu-like symptoms, followed by acute rabies encephalitis. Once symptomatic, rabies is virtually always fatal.

media.title: Rabies fact sheet and mortality map

Bk0zJT.title: Pneumothorax
Bk0zJT.description: A collapsed lung caused by the loss of negative pressure between the visceral and parietal pleural membranes that occurs when air abnormally enters the pleural space. Manifestations include pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and reduced breath sounds on the ipsilateral side.

zk0rqT.title: Intussusception
zk0rqT.description: The invagination of a segment of the intestine into an adjacent section of the intestine, potentially causing bowel obstruction and/or intestinal ischemia. Most common in children < 2 years of age. Clinical features include acute abdominal pain, vomiting, palpable abdominal mass in the RUQ, and blood in the stool.

-k0DqT.title: Carcinoid tumor
-k0DqT.description: Historically used interchangeably with “neuroendocrine neoplasm” or to refer to gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors. Currently only used to describe carcinoid lung tumors and ovarian carcinoid tumors.

media.title: Liver metastases from pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor

ZO0ZIT.title: Inguinal hernia
ZO0ZIT.description: An abnormal protrusion of intra-abdominal contents either through the deep inguinal ring (indirect inguinal hernia; lateral to the inferior epigastric artery) or through the weakened posterior wall of the inguinal canal (direct inguinal hernia; medial to the inferior epigastric artery).

0O0eIT.title: Internal hernia
0O0eIT.description: The protrusion of an internal organ (most commonly bowel) through an opening within the peritoneal cavity (most commonly a surgical adhesion or mesenteric defect). Much less common than external hernias. Can present with features of acute bowel obstruction (e.g., pain, nausea, vomiting).

aO0QIT.title: Femoral hernia
aO0QIT.description: A protrusion of intra-abdominal contents (e.g., intraperitoneal fat, mesentery, bowels) into the femoral canal through the femoral ring.

bO0HIT.title: Acute appendicitis
bO0HIT.description: An inflammation of the vermiform appendix. Manifestations include fever, periumbilical abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, nausea, and vomiting. Most commonly develops during childhood and adolescence but can manifest at any age.

XO09IT.title: Pilonidal disease
XO09IT.description: A condition characterized by recurrent abscesses and formation of sinus tracts due to localized infection in the skin and subcutaneous tissue near the gluteal cleft. Predisposing factors include excessive hair, deep gluteal cleft, and sedentary lifestyle.

media.title: Stages and features of pilonidal disease
Pilonidal cyst with broken hair roots

1O02rT.title: Anal fissures
1O02rT.description: A painful, longitudinal tear in the anoderm, typically located distal to the dentate line in the posterior midline. Most commonly caused by increased anal sphincter tone.

WO0PrT.title: Hemorrhoids
WO0PrT.description: Dilated submucosal vascular cushions within the anal canal that may abnormally enlarge, protrude, and cause perianal pruritus or scanty intermittent hematochezia. Hemorrhoids may be internal (above the dentate line), external (below the dentate line), or mixed.

dO0orT.title: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid
dO0orT.description: A complication of external hemorrhoids caused by localized thrombosis of an inferior hemorrhoidal venous plexus. Manifests as a palpable, tender, dark red to purplish nodule at the anal verge or just within the anal canal.

VO0GrT.title: Rectal prolapse
VO0GrT.description: A protrusion of the rectal mucosa (mucosal prolapse) or the entire rectum (full-thickness prolapse) through the anal opening, usually manifesting with a painless rectal mass that appears on straining. Risk factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., excessive straining), weakness of the pelvic floor muscles (e.g., as a result of old age, multiple pregnancies), and cystic fibrosis.

2O0T7T.title: Bowel obstruction
2O0T7T.description: The interruption of the normal passage of bowel contents either due to a functional (e.g., ileus) or mechanical cause.

TO067T.title: Salter-Harris fractures
TO067T.description: A fracture that involves the growth plate (physis) and/or epiphysis of long bones in children.

gO0F7T.title: Compartment syndrome
gO0F7T.description: A condition caused by tissue ischemia due to increased pressure within a fascial compartment. Acute compartment syndrome of the extremities is a surgical emergency that can lead to tissue necrosis if untreated, while chronic compartment syndrome is associated with exercise or exertion and can often be managed conservatively. Abdominal compartment syndrome is caused by increased pressure within the abdominal cavity and can lead to organ failure.

SO0y7T.title: Complex regional pain syndrome
SO0y7T.description: A condition typically characterized by severe, debilitating pain of the extremities with associated sensory, motor, and/or autonomic changes. Typically associated with a specific precipitating trauma and restricted to a specific nerve territory. The underlying mechanism is unknown but thought to be related to inflammation and dysfunction of pain perception.

media.title: Osteopenia in complex regional pain syndrome (1/2)
Osteopenia in complex regional pain syndrome (2/2)

3O0SHT.title: Acromioclavicular joint separation
3O0SHT.description: A stretching or tear of the ligaments connecting the acromion and the clavicle. Can lead to a complete separation of the scapula and the clavicle. Typically caused by falling onto an adducted arm. Most common in individuals participating in contact sports.

RO0lHT.title: Humerus fracture
RO0lHT.description: A partial or complete break of the humerus bone. Categorized by location (proximal, humeral shaft, distal). Typically manifests with localized pain and swelling. Can result in shortening of the arm in the setting of a displaced fracture.

media.title: Anatomical structures at risk in humerus fractures

iO0JHT.title: Shoulder dislocation
iO0JHT.description: A displacement of the humeral head from the glenoid fossa, usually caused by falling on an outstretched hand. Anterior dislocations (> 95% of cases) cause external rotation and abduction of the arm and flattening of the shoulder contour. Posterior dislocations (< 5% of cases) cause internal rotation and adduction of the arm, prominence of the posterior shoulder with anterior flattening, and a prominent coracoid process.

QO0uHT.title: Radial head subluxation
QO0uHT.description: A partial dislocation of the head of the radius at the level of the radio-humeral joint. Most commonly occurs in young children after sudden tugging of the outstretched and pronated arm. Manifests with painful and limited movement of the upper extremity and guarding, with the arm held in a flexed and pronated position.

PO0WsT.title: Scaphoid bone fracture
PO0WsT.description: The most common carpal bone fracture. Classically caused by a fall on an outstretched hand.

lO0vsT.title: Femoral neck fracture
lO0vsT.description: A type of intracapsular fracture of the femur that typically manifests with groin pain and a shortened and externally rotated leg. Patterns of femoral neck fractures are described in the Garden classification.

media.title: Garden classification of femoral neck fractures
Clinical presentation of femoral neck fracture

MO0MGT.title: Achilles tendon rupture
MO0MGT.description: A partial or complete rupture of the Achilles tendon, which compromises the attachment of the soleus and gastrocnemius muscles to the calcaneus. Most commonly caused by indirect trauma related to exercise. Rupture typically results in the sudden onset of sharp pain in the tendon at the back of the ankle, usually accompanied by a popping or snapping sound or sensation.

nO07GT.title: Seronegative spondyloarthropathy
nO07GT.description: A group of chronic inflammatory arthritic diseases that are negative for rheumatoid factor (RF) and have a strong genetic association with HLA-B27. The most important diseases in this group are ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis. Men are disproportionately affected, with symptom onset generally occurring before the age of 45. The cardinal sign is slowly progressive pain in the lower back and sacroiliac joints (especially at night). Asymmetrical oligoarthritis and enthesopathy are also common.

LO0wGT.title: Meningioma
LO0wGT.description: A slow-growing, extra-axial tumor that arises from arachnoid cap cells of the arachnoid villi. The most common primary brain tumors among adults and almost always benign.

media.title: Extra-axial brain tumor with dural tail sign

oO00tT.title: Acoustic neuroma
oO00tT.description: A type of schwannoma that arises from Schwann cells around the vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII. Commonly manifests with tinnitus and progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

KO0UtT.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
KO0UtT.description: A neurologic condition of unknown etiology that is characterized by chronically elevated intracranial pressure without evidence of hydrocephalus or a space-occupying lesion within the cranium. Clinical features include headaches, visual disturbances (e.g., diplopia, vision loss), and pulsatile tinnitus. Primarily affects obese women between 15 and 45 years of age.

6O0jtT.title: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
6O0jtT.description: A form of communicating hydrocephalus that primarily affects adults > 60 years of age. Intracranial pressure is normal or only mildly elevated, and patients present with the classic triad of urinary incontinence, dementia, and gait abnormalities.

pO0LtT.title: Major neurocognitive disorder
pO0LtT.description: An acquired disorder of cognitive function that is commonly characterized by impairments in memory, speech, reasoning, intellectual function, and/or spatiotemporal awareness. Potential causes of dementia are diverse, but the disorder is mainly due to neurodegenerative (e.g., Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease) and/or vascular disease (e.g., multi-infarct dementia).

qO0CtT.title: Frontotemporal dementia
qO0CtT.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive neuronal loss in the frontal, insular, and/or temporal cortices. Clinical features typically include personality and behavioral changes and/or speech and language impairment. Intelligence, orientation, and memory are initially preserved.

IO0YFT.title: Vascular dementia
IO0YFT.description: A type of cognitive impairment caused by cerebral ischemia. Symptoms depend on extent, location, and severity of vascular compromise and may develop gradually and/or in a stepwise manner.

7O04FT.title: Tremor
7O04FT.description: Rhythmic, oscillatory, involuntary movement of one or more body parts. Classified as resting or action tremor.

HO0KFT.title: Parkinson-plus syndromes
HO0KFT.description: A group of rare, adult-onset neurodegenerative disorders manifesting with parkinsonism and additional features. Key indicators include a poor levodopa response, rapid progression, prominent early cognitive decline, and significant autonomic dysfunction. Management is primarily symptomatic and supportive. Prognosis is less favorable than in Parkinson disease, with a more accelerated progression.

sO0tFT.title: Huntington's disease
sO0tFT.description: An autosomal-dominant neurodegenerative movement disorder characterized by chorea (involuntary and irregular movements of the limbs, neck, head, and/or face), dementia, and psychiatric symptoms. Caused by mutations in the huntingtin gene that lead to an increased number of CAG trinucleotide repeats.

tO0X8T.title: Ballismus
tO0X8T.description: A condition of uncontrolled, large amplitude movements of the arms (and sometimes legs) that can have a flailing quality. Unilateral ballismus (hemiballismus) occurs following contralateral subthalamic nucleus damage, usually from ischemia.

FO0g8T.title: Restless legs syndrome
FO0g8T.description: A neurological sleep disorder characterized by an urge to move the legs that is triggered and/or worsened with rest and is usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations (e.g., pain, pins and needles, itching, tickling, crawling sensation). May be idiopathic or result from an underlying condition (e.g., iron deficiency, uremia) or medication (e.g., H1 antihistamines).

8O0O8T.title: Meningitis
8O0O8T.description: An inflammation of the protective membranes surrounding the brain and the spinal cord, most commonly caused by a viral or bacterial infection. Typically manifests with fever, signs of meningism (e.g., headache, neck stiffness), and altered mental status.

uO0p8T.title: Herpes simplex encephalitis
uO0p8T.description: An inflammation of the brain parenchyma, typically in the medial temporal lobe, that is caused by either herpes simplex virus type-1 (HSV-1) or type-2 (HSV-2). Patients typically present with a prodrome of headaches and fever, followed by sudden focal neurological deficits, seizures, and altered mental status.

vO0A8T.title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
vO0A8T.description: The most common human prion disease. Characterized by myoclonus and rapidly progressive neurological deterioration resulting in death, typically within 1 year of symptom onset. The majority of cases are sporadic; familial and iatrogenic causes have been reported.

9O0NuT.title: Subdural hematoma
9O0NuT.description: A type of intracranial hemorrhage caused by head trauma characterized by bleeding between the dura mater and arachnoid membrane. It is caused by a tear in the bridging veins, presenting with acute, subacute, or chronic onset of headache and signs of increased intracranial pressure.

CO0quT.title: Epidural hemorrhage
CO0quT.description: A type of intracranial hemorrhage characterized by a collection of blood between the skull (calvarium) and the dura mater. Most commonly caused by head injury and subsequent acute bleeding, primarily from the middle meningeal artery.

media.title: Cranial vault fracture with epidural hematoma

yO0dET.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
yO0dET.description: A type of intracranial hemorrhage characterized by bleeding into the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid layer and the pia mater. Most commonly caused by head trauma. Nontraumatic etiologies include ruptured cerebral aneurysm and arteriovenous malformation.

AO0RET.title: Intracerebral hemorrhage
AO0RET.description: A type of intracranial hemorrhage characterized by bleeding within the brain parenchyma. Most commonly caused by arterial hypertension.

zO0rET.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome
zO0rET.description: A systemic autoimmune disease characterized by thrombotic (e.g., DVT, stroke) and/or obstetrical complications (e.g., recurrent early miscarriages, severe preeclampsia) in patients with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies. Other clinical manifestations include livedo reticularis, thrombocytopenia, and valvular heart disease.

-O0DET.title: Fibromuscular dysplasia
-O0DET.description: A disease characterized by stenosis of the small and medium-sized arteries as a result of proliferation of connective tissue and muscle fibers within the arterial vessel walls. Primarily affects young and middle-aged women. The renal, internal carotid, and vertebral arteries are predominantly involved.

media.title: String of beads sign in fibromuscular dysplasia

Zl0ZvT.title: Seizures and epilepsy
Zl0ZvT.description: A group of conditions that causes recurrent, unprovoked seizure activity with at least 2 episodes occurring > 24 hours apart. Can also be characterized by 1 unprovoked seizure with a high probability of further seizures occurring within the next 10 years (e.g., in the case of structural lesions, stroke, central nervous system infection).

0l0evT.title: Focal-onset seizure
0l0evT.description: The clinical manifestation of abnormal, excessive, synchronous brain activity (a seizure) occurring in only one hemisphere of the brain. The temporal lobe is the most common lobe to be affected, but all lobes may be affected. Such seizures may or may not involve impairment of consciousness.

media.title: Anterior temporal spikes and sharp waves

Yl0nvT.title: Transient global amnesia
Yl0nvT.description: An idiopathic, self-limited neurological disorder characterized by acute, transient memory loss lasting ≤ 24 hours. Affected individuals often present with mild agitation, anxiety, and disorientation but are typically alert and oriented to self.

bl0HvT.title: Narcolepsy
bl0HvT.description: A neurologic disorder that disrupts the circadian sleep-wake rhythm. Often begins in adolescence with short diurnal sleep attacks. Manifestations include excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hallucinations upon waking or falling asleep, and sleep paralysis.

Xl09vT.title: Syringomyelia
Xl09vT.description: A condition in which an abnormal fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) develops within the central canal of the spinal cord. The syrinx is a result of disrupted cerebrospinal fluid drainage from the central canal, commonly caused by a Chiari malformation or previous trauma to the cervical or thoracic spine. Symptoms include a cape-like distribution of decreased sensitivity to pain and temperature and flaccid atrophic paralysis in the upper extremities.

media.title: Cross section of the spinal cord

cl0aDT.title: Incomplete spinal cord syndromes
cl0aDT.description: A collection of conditions characterized by dissociated sensory loss caused by lesions that affect only select parts of the ascending or descending spinal tracts. Etiologies include trauma, spinal compression, and occlusion of spinal arteries. Examples include central cord syndrome, anterior cord syndrome, posterior cord syndrome, and Brown-Séquard syndrome.

1l02DT.title: Anterior spinal artery syndrome
1l02DT.description: A condition caused by damage to the anterior ⅔ of the spinal cord as a result of occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (a branch of the aorta). Manifests with complete, bilateral paralysis, loss of pain, and loss of temperature sensation below the level of the lesion. Vibration and proprioception are spared (intact dorsal column). Common causes include aortic aneurysms, aortic surgery.

media.title: Anterior spinal artery syndrome at T8 level

Wl0PDT.title: Spinal muscular atrophy
Wl0PDT.description: A group of autosomal recessive motor neuron diseases that are caused by apoptosis of lower motor neurons. Patients typically present during infancy or early childhood with progressive weakness, hypotonia, muscle atrophy, hyporeflexia/areflexia, and varying degrees of bulbar weakness.

dl0oDT.title: Bulbar palsy
dl0oDT.description: A lower motor neuron palsy caused by bilateral damage or injury of the nerve nuclei of cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII. Clinical features include dysphagia, drooling, anarthria, fasciculations of the tongue, and loss of the gag reflex.

destinations.label: Bulbar palsy and pseudobulbar palsy → Subtypes and variants

el0xDT.title: Hereditary spastic paraplegia
el0xDT.description: A group of rare, inherited, neurodegenerative diseases that affect the corticospinal tract and the dorsal column. Presents with upper motor neuron palsy of bilateral lower limbs, gait abnormalities, and urinary urgency and incontinence.

Ul0bwT.title: Friedreich ataxia
Ul0bwT.description: An autosomal recessive disorder involving trinucleotide repeat expansion that leads to progressive neurodegeneration. It affects multiple spinal cord tracts, causing muscle weakness and impaired coordination of all limbs. A staggering gait in childhood is the resulting main symptom. Other features include skeletal abnormalities, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes.

2l0TwT.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency
2l0TwT.description: A condition characterized by insufficient levels of vitamin B12 (cobalamin), an enzyme cofactor in DNA synthesis. Typically caused by malabsorption (e.g., in pernicious anemia), dietary insufficiency, or increased demand. Vitamin B12 deficiency can result in megaloblastic anemia and neurological disorders (e.g., subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord).

fl0kwT.title: Spinocerebellar ataxia
fl0kwT.description: A group of mostly autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative diseases. Manifests with cerebellar ataxia, sometimes coupled with dyssynergia and dysmetria.

Tl06wT.title: Spinal stenosis
Tl06wT.description: A disease caused by narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recess, and/or neural foramen. Can be congenital or acquired. Commonly caused by degenerative spinal changes (i.e., spondylosis) and spondylolisthesis.

media.title: Vertebral arch fracture deformity with spinal stenosis

Sl0ywT.title: Guillain-Barré syndrome
Sl0ywT.description: An acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy that typically manifests with bilateral ascending flaccid paralysis and sensory involvement, e.g., paresthesia. Symptoms are often preceded by a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (typically due to Campylobacter jejuni). Subtypes include acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and acute motor axonal neuropathy.

hl0c9T.title: Shingles
hl0c9T.description: A dermatomal rash with painful blistering caused by the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus (VZV). Pain can precede the rash. Initial infection with VZV usually occurs early in life, presenting as chickenpox (varicella), and the virus subsequently remains dormant in dorsal root ganglia. Immunosuppressed individuals are at particular risk of VZV reactivation.

3l0S9T.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
3l0S9T.description: A peripheral neuropathy caused by chronic or acute compression of the median nerve by the transverse carpal ligament. Characterized by both sensory disturbances (pain, tingling, and numbness) and motor symptoms (weakness and clumsiness of the thumb) in the area innervated by the median nerve distal to the carpal tunnel.

Ql0u9T.title: Progressive muscular dystrophies
Ql0u9T.description: A group of inherited disorders characterized by progressive weakness and atrophy of muscles. Examples include Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Becker muscular dystrophy, and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

jl0_9T.title: Myotonic syndromes
jl0_9T.description: A group of inherited disorders characterized by muscle fiber hyperexcitability. Myotonic dystrophies, the most prevalent among myotonic syndromes, are one of the most common forms of adult-onset muscular dystrophy.

4l03CT.title: Inborn errors of metabolism
4l03CT.description: A group of inherited genetic disorders characterized by enzyme defects and the subsequent accumulation of toxic substances in the body.

kl0mCT.title: Myasthenia gravis
kl0mCT.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular disease characterized by generalized muscle weakness. It most commonly affects adults between the third and fourth as well as the seventh and eighth decades of life. The pathophysiology involves autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AchR), which induce T-cell mediated destruction of those receptors.

Ol0ICT.title: Stiff person syndrome
Ol0ICT.description: A rare neurological disorder characterized by progressive rigidity and stiffness, primarily affecting the truncal muscles. The stiffness occurs in combination with muscle spasms, causing postural deformities.

ll0vCT.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
ll0vCT.description: A syndrome resulting from the combination of two neurological complications of thiamine (B1) deficiency – Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia) and chronic Korsakoff syndrome (selective anterograde and retrograde amnesia with preservation of long-term memory). Primarily affects individuals with alcohol use disorder.

Nl0-CT.title: Cerebellar syndromes
Nl0-CT.description: A characteristic set of symptoms associated with dysfunction of the cerebellum. Typical symptoms include ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements (dysmetria), dysarthria, and oculomotor disorders (e.g., nystagmus). Acute onset is considered a medical emergency and is usually due to stroke, hemorrhage, or cerebral edema. Chronic cerebellar syndromes are either acquired (e.g., alcoholism, tumors, paraneoplastic) or genetic.

ml0VxT.title: Ulnar nerve entrapment
ml0VxT.description: An impairment of ulnar nerve function caused by trauma or compression. Clinical features include hypoesthesia of the 5th and medial 4th fingers, weak thumb adduction (Froment sign), persistent 5th finger abduction (Wartenberg sign), and/or ulnar claw hand deformity. Common causes include cubital tunnel syndrome and ulnar tunnel syndrome.

5l0ixT.title: Radial nerve palsy
5l0ixT.description: Impairment of the radial nerve function due to damage or repeated/prolonged compression. Separated into "high" and "low" lesions. High lesions usually occur where the radial nerve is most vulnerable – at the level of the mid-humerus where it travels in the spiral groove (e.g., associated with wrist drop and sensory impairment). Low lesions occur from damage to the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), a branch of the radial nerve (e.g., associated with paralysis of the finger extensors).

Ml0MxT.title: Median nerve neuropathy
Ml0MxT.description: A nerve injury that usually occurs secondary to trauma and/or compression of the median nerve as it travels through the carpal tunnel. Manifestations include tingling and numbness over thumbs, index and middle finger, and radial side of the 4th finger. Patients can also develop thenar muscle atrophy and difficulty with index finger flexion and thumb movement.

media.title: Proximal and distal median nerve lesions

Ll0wxT.title: Neuralgic amyotrophy
Ll0wxT.description: Idiopathic inflammation of the brachial plexus. Patients present with severe, acute or subacute shoulder pain. Following pain resolution, which happens over days or weeks, the patient develops patchy weakness, sensory deficits, and/or paresthesias. These neurological deficits also resolve spontaneously after a few months.

ol00BT.title: Persistent vegetative state
ol00BT.description: A condition in which function of the cortex is impaired and function of the brainstem is preserved. Etiologies include traumatic brain injury and diffuse cerebral hypoxia. Patients can appear awake but are not aware or conscious, and they are unable to communicate with others or purposefully interact with their environment. Spontaneous breathing, sleep-wake cycles, and (at least partial) autonomic functions are preserved.

Kl0UBT.title: Locked-in syndrome
Kl0UBT.description: A neurologic disorder characterized by quadriplegia and bulbar or pseudobulbar palsy with preserved consciousness. Blinking and vertical eye movements are generally preserved. Caused by bilateral damage to the ventral pons, most often due to stroke.

6l0jBT.title: Lateral medullary syndrome
6l0jBT.description: A collection of neurological symptoms related to lateral medullary ischemia, secondary to interruption of flow (e.g., due to occlusion, vertebral artery dissection, embolus) in the vertebral artery and/or the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Symptoms may include ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia, dysphonia, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and facial paresthesia, and contralateral limb paresthesia.

pl0LBT.title: Complete spinal cord injury
pl0LBT.description: A spinal cord injury in which there is complete sensory and motor loss below the injured site. Typically manifests with spastic paresis, hyperreflexia, and continued sensory loss.

Jl0sBT.title: Horner syndrome
Jl0sBT.description: A neurologic disorder that causes a triad of miosis (an abnormally small pupil), partial ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid), and facial anhidrosis (absence of sweating). Caused by lesions that interrupt the sympathetic nervous supply (stellate ganglion). Most cases are idiopathic, but etiologies include brainstem stroke, carotid dissection, and neoplasm.

ql0CBT.title: Carotid-cavernous fistula
ql0CBT.description: An abnormal communication between the carotid artery and the cavernous sinus. Mostly caused by trauma. Characterized by diplopia, pulsatile tinnitus, proptosis, and headaches.

Il0YyT.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Il0YyT.description: A condition caused by dislodged otoliths in the semicircular canals that move through the endolymph, which stimulate the vestibular system and lead to sudden, short vertigo attacks that usually last for several seconds. Attacks are triggered by particular body or head movements such as lying down or turning the head quickly.

media.title: Receptive fields of the vestibular system
Cupulolithiasis and canalithiasis in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)

rl0fyT.title: Meniere disease
rl0fyT.description: An idiopathic condition characterized by impaired resorption of endolymphatic fluid, resulting in endolymphatic hydrops. Usually presents with episodes of vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus lasting from minutes to hours.

7l04yT.title: Vestibular neuritis
7l04yT.description: An idiopathic inflammation of the vestibular nerve. Typically manifests with acute-onset vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and gait instability with increased risk of falling to the affected side. Prognosis is good with vestibular rehabilitation therapy.

Hl0KyT.title: Migraine
Hl0KyT.description: A type of headache characterized by recurrent, debilitating episodes that are typically unilateral, throbbing or pulsatile in quality, and frequently accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound.

sl0tyT.title: Tension-type headache
sl0tyT.description: The most common type of headache. May be triggered by fatigue, lack of sleep, poor posture, anxiety, stress, depression. Typical pain is described as bilateral, band-like, or vice-like.

Gl0ByT.title: Cluster headache
Gl0ByT.description: A recurrent, sudden-onset, severe headache that is strictly unilateral and associated with ipsilateral symptoms of increased cranial autonomic activity (e.g., lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, partial Horner syndrome). Mostly affects adult men.

tl0XAT.title: Trigeminal neuralgia
tl0XAT.description: A condition that affects the trigeminal nerve and is characterized by excruciating shooting or stabbing facial pain followed by a burning ache. It is caused by either neurovascular compression from a neighboring vessel or nerve damage resulting from an underlying condition such as multiple sclerosis. Trigeminal neuralgia is managed conservatively with carbamazepine as the drug of choice.

8l0OAT.title: Dissection of the carotid and the vertebral artery
8l0OAT.description: A separation of the tunica media and tunica intima of either the carotid or vertebral arteries. Usually diagnosed by CT angiography.

destinations.label: Dissection of the carotid and the vertebral arteries

ul0pAT.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract
ul0pAT.description: Any structural abnormality of the urinary system (i.e., urethra, bladder, ureters, kidneys) present at birth. Includes ureteropelvic junction obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, duplex collecting system, and kidney malformation, such as renal agenesis, renal dysplasia, or renal hypoplasia; horseshoe kidney; and multicystic dysplastic kidney. May be detected incidentally on prenatal ultrasound or as a result of complications (e.g., severe and/or recurrent UTIs). Long-term complications include renal scarring, chronic hypertension, and end-stage renal disease.

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

vl0AAT.title: Urinary tract obstruction
vl0AAT.description: A blockage of urine passage anywhere along the urinary tract, from the renal papilla to the urethral meatus. Common causes include nephrolithiasis and prostatic hyperplasia. Can be asymptomatic (if mild) or manifest with acute abdominal pain, hydronephrosis, and/or acute kidney injury (if severe).

9l0N_T.title: Testicular torsion
9l0N_T.description: A condition in which the spermatic cord suddenly becomes twisted within the scrotum, which leads to venous engorgement that causes arterial compromise and irreversible damage if the torsion is not resolved after 6–12 hours.

Cl0q_T.title: Phimosis
Cl0q_T.description: A congenital or acquired constriction of the foreskin (prepuce) causing inability to retract it. Most cases occur secondary to balanoposthitis (inflammation of the foreskin and glans).

destinations.label: Disorders of the glans penis and foreskin → Phimosis

xl0E_T.title: Renal cell carcinoma
xl0E_T.description: A malignant tumor that arises from the renal tubular epithelium. Important risk factors include smoking, acquired cystic kidney disease, nephrolithiasis, and chronic acetaminophen use. Typical clinical features include hematuria, flank pain, a flank mass, anemia, weight loss, and possibly paraneoplastic manifestations (e.g., hypertension, hypercalcemia, or polycythemia).

Bl0z_T.title: Urothelial cancer
Bl0z_T.description: A malignant tumor originating in the mucosa of the urinary tract. Most common type is bladder cancer. Often an incidental finding, as the tumor is typically asymptomatic or associated with painless hematuria.

yl0dzT.title: Benign prostatic syndrome
yl0dzT.description: A collection of lower urinary tract symptoms caused by benign hyperplasia of the transitional zone of the prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia, or BPH). Clinical findings include irritative symptoms (i.e., urinary frequency, urinary urgency, urge incontinence, and dysuria) and obstructive symptoms (i.e., hesitancy, straining to urinate, poor and/or intermittent stream, prolonged terminal dribbling, and sensation of incomplete voiding).

Al0RzT.title: Prostate cancer
Al0RzT.description: The second most common cancer affecting American men following skin cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death in men following lung cancer. Arises most often from the posterior lobe of the prostate. Risk increases with age.

_l05zT.title: Testicular tumors
_l05zT.description: The most common solid malignancy in men 20-35 years of age. Classified as germ-cell tumors (seminomas, yolk sac tumors, teratomas, choriocarcinomas, and embryonal carcinomas), non-germ cell tumors (Leydig cell and Sertoli cell tumors), and lymphomas.

-l0DzT.title: Cystitis
-l0DzT.description: An inflammation of the bladder wall typically caused by a lower urinary tract infection. Less common causes include radiation or cyclophosphamide induced cystitis, interstitial cystitis, schistosomiasis, and tuberculosis.

ZN0Z-T.title: Pyelonephritis
ZN0Z-T.description: An infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma that is usually associated with an ascending bacterial infection of the bladder. Typically presents with flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, fever, and features of cystitis (e.g., dysuria, frequency).

0N0e-T.title: Perinephric abscess
0N0e-T.description: A localized infection of the perinephric space between the renal capsule and the Gerota fascia. Usually occurs as a complication of pyelonephritis or, less commonly, due to hematogenous spread. Manifests with abdominal pain and constitutional symptoms (e.g., fever, fatigue).

aN0Q-T.title: Prostatitis
aN0Q-T.description: An inflammation of the prostate gland. Can be of infectious origin (acute and chronic bacterial prostatitis) or noninfectious origin (chronic pelvic pain syndrome).

YN0n-T.title: Epididymitis
YN0n-T.description: An inflammation of the epididymis that is commonly caused by bacterial urinary tract infections or sexually transmitted infections.

bN0H-T.title: Urethritis
bN0H-T.description: An inflammation of the urethral mucosa, typically secondary to sexually transmitted infection. Clinical features include dysuria, burning or itching of the urethral meatus, urethral discharge, and initial hematuria. Can also be asymptomatic. Common causal organisms include C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhea.

WN0PZg.title: Priapism
WN0PZg.description: A penile erection lasting > 4 hours that continues hours beyond or is unrelated to sexual stimulation. Causes include treatment for erectile dysfunction, sickle cell disease, and trauma. Nonischemic priapism often self-resolves. Ischemic priapism is a medical emergency.

dN0oZg.title: Penile fracture
dN0oZg.description: A rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum with hematoma extravasation into the perineum. Typically secondary to blunt trauma to an erect penis. This is a urologic emergency that requires immediate surgical exploration.

VN0GZg.title: Urgency urinary incontinence
VN0GZg.description: A condition characterized by a sudden, strong need to urinate that results in the involuntary loss of urine. Considered a severe form of overactive bladder.

destinations.label: Overactive bladder and urgency urinary incontinence → Definitions

eN0xZg.title: Stress urinary incontinence
eN0xZg.description: A type of urinary incontinence characterized by the leakage of urine following activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing, sneezing). Caused by conditions in which an increase in bladder pressure exceeds sphincter resistance (e.g., pelvic floor weakness, intrinsic sphincter deficiency).

UN0b0g.title: Semen analysis
UN0b0g.description: A test to assess male fertility. Parameters tested include the number, morphology, and mobility of sperm, the semen volume, and the semen pH.

2N0T0g.title: Nephroblastoma
2N0T0g.description: The most common renal malignancy in children, typically affecting those 2–5 years of age. It is most commonly an incidental finding that presents as a large abdominal mass, sometimes associated with hematuria and abdominal pain, especially in tumors that are large, ruptured, or metastasized. A minority of cases are associated with specific syndromes (e.g., WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann) and gene mutations (e.g., WT1).

fN0k0g.title: Vesicoureteral reflux
fN0k0g.description: The retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter. May be primary, due to a congenital defect of the terminal portion of the ureter (most common), or secondary, e.g., due to bladder outlet obstruction, cystitis, or congenital ureteral anomalies. Patients are usually asymptomatic unless reflux sequelae are present such as urinary tract infections, hypertension, uremia, or kidney failure.

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

TN060g.title: Urinary incontinence
TN060g.description: The involuntary leakage of urine. Subtypes include stress, urgency, mixed, and overflow incontinence. Treatment options include medication (e.g. anticholinergics), surgery, and pelvic rehabilitation therapy.

gN0F0g.title: Proteinuria
gN0F0g.description: A condition of urinary protein excretion of > 150 mg/day. Classified as microproteinuria (≤ 300 mg/day) and overt proteinuria (> 300 mg/day). Can be caused by damage to the glomeruli (e.g., minimal change disease, diabetic nephropathy), damage to the tubules (e.g., Fanconi syndrome), or overproduction of proteins (e.g., multiple myeloma). Isolated (i.e. benign) proteinuria can occur in younger patients with fever or after heavy exercise.

3N0Sag.title: Chlorhexidine-based solution
3N0Sag.description: A solution used to disinfect the skin, e.g., prior to surgery. Disrupts the bacterial cell membrane and denatures proteins. Does not have a sporicidal effect.

jN0_ag.title: Dupuytren's contracture
jN0_ag.description: A fibroproliferative disorder of unclear etiology. It is characterized by nodules and cords in the palmar fascia which cause flexion contractures of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. The 4th and 5th digits are most commonly affected.

PN0WYg.title: Tenosynovitis
PN0WYg.description: Inflammation or thickening of a tendon and/or its synovial sheath. Most commonly affects the fingers, wrists, or feet. Often caused by tendon overuse (e.g., texting, typing, ballet) but can result from systemic disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis) or infection following a penetrating injury (e.g., animal or human bite, thorn prick injury). Typically manifests with edema and pain that worsens with activity or stretching of the tendon.

kN0mYg.title: Thoracic outlet syndrome
kN0mYg.description: An umbrella term for conditions involving the compression of neurovascular structures (e.g., the brachial plexus or the subclavian artery or vein) as they pass from the lower neck to the armpit. May be caused by trauma, tumors, or the presence of a cervical rib.

media.title: Thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to muscle hypertrophy or cervical rib
Thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to clavicle fracture

ON0IYg.title: Juvenile kyphosis
ON0IYg.description: A juvenile musculoskeletal condition in which uneven vertebral growth leads to thoracic kyphosis. This causes varying degrees of chronic neck and back pain, as well as a characteristic rounded upper back (hunchback).

NN0-Yg.title: Idiopathic scoliosis
NN0-Yg.description: A lateral curvature of the spine with a Cobb angle ≥ 10° on x-ray and no underlying organic cause. Simultaneous rotation of the involved vertebrae also occurs.

5N0ibg.title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
5N0ibg.description: A congenital deformation affecting either the femoral head, the acetabulum, or the supportive structures around them. Depending on the affected structures, it can cause hip instability, subluxation of the femoral head, hip dislocation, and/or acetabular dysplasia.

media.title: Early-onset osteoarthritis in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
Left hip dislocation in acetabular dysplasia

MN0Mbg.title: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
MN0Mbg.description: A self-limited, idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that typically affects children 4–10 years of age. Characterized by antalgic gait, restricted range of motion (especially internal rotation and abduction) of the affected hip, and pain in the hip, upper leg, and/or knee. Bilateral in 10-20% of patients.

nN07bg.title: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head
nN07bg.description: A necrosis of the head of the femur due to insufficient arterial supply. Can be idiopathic or result from corticosteroid therapy, smoking, heavy alcohol use, thrombophilic states (e.g., sickle cell anemia, myeloproliferative diseases), femoral neck fractures, hip dislocation, or pediatric hip disorders (e.g., slipped capital femoral epiphysis).

media.title: Bilateral avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head

LN0wbg.title: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
LN0wbg.description: A condition in which the shear forces on the proximal femur are stronger than the epiphyseal growth plate, resulting in superior and anterolateral displacement of the femoral neck. On x-ray, the epiphysis appears to "slip" from the femoral neck. The cause is unknown. The condition most commonly occurs in boys aged 10–16 years. Risk factors include obesity, endocrine disorders, and trauma.

media.title: Assessment of slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (slipped upper femoral epiphysis)

KN0UXg.title: Meniscus tear
KN0UXg.description: A rupture or tear to the meniscus. Categorized based on location and pattern. Injury to the inner, poorly vascularized region of the meniscus is more likely to require treatment than injury to the outer, well-vascularized region.

media.title: Meniscus tear - classification according to tear morphology
Horizontal tear of the medial meniscus

6N0jXg.title: Patellar dislocation
6N0jXg.description: Displacement of the patella out of the femoral trochlear groove, often laterally. Usually occurs following torsion of a semiflexed knee. May be associated with underlying biomechanical abnormalities, such as hyperlaxity of the medial patellofemoral ligament, high-riding patella, genu valgum, and/or patellofemoral dysplasia.

JN0sXg.title: Osteochondritis dissecans
JN0sXg.description: A focal, aseptic necrosis of cartilage and subchondral bone (most often the knee, elbow, or ankle) caused by mechanical stress and/or repetitive trauma. Can result in the detachment of bone-cartilage fragments that become displaced within in the joint space and cause pain and progressive joint stiffness.

rN0fcg.title: Avascular necrosis
rN0fcg.description: The death of bone tissue due to interruption of blood supply. Most cases are associated with alcohol use, corticosteroid therapy, or trauma.

media.title: Bilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral head

sN0tcg.title: Paget disease of bone
sN0tcg.description: A slowly progressive skeletal disease characterized by increased bone turnover. Causes normal lamellar bone to be replaced by weak, woven bone. Most likely genetic.

media.title: Paget disease of bone fact sheet

GN0Bcg.title: Insertional tendinopathy
GN0Bcg.description: An inflammation of tendon fibers caused by repetitive strain on tendons at their point of origin or insertion on a bone. Typically caused by overload or overuse injury and commonly occurs in athletes.

EN081g.title: Metal toxicity
EN081g.description: A toxicity caused by acute or chronic exposure to metals (e.g., lead, mercury, arsenic, gold). Symptoms vary by agent. Acute findings include gastrointestinal discomfort and nephrotoxicity. Chronic findings include abnormal physical development, cancer, and neuropathy. Treatments vary depending on the agent ingested and include dimercaprol, dimercaptosuccinic acid (succimer), and D-penicillamine.

DN01Wg.title: Organic solvent toxicity
DN01Wg.description: A spectrum of toxicities caused by chronic exposure to organic solvents (e.g., aromatic amines, hydrocarbons). Manifestations include mucocutaneous irritation, peripheral neuropathy, chronic toxic encephalopathy, and an increased risk of developing certain cancers.

9N0NWg.title: Rare pneumoconioses
