9N0NWg.description: A group of restrictive interstitial lung diseases caused by the inhalation of certain dusts. Often affects miners and agricultural workers. Asbestosis and silicosis are the most common types. Rare forms of pneumoconiosis include aluminosis, anthracosis, berylliosis, and pulmonary siderosis.

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Overview of pneumoconioses

0m0eVg.title: Otitis externa
0m0eVg.description: A condition of inflammation of the external auditory canal, which is most often the result of local bacterial infection. Risk factors include injury to the skin of the external auditory canal and/or exposure to water.

am0QVg.title: Chronic otitis media
am0QVg.description: A group of chronic inflammatory diseases of the middle ear. Includes chronic otitis media with effusion and chronic suppurative otitis media. More common in children than adults.

Ym0nVg.title: Acute otitis media
Ym0nVg.description: An infection of the middle ear that most commonly develops after an upper respiratory tract infection in children < 5 years of age. Most commonly caused by S. pneumoniae. Characterized by the acute onset of otalgia and fever. Examination typically shows a bulging tympanic membrane and effusions. Complications include acute mastoiditis (most common), facial palsy, labyrinthitis, and intracranial abscesses.

bm0HVg.title: Cholesteatoma
bm0HVg.description: A special form of chronic otitis media in which keratinizing squamous epithelium grows from the tympanic membrane or the auditory canal into the middle ear mucosa. Can be congenital or acquired later in life.

Xm09Vg.title: Glomus tumors
Xm09Vg.description: A type of rare, benign neoplasm that originates from glomus bodies in the skin, which are involved in temperature regulation. Most commonly manifest as a singular, paroxysmally painful, blue-red soft mass in the subungual regions of the digits or the deep dermis of the palm, wrist, forearm, and foot.

Wm0Peg.title: Noise-induced hearing loss
Wm0Peg.description: A type of sensorineural hearing loss caused by damage to the stereocilia of cochlear hair cells due to exposure to loud sound. Repeated exposure to sounds louder than 85 dB (or even a single exposure to sounds greater than 140 dB) can cause injury.

Vm0Geg.title: Epistaxis
Vm0Geg.description: A condition of bleeding from the nose. Causes include trauma, mucosal irritation or inflammation, hemostatic disorders, and telangiectasias. Typically self-limited but can cause significant blood loss in rare cases.

media.title: Arterial supply of the nasal septum

em0xeg.title: Sinusitis
em0xeg.description: An inflammation of the mucous membrane of the paranasal sinuses that usually occurs concurrently with inflammation of the nasal mucosa (rhinitis). Therefore, concurrence of the two conditions is commonly referred to as rhinosinusitis. Although viral etiologies are most common, bacterial and fungal pathogens can also cause sinusitis.

2m0TUg.title: Rhinitis
2m0TUg.description: The inflammation of the nasal mucosa. Etiologies include nonallergic rhinitis, type I hypersensitivity reaction (allergic rhinitis), and upper respiratory tract infection (infectious rhinitis or rhinosinusitis). Clinical manifestations include nasal congestion, sneezing, rhinorrhea, and post-nasal drip.

Tm06Ug.title: Acute tonsillitis
Tm06Ug.description: An inflammation of the pharyngeal tonsils. It frequently arises in combination with inflammation of the pharynx; for this reason, the terms tonsillitis and pharyngitis are often used interchangeably or in combination (tonsillopharyngitis). It is commonly caused by viruses and group A streptococci.

hm0c2g.title: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
hm0c2g.description: A locally invasive, benign vascular tumor which originates from the region of the middle turbinate in the nose; classically seen in adolescent males.

im0J2g.title: Laryngeal carcinoma
im0J2g.description: A malignant tumor (most commonly a squamous cell carcinoma) arising from the supraglottic, glottic, or subglottic region of the larynx. Risk factors include tobacco and alcohol use.

Pm0Wfg.title: Sjogren syndrome
Pm0Wfg.description: A chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of glandular and nonglandular organs, leading to cell death. Most commonly manifests with sicca syndrome but can also manifest with systemic symptoms such as arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and GI involvement.

4m03fg.title: Speech and language disorder
4m03fg.description: A delayed and/or impaired ability to articulate language (e.g., due to distortion of speech sound, rate, rhythm, pitch, and/or loudness). Further subdivided into articulation disorders, fluency disorders, and voice disorders.

lm0vfg.title: Amyloidosis
lm0vfg.description: The extracellular deposition of abnormal, insoluble proteins in tissues. Further divided into localized (single organ) and systemic (throughout the body) forms.

mm0VTg.title: Major depressive disorder
mm0VTg.description: An episodic mood disorder that is characterized by depressed mood and/or anhedonia for at least 2 weeks. Additional symptoms include sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia), feelings of guilt/worthlessness, fatigue/loss of energy, diminished concentration/ability to think/make decisions, changes in appetite, psychomotor agitation/retardation, and suicidal ideation. Substance use, underlying medical condition, bipolar disorder, and psychosis must be excluded before making the diagnosis of MDD.

5m0iTg.title: Bipolar affective disorder
5m0iTg.description: A psychiatric condition characterized by episodes of mania (or hypomania) and major depression, interspersed with periods of normal mood and functioning.

Mm0MTg.title: Phobia
Mm0MTg.description: A persistent, irrational fear of an object or situation, triggered by its presence or the anticipation of it.

nm07Tg.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
nm07Tg.description: A psychiatric disorder characterized by obsessions (recurrent and intrusive thoughts or urges) that cause significant distress and/or by compulsions (behaviors or mental acts to alleviate anxiety caused by obsessions or to prevent an unwanted event). Treatment includes cognitive behavioral therapy and/or SSRIs.

Lm0wTg.title: Trauma- and stressor-related disorders
Lm0wTg.description: A group of psychiatric disorders that arise following a stressful or traumatic event. Includes acute stress disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and adjustment disorder. Treatment involves psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy.

om00gg.title: Dissociative disorders
om00gg.description: A group of psychiatric conditions characterized by disruption and/or discontinuity of normal consciousness, memory, identity, and perception. Includes dissociative identity disorder, dissociative amnesia (with or without dissociative fugue), and depersonalization disorder.

Km0Ugg.title: Child maltreatment
Km0Ugg.description: Any act or failure to act that results in potential or actual harm to a child, usually involving a caregiver. Types of child maltreatment include neglect, physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological maltreatment, and medical child abuse.

destinations.label: Ethics of communicating medical information → Reporting

pm0Lgg.title: Personality disorders
pm0Lgg.description: A class of mental disorders that are characterized by rigid, abnormal patterns of thinking and behavior that result in impaired function (cognition, mood, interpersonal relationships, impulse control) and may cause significant distress. Onset typically occurs in late childhood or early adolescence. Examples include borderline personality disorder, antisocial personality disorder, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder.

Jm0sgg.title: Borderline personality disorder
Jm0sgg.description: A cluster B personality disorder characterized by the inability to maintain interpersonal relationships, impulsivity without regard for consequences, and a distorted self-image. Patients typically experience affective and behavioral dysregulation.

Im0YSg.title: Alcohol use disorder
Im0YSg.description: A pattern of alcohol use that causes significant physical and psychosocial impairment or distress. Alcohol abuse and dependence were separate substance use disorders according to DSM-IV, but these were combined into a single diagnosis of alcohol use disorder in DSM-5.

media.title: Changes in liver metabolism due to risky alcohol use

7m04Sg.title: Schizophrenia
7m04Sg.description: A psychiatric disorder that commonly causes hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking/speech, disorganized behavior, and social withdrawal. Patients are at high risk for suicide. Usually, schizophrenia manifests in the late teens to early twenties (later in women). Symptoms must be present for longer than 6 months. First-line treatment involves antipsychotic medications.

Hm0KSg.title: Autism spectrum disorder
Hm0KSg.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent impairment in social interaction and communication and restricted stereotyped patterns of behavior, interests, and activities.

sm0tSg.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
sm0tSg.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impulsivity, hyperactivity, and inattention, with impairment of social, occupational, and/or academic performance. A diagnosis of ADHD requires that symptoms first appear before 12 years of age, be present for ≥ 6 months, and occur in ≥ 2 settings (e.g., school and home).

Gm0BSg.title: Elimination disorders
Gm0BSg.description: A group of psychiatric disorders that manifest in childhood or adolescence as repeated voiding of urine or defecation that is inappropriate for the developmental age. Management strategies include psychoeducation, behavioral training, and pharmacologic treatment.

tm0Xhg.title: Tic disorder
tm0Xhg.description: A neurological condition characterized by sudden, rapid, and involuntary movements and/or vocalizations. Primary tic disorders begin in childhood and include provisional tic disorder, Tourette syndrome, and persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder. Secondary tics may result from a medical condition (e.g., brain lesions, brain injury, neurodegenerative disease) or substance use.

Fm0ghg.title: Anorexia nervosa
Fm0ghg.description: An eating disorder characterized by restricted energy intake, resulting in significantly low body weight. Typically accompanied by a pathological fear of weight gain, distorted body image, and/or behaviors that prevent weight gain such as exercising excessively.

8m0Ohg.title: Sleep disorders
8m0Ohg.description: A category of disorders that affect the sleep-wake cycle. Can be primary (due to an intrinsic problem with the sleep-wake cycle) or secondary (due to an underlying condition). Primary sleep disorders are further divided into dyssomnias or parasomnias. Symptoms include difficulty falling asleep, difficulty remaining asleep, or abnormal behavior during sleep.

um0phg.title: Suicidality
um0phg.description: Feelings of suicidal ideation or intent, indicating a risk of suicide.

Dm013g.title: Livor mortis
Dm013g.description: A postmortem discoloration of the skin due to pooling of blood in gravity-dependent areas.

wm0h3g.title: Rigor mortis
wm0h3g.description: A stiffening of the muscles after death. Caused by persistent attachment of actin and myosin due to lack of ATP. Begins within 1-4 hours after death and begins to resolve ~ 24 hours after death (due to decomposition).

Bm0z3g.title: Drowning
Bm0z3g.description: Respiratory impairment and/or the sensation of respiratory distress caused by submersion or immersion in a liquid, most commonly a body of water. Complications include respiratory distress, hypoxia, cardiac arrest, and brain injury.

_m05Rg.title: Thermal injuries
_m05Rg.description: A localized injury (e.g., burn, frostbite) caused by exposure to extreme hot (e.g., fire, hot liquid) or cold temperatures (e.g., freezing conditions).

zm0rRg.title: Factitious disorder
zm0rRg.description: A psychiatric condition in which patients intentionally falsify signs and symptoms in order to assume the role of a sick patient (primary gain). Associated with a history of significant exposure to health care and personality disorders.

destinations.label: Somatic symptom and related disorders → Factitious disorders

-m0DRg.title: Neonate
-m0DRg.description: A child under 28 days of age.

050eig.title: Short stature
050eig.description: A condition defined as height that is at least two standard deviations below the mean for children of the same age and sex. In adults, the condition is commonly defined as a height of 5'1'' (155 cm) or less in men and 4'10″ (147 cm) or less in women.

Y50nig.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Y50nig.description: A group of autosomal recessive defects in enzymes that are responsible for cortisol, aldosterone, and androgen synthesis. Characterized by low levels of cortisol, high levels of ACTH, and adrenal hyperplasia. The most common form (caused by a deficiency of 21β-hydroxylase) presents with hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, ambiguous genitalia and virilization (in females), and/or precocious puberty (in both males and females).

b50Hig.title: TORCH infections
b50Hig.description: An acronym for the most common vertically transmitted infections associated with congenital anomalies: Toxoplasmosis, Other (varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus infection (CMV), Herpes infections, HIV infection, and Syphilis.

X509ig.title: Teratogenic birth defects
X509ig.description: A set of permanent structural or functional malformations of a fetus or embryo caused by environmental factors (i.e., teratogens). Possible teratogens are maternal illnesses (e.g., diabetes mellitus, thyroid disorders), toxic substances (e.g., alcohol, nicotine, medications, metals), and radiation.

1502Qg.title: Trisomy 21
1502Qg.description: A common autosomal chromosome aberration characterized by the presence of three copies of chromosome 21. Risk increases with increased maternal age. Causes a characteristic appearance that includes upward-slanting palpebral fissures and a single transverse palmar crease, organ malformations (e.g., heart defects, duodenal stenosis, and a hypoplastic thyroid), and intellectual disability.

media.title: Common facial and cranial features of Down Syndrome

d50oQg.title: Sudden infant death syndrome
d50oQg.description: The sudden, unexpected death of a child < 1 year of age in which the cause of death remains unexplained after a complete postmortem examination. Usually presumed to have occurred during sleep.

media.title: Safe sleep practices to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome

V50GQg.title: Craniosynostosis
V50GQg.description: A condition characterized by the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures. Caused by a mutation in genes that code for fibroblast growth factor. Most affected infants are asymptomatic. Diagnosis is clinical, although imaging can help assess the extent of disease. Treated with surgery.

e50xQg.title: Birth traumas
e50xQg.description: A group of injuries to the newborn caused by mechanical forces during birth. Includes soft tissue injuries (e.g., benign cephalohematoma, caput succedaneum), musculoskeletal injuries (e.g., torticollis, clavicle fracture), and nerve damage (e.g., brachial plexus injury, facial nerve palsy).

U50bjg.title: Perinatal asphyxia
U50bjg.description: A condition of oxygen deprivation that occurs near the time of birth. Etiologies include maternal hypoventilation or hypotension, placental insufficiency, and knotting of the umbilical cord. Symptoms range from irritability and poor feeding to lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures, and death. Common complications include developmental delays and cerebral palsy.

destinations.label: Perinatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy → Definitions

250Tjg.title: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
250Tjg.description: A syndrome seen in premature infants that is characterized by pulmonary surfactant deficiency, resulting in alveolar collapse. Typically manifests with signs of increased breathing effort (e.g., tachypnea, nasal flaring) and cyanosis, and may lead to severe complications such as severe respiratory insufficiency and cardiovascular arrest.

f50kjg.title: Neonatal jaundice
f50kjg.description: A common neonatal condition characterized by a serum bilirubin concentration > 5 mg/dL. Most commonly caused by increased unconjugated bilirubin (e.g., from hemolysis of fetal hemoglobin, immature hepatic metabolism of bilirubin). If severe, it can result in drowsiness, failure to thrive, and neurologic damage (kernicterus).

T506jg.title: Hemolytic disease of the newborn
T506jg.description: A condition characterized by the destruction of fetal red blood cells (RBC) and anemia. Most frequently caused by Rhesus (more severe) or ABO incompatibility (milder) between the mother and fetus, leading to immune-mediated hemolysis in the fetus/neonate. Newborn infants may present with pallor, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly. In severe cases, intrauterine hydrops fetalis develops.

destinations.label: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

g50Fjg.title: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn
g50Fjg.description: A bleeding disorder of newborns caused by a deficiency of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors that manifests with spontaneous bleeding (e.g., intracranial, subgaleal, gastrointestinal, or nasal bleeds.

destinations.label: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn

S50yjg.title: Acyanotic congenital heart defects
S50yjg.description: A group of heart anomalies that result in left-to-right shunting. The most common include ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus.

media.title: Cardiac hemodynamics in patent ductus arteriosus
Cardiac hemodynamics in atrial septal defect
Cardiac hemodynamics in ventricular septal defect

h50cPg.title: Choanal atresia
h50cPg.description: A congenital condition characterized by a bony and/or membranous obstruction of the posterior nasal passage. Unilateral choanal atresia often presents late with chronic inflammation (e.g., rhinorrhea, congestion) of the affected nasal passage. Bilateral choanal atresia manifests as obstructed nasal breathing with intermittent cyanosis immediately after birth; breathing improves when crying, as it allows the infant to breathe through his or her mouth.

R50lPg.title: Cystic fibrosis
R50lPg.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, which leads to defective chloride channels and hyperviscosity of exocrine gland secretions. Can result in meconium ileus, chronic respiratory infections leading to bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, and obstructive azoospermia in males. Associated with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.

i50JPg.title: Necrotizing enterocolitis
i50JPg.description: A dangerous hemorrhagic inflammation of the intestinal wall that is caused by impaired bowel perfusion and defective immunity. It most often affects premature infants. The pathognomonic finding on abdominal x-ray is pneumatosis intestinalis.

media.title: Pneumatosis intestinalis and free air in necrotizing enterocolitis

Q50uPg.title: Esophageal atresia
Q50uPg.description: A congenital obstruction of the esophagus caused by abnormal tracheoesophageal septum development. The most common type is Gross type C atresia (esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula). In this condition, the esophagus is not connected to the stomach and ends in a blind-ended pouch, from which the ingested fluids overflow into the trachea via the fistula.

j50_Pg.title: Duodenal atresia and stenosis
j50_Pg.description: A congenital malformation with complete occlusion or absence of the duodenal lumen. Associated with chromosomal abnormalities, especially Down syndrome, in 30% of cases. Manifests in neonates with a distended upper abdomen, delayed meconium passage, bilious vomiting, and a double bubble sign on x-ray.

destinations.label: Congenital visceral malformations → Duodenal atresia and stenosis

P50W4g.title: Congenital visceral malformations
P50W4g.description: A group of abnormalities that can occur during organogenesis; malformations can occur in isolation or in association with other malformations. Includes anal atresia, omphalocele, gastroschisis, and biliary atresia.

45034g.title: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
45034g.description: A condition of hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric sphincter that typically manifests in the first months of life with postprandial, projectile, nonbilious vomiting. A mass measuring 1–2 cm may be palpable in the epigastrium. Diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasonography, which shows pyloric thickening.

k50m4g.title: Hirschsprung disease
k50m4g.description: An inherited disorder primarily affecting newborns. Caused by failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the distal colon during the 4-7th week of development. Characterized by an aganglionic colon segment, usually the rectosigmoid region, which fails to relax, leading to functional intestinal obstruction.

media.title: Gaseous distention of multiple loops of bowel

O50I4g.title: Chickenpox
O50I4g.description: A primary infection with varicella zoster virus that occurs most frequently during childhood and causes a characteristic itchy rash, with macules that rapidly develop into papules and then vesicles.

N50-4g.title: Rubella
N50-4g.description: Infectious disease caused by the rubella virus. Symptoms may include nonspecific flu-like symptoms, post-auricular and/or suboccipital lymphadenopathy, and a rash that typically starts behind the ears and progresses distally, developing into a generalized maculopapular exanthem.

media.title: Congenital rubella infection TORCH fact sheet

m50Vkg.title: Mumps
m50Vkg.description: A highly contagious viral infection that is spread via droplet transmission. Classically manifests with parotitis, low-grade fever, malaise, headache, and possibly swelling of other salivary glands or orchitis in post-pubertal male individuals.

550ikg.title: Roseola infantum
550ikg.description: An infectious disease most commonly caused by human herpesvirus 6 in children < 2 years. Characterized by abrupt onset and resolution of high fever lasting ~ 3 days, followed by the sudden manifestation of a patchy, nonpruritic rash with macules and papules that starts on the trunk and sometimes spreads to the face and extremities.

M50Mkg.title: Erythema infectiosum
M50Mkg.description: A clinical syndrome caused by parvovirus B19 infection. Symptoms initially include mild febrile illness followed by a rash with macules and papules that occurs several days later on the cheeks before spreading to the trunk and extremities. Can also cause a self-limited, symmetrical, nondestructive polyarthritis, which is more commonly seen in infected adults.

destinations.label: Parvovirus B19 infections → Subtypes and variants

n507kg.title: Poliomyelitis
n507kg.description: An infectious disease caused by poliovirus. 90 to 95% of cases are asymptomatic. In 1% of cases, the virus can enter the CNS and cause severe muscle weakness or paralysis. Both bulbar and spinal regions can be affected. Death occurs in 5 to 10% of patients with paralytic polio and is typically caused by paralysis of the respiratory muscles. Thanks to the polio vaccine, this disease has almost been eradicated.

L50wkg.title: Scarlet fever
L50wkg.description: An acute syndrome caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, a highly contagious, toxin-producing group A Streptococcus. Most commonly occurs in children. Manifests with fever, pharyngeal erythema, flushed cheeks with perioral pallor, strawberry tongue, and an erythematous rash with sandpaper-like texture.

o500Og.title: Pertussis
o500Og.description: A respiratory illness caused by Bordetella pertussis that is characterized by paroxysmal coughing with a distinctive whooping sound. Typically a childhood disease. Prophylaxis is provided by the DTaP vaccine (< 7 years of age) or Tdap vaccine (≥ 7 years of age).

K50UOg.title: Coxsackievirus infection
K50UOg.description: A group of infections caused by coxsackieviruses. Can manifest with flu-like illness and cause various conditions, including hand, foot, and mouth disease, meningitis, encephalitis, and respiratory illness (e.g., pneumonia). Mainly transmitted through fecal-oral spread and airborne droplets.

650jOg.title: Asplenia
650jOg.description: A term that can refer to anatomical asplenia (i.e., postsurgical resection) or functional asplenia (e.g., secondary to sickle cell disease). Due to an increased risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria, immunization against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B is recommended for patients with asplenia.

p50LOg.title: Febrile seizure
p50LOg.description: A seizure that occurs in children aged 6 months to 5 years and is associated with fever in the absence of CNS infection, metabolic abnormalities, or a history of afebrile seizures. The exact pathophysiology is unknown. Most febrile seizures end spontaneously and do not require any treatment.

J50sOg.title: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
J50sOg.description: A broad term referring to childhood rheumatic diseases that begin before the age of 16 and involve joint inflammation lasting more than six weeks. Classified into various types based on the pattern of joint involvement, the presence of extra-articular manifestations (e.g., uveitis, rashes, nail changes, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly), laboratory findings, and disease prognosis.

media.title: Pattern of joint involvement and iridocyclitis in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)
Systemic-, psoriatic-, and enthesitis-related juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)

q50COg.title: Neuroblastoma
q50COg.description: A malignant neuroendocrine tumor of the sympathetic nervous system that originates from neural crest cells. Primarily affects children and infants. Composed of blastematous, stromal, and/or epithelial components. Diagnosed by increased urinary catecholamines.

I50Ylg.title: Retinoblastoma
I50Ylg.description: An intraocular malignancy that typically manifests during childhood with leukocoria (white fundal reflex instead of the usual red) and strabismus. Associated with loss of heterozygosity of the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor gene (RB1).

r50flg.title: Atopic dermatitis
r50flg.description: An inflammatory skin condition that most commonly manifests in early childhood and can persist into adulthood. Risk factors include personal and/or family history of atopy, genetic mutations in the filaggrin gene, and environmental factors. Major clinical features include a chronic and/or relapsing course, intense pruritus, and typical eczematous skin lesions that follow age-specific distribution patterns (e.g, face and extensor surfaces in infants and flexural surfaces and creases in older individuals). Triggers (e.g., heat, dry climate, skin irritation) can exacerbate and/or induce flares.

H50Klg.title: Molluscum contagiosum
H50Klg.description: A skin infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (a DNA poxvirus). Typically manifests with multiple, benign, nontender, skin-colored, pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Common in young children and adolescents. Usually self-limited but can be widespread and persistent in immunocompromised individuals.

s50tlg.title: Pityriasis versicolor
s50tlg.description: A benign, superficial skin infection most commonly caused by the yeast species Malassezia furfur and Malassezia globosa. Particularly common in hot, humid climates and in individuals with hyperhidrosis. Manifests as a well-demarcted macules that may be hyperpigmented, hypopigmented, or erythematous with a fine scale. The rash may be more noticeable in summer as the macules fail to tan.

G50Blg.title: Erythrasma
G50Blg.description: A superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum that causes scaly, pruritic, hyperpigmented, or erythematous patches that typically appear in intertriginous areas.

t50XNg.title: Impetigo
t50XNg.description: A highly contagious skin infection of the upper layers of the epidermis. Most common skin infection in children. Nonbullous impetigo (70%) is caused by S. aureus or Group A streptococci and presents with small vesicles, pustules, and/or honey-colored crusts on an erythematous base, along with regional lymphadenopathy. Bullous impetigo (30%) is caused by S. aureus and presents with flaccid, intraepidermal bullae on a non-erythematous base.

F50gNg.title: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
F50gNg.description: A blistering skin disorder caused by exfoliative toxins produced by S. aureus following a local infection (e.g., pharyngitis, bullous impetigo). Typically affects children < 6 years. Fever and diffuse, tender erythema occur, followed by extensive flaccid intraepidermal blisters and sloughing off of the superficial layer of skin to reveal moist, red tissue underneath, giving the area a "scalded” appearance. Mucous membranes are typically spared.

850ONg.title: Scabies
850ONg.description: A parasitic skin infestation caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, primarily transmitted through direct and prolonged contact with an affected individual. Manifests with erythematous, pruritic papules, scattered vesicles, and thin, curvilinear burrow tracks, especially on the wrists and interdigital folds.

u50pNg.title: Lice infestation
u50pNg.description: The presence of at least one viable louse on the head (head lice infestation), or nits and/or lice on clothing (body lice infestation), pubic area (pubic lice infestation), or eyelashes (eyelash lice infestation).

media.title: Developmental stages of the body louse

E508Ng.title: Photodermatoses
E508Ng.description: A group of skin conditions that develop as a result of increased sensitivity to ultraviolet radiation. Causes can be primary (e.g., immune-mediated, drug or chemical induced) or secondary (e.g., genetic). Characterized by an erythematous, painful, pruritic photodistributed rash.

v50ANg.title: Seborrheic dermatitis
v50ANg.description: An inflammatory skin condition that affects areas with high sebaceous activity (e.g., scalp). The exact pathophysiology is unknown but contributing factors include microbial colonization of the skin (esp. Malassezia), immunological factors, climate, and stress. Presents with symptomatic flares (e.g., with itching, burning) alternating with asymptomatic periods. Examination typically shows erythematous patches or plaques with scaling and greasy yellow crusts.

w50hmg.title: Angioedema
w50hmg.description: A self-limited, localized swelling of the dermis, subcutaneous tissues, and/or submucosal tissues caused by fluid leakage into the interstitial tissue. Mediated by vasoactive substances and can be classified as either mast cell-mediated (often secondary to allergic reactions and NSAIDs), bradykinin-mediated (due to ACE inhibitor use or enzyme deficiencies), or idiopathic. Life-threatening laryngeal edema may occur and requires immediate airway protection.

950Nmg.title: Erythema multiforme
950Nmg.description: A rare, acute type IV hypersensitivity reaction triggered by certain infections (e.g., Mycoplasma pneumoniae, herpes simplex virus, SARS-CoV-2), medications (e.g., sulfonamides), or vaccines (e.g., influenza vaccine). Manifests as a polymorphic rash that develops into target lesions. Disease severity ranges from minimal mucosal involvement and localized lesions (erythema multiforme minor) to severe mucosal involvement and extensive lesions with or without systemic symptoms (erythema multiforme major).

C50qmg.title: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
C50qmg.description: A genetic disorder caused by mutations in the genes controlling the synthesis of collagen. There can be a wide range of clinical features depending on the specific mutation, but the classical presentation involves hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, and a tendency to bleed.

destinations.label: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome → Summary

B50zmg.title: Ichthyosis
B50zmg.description: A heterogeneous group of skin conditions characterized by dry and scaly skin due to impaired keratinization.

y50d5g.title: Autoimmune blistering diseases
y50d5g.description: A group of skin conditions characterized by autoimmune destruction of cellular or extracellular adhesion molecules that causes blisters. The three most common autoimmune blistering diseases are bullous pemphigoid, pemphigus vulgaris, and dermatitis herpetiformis.

A50R5g.title: Pityriasis rosea
A50R5g.description: A self-limited pruritic rash. Manifests as a single ovoid macule (herald patch) followed by a secondary eruption of multiple scaly papules distributed in a classic Christmas tree pattern on the trunk. Typically resolves within 6-12 weeks.

_5055g.title: Psoriasis
_5055g.description: A common, chronic inflammatory skin disorder that typically manifests as sharply demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of the knees and elbows but can also affect the scalp and back. Other common clinical findings include nail pitting and arthritis.

z50r5g.title: Parapsoriasis
z50r5g.description: A large group of idiopathic cutaneous diseases characterized by asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, erythematous, scaly patches with a chronic course. Includes large and small plaque parapsoriasis. Treatment includes topical steroid therapy and phototherapy.

-50D5g.title: Paraneoplastic syndrome
-50D5g.description: A set of clinical features that are caused by either an altered immune response to a systemic malignancy or by substances produced by tumors (e.g., hormones, cellular proteins).

ZM0ZMg.title: Xanthomas
ZM0ZMg.description: A nodular, papular, or planar lesion formed by the deposition of lipids in skin, subcutaneous tissue, and/or tendons. Typically pink or yellow in color and occur together with primary or secondary hyperlipidemia and histiocytic disorders.

0M0eMg.title: Porphyrias
0M0eMg.description: A group of inherited or (rarely) acquired metabolic disorders in which defective enzymes impair the biosynthesis of heme in the liver and/or bone marrow. All porphyrias are characterized by the accumulation of porphyrin, or intermediates of its biosynthesis, which can cause a variety of symptoms depending on the organs involved (e.g., skin, liver, CNS). Specific forms include porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) and acute intermittent porphyria (AIP).

YM0nMg.title: Acne vulgaris
YM0nMg.description: A chronic skin condition characterized by noninflammatory comedones and/or inflammatory skin lesions (e.g., papules, pustules, nodules, and/or cysts). Lesions are often located on the face, shoulders, upper chest, and back. Most commonly affects adolescents and young adults.

bM0HMg.title: Rosacea
bM0HMg.description: A chronic inflammatory skin disease that may be exacerbated by various triggers (e.g., heat, alcohol). Clinical features include central facial erythema, papules and pustules, and telangiectasias. Severe cases include phymatous changes (e.g., skin thickening, enlarged pores) due to underlying inflammation.

dM0ong.title: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
dM0ong.description: A slow-growing, locally destructive malignant cancer of the skin that arises from keratinocytes in the stratum spinosum of the epidermis. Typically manifests as a painless, ulcerated lesion with everted edges.

VM0Gng.title: Basal cell carcinoma
VM0Gng.description: A slow-growing, locally invasive malignant neoplasm of the skin that arises from basal epithelial cells. Most common type of skin cancer. Typically develops in sun-exposed areas as a pearly, indurated, nodular, nontender lesion with a rolled border and central ulceration.

eM0xng.title: Vitiligo
eM0xng.description: A benign skin condition characterized by well-demarcated macules and patches of complete depigmentation. Believed to be caused by autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, oxidative stress, and/or intrinsic melanocyte defects in genetically predisposed individuals.

UM0bLg.title: Gonorrhea
UM0bLg.description: A sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Most commonly manifests as an infection of the genitourinary tract, e.g., urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, or epididymitis.

2M0TLg.title: Syphilis
2M0TLg.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Treponema pallidum. The disease has 4 clinical stages, with primary syphilis typically manifesting with a painless chancre on the genitals.

TM06Lg.title: Alopecia
TM06Lg.description: The loss of hair from any hair-bearing area of the body (most often the scalp). Can be congenital or acquired, circumscribed or diffuse, and scarring (cicatricial) or nonscarring. Androgenetic alopecia is the most common type.

gM0FLg.title: Erythema nodosum
gM0FLg.description: A type of panniculitis that manifests with the sudden onset of painful, subcutaneous nodules on the anterior aspect of the lower legs. Often idiopathic but can also be caused by infections, pregnancy, drugs, autoimmune disease, and malignancies.

iM0Jog.title: Androgen insensitivity syndrome
iM0Jog.description: A disorder of sexual development caused by an X-linked recessive loss of function mutation in the gene encoding the androgen receptor. Patients are karyotypically male (XY). Complete androgen insensitivity results in female external genitalia at birth and breast development during puberty. However primary amenorrhea and infertility occur (atretic uterus and blind vaginal pouch), body and pubic hair are absent, and undescended testes are present. A partial form of the disease may result in ambiguous external genitalia at birth and variable degrees of virilization during puberty.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Androgen insensitivity syndrome

PM0WKg.title: Mastitis
PM0WKg.description: Inflammation of the breast parenchyma that most commonly manifests with breast pain, swelling, warmth, and redness. May or may not result in infection (e.g., due to Staphylococcus aureus). Mastitis is classified as either puerperal (i.e., in lactating individuals) or nonpuerperal.

4M03Kg.title: Breast cancer
4M03Kg.description: A malignancy that originates in breast tissue (either ductal or lobular tissue). The most common malignancy in women. Treatment approach depends on the histopathologic classification and the disease stage and involves a combination of surgical management, radiation therapy, and systemic therapy.

kM0mKg.title: Uterine leiomyoma
kM0mKg.description: A benign, hormone-sensitive smooth muscle tumor of the uterus that arises from a single myometrial cell and can be submucosal, intramural, or subserosal. It causes upregulation of hormone receptors and excessive production of extracellular matrix (hence "fibroids"), resulting in an overgrowth of smooth muscle cells and connective tissue. The myometrium also develops vascular changes (e.g., increased arterioles and venules, dilated veins).

OM0IKg.title: Endometriosis
OM0IKg.description: A chronic condition characterized by growth of benign endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, e.g., on the peritoneal surface, ovaries, fallopian tubes, rectouterine pouch, bowel, and/or bladder. Symptoms include chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, abnormal uterine bleeding, and infertility.

lM0vKg.title: Invasive cervical cancer
lM0vKg.description: Malignant neoplasia of the ectocervix and/or endocervix (most commonly squamous cell carcinoma), which is often associated with HPV infections.

media.title: Pathophysiology of the development of cervical cancer

NM0-Kg.title: Endometrial cancer
NM0-Kg.description: The most common cancer of the female genital tract in the US. It is classified into 2 types: Type I comprises endometrioid adenocarcinomas and is related to long-term unopposed estrogen exposure. Type II comprises tumors of nonendometrioid histology (serous, clear cell, mucinous, etc) that are estrogen independent and are associated with p53 mutations.

mM0V6g.title: Ovarian tumors
mM0V6g.description: A tumor arising from the ovaries. Ovarian tumors are the most common ovarian mass in women > 55 years of age.

5M0i6g.title: Vulvar cancer
5M0i6g.description: A rare carcinoma (most frequently squamous cell carcinoma) that predominantly occurs after menopause. Risk factors include HPV infection and the presence of precursor lesions (e.g., lichen sclerosus). Manifestations include vulvar pruritus and the formation of one or more lesions (e.g., plaques or masses).

destinations.label: Vulvar and vaginal cancer → Vulvar cancer

MM0M6g.title: Pregnancy
MM0M6g.description: A process that begins with fertilization of the ovum and subsequent implantation into the uterine wall. The duration of pregnancy is counted in weeks of gestation from the first day of the last menstrual period and on average lasts 40 weeks.

media.title: Overview of the 1st week of pregnancy and embryogenesis

nM076g.title: Hypertensive pregnancy disorders
nM076g.description: A group of disorders characterized by elevated blood pressure during pregnancy. Includes chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and eclampsia.

LM0w6g.title: Placental abruption
LM0w6g.description: A premature separation of a normally implanted placenta before the delivery of the fetus. Patients typically manifest with abdominal pain, antepartum hemorrhage during the third trimester, and/or features of shock (if antepartum hemorrhage is severe).

media.title: Types of hemorrhage in placental abruption

oM00pg.title: Gestational trophoblastic disease
oM00pg.description: A spectrum of diseases in pregnancy that are caused by a proliferation of trophoblasts within the uterus. Includes partial and complete hydatidiform moles (benign placental tumors with malignant potential) and gestational trophoblastic neoplasias (placental tumors with malignant behavior), such as invasive moles, postmolar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, gestational choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumors, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors.

KM0Upg.title: Ectopic pregnancy
KM0Upg.description: A pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum is implanted in a location other than the endometrium, most commonly the fallopian tube. Symptoms include amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Can rupture and result in life-threatening intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

JM0spg.title: Uterine rupture
JM0spg.description: A life-threatening obstetric condition for the mother and the baby that usually arises during labor and manifests with a sudden pause in contractions, an abnormal fetal heart rate (usually bradycardia), severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, loss of fetal station, and hemodynamic instability. Previous c-section predisposes to uterine rupture.

qM0Cpg.title: Postpartum period
qM0Cpg.description: The 12 weeks after childbirth during which the body recovers from the physiological changes of pregnancy and labor.

sM0tJg.title: Inflammation of the eyelids
sM0tJg.description: Redness, swelling, and/or irritation caused by various maladies (e.g., superficial skin irritation) affecting, e.g., eyelid follicles or eye glands. Common causes include hordeola, chalazia, blepharitis, and eyelid dermatitis.

FM0gqg.title: Conjunctivitis
FM0gqg.description: An inflammation of the conjunctiva due to an infectious (e.g., bacterial, viral) or noninfectious (e.g., allergic) etiology. Characterized by conjunctival hyperemia (pink eye), watery or purulent eye discharge, and foreign-body sensation in the eye.

uM0pqg.title: Keratitis
uM0pqg.description: Inflammation of the cornea, caused by infection (most common), UV light exposure, chemical injury, or hypoxic injury.  Clinical features include pain, photophobia, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing.

EM08qg.title: Scleritis
EM08qg.description: A condition characterized by inflammation of the sclera. Causes piercing eye pain (typically worse at night and with eye movement) and diffuse, bright red injection. Complications include keratitis, uveitis, cataract formation, and glaucoma.

DM01Ig.title: Cataract
DM01Ig.description: A condition in which the normally clear lens of the eye becomes opaque, which results in decreased or blurry vision.

CM0qIg.title: Glaucoma
CM0qIg.description: A group of eye diseases characterized by progressive optic neuropathy that results in a specific pattern of irreversible optic disc changes and visual field defects. Frequently associated with raised intraocular pressure. Further subdivided into open-angle glaucoma and angle-closure glaucoma.

media.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of secondary open-angle glaucoma

BM0zIg.title: Retinal vessel occlusion
BM0zIg.description: An occlusion of the central retinal artery and/or its branches, usually as a result of thromboembolic phenomena. Characterized by sudden, painless loss of vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect.

media.title: Central retinal artery occlusion with cilioretinal artery sparing
Hollenhorst plaque causing branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO)

AM0Rrg.title: Age-related macular degeneration
AM0Rrg.description: A degenerative disease of the retina typically leading to central vision impairment caused by deposits under the retinal pigment epithelium (in dry AMD) or neovascularization in the subretinal space (in wet AMD).

media.title: Drusen in nonexudative age-related macular degeneration

_M05rg.title: Retinal detachment
_M05rg.description: The detachment of the inner layer of the retina (neurosensory retina) from the retinal pigment epithelium.

Xn097g.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
Xn097g.description: An endocrinologic disorder characterized by oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, infertility, obesity, virilization and presence of polycystic ovaries. Although the exact pathophysiology is unknown, it is thought to be due to reduced peripheral insulin sensitivity, causing excess androgen production.

cn0aHg.title: Human papillomavirus infection
cn0aHg.description: A viral infection of the skin and mucosal epithelium. Manifestations include common warts (verrucae vulgaris), benign anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata), and a variety of mucosal lesions (e.g., oral warts, respiratory papillomatosis, and squamous intraepithelial lesions of the cervix). Infection with oncogenic types may lead to malignant disease (e.g., cervical, genital, and oropharyngeal cancer).

Wn0PHg.title: Placental insufficiency
Wn0PHg.description: A disorder of the fetomaternal circulation that results in inadequate blood flow to the placenta and impairment in substance exchange (e.g., oxygen) between the mother and fetus. The condition may be either acute (e.g., due to placental abruption) or chronic (e.g., due to maternal drug use, postterm pregnancy).

dn0oHg.title: Multifetal gestation
dn0oHg.description: A pregnancy in which more than one fetus develops simultaneously in the uterus. Associated with an increased the risk of prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, preeclampsia, and other pregnancy and neonatal complications.

2n0Tsg.title: Staphylococcal diseases
2n0Tsg.description: A group of diseases caused by staphylococci, a type of gram-positive bacteria. Includes localized infections (e.g., impetigo), systemic infections (e.g. bacteremia), and reactions to staphylococcal toxins (e.g., food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome).

fn0ksg.title: Neural tube defects
fn0ksg.description: A collection of conditions characterized by incomplete closure of the neural tube in the first weeks of embryonic development. Leads to defects in the spinal cord or brain. Includes spina bifida, myelomeningocele, anencephaly, and encephalocele. May be associated with folate deficiency.

gn0Fsg.title: Rapid sequence intubation
gn0Fsg.description: A method of endotracheal tube intubation used for emergency airway management that involves rapid induction of unconsciousness followed by administration of a paralytic agent. This method differs from traditional intubation in that it uses weight-based bolus doses of short-acting medications (rather than gradually titrating the dose) in order to forego bag-valve-mask ventilation and achieve more rapid intubation.

Sn0ysg.title: Local and regional anesthesia
Sn0ysg.description: A collection of techniques involving the application or infiltration of local anesthetic agents to reversibly block nerve endings, nerves, or nerve bundles, thereby numbing pain conduction in target tissues. Typically used to minimize pain during procedures while preserving consciousness and spontaneous vital functions.

hn0cGg.title: Airway management
hn0cGg.description: The practice of maintaining or restoring a safe, effective pathway for oxygenation and ventilation. Indicated in patients with airway obstruction, respiratory failure, or a need for airway protection (e.g., for general anesthesia or due to an aspiration risk).

Rn0lGg.title: Endarterectomy
Rn0lGg.description: A surgical procedure in which the inner lining of an artery is removed, along with any associated deposits; typically used to remove atherosclerotic deposits in the carotid artery or peripheral arteries of the legs.

in0JGg.title: Tumor markers
in0JGg.description: A biological substance (e.g., protein, DNA) that can be detected in the blood, urine, or tissue of patients with certain tumors. These substances are produced by, shed from, and/or are present in the abnormal cells. While some tumor markers can help diagnose cancer, they are primarily used to aid treatment selection, monitor treatment response, and/or detect recurrence.

jn0_Gg.title: Electrocardiography
jn0_Gg.description: The use of external electrodes to measure and record electrical conduction signals of the heart. Facilitates examination of axis, rate, and rhythm, as well as the amplitudes of specific parts of the heart (e.g., the P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment).

Pn0Wtg.title: Artificial cardiac pacemaker
Pn0Wtg.description: A cardiac implantable electronic device used to monitor the electrical rhythm of the heart and deliver electrical impulses in bradycardia (i.e., antibradycardia pacing).

destinations.label: Cardiac implantable electronic devices → Permanent pacemakers

4n03tg.title: Cardiac catheterization
4n03tg.description: A percutaneous procedure in which a catheter is inserted through a vessel in the groin, arm, or neck and passed into the coronary vessels and/or chambers of the heart. Facilitates the diagnosis of heart diseases and/or therapeutic interventions.

media.title: Cardiac catheterization based on the Seldinger technique

kn0mtg.title: Blood culture
kn0mtg.description: A microbiological culture of the blood. Performed to identify bacteria and fungi in the bloodstream as well as to enable antibiotic resistance testing.

Nn0-tg.title: Pulmonary function testing
Nn0-tg.description: A range of tests that measure the different lung volumes and other metrics of pulmonary function such as the lung's oxygen diffusion capacity. These tests can be used in diagnosing and managing pulmonary disorders, differentiating between obstructive and restrictive lung diseases, and preoperatively evaluating select patients.

mn0VFg.title: Pulse oximetry
mn0VFg.description: A technique that uses red and infrared light detection to measure oxygen saturation based on differences in the light absorption properties of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin. A resting oxygen saturation >95% is considered normal on room air in an otherwise healthy patient.

nn07Fg.title: Conservative treatment of fractures
nn07Fg.description: A collection of nonoperative techniques to manage fractures. Includes closed reduction, splinting, casting, traction, and supportive care.

media.title: Distal radius fracture reduction using finger trap

Ln0wFg.title: Hemithyroidectomy
Ln0wFg.description: The surgical removal of one thyroid lobe and the isthmus.

pn0L8g.title: Lumbar puncture
pn0L8g.description: A procedure that collects cerebrospinal fluid for diagnostic analysis. Common indications include suspected meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, multiple sclerosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Can also be used therapeutically to administer intrathecal antibiotics or chemotherapy. Relatively contraindicated in patients with uncorrected coagulopathy, infection at the proposed puncture site, and clinically suspected elevated intracranial pressure.

media.title: Anatomical structures in lumbar puncture, spinal anesthesia, and epidural anesthesia
Lumbar puncture (1/2): materials, patient positioning, and puncture site

Gn0Bug.title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Gn0Bug.description: An emergency procedure that maintains circulation in patients with cardiac arrest until cardiac function can be restored. Most commonly refers to Basic Life Support (BLS) or Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) algorithms. Consists of chest compression, rescue breathing, and defibrillation.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)

Fn0gEg.title: Computed tomography scan
Fn0gEg.description: A radiographic technique that employs using a rotating x-ray generator and multiple detectors to produce cross-sectional images, which can be digitally reconstructed into a 3D image.

8n0OEg.title: Magnetic resonance imaging
8n0OEg.description: An imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, a radiofrequency current, and a computer to create three-dimensional anatomic images. Intravenous injection of gadolinium (a contrast material) may be required to enhance certain structures. MRI is particularly sensitive for detecting and evaluating changes or damage to soft tissue.

vn0AEg.title: Parasympathomimetic drugs
vn0AEg.description: A group of drugs that activates the parasympathetic nervous system. Further classified as direct or indirect agonists of acetylcholine receptors. Used in the management of a variety of conditions (e.g., postoperative ileus, myasthenia gravis, glaucoma) due to the selectivity of different agents for specific tissues.

Dn01vg.title: Parasympatholytics
Dn01vg.description: A group of drugs that inhibit the parasympathetic nervous system. Includes muscarinic receptors antagonists (e.g., benztropine, ipratropium) and nicotinic receptor antagonists (e.g., vecuronium, succinylcholine).

wn0hvg.title: Beta-2 adrenergic agonists
wn0hvg.description: A drug that stimulates β2 adrenergic receptors, resulting in dilation of certain smooth muscles. Primarily used as bronchodilators to treat bronchial asthma and COPD. Obstetric use includes inducing tocolysis in preterm or undesired contractions. Adverse effects include tachycardia, arrhythmias, tremor, hyperglycemia, and hypokalemia.

9n0Nvg.title: Sympathomimetic drugs
9n0Nvg.description: A group of drugs that mimic or enhance the actions of endogenous catecholamines of the sympathetic nervous system (“fight-or-flight” response). Direct agonists directly activate adrenergic receptors, while indirect agonists enhance the actions of endogenous catecholamines. Clinical indications for sympathomimetics include asthma, heart failure, shock, and anaphylaxis. Adverse effects include hypertension, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, anxiety, and tremor.

Cn0qvg.title: Antisympathetic drugs
Cn0qvg.description: A group of drugs that inhibit the activity of the sympathetic nervous system. Act by blocking adrenergic receptors in target organs (e.g., alpha and beta receptors) or by inhibiting the synthesis, storage, or release of endogenous catecholamines (mainly norepinephrine). Used in the management of a variety of conditions (e.g., ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and urinary retention) due to the selectivity of different agents for specific tissues.

xn0Evg.title: Beta blockers
xn0Evg.description: A group of drugs that inhibit sympathetic activation of β adrenergic receptors. Cardioselective blockers (e.g., bisoprolol) primarily block β1 receptors (the main β receptor of the heart), which causes decreased heart rate and cardiac contractility, slower AVN conduction, and decreased cardiac workload. Nonselective β blockers (e.g., propranolol) inhibit all β receptors and thus are associated with more adverse effects.

Bn0zvg.title: Inhalational anesthetics
Bn0zvg.description: A group of drugs used for the induction and maintenance of general anesthesia and sedation. Agents include sevoflurane, desflurane, and nitrous oxide.

yn0dDg.title: IV anesthetics
yn0dDg.description: A group of drugs used to induce a state of impaired awareness or complete sedation. Agents include propofol, etomidate, ketamine, and barbiturates (e.g., thiopental, phenobarbital).

An0RDg.title: Skeletal muscle relaxants
An0RDg.description: A group of drugs used to decrease muscle tone in skeletal muscles. Further classified as neuromuscular blockers or spasmolytics. Common uses include treatment of spasticity and musculoskeletal pain (e.g., fibromyalgia).

zn0rDg.title: Benzodiazepines
zn0rDg.description: A group of drugs that act by binding GABA-A receptors and increasing the frequency that they are open. Predominantly used to treat stress and anxiety disorders, sleep disorders, and seizures but can also be used for muscle relaxation in minor orthopedic procedures and perioperative sedation. Adverse effects include confusion, impaired motor coordination, amnesia, drowsiness, and respiratory depression.

ZL0Zwg.title: Non-opioid analgesics
ZL0Zwg.description: A group of analgesics consisting of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), selective COX-2 inhibitors, and acetaminophen.

aL0Qwg.title: Antipsychotics
aL0Qwg.description: A type of drug primarily used to treat psychosis (e.g., paranoia, delusions, hallucinations). Antipsychotics are mainly used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, although they may also be used for anxiety disorders and depression.

YL0nwg.title: Antidepressants
YL0nwg.description: A group of drugs primarily used to treat major depressive disorder but also used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorders, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, and neuropathic pain. Drug classes include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SSNRIs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).

bL0Hwg.title: Lithium
bL0Hwg.description: An antimanic agent used to treat bipolar disorder. The exact mechanism of action is unclear, but it is believed to alter cation transport in neurons and myocytes, affecting serotonin and norepinephrine levels.

XL09wg.title: Anticonvulsant drugs
XL09wg.description: A group of drugs used to treat and prevent seizures. Classified as first-generation (classic) or second-generation anticonvulsants. Drug choice is often guided by the type of seizure. Also used in the management of pain and mood disorders.

1L029g.title: Statin
1L029g.description: A class of drugs that reduce the lipid levels in the blood by inhibiting cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Statins are the most effective drug for reducing LDL levels and can also improve HDL and triglyceride levels. Adverse effects include abnormalities in liver function tests and myalgia.

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

WL0P9g.title: Second-line lipid-lowering agents
WL0P9g.description: A group of drugs used in the management of hypercholesterolemia. Typically used when cholesterol levels are inadequately controlled with statin monotherapy or when patients have persistent adverse effects from statins (e.g., myositis, myalgia). Includes fibrates, bile acid resins, niacin, and cholesterol absorption inhibitors.

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

dL0o9g.title: Amiodarone
dL0o9g.description: A class III antiarrhythmic drug that is most commonly used to treat ventricular tachyarrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.

VL0G9g.title: Calcium channel blockers
VL0G9g.description: A group of drugs that inhibit L-type voltage-gated calcium channels found in cardiomyocytes and arterial smooth muscle cells. In the heart, CCBs cause negative inotropic, chronotropic, and dromotropic effects. In arteries, they lead to muscle relaxation and vasodilation. Three main classes of CCBs are phenylalkylamines (e.g., verapamil), benzothiazepines (e.g., diltiazem), and dihydropyridines (e.g., nifedipine, amlodipine). Mainly used to treat hypertension, coronary artery disease, and cardiac arrhythmias.

eL0x9g.title: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors
eL0x9g.description: A group of drugs that inhibits the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Consists of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs), and direct renin inhibitors. Typically used in the management of hypertension, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and myocardial infarction.

media.title: Mechanism of action: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors

UL0bCg.title: Nitrates
UL0bCg.description: A chemical compound that contains NO₃⁻. May refer to medications that increase the release of nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle cells (e.g., nitroglycerin), leading to vasodilation, or chemicals found in various food items (e.g., foods preserved by curing or smoking).

media.title: Mechanism of action: nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors

fL0kCg.title: Cardiac glycosides
fL0kCg.description: A cardiac glycoside that inhibits Na+/K+- ATPases in cardiomyocytes. Increased intracellular Na+ levels result, which in turn reduce the efficacy of Na+/Ca2+ exchangers and lead to higher intracellular Ca2+ concentrations. As a result, the force of contraction becomes stronger (positive inotropic effect) and the electrical conduction in the heart is slowed down (negative dromotropic effect).

TL06Cg.title: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors
TL06Cg.description: A class of drugs that inhibit phosphodiesterase enzymes (PDEs). Classified as nonspecific, PDE3, PDE4, and PDE5 inhibitors. Typically used in the management of acute heart failure and peripheral vascular disease (PDE3 inhibitors), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (PDE4 inhibitors), and pulmonary hypertension and erectile dysfunction (PDE5 inhibitors). Contraindications include nitrate and alpha-blocker use due to risk of life-threatening hypotension.

SL0yCg.title: Heparin
SL0yCg.description: A mixture of sulfated mucopolysaccharides that indirectly inhibits the action of thrombin and factor Xa by increasing the activity of antithrombin (an endogenous anticoagulant). Heparin is indicated for the treatment and prophylaxis of venous thrombosis. Two forms of heparin are in clinical use: Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin.

3L0Sxg.title: Diuretics
3L0Sxg.description: A group of drugs that induce increased production of urine. Classes include thiazides, loop diuretics, and potassium-sparing diuretics. Depending on the class, diuretics act on different renal structures and cause varying changes in the volume and composition of urine as well as the electrolyte balance.

RL0lxg.title: Thiazide diuretics
RL0lxg.description: A group of diuretic agents that act as Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter inhibitors in the early distal renal tubule. Used mainly to treat hypertension. Examples include hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone. Adverse effects include metabolic alkalosis, electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia), metabolic effects (hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia), and sulfonamide hypersensitivity.

iL0Jxg.title: Loop diuretics
iL0Jxg.description: A group of drugs that block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporters in the thick ascending loop of Henle. This causes the gradient between the renal medulla and cortex to diminish over time and reduces the nephron's capacity to concentrate the urine, which leads to diuresis. Associated with the following metabolic imbalances: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hypochloremia, hyponatremia, and metabolic alkalosis. Agents include furosemide and torsemide.

QL0uxg.title: Potassium-sparing diuretics
QL0uxg.description: A class of diuretics consisting of aldosterone receptor antagonists (e.g., spironolactone, eplerenone) and epithelial sodium channel blockers (e.g., triamterene, amioloride). All agents in this class reduce the reabsorption of sodium and the excretion of potassium. Typically used in the management of hypertension and congestive heart failure. Adverse effects include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gastrointestinal disturbances, and endocrine disturbances (e.g., gynecomastia, impotence, amenorrhea, hirsutism).

4L03Bg.title: Glucocorticoids
4L03Bg.description: A type of corticosteroid hormone produced naturally in the adrenal glands. Synthesized versions are used therapeutically to treat allergic, neoplastic, and autoimmune conditions, among other conditions. Commonly used agents include prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, and beclometasone.

OL0IBg.title: Cephalosporins
OL0IBg.description: A class of broad-spectrum, bactericidal, beta-lactam antibiotics. First-generation cephalosporins are active against gram-positive bacteria; successive generations typically have increased activity against gram-negative bacteria and decreased activity against gram-positive organisms. Adverse effects include allergy, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and vitamin K deficiency.

lL0vBg.title: Fluoroquinolones
lL0vBg.description: A subtype of quinolones with a fluorine atom in their structure, which significantly increases their antibacterial spectrum. Effective against, e.g., streptococci and gram-negative organisms. Examples are ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.

5L0iyg.title: Antiemetics
5L0iyg.description: A group of drugs used to treat various causes of nausea and vomiting. Different antiemetics act on different receptors, including the 5-HT3 receptor (e.g., ondansetron), M2 receptors (e.g., scopolamine), and D2 receptors (e.g., metoclopramide).

ML0Myg.title: Proton pump inhibitors
ML0Myg.description: A family of drugs that decrease acid production in the stomach by irreversibly inhibiting hydrogen/potassium ATPase. Examples include omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole, and dexlansoprazole.

LL0wyg.title: Insulin
LL0wyg.description: An anabolic hormone that is naturally produced by pancreatic β cells to counteract hyperglycemia. Exogenous insulin is used as a medication for diabetes mellitus and is typically administered subcutaneously.

KL0UAg.title: Thyrostatics
KL0UAg.description: Drugs used to treat hyperthyroidism that either decrease thyroid hormone synthesis (thionamides) or thyroid hormone release (iodides).

6L0jAg.title: Hormonal contraceptives
6L0jAg.description: A type of contraceptive that uses estrogen and/or progestin analogs to prevent pregnancy. May take the form of oral contraceptives, the contraceptive patch, the vaginal ring, injectable progestin, hormonal intrauterine devices, or subdermal progestin implants.

JL0sAg.title: Influenza
JL0sAg.description: A highly contagious, viral infection that typically occurs during the winter months. Manifestations include sudden-onset high fever, headache, rhinorrhea, nonproductive cough, malaise, and myalgia.

IL0Y_g.title: Vaccinations
IL0Y_g.description: The administration of a biological product to induce adaptive immunity to a specific infectious disease. Vaccines typically contain antigens derived from the target pathogen (e.g., live attenuated micro-organisms, protein, DNA) and adjuvants to enhance the immune response.

sL0t_g.title: Syncope
sL0t_g.description: A sudden, completely reversible loss of consciousness secondary to an acute reduction of cerebral perfusion, which may last from several seconds up to minutes. The most common type is vasovagal syncope, which is triggered by emotional stress or prolonged standing. Possible underlying causes of syncope include cardiovascular disease (cardiac syncope), autonomic dysfunction (reflex syncope), and insufficient counterregulation during blood pressure changes when standing up (orthostatic syncope).

media.title: Mean blood pressure in different regions of the body (standing position)

GL0B_g.title: Cervical myelopathy
GL0B_g.description: A degenerative process involving the cervical spine that results in either compression of the cervical spinal cord or its arterial supply. Most commonly presents with radicular pain, sensory deficits, and lower motor neuron signs at the level of the lesion.

8L0Ozg.title: Yellow fever
8L0Ozg.description: An acute viral hemorrhagic fever caused by a virus of the Flaviviridae family and transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Yellow fever is endemic in tropical Africa, and parts of Middle and South America (so-called yellow fever belt). Clinical findings include hepatic dysfunction, renal failure, DIC, and shock.

media.title: Geographic distribution of yellow fever (risk of transmission)

uL0pzg.title: Zoonotic diseases
uL0pzg.description: A group of infections that are transmitted from animals to humans. Typically endemic to specific geographical regions. Examples include Q fever, babesiosis, and epidemic typhus.

EL08zg.title: Epiglottitis
EL08zg.description: Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures. Historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, but many cases are now caused by streptococci. Peak incidence between 6–12 years. Classically manifests with respiratory distress, anxiety, and the characteristic "tripod" or "sniffing" posture. Lateral neck x-ray shows an enlarged epiglottis (thumb sign).

DL01-g.title: Renal replacement therapy
DL01-g.description: A treatment used to remove toxins, metabolites, and water from the body if kidney function is transiently or persistently lost. Can also be used in certain cases of poisoning or overdose. There are three main modalities used to replace renal function: dialysis (either hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis), hemofiltration, and kidney transplantation.

wL0h-g.title: Dengue
wL0h-g.description: A mosquito-borne tropical disease. Most often asymptomatic or with nonspecific mild symptoms (e.g., fever, headache). Additional clinical manifestations include myalgia, exanthem, hemorrhage, and/or shock.

CL0q-g.title: Fever
CL0q-g.description: An elevated body temperature (typically defined as > 38°C) due to an increase in the hypothalamic temperature setpoint, usually as a response to endogenous pyrogens, e.g., cytokines. Causes of fever can be infectious (e.g., viral, bacterial, fungal) or noninfectious (e.g., malignancy, systemic rheumatic disease, drug reaction).

_L05ZS.title: Aortic dissection
_L05ZS.description: A tear in the intima of the aortic wall that leads to blood entering between the intima and media or adventitia at high pressure and separating these layers, which creates a false lumen. Propagation of the tear can lead to obstruction of aortic branches and subsequent ischemia (e.g., neurological deficits, renal infarction), aortic regurgitation, and/or cardiac tamponade.

-L0DZS.title: Radiation therapy
-L0DZS.description: A therapy used to treat neoplasms through the cell-damaging effect of ionizing radiation. Radiation therapy can be applied either internally via radioactive substances or externally using of special irradiation devices.

Zo0Z0S.title: Neurological examination
Zo0Z0S.description: A part of the physical examination. Assess mental status, cranial nerves, muscles (e.g., bulk, tone, strength), sensation (e.g., sensation to dullness, sharpness, pain, temperature, light touch, vibration, and proprioception), and reflexes. Compare upper and lower extremities and laterality of findings to identify the location of a lesion with the nervous system.

0o0e0S.title: Foreign body aspiration
0o0e0S.description: A potentially life-threatening emergency in which an aspirated object becomes stuck in the larynx, trachea, or bronchi. Most commonly occurs in children < 3 years of age. FBA typically manifests with a sudden onset of coughing and choking, followed by stridor and dyspnea. Aspirated foreign bodies are found more often in the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

media.title: Distribution of affected bronchi in foreign body aspiration

ao0Q0S.title: Chancroid
ao0Q0S.description: A sexually transmitted disease caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Patients present with one or more painful genital ulcers and painful, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy. Commonly seen in Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America.

Yo0n0S.title: Atrioventricular block
Yo0n0S.description: An arrhythmia characterized by interrupted or delayed conduction between the atria and the ventricles. Divided into three different degrees depending on the extent of the interruption or delay.

bo0H0S.title: Astrocytoma
bo0H0S.description: A neuroepithelial tumor (glioma) that arises from the supportive tissue of the brain. Presents with general symptoms initially (e.g., headaches, seizures) and focal symptoms (e.g., progressive paralysis, aphasia) later in the course of disease. While low-grade (benign) astrocytomas occur predominantly in children and adults aged 20–40, grade IV (highly malignant) astrocytomas (glioblastomas) are the most common brain tumors in adults aged 50–60.

1o02aS.title: Pleural effusion
1o02aS.description: The presence of fluid in the pleural cavity. Classified as transudative (e.g., due to congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis) or exudative (e.g., pneumonia, malignancies, pulmonary embolism), depending on the underlying cause. Typically manifests with dyspnea and a dry cough.

media.title: Fluid in the right costodiaphragmatic recess
Fluid in the left costodiaphragmatic recess

Wo0PaS.title: Esophageal barium swallow
Wo0PaS.description: A diagnostic test in which serial x-rays of the chest are taken while a patient swallows liquid barium, a contrast medium. Barium coats the walls of the esophagus and can be used to identify anatomical defects in the esophagus (e.g., strictures, rings, dilation). Performed to evaluate symptoms such as painful and/or difficult swallowing.

eo0xaS.title: Laparoscopic surgery
eo0xaS.description: A minimally invasive surgical procedure in which instruments and a camera are introduced into the abdominal cavity ("keyhole surgery") for examination and/or treatment with reduced soft tissue damage.

media.title: Peritoneal access with closed technique (using Veress needle)

To06YS.title: Septic arthritis
To06YS.description: A joint infection that causes severe pain, swelling, erythema, warmth, and loss of function of the affected joint. Also frequently causes systemic signs such as fever.

media.title: Synovial fluid analysis in septic arthritis

ho0cbS.title: Subclavian steal syndrome
ho0cbS.description: A condition in which the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery narrows or becomes occluded, usually due to atherosclerosis. This blockage results in a lack of blood reaching the ipsilateral arm through the subclavian artery, which can lead to a reversal of blood flow in the affected vertebral artery so that blood from the contralateral side can flow through the circle of Willis to supply the affected arm. Presents with ischemic symptoms on the affected arm, sometimes associated with neurologic symptoms (e.g., lightheadedness). Causes arm blood pressure discrepancy > 15 mmHg.

jo0_bS.title: Transfusion
jo0_bS.description: The intravenous administration of whole blood or blood products. The most common blood transfusion products are packed red blood cells and are used for the treatment of acute or chronic blood loss. Platelet transfusions, clotting factor transfusions, fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and cryoprecipitate are also available.

media.title: Blood type O+ RBC transfusion compatibility
Blood type AB+ RBC transfusion compatibility

ko0mXS.title: Chorioamnionitis, neonatal infection, and omphalitis
ko0mXS.description: Chorioamnionitis is an infection of the amniotic fluid, fetal membranes, and placenta that is most commonly caused by ascending cervicovaginal bacteria.

Oo0IXS.title: Edema
Oo0IXS.description: An abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitium due to an imbalance in fluid hemostasis.

mo0VcS.title: Food allergies
mo0VcS.description: A hypersensitivity reaction to allergens contained in food. Most common cause of anaphylaxis-related emergency admissions. Clinical features include urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, rhinorrhea, and abdominal pain.

Mo0McS.title: Puberty
Mo0McS.description: The phase of development between childhood and adulthood during which complete functional maturation of the reproductive glands and external genitalia occurs. Characterized by the development of secondary sex characteristics, growth spurts, and psychosocial changes. Typically begins between 8–13 years in girls and 9–14 years in boys.

no07cS.title: Endophthalmitis
no07cS.etymology: Latin: endo-: within; ophthalmos: eye; -itis: pertaining to inflammation
no07cS.description: Inflammation of the vitreous humor (the innermost "layer" of the eye) with possible involvement of surrounding structures, usually due to microbial infection.

Lo0wcS.title: Mitral valve prolapse
Lo0wcS.description: A valvular lesion characterized by bulging of a mitral valve leaflet into the left atrium during systole. Most commonly idiopathic but can also be associated with connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan syndrome) or occur as a complication of infective endocarditis, acute rheumatic heart disease, or myocardial infarction. On auscultation (best heard over the apex), typically characterized as a late systolic crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click due to sudden tensing of the chordae tendinae.

media.title: Heart murmur in mitral valve prolapse

oo001S.title: Glycogen storage disorders
oo001S.description: A heterogeneous group of diseases that occur due to a deficient enzyme in glucose metabolism, which leads to excessive accumulation of glycogen in various organs, particularly the heart, liver, and muscles. Several subtypes of glycogen storage disease (GSD) exist, with the most notable being Von Gierke disease (GSD type I), Pompe disease (GSD type II), Cori disease (GSD type III), Andersen disease (GSD type IV), and McArdle disease (GSD type V).

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Glycogen storage disorders (GSD)

Ko0U1S.title: Uveal melanoma
Ko0U1S.description: A melanoma of the uveal tract (e.g., iris, ciliary body, choroid). Often asymptomatic but can manifest with flashes, floaters, and/or visual field defects. Risk factors include congenital ocular melanocytosis, light eye and skin color, and cutaneous and iris nevi.

6o0j1S.title: Postpartum hemorrhage
6o0j1S.description: A blood loss ≥ 1,000 mL or bleeding associated with signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of delivery. Causes for early/primary postpartum hemorrhage (< 24 hours after delivery) include atonic uterus (most common cause), retained placenta, coagulopathy, and trauma. Causes for late/secondary postpartum hemorrhage (> 24 hours after delivery) include retained placental remnants (most common cause), endometritis, and bleeding from the C-section or episiotomy wound.

Jo0s1S.title: Pelvic organ prolapse
