qs0CDh.description: Urinalysis findings seen in glomerulonephritis. Abnormalities include dysmorphic red blood cells (acanthocytes), red blood cell casts, mild to moderate proteinuria (< 3.5 g/24 h), and sterile pyuria.

Is0Ywh.title: Nephrotic sediment
Is0Ywh.description: Urine microscopy findings that suggest nephrotic syndrome, including lipiduria, fatty casts (hyaline casts composed of fat globule inclusions and proteins with Maltese cross appearance under polarized light), and renal tubular epithelial cell casts.

Hs0Kwh.title: Nephritic syndrome
Hs0Kwh.description: A clinical syndrome characterized by glomerular inflammation that causes glomerular hematuria (e.g., with red blood cell casts), sterile pyuria, and mild to moderate proteinuria. Results in hypertension, oliguria, and/or fluid retention with mild to moderate peripheral edema. Causes include various autoimmune disorders, hereditary disorders, and infectious diseases.

Gs0Bwh.title: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Gs0Bwh.description: A condition characterized by focal segmental glomerular lesions with sclerosis and hyalinosis on light microscopy and effacement of podocytes on electron microscopy. On immunofluorescence microscopy, nonspecific IgM, C3, and C1 deposits may be present. Can be idiopathic or secondary to other conditions. Associated with HIV, intravenous drug use, and obesity.

ts0X9h.title: Membranous nephropathy
ts0X9h.description: The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in white adults. Can be idiopathic or associated with infections (hepatitis B and C), SLE, tumors, or medications. Characterized by thickened glomerular capillary loops on light microscopy and subepithelial dense deposits (spike and dome appearance) on electron microscopy.

Fs0g9h.title: Minimal change glomerulonephritis
Fs0g9h.description: A common cause of nephrotic syndrome, especially in children following a viral infection. Common features include edema, proteinuria (causing frothy urine), and low serum albumin. The glomerulus looks normal under light microscopy; electron microscopy shows podocyte effacement and vacuolization.

media.title: Podocyte foot processes fusion in minimal change disease

8s0O9h.title: Spot urinary collection
8s0O9h.description: The collection of a single sample of urine (in contrast to a 24-hour urine collection). Some test results (e.g., urine protein/creatinine ratio) obtained using spot urinary collection correlate highly with those obtained using 24-hour urine collections.

us0p9h.title: Renal vein thrombosis
us0p9h.description: A complication of hypercoagulable states (e.g., malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome) and typically presents with flank pain and hematuria, as well as anuria and elevated creatinine levels if bilateral thrombosis occurs.

vs0A9h.title: Goodpasture disease
vs0A9h.description: An autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of circulating antibodies against type IV collagen in the glomerular and pulmonary capillary basement membranes. Can cause a spectrum of illness, ranging from minimally symptomatic disease to pulmonary-renal syndrome with hemoptysis, cough, dyspnea, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Ds01Ch.title: Pulmonary-renal syndrome
Ds01Ch.description: A combination of glomerulonephritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Common causes include ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome, microscopic polyangiitis), SLE, and Goodpasture disease.

ws0hCh.title: Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis
ws0hCh.description: An acute inflammation of the renal interstitium and tubules that is most commonly due to drug hypersensitivity. Causes a decline in renal function over a period of days to weeks.

xs0ECh.title: Aristolochic acid nephropathy
xs0ECh.description: A form of toxic interstitial nephropathy caused by the ingestion of aristolochic acid, often in the form of herbal weight-loss pills or food contaminated with environmental pollutants.

Bs0zCh.title: Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis
Bs0zCh.description: A condition of chronic inflammation of the renal interstitium and tubules most commonly due to the progression of acute tubulointerstitial nephritis but also caused by autoimmune, metabolic, systemic, or environmental processes. Patients typically present with an indolent course, with clinical features characteristic of the underlying etiology. In addition to laboratory findings consistent with chronic kidney disease, typical urinalysis findings are sterile pyuria, subnephrotic-range proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria. May progress to end-stage renal disease.

-s0Dxh.title: Analgesic nephropathy
-s0Dxh.description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) resulting from the chronic use of analgesics, particularly when multiple agents are used in combination (e.g., acetaminophen with aspirin).

0G0eBh.title: Myeloma cast nephropathy
0G0eBh.description: A form of tubulointerstitial renal disease seen in patients with multiple myeloma. It occurs when excessive amounts of immunoglobulin light chains are produced and filtered into the primary urine, resulting in their precipitation within the renal tubules and leading to tubular obstruction and toxicity to renal tissue.

aG0QBh.title: Calcium oxalate stones
aG0QBh.description: A common type of kidney stone that can occur due to hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypocitraturia. On urinalysis, they appear as biconcave dumbbells or bipyramidal envelopes. Radiopaque on imaging. Associated with low urinary pH. Preventive measures include dietary modification, urine alkalinization, and thiazide diuretics.

YG0nBh.title: Struvite stones
YG0nBh.description: A type of radiopaque urinary stone associated with chronic upper urinary tract infections, urease-producing organisms (most commonly Proteus mirabilis), and alkaline urine. Very large stones that fill the entire renal pelvis and calyces are referred to as staghorn calculi.

bG0HBh.title: Uric acid stones
bG0HBh.description: A type of kidney stone that occurs due to persistently acidic urine, gout, and hyperuricemia. Appear on urinalysis as rounded, rhomboid or needle-shaped stones in urinalysis. Radiolucent on imaging. Associated with low urinary pH. Preventive measures include a low-purine diet and urine alkalinization.

XG09Bh.title: Calcium phosphate stones
XG09Bh.description: A type of kidney stone that can occur due to hyperparathyroidism and type 1 renal tubular acidosis. Appear on urinalysis as wedge-shaped prisms; radiopaque on imaging. Associated with high urinary pH. Urine acidification is a preventive measure.

cG0ayh.title: Cystine stones
cG0ayh.description: An uncommon type of kidney stone that develops in patients with cystinuria, often as early as childhood. Appear on urinalysis as hexagon-shaped crystals. Radiopaque and associated with low pH. Prevention strategies include a low-sodium diet, urine alkalinization, and administration of chelating agents.

1G02yh.title: Cystinuria
1G02yh.description: An autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defective intestinal or renal tubular transport of dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, arginine, lysine). Causes aminoaciduria and cysteine accumulation in the urine, ultimately resulting in recurrent cystine stones.

VG0Gyh.title: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy
VG0Gyh.description: A noninvasive method of stone fragmentation using an acoustic pulse. Primarily used for the treatment of urolithiasis and, less commonly, gallstones.

TG06Ah.title: Hyperkalemia
TG06Ah.description: A serum potassium concentration > 5 mEq/L. Etiologies include decreased potassium excretion (e.g., due to chronic kidney disease), potassium release from cells (e.g., from rhabdomyolysis), and extracellular shift of potassium ions (e.g., secondary to acidosis or insulin deficiency). Manifestations include cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, and gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., constipation).

gG0FAh.title: Hypokalemia
gG0FAh.description: A serum potassium concentration < 3.5 mEq/L. Etiologies include renal and/or gastrointestinal potassium losses and intracellular shift of potassium ions (e.g., secondary to alkalosis or insulin therapy). Manifestations include cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., constipation), and fatigue.

SG0yAh.title: Hypercalcemia of malignancy
SG0yAh.description: A paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by highly elevated serum calcium. Causes include the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide, ectopic calcitriol D production, bone osteolysis by the malignancy, and ectopic parathyroid hormone production (rare).

3G0S_h.title: Parathyroid hormone
3G0S_h.description: A hormone involved in calcium regulation. Increases the concentration of serum ionized calcium by stimulating the release of calcium and phosphate from bone, calcium reabsorption from the renal distal tubule, and renal production of calcitriol (which in turn increases the intestinal absorption of calcium).

destinations.label: Hypocalcemia → Calcium homeostasis and calcium physiology

media.title: Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism

RG0l_h.title: Vitamin D
RG0l_h.description: A cholesterol-derived vitamin that is largely synthesized in the skin, with ultraviolet light serving as a catalyst. It plays a prominent role in regulation of calcium homeostasis, and intestinal absorption of calcium. Ergocalciferol and cholecalciferol are precursors of vitamin D. Deficiency leads to rickets (in children) or osteomalacia (in adults).

media.title: Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism

iG0J_h.title: Cholecalciferol
iG0J_h.description: An inactive intermediate in the vitamin D biosynthesis pathway. Synthesized from 7-dehydrocholesterol with sun exposure (UVB light). Commonly used as a supplement for the treatment of vitamin D deficiency.

QG0u_h.title: 25-hydroxyvitamin D
QG0u_h.description: An intermediate in the vitamin D biosynthesis pathway that is the major circulating form of vitamin D in the body. Used as an indicator of vitamin D supply. Levels < 20 ng/mL suggest vitamin D deficiency.

jG0__h.title: Calcitriol
jG0__h.description: A form of vitamin D that becomes hormonally active in the kidneys. Increases calcium absorption in the small bowel and renal tubules and increases calcium release from bones.

media.title: Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism

OG0Izh.title: Calcitonin
OG0Izh.description: A hormone produced by parafollicular cells (C cells) in the thyroid gland that inhibits osteoclast activity and renal reabsorption of calcium and phosphate to reduce serum calcium; it may be used therapeutically, e.g., in osteoporosis, or diagnostically, as it is often elevated in medullary thyroid cancer.

destinations.label: Hypocalcemia → Calcium homeostasis and calcium physiology

media.title: Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism

NG0-zh.title: Tetany
NG0-zh.description: A condition of increased neuromuscular irritability caused by hypocalcemia. Manifests as involuntary muscular contractions (cramps and spasms), hyperreflexia, and (perioral) paresthesia.

mG0V-h.title: Hyperventilation-induced tetany
mG0V-h.description: A rare state of neuromuscular hyperexcitability induced by alkalosis/hypocapnia (secondary to hyperventilation). Clinical manifestations are similar to those seen in hypocalcemia tetany, including paresthesias in the extremities and/or the perioral area, the Chvostek sign, and the Trousseau sign.

5G0i-h.title: Chvostek sign
5G0i-h.description: Contraction of the facial muscles elicited by tapping the facial nerve in the area of the cheek. It is a sign of nerve hyperexcitability usually seen in tetany.

MG0M-h.title: Thrombophlebitis migrans
MG0M-h.description: A form of superficial thrombophlebitis that is recurrent and migratory (i.e., occurring in various locations, resolving, then appearing elsewhere). Referred to as Trousseau syndrome if related to underlying malignancy (most commonly pancreatic adenocarcinoma and bronchial carcinoma). It is also a finding of thromboangiitis obliterans and Behçet disease.

LG0w-h.title: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
LG0w-h.description: A genetic disorder that is characterized by decreased urinary calcium excretion and (usually asymptomatic) hypercalcemia. PTH levels are normal in most patients. Caused by an autosomal dominant mutation of a calcium-sensing receptor in the kidneys and parathyroid gland (CaSR gene).

oG00Z3.title: Severe hypercalcemia
oG00Z3.description: A serum calcium concentration > 14 mg/dL (> 3.5 mmol/L) or an ionized (free) calcium concentration > 10 mg/dL (> 2.5 mmol/L). Manifestations include dehydration, oliguria or anuria, cardiac arrhythmias, and an altered level of consciousness, together with the typical symptoms of hypercalcemia (e.g., abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting).

KG0UZ3.title: Dantrolene
KG0UZ3.description: A postsynaptic skeletal muscle relaxant that acts by inhibiting the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum and thereby prevents the release of calcium into the myocyte cytoplasm. The result is impaired muscle contraction. Used to treat malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or severe spasticity.

media.title: Pathomechanisms and therapeutic approach in malignant hyperthermia

6G0jZ3.title: PaO2/FiO2 ratio
6G0jZ3.description: The ratio of arterial oxygen partial pressure on arterial blood gas analysis (PaO2) to the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2). Commonly used as a clinical indicator for hypoxemia. A value of approx. 500 mm Hg is considered normal.

pG0LZ3.title: Right-to-left pulmonary shunt
pG0LZ3.description: A functional shunt. Blood (from the right heart) still flows through alveoli that are not ventilated (e.g., in atelectasis), which results in decreased oxygenation (to the left heart).

IG0Y03.title: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
IG0Y03.description: An adverse effect of transfusion of blood products characterized by acute-onset, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Manifests with dyspnea, severe hypoxemia, hypotension, and fever that typically occurs within 6 hours after transfusion.

GG0B03.title: Lung protective ventilation
GG0B03.description: A mechanical ventilation strategy used primarily in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) to minimize the risk of ventilator-associated lung injury. May also be used to reduce risk of postoperative pulmonary complications in patients undergoing general anesthesia. Incorporates permissive hypercapnia, low tidal volumes (4–8 mL/kg IBW), plateau pressure limits (< 30 cm H2O), and PEEP titration. Associated with improved clinical outcomes.

tG0Xa3.title: Permissive hypercapnia
tG0Xa3.description: Acceptance of hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mm Hg) as a side effect of the most appropriate mechanical ventilation strategy for a patient. Examples include lung-protective ventilation for patients with ARDS and obstructive lung disease ventilation strategy for a patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD.

FG0ga3.title: Traction diverticulum
FG0ga3.description: A herniation of the gastrointestinal wall (most commonly in the esophagus) caused by scarring and retraction from inflammatory processes (e.g., fungal infections, tuberculosis). Usually all layers of the wall are involved (true diverticulum).

8G0Oa3.title: Pulsion diverticulum
8G0Oa3.description: A herniation of the gastrointestinal wall caused by increased intraluminal pressure (e.g., due to achalasia). Usually only the mucosal tissue is involved (false diverticulum). Examples include Zenker diverticula and colonic diverticula in diverticulosis.

uG0pa3.title: Gastroesophageal reflux
uG0pa3.description: The movement of stomach contents into the esophagus due to transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Can be a normal physiological process (e.g., in infants, occasionally after meals) or a feature of a disease (e.g., gastroesophageal reflux disease).

EG08a3.title: Nonerosive reflux disease
EG08a3.description: Characteristic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease in the absence of esophageal injury, such as reflux esophagitis, on endoscopy.

wG0hY3.title: Esophageal pH monitoring
wG0hY3.description: Test which uses a nasogastric tube with a pH probe to quantify esophageal exposure to gastric acid over a 24-hour period.

9G0NY3.title: Eosinophilic esophagitis
9G0NY3.description: Chronic immune-mediated eosinophil-predominant inflammation of the esophageal mucosa. Associated with allergic diseases (allergic asthma, allergic rhinitis) in 50% of cases.

xG0EY3.title: Nissen fundoplication
xG0EY3.description: A surgical procedure in which the gastric fundus is completely (i.e., 360°) wrapped around the lower esophagus to form a cuff, effectively narrowing the distal esophagus and the gastroesophageal junction to prevent reflux of stomach contents and the fundus from sliding through the esopageal hiatus. Used to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and hiatal hernia.

AG0Rb3.title: Barrett esophagus
AG0Rb3.description: A condition in which the esophageal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium and goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia) due to long-term reflux esophagitis. Considered a precancerous condition for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Zt0ZX3.title: Intestinal metaplasia
Zt0ZX3.description: Transformation of the epithelium that is characteristic of certain hollow organs, e.g., the esophagus, stomach, or bladder, into intestinal epithelium. Characterized by the presence of goblet cells with or without intestinal columnar epithelial cells. Occurs due to chronic inflammation or trauma of the epithelial lining of the organ.

Yt0nX3.title: Type I hiatal hernia
Yt0nX3.description: The temporary protrusion of the gastroesophageal junction and the gastric cardia through the esophageal hiatus into the chest. The gastric fundus remains below the diaphragm. It is the most common type of hiatal hernia.

bt0HX3.title: Type II hiatal hernia
bt0HX3.description: The protrusion of part of the gastric fundus through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax. The gastroesophageal junction remains below the diaphragm.

et0xc3.title: Hiatoplasty
et0xc3.description: A surgical procedure that narrows the esophageal hiatus using a mesh or by bringing part of the diaphragm together with sutures.

Ut0b13.title: Saint's triad
Ut0b13.description: A rare combination of cholelithiasis, diverticulosis, and hiatal hernia.

ft0k13.title: Mediastinitis
ft0k13.description: A potentially life-threatening inflammation of the mediastinum (i.e., the central compartment of the chest between the lungs), most commonly of infectious origin. It is often caused by extension of retropharyngeal infections into the mediastinum or develops secondary to perforation of mediastinal organs, e.g., the esophagus.

gt0F13.title: Autoimmune gastritis
gt0F13.description: A form of atrophic gastritis characterized by autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, leading to gland loss, loss of intrinsic factor, achlorhydria, and vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia). Associated with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis) and increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumor.

Rt0lW3.title: Environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis
Rt0lW3.description: The most common type of atrophic gastritis, usually caused by Helicobacter pylori infection. Characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa that manifests with atrophy, gland loss, and metaplastic changes.

media.title: Gastritis: granulocyte infiltration in Helicobacter pylori infection

4t03d3.title: Reactive gastropathy
4t03d3.description: Injury to the gastric mucosa caused by chronic exposure to irritant endogenous (e.g., bile reflux) or exogenous substances (e.g., alcohol, NSAIDs, aspirin). Histopathology shows mucosal edema in the absence of inflammation.

5t0iV3.title: Urea breath test
5t0iV3.description: A rapid diagnostic test for H. pylori infection that is based on the ability of H. pylori to produce urease, an enzyme that converts urea to carbon dioxide and ammonia. Urea that is labeled with C-13 or C-14 isotopes is swallowed by the patient and the amount of isotope-labeled carbon dioxide that is exhaled by the patient is measured after 20–30 minutes.

Mt0MV3.title: Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
Mt0MV3.description: A combination of acid-blocking medication and antibiotics (e.g., optimized bismuth quadruple therapy) aimed at eliminating Helicobacter pylori infection from the gastrointestinal tract. Should be provided to all patients with a confirmed active H. pylori infection.

Kt0Ue3.title: Stress ulcer
Kt0Ue3.description: An ulcer caused by acute damage to the gastric mucosa. Subtypes include Curling ulcers and Cushing ulcers.

destinations.label: Peptic ulcer disease → Subtypes and variants

6t0je3.title: Gastric cardia
6t0je3.description: The most proximal region of the stomach. Connects the esophagus to the fundus and body of the stomach.

Jt0se3.title: Gastric fundus
Jt0se3.description: The superior portion of the stomach.

Gt0BU3.title: Pyloric canal
Gt0BU3.description: The region of the pylorus that connects the pyloric antrum to the duodenum.

tt0X23.title: Dieulafoy lesion
tt0X23.description: An abnormally dilated submucosal artery of the GI tract, most commonly the stomach. Minor mucosal trauma can lead to major GI bleeding.

8t0O23.title: Billroth I
8t0O23.description: Gastroduodenal reconstruction to restore gastrointestinal continuity. Performed after a partial gastrectomy done for conditions such as gastric cancer, large duodenal perforation, or intractable bleeding from a peptic ulcer.

ut0p23.title: Billroth II
ut0p23.description: A reconstructive surgical procedure in which the distal ⅔ of the stomach are resected and the remaining stomach is reconnected with an end-to-side gastro-jejunostomy, while the duodenal stump ends blind. Most often performed to treat refractory peptic ulcer disease.

Et0823.title: Vagotomy
Et0823.description: A division of the main trunk or branches of the vagus nerve. Can be used to decrease gastric acid secretion in patients with recurrent or complicated peptic ulcer disease that is not responding to medical therapy.

yt0dT3.title: Virchow's node
yt0dT3.description: An enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node. Classically associated with metastatic gastric cancer but can develop in other abdominopelvic malignancies (e.g., gallbladder, pancreas, kidneys, testicles, prostate, ovaries).

At0RT3.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
At0RT3.description: A rare malignant tumor of the GI tract that arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal. The most common site of a GIST is the stomach.

media.title: Liver metastasis of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST)

zt0rT3.title: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
zt0rT3.description: A surgical procedure in which a distal portion of the gastrointestinal tract is cut and reattached to a more proximal part. Can be used to bypass the stomach (i.e., gastric bypass) for bariatric surgery. Other indications include reconstruction following gastrectomy for stomach cancer and creation of a hepaticojejunostomy to treat bile duct obstruction.

aF0Qg3.title: Dumping syndrome
aF0Qg3.description: A complication of dysfunctional or bypassed pyloric sphincter (e.g., post-gastrectomy) with symptoms occuring due to rapid gastric emptying. There are two types of dumping syndrome: early and late, referring to the timing of symptoms after meals.

cF0aS3.title: Early dumping
cF0aS3.description: A complication of procedures compromising the pyloric sphincter (e.g., distal gastrectomy) that presents with gastrointestinal discomfort (nausea, vomiting, cramps, diarrhea) and vasomotor symptoms (sweating, palpitations, flushing) shortly after eating (within 15–20 minutes). Symptoms result from fast emptying of carbohydrate-rich chyme into the small intestine.

WF0PS3.title: Late dumping
WF0PS3.description: A complication of procedures compromising the pyloric sphincter (e.g., distal gastrectomy) that presents with gastrointestinal discomfort (nausea, vomiting, cramps, diarrhea), shakiness, hypoglycemia, hunger, and decreased level of consciousness late after eating (after hours). Symptoms result from absorption of carbohydrate-rich chyme in the small intestine and subsequent hyperglycemia and excessive release of insulin, leading to compensatory hypoglycemia and a surge in catecholamines.

TF06h3.title: Blind loop syndrome
TF06h3.description: Bacterial overgrowth of the small intestine caused by stasis in a bypassed segment (blind loop), e.g., following partial gastrectomy with Billroth II or Roux-en-Y anastomosis. Often results in dysfunctional intestinal digestion and malabsorption. Symptoms include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and flatulence.

hF0c33.title: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
hF0c33.description: Gastrointestinal bleeding that originates from the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). Overt UGIB typically manifests with hematemesis and/or melena, or less commonly with hematochezia. Occult UGIB can manifest with nonspecific symptoms due to iron deficiency anemia (e.g., fatigue, pallor). Causes include erosive lesions (e.g., gastric or duodenal ulcers, esophagitis), vascular lesions (e.g., esophageal varices), malignancy, and trauma.

media.title: Management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Forrest classification of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhages

RF0l33.title: Lower gastrointestinal bleeding
RF0l33.description: Gastrointestinal bleeding that originates from the colon or rectum. Overt LGIB typically manifests with hematochezia and/or melena. Occult LGIB typically manifests with nonspecific symptoms due to iron deficiency anemia (e.g., fatigue, pallor). Causes include diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, and hemorrhoids.

media.title: Management of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding

jF0_33.title: Melena
jF0_33.description: Black, tarry stool. Results from the presence of hematin, which forms when heme is oxidized (e.g., by gastric acid). Most commonly caused by upper gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., peptic ulcer disease, esophageal varices, coagulopathies).

4F03R3.title: Double‑balloon enteroscopy
4F03R3.description: An enteroscopic technique for visualizing the entire small bowel. The device consists of an overtube and two balloons. With alternate insufflation and deflation of the balloons, the enteroscope and its overtube can be moved along the length of the small bowel.

OF0IR3.title: Capsule endoscopy
OF0IR3.description: A diagnostic procedure using a small (1-3 cm) wireless camera fitted inside a capsule that is swallowed by the patient to take pictures of the mucosa in the GI tract. Pictures are analyzed after the capsule is excreted 24–48 hours later.

5F0ii3.title: Maldigestion
5F0ii3.description: An inadequate breakdown of food in the intestinal lumen. Can be caused by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (e.g., due to decreased pancreatic enzyme secretion) and bile acid deficiency.

nF07i3.title: Whipple disease
nF07i3.description: A very rare, multisystem infectious disease caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei. Early manifestations include migrating polyarthralgias, fever, and fatigue. This is typically followed by gastrointestinal manifestations such as abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, and significant weight loss. Important extraintestinal symptoms include neurological symptoms, cardiac symptoms, and lymphadenopathy.

media.title: PAS-positive foam cells in Whipple's disease

oF00Q3.title: D-xylose absorption test
oF00Q3.description: A diagnostic tool for assessing the passive absorptive function of the upper small intestinal mucosa. Urine or serum D-xylose levels are measured 5 hours after oral administration of D-xylose. Low levels indicate insufficient absorption caused by damage to the intestinal mucosa (e.g., in celiac disease), and the test is considered positive.

KF0UQ3.title: Hydrogen breath tests
KF0UQ3.description: A set of noninvasive tests that measure breath hydrogen levels after the ingestion of specific sugar solutions (e.g., lactose, glucose, lactulose, fructose). Elevated breath hydrogen levels indicate carbohydrate malabsorption or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

6F0jQ3.title: Lactulose breath test
6F0jQ3.description: A test used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). The patient swallows an oral solution of lactulose. When bacteria are present, they break down the lactulose, generating hydrogen. An increase in exhaled hydrogen of ≥ 20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes confirms SIBO.

pF0LQ3.title: Glucose hydrogen breath test
pF0LQ3.description: A test used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. The patient swallows an oral glucose solution. Bacterial digestion of glucose creates hydrogen, and high breath hydrogen levels indicate higher levels of bacteria. An increase of exhaled hydrogen ≥ 20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes confirms SIBO.

qF0CQ3.title: Protein-losing enteropathy
qF0CQ3.description: A condition characterized by massive loss of protein that can occur as a complication of several gastrointestinal disorders, including inflammatory bowel disease, infection, and celiac disease. Characterized by hypoproteinemia and peripheral edema. Treatment involves managing the underlying disease and supportive care (e.g., nutritional support and correction of electrolyte abnormalities).

HF0Kj3.title: Acrodermatitis enteropathica
HF0Kj3.description: An autosomal recessive cause of congenital zinc deficiency. Results from a mutation in the gene for a transmembrane protein responsible for zinc uptake. Symptoms are typical of zinc deficiency, including periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea, and impaired wound healing.

sF0tj3.title: Lactose tolerance test
sF0tj3.description: A test used to diagnose lactose intolerance. Involves administering lactose and measuring the response in blood glucose levels. In the presence of lactase deficiency, lactose cannot be digested and glucose cannot be absorbed into the bloodstream; a decreased rise in glucose levels is considered pathologic. This test has been largely replaced by other alternatives (e.g., hydrogen breath test).

GF0Bj3.title: Acute mesenteric ischemia
GF0Bj3.description: Acute decrease in intestinal blood flow, usually due to thromboembolic occlusion of a mesenteric artery. A less common cause is vasospasm (non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia) in critically ill patients on vasopressors. The classic presentation is abdominal pain out of proportion to abdominal examination. Bowel infarction develops within 6 hours, resulting in bloody diarrhea, abdominal distention, and peritonitis.

tF0XP3.title: Chronic mesenteric ischemia
tF0XP3.description: A condition in which two or more major visceral arteries are narrowed or occluded, resulting in an inability of the blood supply to meet the metabolic needs of the visceral organs. It most commonly manifests as long-standing post-prandial abdominal pain with weight loss.

DF0143.title: Diverticulitis
DF0143.description: A condition of inflammation and/or infection of diverticula. Clinical features include low-grade fever, left lower quadrant pain, a tender, palpable abdominal mass, and changes in bowel habits. Can be complicated by an ileus, abscess formation, perforation, and peritonitis.

wF0h43.title: Pseudodiverticula
wF0h43.description: An outpouching in the wall of a hollow organ, most commonly the intestine, that forms when a layer of mucosa and submucosa herniate through the organ's muscular layer (i.e., the muscularis propria).

_F05k3.title: Toxic megacolon
_F05k3.description: A rare, life-threatening complication of colitis with acute dilation of the colon that presents with bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain and distention, and sepsis, increasing the risk of perforation. Causes include inflammatory bowel disease, pseudomembranous colitis, and infectious colitis.

zF0rk3.title: Crohn Disease Activity Index
zF0rk3.description: A tool used to assess the disease activity of Crohn disease. Calculated using variables such as the number of liquid stools per day, abdominal pain, and the presence of complications. Its use in clinical practice may be limited by its complexity but it is commonly used in clinical trials.

Z80ZO3.title: Pyoderma gangrenosum
Z80ZO3.description: An inflammatory skin condition characterized by a single or multiple rapidly progressive, painful skin ulcers with neutrophilic infiltration. Associated with autoimmune conditions (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis) and malignancies (e.g., hematologic malignancies).

080eO3.title: MRI enteroclysis
080eO3.description: An imaging technique that involves the administration of a contrast medium (e.g., mannitol solution) via a nasoduodenal tube, small bowel distention via an infusion pump, and magnetic resonance imaging. Used to assess for intestinal, perianal, and pelvic inflammation. Highly sensitive and specific for inflammatory bowel disease.

c80al3.title: Snail trails
c80al3.description: A physical examination finding characterized by longitudinal ulcerations in the oral mucosa. Associated with Crohn disease.

W80Pl3.title: Cobblestone sign
W80Pl3.description: Inflamed sections of mucosa with neighboring deep ulcerations that resemble uneven cobblestones. A characteristic finding on ileocolonoscopy in Crohn disease.

d80ol3.title: Skip lesions
d80ol3.description: A histopathologic finding of patchy, discontinuous inflammation (i.e., areas of inflammation interspersed with normal tissue). Seen in conditions such as Crohn disease and giant cell arteritis.

f80kN3.title: Microscopic colitis
f80kN3.description: An idiopathic inflammatory disease of the colon characterized by chronic, nonbloody, watery diarrhea; a normal-appearing bowel on colonoscopy; and collagenous or lymphocytic infiltrates on microscopy.

T806N3.title: Collagenous colitis
T806N3.description: A histological subtype of microscopic colitis characterized by the proliferation of collagenous connective tissue that forms a thick subepithelial collagen band.

g80FN3.title: Lymphocytic colitis
g80FN3.description: A histological subtype of microscopic colitis characterized by lymphocytic infiltrates and little to no proliferation of connective tissue.

S80yN3.title: 5-aminosalicylic acid derivatives
S80yN3.description: A group of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that include mesalazine, sulfasalazine, and olsalazine. Used to treat ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Available in oral and rectal suppository forms.

destinations.label: Ulcerative colitis → Pharmacological therapy for ulcerative colitis

R80lm3.title: Mesalamine
R80lm3.description: The active component of sulfasalazine. Used to treat inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease). Mechanism of action is unknown but thought to involve downregulation of the inflammatory and immune responses.

destinations.label: Ulcerative colitis → Pharmacological therapy for ulcerative colitis

i80Jm3.title: Sulfasalazine
i80Jm3.description: A pro-drug that is converted into the active metabolite, 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), which acts as an anti-inflammatory. It can be used to treat inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

destinations.label: Ulcerative colitis → Pharmacological therapy for ulcerative colitis

O80I53.title: Tubulovillous adenoma
O80I53.description: A colonic polyp that contains both tubular and villous cells. They are relatively uncommon (5–10%) but convey a risk of malignant transformation (~20%).

N80-53.title: Villous adenoma
N80-53.description: A rare (5–15%) form of adenomatous colonic polyp that shows finger-like projections lined by dysplastic epithelium on histology. These lesions are typically the largest of the adenomatous polyps, are most commonly found near the rectum, and generally sessile in appearance. Larger polyps can convey a risk of malignant transformation of up to 50%.

n807M3.title: Hereditary polyposis syndromes
n807M3.description: A group of conditions characterized by numerous gastrointestinal polyps and an increased risk of gastrointestinal and extraintestinal malignancy. More commonly inherited but can occur from de novo mutations.

L80wM3.title: Familial adenomatous polyposis
L80wM3.description: An autosomal dominant adenomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation in the APC tumor suppressor gene. Characterized by the presence of hundreds to thousands of adenomatous intestinal polyps that have a high potential for malignant transformation. Variants include attenuated FAP, Gardner syndrome, and Turcot syndrome.

K80Un3.title: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
K80Un3.description: An autosomal dominant, hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by the presence of polyps (typically < 20) throughout the gastrointestinal tract (mainly the jejunum). Associated with mutation of the STK11 gene on chromosome 19p13.3. Manifests with hematochezia, constipation, diarrhea, mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, and an increased risk of colorectal, ovarian, breast, and pancreatic cancer.

680jn3.title: Muir-Torre syndrome
680jn3.description: A phenotypic variant of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma syndrome (Lynch syndrome). Caused by mutations in the MLH1, MSH2, or MLH6 genes that are typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Causes the formation of several cutaneous tumors (e.g., sebaceous adenomas and carcinomas, keratoacanthomas) and visceral malignancies (e.g., colorectal, endometrial and ovarian, urothelial).

J80sn3.title: Fecal occult blood test
J80sn3.description: A test used to detect the presence of blood in feces that is not visibly apparent. Used as a screening tool for colorectal carcinoma, but upper gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., from a peptic ulcer) can also yield positive results. A positive result merits additional follow-up (e.g., upper endoscopy, colonoscopy). This test has poor sensitivity for detecting polyps.

7804L3.title: Small-bowel cancer
7804L3.description: A neoplasia of the small bowel. Clinical signs are often nonspecific and include a change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, and weight loss. Represents < 5% of all gastrointestinal cancers.

H80KL3.title: FOLFOX
H80KL3.description: A chemotherapy regimen consisting of leucovorin calcium (folinic acid; FOL), fluorouracil (F), and oxaliplatin (OX) that is used to treat advanced colorectal cancer. Common adverse effects include sensory neuropathy, pancytopenia, fatigue, and nausea.

s80tL3.title: FOLFIRI
s80tL3.description: A chemotherapy regimen consisting of leucovorin calcium (folinic acid; FOL), fluorouracil (F), and irinotecan (IRI) used to treat advanced colorectal and gastric cancer. Common adverse effects include pancytopenia, fatigue, and nausea.

G80BL3.title: XELOX
G80BL3.description: A chemotherapy regimen consisting of capecitabine (XEL) and oxaliplatin (OX). Used to treat advanced colorectal cancer. Common adverse effects include sensory neuropathy, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.

v80Ao3.title: Cullen sign
v80Ao3.description: A physical examination characterized by periumbilical ecchymosis and bluish-red discoloration. Can be seen in any disease that causes retroperitoneal hemorrhage (e.g., ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm). Classically associated with pancreatitis.

D801K3.title: Grey Turner sign
D801K3.description: A physical examination finding of flank ecchymosis due to retroperitoneal bleeding that dissects through fascial planes. Can be seen in any disease that causes retroperitoneal hemorrhage (e.g., ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm). Classically associated with pancreatitis.

w80hK3.title: Fox sign
w80hK3.description: A physical examination finding characterized by ecchymosis over the inguinal ligament. Associated with acute pancreatitis.

C80qK3.title: Ranson criteria
C80qK3.description: A scoring system used to predict severity and prognosis in acute pancreatitis. Five factors (age, WBC, blood glucose, serum LDH, and AST) are evaluated on admission and six factors (hematocrit decrease, BUN increase, calcium, blood oxygenation, estimated amount of third space fluid, and base deficit) are evaluated after 48 hours.

destinations.label: Acute pancreatitis → Severity grading and prognostic scores

x80EK3.title: Pancreatic pseudocyst
x80EK3.description: A fluid collection that is rich in pancreatic enzymes surrounded by a nonepithelialized wall consisting of fibrin and granulation tissue. Usually occurs several weeks after pancreatitis. Thought to occur due to disruptions of the pancreatic duct from pancreatitis and extravasation of pancreatic enzymes.

B80zK3.title: Courvoisier’s sign
B80zK3.description: The finding of painless obstructive jaundice and a palpable, nontender gallbladder should be presumed to be due to an obstructive pancreatic, periampullary, or biliary malignancy until proven otherwise.

-80D63.title: Double-duct sign
-80D63.description: A radiologic sign suggestive of bile drainage blockage (e.g., from tumors of the pancreatic head) in both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct, leading to dilation of both structures on imaging.

media.title: Double duct sign in pancreatic head carcinoma

au0Qp3.title: Celiac ganglion block
au0Qp3.description: A procedure used to treat severe visceral pain. Most commonly performed using CT-guided radiologic or endosonographic transgastric puncture of the celiac ganglion. After instillation of a test dose of local anesthetic, 95% ethanol is used to destroy the nerve tissue.

bu0Hp3.title: Jaundice
bu0Hp3.description: A yellowish discoloration of the skin, sclerae, and mucous membranes due to the deposition of bilirubin.

1u02J3.title: Scleral icterus
1u02J3.description: A yellowing of the whites of the eyes resulting from an increased serum bilirubin (at least 2.5 mg/dL) of any etiology (e.g., cholestasis, biliary conjugation defects, advanced cirrhosis, acute liver failure).

du0oJ3.title: Pseudojaundice
du0oJ3.description: A yellowish discoloration of the skin due to deposition of carotene in the skin following excessive consumption of fruits and vegetables rich in carotene or multivitamin supplements. Does not lead to scleral icterus. Can also refer to yellowish skin discoloration from rifabutin therapy.

Vu0GJ3.title: Cholestasis
Vu0GJ3.description: A condition that impairs bile production or secretion (nonobstructive intrahepatic cholestasis), causes biliary obstruction within the liver (obstructive intrahepatic cholestasis), or causes biliary obstruction between the liver and the duodenum (obstructive extrahepatic or posthepatic cholestasis). Manifestations include jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus, and symptoms of fat malabsorption (e.g., steatorrhea, weight loss). Diagnostic workup includes liver function tests (particularly alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and bilirubin) and imaging.

2u0Tq3.title: AST/ALT ratio
2u0Tq3.description: A measure commonly used to determine the etiology of hepatocellular injury.

fu0kq3.title: Double-barrel shotgun sign
fu0kq3.description: An echographic sign that indicates dilation of the intrahepatic common bile duct (CBD) and suggests biliary obstruction. The dilated CBD runs parallel to the portal veins through the liver, resulting in the appearance of a double-barrel shotgun.

media.title: Dilated intrahepatic bile ducts (double-barrel shotgun sign)

Su0yq3.title: Indirect bilirubin
Su0yq3.description: A water-insoluble byproduct of hemoglobin degradation. Serum concentrations increase in the setting of impaired conjugation, hemolysis, and ineffective erythropoiesis.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Metabolism of erythrocytes

3u0SI3.title: Direct bilirubin
3u0SI3.description: A water-soluble product formed by addition of glucuronic acid to indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin in the liver. Serum concentrations increase in the setting of biliary tract obstruction.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Metabolism of erythrocytes

Ru0lI3.title: Urobilinogen
Ru0lI3.description: A breakdown product of bilirubin that results from bacterial reduction of bilirubin in the intestines. Approximately 50% is reabsorbed by the intestines, and 50% is further metabolized and excreted in feces. Urobilinogen is water soluble and can also be excreted in the urine.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Metabolism of erythrocytes

ju0_I3.title: Intrahepatic jaundice
ju0_I3.description: A type of jaundice caused by decreased excretion and/or impaired hepatic reuptake of bilirubin. Etiologies include hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hereditary hyperbilirubinemia (e.g., Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome).

Ou0Ir3.title: Cardiac cirrhosis
Ou0Ir3.description: A complication of right-sided heart failure characterized by cirrhosis due to chronic hepatic vein congestion. Associated with "nutmeg liver" (diffuse mottling on imaging due to ischemia and fatty degeneration).

lu0vr3.title: Child-Pugh score
lu0vr3.description: A prognostic grading scale for cirrhosis. Scored on the basis of bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, and degree of ascites and encephalopathy. Graded A (mild), B (moderate), and C (severe).

nu0773.title: Spider angiomata
nu0773.description: A small (< 1 cm), subcutaneous, vascular lesion composed of a central arteriole from which multiple, small vessels radiate outward, resembling the shape of a spider. Typically distributed on the neck, shoulders, and chest and blanches with pressure. Typically occurs in patients with hyperestrogenic conditions (e.g., chronic liver failure, pregnancy).

pu0LH3.title: Hepatorenal syndrome
pu0LH3.description: Kidney injury in patients with cirrhosis. May be further differentiated into acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) and non-acute kidney injury (HRS-NAKI). Patients with HRS have a poor prognosis and a liver transplant is the only curative treatment.

su0ts3.title: Hepatitis B serology
su0ts3.description: Serological testing in the assessment for HBV infection. The initial tests obtained are HBsAg, anti-HBc titers, and anti-HBs titers. If results indicate infection, HBeAg, anti-HBe, and HBV DNA are measured to assess disease activity.

media.title: Serology time course of acute and resolved hepatitis B infection

Gu0Bs3.title: Interface hepatitis
Gu0Bs3.description: A histopathologic finding characterized by periportal liver cell necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration. Indicates chronic active hepatitis.

media.title: Liver cirrhosis in chronic hepatitis B

Fu0gG3.title: Ground glass hepatocytes
Fu0gG3.description: A histopathological hallmark of hepatitis B infection characterized by hepatocytes with swollen, transparent cytoplasm. Caused by hyperplasia of the endoplasmic reticulum due to increased production of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Eu08G3.title: Hepatitis D virus
Eu08G3.description: A virusoid, defective enveloped virus with a circular RNA. The hepatitis D (Delta) virus (HDV) can only cause infection if cells are coinfected with Hepatitis B virus (HBV), which provides the HbsAg (a process called complementation).

destinations.label: Overview of viral hepatitides → Hepatitis D

vu0AG3.title: Acute hepatitis C infection
vu0AG3.description: The initial period of hepatitis C infection (i.e., 6 months after exposure). Can resolve spontaneously or progress to chronic infection (75-85% of cases). Patients may be asymptomatic or develop manifestations of acute viral hepatitis and impaired liver function.

Du01t3.title: Chronic hepatitis C infection
Du01t3.description: A hepatitis C infection that persists for ≥ 6 months after initial exposure. Can result in cirrhosis and liver cancer. Patients may be asymptomatic or develop manifestations of chronic liver disease and/or impaired liver function.

9u0Nt3.title: Direct-acting antivirals
9u0Nt3.description: A class of drugs used to treat hepatitis C infection. These drugs inhibit specific components of the viral replication cycle, including NS3/4A protease, NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and NS5A protein.

Cu0qt3.title: Hepatic steatosis
Cu0qt3.description: The accumulation of triglycerides and other fats in hepatocytes, leading to microvesicular and macrovesicular steatotic changes, which can be seen on histopathology. Etiologies include harmful alcohol use (alcohol-associated liver disease), diet (e.g., protein-energy malnutrition), drug-induced changes (e.g., due to amiodarone, corticosteroids), and genetic predisposition (e.g., metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease). Hepatic steatosis can lead to cirrhosis.

xu0Et3.title: Steatohepatitis
xu0Et3.description: Hepatic inflammation caused by the accumulation of fat. Most commonly due to heavy alcohol use and/or metabolic syndrome. Characteristic histological findings include hepatocyte ballooning and Mallory bodies. Fibrosis may be present.

Bu0zt3.title: Alcohol-associated steatohepatitis
Bu0zt3.description: Hepatocellular injury and degeneration caused by chronic harmful alcohol use. Characteristic histological features include hepatocyte ballooning and neutrophil-mediated inflammation of the parenchyma, with possible formation of Mallory‐Denk bodies. Fibrosis may be present.

Au0RF3.title: Alcohol-associated steatosis
Au0RF3.description: A potentially reversible manifestation of alcohol-associated liver disease caused by chronic harmful alcohol use. Often asymptomatic, but hepatomegaly may be present. Imaging may show steatotic infiltration of the liver (i.e., hepatic steatosis).

_u05F3.title: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis
_u05F3.description: A subtype of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease characterized by chronic hepatocyte inflammation and damage due to lipid accumulation, with a high risk of progression to fibrosis and cirrhosis. Patients are typically asymptomatic. Previously referred to as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

destinations.label: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease → Definitions

0E0e83.title: Zieve syndrome
0E0e83.description: A rare condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, hyperlipidemia, and jaundice that can occur in individuals with alcohol-associated liver disease.

aE0Q83.title: Ursodeoxycholic acid
aE0Q83.description: A bile acid that inhibits intestinal absorption of cholesterol and reduces hepatic synthesis and secretion of endogenous cholesterol. Can be used to treat primary biliary cholangitis because of its antiapoptotic and immunomodulatory effects. Also used for nonsurgical treatment of cholesterol gallstones.

1E02u3.title: Portosystemic anastomosis
1E02u3.description: A type of anastomosis between veins of the portal circulation and the systemic circulation. In portal hypertension, these anastomoses become distended (varices) in an attempt to relieve increased intraluminal pressure. Portosystemic anastomosis can, e.g., involve the left gastric and azygos veins (esophageal varices), paraumbilical and epigastric veins (caput medusae), and superior rectal and middle and inferior rectal veins (rectal varices).

destinations.label: Abdominal cavity → Important anastomoses and collateral circulation

dE0ou3.title: Caput medusae
dE0ou3.description: A pathognomonic sign of portal hypertension characterized by the presence of engorged, tortuous paraumbilical veins. Caused by the portosystemic shunting of blood between the portal paraumbilical veins and the systemic superficial epigastric veins. Obstruction of the vena cava is an uncommon cause of caput medusae.

destinations.label: Abdominal cavity → Important anastomoses and collateral circulation

UE0bE3.title: Esophageal variceal hemorrhage
UE0bE3.description: Bleeding from dilated submucosal veins (varices) in the distal esophagus due to portal hypertension. The most common form of upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in patients with cirrhosis.

destinations.label: Esophageal varices → Management of esophageal variceal hemorrhage

fE0kE3.title: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt
fE0kE3.description: Implantation of a stent between a hepatic vein radicle and an intrahepatic branch of the portal vein to decrease portal venous pressure in patients with portal hypertension.

RE0lv3.title: Distal splenorenal shunt
RE0lv3.description: A surgical end-to-side anastomosis between the distal end of the splenic vein and the left renal vein. DSRS prevents increased pressure within the portal vein from being transmitted to the gastroesophageal collaterals. Used for secondary prophylaxis of recurrent variceal bleeding. Associated with a lower risk of hepatic encephalopathy than other types of portal shunts (portal venous drainage to the liver remains largely intact).

QE0uv3.title: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
QE0uv3.description: A bacterial infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of other intraabdominal causes. Most often seen in patients with liver cirrhosis. Defined as > 250 granulocytes/mm³ ascitic fluid.

lE0vD3.title: Metastatic liver disease
lE0vD3.description: The presence of metastases in the liver, usually originating from the colon, stomach, pancreas, lung, or breast. Liver metastases are more common than primary liver tumors.

mE0Vw3.title: Apoceruloplasmin
mE0Vw3.description: The major carrier of copper in the blood and an important enzyme with ferroxidase activity. Ceruloplasmin is synthesized by hepatocytes and secreted into the blood. When ceruloplasmin is bound to copper, it is called holoceruloplasmin. When it is not bound to copper, it is called apoceruloplasmin.

ME0Mw3.title: Trientine hydrochloride
ME0Mw3.description: A copper chelating agent that induces urinary excretion of copper (cupriuresis). Indicated for treatment of Wilson disease if penicillamine cannot be used.

KE0U93.title: Cardiac asthma
KE0U93.description: A manifestation of congestive heart failure that mimics asthma, with shortness of breath, wheezing, and coughing. The underlying mechanism is increased capillary pressure in the bronchial arteries, which leads to airway compression and bronchospasm.

pE0L93.title: Heart failure cells
pE0L93.description: A type of macrophage filled with hemosiderin due to the phagocytosis of blood that has leaked into the lungs. Associated with pulmonary congestion caused by congestive heart failure.

JE0s93.title: Nutmeg liver
JE0s93.description: A macroscopic or radiographic finding in patients with cardiac cirrhosis or Budd-Chiari syndrome where the liver resembles a grated nutmeg seed (diffuse mottling on imaging). Caused by ischemia and fatty degeneration from hepatic venous congestion.

IE0YC3.title: Hepatic venous congestion
IE0YC3.description: A state of increased pressure and impaired drainage in the hepatic venous system that can lead to hepatic injury (congestive hepatopathy) and progress to cirrhosis, which is referred to as cardiac cirrhosis if the underlying cause is right-sided heart failure.

7E04C3.title: Clinical features of right-sided heart failure
7E04C3.description: Features include peripheral pitting edema, abdominal pain and jaundice (from hepatic venous congestion), hepatojugular reflux, hepatosplenomegaly, and jugular venous distention.

HE0KC3.title: NYHA functional classification
HE0KC3.description: A staging system used to classify the severity of heart failure. The four stages (NYHA I-IV) classify patients based on the severity of symptoms, from no symptoms (Class I) to severe limitations in daily life (Class IV). An additional stage, NYHA V, is sometimes used for patients with an otherwise undetermined class of heart failure.

GE0BC3.title: Brain natriuretic peptide
GE0BC3.description: A hormone with vasodilator and diuretic properties that is secreted by cardiomyocytes. Production is increased during cardiomyocyte stretch and ventricular wall stress. Causes of elevated BNP include heart failure, renal failure, and atrial fibrillation.

tE0Xx3.title: Hepatojugular reflux
tE0Xx3.description: A clinical sign in which jugular venous pressure increases on applying pressure over the liver (right hypochondrium) for 10-15 seconds. In healthy individuals, a mild increase in JVP (approx. 1 cm H₂O) occurs with this maneuver. In states of fluid overload or right heart failure, an increase in JVP that is > 3 cm H₂O occurs and it persists for > 15 seconds. In patients with IVC obstruction (e.g., Budd-Chiari syndrome), the hepatojugular reflux is characteristically absent.

media.title: Testing the Hepatojugular Reflux - Clinical Examination

8E0Ox3.title: NT-proBNP
8E0Ox3.description: An inert biomarker that is used in the diagnosis and monitoring of heart failure. It is produced in cardiomyocytes from the cleaving of the prohormone proBNP into BNP and NT-proBNP. Production is increased during cardiomyocyte stretch and ventricular wall stress. Elevated levels are suggestive of heart failure. Recommended cut-off levels vary according to heart failure acuity and patient age.

uE0px3.title: Chest x-ray findings in cardiogenic pulmonary edema
uE0px3.description: Findings include enlarged heart shadow, Kerley B lines, prominent pulmonary vessels, bilateral pleural effusions, and peribronchial cuffing.

EE08x3.title: Heart transplantation
EE08x3.description: The transplantation of a heart from a deceased donor. Indicated in patients with end-stage heart failure, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, and certain congenital heart defects. Complications include graft rejection, post-transplant infection, and pulmonary hypertension.

vE0Ax3.title: Pulmonary edema
vE0Ax3.description: The accumulation of fluid in the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli. Causes can be cardiogenic (e.g., secondary to acute heart failure) or noncardiogenic (e.g., ARDS). Typically manifests with cough, progressive dyspnea, signs of hypoxia, and dullness and rales on pulmonary examination.

DE01B3.title: Bradyarrhythmias
DE01B3.description: A heart rate of less than 60 beats/min in adults. Children have their own age-specific values for the minimum heart frequency. Bradyarrhythmias may be atrial in origin (e.g. respiratory sinus arrhythmia, sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial pause or arrest, and tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome) or may originate in the AV node (e.g. atrioventricular block).

media.title: Sinus block (variant of sinus node dysfunction)

wE0hB3.title: Supraventricular arrhythmias
wE0hB3.description: A group of tachyarrhythmias that originate in the atria or AV node (i.e., above the ventricles). Typically characterized by a narrow QRS complex, although this can be wide if there is aberrant conduction (including accessory pathways). Examples include AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia, junctional tachycardia, as well as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter.

CE0qB3.title: Ventricular arrhythmias
CE0qB3.description: A group of tachyarrhythmias that originate below the atrioventricular node. Includes ventricular ectopics (premature ventricular contractions), ventricular tachycardia (monomorphic or polymorphic), ventricular flutter, and ventricular fibrillation.

AE0Ry3.title: Adenosine
AE0Ry3.description: A class V anti-arrhythmic drug that causes a short-term heart block by slowing down conduction in the atrioventricular node. In reference to molecular biology, it is also a nucleoside unit in RNA that is derived from the purine adenine.

zE0ry3.title: Antiarrhythmic drugs
zE0ry3.description: Group of drugs that are used to restore sinus rhythm in patients presenting with cardiac arrhythmias, as well as to prevent recurrent arrhythmias. Antiarrhythmic agents are classified into 5 classes according to their electrophysiological effect on the myocardium (i.e., sodium channel blocker, beta blocker, potassium channel blocker, calcium channel blocker, and others). Because all antiarrhythmic drugs are potentially proarrhythmic, they should be administered under ECG monitoring.

Zv0ZA3.title: Quinidine
Zv0ZA3.description: A class Ia antiarrhythmic that blocks cardiac sodium channels and prolongs the action potential duration through prolongation of the QT and QRS segments. Used to treat ventricular arrhythmias.

av0QA3.title: Ivabradine
av0QA3.description: A drug that decreases the funny current in pacemaker cells by blocking the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel. It decreases myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing heart rate in a dose-dependent manner but it does not affect heart contractility. It is used to treat chronic stable angina in patients who cannot take beta blockers, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

Xv09A3.title: Holiday heart syndrome
Xv09A3.description: An abnormal heart rhythm (usually atrial fibrillation) that is classically triggered by excessive alcohol consumption, though it may also be caused by stress, dehydration, and/or lack of sleep.

cv0a_3.title: Valvular atrial fibrillation
cv0a_3.description: A term previously used to categorize atrial fibrillation occurring in patients with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves. These valvulopathies significantly increase the risk of thromboembolism.

ev0x_3.title: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
ev0x_3.description: Atrial fibrillation with a heart rate > 100–110/minute.

media.title: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

2v0Tz3.title: Atrial flutter
2v0Tz3.description: A supraventricular tachyarrhythmia usually caused by a single macroreentrant rhythm within the atria that is classically characterized on ECG by the sawtooth appearance of P waves, also known as "flutter waves", with narrow QRS complexes.

media.title: Atrial flutter with variable atrioventricular (AV) block

Tv06z3.title: Cardioversion
Tv06z3.description: The restoration of normal heart rhythm in patients with tachycardia or arrhythmia using electric current (electric cardioversion) or drugs (chemical cardioversion).

gv0Fz3.title: Pharmacologic cardioversion
gv0Fz3.description: A therapy used to restore sinus rhythm in patients with arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia and ventricular tachycardia. Common antiarrhythmic drugs that are used include flecainide, propafenone, ibutilide, and dofetilide. Less effective than electrical cardioversion (external direct current).

Sv0yz3.title: Pill in the pocket
Sv0yz3.description: A pharmacological treatment regime for paroxysmal tachyarrhythmias. At the onset of symptoms, patients self-administer a single dose of a rapid-acting antiarrhythmic (e.g., flecainide) to terminate the episode.

hv0c-3.title: Electrical cardioversion
hv0c-3.description: The application of electrical current to convert cardiac arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia) to a normal sinus rhythm. In contrast to defibrillation, the electrical current delivered is low-energy and synchronized to the QRS complex.

destinations.label: Management of tachycardia → Unstable tachycardia with pulse

media.title: Placement of paddles for defibrillation or electrical cardioversion
Placement of adhesive electrode pads for defibrillation, electrical cardioversion, or transcutaneous pacing

Rv0l-3.title: CHA2DS2-VASc score
Rv0l-3.description: A score used to assess thromboembolic risk and the risk for stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Also an acronym for the risk factors. Major risk factors count for two points (indicated in the subscript of the acronym): Age ≥ 75 years; Stroke, transient ischemic attack, or thromboembolism. Other risk factors count for one point each: Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Diabetes mellitus, Vascular disease (prior MI, peripheral artery disease, or aortic plaque), Age 65–74 years, Sex category (female sex).

Qv0u-3.title: Valsalva maneuver
Qv0u-3.description: Forced exhalation against a closed upper airway (i.e., mouth, nose, and/or glottis). Has multiple effects throughout the body (e.g., a reduction in cardiac output and heart rate; stimulation of the vagus nerve; increased intrathoracic, intra-abdominal, and intracranial pressure). Can be used in the diagnosis (e.g., pelvic organ prolapse, abdominal hernia, Chiari malformation) and treatment (e.g., Eustachian tube dysfunction, supraventricular tachycardia) of several conditions.

jv0_-3.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
jv0_-3.description: A congenital condition characterized by intermittent tachycardia and a ventricular pre-excitation pattern on ECG, which both arise from an accessory pathway, known as the “bundle of Kent,” that connects the atria and ventricles, bypassing the AV node. Typical resting ECG findings include a shortened PR interval and a "slurred" upstroke in the QRS complex, called a "delta wave."

kv0mZR.title: Delta wave (ECG)
kv0mZR.description: A slurred upstroke in the QRS complex that appears as a triangle or delta on ECG. Caused by pre-excitation of the ventricles (e.g., from Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome).

Ov0IZR.title: Bigeminy
Ov0IZR.description: An ECG finding in which every normal complex is followed by a premature complex, which are most commonly ventricular (wide QRS complex) but may also be atrial (narrow QRS complex).

mv0V0R.title: R-on-T phenomenon
mv0V0R.description: A phenomenon seen on ECG in which a premature ventricular complex occurs in the downslope of the preceding T wave. May initiate sustained ventricular tachycardia.

nv070R.title: Torsades de pointes
nv070R.description: A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a shifting ECG axis that is triggered by early afterdepolarizations of the left ventricle in patients with a prolonged QTc interval. Associated with electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia), certain drugs, and congenital heart disease. It often reverts spontaneously to sinus rhythm but a life-threatening ventricular fibrillation may sometimes develop.

destinations.label: Management of tachycardia → Stable wide-complex tachycardia

media.title: Comparison of monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT), including torsades de pointes

Kv0UaR.title: Ventricular flutter
Kv0UaR.description: An arrhythmia originating in the ventricles and characterized on EGG by a regular, sinusoidal waveform ~300/minute. Often progresses to life-threatening ventricular fibrillation.

Jv0saR.title: Atherosclerosis
Jv0saR.description: The formation of lipid, cholesterol, and/or calcium-laden plaques within the tunica intima of the arterial wall, which can restrict blood flow. Rupture can cause intraluminal thrombosis that results in myocardial infarction, unstable angina, and/or ischemic stroke.

qv0CaR.title: Coronary artery disease
qv0CaR.description: Atherosclerotic changes in the epicardial coronary arteries that can reduce myocardial blood supply and lead to myocardial ischemia. Clinical presentations include stable coronary artery disease and acute coronary syndrome.

media.title: Types of plaques in coronary artery disease

Iv0YYR.title: Risk factors for atherosclerosis
Iv0YYR.description: A set of patient characteristics and comorbidities associated with the development of atherosclerosis. These factors include advanced age, male sex, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, smoking history, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, obesity, and known inflammatory states.

Fv0gbR.title: Foam cells
Fv0gbR.description: Macrophages that become filled with lipids (e.g., cholesterol from oxidized LDL), giving them a "foamy" appearance. Foam cells can be found in various diseases (e.g., atherosclerosis, Niemann-Pick disease).

8v0ObR.title: Fatty streaks
8v0ObR.description: A macroscopically visible type of atherosclerotic lesion. Mainly formed by foam cells located within the intima of vessels and extracellular droplets of lipid.

Ev08bR.title: Angina pectoris
Ev08bR.description: A condition characterized by paroxysmal attacks of retrosternal chest discomfort, tightness, or pressure due to myocardial ischemia. Most commonly occurs in individuals with coronary heart disease. Triggers include exertion and stress, which result in increased myocardial oxygen demand.

Dv01XR.title: Vasospastic angina
Dv01XR.description: A condition characterized by episodic chest pain caused by coronary artery spasm. Symptoms can occur at rest. Triggers include smoking, stimulants (e.g., cocaine), triptans, alcohol, and stress. Associated with reversible ST elevations on ECG. Does not cause an increase in serum concentrations of cardiac biomarkers.

destinations.label: Chronic coronary disease → Ischemia with nonobstructive coronary arteries (INOCA)

xv0EXR.title: Cardiac stress test
xv0EXR.description: Cardiac stress testing is an umbrella term for diagnostic studies that evaluate cardiac function using ECG or cardiac imaging while stress is induced in the heart. Imaging modalities include echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging, and cardiac MRI. Cardiac stress testing is most commonly used to assess for stress-induced cardiac ischemia.

yv0dcR.title: Radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging
yv0dcR.description: A nuclear scan that utilizes a radioactive tracer to evaluate myocardial viability, detect ischemia, and assess perfusion and left ventricular function during rest or exercise. Techniques include single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and positron emission tomography (PET).

destinations.label: Coronary artery disease → Cardiac stress testing

_v05cR.title: Hibernating myocardium
_v05cR.description: A state in which myocardial tissue exhibits abnormal contractility due to repetitive or persistent ischemia. Myocardium can regain function when adequate oxygen supply is restored. May be seen in patients with angina pectoris, dysfunction of the left ventricle, and/or heart failure.

aD0Q1R.title: Unstable angina
aD0Q1R.description: A form of acute coronary syndrome. Characterized by symptoms typical of myocardial infarction (≥ 20 min) at rest or after minimal exertion. In contrast to NSTEMI, troponin levels are normal. Angina is also considered unstable if the symptoms appear after a recent myocardial infarction, for the first time (new-onset angina), or increase in frequency or duration (crescendo angina).

XD091R.title: Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
XD091R.description: A myocardial infarction that is not associated with elevation of the ST segment on ECG but manifests with rest angina or other typical symptoms that last > 20 minutes and a rise in troponins. Usually the result of a small subendocardial infarction. ECG can be normal or associated with changes of myocardial ischemia (e.g., ST depression, T wave inversion).

1D02WR.title: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
1D02WR.description: Acute myocardial infarction characterized by persistent ST-segment elevation in at least two contiguous leads on ECG.

media.title: Acute anterior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
Inferior myocardial infarction with anterior ST-elevations
Management of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

eD0xWR.title: Cardiac biomarkers
eD0xWR.description: A group of cardiac-specific and nonspecific proteins that are released when cardiac myocytes undergo stress or injury. Examples include troponin T, high-sensitivity troponin, BNP, NT-proBNP, CK-MB, and myoglobin.

UD0bdR.title: Troponin T/I
UD0bdR.description: A group of muscle proteins found in skeletal and cardiac muscle that are involved in muscle contraction. In acute myocardial injury, troponins and other cardiac biomarkers are released into the blood. Used as a highly sensitive and specific biomarker for cardiac muscle cell death (e.g., from myocardial ischemia in acute myocardial infarction).

media.title: Cardiac enzymes and biomarkers in myocardial infarction

fD0kdR.title: Myoglobin
fD0kdR.description: An iron- and oxygen-binding protein found in muscle tissue. Presence in the blood or urine can indicate muscle injury (e.g., in rhabdomyolysis or infarction). High concentrations can cause acute kidney injury.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve

TD06dR.title: Creatine kinase-muscle/brain
TD06dR.description: An enzyme present in myocardial cells that is released into the serum when myocardial cells are damaged (e.g., acute myocardial infarction, myocarditis). Used as a cardiac biomarker that can help diagnose acute MI, in which levels typically rise 3–12 hours after an infarction, peak at 12–24 hours, and normalize after 2–3 days, making it a good marker for evaluation of myocardial reinfarction as well.

SD0ydR.title: Costochondral junction syndrome
SD0ydR.description: A rare condition characterized by painful swelling of the costosternal, sternoclavicular, and/or costochondral joints (usually only one area is involved). Most commonly affects young adults.

hD0cVR.title: Ventricular aneurysm
hD0cVR.description: A focal enlargement and/or bulge in the cardiac ventricle caused by thinning of the myocardium, most commonly secondary to myocardial infarction. Can lead to life-threatening complications such as ventricular rupture, thromboembolism, acute cerebrovascular accident (stroke), and heart failure.

jD0_VR.title: Erythema marginatum
jD0_VR.description: A dermatologic manifestation of rheumatic fever. Appears as a centrifugally expanding pink or light red rash with a well-defined outer border and central clearing. The trunk and limbs are affected, while the face is spared. May rapidly appear and disappear at different locations. Painless and nonpruritic.

lD0veR.title: Anitschkow cells
lD0veR.description: An enlarged macrophage found within Aschoff bodies in patients with rheumatic heart disease. Characterized by an ovoid nucleus containing a wavy, caterpillar-like bar of chromatin.

ND0-eR.title: Aschoff bodies
ND0-eR.description: A histologic finding in myocardial biopsies associated with rheumatic fever. Characterized by granulomatous foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by multinucleated giant cells (Aschoff cells) and other inflammatory cells.

mD0VUR.title: HACEK organisms
mD0VUR.description: A group of fastidious organisms that are normally part of the oral and pharyngeal flora. Members of this group include species of the Haemophilus genus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae. HACEK organisms can cause infective endocarditis.

5D0iUR.title: Janeway lesions
5D0iUR.description: Nontender erythematous macules and papules on the palms and soles that can occur in infective endocarditis. The lesions are thought to be caused by septic embolization from the infected valve.

nD07UR.title: Osler nodes
nD07UR.description: A dermatologic finding of painful subcutaneous nodules on the pads of the fingers and toes that typically develop in association with infective endocarditis. Caused by immune complex-mediated vasculitis that most likely occurs as a sequela of microthrombi occluding the vasculature.

oD002R.title: Subacute endocarditis
oD002R.description: Form of endocarditis in which typically mild constitutional symptoms (low fever, mild fatigue) develop over a period of weeks to months. Most commonly caused by viridans streptococci species and generally affects individuals with pre-existing damage to the heart valves, structural heart defects, or the presence of prosthetic valves.

pD0L2R.title: Modified Duke criteria
pD0L2R.description: A set of diagnostic criteria for infective endocarditis. Replaced by the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria, which are more comprehensive (e.g., additional imaging modalities) and have higher sensitivity.

8D0OTR.title: Libman-Sacks endocarditis
8D0OTR.description: A form of noninfectious endocarditis seen in systemic lupus erythematosus. Can result in the formation of systemic emboli, leading to hemorrhages under the nails, skin, and retina.

vD0ATR.title: Prophylaxis for endocarditis
vD0ATR.description: The administration of antibiotics prior to procedures with a high risk of bacteremia (e.g., dental procedures) in order to prevent infective endocarditis. Recommended only for certain procedures in selected high-risk patients.

wD0hgR.title: Pericarditis
wD0hgR.description: An inflammation of the pericardium. Etiologies include infection, complications of myocardial infarction, and systemic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Manifestations include fever, pleuritic chest pain, and a pericardial friction rub heard on auscultation.

CD0qgR.title: Constrictive pericarditis
CD0qgR.description: A condition characterized by chronic pericardial inflammation with subsequent thickening and rigidity of the pericardium, which results in decreased ventricular compliance and diastolic heart failure. Causes include idiopathic or viral pericarditis, radiotherapy, cardiac surgery, connective tissue diseases, and tuberculosis. Manifestations include fatigue, dyspnea, jugular vein distention (with a prominent y descent), peripheral edema, Kussmaul sign, pulsus paradoxus, and a pericardial knock.

yD0dSR.title: Prosthetic heart valve
yD0dSR.description: A device implanted to replace a patient's native heart valve. Includes mechanical valves, which are entirely artificial, and bioprosthetic valves, which are xenografts created from animal tissue.

AD0RSR.title: Mechanical prosthetic valve
AD0RSR.description: A nonbiological replacement cardiac valve. Placed via an open surgical procedure in which a valve is replaced with mechanical valve leaflets made of titanium or carbon attached to an artificial outer ring. Compared to biological prosthetic valves, mechanical prosthetic valves have a longer lifespan and require lifelong anticoagulation. Typically used in patients < 65 years of age and previously anticoagulated patients.

_D05SR.title: Biological prosthetic valve
_D05SR.description: A replacement cardiac valve typically made from either bovine (cow) or porcine (pig) material. In contrast to mechanical valves, biological prosthetic valves degrade more quickly due to sclerotic generation but require only temporary anticoagulation. Typically used in patients > 65 years of age, patients with a high risk of bleeding (contraindication for anticoagulation), and women with a desire to have children.

-D0DSR.title: de Musset's sign
-D0DSR.description: A physical exam finding consisting of head bobbing (or rhythmic nodding) in synchrony with the patient's pulse. It is considered a symptom of high pulse pressure and is associated with aortic regurgitation.

Zw0ZhR.title: Austin Flint murmur
Zw0ZhR.description: A low-pitched, rumbling, mid-to-late diastolic murmur at the apex that is heard in some patients with aortic regurgitation. Occurs because of the regurgitant jet of blood from the aortic valve. It was initially thought to cause a functional mitral stenosis, however most studies with Echo have shown the murmur is from the jet hitting the left ventricular free wall.

Yw0nhR.title: Quincke sign
Yw0nhR.description: A capillary pulse visible as alternating blanching and erythema of the nailbed. Tested by applying gentle pressure on the edge of the nail. Seen in patients with severe aortic insufficiency.

1w023R.title: Secondary hypertension
1w023R.description: Hypertension due to an identifiable cause. Accounts for 5–15% of cases of hypertension.
