Important causes include renal disease, renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism, hyperaldosteronism, hypercortisolism, obstructive sleep apnea, raised intracranial pressure, and certain drugs (e.g., sympathomimetics).

Ww0P3R.title: Renal hypertension
Ww0P3R.description: A type of secondary arterial hypertension caused by decreased renal perfusion (e.g., in renal failure or renal artery stenosis), which in turn leads to increased secretion of renin and activation of the renin angiotensin aldosterone pathway.

dw0o3R.title: Endocrine hypertension
dw0o3R.description: A term used to describe secondary arterial hypertension caused by a range of endocrine disorders, including primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, and thyroid disorders.

Vw0G3R.title: Hypertensive urgency
Vw0G3R.description: An increase in blood pressure > 180/120 mm Hg without symptoms or signs of organ damage.

ew0x3R.title: Hypertensive emergency
ew0x3R.description: An increase in blood pressure > 180/120 mm Hg in combination with acute end-organ damage (e.g., focal neurologic symptoms, retinopathy, dyspnea, cardiac symptoms, hematuria).

Uw0bRR.title: Renal artery stenosis
Uw0bRR.description: A narrowing of one or both renal arteries, usually due to atherosclerosis (most commonly) or fibromuscular dysplasia. Findings include abdominal bruits and signs of hyperaldosteronism (e.g., hypertension), from activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Can also lead to findings of decreased kidney function secondary to ischemic renal injury.

2w0TRR.title: White coat hypertension
2w0TRR.description: A subtype of hypertension in which blood pressure readings are elevated when measured in a clinical setting but are normal when measured outside of a clinical setting. Anxiety and stress in clinical settings may be contributory. Out-of-office blood pressure measurement is required for diagnosis. The term "white coat effect" refers to patients who are already diagnosed with hypertension and experience an additional temporary increase in blood pressure when in a clinical environment.

Sw0yRR.title: Vasodilators
Sw0yRR.description: A class of agents that relax the smooth muscle cells lining the blood vessels and thus increase the flow of blood by decreasing vascular resistance. Dilation of arterial blood vessels decreases blood pressure. Two agents widely used to treat hypertensive emergency include hydralazine and nitroprusside.

iw0JiR.title: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
iw0JiR.description: A renal vascular injury caused by chronic arterial hypertension. Characterized on renal biopsy by vascular, glomerular, and tubulointerstitial changes with arterial and arteriolar sclerosis and hyalinosis (due to chronic ischemic damage).

jw0_iR.title: Hypertensive retinopathy
jw0_iR.description: A retinal abnormality (e.g., arterial narrowing or nicking, blot- and flame-shaped hemorrhage, microaneurysms) seen in patients with hypertension.

nw07jR.title: Ankle-brachial index
nw07jR.description: The ratio of systolic ankle blood pressure to systolic brachial blood pressure. This is a fast, easy, and inexpensive way to screen for and diagnose peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Normal resting ABI is 0.91–1.4; in patients with clinical features of PAD, values ≤ 0.9 confirm the diagnosis; values > 1.4 indicate a noncompressible calcified vessel.

ow00PR.title: Buerger sign
ow00PR.description: A maneuver used to evaluate peripheral arterial disease of the lower limbs. Pallor of the feet upon elevation of the lower limbs, and reactive hyperemia of the feet and prolonged time to venous refilling on limb dependency indicate arterial insufficiency.

rw0f4R.title: Popliteal artery aneurysm
rw0f4R.description: An aneurysm of the popliteal artery. Can present with obstruction and ischemic symptoms of the lower leg and foot. Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, male sex, age, and other vessel aneurysms.

sw0t4R.title: Peripheral cyanosis
sw0t4R.description: A blue discoloration of the extremities (and sometimes the circumoral and periorbital regions) caused by poor peripheral circulation. Unlike in central cyanosis, which is caused by hypoxia, discoloration is not seen in the mucous membranes.

Gw0B4R.title: Erythromelalgia
Gw0B4R.description: A rare condition characterized by intermittent hyperperfusion of the feet and (less frequently) hands that is associated with intense burning pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. May be genetic (primary erythromelalgia) or occur in association with myeloproliferative disorders, connective tissue diseases, cancer, infections, and poisoning.

media.title: Erythromelalgia in hereditary small fiber neuropathy

Fw0gkR.title: Hereditary thrombophilia
Fw0gkR.description: A group of genetic disorders in which an individual is predisposed to thrombosis or thromboembolism. Includes factor V Leiden mutation, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, elevated factor VIII, prothrombin mutation, hyperhomocysteinemia, and sickle cell anemia.

Ew08kR.title: Factor V Leiden
Ew08kR.description: A common inherited thrombophilia. Caused by a mutation in the factor V gene that causes resistance to protein C inactivation of factor V. Results in increased risk of venous thromboembolism.

Dw01OR.title: Prothrombin mutation
Dw01OR.description: An autosomal dominant hereditary thrombophilia that results from a mutation (G20210A) in the promoter region of the prothrombin gene. This mutation increases the expression of prothrombin and leads to increased prothrombin serum levels. Thrombin (factor II) cleaves fibrinogen to form fibrin.

ww0hOR.title: Protein S deficiency
ww0hOR.description: A hereditary thrombophilia that causes a decrease in either the total amount of protein S or its functionality. Results in the decreased inhibition of factors Va and VIIIa, leading to an increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Most often autosomal dominant.

9w0NOR.title: Protein C deficiency
9w0NOR.description: An autosomal dominant congenital hypercoagulable disease caused by an overactivity of factors V and VIII, which are normally inhibited by protein C.

Cw0qOR.title: Antithrombin III deficiency
Cw0qOR.description: An autosomal dominant hereditary thrombophilia. A deficiency in AT III may also be acquired secondary to conditions such as nephrotic syndrome or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). AT III's inhibitory effect on coagulation, by binding to and inactivating the coagulation factors II (thrombin) and X, is decreased. Heparin's therapeutic effect is reduced because its mechanism of action requires AT III.

_w05lR.title: Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis
_w05lR.description: A scoring system used to estimate the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Includes medical history (presence of active cancer, history of previous DVT), history of immobilization (paralysis or recent immobilization of a lower extremity, recent history of major surgery of remaining bedridden), and clinical symptoms (localized tenderness along the deep venous system, leg swelling, asymmetrical calf swelling, unilateral pitting edema, and presence of collateral, non-varicose superficial veins).

media.title: Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis

zw0rlR.title: Virchow's triad
zw0rlR.description: A combination of pathophysiological factors that promote thrombus formation, including endothelial damage (e.g., inflammation, trauma), venous stasis (e.g., varicosis, immobilization), and hypercoagulability (e.g., increased platelet adhesion, thrombophilia).

Z90ZNR.title: Thrombophlebitis
Z90ZNR.description: The inflammation of a vein related to blood clot formation.

090eNR.title: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens
090eNR.description: A severe form of deep vein thrombosis characterized by venous obstruction of an entire extremity, leading to impaired arterial inflow. Manifests with severe swelling, edema, pain, cyanosis, coldness, and absent pulses.

destinations.label: Deep vein thrombosis → Subtypes and variants

a90QNR.title: Primary upper extremity deep vein thrombosis
a90QNR.description: A deep vein thrombosis in the upper extremity due to thoracic outlet syndrome, repetitive strenuous activity involving the upper extremities (effort thrombosis), or an unknown cause.

destinations.label: Deep vein thrombosis → Subtypes and variants

X909NR.title: Homans sign
X909NR.description: A nonspecific and insensitive clinical sign for deep vein thrombosis. Positive if dorsiflexion of the foot elicits calf tenderness.

1902mR.title: Varicose veins
1902mR.description: A dilated, often tortuous, subcutaneous vein with a diameter ≥ 3 mm. Can develop in the lower extremities due to venous insufficiency. Corresponds to CEAP class C2 venous disease.

V90GmR.title: Stasis dermatitis
V90GmR.description: An inflammatory skin condition characterized by poorly defined erythematous and eczematous patches and plaques on the lower legs. In acute forms, may also manifest with pruritus and weeping. Caused by edema due to chronic venous insufficiency. May result in secondary bacterial infections.

e90xmR.title: Venous ulcers
e90xmR.description: An ulceration of the skin caused by chronic venous insufficiency. Classically develops superior to the medial ankle. Often associated with skin changes (e.g., hyperpigmentation) and unilateral edema.

media.title: Venous leg ulcer in chronic venous insufficiency
Features of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers

290T5R.title: Trendelenburg test
290T5R.description:
There are 2 different tests with this name:
1. Used to diagnose valve incompetency in the superficial and deep veins of the legs. While supine, a tourniquet is applied to compress the superficial great saphenous vein. Rapid filling of the superficial veins as soon as the patient stands indicates valve incompetence in the deep veins. If there is no rapid refilling, the tourniquet is released, at which point rapid refilling indicates incompetence in the superficial veins.
2. Used to evaluate gluteus medius strength by asking the patient to pick up one leg and balance their weight onto the other. If one side tilts downward. The test is positive for weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the contralateral side (Trendelenburg sign).

f90k5R.title: Perthes' manoeuvre
f90k5R.description: A test used to assess the patency of deep veins in patients with chronic venous disease. For this test, the examiner uses a tourniquet to compress the great saphenous vein (a superficial vein) and asks the patient to take a few steps, allowing blood to flow through the deep venous system. The test is positive if the varices fill due to deep vein obstruction.

T9065R.title: Venous plethysmography
T9065R.description: A noninvasive test that evaluates changes in limb volume in order to measure blood flow in the extremities and detect reflux and/or occlusion. Methods include air plethysmography (using a cuff) and photoplethysmography (using a diode).

g90F5R.title: Bronchiolitis
g90F5R.description: A lower respiratory tract infection (RTI) in which the bronchioles become inflamed, most commonly due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. Occurs mainly in children < 2 years of age and is characterized by initial upper RTI symptoms (e.g., low-grade fever, stuffy nose) followed by cough and possibly signs of respiratory distress (e.g., tachypnea, wheezing, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, cyanosis).

media.title: Bilateral hyperinflation and right lung consolidation

h90cMR.title: Expectorants
h90cMR.description: A group of medications used for symptomatic treatment of cough. Expectorants thin bronchial secretions and make cough more productive.

Q90uMR.title: Mucolytics
Q90uMR.description: A group of medications that liquefy mucus by reducing the disulfide bonds of mucoproteins. Examples include N-acetylcysteine, carbocysteine, erdosteine, and fudosteine.

P90WnR.title: Chronic bronchitis
P90WnR.description: A former subclass of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease defined as chronic inflammation of the airways with productive cough for ≥ 3 months each year for ≥ 2 consecutive years.

k90mnR.title: Emphysema
k90mnR.description: An abnormal, permanent dilation of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles. Results in hyperinflation, hypoxia, and dyspnea. Caused by destruction of the alveolar walls and capillaries required for gas exchange. Risk factors include smoking, air pollution, and inhalation of chemical fumes and dust.

L90wLR.title: Pursed lip breathing
L90wLR.description: A style of breathing in which an individual breathes in through the nose and breathes out slowly through pursed lips. This technique increases airway pressure and prevents bronchial collapse during the last phase of expiration. Most commonly seen in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

destinations.label: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease → Clinical features

o900oR.title: Theophylline
o900oR.description: A methylxanthine derivative with anti-inflammatory and mild bronchodilatory effects. May be used in maintenance therapy of COPD if other bronchodilators are not available. No longer routinely recommended for asthma.

7904KR.title: Montelukast
7904KR.description: A leukotriene-receptor antagonist used in maintenance treatment of asthma and allergic rhinitis. Acts to decrease bronchoconstriction and inflammation. Not used for treatment of acute asthma attacks.

t90X6R.title: Status asthmaticus
t90X6R.description: A severe asthma exacerbation that does not respond to initial treatment with bronchodilators.

u90p6R.title: Farmer's lung
u90p6R.description: A type of hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to exposure to thermophilic actinomyces spores present in moldy hay.

w90hpR.title: Caplan syndrome
w90hpR.description: A syndrome that occurs in individuals with both rheumatoid arthritis and occupational pneumoconiosis (e.g., silicosis, asbestosis, berylliosis, anthracosis). Characterized by rapidly progressive shortness of breath and the development of basilar nodules.

990NpR.title: Eggshell calcification
990NpR.description: Well-defined, sickle-shaped calcification of the edges of hilar lymph nodes. This radiologic sign is characteristic for silicosis, though it can also be seen in other diseases, e.g., sarcoidosis.

C90qpR.title: Mesothelioma
C90qpR.description: A malignant neoplasm that develops from mesothelial cells (which line several body cavities) and most commonly manifests as pleural mesothelioma. Highly associated with asbestos exposure. Has a latency period of about 30 years and a poor prognosis.

y90dJR.title: Pleural mesothelioma
y90dJR.description: The common type of mesothelioma. Develops in mesothelial cells in the pleural cavity and is most commonly caused by asbestos exposure. Often manifests with constitutional symptoms, pleural thickening, and pleural effusion 30–50 years after exposure. Prognosis is poor.

_905JR.title: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia
_905JR.description: A rare, noninfectious type of pneumonia that is characterized by inflammation of the bronchioles and the surrounding structures. Can be caused by chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) or certain drugs (e.g., amiodarone).

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias

ZC0ZqR.title: Acute interstitial pneumonia
ZC0ZqR.description: A rare, severe type of idiopathic interstitial lung disease with an acute onset that can progress rapidly to respiratory failure. Usually affects individuals without a preexisting lung condition. Manifestations include rapidly progressive dyspnea, fever, and cough. Imaging findings include bilateral ground-glass opacities, traction bronchiectasis, and consolidation areas.

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias

aC0QqR.title: Typical pneumonia
aC0QqR.description:
Pneumonia featuring classic symptoms (e.g., sudden onset of severe malaise, high fever and chills, productive cough with purulent sputum, tachypnea, and dyspnea) and typical findings on auscultation and percussion (e.g., crackles, bronchial, and decreased breath sounds on auscultation, dullness on percussion).
Manifests as lobar pneumonia or bronchopneumonia. Most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

YC0nqR.title: Atypical pneumonia
YC0nqR.description: An indolent type of pneumonia characterized by interstitial inflammation. Manifests as a nonproductive, dry cough, dyspnea, fatigue, headache, sore throat, myalgias, and malaise. Most commonly caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and viral infections.

media.title: Atypical pneumonia manifesting as upper lobe-predominant opacities

XC09qR.title: Air bronchogram
XC09qR.description: A radiographic sign present in many pulmonary conditions, e.g., pulmonary consolidation, edema, and neoplasms. Characterized by a dark (radiolucent) linear zone, representing alveoli filled with substances such as fluid or pus, surrounded by a white or gray (radiopaque) zone, representing normal air-filled bronchi.

dC0oIR.title: CURB-65 score
dC0oIR.description:
A score used to decide whether patients with pneumonia require hospitalization. Each of the following is assigned 1 point:
- Confusion
- Urea (blood) > 7 mmol/L (20 mg/dL)
- Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min
- Blood pressure (systolic) ≤ 90 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≤ 60 mm Hg
- ≥ 65 years (of age)
If the CURB-65 score is ≥ 2, hospitalization is indicated.

TC06rR.title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
TC06rR.description: A nonmotile, aerobic, gram-positive, acid-fast bacillus with a rich lipid cell wall. Able to survive in aerosols and gastric secretions. Due to its cell wall, antibiotic therapy requires long duration. Causes tuberculosis with spread via droplets. Humans are the predominant host.

SC0yrR.title: Primary tuberculosis
SC0yrR.description: A form of tuberculosis that occurs after initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Includes latent tuberculosis infection and active primary tuberculosis.

RC0l7R.title: Latent tuberculosis infection
RC0l7R.description: A condition in which a person is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis but does not have any symptoms of disease (e.g., fever, night sweats, weight loss, productive cough) and is not infectious. The tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay are positive.

iC0J7R.title: Active tuberculosis
iC0J7R.description: A condition in which the infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis becomes symptomatic, often due to the patient being immunocompromised. Symptoms may include fever, night sweats, weight loss, and/or productive cough (if the lungs are affected).

4C03HR.title: Ghon complex
4C03HR.description: A granuloma with an associated lymph node that forms as a sequela of tuberculosis infection. Usually found in the middle or lower lobes of the lung. Can retain bacteria and therefore become a source of reinfection. Fibrosed and calcified Ghon complexes are known as Ranke complexes.

lC0vHR.title: Reactivation tuberculosis
lC0vHR.description: A condition in which a latent infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis becomes symptomatic (e.g., due to the patient becoming immunocompromised) and contagious. Manifestations include fever, night sweats, weight loss, and productive cough.

NC0-HR.title: Urogenital tuberculosis
NC0-HR.description: Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that has spread to the urinary tract (kidneys, ureter, and/or bladder). Clinical features include dysuria, flank pain, hematuria, pyuria, and a low-grade fever. In addition, men may present with symptoms of prostatitis and women with secondary amenorrhea, lesions of the fallopian tubes, and possibly pyosalpinx leading to infertility/sterility.

nC07sR.title: Postprimary inoculation tuberculosis
nC07sR.description: A form of cutaneous tuberculosis that can develop in individuals with prior tuberculosis infection. Occurs following the inoculation of injured skin with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Manifests as a hyperkeratotic papule that typically persists for months to years.

LC0wsR.title: Lupus vulgaris
LC0wsR.description: A cutaneous form of tuberculosis that is caused by hematogenous, lymphatic, or contiguous spread of tuberculosis to the skin in individuals with high TB sensitivity. Manifests as plaques or nodules with ulceration and scarring over the face and neck. Diascopy reveals apple jelly nodules.

KC0UGR.title: Scrofuloderma
KC0UGR.description: A cutaneous form of tuberculosis caused by contiguous involvement of skin overlying a deeper structure (e.g., lymph node, bone, joint, epididymis) that has been infected by tuberculosis. Manifests as a firm, painless nodule or mass, which may ulcerate to form a discharging sinus tract.

pC0LGR.title: Tuberculid
pC0LGR.description: A group of cutaneous conditions that develop as a result of hypersensitivity reactions to mycobacterial antigens. Includes papulonecrotic tuberculid, lichen scrofulosorum, and erythema induratum of Bazin.

sC0ttR.title: Tuberculous pleurisy
sC0ttR.description: Inflammation of the pleura that usually presents concurrently with pulmonary tuberculosis. Typically presents with a unilateral, lymphocyte-predominant, exudative pleural effusion with an adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 40 U/L.

GC0BtR.title: Miliary tuberculosis
GC0BtR.description: The widespread, hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The most commonly involved sites are the lungs (characterized by the presence of small nodules that resemble millet seeds), the central nervous system, bones and joints, liver, adrenal glands, and the lymphatic system. Manifestations include fevers, night sweats, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and skin lesions.

tC0XFR.title: Tuberculous meningitis
tC0XFR.description: A type of meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Manifests with a subacute course over several weeks or months that can include intermittent fever, cranial nerve deficits, and focal neurological deficits due to hematogenous dissemination of cranial arteritis.

uC0pFR.title: Purified protein derivative tuberculin skin test
uC0pFR.etymology: Abbreviations: PPD TST, PPD, or TST
uC0pFR.description: A test to assess for latent TB, in which 5 units of purified protein derivative tuberculin is injected intradermally. The diameter of the induration at the injection site is measured after 48–72 hours, and determines if further TB testing is necessary.

vC0AFR.title: Interferon-γ release assay
vC0AFR.description: An ELISA test that measures the level of interferon-γ expressed by T cells after coming into contact with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Used to diagnose latent tuberculosis infection in at-risk populations. Elevated interferon-γ levels indicate a positive result. In contrast to tuberculin skin testing, there are no false-positive results with IGRA in patients who received the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. Commercially available, FDA-approved tests include the QuantFERON-TB Gold In-Tube assay and the T-SPOT.TB assay.

xC0E8R.title: Caseous necrosis
xC0E8R.description: A type of necrosis characterized by granular debris that results from macrophages walling off a pathogen. Seen in tubercular, fungal, and Nocardia infection. Histopathological examination shows cellular debris, lymphocytes, and macrophages that form granulomas.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

_C05uR.title: Isoniazid
_C05uR.description: A prodrug activated by bacterial catalase-peroxidase. It inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, which is a vital component of mycobacterial cell walls. Mainly used in treatment and prophylaxis of tuberculosis. It is a P450 cytochrome inhibitor with many drug-drug interactions.

zC0ruR.title: Rifampicin
zC0ruR.description: An antibiotic that obstructs bacterial protein synthesis by preventing transcription. Commonly used to treat tuberculosis and leprosy. Drug of choice for Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae infection chemoprophylaxis.

-C0DuR.title: Pyrazinamide
-C0DuR.description: An antimycobacterial drug with an unknown mechanism of action that is used in combination with isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. Adverse effects are hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity.

Zx0ZER.title: Ethambutol
Zx0ZER.description: An antimycobacterial drug that inhibits arabinosyltransferase and thereby stops carbohydrate polymerization of the mycobacterial cell wall. Can cause optic neuropathy with red-green color blindness.

0x0eER.title: Acute sarcoidosis
0x0eER.description: A type of sarcoidosis that typically has a sudden onset and remits spontaneously within ~ 2 years. Manifestations include fever, malaise, lack of appetite, weight loss, dyspnea, cough, chest pain, arthritis, anterior uveitis, and erythema nodosum. Can rarely progress to chronic sarcoidosis.

bx0HER.title: Chronic sarcoidosis
bx0HER.description: A variant of sarcoidosis typically characterized by an insidious onset of symptoms. Most commonly causes respiratory symptoms (e.g., exertional dyspnea, dry cough), though other systemic manifestations can be seen.

Wx0PvR.title: Heerfordt syndrome
Wx0PvR.description: A rare, subacute manifestation of sarcoidosis that includes fever, parotitis, uveitis (iridocyclitis), and facial nerve palsy.

Vx0GvR.title: Lofgren syndrome
Vx0GvR.description: An acute presentation of sarcoidosis that manifests with fever, migratory polyarthritis, erythema nodosum, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

Ux0bDR.title: Lupus pernio
Ux0bDR.description: An extrapulmonary manifestation of sarcoidosis that most commonly manifests with erythematous to violaceous, indurated lesions on the central face.

destinations.label: Collection of dermatological disorders → Cutaneous granulomas

fx0kDR.title: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
fx0kDR.description: The bilateral enlargement of the lymph nodes of the pulmonary hila. Etiologies include sarcoidosis, infections (e.g., tuberculosis, histoplasmosis), malignancy (lymphomas), and inorganic dust diseases (silicosis).

media.title: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy due to sarcoidosis
Bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy

gx0FDR.title: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
gx0FDR.description: A syndrome characterized by clubbing and painful joint swelling (periostitis). Associated with a variety of conditions; most commonly associated with lung adenocarcinoma (as a paraneoplastic syndrome).

hx0cwR.title: Pancoast tumor
hx0cwR.description: A peripheral lung carcinoma (predominantly non-small cell lung cancer) located in the superior sulcus of the lung. Can compress local structures, including the recurrent laryngeal nerve (causes hoarseness), the stellate ganglion (causes Horner syndrome), the superior vena cava (causes superior vena cava syndrome), the brachiocephalic vein (causes brachiocephalic syndrome), and the brachial plexus (causes sensorimotor deficits).

3x0SwR.title: Pancoast syndrome
3x0SwR.description: A constellation of signs and symptoms associated with a Pancoast tumor (peripheral lung carcinoma located in the superior sulcus of the lung). Characterized by severe pain in the axilla and shoulder, Horner syndrome, atrophy of arm and hand muscles, and edema of the arm with facial swelling.

media.title: Pancoast tumor with chest wall extension

jx0_wR.title: Non-small cell lung cancer
jx0_wR.description: A group of heterogeneous lung cancer types that accounts for ~ 85% of all lung cancers. Includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma of the lung. In contrast to small cell lung cancer, NSCLC is often managed surgically (with or without chemotherapy, molecularly targeted therapy, and/or immunotherapy).

Ox0I9R.title: Small cell lung cancer
Ox0I9R.description: A pulmonary neuroendocrine tumor that most commonly develops in the central region of the lung. Associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes, including syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and Cushing syndrome, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

Mx0MCR.title: Apnea
Mx0MCR.description: A respiratory arrest that lasts for ≥ 10 seconds. Can be voluntary (breath-holding), mechanical (choking, airway obstruction), or due to neurological conditions or trauma. Prolonged apnea results in decreased arterial oxygen content and a rise in CO₂ (hypercapnia).

destinations.label: Respiratory failure and arrest → Initial management

nx07CR.title: Hypopnea
nx07CR.description: A decrease in airflow that is insufficient to meet the criteria for an apnea event. Definitions vary. The set of criteria recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine are: peak signal excursion decrease by ≥ 30% for a ≥10-second duration, associated with ≥ 3% oxygen desaturation or arousal.

Lx0wCR.title: Apnea-hypopnea index
Lx0wCR.description: The number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep, usually measured by in-laboratory polysomnography.

Kx0UxR.title: Respiratory effort-related arousal
Kx0UxR.description: An arousal from sleep due to increased respiratory effort for at least 10 seconds without meeting the criteria for a hypopnea or apnea event.

px0LxR.title: Respiratory disturbance index
px0LxR.description: The number of apneas plus hypopneas plus RERAs per hour of sleep, usually measured by in-laboratory polysomnography.

qx0CxR.title: Obstructive sleep apnea
qx0CxR.description: A sleep disorder characterized by obstruction of the upper airways due to collapse of the pharyngeal muscles during sleep, causing apneic episodes. Subsequent hypoxia and poor quality of sleep lead to daytime sleepiness, impaired cognitive functions, and depressive mood changes. Commonly associated with obesity, alcohol use, and smoking.

rx0fBR.title: Central sleep apnea
rx0fBR.description: A sleep disorder characterized by repetitive cessation or decrease of respiratory effort during sleep due to impaired function of the respiratory center. Subsequent hypoxia and poor quality of sleep can lead to daytime sleepiness, impaired cognitive function, and depressive mood changes.

7x04BR.title: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
7x04BR.description: A breathing disorder that affects obese individuals only (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2). It is characterized by diurnal hypercapnia secondary to alveolar hypoventilation and is frequently accompanied by obstructive sleep apnea.

Gx0BBR.title: Home sleep apnea testing
Gx0BBR.description: A type of sleep study that can be used to diagnose obstructive sleep apnea using ventilation and oxygenation parameters, especially in patients with high pretest probability. In contrast to in-laboratory polysomnography, this method includes fewer parameters, and it cannot assess sleep stages or arousal from sleep. Not suitable for patients with comorbid cardiopulmonary conditions, such as COPD or heart failure.

tx0XyR.title: Polysomnography
tx0XyR.description: A type of sleep study that is usually performed in a supervised facility and that assesses physiologic variables (e.g., sleep stages, oxygen saturations, airflow, and respiratory effort) via ≥ 7 channels, including EEG, EMG, EOG, and ECG. It is the gold standard for diagnosing obstructive sleep apnea and other forms of sleep-disordered breathing. Can also be used to titrate positive airway pressure if obstructive sleep apnea is detected, and to diagnose other sleep disorders.

ux0pyR.title: Slow-wave sleep
ux0pyR.description: A phase of NREM sleep that constitutes 10–20% of total sleep time. Associated with delta waves of 0–4 Hz with high amplitudes (> 75 microvolts). Parasomnias (e.g., sleepwalking, night terror disorder, bedwetting) occur during slow-wave sleep.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Sleep physiology

Dx01AR.title: REM sleep
Dx01AR.description: A stage of deep sleep that lasts 10-30 minutes, characterized by predominant beta waves on EEG. During REM sleep there is a high waking threshold, maximum muscle relaxation with simultaneously rapid eye movement (REM), activation of autonomic functions, and high dream activity.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Sleep physiology

9x0NAR.title: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
9x0NAR.description: The surgical dilation of the upper airway via resection of the uvula and redundant retrolingual, soft palate, and tonsillar tissue. Can be used to treat obstructive sleep apnea if conservative therapy is unsuccessful.

Ax0R_R.title: Wells score
Ax0R_R.description:
A term used for two different diagnostic scoring systems, including:
1. Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis
2. Wells criteria for pulmonary embolism.
Although there are overlapping components between the two, each set of criteria is unique.

destinations.label: Pulmonary embolism → Pretest probability of pulmonary embolism

_x05_R.title: D-dimer
_x05_R.description: A fibrin degradation product released when plasmin cleaves crosslinked fibrin. Increased serum concentrations of D-dimer indicate recent intravascular coagulation and/or fibrinolysis (e.g., from deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, disseminated intravascular coagulation).

XB09zR.title: Westermark sign
XB09zR.description: A radiographic sign on chest x-ray associated with pulmonary embolism. The findings include dilation of the pulmonary arteries proximal to the embolus, and the collapse of the distal vasculature, creating the appearance of a sharp cut-off. Seen in about 2% of patients, it has low sensitivity but high specificity for PE.

cB0a-R.title: Hampton hump
cB0a-R.description: A radiographic finding caused by pulmonary infarction. The finding refers to a shallow wedge-shaped opacity in the periphery of the lung, with its base against the pleural surface. Although it may aid in the diagnosis of PE, it has low sensitivity and intraobserver reliability.

WB0P-R.title: Perfusion and ventilation scintigraphy
WB0P-R.description: A nuclear medicine scan that uses radioactive material to examine ventilation (V) and blood flow (Q) in the lungs. It can be used to diagnose pulmonary emboli, which show up as areas that are ventilated but not perfused (mismatch).

media.title: Mismatched perfusion defects from pulmonary emboli

dB0o-R.title: Pulmonary angiography
dB0o-R.description: A radiologic procedure performed with contrast dye to visualize the pulmonary vasculature and identify intraluminal filling defects. Can entail an invasive procedure in which contrast dye is injected into the pulmonary arteries or a non-invasive procedure in which intravenous contrast dye is injected into a peripheral vein and a timed radiologic study (e.g., CT scan) is performed.

eB0x-R.title: Pulmonary infarction
eB0x-R.description: An infarction of the lung parenchyma that results from embolic occlusion of the smaller segmental arteries (segmental pulmonary embolism), leading to a wedge-shaped area of hemorrhage and necrosis. Anastomoses between pulmonary arteries and bronchial arteries prevent infarction when medium-sized pulmonary arteries are occluded.

media.title: Peripheral opacity (Hampton hump) from pulmonary embolism

fB0kZi.title: Rule of nines
fB0kZi.description: A clinical tool used to rapidly assess the extent of body surface area affected by burns. The body surface of an adult can be divided into 11 regions (head, anterior chest, abdomen, upper back, lower back, arms x2, thighs x2, lower legs x2) each of which comprises ~ 9% of total body surface. The external genitalia accounts for the remaining 1%.

gB0FZi.title: Parkland formula
gB0FZi.description: A formula used to guide fluid therapy during the first 24 hours after burn injuries. The volume of lactated Ringer's solution to be administered within a period of 24 h = 4 mL x % of body surface involved in 2nd or 3rd-degree burn x body weight (in kg). The Advanced Trauma Life Support and American Burn Association guidelines now recommend only using half of the fluid volume as calculated by the Parkland formula.

SB0yZi.title: Inhalation injury
SB0yZi.description: A condition caused by inhalation of hot smoke and/or toxic gases. Clinical features include laryngeal edema (which can cause airway obstruction), pneumonitis, and manifestations of carbon monoxide and cyanide toxicity. Should be suspected in patients with a history of being trapped in a confined space during a fire.

media.title: Inhalation injury of the upper airways

hB0c0i.title: Necrotizing fasciitis
hB0c0i.description: Rapidly progressive infection resulting in extensive necrosis of deep tissue (subcutaneous tissue, fascia, and muscle) and a systemic response that can develop into a life-threatening condition within hours. The most common causative organism is group A Streptococcus but mixed infection (typically with aerobic and anaerobic gram-negative bacteria) are common. One rare, specific subtype is gas gangrene, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTIs)

RB0l0i.title: Paronychia
RB0l0i.description: Inflammation of the nail folds that most frequently affects the fingernails. Commonly caused by bacterial infections secondary to trauma (e.g., cuts) or chronic skin damage/irritation (e.g., from the use of cleaning agents).

iB0J0i.title: Felon
iB0J0i.description: A distal pulp space infection of the fingertip. Usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

4B03ai.title: Negri bodies
4B03ai.description: A histopathologic finding characterized by eosinophilic inclusion bodies in the cytoplasm of neurons in the hippocampus and cerebellum. Associated with rabies.

OB0Iai.title: Osteomyelitis
OB0Iai.description: An infection of the bone. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Hematogenous osteomyelitis is caused by seeding from a remote source and is most common among IV drug users and children. Exogenous osteomyelitis is more common in adults and results from direct inoculation through trauma or contiguous spread from infected adjacent tissue.

media.title: Lytic lesion in long bone from subacute osteomyelitis
Foot ulcer with abscess and osteomyelitis

lB0vai.title: Vertebral osteomyelitis
lB0vai.description: An infection of the vertebrae (e.g., due to hematogenous spread). Manifests with latent, nonspecific symptoms such as back and/or neck pain, spinal tenderness, and possibly fever.

media.title: Retropharyngeal abscess with spondylodiscitis and osteomyelitis
Spondylodiscitis with prevertebral and paravertebral abscess formation

5B0iYi.title: Discitis
5B0iYi.description: An infection of the intervertebral disc space secondary to contiguous spread from an adjacent infection (e.g., vertebral osteomyelitis), hematogenous spread of an infection (e.g., urinary tract infection, pneumonia, skin infection), or direct inoculation (e.g., surgery, injection of disc space).

nB07Yi.title: Tuberculous spondylitis
nB07Yi.description: A form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Usually involves > 1 vertebra. If untreated, the condition can result in collapse of the vertebral bodies, kyphosis, and spinal cord compression and thus lead to neurologic deficits.

media.title: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with gibbus deformity

JB0sbi.title: Bony sequestrum
JB0sbi.description: A necrotic bone fragment that has become detached from the original bone.

qB0Cbi.title: Spontaneous pneumothorax
qB0Cbi.description: The development of a collection of air within the pleural space (in between the lung and the chest wall) without a precipitating event. Spontaneous pneumothorax can be further classified into primary spontaneous pneumothorax (no underlying pulmonary disease present) and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (underlying pulmonary disease present). Typically manifests with sudden, severe, ipsilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Can lead to partial or complete pulmonary collapse, and can develop into a tension pneumothorax.

IB0YXi.title: Tension pneumothorax
IB0YXi.description: A life-threatening variant of a pneumothorax in which a one-way valve mechanism (e.g., from a puncture wound) allows air into the pleural space while the chest wall expands during inspiration but does not allow it to escape during expiration. Air progressively accumulates in the pleural space and builds up pressure that causes collapse of the ipsilateral lung and compression of the contralateral lung, heart, and superior vena cava. This culminates in hypoxia and hemodynamic compromise.

rB0fXi.title: Mediastinal flutter
rB0fXi.description: A phenomenon associated with open pneumothorax in which the mediastinum shifts toward the uninjured hemithorax during inspiration and toward the injured hemithorax during expiration. Can impair venous return to the heart and cause severe hemodynamic instability.

7B04Xi.title: Hemothorax
7B04Xi.description: The presence of blood in the pleural cavity. Presents with diminished breath sounds and hyporesonant chest percussion. Usually the result of chest trauma but may rarely occur spontaneously in patients with a coagulopathy, pulmonary neoplasm, tuberculosis, or a vascular malformation.

tB0Xci.title: Chest tube placement
tB0Xci.description: The insertion of a flexible tube into the thoracic cavity to drain air or fluid (e.g., in pneumothorax or hemothorax) in order to facilitate lung reexpansion. Most commonly inserted at the 4th–5th intercostal space (nipple line), between the anterior and midaxillary lines (safe triangle).

media.title: Chest tube placement equipment, patient positioning, and insertion site

yB0dWi.title: Carcinoid syndrome
yB0dWi.description: A paraneoplastic condition caused by intermittent secretion of serotonin and other vasoactive substances (e.g., kallikrein, histamine) by neuroendocrine neoplasms. Most often associated with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors in the gastrointestinal tract. Features include diarrhea, cutaneous flushing, and wheezing.

zB0rWi.title: VIPoma
zB0rWi.description: A neuroendocrine tumor most often found in the pancreas that secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), causing secretory diarrhea.

-B0DWi.title: WDHA syndrome
-B0DWi.description: A triad of classic clinical features of VIPoma: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria.

0y0edi.title: Lichtenstein repair
0y0edi.description: A surgical technique for the treatment of inguinal hernias. Involves reinforcement by implementation of a synthetic mesh between the abdominal internal oblique muscle and the aponeurosis of the abdominal external oblique muscle.

ay0Qdi.title: Shouldice repair
ay0Qdi.description: A surgical technique for the treatment of inguinal hernias. Involves doubling of the transverse fascia and fixation of the abdominal internal oblique muscle and transverse muscle at the inguinal ligament using suture (nonmesh repair).

by0Hdi.title: Signs of appendicitis
by0Hdi.description: A group of clinical signs of appendicitis, including Blumberg sign (rebound tenderness caused upon suddenly ceasing deep palpation of the RLQ), McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing sign (referred pain to the RLQ upon deep palpation of the LLQ), psoas sign (RLQ pain with extension of the right leg against resistance), and obturator sign (RLQ pain with flexion and internal rotation of the right leg).

Xy09di.title: McBurney
Xy09di.description: An anatomical area in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen located one third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Tenderness in this area is a sign of appendicitis and referred to as McBurney sign.

cy0aVi.title: Lanz point
cy0aVi.description: An anatomical area located one third of the distance from the right iliac spine to the left iliac spine. Tenderness in this area is associated with appendicitis.

Wy0PVi.title: Sherren's triangle
Wy0PVi.description: A triangular area on the anterior abdominal wall bounded by the anterior superior iliac spine, umbilicus, and symphysis pubis. Tenderness in this area is associated with appendicitis.

dy0oVi.title: Rovsing's sign
dy0oVi.description: A physical finding characterized by referred pain to the right lower quadrant after deep palpation of the left lower quadrant. Indicates right-sided peritoneal irritation. Associated with appendicitis.

Vy0GVi.title: Pain in the Pouch of Douglas
Vy0GVi.description: A physical finding characterized by pain elicited by palpation of the recto-uterine pouch on rectal examination. Associated with appendicitis and endometriosis.

ey0xVi.title: Psoas sign
ey0xVi.description: A physical finding characterized by pain (usually in the abdomen, groin, or back) triggered by active flexion against resistance or passive extension of the hip. Caused by inflammation or irritation of the iliopsoas muscle group (e.g., due to psoas muscle abscess, psoas hematoma, or retrocecal appendix). A positive right-sided psoas sign is associated with acute appendicitis.

fy0kei.title: Target sign
fy0kei.description: The appearance of concentric circles of different densities or echogenicities on abdominal imaging. May be seen in intussusception, acute appendicitis, and biliary disease.

Oy0I2i.title: Meckel diverticulum
Oy0I2i.description: A congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract characterized by an outpouching of the ileal wall. Caused by an incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct.

ly0v2i.title: Appendectomy
ly0v2i.description: Surgical removal of the appendix. Can be performed via an open procedure or laparoscopically.

my0Vfi.title: Periappendiceal abscess
my0Vfi.description: Collection of pus near the appendix secondary to extension of infection in acute appendicitis, especially with perforation of the appendix.

Ly0wfi.title: Anal skin tags
Ly0wfi.description: A painless, benign fold of perianal skin formed at the site(s) of previous perianal inflammation or thrombosed external hemorrhoids.

Ky0UTi.title: Milligan‑Morgan approach
Ky0UTi.description: A surgical approach for submucosal hemorrhoidectomy that involves excision of the hemorrhoid followed by healing of the mucosal defect by secondary intention.

6y0jTi.title: Cholelithiasis
6y0jTi.description: The presence of gallstones in the gallbladder. Not considered a disease unless it causes symptoms.

media.title: Pathophysiology for different types of gallstones

Jy0sTi.title: Choledocholithiasis
Jy0sTi.description: The presence of gallstones in the common bile duct. Complications of choledocholithiasis include cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, and/or obstructive jaundice.

qy0CTi.title: Cholecystitis
qy0CTi.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder. May be acute (typically caused by an obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone) or chronic (usually secondary to chronic irritation of the gallbladder wall by gallstones).

Iy0Ygi.title: Acute cholangitis
Iy0Ygi.description: An ascending bacterial infection of the biliary tract facilitated by bile stasis. Causes of stasis include bile duct stones (most common), strictures, fluke infection, ERCP, indwelling stent, and obstructed biliary enteric anastomosis. Common causative pathogens include E. coli, Klebsiella, S. faecalis, Enterobacter, and Bacteroides.

Hy0Kgi.title: Charcot cholangitis triad
Hy0Kgi.description: The triad of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and fever. Classically seen in acute cholangitis.

sy0tgi.title: Mirizzi syndrome
sy0tgi.description: A condition of compression of the extrahepatic bile duct by a gallstone at the neck of the gall bladder or the cystic duct. Mirizzi syndrome results in obstructive jaundice along with gallbladder dilation (one of the exceptions to Courvoisier's law).

media.title: Concrement of Cystic duct and Mirizzi syndrome (modified classification by McSherry)

ty0XSi.title: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
ty0XSi.description: A diagnostic and/or therapeutic procedure in which a side-viewing endoscope is inserted into the duodenum and contrast is injected via the ampulla of Vater into the bile ducts. Different instruments can then be introduced via the endoscope to cannulate the common bile duct. If necessary, a sphincterotomy of the ampulla of Vater or removal of gallstones from the common bile duct can also be performed.

8y0OSi.title: Murphy sign
8y0OSi.description: The act of the patient suddenly pausing during inspiration upon deep palpation of the right upper quadrant due to pain. A strong indicator of cholecystitis.

Ey08Si.title: Papillotomy
Ey08Si.description: An endoscopic technique (performed in combination with ERCP) that widens the ampulla of Vater by cutting through the sphincter muscle. Facilitates better passage of bile, pancreatic secretions, and possibly gallstones.

vy0ASi.title: Gallbladder empyema
vy0ASi.description: A pus-filled, distended gallbladder. May occur as a complication of acute cholecystitis or as a secondary infection of a gallbladder mucocele.

Dy01hi.title: Gallstone ileus
Dy01hi.description: Mechanical bowel obstruction by a gallstone that has eroded through the biliary system into the gastrointestinal system, creating a fistula.

wy0hhi.title: Gallbladder mucocele
wy0hhi.description: A distended gallbladder filled with mucoid fluid due to prolonged cystic duct obstruction (e.g., due to cholelithiasis) and subsequent absorption of bilirubin in the gallbladder.

9y0Nhi.title: Porcelain gallbladder
9y0Nhi.description: A fibrotic and calcified gallbladder caused by chronic inflammation (e.g., from chronic cholecystitis). Associated with an increased risk of developing gallbladder malignancy (typically adenocarcinoma).

By0zhi.title: Klatskin tumor
By0zhi.description: Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma occuring at the junction of the right and left hepatic bile ducts.

_y053i.title: Mechanical bowel obstruction
_y053i.description: The interruption of the normal passage of bowel contents due to a structural barrier. Classified according to the location as either small bowel obstruction (SBO) or large bowel obstruction (LBO) and, depending on the extent of obstruction, as partial or complete.

zy0r3i.title: Paralytic ileus
zy0r3i.description: A temporary disturbance of peristalsis in the gastrointestinal tract in the absence of mechanical obstruction, most commonly caused by intraabdominal surgery. Other causes include peritonitis, trauma, metabolic or endocrine disturbances (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hypokalemia), and certain medication (e.g., anticholinergics, opioids).

aA0QRi.title: Pathologic fracture
aA0QRi.description: A fracture that occurs in damaged bone tissue (e.g., due to metastasis, neoplasia, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoid use) following minor trauma or physical activity that would not typically cause a fracture (e.g., lifting something, bending over, sneezing).

destinations.label: General principles of fractures → Subtypes and variants

XA09Ri.title: Comminuted fracture
XA09Ri.description: A fracture with > 2 fracture lines, resulting in multiple bone fragments.

eA0xii.title: Fracture signs
eA0xii.description: Features observed or elicited on physical examination that suggest an underlying fracture. Includes: localized pain, edema, and erythema at the site of injury; deviation from the normal longitudinal axis of the body part; a palpable unevenness or gap along the surface of the bone; bone crepitus when the fracture fragments are moved.

destinations.label: General principles of fractures → Clinical features

2A0TQi.title: Complications of fractures
2A0TQi.description: Early complications include acute compartment syndrome, injury to nerves and vessels, fat embolism, and wound infection. Late complications include poor healing (e.g., nonunion, malunion), growth disturbances in children, complex regional pain syndrome, avascular necrosis, posttraumatic arthritis, tendinopathy, contractures, and cosmetic deformity.

TA06Qi.title: Greenstick fracture
TA06Qi.description: A type of incomplete bone fracture characterized by discontinuity in the cortex on one side of the bone with a continuous cortex on the other side (as when one tries to snap a flexible, young, "green" twig or stick). The intact cortex may, however, bend or buckle. Greenstick fractures are seen most commonly in children.

media.title: Greenstick fracture of the distal radius

jA0_ji.title: Spinal cord stimulation
jA0_ji.description: A neuromodulation technique to relieve chronic neuropathic pain by using a mild electric current that is administered percutaneously or through electrodes implanted in the epidural space.

kA0mPi.title: Hill-Sachs lesion
kA0mPi.description: A depression fracture of the humeral head that occurs with forceful impact of the humerus against the glenoid rim. Associated with anterior shoulder dislocation.

lA0vPi.title: Bankart lesion
lA0vPi.description: Damage to the anterior inferior labrum of the glenoid fossa caused by anterior shoulder dislocation.

destinations.label: Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder → Glenoid labrum injuries

NA0-Pi.title: Stimson technique
NA0-Pi.description: An anterior shoulder dislocation reduction technique in which the patient is placed prone with the affected arm hanging off the bed with approximately 10–15 pounds of weights attached. Reduction should occur after 15–30 minutes.

MA0M4i.title: Milch technique
MA0M4i.description: A reduction technique for anterior shoulder dislocations in which the affected arm is abducted and externally rotated before applying traction while guiding the humeral head into place.

KA0Uki.title: Hippocratic technique
KA0Uki.description: An anterior shoulder dislocation reduction method. With the patient supine, the provider adducts the patient's extended arm, applies traction, and then places their heel in the patient's axilla to apply a counterforce.

pA0Lki.title: Kocher technique
pA0Lki.description: An anterior shoulder dislocation reduction method. The patient's arm is adducted at the shoulder and flexed at the elbow. The provider first externally rotates the arm with or without flexion and further adduction at the shoulder joint, then internally rotates the arm to reduce the shoulder.

HA0KOi.title: Colles fracture
HA0KOi.description: A distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment. Classically occurs after a fall on an outstretched hand and is common in patients with osteoporosis.

sA0tOi.title: Smith fracture
sA0tOi.description: A fracture of the distal radius associated with volar (radial and ventral) angulation of the distal fracture fragment. Typically caused by a fall on a flexed wrist or direct injury to the back of the wrist.

GA0BOi.title: Galeazzi fracture
GA0BOi.description: A radial shaft fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint. It is more common in children and is usually caused by a fall on an outstretched arm.

DA01Ni.title: Trans-scaphoid-perilunate dislocation
DA01Ni.description: Dorsal dislocation of the wrist around the fixated, unmoved lunate bone with a fractured scaphoid bone. Mostly due to a fall onto a hyperextended wrist that is deviated towards the ulna.

9A0NNi.title: Carpal bones
9A0NNi.description: A set of eight bones, arranged in two rows of four bones each, that make up the wrist joint. The proximal row includes (lateral to medial) the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform bones. The distal row includes (lateral to medial) the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate bones.

destinations.label: Forearm, wrist, and hand → Bones and joints

CA0qNi.title: Scaphoid view
CA0qNi.description: A posteroanterior x-ray of the wrist taken in ulnar deviation to obtain ideal visualization of the scaphoid bone. Indicated in suspected scaphoid fractures.

X_095i.title: Whiplash injury
X_095i.description: An injury pattern caused by abrupt flexion/extension movement of the neck. Most commonly seen after motor vehicle accidents. Symptoms usually develop hours to days after the inciting event and include headache, neck ache (possibly radiating into the shoulders and arms), increased muscle tension of the neck, and arm and hand paresthesia.

W_0PMi.title: Spondylodesis
W_0PMi.description: A surgical procedure for the treatment of vertebral fractures (particularly unstable fractures in patients presenting with neurological symptoms), symptomatic spondylolisthesis, and severe scoliosis. Involves fusion of two or more vertebral bodies via internal fixation using plates, rods, screws, or cages.

d_0oMi.title: Kyphoplasty
d_0oMi.description: A minimally invasive procedure for the treatment of vertebral fractures. Involves reexpansion of the fracture through insertion of an inflatable balloon into the vertebral body and injection of bone cement. Indications include stable vertebral compression fractures with progressive pain and kyphosis refractory to conservative treatment.

V_0GMi.title: Garden Classification
V_0GMi.description: A classification system for femoral neck fractures: undisplaced, incomplete fractures (stage I); undisplaced, complete fractures (stage II); incompletely displaced, complete fractures (stage III); and completely displaced, complete fractures (stage IV).

Q_0uLi.title: Trimalleolar fracture
Q_0uLi.description: An unstable fracture of the ankle involving the medial, lateral, and posterior malleoli.

O_0Ioi.title: Thompson test
O_0Ioi.description: A test to diagnose Achilles tendon rupture. The patient lies prone with the feet hanging off the end of the bed, and the clinician squeezes the patient's calf. Normally, passive plantar flexion is present. In complete Achilles tendon rupture, passive plantar flexion is absent.

m_0VKi.title: Mini-Mental State Examination
m_0VKi.description: A screening tool that assesses cognitive impairment in individuals with suspected dementia. Includes testing of orientation to time and place, registration (immediate repetition of named prompts), attention and calculation, recall (of previous prompts), language, repetition of a complex phrase, and complex commands. The maximum number of points is 30. Patients who score fewer than 24 points are generally considered to have dementia.

L_0wKi.title: Clock-drawing test
L_0wKi.description: A nonverbal screening tool used to assess deficits common in the early stages of dementia, including visual-spatial, numerical sequencing, and planning abilities. The patient is given a sheet of paper with an empty circle on which they are asked to draw a clock indicating 10 minutes past 11 o'clock. An incorrect drawing has 85% sensitivity and 86% specificity for dementia.

o_006i.title: Pseudodementia
o_006i.description: A condition in which patients with mental disorders, especially major depression, exhibit symptoms that resemble dementia (e.g., memory loss). Often reversible with psychiatric treatment. More prevalent in older individuals.

p_0L6i.title: Donepezil
p_0L6i.description: A drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase in the central nervous system and allows build-up of the transmitter acetylcholine, which is decreased in various forms of dementia such as Alzheimer's disease. The drug has been shown in trials to improve cognition in patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

J_0s6i.title: Rivastigmine
J_0s6i.description: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to treat dementia associated with Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease.

I_0Ypi.title: Memantine
I_0Ypi.description: An NMDA receptor antagonist used to treat moderate to severe dementia. Although the mechanism of action is unclear, memantine is thought to be neuroprotective. Glutamate agonizes NMDA receptors in certain neurons linked to memory in the hippocampus; excessive stimulation of these neurons may lead to damage (i.e., excitotoxicity). By blocking NMDA receptors, memantine may prevent excitotoxicity.

H_0Kpi.title: Parkinsonism
H_0Kpi.description: A syndrome that includes bradykinesia and either resting tremor or rigidity (or both). Caused by neurodegenerative diseases (Parkinson disease, Parkinson-plus syndromes) or secondary to medication, intoxication, or head trauma.

E_08Ji.title: Bradykinesia
E_08Ji.description: A decreased speed of voluntary and involuntary movements. Can manifest with gait abnormalities (e.g., dragging feet, unsteadiness) and decreased manual dexterity. Typically seen in patients with damage to the basal ganglia (e.g., from Parkinson disease).

v_0AJi.title: Akinesia
v_0AJi.description: A condition of severely reduced or absent voluntary and involuntary movements. Typically seen in patients with severe damage to the basal ganglia (e.g., from Parkinson disease).

w_0hqi.title: Cogwheel rigidity
w_0hqi.description: A physical examination finding of jerking muscle resistance and relaxation in response to passive movement. Seen in some patients with Parkinson disease.

9_0Nqi.title: Postural instability
9_0Nqi.description: A symptom of imbalance and tendency to fall. Caused by impairment of the righting reflexes (i.e., small balancing movements).

x_0Eqi.title: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder
x_0Eqi.description: A parasomnia characterized by dream enactment (e.g., purposeful movements, such as reaching for objects) due to loss of REM sleep atonia. Associated with Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, and dementia with Lewy bodies.

A_0RIi.title: DaTSCAN
A_0RIi.description: An imaging technique in which a radiotracer (123I-ioflupane) in a single-photon emission CT is used to visualize striatal dopamine transporters (DaTs). Used to differentiate between Parkinson disease (reduced DaT activity) and essential tremor.

z_0rIi.title: Anticipation (psychiatry)
z_0rIi.description: Anticipation is a type IV (mature) ego defense mechanism characterized by realistic planning or premature worrying about future discomforts.

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Defense mechanisms

Zz0Zri.title: Blepharospasm
Zz0Zri.description: A focal dystonia characterized by increased blinking or involuntary twitching of the eyelid.

bz0Hri.title: Dopa-responsive dystonia
bz0Hri.description: A rare, genetic disorder characterized by Parkinsonism and dystonia manifesting in childhood. Responds well to treatment with levodopa.

dz0o7i.title: Spasmodic torticollis
dz0o7i.description: A neurologic disorder characterized by sudden, painful contractions of neck muscles that results in abnormal head movements or fixed head posture.

fz0kHi.title: Brudzinski's sign
fz0kHi.description: A physical finding in which forced flexion of the neck elicits an involuntary flexion of the knees and hips. It can occur in patients with meningeal irritation secondary to meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Tz06Hi.title: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Tz06Hi.description: The analysis of fluid from the subarachnoid space. Components include opening pressure, gross appearance, total protein, cell counts, bacterial cultures, PCR, and concentrations of glucose and lactate dehydrogenase.

gz0FHi.title: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
gz0FHi.description: A life-threatening complication of bacterial septicemia (most commonly following meningococcal meningitis), characterized by disseminated intravascular coagulation and hemorrhagic necrosis of the adrenal glands with resulting acute adrenal insufficiency.

hz0csi.title: Meningococcal conjugate vaccine
hz0csi.description: An inactivated, polysaccharide-based conjugate vaccine against Neisseria meningitidis. Recommended for children at 11-12 and 16 years of age, as well as for individuals at risk for meningococcal infections, e.g., individuals with asplenia or complement deficiencies.

3z0Ssi.title: Neonatal meningitis
3z0Ssi.description: Meningitis that occurs within the first 28 days of life. Symptoms are often nonspecific (e.g., irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, hypotonia, hypothermia, respiratory distress) without the classic signs of meningismus (e.g., nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign).

destinations.label: Neonatal bacterial infections → Neonatal bacterial meningitis

Qz0usi.title: Uhthoff's phenomenon
Qz0usi.description: A reversible exacerbation of neurological symptoms after physical exertion, exposure to heat (e.g., warm baths), or fever. Seen in patients with multiple sclerosis. Thought to be due to worsened impulse conduction of demyelinated nerves.

Mz0Mti.title: Lhermitte sign
Mz0Mti.description: A shooting electric sensation that travels down the spine upon flexion of the neck. Typical in multiple sclerosis and may occur in other demyelinating diseases.

oz00Fi.title: McDonald Criteria
oz00Fi.description: A scoring system used to estimate the likelihood of multiple sclerosis. Includes evaluation of the number of exacerbations and clinical manifestations, including spatial and temporal dissemination on MRI.

Kz0UFi.title: Dissemination in space
Kz0UFi.description: A term most commonly used in multiple sclerosis that refers to the formation of demyelinating lesions in different anatomical regions within the CNS. It can be demonstrated either by objective clinical evidence of at least two distinct lesions (e.g., optic disc pallor and hemiparesis confirmed by neurological examination in a person who presents with monocular scotoma and limb weakness) or MRI evidence of at least one lesion seen in at least two different CNS regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and/or spinal).

6z0jFi.title: Dissemination in time
6z0jFi.description: A term most commonly used in the evaluation of multiple sclerosis to describe lesions that develop in the CNS at different time points. It can be confirmed by the presence of at least two documented MS excacerbations or by MRI demonstrating a simultaneous presence of gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at any time or a new T2-hyperintense or enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI.

pz0LFi.title: Neuromyelitis optica
pz0LFi.description: An immune-mediated, chronic inflammatory disease of the CNS; characterized by optic neuritis and other forms of myelitis. Clinically presents with (usually bilateral) optic neuritis and progressive paraplegia. Diagnosed by the combination of clinical symptoms, a normal MRI (to rule out MS), and serological evidence of antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4).

qz0CFi.title: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
qz0CFi.description: A rare immune-mediated, demyelinating CNS disease caused by cross-reaction hypersensitivity between viral antigens and myelin. It usually develops after viral infections or, rarely, after vaccination. Clinical features resemble those of multiple sclerosis (e.g., optic neuritis).

7z048i.title: Glatiramer acetate
7z048i.description: A synthetic oligopeptide derived from myelin basic protein (MBP). This is disease-modifying therapy used for long-term management of multiple sclerosis (MS) to prevent relapses. While its complete mechanism of action is unknown, it is known that glatiramir induces Th2 regulatory cell production. In addition, as an MBP-derivative, it can act as a decoy target for the immune system so that the immune system does not target neuronal myelin.

Hz0K8i.title: Mitoxantrone
Hz0K8i.description: An antineoplastic drug used in the treatment of acute non-lymphocytic leukemia and prostate cancer. Mitoxantrone is also approved for use as a disease-modifying drug in multiple sclerosis.

sz0t8i.title: Dimethyl fumarate
sz0t8i.description: An immunomodulator used in disease-modifying therapy for patients with MS. Particularly efficacious in patients with relapse-remitting MS.

Gz0B8i.title: Teriflunomide
Gz0B8i.description: A drug that inhibits the proliferation of rapidly dividing T and B cells. It works by inhibiting the mitochondrial enzyme dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase. Used as a disease-modifying drug in multiple sclerosis.

tz0Xui.title: Fingolimod
tz0Xui.description: A sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator. Used as a disease-modifying drug in multiple sclerosis

8z0Oui.title: Bridging veins
8z0Oui.description: The veins that connect the superficial cerebral veins to the meningeal veins and dural venous sinuses. Shearing leads to subdural hematoma.

uz0pui.title: Levels of consciousness
uz0pui.description: An individual's level of arousability and response to stimuli. Typically measured by assessing the response to a stimulus (e.g., shouting in the ear, sternal rub) and by the Glasgow coma scale score (eye opening, verbal, and motor responses).

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Sensorium and cognition

Ez08ui.title: Somnolence
Ez08ui.description: A state of drowsiness from which a patient can be easily aroused.

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Sensorium and cognition

9z0NEi.title: Coma
9z0NEi.description: A state of complete unarousable unresponsiveness that typically lasts for 2–4 weeks. Characterized by closed eyes and decreased or absent reflex responses and motor activity. Circulatory function and breathing drive are preserved.

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Sensorium and cognition
Altered mental status and coma → Summary

_z05vi.title: Vestibuloocular reflex
_z05vi.description: A brainstem reflex elicited by activating the vestibular system (e.g., via head movement or caloric stimulation). Normally, the eyes move in the opposite direction to the head movement/caloric stimulation with warm water to stabilize the image in the center of the visual field. The reflex is mediated by the afferent sensory pathway of CN VIII and the efferent motor pathway of the contralateral CN VI and the ipsilateral CN III.

media.title: Testing the vestibuloocular reflex with oculocephalic maneuver

a-0QDi.title: Cerebral edema
a-0QDi.description: A swelling of the brain that causes intracranial hypertension. Can lead to brain herniation in severe cases.

destinations.label: Elevated intracranial pressure and brain herniation → Complications

b-0HDi.title: Glasgow coma scale
b-0HDi.description: A standardized scale used to assess level of consciousness and neurological status. The scale scores the patient's eye response (1–4 points), verbal response (1–5 points), and motor response (1–6 points). A maximum score of 15 points indicates full consciousness, while a minimum score of 3 points can indicate deep coma or brain death. Commonly used to classify traumatic brain injury severity.

destinations.label: Altered mental status and coma → Coma scores

T-069i.title: Manifestations of increased intracranial pressure
T-069i.description: A collection of symptoms that include early findings of positional headache and confusion and late findings of altered mental status, papilledema, and Cushing triad (i.e., irregular breathing, widening pulse pressure, and bradycardia).

destinations.label: Elevated intracranial pressure and brain herniation → Clinical features

m-0VBi.title: Paradoxical embolism
m-0VBi.description: A form of embolism in which the embolus (often a venous thromboembolus) passes through a shunt (e.g., patent foramen ovale) into arterial circulation and causes end-organ infarction (e.g., stroke). Considered a diagnosis of exclusion that should be suspected in patients < 60 years old who present with end-organ ischemia (e.g., stroke) despite no clear risk factors.

n-07Bi.title: Transient ischemic attack
n-07Bi.description: A temporary episode (usually lasting < 1 hour) of focal cerebral ischemia that results in completely reversible neurological deficits. There is no imaging evidence of cerebral infarction and no long-term loss of CNS function.

7-04Ai.title: Lacunar infarcts
7-04Ai.description: A subcortical stroke that is primarily associated with hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Lipohyalinotic thickening of vessel walls results in the occlusion of small, penetrating arteries that supply the subcortical regions of the brain (internal capsule, pons, thalamus, putamen, and caudate). Typically presents as specific lacunar syndromes that are characterized by the absence of cortical signs (e.g., aphasia, hemianopsia, agnosia, apraxia).

H-0KAi.title: Watershed stroke
H-0KAi.description: A stroke in the region between two major vessels that supply the brain, usually as a result of a sudden decrease in blood pressure or cessation of blood flow through both vessels. This occurs because the region between the two territories is least perfused and most susceptible to ischemia.

8-0O_i.title: Kluver-Bucy syndrome
8-0O_i.description: A rare behavioral syndrome that results from bilateral damage to the medial parts of the anterior temporal lobes (amygdala, hippocampus), e.g., due to herpes encephalitis, head trauma, or infarction. Clinical features include hyperorality, hypersexuality, emotional lability, and cognitive dysfunction.

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → Kluver Bucy syndrome

u-0p_i.title: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
u-0p_i.description: A transient decrease in blood flow in the posterior circulation of the brain (which supplies the medulla, cerebellum, pons, midbrain, thalamus, and occipital cortex). Symptoms include vertigo, syncope, nausea, visual or auditory disturbances, dysphagia, and hemiparesis. Etiologies include atherosclerosis, hypotension, and compression of vertebral arteries by cervical osteophytes.

destinations.label: Overview of stroke → Stroke symptoms by affected vessel

w-0hzi.title: Medial medullary syndrome
w-0hzi.description: A neurologic condition caused by occlusion of the paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery, which supply the medial part of the medulla. Manifestations include a triad of contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sensations, and ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy.

destinations.label: Overview of stroke → Stroke symptoms by affected region

x-0Ezi.title: Hyperdense MCA sign
x-0Ezi.description: Increased signal intensity of a portion of the intracranial middle cerebral artery on CT scan, which suggests a large thrombus at that position in the artery.

media.title: Acute ischemic stroke with hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign

B-0zzi.title: Perfusion-diffusion mismatch MRI
B-0zzi.description: An MRI finding describing the difference between the size of a lesion in DWI and PWI sequences. Regions with both reduced diffusion and perfusion suggest irreversibly damaged cerebral tissue, while regions with only perfusion abnormalities and normal diffusion are likely still viable ischemic tissue (i.e., penumbra).

z-0r-i.title: Thrombolytic therapy
z-0r-i.description: The pharmacologic breakdown of blood clots formed in vessels. Indications include STEMI, stroke, massive pulmonary embolism, severe deep vein thrombosis, and acute limb ischemia. Agents used include streptokinase and alteplase.

aZaQZQ.title: Subarachnoid space
aZaQZQ.description: The space between the arachnoid layer and pia mater that contains cerebrospinal fluid. The major arteries of the brain, including the circle of Willis, lie in the subarachnoid space.

destinations.label: The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system → Meninges, falces, and spaces

YZanZQ.title: Cushing reflex
YZanZQ.description: A hypothalamic response to maintain cerebral perfusion in patients with elevated ICP. Results in the Cushing triad, which consists of increased systolic blood pressure, bradycardia, and irregular breathing

bZaHZQ.title: Thunderclap headache
bZaHZQ.description: A sudden-onset, severe headache that reaches maximum intensity almost instantly. Classically associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage due to a ruptured aneurysm; however, various etiologies are now recognized.

XZa9ZQ.title: Sentinel leaks
XZa9ZQ.description: A sudden, severe headache that precedes ~ 25% of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhages by 6-20 days. Thought to be due to a minor hemorrhage of the aneurysm.

2ZaTaQ.title: Epileptic seizure
2ZaTaQ.description: A condition of irregular electrical activity in the brain caused by the hyperexcitability of neurons, especially in cortical areas. Depending on the origin and the type of the seizure, various temporary motor, sensory, autonomic, or psychological symptoms may occur. The most frequent clinical presentation involves rhythmic twitching and loss of consciousness (tonic-clonic seizure).

gZaFaQ.title: Primarily generalized seizures
gZaFaQ.description: A seizure disorder caused by disturbances in both hemispheres. Manifests with impairment or loss of consciousness of varying length. Motor symptoms include tonic-clonic seizures (grand mal seizure), myoclonic or atonic seizures.

hZacYQ.title: Absence seizures
hZacYQ.description: A generalized seizure characterized by transient unresponsiveness (usually lasting < 20 seconds) without a preceding aura or postictal lethargy or confusion. Generalized stiffness and rhythmic jerking seen in tonic-clonic seizures is not seen, but myoclonic jerks or automatisms of the face may be present. An EEG typically reveals a spike and wave pattern with a frequency of 2.5–3.5 Hz.

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndromes

iZaJYQ.title: Tonic-clonic seizure
iZaJYQ.description: A primarily generalized seizure condition characterized by a loss of consciousness and generalized violent muscle contractions followed by rhythmic muscle jerks. Caused by abnormal, unregulated electrical activity.

4Za3bQ.title: Status epilepticus
4Za3bQ.description: A state of continuous seizure lasting ≥ 5 min, or ≥ 2 repetitive, separate seizures with consciousness not fully regained in the interictal period.

OZaIbQ.title: Cataplexy
OZaIbQ.description: A symptom of narcolepsy present in 80% of cases. Characterized by sudden muscle weakness in a fully conscious patient that is triggered by strong emotions (e.g., patients may experience buckling of the knees upon laughing). Self-resolves in < 2 minutes.

lZavbQ.title: Sleep paralysis
lZavbQ.description: A condition in which complete paralysis occurs for 1–2 minutes after waking or before falling asleep. External stimuli (e.g., stirring or addressing the patient) can release a patient from this condition.

nZa7XQ.title: Pseudobulbar palsy
nZa7XQ.description: An upper motor neuron palsy caused by injury to the corticobulbar tracts of cranial nerves V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII. Clinical features include dysarthria, dysphagia, lack of facial expression, difficulty chewing, and emotional lability.

destinations.label: Bulbar palsy and pseudobulbar palsy → Subtypes and variants

oZa0cQ.title: Cobalamin
oZa0cQ.description: A water-soluble vitamin involved in heme synthesis, fatty acid and amino acid metabolism, and, most importantly, DNA synthesis. Significant amounts are contained in red meat, fish, and dairy products. Body stores are very large and last for several years even if an individual completely stops its consumption.

6ZajcQ.title: Pernicious anemia
6ZajcQ.description: A condition characterized by vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia in patients with autoimmune gastritis (AIG). Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells in AIG leads to reduced intrinsic factor production, causing vitamin B12 deficiency. Antibodies to intrinsic factor are also often present. Intrinsic factor is necessary for absorption of vitamin B12 at the terminal ileum.

qZaCcQ.title: Schilling test
qZaCcQ.description: A test to determine the cause of B12 deficiency. Patients ingest radiolabelled B12 and then its urinary excretion is measured. Excretion will be normal if the cause is a dietary deficiency. If excretion is low (suggesting malabsorption), the test is repeated with orally administered intrinsic factor (IF). If excretion normalizes, the cause is IF deficiency. If excretion still remains low, the test is repeated with antibiotics, and then pancreatic enzymes to rule out bacterial overgrowth and pancreatic insufficiency, respectively.

IZaY1Q.title: Folate deficiency
