IZaY1Q.description: A condition characterized by insufficient levels of folate (vitamin B9), an enzyme cofactor in DNA synthesis. Typically caused by dietary insufficiency (e.g., in alcohol use disorder), malabsorption, increased requirement (e.g., in hemolytic anemia) or medications. Can cause neural tube defects in pregnancy and megaloblastic anemia.

rZaf1Q.title: Neurogenic claudication
rZaf1Q.description: A hallmark symptom of lumbar spinal stenosis. Manifests with bilateral or unilateral leg pain that may be accompanied by weakness or numbness. Symptoms are exacerbated by walking, standing, or postures that involve lumbar extension; symptoms are relieved by sitting, lying down, or other postures that involve lumbar flexion.

media.title: Posture-dependent pain in lumbar spinal stenosis (neuropathic claudication)

sZat1Q.title: Hereditary motor sensory neuropathies
sZat1Q.description: A group of progressive hereditary nerve disorders (typically autosomal dominant). Usually caused by defects in proteins involved in the function and structure of axons and/or the myelin sheath. Typical manifestations include distal muscle weakness and atrophy, sensory deficits, and foot deformities (e.g., high arches, hammer toes).

FZagWQ.title: Refsum disease
FZagWQ.description: A rare autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder caused by insufficient α-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids. Consequently, phytanic acid builds up leading to adolescent onset of progressive ataxia, sensorineural hearing loss, scaling skin, cataracts, and night blindness. A short 4th toe may also be seen.

uZapWQ.title: Miller-Fisher syndrome
uZapWQ.description: A rare clinical variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that is characterized by the triad of areflexia, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Associated with anti-GQ1b and anti-GT1a antibodies. Overlap of symptoms with the classic sensorimotor presentation or other clinical variants is common.

EZa8WQ.title: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
EZa8WQ.description: An acquired, autoimmune, demyelinating polyneuropathy characterized by ascending neurologic deficits that develop over a period of ≥ 8 weeks.

wZahdQ.title: Multifocal motor neuropathy
wZahdQ.description: A type of neuropathy that solely affects motor neurons. Associated with anti-GM1 autoantibodies and characterized by asymmetric paresis and areflexia that typically start at the distal upper extremities. Muscle atrophy is rare. Typical diagnostic findings include motor nerve conduction block on EMG and normal protein levels in CSF.

CZaqdQ.title: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
CZaqdQ.description: A reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Causes a prodrome of fever, malaise, and pain. Vesicles typically develop on the ipsilateral forehead, eyelid, and nose. Can cause conjunctivitis, decreased corneal sensitivity, keratitis, and iritis and is potentially sight-threatening.

xZaEdQ.title: Herpes zoster oticus
xZaEdQ.description: Reactivation of VZV in the geniculate ganglion, affecting the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) cranial nerves. Also known as Ramsay Hunt syndrome, it typically manifests with fever, pain, and a vesicular rash in the auditory canal and pinna, as well as facial paralysis, vertigo, and sensorineural hearing loss. The term herpes zoster oticus is sometimes used to refer only to the ear rash and Ramsay Hunt syndrome to refer to the combination of ear rash and facial paralysis.

BZazdQ.title: Postherpetic neuralgia
BZazdQ.description: A complication of shingles characterized by attacks of acute, intense pain in areas previously affected by the rash. Presents in 10–15% of cases and has a strong association with advanced age. Symptoms may subside with time or persist. Treatments include tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline) and gabapentin.

AZaRVQ.title: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
AZaRVQ.description: A compression neuropathy in which the posterior tibial nerve is compressed within the tarsal tunnel. Manifestations include neuropathic pain, paresthesia, and numbness in the posteromedial ankle, heel, and toes.

media.title: Tarsal tunnel (malleolar canal) with flexor retinaculum of the foot

zZarVQ.title: Tinel sign
zZarVQ.description: A tingling sensation produced on percussion of a damaged or irritated nerve.

destinations.label: Orthopedic examination → Arm and hand examination

media.title: Tinel sign in carpal tunnel syndrome

-ZaDVQ.title: Phalen test
-ZaDVQ.description: A highly specific test for median nerve entrapment in the carpal tunnel. The wrist is actively or passively held in full flexion. If paresthesia in the fingers innervated by the median nerve (right thumb, index finger, middle finger, lateral ring finger) occurs within one minute, the test is positive for carpal tunnel syndrome.

destinations.label: Orthopedic examination → Arm and hand examination

media.title: Phalen maneuver and reverse Phalen maneuver
Phalen maneuver supported by the examiner

Z0aZeQ.title: Bell palsy
Z0aZeQ.description: The most common cause of facial paralysis. Caused by a lower motor neuron lesion. Typically manifests with unilateral facial sag and forehead weakness (e.g., inability to raise eyebrows, decreased forehead wrinkling). Changes in hearing and taste can also occur.

a0aQeQ.title: Central facial nerve palsy
a0aQeQ.description: A unilateral lesion affecting the upper motor neuron (between the cortex and brainstem nuclei) that results in contralateral hemiparesis of the lower facial muscles, while the forehead is spared.

media.title: Examination findings in facial nerve palsy

Y0aneQ.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Y0aneQ.description: An X-linked recessive genetic disease in which mutations in the dystrophin gene result in a defective protein product. Results in subsequent degeneration of muscle fibers, causing proximal muscle weakness along with cardiomyopathy and bone fragility. Progresses relatively rapidly; most patients become wheelchair-dependent in late childhood and die during or before the third decade of life due to respiratory insufficiency or cardiomyopathy.

media.title: Progressive muscular dystrophy (Duchenne and Becker subtypes)
Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Becker muscular dystrophy fact sheet

b0aHeQ.title: Gower maneuver
b0aHeQ.description: A physical examination finding in which the patient walks their hands along their thighs as support to rise from a sitting position. Indicates proximal muscle weakness.

X0a9eQ.title: Calf pseudohypertrophy
X0a9eQ.description: A physical finding associated with progressive muscular dystrophy characterized by large calf muscles. Caused by necrosis of muscle cells and subsequent replacement with connective and fat tissue.

c0aaUQ.title: Becker muscular dystrophy
c0aaUQ.description:
An X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Results in the degeneration of muscle fibers and progressive proximal muscle weakness. Affected individuals usually survive past the third decade of life.

The term "Becker muscular dystrophy" .is named after Peter Emil Becker, a German neurologist and member of a paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party who was formally de-Nazified in 1947. Although we refrain from eponyms whenever possible, there is no accepted replacement term at this time.

media.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Becker muscular dystrophy fact sheet

10a2UQ.title: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
10a2UQ.description: A genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness that develops in childhood or adolescence and primarily affects the pelvic and shoulder girdle. Caused by mutations of the calpain-3 gene, which encodes a protease involved in calcium regulation and sarcomere function.

d0aoUQ.title: Myotonia
d0aoUQ.description: A very slow relaxation of the muscle after cessation of contraction. Occurs as a result of prolonged depolarization of muscle fibers due to instability of the sarcolemmal membrane. Patients usually complain of muscle stiffness, or a difficulty letting go of objects after gripping them (grip myotonia). Percussion of the thenar eminence causes the thumb to abduct and then relax slowly (percussion myotonia). Causes of myotonia include myotonic dystrophy and certain channelopathies (e.g., myotonia congenita).

V0aGUQ.title: Myotonic dystrophy type I
V0aGUQ.description: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by a CTG trinucleotide expansion in the DMPK gene. Clinical features include muscle weakness, myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction abnormalities, infertility, hypersomnia, and cognitive dysfunction.

U0ab2Q.title: Myotonic dystrophies
U0ab2Q.description: An autosomal dominant myopathy characterized by myotonia (slow relaxation of muscles after cessation of contraction) and slowly progressive weakness of muscles in the face and/or limbs. Type 1 myotonic dystrophy predominantly affects distal muscles, while type 2 myotonic dystrophy affects proximal muscles. Other systemic manifestations such as cardiomyopathy, cataracts, smooth muscle weakness, and endocrine deficiency may also be present.

R0alfQ.title: Simpson test
R0alfQ.description: A clinical test used historically to demonstrate fatigable eyelid muscle weakness in patients with myasthenia gravis.

i0aJfQ.title: Edrophonium test
i0aJfQ.description: A test that was historically used for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis and to differentiate a myasthenic crisis from a cholinergic crisis. Edrophonium (Tensilon®), an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, results in an increase of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction. Considered positive if symptoms of muscular weakness improve, which supports the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. The FDA discontinued edrophonium testing in 2018 due to its high false-positive rates; more specific testing (i.e., for antiacetylcholine receptor antibodies) is preferred.

Q0aufQ.title: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Q0aufQ.description: An autoimmune condition caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels in the neuromuscular junction, which inhibits the release of acetylcholine. Manifests as muscle weakness that improves with repetitive stimulation and autonomic dysfunction. Often a paraneoplastic syndrome, most commonly from small cell lung cancer.

j0a_fQ.title: Confabulations
j0a_fQ.description: A cognitive disturbance in which individuals fabricate, distort, and/or misinterpret memories without the intention to deceive. Seen in patients with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

destinations.label: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome → Clinical features
Mental status examination → Sensorium and cognition

P0aWTQ.title: Korsakoff syndrome
P0aWTQ.description: Chronic neurologic condition characterized by selective anterograde and retrograde amnesia with relative preservation of long-term memory. Occurs as a consequence of long-term thiamine deficiency, generally after already experiencing signs of Wernicke encephalopathy. Typically occurs in alcoholics.

destinations.label: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome → Clinical features

40a3TQ.title: Wernicke encephalopathy
40a3TQ.description: An acute neurological syndrome caused by thiamine deficiency that is characterized by a triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Requires emergency treatment with thiamine repletion. Typically occurs in individuals with alcohol use disorder.

destinations.label: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome → Clinical features

k0amTQ.title: Gait ataxia
k0amTQ.description: An abnormal, unsteady, staggering gait with irregular, uncoordinated movements of the pelvic girdle and/or lower limbs. Typically caused by cerebellar dysfunction (cerebellar ataxia), frontal lobe dysfunction (frontal ataxia), or damage to the proprioceptive sensory pathways (sensory ataxia).

O0aITQ.title: Truncal ataxia
O0aITQ.description: The inability to maintain truncal stability and coordinate central trunk muscles. Most commonly manifests with an inability to sit upright and/or stand without support.

N0a-TQ.title: Finger-to-nose test
N0a-TQ.description: A test of coordination that evaluates for appendicular (limb) ataxia. Patients are asked to extend their hands and touch the tip of their nose with their index finger. Cerebellar lesions typically manifest with ipsilateral dysmetria and/or intention tremor.

m0aVgQ.title: Heel-knee-shin test
m0aVgQ.description: A test of coordination that evaluates for appendicular (limb) ataxia. While lying supine, the patient is asked to place one heel on the contralateral knee and slide the heel down along the shin toward the ankle. The test is repeated on the other leg. An abnormal test may indicate an ipsilateral cerebellar lesion.

50aigQ.title: Canal of Guyon
50aigQ.description: A 4-cm long, fibro-osseous canal on the medioventral portion of the wrist that contains the ulnar artery and ulnar nerve. The floor of the canal is formed by the transverse carpal ligament, the roof by the palmar carpal ligament, the ulnar (medial) border by the pisiform bone, and the radial (lateral) border by the hook of the hamate bone.

destinations.label: Forearm, wrist, and hand → Muscles and fascia

media.title: Cross-section of wrist showing the carpal tunnel and Guyon canal

M0aMgQ.title: Cubital tunnel syndrome
M0aMgQ.description: A condition characterized by compression of the ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Can be caused by leaning on the elbow, prolonged elbow flexion, trauma, and repetitive use of the forearm flexors (e.g., baseball players, bodybuilders, wrestlers). Symptoms include numbness/paresthesias along the ring and little fingers that can be reproduced by tapping on the medial epicondyle (Tinel test) and elbow pain that radiates to the forearm.

destinations.label: Ulnar nerve entrapment → Overview of ulnar nerve entrapment

L0awgQ.title: Claw hand deformity
L0awgQ.description: A deformity characterized by flexion of the proximal and/or distal interphalangeal joint, and extension of the metacarpophalangeal joint. It is caused by weakness of the lumbrical muscle, which flexes the metacarpophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joint.

o0a0SQ.title: Froment sign
o0a0SQ.description: An inability to keep the thumb's interphalangeal joint extended when tightly pressing together the tips of the index finger and thumb, or when tightly adducting the thumb against the 2nd metacarpal (e.g., pinching a piece of paper using the thumb). Froment sign is seen in ulnar nerve palsy because the flexor pollicis longus (innervated by the intact median nerve) compensates for the action of the weak adductor pollicis but simultaneously causes flexion of the thumb's interphalangeal joint.

p0aLSQ.title: Radial tunnel syndrome
p0aLSQ.description: A condition characterized by purely by lateral elbow pain without symptoms of nerve palsy (i.e., no weakness, sensory deficits, or paresthesias). The pain results from compression of the posterior interosseous nerve within the radial tunnel, an anatomical space on the lateral aspect of the elbow that extends from the radial head to the distal margin of supinator muscle.

J0asSQ.title: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome
J0asSQ.description: A syndrome characterized by weakness of muscles in the extensor compartment of the forearm as a result of compression of the posterior interosseous nerve (a motor branch of the radial nerve). The most common site of compression is within the radial tunnel, at the proximal border of the superficial head of the supinator (arcade of Frohse).

I0aYhQ.title: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome
I0aYhQ.description: A pure motor deficit caused by damage to the median nerve distal to the elbow. Results in impaired flexion of distal joints of thumb and index finger (i.e., inability to pinch with the thumb and second finger). Does not typically cause pain.

70a4hQ.title: Hand of benediction
70a4hQ.description: A distortion of the hand that occurs in individuals with proximal median nerve injury. When asked to make a fist, the patient can only flex the ring finger and little finger and is unable to oppose and abduct the thumb and flex the index and middle finger. Chronic nerve lesions lead to thenar muscle atrophy. Typically accompanied by sensory deficits over the first three digits and the radial side of the ring finger.

media.title: Proximal and distal median nerve lesions

H0aKhQ.title: Pinch sign
H0aKhQ.description: An inability to pinch a small object due to an impairment in flexing the distal joints of the thumb and index finger (due to weakness of the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus). The distal joints of both fingers remain extended. Typically seen in patients with anterior interosseous nerve syndrome.

s0athQ.title: Triad of Horner syndrome
s0athQ.description: A group of physical findings characteristic of Horner syndrome, including ipsilateral miosis, partial ptosis, and anhidrosis on the face and arm.

G0aBhQ.title: Otoliths
G0aBhQ.description: Calcium carbonate structures located on top of the otolith organs (utricle and saccule). Because the gelatinous otolithic membrane is heavier than the surrounding endolymph, otoconia are especially sensitive to gravity and linear acceleration.

t0aX3Q.title: Dix-Hallpike test
t0aX3Q.description: A test used to diagnose benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and identify the affected side by provoking an attack.

F0ag3Q.title: Epley repositioning maneuver
F0ag3Q.description: A method for treating benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) by removing the otoliths from the semicircular canals using gravity and targeted movement.

media.title: Epley maneuver for right posterior semicircular canal BPPV
Epley maneuver for left posterior semicircular canal BPPV

80aO3Q.title: Endolymphatic hydrops
80aO3Q.description: A distortion and distention of the labyrinthine system of the inner ear caused by the accumulation of fluid in the endolymphatic sac. Considered the classic pathologic lesion of Ménière disease but can also be seen as a result of trauma, metabolic conditions, and autoimmune conditions.

C0aqRQ.title: Aura
C0aqRQ.description: A group of paroxysmal, reversible, neurological symptoms that typically precede an attack of migraine or seizure and vary in intensity and duration. Aura can manifest with a multitude of symptoms: e.g., visual (e.g., flashing lights, scotoma), motor (e.g., paresis), somatosensory (e.g., paresthesia), vestibular (e.g., dizziness), vocal (e.g., aphasia), or olfactory (e.g., hyperosmia) symptoms.

y0adiQ.title: Retinal migraine
y0adiQ.description: A condition characterized by migraine with concurrent monocular visual deficits such as scotomas, light flashes, or, in rare cases, complete monocular blindness.

A0aRiQ.title: Medication overuse headache
A0aRiQ.description: A secondary headache disorder caused by frequent use of analgesics (usually ≥ 10 days/month for more than 3 months), most commonly drugs that are themselves used to treat headaches (e.g., NSAIDs, triptans, ergotamine).

z0ariQ.title: Triptans
z0ariQ.description: A group of 5-HT receptor agonists that act by vasoconstriction of (dilated) cranial and basilar arteries. Used for acute treatment of migraine and cluster headaches. Most effective if taken early after the onset of symptoms. Adverse effects include include a temporary increase in blood pressure.

-0aDiQ.title: Status migrainosus
-0aDiQ.description: A severe, debilitating migraine attack that lasts ≥ 72 hours.

0aaeQQ.title: Paroxysmal hemicrania
0aaeQQ.description: A disorder characterized by severe, unilateral attacks of periorbital pain that occur several times per day. Associated with cranial autonomic dysfunction (e.g., lacrimation, conjunctival injection).

1aa2jQ.title: Low back pain
1aa2jQ.description: Pain and/or stiffness localized to the lower back (below the costal margin) and above the buttocks. May be accompanied by pain radiating down the legs.

WaaPjQ.title: Radiculopathy
WaaPjQ.description: Compression or irritation of a nerve root that manifests with pain, paresthesia, weakness, and/or hyporeflexia along the distribution of the nerve root.

faakPQ.title: C7 radiculopathy
faakPQ.description: A compression of the C7 spinal nerve root. Main clinical features include weakness of the triceps and wrist flexor muscles, a reduced triceps reflex, and a sensory deficits of the dorsomedial forearm and hand and the palmar aspects of digits II–IV.

gaaFPQ.title: L3 radiculopathy
gaaFPQ.description: Injury or compression of the L3 nerve root (e.g., from L2/L3 intervertebral disc herniation). Classically results in sensation abnormalities along the anterior lateral area of the thigh (stretching diagonally from thigh to upper area of the medial knee). Patellar and adductor reflexes may be impaired.

SaayPQ.title: L4 radiculopathy
SaayPQ.description: L4 spinal nerve root compression. Characteristic symptoms include: diminished sensation from the distal lateral thigh area over the patella up to the inner side of the lower leg and tibialis anterior muscle weakness (weak foot dorsiflexion), leading to difficulty heel walking. The most common causes are lumbar disc herniation and spinal stenosis.

haac4Q.title: L5 radiculopathy
haac4Q.description: Compression of the L5 nerve root which can lead to pain and reduced sensitivity in the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. It may also cause weakness in foot dorsiflexion and eversion, as well as extension of the big toe

media.title: Intervertebral disk herniation and nerve root compression

3aaS4Q.title: S1 radiculopathy
3aaS4Q.description: A condition caused by S1 spinal nerve root compression. Characteristic symptoms include reduced sensation over the lateral foot, weakness in plantar flexion and eversion, and decreased Achilles tendon reflex. Common causes are lumbar disc herniation and spinal stenosis.

Raal4Q.title: Conus medullaris syndrome
Raal4Q.description: A syndrome caused by damage to the spinal cord at the level of T12-L2. Manifestations include sudden-onset lower back pain, symmetrical and hyperreflexic distal paresis of the lower limbs, perianal numbness, and bladder and fecal incontinence.

media.title: Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes

Qaau4Q.title: Cauda equina syndrome
Qaau4Q.description: A clinical syndrome caused by compression of nerves in the cauda equina (involving ≥ 2 of the L2–S5 nerve roots). Can cause bowel or bladder dysfunction, perianal or saddle anesthesia, variable lower extremity neurological deficits, and back pain. Can lead to irreversible disability, especially if not promptly diagnosed using MRI and treated with surgical decompression.

media.title: Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes

4aa3kQ.title: Straight leg raise test
4aa3kQ.description: An assessment for nerve root impingement in the lumbosacral region that is often caused by disk herniation. With the patient in a supine position, the examiner lifts the leg 30º-70º with the knee in extension. The test is considered positive if the patient experiences pain radiating down the same leg, below the knee.

5aaiOQ.title: Bragard sign
5aaiOQ.description: A physical examination sign for lumbar disc herniation. The examiner lifts the supine patient's leg while the knee is straight until pain is elicited. The leg is then lowered just below this point. The ankle is then dorsiflexed. If pain is reproduced, it is a positive test.

MaaMOQ.title: Kernig sign
MaaMOQ.description: A physical finding elicited by placing the patient in supine position, flexing the thigh at the hip, and subsequently extending the knee. Considered positive if extension of the knee causes pain and resistance. Suggests meningeal or nerve root irritation.

JaaslQ.title: Periradicular therapy
JaaslQ.description: CT-navigated injection of a local anesthetic (e.g., ropivacaine) and glucocorticoids at the intervertebral foramen to reduce inflammation and edema at the affected nerve root.

raafNQ.title: Dissection of the carotid artery
raafNQ.description: Separation of the tunica media and tunica intima of the carotid artery. Typically manifests with a headache and neck pain. Can cause focal neurologic deficits secondary to stenosis of the carotid artery (may lead to cerebral hypoperfusion) or thrombus formation (may lead to embolic stroke). Usually diagnosed by CT angiography. Treatment typically includes antithrombotic agents, thrombolysis, and/or surgery.

destinations.label: Dissection of the carotid and the vertebral arteries → Clinical features

7aa4NQ.title: Dissection of the vertebral artery
7aa4NQ.description: Separation of the tunica media and tunica intima of the vertebral artery. Typically manifests with a headache and neck pain. Can cause focal neurologic deficits secondary to stenosis of the vertebral artery (may lead to cerebral hypoperfusion) or thrombus formation (may lead to embolic stroke). Usually diagnosed by CT angiography. Treatment typically includes antithrombotic agents, thrombolysis, and/or surgery.

destinations.label: Dissection of the carotid and the vertebral arteries → Clinical features

GaaBNQ.title: Horseshoe kidney
GaaBNQ.description: A congenital disorder characterized by the fusion of both kidneys into a horseshoe shape. Kidney function in itself is not impaired, but the abnormal anatomy increases the risk of ureteropelvic junction obstruction and kidney stones with subsequent inflammation.

destinations.label: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys → Overview

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

uaapmQ.title: Renal agenesis
uaapmQ.description: The congenital absence of one or both kidneys, which is caused by the failure of the uretic (kidney) bud to form during fetal development.

destinations.label: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys → Overview

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

vaaAmQ.title: Renal dysplasia
vaaAmQ.description: An abnormal development of the kidney characterized by disorganized nephrons, decreased number of nephrons, and inappropriate differentiation of renal tissue. Associated with collecting system anomalies that predispose to urinary tract infection. Unilateral dysplasia is usually asymptomatic; bilateral dysplasia leads to early renal insufficiency and can lead to renal failure.

destinations.label: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys → Overview

xaaE5Q.title: Duplex collecting system
xaaE5Q.description: A complete or incomplete duplication of the collecting system (i.e. pelvicalyceal system and ureter), which results in varying clinical manifestations based on the degree of fusion. Results in a kidney with two separate pelvicalyceal systems and either a single ureter (i.e., bifid renal pelvis), two ureters that merge before entering the bladder (i.e., Y-shaped ureter or bifid ureter), or two ureters that merge into separate orifices in the bladder (i.e., duplex ureter).

destinations.label: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys → Overview

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

Baaz5Q.title: Double ureter
Baaz5Q.description: A congenital abnormality in which the ureter is duplicated with two separate orifices that merge into the bladder.

destinations.label: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys → Overview

ZYaZnQ.title: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
ZYaZnQ.description: An autosomal recessive hereditary disease characterized by cystic dilation of the renal collecting ducts. Severe ARPKD manifests soon after birth with abdominal distention, respiratory failure, craniofacial abnormalities, hematuria, and/or renal failure. Patients who survive infancy often live > 10 years, but congenital hepatic and portal fibrosis are common.

cYaaLQ.title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
cYaaLQ.description: An autosomal dominant hereditary disease characterized by the development of multiple cysts in the kidneys. Clinical features include chronic kidney disease, recurrent UTIs, and nephrolithiasis. Extrarenal manifestations include multiple benign hepatic cysts, heart valve defects, colonic diverticulosis, and intracranial saccular aneurysms.

media.title: Liver involvement in polycystic kidney disease

UYaboQ.title: Medullary sponge kidney
UYaboQ.description: A rare congenital disorder characterized by calcified cysts in the collecting ducts of one or both kidneys. Typically asymptomatic but associated with an increased risk of nephrolithiasis and urinary tract infections.

TYa6oQ.title: Acoustic enhancement
TYa6oQ.description: An ultrasonographic phenomenon characterized by increased echogenicity behind structures that transmit ultrasound waves well (e.g., fluid-filled cysts).

3YaSKQ.title: Prehn sign
3YaSKQ.description: A physical examination finding in which elevation of the scrotum relieves testicular pain. A positive Prehn sign is associated with epididymitis; a negative Prehn sign is associated with testicular torsion.

RYalKQ.title: Hydatid of Morgagni torsion
RYalKQ.description: A rotation of the hydatid of Morgagni, an embryological remnant at the upper pole of the testes, around its own axis, causing ischemia.

iYaJKQ.title: Paraphimosis
iYaJKQ.description: A urological emergency in which the foreskin is trapped behind the glans penis in uncircumcised or partially circumcised individuals, causing constriction of the penis. Often caused by failure to reduce the foreskin after retraction (e.g., during Foley catheter insertion).

destinations.label: Disorders of the glans penis and foreskin → Paraphimosis

QYauKQ.title: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
QYauKQ.description: An autosomal dominant condition characterized by the formation of benign skin hamartomas on the head and neck, pulmonary cysts (which can result in spontaneous pneumothorax), and an increased risk of developing renal cell carcinoma.

PYaW6Q.title: Stauffer syndrome
PYaW6Q.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome associated with renal cell carcinoma. Manifestations include transaminemia, thrombocytosis, a prolonged prothrombin time, hepatosplenomegaly. Thought to be caused by an increased serum IL-6 concentration.

4Ya36Q.title: Angiomyolipoma
4Ya36Q.description: A benign renal tumor that arises from perivascular epithelioid cells and consists of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and mature fat cells. May be sporadic or associated with certain syndromes (e.g., tuberous sclerosis). Mostly asymptomatic, but large angiomyolipomas may present with hematuria, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, and impaired renal function.

kYam6Q.title: Oncocytoma
kYam6Q.description: A tumor composed of oncocytes, which are large, acidophilic, mitochondria-rich cells derived from the epithelium. It is typically benign. It can develop in the kidneys, salivary gland, thyroid gland, pancreas, or the pituitary gland.

oYa0JQ.title: Lower urinary tract symptoms
oYa0JQ.description: A nonspecific term used to encompass symptoms of bladder irritation or bladder outlet obstruction. Irritative symptoms include urinary frequency, nocturia, urgency, and urge incontinence. Obstructive symptoms include urinary hesitancy, straining to urinate, poor urinary stream, prolonged terminal dribbling, and sensation of incomplete voiding.

GYaBqQ.title: 5α-reductase inhibitor
GYaBqQ.description: A class of substances that block the activity of the enzyme 5α-reductase, thereby preventing the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. This, in term, reduces prostate size. Agents include finasteride and dutasteride.

FYagIQ.title: Finasteride
FYagIQ.description: A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor that is used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia (male pattern baldness). It is also sometimes used to treat hirsutism (e.g., in polycystic ovary syndrome) in women.

media.title: Drugs influencing the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal-axis

8YaOIQ.title: Transurethral resection of the prostate
8YaOIQ.description: A minimally invasive surgical procedure for benign prostatic hyperplasia wherein hyperplastic prostatic tissue is resected under cystoscopic guidance using a cautery resectoscope. Indicated in patients with enlarged prostates that cause complications (e.g., urinary retention, recurrent UTIs, hydronephrosis) or severe symptoms that affect the patient's quality of life (e.g., frequent nocturia interfering with sleep, prolonged micturition).

EYa8IQ.title: Transurethral resection syndrome
EYa8IQ.description: A condition of dilutional hyponatremia that results as a complication of endoscopic or surgical procedures in which a large amount of irrigation fluid is used. Caused by the absorption of irrigant by the vasculature.

vYaAIQ.title: Prostate specific antigen
vYaAIQ.description: An enzyme produced exclusively by the prostate, which physiologically splits the semenogelin-1 protein and thereby liquefies semen. Controversially used as a screening tool for prostate cancer and as a tumor marker during follow-up of prostate cancer. Reasons for elevation include cancer, benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH), urinary tract infection, prostatitis, trauma, and prostate gland manipulation. Malignancy is suspected if PSA levels are > 4 ng/mL.

DYa1rQ.title: Prostate biopsy
DYa1rQ.description: The sampling of prostate tissue under image guidance (e.g., transrectal ultrasound or mpMRI). Primarily performed to evaluate for prostate cancer in patients with suspicious findings on digital rectal exam (e.g. nontender prostatic nodularity) and/or elevated prostate-specific antigen levels. Complications include UTI, prostatitis, hematuria, hematospermia, and acute urinary retention.

9YaNrQ.title: Gleason score
9YaNrQ.description: A score used to grade prostate cancer based on histological findings on transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy or radical prostatectomy samples.

xYaErQ.title: Radical prostatectomy
xYaErQ.description: A surgical procedure that involves removal of the entire prostate gland, including the capsule, seminal vesicles, and vas deferens. Indicated in cases of localized prostate cancer or in cases of prostate cancer where primary radiation therapy has failed to control the disease (salvage prostatectomy).

AYaR7Q.title: Seminoma
AYaR7Q.description: A germ cell tumor of the testicle that originates in the germinal epithelium of the seminiferous tubules. Typically manifests as a painless, testicular lump. Ultrasonography usually shows a well-defined, hypoechoic lesion without cystic areas.

zYar7Q.title: Lugano classification
zYar7Q.description: A classification system used for staging and assessing response to treatment in Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

0baeHQ.title: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection
0baeHQ.description: A urinary tract infection in immunocompetent women who do not have a condition that predisposes them to an increased risk of infection or failed therapy (e.g., pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, recent history of any instrumentation).

YbanHQ.title: Complicated urinary tract infection
YbanHQ.description: A urinary tract infection associated with factors that predispose a patient to an increased risk of infection or failed therapy. These factors include male sex, pregnancy, functional or anatomical abnormalities (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia, kidney cysts, stones), immunocompromise, recent catheterization or instrumentation, and features of atypical pediatric UTI.

Xba9HQ.title: Recurrent urinary tract infections
Xba9HQ.description: ≥ 2 urinary tract infections within 6 months or ≥ 3 urinary tract infections within 1 year.

cbaasQ.title: Honeymoon cystitis
cbaasQ.description: A lower urinary tract infection that occurs in women after recent sexual activity, which can cause irritation of the urethral meatus and facilitate bacterial entry into the urethra (e.g., from the genital and/or anal region).

1ba2sQ.title: Significant bacteriuria
1ba2sQ.description: The number of colony-forming units/mL (CFU/mL) of urine that indicate true intravesical colonization rather than contamination. A threshold of > 100,000 CFU/mL is widely used but levels vary depending on collection method; e.g., in urine samples collected from suprapubic catheters, any CFUs are often considered significant.

WbaPsQ.title: Interstitial cystitis
WbaPsQ.description: A chronic pelvic pain syndrome characterized by pain with bladder filling, lower urinary tract symptoms (urinary urgency and increased frequency, nocturia), and suprapubic and/or pelvic pain. Diagnosed clinically in patients with symptoms lasting ≥ 6 weeks after exclusion of alternative diagnoses (e.g., urinary tract infection).

VbaGsQ.title: Nitrofurantoin
VbaGsQ.description: A bactericidal antibiotic that binds nonspecifically to bacterial ribosomal proteins to impair cellular function. Used in the treatment of and prophylaxis against lower urinary tract infections (e.g., urethritis, cystitis).

fbakGQ.title: Paranephric abscess
fbakGQ.description: An infection in the retroperitoneal space adjacent to the kidney and outside the Gerota fascia. Usually secondary to perinephric abscess and rupture of the Gerota fascia.

Tba6GQ.title: Transudate
Tba6GQ.description: A type of fluid that is low in proteins and cells and typically due to the permeation of fluid from intact vessels into a cavity. Causes include increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (e.g., pleural effusion in congestive heart failure) and/or decreased capillary oncotic pressure (e.g., edema due to lack of albumin).

gbaFGQ.title: Exudate
gbaFGQ.description: A protein-rich fluid that occurs as a result of increased vascular permeability from inflammation. Analysis of the fluid reveals a cellular (cloudy) fluid with high protein and low glucose concentration. Can accumulate in cavities (e.g., pleural space, pericardial space).

SbayGQ.title: Chylothorax
SbayGQ.description: Lymphatic fluid from the thoracic duct (chyle) in the pleural cavity. Chyle is a cloudy milky fluid with high concentrations of lipids (↑ triglycerides, cholesterol, chylomicrons, and fat-soluble vitamins).

RbaltQ.title: Pleurodesis
RbaltQ.description: An invasive procedure in which the pleural space is obliterated. Used to prevent recurrent pneumothorax or recurrent pleural effusion (either benign or malignant). A chest tube is inserted in the pleural space, through which a chemical (talc, bleomycin) is dispersed. This leads to inflammation and fibrosis of both visceral and parietal pleura, which results in adhesion and obliteration of the potential space where effusions/pneumothorax develop.

ibaJtQ.title: Reexpansion pulmonary edema
ibaJtQ.description: A self-limited, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that develops within 24 hours of rapid re-expansion of lung tissue (e.g., after therapeutic thoracentesis) that has collapsed as a result of air, pleural fluid, or mucus plugging. Characterized by respiratory distress that may necessitate oxygen and ventilatory support. Risk factors include removal of large volumes of pleural fluid, long duration of lung collapse, and associated pneumothorax.

QbautQ.title: Acute bacterial prostatitis
QbautQ.description: An infection of the prostate gland that typically causes urinary tract symptoms (e.g., dysuria, genitourinary pain, urgency) and fever. The most common cause is E. coli. Early antibiotic treatment is important to avoid complications such as sepsis and prostatic abscess.

PbaWFQ.title: Chronic bacterial prostatitis
PbaWFQ.description: A chronic, bacterial infection (most commonly E. coli) of the prostate gland that typically causes recurrent symptoms of urinary tract infections (e.g., dysuria, increased urinary frequency, urgency).

4ba3FQ.title: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome
4ba3FQ.description: A condition characterized by chronic urogenital pain with no evidence of urinary tract infection. Affected individuals may also experience lower urinary tract symptoms (e.g., increased urinary frequency and urgency) and erectile dysfunction. The etiology is unclear. A multimodal treatment approach with a symptomatic focus is recommended.

ObaIFQ.title: Four-glass test
ObaIFQ.description: A fractional urine examination to diagnose chronic bacterial prostatitis. Urine cultures are obtained from a urethral sample, midstream urine, and samples during and after prostate massage. The prostate is confirmed as the source of infection if the bacterial count in one of the prostatic samples is 10-fold higher than the midstream urine sample. Has largely been replaced by the more simple two-glass test.

lbavFQ.title: Hydrocele
lbavFQ.description: An accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis of the scrotum surrounding one or both testicles. Most commonly idiopathic but may occur secondary to trauma, a tumor, or lymphatic filariasis. Further subdivided into communicating hydroceles (usually discovered in infancy; contain peritoneal fluid) and noncommunicating hydroceles (no connection to the peritoneal cavity, fluid derives from the tunica vaginalis).

Nba-FQ.title: Varicocele
Nba-FQ.description: A pathological dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum. Usually left-sided since the left testicular vein is longer (more gravitational pull) and drains into the left renal vein at a right angle without an antireflux valve at the junction, leading to poor outflow of blood and an increased reflux.

mbaV8Q.title: Fournier gangrene
mbaV8Q.description: A condition of necrotizing fasciitis affecting the genital or perianal areas.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTIs)

Lbaw8Q.title: Urinary urgency
Lbaw8Q.description: A strong urge or perceived need to void that may be accompanied by pain or a fear of urine leakage.

destinations.label: Overactive bladder and urgency urinary incontinence → Clinical features

pbaLuQ.title: WAGR syndrome
pbaLuQ.description: A genetic syndrome caused by deletion of the WT1 gene that is named for its features: Wilms' tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies (e.g., cryptorchidism, streak ovaries), and intellectual disability (mental Retardation).

JbasuQ.title: Retrograde pyelography
JbasuQ.description: A diagnostic procedure in which x-rays are taken as a water-soluble contrast agent is injected into the ureter via cystoscopy. Used to visualize filling defects within the ureter and/or renal pelvis (e.g., tumor, stones, contrast extravasation).

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

qbaCuQ.title: Reflex incontinence
qbaCuQ.description: Unpredictable urinary leakage that occurs when the bladder is full or otherwise stimulated (e.g., by cold air). Due to simultaneous dyssynergistic contractions of the sphincter and the detrusor muscle, brought about by an underlying neurologic condition like multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury.

rbafEQ.title: Subacromial impingement syndrome
rbafEQ.description: A spectrum of clinical findings caused by compression of subacromial structures (e.g., rotator cuff tendons, subacromial bursa) between the humeral head and the acromion. Typically manifests as shoulder pain and dysfunction. Usually caused by repetitive overhead sports or activities and can eventually lead to a rotator cuff tear.

destinations.label: Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder → Subacromial impingement syndrome

GbaBEQ.title: Frozen shoulder
GbaBEQ.description: A condition of inflammation and fibrosis of the joint capsule that leads to contracture of the shoulder joint. Can be idiopathic, a complication of proximal humerus fracture, or a postoperative complication due to immobility.

destinations.label: Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder → Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

8baOvQ.title: Biceps tendinopathy
8baOvQ.description: Inflammation (tendinitis) and/or chronic degeneration (tendinosis) of the biceps tendon, most commonly affecting the proximal long head near its origin at the superior glenoid tubercle. If left untreated, it can progress to rupture of the tendon.

destinations.label: Biceps tendinopathy and biceps tendon rupture → Definitions

ubapvQ.title: Calcific tendinitis
ubapvQ.description: An idiopathic deposition of calcium crystals within the periarticular soft tissue, most commonly the rotator cuff tendons, especially at the supraspinatus insertion. Occurs more commonly in women than men and can manifest acutely, with pain and restricted joint movement, or as chronic pain syndrome.

destinations.label: Basic calcium phosphate crystal deposition diseases → Calcific tendinitis

media.title: Basic calcium phosphate-associated calcific periarthritis (calcific tendinitis)

9baNDQ.title: Rotator cuff tear
9baNDQ.description: A large tear in the tendon of one or more muscles in the rotator cuff. Often results from progression of smaller tears and inflammation; may be degenerative or traumatic in nature.

destinations.label: Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder → Rotator cuff disease

CbaqDQ.title: Peyronie's disease
CbaqDQ.description: An acquired fibrosis of the tunica albuginea that leads to abnormal curvature of the penis. Commonly causes pain, deformity, and erectile dysfunction.

BbazDQ.title: Camptodactyly
BbazDQ.description: A congenital, fixed digital flexion deformity most often seen in the 5th digit. Associated with several congenital syndromes, including Down syndrome.

ybadwQ.title: Finkelstein test
ybadwQ.description: A clinical test to diagnose de Quervain tenosynovitis. The examiner grasps the thumb of the affected hand and exerts longitudinal traction, passively pulling the thumb across the palm to cause ulnar deviation of the wrist. This stretches the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Test is positive if the maneuver elicits pain or discomfort over the dorsoradial wrist.

destinations.label: Orthopedic examination → Arm and hand examination

AbaRwQ.title: Trigger finger
AbaRwQ.description: An inflammation of the flexor tendon sheath leading to a stenosing tenosynovitis. Patients experience a locking or catching sensation during active flexion-extension activity and often have a palpable nodule along the axis of the flexor tendon. The cause is unknown.

zbarwQ.title: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
zbarwQ.description: Noninflammatory thickening of the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment of the extensor retinaculum, overlying the radial styloid process. Thought to be caused by repetitive abduction and/or extension of the thumb.

UXabxQ.title: Spondylolysis
UXabxQ.description: A lytic defect or fracture in the pars interarticularis of the vertebral arch. This defect occurs almost exclusively in the lumbar vertebrae and, when bilateral, can progress to spondylolisthesis.

2XaTxQ.title: Spondylolisthesis
2XaTxQ.description: A condition in which a vertebral body slips forward in relation to the subjacent vertebra. The two main causes are degenerative changes, which affect individuals > 50 years of age, and defects in the pars articularis (spondylolysis), which most commonly affect children and adolescents. Can be asymptomatic or cause lower back pain that is exacerbated by exertion, gait problems, and radiculopathy.

gXaFxQ.title: Step-off sign
gXaFxQ.description:
1) A physical examination finding in spondylolisthesis or fracture in which there is a palpable step on examination of the vertebrae due to displacement (may also be used to describe the x-ray).
2) A deformity seen on lateral spinal x-ray in sickle cell disease and Gaucher disease in which there is end-plate vertebral body depression (also known as H-vertebrae)
3) A physical examination finding of a posterior cruciate ligament tear in which there is a loss of the normal step off in a hypothetical line between the femur and the tibia
4) An x-ray finding of Lisfranc injury caused by dorsal displacement of the second metatarsal on a lateral view

iXaJBQ.title: Facet joint syndrome
iXaJBQ.description: A cause of lower back pain resulting from arthritic changes of the zygapophyseal joints (also known as the facet joints). Largely a degenerative disease of older adults. Symptoms can be nonspecific but often include radiating pain to the buttocks or groin. It is differentiated from other spinal pathologies (especially discogenic pain) by the fact that pain is not exacerbated with increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., Valsalva maneuver).

jXa_BQ.title: Cobb angle
jXa_BQ.description: A radiographic measurement used to assess the degree of spinal curvature (e.g., in scoliosis or kyphosis). Lines are drawn parallel to the top of the uppermost and bottom of the lowermost tilted vertebrae. A perpendicular line is drawn between the two lines to form a parallelogram, and the intersecting angle is measured.

4Xa3yQ.title: Risser stage
4Xa3yQ.description: A radiographic measurement of the ossification of the iliac apophysis used to estimate skeletal maturity and remaining growth potential. The stages range from 0-5 and are inversely related to remaining growth potential (i.e., stage 0 indicates high growth potential, and stage 5 indicates no remaining growth potential). Commonly used to guide management in patients with scoliosis.

OXaIyQ.title: Asymmetrical gluteal folds
OXaIyQ.description: A sign in pediatric patients that is associated with hip dysplasia.

destinations.label: Developmental dysplasia of the hip → Clinical features

lXavyQ.title: Ortolani test
lXavyQ.description: A physical examination maneuver used to evaluate infantile hip dysplasia. The child's hips are placed in 90° of flexion and the examiner abducts the leg and applies upward pressure. A palpable clunk represents a subluxation of the examined hip (positive Ortolani sign).

destinations.label: Developmental dysplasia of the hip → Diagnosis

media.title: Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)

NXa-yQ.title: Barlow test
NXa-yQ.description: A physical examination maneuver used to evaluate infantile hip dysplasia. The child's hips are placed in 90° of flexion and the examiner adducts the leg and applies downward pressure. A palpable clunk represents a subluxation of the examined hip (positive Barlow sign).

destinations.label: Developmental dysplasia of the hip → Diagnosis

media.title: Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)

mXaVAQ.title: Graf's classification
mXaVAQ.description: A classification system for developmental hip dysplasia that ranges from I (normally developed) to IV (dislocated). Includes the angle of the joint, the anatomical position of the lower extremities, and the age of the child.

rXafzQ.title: Transient synovitis
rXafzQ.description: A self-limited inflammation of the synovium of the hip joint, causing hip pain and a limp. Most commonly affects children aged 3–8 years. Associated with a preceding viral illness.

8XaO-Q.title: Drehmann sign
8XaO-Q.description: A sign of slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Characterized by obligatory external rotation upon flexion of the hip in the supine position.

destinations.label: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis → Clinical features

DXa1Zj.title: Patellar grind test
DXa1Zj.description: A physical examination maneuver used to evaluate patellofemoral pain. With the patient supine, the examiner pushes the patella distally with both thumbs and stabilizes it. Pain that occurs when the patient contracts the quadriceps muscle indicates patellofemoral osteoarthritis.

destinations.label: Osteoarthritis of the hip and knee → Clinical features

wXahZj.title: Buffer insoles
wXahZj.description: A supportive insert placed in the shoe for the treatment of various musculoskeletal conditions, particularly involving the foot and ankle, e.g., flatfoot, uneven limb length.

9XaNZj.title: Hip replacement
9XaNZj.description: A surgical procedure that completely or partially replaces the articular surfaces of the hip joint with a prosthesis. Commonly performed in patients with osteoarthritis who have persistent pain and functional impairment despite conservative management, and those with femoral neck fractures.

xXaEZj.title: Total hip replacement
xXaEZj.description: A surgical procedure that replaces both the ball (femoral head) and socket (acetabulum) of the hip joint with a prosthesis. Commonly performed in patients with severe osteoarthritis who have persistent pain and functional impairment despite conservative management.

media.title: Main components of a hip prosthesis

AXaR0j.title: Knee joint replacement
AXaR0j.description: A surgical procedure that completely or partially replaces the articular surfaces (femoral, tibial) of the knee joint with a prosthesis. Commonly performed in patients with osteoarthritis who have persistent pain and functional impairment despite conservative management.

ZcaZaj.title: Unicondylar knee replacement
ZcaZaj.description: A surgical procedure that replaces a single compartment of the knee joint with a prosthesis. Commonly performed in patients with osteoarthritis affecting just one compartment of the knee that is not responsive to conservative management. Types include medial unicompartmental knee replacement (most common), lateral unicompartmental knee replacement, and patellofemoral joint replacement.

acaQaj.title: Bicondylar knee prosthesis
acaQaj.description: A surgical procedure that replaces two of the three compartments of the knee joint with a prosthesis. Commonly performed in patients with osteoarthritis that has not improved with conservative management.

bcaHaj.title: Total knee replacement
bcaHaj.description: A surgical procedure that replaces all three compartments of the knee joint with a prosthesis. The femoral and tibial components are often metal, separated by a plastic spacer (usually polyethylene) to facilitate movement. Commonly performed in patients with osteoarthritis who have persistent pain and functional impairment despite conservative management.

1ca2Yj.title: Patellofemoral joint replacement
1ca2Yj.description: A partial knee replacement procedure in which part of the femur and patella are replaced by a prosthesis.

dcaoYj.title: Soft tissue ossification
dcaoYj.description: The formation of bone in soft tissue and/or muscle that can occur after tissue injury. Typically results in muscle stiffness and restriction of movement.

destinations.label: Collection of orthopedic conditions → Myositis ossificans

gcaFbj.title: Bucket-handle tear
gcaFbj.description: A displaced and extensive longitudinal meniscal tear that splits the meniscus into two parts that remain connected to each other at the anterior and posterior ends.

media.title: Bucket handle tear and flipped meniscus

3caSXj.title: Steinman test
3caSXj.description: A physical examination maneuver to assess for meniscal tear.

icaJXj.title: Bohler sign
icaJXj.description: A sign of knee meniscus injury. With the patient supine and the knee and hip slightly flexed, the examiner lifts the leg with one hand while maintaining the knee in an attitude of flexion. With the other hand, the examiner grasps the lower leg and applies adducting (varus) and abducting (valgus) forces on the knee joint. Pain during adduction (varus stress) is a sign of medial meniscus injury; pain during abduction (valgus stress) is a sign of lateral meniscus injury.

QcauXj.title: Apley grind test
QcauXj.description: A physical examination maneuver to assess for meniscal tear. With the patient prone, the examiner flexes the knee to 90° while holding the medial knee in one hand and ankle in the other hand. The examiner then stabilizes the thigh and internally and externally rotates the leg. Pain during external rotation indicates medial meniscus injury; pain during internal rotation indicates lateral meniscus injury.

OcaIcj.title: Panner disease
OcaIcj.description: A form of osteochondrosis that affects the capitulum of the humerus. Manifests with pain, limited range of motion, and swelling in the elbow. Typically affects the dominant arm and is usually caused by repetitive strain injury due to overuse of the elbow (e.g., from pitching baseballs). Most commonly affects boys between 5-10 years of age.

media.title: Osteochondrosis of the humeral capitellum (Panner disease)

lcavcj.title: Kienbock disease
lcavcj.description: Avascular necrosis of the lunate bone in the hand. It is associated with repetitive impact or trauma to the hand (e.g., volleyball). Clinical features include pain in the dorsum of the wrist.

Nca-cj.title: Ahlback disease
Nca-cj.description: An insufficiency fracture in the subchondral area of the distal femur that is not preceded by significant trauma. Manifests with acute knee pain. Most commonly affects women between 55-70 years of age. Can lead to osteonecrosis localized to the fracture area.

media.title: Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIF/SIFK)
Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIF/SIFK)

mcaV1j.title: Blount disease
mcaV1j.description: Varus deformity of the proximal tibia caused by disrupted cartilage growth. Primarily affects young children or adolescents. Risk factors include early walking, obesity, and African-American ethnicity. Causes severe and progressive inward angling of the proximal tibia, presenting as a bow leg deformity.

destinations.label: Angular deformities of the lower extremities → Subtypes and variants

5cai1j.title: Osgood-Schlatter disease
5cai1j.description: A traction apophysitis that occurs where the patellar tendon inserts onto the tibial tuberosity. Characterized by progressive anterior knee pain that is exacerbated by activity (typically jumping, kneeling, running, squatting), with focal swelling and tenderness at the tibial tuberosity. Most commonly affects adolescents.

McaM1j.title: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease
McaM1j.description: A traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella where the patellar tendon attaches. Characterized by anterior knee pain that worsens with activities such as jumping, kneeling, running, and squatting. Often accompanied by tenderness and swelling over the inferior patella. Most commonly affects young adolescents.

nca71j.title: Sever disease
nca71j.description: An inflammatory condition caused by a stress fracture. Manifests with heel pain at the insertion point of the Achilles tendon. Occurs in growing children, especially young athletes who engage in repetitive running and/or jumping.

oca0Wj.title: Metatarsal avascular necrosis
oca0Wj.description: A condition of osteonecrosis of the metatarsals, most often affecting the second or third metatarsal head. Thought to be caused by repetitive trauma.

KcaUWj.title: Fibrous dysplasia
KcaUWj.description: A benign developmental disorder of bone that causes normal skeletal tissue to be replaced by fibrous tissue. Appears on x-ray as well-defined, intramedullary, osteolytic lesions. Usually monostotic but is polyostotic in 25% of cases. Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia may be associated with café-au-lait spots and precocious puberty (McCune-Albright syndrome).

JcasWj.title: McCune-Albright syndrome
JcasWj.description: A genetic syndrome caused by a mosaic mutation in G-protein signaling and subsequent continuous stimulation of endocrine functions. Typical features include precocious puberty, café-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and endocrine abnormalities (e.g., Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, thyrotoxicosis).

media.title: Fibrous dysplasia in McCune Albright syndrome

IcaYdj.title: Osteopetrosis
IcaYdj.description: A heritable bone disease caused by defective osteoclastic resorption of immature bone.

rcafdj.title: Achilles tendinopathy
rcafdj.description: An overuse injury of the Achilles tendon that typically manifests with pain and tenderness 2–6 cm above the insertion of the Achilles tendon.

7ca4dj.title: Lateral epicondylitis
7ca4dj.description: An overuse injury typically caused by activities that involve repetitive wrist extension and/or repetitive forearm supination-pronation with the elbow in near complete extension (e.g., racket sports). Results in microtears at the common tendinous origin of the extensor muscles in the forearm.

HcaKdj.title: Medial epicondylitis
HcaKdj.description: An overuse injury typically caused by activities that involve repetitive valgus stress on the elbow, forearm pronation, and/or wrist flexion. Results in microtears at the common tendinous origin of the flexor muscles in the forearm. This common tendon is attached to the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

tcaXVj.title: Patellar tendinitis
tcaXVj.description: An overuse injury of the patellar tendon distal to the kneecap that often develops in athletes who jump frequently. Manifests with pain over the anterior aspect of the knee that worsens with climbing stairs, walking downhill, and after prolonged sitting.

ucapVj.title: Iliotibial band syndrome
ucapVj.description: An overuse injury most common in cyclists and runners that causes pain along the lateral aspect of the knee as a result of inflammation of the iliotibial band. Caused by friction between the lateral femoral condyle and the iliotibial band near its insertion at the Gerdy tubercle.

Eca8Vj.title: Malignant otitis externa
Eca8Vj.description: A subtype of otitis externa characterized by a necrotizing inflammation of the external auditory canal. Most frequently caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Risk factors include poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and immunosuppression.

Dca1ej.title: Bullous myringitis
Dca1ej.description: An infection of the tympanic membrane that manifests with painful vesicles and bullae. Most commonly caused by a viral or bacterial infection.

wcahej.title: Mastoiditis
wcahej.description: An inflammation of the mastoid air cells. Most commonly occurs in children < 2 years of age as a complication of acute otitis media. Typical manifestations include a tender and edematous mastoid and anterolateral protrusion of the auricle.

9caNej.title: Labyrinthitis
9caNej.description: An inflammation of the inner ear (labyrinth) that causes severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss. Usually idiopathic (possibly viral) but can also be bacterial (e.g., complication of acute otitis media). Sometimes used to describe vestibular neuritis with associated hearing impairment. In practice, the terms labyrinthitis and vestibular neuritis are often used interchangeably.

Bcazej.title: Paracusis willisii
Bcazej.description: A phenomenon in certain forms of conductive hearing loss (especially otosclerosis) in which the patient hears conversation better in noisy rather than silent surroundings. This phenomenon occurs because the other person involved in the conversation speaks louder to adjust to ambient noise, and ambient noise, which is typically low-pitched, is masked by the low-tone deafness that is characteristic of conductive hearing loss.

Z1aZ2j.title: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome
Z1aZ2j.description: An autosomal dominant genetic disorder causing abnormal vascular development in the mucous membranes, skin, GI tract, genitourinary tract, lungs, liver, and/or brain. It commonly presents with nosebleeds but can also cause acute or chronic bleeding from the GI tract, requiring blood transfusions and iron supplementation.

a1aQ2j.title: Acute sinusitis
a1aQ2j.description: An inflammation of the paranasal sinuses and adjacent nasal cavity that causes purulent nasal drainage as well as nasal obstruction or facial tenderness over the affected sinus for up to 4 weeks. Usually viral but can less commonly be caused by bacteria. Fungal causes are usually only found in immunocompromised patients.

Y1an2j.title: Chronic sinusitis
Y1an2j.description: An inflammation of the paranasal sinuses and adjacent nasal cavities with purulent nasal drainage and nasal obstruction or facial tenderness lasting > 12 weeks. The diagnosis relies on objective confirmation with CT, nasal endoscopy, or anterior rhinoscopy. May be caused by an underlying medical conditions, e.g., polyps. Considered an inflammatory disease with occasional bacterial exacerbations.

b1aH2j.title: Nasal polyps
b1aH2j.description: Benign lesions of the nasal mucosa or paranasal sinuses that develop due to chronic mucosal inflammation, commonly in the context of chronic rhinosinusitis.

X1a92j.title: Chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps
X1a92j.description: A subtype of chronic rhinosinusitis characterized by the presence of nasal polyps and typical manifestations of rhinosinusitis (e.g., rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, hyposmia, facial pressure/pain).

11a2fj.title: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
11a2fj.description: A rare, autosomal recessive disorder caused by dysfunctional or absent cilia (e.g., due to mutations in the dynein arm or assembly proteins). Clinical features include recurrent otitis, sinusitis, chronic productive cough, and situs inversus. Fertility is usually reduced due to decreased sperm motility or dysfunctional fallopian tube cilia.

V1aGfj.title: Atrophic rhinitis
V1aGfj.description: A chronic type of nonallergic rhinitis characterized by the thinning and degeneration of the nasal mucosa and underlying structures that leads to dryness, crusting, nasal congestion, foul odor, and, sometimes, nasal deformity. Can be primary (often associated with bacterial colonization) or secondary (e.g., resulting from granulomatous infections or trauma).

21aTTj.title: Allergic rhinitis
21aTTj.description: An allergic reaction to environmental allergens (e.g., pollen) causing rhinorrhea or nasal congestion, sneezing, itchy eyes or skin, and fatigue. Symptoms may occur at the same time every year (seasonal) or persist throughout the year (perennial).

h1acgj.title: Stable angina pectoris
h1acgj.description: A type of angina that occurs upon exertion, mental stress, and/or exposure to cold and usually subsides within 20 minutes of rest or after administration of nitroglycerin. Occurs due to a mismatch in myocardial oxygen supply and oxygen demand from underlying coronary artery disease.

k1amSj.title: Herpangina
k1amSj.description: A highly contagious seasonal infection most commonly caused by group A coxsackieviruses. Typically manifests with fever and painful oral and pharyngeal lesions. Most commonly affects children < 5 years of age. Similar to hand, foot, and mouth disease, which manifests with additional cutaneous lesions.

destinations.label: Coxsackievirus infections → Hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina

O1aISj.title: Vincent angina
O1aISj.description: An acute necrotizing periodontal bacterial infection that also involves the tonsils and pharynx.

destinations.label: Acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis → Differential diagnoses

N1a-Sj.title: Ludwig angina
N1a-Sj.description: A rare, life-threatening, and rapidly spreading soft tissue infection of the floor of the mouth that can lead to airway compromise. Most commonly caused by polymicrobial odontogenic infections and occurs more frequently in individuals with poor dentition and/or immunosuppression. The classic presentation includes a woody or indurated floor of the mouth, submandibular swelling, and tongue elevation.

51aihj.title: Total tonsillectomy
51aihj.description: A surgical procedure in which the entire tonsils and tonsillar capsule are typically removed.

M1aMhj.title: Subtotal tonsillectomy
M1aMhj.description: A surgical procedure to remove only part of the tonsils and leave the tonsillar capsule intact. This procedure is carried out in children more often than adults, particularly in cases of sleep apnea secondary to tonsillar hypertrophy. Partial tonsillectomy is also an option in recurrent and chronic tonsillitis, or tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess.

L1awhj.title: Oral cavity cancer
L1awhj.description: A cancer of the oral mucosa, tonsils, or salivary glands. Associated with smoking, chronic alcohol consumption, and certain subtypes of human papillomavirus (e.g., HPV 16). Manifestations include dysphagia, nonhealing ulcers, bleeding, and lymphadenopathy.

K1aU3j.title: Tonsil cancer
K1aU3j.description: A malignant neoplasia (most commonly squamous cell carcinoma) of the tonsils. It is the most common form of oropharyngeal malignancy. Manifestations include otalgia and the sensation of a mass in the throat (globus sensation). Often associated with human papillomavirus infection.

I1aYRj.title: Sicca syndrome
I1aYRj.description: A condition characterized by xerophthalmia and xerostomia. Common in patients with Sjogren syndrome (due to focal lymphocytic infiltration) and systemic sclerosis (due to fibrosis). Nonautoimmune causes include radiation therapy to the head, medications (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants), and infections (e.g., HCV, HIV).

v1aAij.title: Persistent depressive disorder
v1aAij.description: A chronic depression characterized by a consistently low mood and other depressive symptoms lasting for ≥ 2 years (≥ 1 year in adolescents and children).

w1ahQj.title: Major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern
w1ahQj.description: A subtype of major depressive disorder characterized by ≥ 2 depressive episodes associated with a seasonal pattern (e.g., the winter season) over ≥ 2 years. Must include absence of depressive episodes in times other than the identified season.

destinations.label: Major depressive disorder → Subtypes and variants

z1arjj.title: Postpartum psychosis
z1arjj.description: An umbrella term for various forms of psychosis that develop following childbirth. Typically manifests within 2 weeks but may occur up to or even after 4 weeks postpartum. Characterized by acute onset of psychotic features (e.g., hallucinations, delusions), mood changes (e.g., mania and/or depression), and cognitive symptoms similar to delirium. May be associated with insomnia and irritability. May result in harm to patient and/or baby and is a psychiatric emergency.

destinations.label: Approach to psychosis → Special patient groups

ZWaZPj.title: Manic episode
ZWaZPj.description: A mood state characterized by ≥ 7 consecutive days of persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood in addition to ≥ 3 (or ≥ 4 if mood is only irritable) of the following symptoms: inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and/or excessive involvement in risky activities. A manic episode results in marked impairment in functioning or hospitalization and can be diagnosed after ruling out other medical conditions or substance use.

YWanPj.title: Rapid cycling
YWanPj.description: A subtype of bipolar disorder characterized by rapidly alternating episodes of mania/hypomania and depression (≥ 4 episodes per year).

cWaa4j.title: Cyclothymia
cWaa4j.description: A psychiatric disorder that is characterized by persistent hypomanic/depressive mood swings over a period of at least 2 years, which are not sufficiently severe to justify a diagnosis of bipolar disorder.

iWaJOj.title: Alcohol withdrawal delirium
iWaJOj.description: A life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal in individuals with chronic alcohol use. Symptoms usually develop 72–96 hours after cessation or reduction of alcohol consumption. It is characterized by an alteration of consciousness (agitation, possibly with hallucinations) and sympathetic hyperactivity (e.g., tachycardia, hypertension).

jWa_Oj.title: Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder
jWa_Oj.description: A complication of alcohol withdrawal occurring within 12–24 hours after cessation of or reduction in heavy alcohol consumption. Typically, patients present with auditory and/or visual hallucinations without the additional symptoms present in alcohol withdrawal delirium (i.e., there is no impaired consciousness and vital signs can be normal).

PWaWlj.title: CAGE
PWaWlj.description:
A series of questions used to screen for alcohol use disorder, includes: 
C: Cut down drinking: (e.g., “Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?”)
A: Annoyed: (e.g., “Have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking?”)
G: Guilty: (e.g., “Have you ever felt guilty about drinking?”)
E: Eye-opener: (e.g., “Have you ever felt you needed a drink first thing in the morning as an "eye-opener" to steady your nerves or to overcome a hangover?”)

kWamlj.title: Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin
kWamlj.description: A transferrin molecule with ≤ 3 sialic acid residues. Typically increased in patients with alcohol use disorder due to a change in the glycosylation patterns of transferrin induced by alcohol consumption.

destinations.label: Overview of alcohol use → Confirmation of alcohol use

5WaiNj.title: Delirium
5WaiNj.description: An acute, complex, organic brain syndrome characterized by a waxing and waning state of confusion, along with disturbances of consciousness, cognitive function, psychomotor behavior (e.g., hypoactivity, hyperactivity), and sleep-wake rhythm. Not associated with focal deficits on neurological examination.

sWat5j.title: Positive symptoms of schizophrenia
sWat5j.description: Abnormal symptoms that are present in patients with schizophrenia. Symptoms include hallucinations, delusions, features of disorganized thought and speech processes, grossly disorganized behavior, and abnormal movement (e.g., catatonia).

GWaB5j.title: Negative symptoms of schizophrenia
GWaB5j.description: A collection of behavioral and emotional symptoms of schizophrenia. Includes flat affect, anhedonia, avolition (decreased purposeful activity), alogia (decreased speech), and social withdrawal.

EWa8Mj.title: Waxy flexibility
EWa8Mj.description: A sign of catatonia characterized by initial resistance to passive limb movement that can be overcome by repositioning of the limb.

wWahnj.title: Catalepsy
wWahnj.description: A state of muscular rigidity and immobility characterized by unresponsiveness to external stimuli. Common causes include neurologic disorders (e.g., Parkinson disease, epilepsy, catatonia) and neuroleptic drug use (e.g., haloperidol).

BWaznj.title: Catatonia
BWaznj.description: A syndrome characterized by markedly decreased or excessive motor activity and/or decreased reactivity to the environment (e.g., during a medical evaluation). Usually associated with a psychiatric condition (e.g., bipolar disorder or schizophrenia) but can also be associated with medical conditions. Manifestations include stupor, staring, mutism, posturing, grimacing, and/or echolalia.

yWadLj.title: Negativism
yWadLj.description: A manifestation of catatonia characterized by opposition or a lack of response to instructions (social negativism) or to external stimuli, e.g., an attempt to passively move the patient's limbs (motor negativism).

Ydanoj.title: Delusional symptoms in the context of a relationship with an individual with prominent delusions
Ydanoj.description: Delusional themes in an individual with delusional disorder are mirrored in the delusional beliefs of another person in the context of a relationship.

1da2Kj.title: Schizotypal personality disorder
1da2Kj.description: A cluster A personality disorder that is characterized by an impaired capacity for social and interpersonal relationships in combination with eccentric behavior or beliefs (e.g., magical thinking, bizarre preoccupations, unusual perceptual experiences, overelaborate or metaphorical speech). Symptoms begin by early adulthood.

fdak6j.title: Psychoeducation
fdak6j.description: A form of counseling on the symptoms, treatments, and prognosis of psychiatric or neurocognitive disorders. Psychoeducation provides patients and their caregivers with tools to manage chronic conditions.

Tda66j.title: Postpsychotic depression
Tda66j.description: A depressive episode that occurs in a patient with schizophrenia following the resolution of psychotic symptoms.

Sday6j.title: Methylphenidate
Sday6j.description: A central nervous system stimulant that functions by blocking norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake by presynaptic neurons. Appears to have an effect on the the cerebral cortex and subcortical structures that is similar to amphetamines. It is the first-line drug for ADHD; also used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness.

Rdalpj.title: Bulimia nervosa
Rdalpj.description: An eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating, the use of measures to counteract weight gain (e.g., inducing vomiting, laxative misuse), and sense of self-worth being disproportionately influenced by the perception of one's weight and/or body shape.

Qdaupj.title: Russell's sign
Qdaupj.description: The formation of calluses on the knuckles as a result of self-induced vomiting, caused by frequent contact of the dorsal skin of the fingers with the upper incisors. Seen in patients with anorexia nervosa with purging behavior and bulimia nervosa.

jda_pj.title: Binge eating disorder
jda_pj.description: An eating disorder characterized by recurrent binge eating episodes, which involve a lack of control over the amount eaten and cause the individual significant distress. Purging behaviors are absent. Commonly associated with obesity.

PdaWJj.title: Refeeding syndrome
PdaWJj.description: A condition caused by abrupt and/or excessive resumption of nutrition in a chronically malnourished patient (e.g., patients with anorexia nervosa, chronic alcohol use, critical illness). Caused by a sudden shift from a catabolic to an anabolic state and massive release of insulin, which causes severe electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) and fluid retention. Clinical features include edema, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and ataxia. Management involves close monitoring of electrolyte levels with repletion as needed and careful reintroduction of nutrition.

kdamJj.title: Suicide
kdamJj.description: The act of intentionally ending one's own life.

Nda-Jj.title: Suicidal ideation
Nda-Jj.description: Thoughts of, or a preoccupation with, ending one's life. Suicidal ideation can be passive (e.g., thoughts or preoccupation with no preparatory behavior or intent) or active (e.g., planning the time, place, and/or method of suicide).

KdaUIj.title: Robertsonian translocation
KdaUIj.description: A chromosomal translocation that involves fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 13, 14, 15, 21, 22). The short arms of two acrocentric chromosomes are lost and the long arms are fused together. Carriers of balanced Robertsonian translocation have a normal phenotype. Offspring of a translocation carrier can inherit a normal karyotype, balanced translocation, or unbalanced translocation (e.g., trisomy 21.)

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Types of mutations

pdaLIj.title: Sandal gap
pdaLIj.description: An abnormally enlarged space between the first and second toe. Associated with trisomy 21.

JdasIj.title: Transverse palmar crease
JdasIj.description: A single palmar crease along the metacarpophalangeal joints perpendicular to the fingers, which is formed by fusion of the two transverse palmar creases. A typical finding in trisomy 21 but can also be a normal variant.

qdaCIj.title: Brachycephaly
qdaCIj.description: A head shape anomaly caused by premature fusion of the coronal sutures (craniosynostosis). Presents with a short, broad, flattened skull.

GdaBrj.title: Scaphocephaly
GdaBrj.description: An abnormally elongated head shape caused by premature fusion of the sagittal suture.

Fdag7j.title: Asphyxia
Fdag7j.description: A deficiency of oxygen supply due to impaired gas exchange (e.g., due to impaired breathing). Typically results in hypercapnia and acidemia.

Eda87j.title: Porencephaly
