Eda87j.description: A disorder characterized by the development of a cerebrospinal fluid-filled cavity in the brain. Can be congenital or develop after a stroke or neonatal infection. Manifestations include developmental delay, spastic contractures, seizures, hypotonia, and hydrocephalus.

wdahHj.title: Periventricular leukomalacia
wdahHj.description: Symmetrical, periventricular injury of cerebral white matter (necrosis and cystic formation) caused by ischemia and/or infection. PVL mainly affects premature infants. Sequelae include spastic cerebral palsy, intellectual impairment, and visual disturbances. Diagnosis is established by brain imaging using ultrasound, cranial CT, or MRI.

9daNHj.title: Selective neuronal necrosis
9daNHj.description: A histopathologic finding characterized by hypoxia-induced, selective destruction of individual nerve cells with sparing of surrounding glial tissue. Etiologies include ischemic damage with subsequent reperfusion (e.g., from temporary cardiac arrest) and epilepsy.

xdaEHj.title: Surfactant
xdaEHj.description: A mixture of phospholipids and proteins produced by alveolar type II cells. The phospholipids reduce alveolar surface tension and thereby prevent the alveoli from collapsing. Deficiency can lead to respiratory distress syndrome, which is most common in preterm infants and often requires tracheal instillation of surfactant.

_da5sj.title: Pulmonary hypoplasia
_da5sj.description: An underdevelopment of the lungs characterized by a decreased number of alveoli and airways. Result in an impaired gas exchange. Associated with oligohydramnios and Potter sequence.

destinations.label: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome → Differential diagnoses

-daDsj.title: Meconium aspiration syndrome
-daDsj.description: A condition in which the fetus/newborn aspirates amniotic fluid after passing meconium in utero. Occurs more frequently in post-term children. The classic presentation includes green/yellow amniotic fluid, neonatal respiratory distress, and consistent findings on chest x-ray (e.g., air trapping, atelectasis).

destinations.label: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome → Differential diagnoses

aVaQGj.title: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
aVaQGj.description: A chronic lung disease that can affect premature infants. Caused by arrested pulmonary development and/or prolonged mechanical ventilation. The most common definition of bronchopulmonary dysplasia is the need for at least 28 days of oxygen therapy in infants born at < 32 weeks' gestation.

YVanGj.title: Kernicterus
YVanGj.description: An irreversible neurological syndrome that occurs in inadequately treated neonates with high levels of serum bilirubin (> 25 mg/dL) as a result of deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and/or brain stem nuclei. Long-term sequelae include hearing impairment, movement disorders (athetosis), intellectual disability, and dental enamel hypoplasia.

bVaHGj.title: Rhesus incompatibility
bVaHGj.description: A hemolytic disease in which Rh antibodies from Rh-negative mothers transfer to an Rh-positive fetus or newborn and result in hemolysis; the severity of clinical presentation ranges from isolated mild anemia to marked anemia causing hydrops fetalis and stillbirth.

destinations.label: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn → Pathophysiology

1Va2tj.title: Anti-D prophylaxis
1Va2tj.description: An antibody against the rhesus D antigen. Commonly used as prophylaxis against hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in Rh(D) negative mothers. Also used in the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

destinations.label: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn → Prevention

eVaxtj.title: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene
eVaxtj.description: A gene located on the long arm of chromosome 7 that encodes the CFTR protein, which is required for proper function of the chloride channel in cell membranes. The chloride channel normally secretes chloride ions in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract. Defects (most commonly a deletion of Phe508) cause cystic fibrosis.

UVabFj.title: Sweat test
UVabFj.description: A laboratory test commonly used to diagnose cystic fibrosis. Involves measuring chloride levels in the patient's sweat after pilocarpine stimulation of the sweat glands; chloride levels ≥ 60 mmol/L on one occasion are consistent with cystic fibrosis. However, usually, two sweat tests on different occasions are obtained to minimize false positives due to technical errors.

fVakFj.title: Meconium ileus
fVakFj.description: An intestinal obstruction caused by failure to pass meconium. Typically manifests in the first three days of life with abdominal distension. Can have associated vomiting. Associated with cystic fibrosis in ~ 90% of cases.

media.title: Microcolon and bowel perforation in meconium ileus

gVaFFj.title: Double bubble sign
gVaFFj.description: A radiographic sign typically seen on abdominal ultrasound/x-ray in patients with duodenal atresia, but may also be present in annular pancreas and midgut volvulus. The two bubbles correlate with the air-filled, distended stomach and duodenum proximal to the obstruction.

destinations.label: Congenital visceral malformations → Duodenal atresia and stenosis

SVayFj.title: Pyloromyotomy
SVayFj.description: A procedure where an incision is made in the muscular layers of the pylorus to widen its lumen.

hVac8j.title: Total colonic aganglionosis
hVac8j.description: A variant of Hirschsprung disease characterized by complete aganglionosis of the colon. Presents with severe symptoms, from incomplete intestinal obstruction to ileus. Associated with significant long-term morbidity and mortality (e.g., enterocolitis, postoperative bowel incontinence).

iVaJ8j.title: Koplik spots
iVaJ8j.description: An enanthem of the buccal mucosa characterized by tiny white or bluish-white spots on an irregular erythematous background. The spots are pathognomonic for measles infection and appear during the prodromal stage.

4Va3uj.title: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
4Va3uj.description: A lethal, generalized, demyelinating inflammation of the brain caused by persistent measles virus infection. SSPE is characterized by dementia, myoclonus, and epilepsy, leading to coma and death. It is a very rare complication that develops several years after initial infection with measles.

MVaMEj.title: Simple febrile seizure
MVaMEj.description: A febrile seizure that is generalized, lasts less than 15 minutes, and does not recur within 24 hours. Usually followed by a quick return to normal without focal neurological deficits.

nVa7Ej.title: Complex febrile seizure
nVa7Ej.description: A febrile seizure that meets any of the following criteria: focal seizure, duration > 15 minutes or interrupted with abortive therapy, or recurrence within less than 24 hours. Around 25% of all febrile seizures are considered complex.

pVaLvj.title: Oligoarticular JIA
pVaLvj.description: A type of juvenile arthritis seen primarily in small children. Affects 4 or less large, weight-bearing joints (e.g., knees, ankles) and is often associated with chronic anterior uveitis.

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

JVasvj.title: Seronegative polyarticular JIA
JVasvj.description: A type of juvenile arthritis characterized by the involvement of 5 or more joints in the first six months of disease onset. May be symmetrical or asymmetrical, and affects both large and small joints. Typical findings include symmetrical interphalangeal arthritis and negative rheumatoid factor in blood tests.

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

qVaCvj.title: Seropositive polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis
qVaCvj.description: A type of juvenile arthritis characterized by the involvement of ≥ 5 joints in the first 6 months of disease onset and the presence of rheumatoid factor. Arthritis is symmetrical and typically affects small joints (e.g., interphalangeal joints).

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

IVaYDj.title: Still disease
IVaYDj.description: A rare condition characterized by recurrent high fever, salmon-pink rash, arthralgia, and/or arthritis. Adult-onset Still disease and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis are increasingly viewed as the same condition with different ages of onset. Serious complications include macrophage activation syndrome and associated interstitial lung disease.

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

media.title: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Still disease) fact sheet

rVafDj.title: Juvenile psoriatic arthritis
rVafDj.description: A type of juvenile arthritis characterized by asymmetrical arthritis of small- to medium-sized joints and psoriasis. May also manifest with dactylitis and nail changes.

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

7Va4Dj.title: Enthesitis-related arthritis
7Va4Dj.description: A type of juvenile arthritis characterized by arthritis and enthesitis occurring either concurrently or independently of each other. Manifests as asymmetric, oligoarticular arthritis of the lower limbs; may also involve peripheral (e.g., fingers) and sacroiliac joints.

destinations.label: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → Subtypes and variants

BVaz9j.title: Intertrigo
BVaz9j.description: An inflammation of the skin that particularly affects skin folds (submammary, inguinal, interdigital). Typically manifests as white macerations on an erythematous base with satellite lesions and possibly scaling. Aggravating factors include obesity, sweat, feces, urine, and vaginal discharge.

AVaRCj.title: Honey-colored crust
AVaRCj.description: A descriptor for the characteristic lesions of impetigo that form when vesicles rupture and the fluid within dries on the skin.

_Va5Cj.title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
_Va5Cj.description: A rare, life-threatening, immune-mediated skin reaction that results in the blistering of skin and extensive epidermal detachment, usually precipitated by medications (e.g., NSAIDs, certain antibiotics, antiepileptics) or, less commonly, viral and bacterial infections (e.g., mycoplasma, herpes simplex virus). When > 30% of the skin is affected, the condition is referred to as toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

-VaDCj.title: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
-VaDCj.description: An immune-mediated, skin reaction that results in extensive blistering of the skin and mucous membranes (a more severe form of Stevens-Johnson syndrome). TEN is usually caused by drugs. Clinical manifestations appear 1–3 weeks after initiating medical therapy. Prodromal symptoms such as fever and malaise may be present. TEN has a high case-fatality rate due to shock.

beaHxj.title: Anaphylaxis
beaHxj.description: A potentially life-threatening type I hypersensitivity reaction that manifests with a variable combination of rash, mucosal swelling, respiratory compromise, hypotension, and/or gastrointestinal symptoms within minutes to hours of exposure to an offending agent.

deaoBj.title: Agranulocytosis
deaoBj.description: A condition characterized by the absence of granulocytes or severe neutropenia. Because of immune suppression, patients with agranulocytosis are at risk for life-threatening infections. Most commonly seen as a toxic effect (myelosuppression) in cytostatic therapy, but it is also an adverse effect of certain drugs, including clozapine, carbamazepine, propylthiouracil, and methimazole. Diseases affecting the bone marrow, such as aplastic anemia and leukemias, can also cause agranulocytosis.

2eaTyj.title: Atopy
2eaTyj.description: A genetic predisposition to produce IgE after antigen exposure. This leads to a tendency toward developing hypersensitivity reactions, especially allergic rhinitis, eczema, and asthma (atopic triad).

destinations.label: Hypersensitivity reactions → Type I hypersensitivity reaction

Tea6yj.title: Skin prick test
Tea6yj.description: A test for a type I hypersensitivity reaction. Tiny amounts of various allergens are applied to the skin. A lancet is then used to prick the surface of the skin, allowing allergens to penetrate the tissue. A wheal (typically within 15–20 minutes) equal to or larger than a histamine control (or greater than 3 mm) indicates a positive reaction to that allergen.

destinations.label: Hypersensitivity reactions → Type I hypersensitivity reaction

ieaJAj.title: Patch test
ieaJAj.description: A diagnostic test that allows the allergens causing allergic contact dermatitis to be determined. The allergen is fixed on a patch and then attached to the arm or back. Erythema, papules, and/or vesicles under the area of contact indicate a positive result.

QeauAj.title: Pseudoallergy
QeauAj.description: A condition characterized by symptoms of a type I hypersensitivity reaction that are not the result of an IgE-mediated process. Typical mechanisms include direct mast cell degranulation, complement-mediated mast cell degranulation (anaphylactoid reactions), and an increase in the production of certain cytokines (e.g., increased leukotriene production in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).

jea_Aj.title: Anaphylactoid reaction
jea_Aj.description: A severe pseudoallergic reaction with symptoms of anaphylaxis (e.g., rash, angioedema). Not IgE-mediated; caused by direct mast cell degranulation (e.g., due to vancomycin or opioid use) or complement-mediated mast cell degranulation.

4ea3_j.title: Allergen immunotherapy
4ea3_j.description: A treatment for type I hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma, allergy to wasp or bee venom). Increasingly greater amounts of a particular allergen are gradually introduced in order to induce tolerance to the antigen by decreasing the body's inflammatory response. Immunological effects include reduced IgE levels, increased IgG levels, and reduced numbers and activation of mast cells, eosinophils, and basophils.

destinations.label: Hypersensitivity reactions → Type I hypersensitivity reaction

Nea-_j.title: Cross-reactive hypersensitivity
Nea-_j.description: A hypersensitivity reaction in which IgE antibodies that are directed against a specific allergen react with another allergen that has a similar antigenic profile (e.g., hypersensitivity to birch pollen among patients who are allergic to apples).

destinations.label: Hypersensitivity reactions → Type I hypersensitivity reaction

meaVzj.title: Histamine-mediated angioedema
meaVzj.description: Angioedema, often accompanied by urticaria and pruritus, that typically develops within 30 minutes to 2 hours after exposure to NSAIDs or allergens (e.g., food, insect bites). Usually resolves within hours to days. Allergens trigger IgE-mediated mast cell activation; NSAIDs trigger IgE but can also trigger mast cells directly.

5eaizj.title: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
5eaizj.description: A hereditary or acquired deficiency or dysfunction of the C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) protein responsible for complement regulation. A lack of C1-INH allows activation of kallikrein and subsequent overproduction of bradykinin, which can trigger bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

Leawzj.title: Hereditary angioedema
Leawzj.description: An autosomal-dominant form of C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency that causes bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Can be triggered by trauma, surgery, dental procedures, infections, and drugs.

oea0-j.title: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema
oea0-j.description: Angioedema that is triggered by increased levels of proinflammatory bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that increases vascular permeability. Urticaria and pruritus are uncommon. Etiologies include C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (both hereditary and acquired) and ACE-inhibitor exposure.

KeaU-j.title: Fixed drug eruption
KeaU-j.description: An adverse cutaneous reaction to a specific drug characterized by the appearance of a well-defined, round, red-purple plaque on the same site of the body every time the drug is taken. The lesion, which is caused by a T-cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction, appears within 30 minutes to 8 hours of taking the drug. The most commonly implicated drugs are NSAIDS, acetaminophen, cotrimoxazole, and tetracycline.

peaL-j.title: Neurofibromatosis type 1
peaL-j.description: A neurocutaneous syndrome caused by mutation of NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. Characterized by café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules (pigmented iris hamartomas), neurofibromas (benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors), and optic pathway gliomas.

media.title: Clinical features of neurofibromatosis type 1 and type 2

Jeas-j.title: Angiofibroma
Jeas-j.description: A benign tumor composed of fibrous tissue, connective tissue, and blood vessels (angiofibroma) that involves the face and appears as reddish nodules in a butterfly appearance around the nose and cheeks (acne-like appearance). Associated with tuberous sclerosis.

qeaC-j.title: Ataxia telangiectasia
qeaC-j.description: An autosomal recessive disease caused by a mutation in the ATM gene, a tumor suppressor gene that assists in the repair of double strand breaks. Affected individuals have severe humoral immunodeficiency (decreased IgA, IgG, and IgE), ataxia due to cerebellar atrophy, and capillary malformations (i.e., telangiectasia). They also have an increased risk of developing lymphomas and leukemias.

7ea4ZP.title: Ungual fibromas
7ea4ZP.description: A benign tumor composed of fibrous or connective tissues that grow under (ungual) or around (periungual) the nails. Typically appears as a smooth, flesh-colored nodule. Associated with tuberous sclerosis.

seatZP.title: Neurofibromatosis type 2
seatZP.description: A hereditary neurocutaneous syndrome caused by mutations in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes the tumor suppressor merlin/schwannomin. Manifestations often include multiple cerebral and spinal tumors, such as acoustic schwannomas (which may be bilateral), gliomas, and meningiomas.

media.title: Clinical features of neurofibromatosis type 1 and type 2

ueap0P.title: Tuberous sclerosis
ueap0P.description: An autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome that is caused by mutation of the TSC1 or TSC2 gene, which encode for hamartin or tuberin protein (both tumor suppressors), respectively. Typically presents with intellectual disability, seizures, and skin manifestations such as adenoma sebaceum, ash-leaf spots, Shagreen patch, and small benign tumors (e.g., brain hamartomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and renal angiomyolipomas).

media.title: Adenoma sebaceum in patient with tuberous sclerosis

veaA0P.title: Herald patch
veaA0P.description: A single ovoid macule or patch with a raised border, central clearing, and surrounding collarette. Typically red with salmon-colored clearing (on light skin) or hyperpigmented with lighter clearing (on dark skin). Appears on the trunk days to weeks before a generalized rash develops in pityriasis rosea.

media.title: Herald patch (mother patch) in pityriasis rosea

9eaNaP.title: Collarette
9eaNaP.description: A fine, ring-like, white scale surrounding a skin lesion. Peripherally adherent with a loosened inner margin. May occur in, e.g., pityriasis rosea, bullous impetigo, mucocutaneous candidiasis, and pustular psoriasis.

xeaEaP.title: Koebner phenomenon
xeaEaP.description: The development of skin lesions in traumatized skin that was previously normal. Koebner's phenomenon is seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo.

AeaRYP.title: Guttate psoriasis
AeaRYP.description: A form of psoriasis characterized by the sudden appearance of numerous small, drop-shaped, erythematous scaly papules. Often precipitated by streptococcal throat infection and primarily affecting the trunk and proximal limbs. Lesions may resolve spontaneously or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis.

-eaDYP.title: Acanthosis
-eaDYP.description: A histopathologic finding characterized by epidermal hyperplasia of the stratum spinosum. Often seen in patients with acanthosis nigricans.

ZUaZbP.title: Parakeratosis
ZUaZbP.description: A histopathological finding characterized by retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum of the epidermis. Often seen in patients with psoriasis.

0UaebP.title: Nail pitting
0UaebP.description: A physical finding of small, round depressions in the nail. Associated with psoriasis.

aUaQbP.title: Oil drop sign
aUaQbP.description: A well-circumscribed, yellow-reddish discoloration of the nail bed (resembles a drop of oil under the nail plate). Typically seen in psoriasis.

YUanbP.title: Brittle nails
YUanbP.description: A nail abnormality characterized by poor strength of the nail plate, which can result in crumbling of the nail with minor trauma. Etiologies include vitamin deficiencies, hypothyroidism, psoriasis, iron deficiency, dermatophyte infections, and peripheral arterial disease.

bUaHbP.title: Psoriatic arthritis
bUaHbP.description: A seronegative inflammatory arthritis found in patients with psoriasis. In 60-80% of patients, psoriasis precedes the arthritis; in 15-20% of patients, arthritis appears before psoriasis. Other common symptoms include enthesitis particularly where the Achilles tendon attaches to the calcaneus, dactylitis, and nail changes.

WUaPXP.title: Pencil-in-cup deformity
WUaPXP.description: A radiographic finding that describes periarticular erosion around the distal interphalangeal joint that gives the appearance of a pencil in a cup. Classically associated with psoriatic arthritis but can be found in patients with other conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and reactive arthritis.

SUaycP.title: Auspitz's sign
SUaycP.description: The appearance of small pinpoint bleeding when scales of a cutaneous lesion are scraped off. Sometimes positive in patients with psoriasis, but neither sensitive nor specific for this condition.

hUac1P.title: Pityriasis rubra pilaris
hUac1P.description: A group of rare, chronic dermatoses characterized by generalized plaques with orange-pink scale, follicular keratosis (i.e., excessive keratin production resulting in small, rough eruptions on the skin), and erythroderma. Typically involves the palms and soles but can affect the entire skin with intermittent sparing.

3UaS1P.title: Erythroderma
3UaS1P.description: A condition that is characterized by generalized erythema, pruritus, and desquamation (typically 2–6 days following onset of the rash). May be idiopathic or arise secondary to an underlying disease (e.g., atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, Sezary syndrome).

RUal1P.title: Phototherapy
RUal1P.description: A treatment for various cutaneous diseases including psoriasis (via impairment of keratinization and induction of apoptosis of pathogenic cells through UVB radiation), atopic dermatitis (with UVA1), and neonatal jaundice (via isomerization of unconjugated, hydrophobic bilirubin to water-soluble bilirubin, which can be excreted in urine and bile, through exposure to blue light with the wavelength 420–480 nm).

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Overview of treatment

iUaJ1P.title: Psolaren and UVA therapy
iUaJ1P.description: A type of phototherapy in which the skin is first sensitized to light by systemically or locally administered psolarens and subsequently exposed to ultraviolet A light (320-400 nm). Used to treat several conditions, including psoriasis, vitiligo, atopic dermatitis, polymorphic light eruptions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Recurrent use is associated with an increased risk of skin cancers.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Overview of treatment

4Ua3WP.title: Wickham's striae
4Ua3WP.description: A dermatologic finding in lesions of lichen planus characterized by fine white lines on the surface of papules or plaques.

kUamWP.title: Mucosal lichen planus
kUamWP.description: An inflammatory disease that can affect the oral, esophageal, and genital mucosa. Manifestations vary depending on the location but often include papules and plaques, Wickham striae, and erosions. The course is typically chronic, and lesions have the potential for malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma.

OUaIWP.title: Hypertrophic lichen planus
OUaIWP.description: A subtype of cutaneous lichen planus that manifests with severely pruritic hyperkeratotic scaly nodules and plaques on the ankles, shins, and interphalangeal joints. The course is typically chronic, and lesions have the potential for malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma.

mUaVdP.title: Lichen sclerosus
mUaVdP.description: A chronic inflammatory dermatosis characterized by pruritic white plaques with epidermal atrophy and scarring. Lichen sclerosis most commonly affects the anogenital area but may also affect extragenital areas (e.g., oral mucosa, back, shoulders). Although lichen sclerosus is a benign condition, genital lesions are associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

nUa7dP.title: Comedonal acne vulgaris
nUa7dP.description: A variant of acne vulgaris characterized by noninflammatory lesions (e.g., closed and open comedones) that typically develop on the forehead, nose, and/or chin.

6UajVP.title: Nodulocystic acne
6UajVP.description: A severe form of inflammatory acne vulgaris in which lesions are > 5 mm in diameter.

JUasVP.title: Hidradenitis suppurativa
JUasVP.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by recurrent follicular inflammation. Manifestations include painful skin lesions (nodules and abscesses), draining sinus tracts, and scarring; the severity of symptoms varies. Lesions are generally located in intertriginous areas (e.g., axillae, inguinal and genital areas).

media.title: Most common sites of hidradenitis suppurativa

IUaYeP.title: Neonatal cephalic pustulosis
IUaYeP.description: A benign skin condition that manifests at a mean age of 3 weeks, affects ~20% of newborns, and is characterized by inflammatory papules and pustules on the face and, sometimes, the scalp. The eruptions usually resolve within 4 months without scarring. The underlying cause remains unclear, but is thought to be inflammatory or fungal.

7Ua4eP.title: Infantile acne
7Ua4eP.description: An uncommon form of acne that occurs in infants. Typically develops 3-4 months after birth and causes inflammatory papules, pustules, and comedones. Usually resolves by the end of infancy. The underlying cause is not well understood.

sUateP.title: Isotretinoin
sUateP.description: A vitamin A derivative primarily used to treat severe acne. Adverse effects include a transient worsening of acne (lasting 2–3 weeks), cheilitis, dry and fragile skin, photosensitivity, hepatic toxicity, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Isotretinoin is known to cause birth defects (e.g., cleft palate and cardiac anomalies).

vUaAUP.title: Nodular melanoma
vUaAUP.description: A rapidly growing and aggressive type of melanoma that most commonly develops on sites of intermittent, intense sun exposure. Typically appears as a blue-black nodule with smooth borders, but may also be amelanotic (e.g., pink or red). May ulcerate and bleed.

wUah2P.title: Lentigo maligna melanoma
wUah2P.description: A subtype of melanoma that often arises from lentigo maligna lesions in older adults. The initial lentigo maligna lesion typically manifests in sun-exposed areas as a tan macule that undergoes slow, horizontal growth into a darkly pigmented, irregularly shaped patch. The transition to lentigo maligna melanoma is characterized by the subsequent development of papules or nodules and variegated tones of red, blue, and white.

9UaN2P.title: Acral lentiginous melanoma
9UaN2P.description: A rare type of malignant melanoma that most commonly manifests on the palms, soles, nail bed, or mucous membranes. More common in patients with darker skin types.

CUaq2P.title: Amelanotic melanoma
CUaq2P.description: A less common variant of melanoma in which the melanocytes produce little or no pigment. Color of the lesion may range from skin-colored to bright pink or red. Diagnosis can be difficult and typically requires histological confirmation.

yUadfP.title: ABCDE criteria
yUadfP.description: A mnemonic summarizing cutaneous changes that are concerning for melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularities, Color variegation, Diameter > 6 mm, and Evolving in size, shape, and/or color.

-UaDfP.title: Breslow depth
-UaDfP.description: The distance between the top of the stratum granulosum or the ulcer base of a melanoma to the deepest tumor cell. Used in melanoma staging. Greater depth is associated with worse prognosis and higher probability of metastasis.

media.title: Breslow depth chart for malignant melanoma

02aeTP.title: Keratoacanthoma
02aeTP.description: A rapidly-growing tumor of the skin derived from the glands surrounding a hair follicle (pilosebaceous glands). Typically presents on hair-bearing areas of skin that are exposed to sun (e.g., face, neck) as a round, erythematous nodule with a central hyperkeratotic crater. Usually heals without treatment, but surgical removal is preferred because of histological resemblance to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

destinations.label: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma → Subtypes and variants

Y2anTP.title: Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome
Y2anTP.description: An autosomal dominant condition characterized by the early development of basal cell carcinomas, medulloblastomas, jaw keratocysts, basaloid follicular hamartomas, and skeletal abnormalities.

destinations.label: Basal cell carcinoma → Subtypes and variants

X2a9TP.title: Superficial basal cell carcinoma
X2a9TP.description: The second most common subtype of basal cell carcinoma. Typically manifests as a thin scaly plaque with a pearl-like appearance, raised borders, and central atrophy. Often located on the trunk and legs. Grows gradually, rarely metastasizes, and has a low likelihood of recurrence after excision.

destinations.label: Basal cell carcinoma → Subtypes and variants

d2aogP.title: Trichoepithelioma
d2aogP.description: A rare, benign tumor of the hair follicle that usually occurs in young individuals and is often mistaken for basal cell carcinoma.

U2abSP.title: Melasma
U2abSP.description: A benign type of hyperpigmentation that occurs after exposure to UV radiation and/or visible light. Commonly associated with pregnancy and the use of certain medications (e.g., oral contraceptives, anticonvulsants). Typical manifestations include nonscaling macules or patches on the face (i.e., centrofacial, malar, or mandibular pattern) and dorsal forearm.

f2akSP.title: Nevus anemicus
f2akSP.description: A congenital nevus characterized by the presence of well-defined, hypopigmented macules and/or patches on the skin. They do not become erythematous in response to friction or heat, unlike the surrounding skin.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

g2aFSP.title: Disseminated gonococcal infection
g2aFSP.description: A systemic infection of N. gonorrhoeae that occurs in <2% of adults with gonorrhea via hematogenous spread. Most commonly manifests as gonococcal arthritis (i.e., arthritis-dermatitis syndrome and/or purulent arthritis). Complications include infective endocarditis, bacterial meningitis, and perihepatitis.

media.title: Pustular skin lesion in disseminated gonococcal infection
Pustular skin lesion in disseminated gonococcal infection

S2aySP.title: Primary syphilis
S2aySP.description: The first clinical stage of syphilis that occurs after an average incubation period of 21 days and presents with a painless, firm, genital ulcer with indurated borders and a smooth base (chancre), which is the site where the treponemes entered the body. Usually concomitant inguinal, nontender lymphadenopathy. Resolves spontaneously within 3–6 weeks, typically without scarring.

media.title: Chancre of the glans penis in primary syphilis

32aShP.title: Secondary syphilis
32aShP.description: A stage of T. pallidum infection in which the spirochetes spread systemically. Symptoms typically arise ~ 10 weeks after infection and include generalized lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, disseminated maculopapular rash affecting the palms and soles, and condyloma lata.

media.title: Condylomata lata of the glans penis in secondary syphilis

j2a_hP.title: Tertiary syphilis
j2a_hP.description: The last stage of syphilis, in which the infection has disseminated to various organs. Can present with tabes dorsalis, chronic meningoencephalitis with cerebral atrophy, an Argyll Robertson pupil, coronary or aortic arch aneurysms, aortic regurgitation, and syphilitic gummas.

N2a-3P.title: Chancre
N2a-3P.description: A painless ulcer (typically solitary) with indurated borders that appears at the site where Treponema pallidum enters the body (e.g., genital region, anus, or oral cavity) during the primary stage of syphilis.

media.title: Chancre of the glans penis in primary syphilis
Chancres on the penile shaft in primary (1º) syphilis

52aiRP.title: Condylomata lata
52aiRP.description: A manifestation of secondary syphilis that causes broad-based, wart-like, papular erosions in the anogenital region, intertriginous folds, and oral cavity.

media.title: Condylomata lata of the glans penis in secondary syphilis

L2awRP.title: Gumma
L2awRP.description: A destructive granulomatous lesion with a necrotic center that tends to ulcerate. Characteristic of tertiary syphilis. Can affect any organ. If gumma are found in the CNS, the disease is classified as stage IV or neurosyphilis.

K2aUiP.title: Neurosyphilis
K2aUiP.description: An involvement of the CNS in a patient with syphilis, causing an inflammatory reaction of the meninges and the surrounding vessels, as well as the cerebral parenchyma. Late manifestation of the disease (tertiary syphilis) that can present with a range of symptoms (e.g., acute meningitis, general paresis, dementia, ataxia).

p2aLiP.title: Tabes dorsalis
p2aLiP.description: Degeneration of the dorsal columns of the spinal cord caused by tertiary syphilis. Manifestations include dysesthesias, gait ataxia, and progressive loss of proprioception.

r2afQP.title: Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption
r2afQP.description: A treponemal test used to diagnose T. pallidum infection with high sensitivity and specificity.

72a4QP.title: VDRL
72a4QP.description: A non-treponemal serological laboratory test for syphilis. Detects nonspecific anti-cardiolipin antibodies and is sensitive, but not specific. Associated with many false-positive results due to cross-reacting antibodies in viral infections, rheumatic fever, lupus, or leprosy.

H2aKQP.title: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
H2aKQP.description: An acute systemic reaction to bacterial endotoxins and pyrogens that are released following initiation of antibiotic treatment, especially for spirochete infections (e.g., syphilis, borreliosis, leptospirosis). Symptoms are typically flu-like (e.g., fever, chills), accompanied by tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and, less commonly, reoccurrence of syphilitic exanthema. Usually self-limited and resolves within 12-24 hours.

F2agjP.title: Dysmenorrhea
F2agjP.description: Lower abdominal and pelvic pain that occurs shortly before and/or during menstruation. Further categorized as primary dysmenorrhea (pain in the absence of pelvic pathology) and secondary dysmenorrhea (resulting from an underlying condition).

u2apjP.title: Primary amenorrhea
u2apjP.description: The absence of menarche by 15 years of age or 5 years after thelarche, whichever comes first. Causes include constitutional delay of growth and puberty, anatomical abnormalities, and congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

E2a8jP.title: Secondary amenorrhea
E2a8jP.description: The absence of menses for > 3 months in individuals with previously regular cycles or > 6 months in individuals with previously irregular cycles. Causes include physiological factors (e.g., pregnancy, breastfeeding, menopause), hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction, primary ovarian insufficiency, anatomical abnormalities, and endocrine conditions (e.g., thyroid dysfunction, polycystic ovary syndrome).

v2aAjP.title: Frequent menstruation
v2aAjP.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by frequent menses, with menstrual cycles < 24 days in length.

D2a1PP.title: Infrequent menstruation
D2a1PP.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by infrequent menses, with menstrual cycles > 38 days in length.

92aNPP.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding
92aNPP.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with quality of life. Other definitions include high flow of bleeding (> 80 mL) and/or prolonged duration (> 8 days). Seen in, e.g., endometriosis, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial cancer.

x2aEPP.title: Light menstruation
x2aEPP.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by abnormally short, light menstrual periods (volume < 25 ml). Seen in conditions such as endometrial atrophy, eating disorders (e.g., anorexia nervosa), and chronic endometritis.

y2ad4P.title: Intermenstrual bleeding
y2ad4P.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by bleeding between menstrual periods. Common causes include ovarian insufficiency, endometrial cancer or hyperplasia, cervical cancer, and oral contraceptive use.

A2aR4P.title: Heavy irregular menstrual bleeding
A2aR4P.description: A type of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by heavy and/or prolonged, irregular menstrual bleeding. Associated conditions include ovarian insufficiency, endometriosis, uterine leiomyoma, and endometrial cancer.

z2ar4P.title: Premenstrual syndrome
z2ar4P.description: Affective (e.g., mood swings, irritability) and/or somatic (e.g., bloating, lethargy) symptoms with an onset in the luteal phase and with resolution following menstruation. Symptoms do not meet the DSM-5 criteria for PMDD.

-2aD4P.title: Breast cancer type 1 susceptibility protein gene
-2aD4P.description: A tumor suppressor gene located on the long arm of chromosome 17. Produces a protein that is involved in homologous recombination DNA repair. Mutations in this gene can predispose to the development of breast and ovarian cancer.

ZfaZkP.title: Breast cancer type 2 susceptibility protein gene
ZfaZkP.description: A tumor suppressor gene located on the long arm of chromosome 13. Produces a protein that is involved in homologous recombination DNA repair. Mutation in this gene can predispose to the development of breast and ovarian cancer.

0faekP.title: Li-Fraumeni syndrome
0faekP.description: A syndrome caused by an autosomal dominant inherited mutation of the tumor suppressor gene TP53. Characterized by multiple malignancies (sarcoma, breast carcinoma, leukemia, adrenocortical carcinoma) that occur at an early age.

afaQkP.title: Ductal carcinoma in situ
afaQkP.description: A noninvasive (in situ) carcinoma of the breast arising from ductal tissue. Usually unifocal and frequently presents with a pattern of grouped microcalcifications. Progresses to invasive carcinoma within 10 years of diagnosis in around 30% of all patients.

destinations.label: Breast cancer → Types of breast cancer

bfaHkP.title: Comedo ductal carcinoma
bfaHkP.description: A high-grade type of ductal carcinoma in situ characterized by extensive central necrosis that can often become calcified.

destinations.label: Breast cancer → Types of breast cancer

1fa2OP.title: Invasive ductal carcinoma
1fa2OP.description: An aggressive, invasive breast tumor that arises from ductal epithelium. The most common type of breast cancer (80% of cases). Usually affects women between the ages of 35 and 60. Most often discovered incidentally as a breast lump during routine examination but may present with bloody or serous nipple discharge, and/or skin changes.

destinations.label: Breast cancer → Types of breast cancer

media.title: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

WfaPOP.title: Invasive lobular carcinoma
WfaPOP.description: A malignant, invasive breast tumor that arises from the lobular epithelium. The second most common type of breast cancer (10–15% of cases). Usually multifocal and may be unilateral or bilateral. Most often discovered incidentally as an abnormal thickening or fullness of the breast during routine examination; may present with bloody or serous nipple discharge and/or skin changes.

destinations.label: Breast cancer → Types of breast cancer

media.title: Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast

dfaoOP.title: Paget disease of the breast
dfaoOP.description: A ductal carcinoma (either in situ or invasive) of the secretory ducts with early infiltration of the nipple and areola. Patients present with a scaly erythematous rash of the nipple and areola.

efaxOP.title: Inflammatory breast cancer
efaxOP.description: A rare form of advanced, invasive carcinoma of the breast. Clinical features include erythematous and edematous (peau d'orange) skin plaques over a rapidly growing breast mass, tenderness, burning, blood-tinged nipple discharge, and axillary lymphadenopathy. 25% of patients have metastatic disease at the time presentation.

media.title: Inflammation of breast with peau d'orange change

2faTlP.title: Mammography
2faTlP.description: An imaging modality used to evaluate breast abnormalities (e.g., palpable breast mass, screening for breast cancer). Typically two low-dose x-rays of each breast are obtained (mediolateral oblique and craniocaudal).

gfaFlP.title: Sentinel lymph node biopsy
gfaFlP.description: A procedure used to identify the lymph nodes that drain tumorous tissue and evaluate them for the involvement of malignancy. A radioactive dye is injected into the tissue surrounding the tumor. The dye accumulates in draining lymph nodes, where it can be detected with lymphoscintigraphy and visual identification. Subsequent excision of the lymph node and intraoperative frozen section are done to detect the lymphatic spread of malignant cells.

hfacNP.title: Trastuzumab
hfacNP.description: A monoclonal antibody against the ERBB2 tyrosine kinase receptor that inhibits cellular signaling and has cytotoxic effects. Used in the treatment of ERBB2-positive breast and gastric cancer. Adverse effects include cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy).

3faSNP.title: Tamoxifen
3faSNP.description: A type of selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is used in breast cancer prevention and treatment. It has antiestrogenic effects in the breast and estrogenic effects in the uterus and bone.

destinations.label: Female sex hormones → Reproductive system drugs

QfauNP.title: Submucosal leiomyoma
QfauNP.description: A uterine leiomyoma located directly below the endometrial layer (uterine mucosa).

media.title: Overview of uterine leiomyoma types and location

jfa_NP.title: Intramural leiomyoma
jfa_NP.description: A uterine leiomyoma located within the myometrial wall. Intramural leiomyomas are the most common type of uterine leiomyomas.

media.title: Overview of uterine leiomyoma types and location

PfaWmP.title: Subserosal leiomyoma
PfaWmP.description: A uterine leiomyoma located in the outer uterine wall beneath the peritoneal surface (serosa). Can be sessile, pedunculated, or intraligamentary (extending into the broad ligament).

media.title: Overview of uterine leiomyoma types and location

OfaImP.title: Uterine artery embolization
OfaImP.description: An interventional radiologic procedure in which the uterine blood supply is blocked by delivering small particles via catheter to the uterine arteries. Used to treat uterine fibroids.

Nfa-mP.title: Adenomyosis uteri
Nfa-mP.description: A disease of unknown etiology characterized by growth of nonmalignant endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Often associated with endometriosis and/or uterine fibroids. Occurs in individuals of reproductive age and manifests with dysmenorrhea, abnormal uterine bleeding, chronic pelvic pain, and uniformly enlarged uterus.

nfa75P.title: Dyspareunia
nfa75P.description: Pain that occurs with vaginal intercourse or penetration. Dyspareunia may be superficial (with vaginal entry), deep (with deeper penetration or thrusting, e.g., pelvic pain), or both. Causes of dyspareunia include vulvar dermatoses, genitourinary infections, and structural abnormalities.

KfaUMP.title: Endometrioma
KfaUMP.description: An ovarian cyst that has endometrium-like tissue in the cyst walls and contains chocolate-colored bloody fluid. May be a true cyst or formed by invagination. Endometriomas are a manifestation of endometriosis.

pfaLMP.title: Pap smear
pfaLMP.description: A test used for screening and surveillance of cervical cancer in which cells are collected from the outer opening of the cervix and analyzed under microscopy to look for abnormalities.

JfasMP.title: The Bethesda system for reporting cervical cytology
JfasMP.description: A cytopathologic classification system used to categorize cervical cancer cytology findings (Pap smear). The categories include: ASC-US (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance), ASC-H (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), and AGC (atypical glandular cells).

ufapLP.title: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia
ufapLP.description: A precursor to squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. Depending on the severity of dysplasia, CIN is categorized into CIN 1 (mild), CIN 2 (moderate), CIN 3 (severe).

Efa8LP.title: CIN1
Efa8LP.description: A low-grade type of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia involving the lower ⅓ or less of the cervical epithelium. Usually caused by human papillomavirus infection and regresses in ~ 60% of cases.

vfaALP.title: CIN2
vfaALP.description: A high-grade type of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia involving ⅓ to ⅔ of the cervical basal epithelium.

Dfa1oP.title: CIN3
Dfa1oP.description: A high-grade type of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia involving more than ⅔ of the cervical basal epithelium, with an intact basement membrane.

wfahoP.title: Conization
wfahoP.description: The excision of a cone-shaped portion of tissue from the cervix using a cold knife, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, or laser. Should include samples from the ectocervix, endocervix, and transformation zone. Performed for diagnosis and/or treatment of cervical cancer.

destinations.label: Invasive cervical cancer → Surgical interventions for cervical cancer

9faNoP.title: Trachelectomy
9faNoP.description: The surgical removal of the cervix followed by anastomosis of the uterus and vagina. En bloc removal of the parametrium with or without bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy along with the cervical tissue is termed radical trachelectomy, which is a treatment option for microinvasive cervical cancer in patients who wish to preserve fertility.

destinations.label: Invasive cervical cancer → Surgical interventions for cervical cancer

CfaqoP.title: Hysterectomy
CfaqoP.description: The surgical removal of the uterus. Can be subtotal (supracervical excision), total (excision of uterus and cervix), or radical (en bloc excision with parametrium and upper vagina).

destinations.label: Invasive cervical cancer → Surgical interventions for cervical cancer

BfazoP.title: 9-valent human papillomavirus vaccine
BfazoP.description: An inactivated vaccine that protects against HPV subtypes that cause anogenital warts and HPV-related cancers (e.g., cervical cancer, anal cancer). The 9-valent vaccine, effective against types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58, is available in the United States.

zfarKP.title: Follicle persistence
zfarKP.description: An abnormal ovarian structure associated with anovulatory cycles. The follicle persists and does not mature, which results in constant estrogen production. Can cause endometrial hyperplasia.

-faDKP.title: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia
-faDKP.description: Proliferation of the endometrium due to increased estrogen stimulation. Manifests clinically with irregular uterine bleeding and histologically with pronounced glandular crowding and clonal, atypical cells with increased mitosis. Has a high risk of progression to and concurrent endometrial cancer.

destinations.label: Benign and premalignant lesions of the endometrium → Endometrial hyperplasia

ZTaZ6P.title: Pyometra
ZTaZ6P.description: An accumulation of pus in the uterine cavity, typically caused by infection resulting from obstruction of the cervical opening. Can develop in patients with duplication of the cervix or as an uncommon complication of gynecological malignancy. Manifestations include purulent vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, and an enlarged uterus.

0Tae6P.title: Ovarian cystadenoma
0Tae6P.description: A benign ovarian tumor of epithelial origin. Can be serous or mucinous, is frequently bilateral, and often shows psammoma bodies on histopathologic examination. Usually asymptomatic and found incidentally. With tumor growth, pelvic pain, urinary symptoms, and/or ovarian torsion can occur.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Epithelial ovarian tumors

YTan6P.title: Endometrioid carcinoma
YTan6P.description: A malignant type of ovarian epithelial cell tumor that is often associated with endometrial cancer and endometriosis.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Epithelial ovarian tumors

bTaH6P.title: Borderline ovarian tumors
bTaH6P.description: A type of epithelial ovarian tumor that grossly appears to have malignant features but lacks frank invasion on histopathologic examination. Occasionally, microscopic invasive implants may be seen.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Epithelial ovarian tumors

cTaapP.title: Teratoma
cTaapP.description:
A germ cell tumor comprised of the derivatives of the three germ cell layers. The tumor can have highly differentiated tissue, which is usually benign, or undifferentiated tissue, which is more likely to be malignant. 
The tumor can occur within the gonads or can be extragonadal, with ovarian and testicular teratomas being the most common gonadal tumor.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

1Ta2pP.title: Dermoid cysts
1Ta2pP.description: A mature cystic teratoma that can occur on the head, the neck, spine, cranium, and in the abdomen (most common ovarian tumor in females). Cysts typically become symptomatic as they grow in size. They are treated with complete surgical excision.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

WTaPpP.title: Struma ovarii
WTaPpP.description: An ovarian teratoma with endodermal differentiation into thyroid tissue that may produce thyroxine; 10% of patients present with hyperthyroidism. Very rarely, malignant transformation into a thyroid carcinoma can occur.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

dTaopP.title: Dysgerminoma
dTaopP.description: Rare type of malignant ovarian germ cell tumor. Predominantly seen in young women (20–30 years of age). Female histological equivalent to male seminoma.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

VTaGpP.title: Yolk sac tumor of the ovary
VTaGpP.description: Ovarian germ cell tumor that is often malignant and occurs mainly in childhood and adolescence. Notable for rapid growth and acute onset of pelvic pain. Contains characteristic Shiller-Duval bodies on microscopy.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

eTaxpP.title: Non-gestational choriocarcinoma
eTaxpP.description: A rare and extremely malignant subtype of ovarian germ cell tumor. Arises from the extraembryonic differentiation of malignant germ cells that become trophoblastic cells. Histologically identical to gestational choriocarcinoma.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Ovarian germ cell tumors

UTabJP.title: Sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary
UTabJP.description: A tumor derived from the primitive sex cords or stromal cells of the ovary. Typically produces hormones (estrogen or testosterone) and is benign.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary

2TaTJP.title: Theca cell tumor
2TaTJP.description: A benign sex-cord stromal tumor of the ovary. Frequently produces estrogen and is most commonly seen in postmenopausal women, in whom it results in postmenopausal bleeding.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary

STayJP.title: Krukenberg tumor
STayJP.description: A metastatic tumor of the ovary, most commonly caused by diffuse gastric cancer (signet ring cell carcinoma). Other primary sites include other types of gastric cancer as well as breast cancer, endometrial cancer, and colon cancer.

3TaSqP.title: Granulosa cell tumor
3TaSqP.description: An estrogen-producing sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary. Most commonly affects postmenopausal women and is usually malignant. The increase in estrogen leads to menstrual irregularities and an increased risk of endometrial cancer. In children, it causes precocious puberty.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary

QTauqP.title: Pseudomyxoma peritonei
QTauqP.description: A condition characterized by peritoneal dissemination of a mucus-producing adenocarcinoma (peritoneal carcinomatosis), which results in progressive accumulation of mucinous ascites throughout the peritoneal cavity. Most commonly caused by mucinous adenocarcinoma of the appendix.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Epithelial ovarian tumors

jTa_qP.title: Meigs' syndrome
jTa_qP.description: Simultaneous occurence of benign ovarian tumor (usually ovarian fibroma), ascites, and pleural effusion.

destinations.label: Overview of ovarian tumors →  Sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary

kTamIP.title: Ovarian cyst
kTamIP.description: Fluid-filled sac within the ovary that typically results from a disruption in the development of follicles or corpus luteum.

NTa-IP.title: Corpus luteum cysts
NTa-IP.description: A type of benign and functional ovarian cyst. Develops from the enlargement and buildup of fluid in the corpus luteum after failed regression following the release of an ovum (in women who are not pregnant) or by the end of the first trimester (in women who are pregnant). Produces progesterone.

nTa7rP.title: Extramammary Paget disease
nTa7rP.description: A rare, intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that typically causes pruritus and eczematous lesions around the vulva and perineum.

destinations.label: Vulvar and vaginal cancer → Vulvar cancer

KTaU7P.title: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
KTaU7P.description: A precancerous vulvar lesion caused by dysplasia of squamous cells, marked with varying degrees of atypia. The epithelial basement membrane is intact and the lesion is thus not invasive (but has invasive potential). Associations include HPV, HSV-2, smoking, immunosuppression, chronic vulvar irritation, and lichen sclerosus.

destinations.label: Vulvar and vaginal cancer → Precursor lesions

6Taj7P.title: Sarcoma botryoides
6Taj7P.description: A rare, highly malignant rhabdomyosarcoma. Most commonly arises in the genitourinary system as a polypoid mass that resembles a bunch of grapes (botryoid in Greek) protruding through the vagina. Peak incidence is before the age of 8.

destinations.label: Vulvar and vaginal cancer → Vaginal cancer

JTas7P.title: Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia
JTas7P.description: A precancerous vaginal lesion caused by dysplasia of squamous cells, marked with varying degrees of atypia. The epithelial basement membrane is intact and the lesion is, therefore, not invasive (but has invasive potential). Risk factors include HPV infection, smoking, and immunosuppression.

qTaC7P.title: Vaginal carcinoma
qTaC7P.description: A carcinoma that typically arises from the nonkeratinized squamous epithelium of the vagina. Often associated with HPV infection. Non-HPV vaginal carcinomas are rare and include clear cell adenocarcinoma (associated with exposure to diethylstilbestrol) and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides).

destinations.label: Vulvar and vaginal cancer → Vaginal cancer

HTaKHP.title: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
HTaKHP.description: Pregnancy-induced hypertension with onset after 20 weeks' gestation.

sTatHP.title: Preeclampsia
sTatHP.description: A condition characterized by pregnancy-induced hypertension with either proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction and an onset after 20 weeks' gestation. Can cause renal insufficiency, thrombocytopenia, evidence of liver damage, pulmonary edema, and cerebral edema. Can progress to HELLP syndrome or eclampsia.

tTaXsP.title: Preeclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension
tTaXsP.description: Evidence of preeclampsia (proteinuria, renal insufficiency, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, pulmonary edema, cerebral edema) that occurs in a patient with chronic hypertension (BP > 140/90 mm Hg before 20 weeks' gestation).

ETa8sP.title: Eclampsia
ETa8sP.description: Preeclampsia with development of new-onset grand mal seizures and/or coma. Treatment involves airway management, anticonvulsive therapy with IV magnesium sulfate, and urgent delivery.

vTaAsP.title: HELLP syndrome
vTaAsP.description: A complication of pregnancy and form of preeclampsia that most commonly occurs > 27 weeks' gestation. Characterized by hemolysis (H), elevated liver (EL) enzymes, and low platelet (LP) count. Other features include abdominal pain and rapid clinical deterioration (due to severe systemic inflammation causes multiorgan failure). Treatment includes stabilization (e.g., fluid resuscitation, antihypertensive therapy) and delivery of the fetus.

wTahGP.title: Placenta previa
wTahGP.description: An obstetric complication in which a portion of the placenta covers the cervical os. A complete previa occurs when the cervical os is completely covered by the placenta. A marginal previa occurs when the leading edge of the placenta is less than 2 cm from the internal os but does not fully cover it. This condition, which typically presents as painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester, is diagnosed by ultrasound.

CTaqGP.title: Low-lying placenta
CTaqGP.description: A placenta with a lower edge < 2 cm from the internal cervical os.

ATaRtP.title: Hydatidiform mole
ATaRtP.description: A benign tumor of the uterus that develops following abnormal fertilization of the ovum. Can be complete (fertilization of an empty egg that does not carry any chromosomes; tumor does not contain any fetal or embryonic parts) or partial (fertilization of a normal egg with two sperms; tumor contains fetal or embryonic parts).

_Ta5tP.title: Invasive mole
_Ta5tP.description: A form of gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by direct invasion of the myometrium by abnormal trophoblastic cells and edematous chorionic villi.

destinations.label: Gestational trophoblastic disease → Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

zTartP.title: Choriocarcinoma
zTartP.description: A highly malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) characterized by invasive, highly vascular, and anaplastic trophoblastic tissue without villi. It is rare but can arise from any type of trophoblastic tissue (molar pregnancy, abortion, ectopic, prior pregnancy). It has the propensity to metastasize to the lungs, vagina, CNS, liver, kidney, and GI tract. Bleeding from these metastatic sites is common.

destinations.label: Gestational trophoblastic disease → Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

-TaDtP.title: Complete hydatidiform mole
-TaDtP.description: A type of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) that results from aberrant fertilization in an embryo and has the potential to invade the uterus and metastasize. Complete moles are diploid and have a higher risk of malignant transformation than partial moles. The main risk factors for GTD are extremes of maternal age and prior history of GTD.

ZgaZFP.title: Partial hydatidiform mole
ZgaZFP.description: A type of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) that is caused by aberrant fertilization in an embryo and has the potential to invade the uterus and metastasize. Partial moles are triploid and usually result from fertilization of an egg with 2 sperm or a diploid sperm.They may be associated with the presence of a fetus; however, intrauterine death due to triploidy is common, and it is commonly mistaken for an incomplete or missed abortion.

1ga28P.title: Stillbirth
1ga28P.description: Fetal death after 20 weeks of gestation.

dgao8P.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss
dgao8P.description: The occurrence of ≥ 2 spontaneous pregnancy losses. Definitions vary.

VgaG8P.title: Threatened abortion
VgaG8P.description: A process of miscarriage that has started but not yet progressed to a state from which recovery is impossible. Manifests before 20 weeks' gestation with vaginal bleeding without opening of the cervical os or expulsion of any products of conception.

egax8P.title: Inevitable abortion
egax8P.description: A condition of vaginal bleeding and cervical dilation without expulsion of products of conception (POC) before 20 weeks' gestation. Typically followed by partial or complete passage of POC.

UgabuP.title: Missed abortion
UgabuP.description: The death of a fetus before 20 weeks' gestation without expulsion of any products of conception. Typically asymptomatic or manifests with cramping. The cervical os is closed, and ultrasonography shows a gestational sac with products of conception and absent fetal cardiac activity.

2gaTuP.title: Incomplete abortion
2gaTuP.description: A condition in which products of conception are retained without continued embryonic or fetal cardiac activity. Clinical features may include vaginal bleeding and painful cramping without expulsion of fetal tissue. May occur after spontaneous or induced abortion.

fgakuP.title: Complete abortion
fgakuP.description: The complete passage of all products of conception (POC) before 20 weeks' gestation.

Tga6uP.title: Anembryonic pregnancy
Tga6uP.description: The formation of a gestational sac without any embryonic structures.

hgacEP.title: Tocolysis
hgacEP.description: The process of slowing cervical dilation by administering tocolytic medications, which decrease uterine contractions, thereby delaying labor (typically up to 48 hours, although some agents may act for several days). Indications include cervical insufficiency, premature contractions at 24–34 weeks' gestation to allow antenatal corticosteroid administration, and to provide time for adequate intervention if complications arise (e.g., for cesarean section).

3gaSEP.title: Tocolytics
3gaSEP.description: A group of drugs that inhibit uterine contractions. Includes beta-mimetics (e.g., terbutaline, ritodrine, isoxsuprine), cyclooxygenase inhibitors (e.g., indomethacin, sulindac), magnesium sulfate, calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine), oxytocin antagonists (e.g., atosiban), and nitric oxide donors (e.g., glyceryl trinitrate). Used to prevent preterm delivery, typically to improve neonatal outcomes (e.g., to complete a corticosteroid course for fetal lung maturity).

RgalEP.title: Induction of fetal lung maturity
RgalEP.description: The administration of betamethasone or dexamethasone to promote surfactant production and fetal lung maturity and reduce the risk of fetal respiratory distress. Recommended for pregnant individuals between 24 0/7 weeks and 33 6/7 weeks of gestation at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days.

igaJEP.title: Dilation and curettage
igaJEP.description: A gynecological procedure in which the cervix is dilated and tissue is removed from the uterus using a suction curette (uterine aspiration) or a sharp curette. Performed for therapeutic purposes (e.g., removal of uterine masses or products of conception) or diagnostic purposes (e.g., obtaining uterine tissue samples for histological examination).

QgauEP.title: Cervical cerclage
QgauEP.description: A procedure in which the cervix is temporarily sutured shut. Cervical cerclage is used in the management of cervical insufficiency associated with pregnancy.

destinations.label: Maternal complications during pregnancy → Cervical insufficiency

jga_EP.title: Emergency contraception
jga_EP.description: Therapy that is given within 5 days of unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure (e.g., condom breakage, missed oral contraceptives) to prevent pregnancy. The most commonly accepted forms of emergency contraception include ulipristal acetate, a progestin-only pill (typically levonorgestrel), or the insertion of a copper IUD.

4ga3vP.title: Septic abortion
4ga3vP.description: An infection of the placenta and fetus before 20 weeks' gestation. Associated with maternal signs of infection (e.g., fever, vaginal or cervical discharge, leukocytosis) and, inevitably, with fetal death.

OgaIvP.title: Bandl ring
OgaIvP.description: A muscular constriction between the upper and lower segments of the uterus that can develop during labor, causing obstructed and/or prolonged labor. The etiology is unclear, but the risk of development is thought to increase with prolonged labor. A Bandl ring that ascends toward the umbilicus can be a sign of impending uterine rupture.

media.title: Signs of impending uterine rupture: Bandl ring

Nga-vP.title: Hypovolemic shock
Nga-vP.description: A type of shock characterized by circulatory failure from intravascular volume loss. Etiologies include hemorrhage and severe fluid loss from the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and/or skin.

mgaVDP.title: Cardiogenic shock
mgaVDP.description: A condition of circulatory failure that results from the heart's inability to maintain adequate cardiac output. Clinical features include those of heart failure alongside tachycardia, hypotension, signs of poor peripheral perfusion, and oliguria. Biomarkers of shock may also be elevated (e.g., lactate).

5gaiDP.title: Distributive shock
5gaiDP.description: A circulatory failure caused by an insult to blood vessels that results in fluid extravasation from the vasculature and loss of adequate intravascular fluid volume. Etiologies include septic shock, anaphylactic shock, and neurogenic shock.

LgawDP.title: Septic shock
LgawDP.description: A type of distributive shock caused by an excessive inflammatory response to disseminated infection, which leads to fluid extravasation from the vascular space and loss of intravascular volume. Diagnostic criteria include the requirement of vasopressors to maintain a median arterial pressure ≥ 65 mm Hg despite adequate fluid therapy, and lactate > 2 mmol/L (> 18 mg/dL) in a normovolemic patient with sepsis.

oga0wP.title: Multiple organ failure
oga0wP.description: A clinical syndrome of progressive failure of two or more organ systems in a critically ill patient. Results from acute, severe illnesses or injuries such as sepsis, multiple trauma, or burns.

IgaY9P.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
IgaY9P.description: A condition characterized by systemic activation of the clotting cascade, platelet consumption, and subsequent exhaustion of clotting factors that leads to widespread thrombosis and hemorrhage. Often associated with trauma, shock, and sepsis.

media.title: ISTH score for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

8gaOCP.title: Posterior capsule opacification
8gaOCP.description: A complication of cataract surgery characterized by a regenerative secondary cataract of the posterior capsule that develop due to proliferation and migration of persistent cells of the lens epithelium.

Dga1xP.title: Open-angle glaucoma
Dga1xP.description: A type of glaucoma characterized by a wide-open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy. Can be idiopathic (primary open-angle glaucoma) or secondary to trabecular clogging, edema, and/or scarring of the episcleral veins (secondary open-angle glaucoma).

media.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of secondary open-angle glaucoma

wgahxP.title: Angle-closure glaucoma
wgahxP.description: A sudden and sharp increase in intraocular pressure caused by an obstruction of aqueous outflow (most commonly as a result of an occlusion of the chamber angle).

xgaExP.title: Neovascular glaucoma
xgaExP.description: A form of secondary glaucoma in which the formation of new blood vessels leads to occlusion of the anterior chamber angle. Most commonly a result of retinal ischemia.

zgarBP.title: Arcuate scotoma
zgarBP.description: A visual field abnormality characterized by an arc-shaped area of reduced or absent vision that starts at the blind spot and courses over the macular area.

destinations.label: Disorders of the visual pathway → Scotoma and anopia

-gaDBP.title: Hormone replacement therapy
-gaDBP.description: A hormone regimen consisting of estrogen and progestin (unless the patient has had a hysterectomy) that is usually employed for the short-term treatment of menopausal symptoms (e.g., hot flashes, mood lability, joint pain, and vaginal dryness/atrophy). Can be administered via the oral route or transdermally. Potential adverse effects include endometrial cancer (only in the case of unopposed estrogen), breast cancer, thromboembolic events, gallbladder disease, and stress urinary incontinence.

0SaeyP.title: Amaurosis fugax
0SaeyP.description: A transient monocular or binocular loss of vision. Causes include cardiovascular, ocular, and neurological conditions.

aSaQyP.title: Photodynamic therapy
aSaQyP.description: A type of phototherapy in which a drug is administered that is activated upon exposure to a light source, which causes cellular destruction. Typically used to treat conditions with dysplastic and hyperproliferative tissue (e.g., hyperproliferative scar tissue, macular degeneration, skin cancer).

YSanyP.title: Menopause
YSanyP.description: The time at which a woman permanently stops menstruating, usually between 45-55 years of age. Diagnosed after 12 months of amenorrhea. Often associated with autonomic symptoms (e.g., hot flashes), mood disorders (e.g., irritability, insomnia, loss of libido), and atrophic changes due to decreased estrogen production (e.g., vulvovaginal atrophy).

bSaHyP.title: Perimenopause
bSaHyP.description: The time leading up to menopause in which patients experience changes in hormonal levels, ovulation, and their menstrual cycle. This period can last up to 10 years.

XSa9yP.title: Postmenopause
XSa9yP.description: The period of time after an individual's final menstrual period.

cSaaAP.title: Premenopause
cSaaAP.description: The reproductive period that begins with menarche and ends with the onset of perimenopause. Menstrual cycles are predominantly regular during this period.

VSaGAP.title: Menopause praecox
VSaGAP.description: The permanent cessation of ovarian function and menses before the age of 40 years. Most common causes are induced menopause and ovarian insufficiency.

eSaxAP.title: Ovarian insufficiency
eSaxAP.description: Impaired ovarian function that affects ovulation and estrogen production. Manifests with amenorrhea or abnormal uterine bleeding, climacteric symptoms (e.g., vaginal dryness, vasomotor symptoms, dyspareunia, and irritability), and infertility or subfertility. May be primary (due to impairment of the ovary itself) or secondary (due to inadequate stimulation of the ovaries by the hypothalamus and/or pituitary gland).

2SaT_P.title: Condylomata
2SaT_P.description: Proliferation of atypical squamous cells, usually seen in genital warts (condylomata acuminata) or secondary syphilis (condylomata lata).

TSa6_P.title: Anogenital warts
TSa6_P.description: Lesions caused by infection with human papillomavirus. Manifest as flat, papular, or exophytic cauliflower-like lesions on the vulva, cervix, urethra (rare), and/or anal region (in female individuals) or the glans penis, foreskin, urethra, and/or anal region (in male individuals). Often asymptomatic but can cause pruritus or pain.

QSauzP.title: Dichorionic-diamniotic
QSauzP.description: A twin pregnancy in which the fetuses have separate chorionic sacs (separate placentas) and separate amniotic sacs. All dizygotic pregnancies and ~ 25% of monozygotic pregnancies are dichorionic-diamniotic. Has a characteristic lambda sign on ultrasonography.

jSa_zP.title: Dizygotic twins
jSa_zP.description: A type of pregnancy in which genetically different twins develop after fertilization of two oocytes with two spermatozoa. Each twin has its own placenta and amniotic sac.

4Sa3-P.title: Monochorionic-diamniotic
4Sa3-P.description: A twin pregnancy where the fetuses share a single chorionic sac (the twins share a placenta) but have a separate, individual amniotic sac. Seen in ~ 75% of monozygotic twin pregnancies and not seen in dizygotic twin pregnancies. On ultrasonography, a thin intertwin membrane that resembles the letter T separates the amniotic sacs within a common chorionic sac.

kSam-P.title: Monochorionic-monoamniotic
kSam-P.description: A twin pregnancy in which the fetuses share a single chorionic sac (the twins share a placenta) and a single amniotic sac. Seen rarely and only in monozygotic twin pregnancies.

OSaI-P.title: Monozygotic twins
OSaI-P.description: A type of pregnancy in which genetically identical twins that develop from one zygote that has split into two embryos. The fetuses typically share the placenta and have individual amniotic sacs (monochorionic-diamniotic).

lSav-P.title: Conjoined twins
lSav-P.description: A rare type of monochorionic-monoamniotic monozygotic pregnancy that occurs when cleavage of the embryo occurs > 13 days after fertilization. Results in fusion between same body parts.

5SaiZ4.title: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
5SaiZ4.description: A condition that occurs in monochorionic twins when one twin (donor) continuously transfers blood to the other (recipient). Leads to dehydration, anemia, growth restriction, and oligohydramnios in the donor and polycythemia and polyhydramnios in the recipient. Mortality is significantly increased for both twins.

nSa7Z4.title: Bennett fracture-dislocation
nSa7Z4.description: An intraarticular two-part fracture-dislocation at the base of the first metacarpal bone. The metacarpal shaft fragment is radially and proximally dislocated by the pull of the abductor pollicis longus muscle.

oSa004.title: Rolando fracture
oSa004.description: An intraarticular, comminuted fracture at the base of the first metacarpal bone. The bony fragments usually form a Y- or T-shaped pattern.

6Saj04.title: Toxic shock syndrome
6Saj04.description: A systemic inflammatory reaction caused by bacterial exotoxins (e.g., toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 produced by Staphylococcus aureus). Manifestations include fever, hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, flu-like symptoms, and an erythematous rash.

media.title: Diffuse maculopapular exanthema in toxic shock syndrome

7Sa4a4.title: Anencephaly
7Sa4a4.description: A lethal cranial neural tube defect that manifests with an absent or underdeveloped cranium, forebrain, and cerebellum. Results in polyhydramnios due to a defective fetal swallowing center. Associated with elevated levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in maternal serum and amniotic fluid.

sSata4.title: Encephalocele
sSata4.description: A congenital CNS malformation characterized by a sac-like protrusion of the brain and the membranes that cover it through an opening in the skull (e.g., suture lines).

GSaBa4.title: Myelomeningocele
GSaBa4.description: A neural tube defect in which the meninges and spinal cord herniate through an abnormal vertebral opening.

tSaXY4.title: Meningocele
tSaXY4.description: A congenital neural tube defect in which the meninges (without neural tissue) herniate through a defect in the vertebrae. Most commonly occurs in the lumbosacral region. Associated with spina bifida cystica.

8SaOY4.title: Spina bifida
8SaOY4.description: A neural tube defect due to failure of vertebrae closure. The overlying skin may remain intact (i.e., spina bifida occulta), or the meninges and/or spinal cord may protrude (i.e., spina bifida cystica). Most commonly found in the lower lumbar or sacral region.

ESa8Y4.title: Spina bifida occulta
ESa8Y4.description: A congenital neural tube defect in which part of the vertebrae fail to close. The spinal cord, spinal meninges, and overlying skin remain intact. Most commonly occurs in the lumbosacral region, and is usually asymptomatic. There may be a visible dimple, collection of fat, or patch of hair on the skin above the defect.

9SaNb4.title: Aspiration pneumonia
9SaNb4.description: A type of pneumonia that develops following aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions and/or gastric contents.

CSaqb4.title: Aspiration pneumonitis
CSaqb4.description: A condition of inflammation of lung tissue caused by recurrent aspiration of gastric acid. Risk factors include altered consciousness (e.g., due to alcohol intoxication, sedation, general anesthesia), neurodegenerative conditions (e.g., Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease), oropharyngeal dysphagia resulting from stroke, and esophageal motility disorders.

xSaEb4.title: Aspiration
xSaEb4.description:
Can refer to:
1. The inhalation of foreign material (e.g., food, drink, vomitus) into the airways.
2. The removal of fluid, gas, or tissue from a body cavity (e.g., pleural cavity, joint space) or sac (e.g., cyst, bursa) using a suction device.

ASaRX4.title: Digital nerve block
ASaRX4.description: A peripheral nerve block of the digital nerves. Used to anesthetize the fingers or toes.

_Sa5X4.title: Epidural anesthesia
_Sa5X4.description: A procedure that involves injection of local anesthetics into the epidural space, which blocks the spinal nerve roots and provides analgesia. It is used during labor and delivery, as well as in surgeries on the lower body (hernia repair, prostate and bladder surgery) and in chronic pain management.

media.title: Spread of effect of epidural anesthesia

zSarX4.title: Spinal anesthesia
zSarX4.description: A form of regional anesthesia involving the injection of local anaesthetic into the subarachnoid space in the lumbar spine to act directly on the spinal cord, blocking all motor and sensory function below the level of injection.

media.title: Spinal anesthesia (1/2): materials and patient positioning
Spread of effect of spinal anesthesia

Xha9c4.title: Total spinal anesthesia
Xha9c4.description: A complication of spinal or epidural anesthesia caused by injection of anesthetic into the subdural or subarachnoid space. Typically develops within minutes after administration of anesthetic, but can also occur due to changes in patient positioning. Manifestations include sympathetic, sensory, and motor block, which can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and dyspnea.

WhaP14.title: Modified Allen test
WhaP14.description: A test to evaluate the patency of the collateral circulation to the hand through the radial and ulnar arteries. The patient is asked to form a fist, after which pressure is applied to both arteries to prevent perfusion, resulting in pallor of the palm. Rapid return to the natural color upon release of an artery indicates patency of that artery. The procedure is repeated with the other artery.

UhabW4.title: Coronary artery bypass grafting
UhabW4.description: A surgical cardiac revascularization technique used to treat patients with significant, symptomatic stenosis of a coronary artery or its branches.
