The stenosed segment is bypassed using an arterial (e.g., internal thoracic artery) or venous (e.g., great saphenous vein) autograft, re-establishing blood flow to the ischemic areas of the myocardium.

media.title: Vessels commonly used in coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)
Main indications for coronary artery bypass grafting
Arterial and venous grafts used in coronary artery bypass grafting

Tha6W4.title: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator
Tha6W4.description: An implanted device capable of detecting and treating cardiac arrhythmias by delivering electrical impulses to convert heart rhythm back into sinus rhythm. Indications include recurrent ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation.

destinations.label: Cardiac implantable electronic devices → Automated implantable cardioverter defibrillators

hhacd4.title: Pacemaker syndrome
hhacd4.description: A condition characterized by atrioventricular dyssynchrony in patients with a single-chamber pacemaker. Pacing of the ventricle alone can lead to the atria contracting against closed mitral and tricuspid valves, resulting in loss of atrial kick and decreased cardiac output. Typically manifests with fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, and worsening signs of heart failure.

Qhaud4.title: Coronary angiography
Qhaud4.description: A procedure that uses contrast dye and radiography to take images of the coronary arteries. Performed via cardiac catheterization by inserting a catheter into an artery of the arm or groin and guiding it to the coronary arteries.

media.title: Illustration of coronary angiography; left coronary artery (LCA)
Illustration of coronary angiography; right coronary artery (RCA)
Coronary angiography in acute anterior myocardial infarction

jha_d4.title: Percutaneous coronary intervention
jha_d4.description: An endovascular procedure in which an inflatable balloon is passed over a wire into a narrowed or obstructed artery. Upon inflation, the balloon widens the arterial lumen, which improves perfusion. A stent is usually placed to keep the artery patent.

media.title: Cardiac catheterization based on the Seldinger technique

mhaVe4.title: Bare metal stent
mhaVe4.description: A bare-surfaced, metallic stent deployed during percutaneous coronary intervention that provides a mechanical framework to keep an artery open.

5haie4.title: Drug-eluting stent
5haie4.description: A type of stent that is coated with antiproliferative substances (e.g., immunosuppressant drugs or cytostatic drugs) to prevent excessive intimal hyperplasia following percutaneous coronary intervention.

Lhawe4.title: Right heart catheterization
Lhawe4.description: The passing of a balloon-tipped, multi-lumen catheter (Swan-Ganz catheter) into the right side of the heart and the pulmonary arteries to monitor pressure within the cardiac chambers (intracardiac pressure) and to assess pulmonary arterial pressure as well as pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (to approximate left atrial pressure). Used primarily to diagnose pulmonary hypertension and cardiogenic shock.

6hajU4.title: Cholesterol embolization syndrome
6hajU4.description: A condition in which cholesterol crystals are released from atherosclerotic plaques and occlude arterial vessels, resulting in end-organ ischemia or infarction. May occur spontaneously but is more commonly caused by vascular interventions (e.g., PCI) or cardiac surgery.

JhasU4.title: Hypoxemic respiratory failure
JhasU4.description: A type of respiratory failure characterized by hypoxemia (↓ PₐO₂) and normocapnia or hypocapnia (↓ PₐCO₂) on arterial blood gas analysis.

qhaCU4.title: Hypercapnic respiratory failure
qhaCU4.description: A type of respiratory failure characterized hypercapnia (↑ PₐCO₂) and normoxemia or hypoxemia (↓ PₐO₂) on arterial blood gas analysis.

HhaK24.title: Respiratory acidosis
HhaK24.description: A pH below 7.35 due to a reduction in alveolar ventilation resulting in retention of CO₂. Common etiologies include COPD exacerbation, bronchial asthma, respiratory muscle weakness, and CNS depression due to head trauma or drug toxicity (opiates, barbiturates, and benzodiazepines).

shat24.title: Respiratory alkalosis
shat24.description: A pH greater than 7.45 and low pCO₂ due to alveolar hyperventilation (increase in respiratory rate and/or tidal volume). Common etiologies include hyperventilation due to pain, anxiety, panic attacks, pregnancy, high altitude, and drug toxicity (theophylline, progesterone, salicylate toxicity).

GhaB24.title: Metabolic acidosis
GhaB24.description: A reduction in the concentration of bicarbonate ions (HCO₃ ̄) that results in a pH < 7.35. Can occur due to excess hydrogen ions (e.g., lactic acid production from hypoxia or ketoacidosis during starvation) or loss of bicarbonate (e.g., diarrhea, renal failure).

thaXf4.title: Metabolic alkalosis
thaXf4.description: An increase in the concentration of bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) that results in a pH > 7.45. Can be due to a loss of hydrogen ions (e.g., resulting from hyperaldosteronism, vomiting) or an increase in bicarbonate ions (e.g., due to milk-alkali syndrome).

Fhagf4.title: Anion gap
Fhagf4.description: The difference between the concentration of measured cations and anions. The anion gap can be calculated by subtracting the concentration of routinely measured cations from routinely measured anions. Serum anion gap = [Na⁺] - ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]). Normal range is 6–12 mEq/L. The anion gap can also be calculated taking potassium levels into account: ([Na⁺] + [K⁺]) - ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]), with a normal range of 10–16 mEq/L.

8haOf4.title: Normal anion gap
8haOf4.description: A metabolic acidosis that is caused by a primary loss of bicarbonate, which results in a compensatory increase in extracellular chloride (the anion gap is therefore unchanged). Common causes include diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis, and certain drugs (e.g., carbonic anhydrase inhibitors).

Eha8f4.title: Oxygen dissociation curve
Eha8f4.description: A sigmoidal curve that plots the oxygen saturation of a substance (e.g., hemoglobin) (Y-axis) versus the partial pressure of oxygen (X-axis). The shape of the curve is determined by the affinity of the substance for oxygen and can be shifted by factors that affect the oxygen carrying capacity.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve

media.title: Oxygen dissociation curves for hemoglobin and myoglobin

xhaET4.title: Hartmann's procedure
xhaET4.description: The surgical resection of the rectosigmoid colon followed by creation of an end colostomy with closure of the rectal stump. Usually an emergent temporary procedure to treat bowel perforation, infection (e.g., diverticulitis), or obstruction if primary anastomosis is deemed unsafe. Can be permanent when carried out as a palliative measure for colon cancer.

zharg4.title: Stoma
zharg4.description: A surgically created bowel outlet for the passage of feces. May be temporary or permanent.

Z3aZS4.title: Loop stoma
Z3aZS4.description: A surgical procedure in which the end of a loop of ileum is diverted to an artificial opening (stoma) in the abdominal wall.

a3aQS4.title: Anastomosis insufficiency
a3aQS4.description: The leakage of intraluminal contents from the site of surgical anastomosis between two hollow viscera (e.g., after bowel or vascular anastomoses).

Y3anS4.title: Wound dehiscence
Y3anS4.description: The spontaneous separation of wound edges following surgical wound repair. Can be superficial (skin and subcutaneous tissue) and/or deep (fascial) as well as partial or complete. Complete wound dehiscence affects all layers and can lead to prolapse of underlying structures or organs.

media.title: Wound dehiscence after inguinal hernia repair

13a2h4.title: Post-lumbar puncture headache
13a2h4.description: A headache that develops within 7 days after a dural puncture. Generally manifests bilaterally, worsens with upright positioning, and improves with lying down. Thought to be due to persistent cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

e3axh4.title: Advanced cardiac life support
e3axh4.description: A structured sequence of management steps performed to maximize survival in cardiac arrest in adults. Includes the provision of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation with minimal interruptions, early defibrillation and drug delivery, investigation and treatment of underlying causes, and goal-directed postresuscitation care.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)

U3ab34.title: Basic life support
U3ab34.description: The immediate life-supporting medical care that is provided to a person with a hyperacute life-threatening illness or injury (e.g., cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, airway obstruction, drowning). Includes assessing scene safety, evaluating patient response, calling for help, assessing for signs of life, and performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Basic life support (BLS)

23aT34.title: Defibrillation
23aT34.description: The application of electrical current to treat cardiac arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia). Also used if synchronized cardioversion is not possible (e.g., polymorphic ventricular tachyarrhythmia). In contrast to electrical cardioversion, the electrical current delivered is high-energy and not synchronized to the QRS complex.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)
Management of tachycardia → Unstable tachycardia with pulse

f3ak34.title: Return of spontaneous circulation
f3ak34.description: The return of a spontaneous perfusing cardiac rhythm after cardiac arrest, as evidenced by the presence of a palpable pulse and/or measurable blood pressure. Additional confirmatory signs may include an increase in EtCO₂, spontaneous breathing, and improved mental status.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Cessation of CPR

g3aF34.title: Shockable rhythms
g3aF34.description: The two cardiac rhythms, ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, that should be treated with defibrillation.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)

h3acR4.title: Nonshockable rhythms
h3acR4.description: The two cardiac rhythms, pulseless electrical activity and asystole, that should not be treated with defibrillation.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)

P3aWi4.title: Pulseless electrical activity
P3aWi4.description: A non-perfusing rhythm resulting in cardiac arrest. Although an electrocardiographic rhythm is present, there is no meaningful ventricular activity (also referred to as electromechanical dissociation). The most common underlying etiologies include hypoxia and hypovolemia.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)

53aiQ4.title: Precordial thump
53aiQ4.description: An intervention in which a sharp, high-velocity blow is delivered to the mid sternum using the ulnar aspect of the fist. Aims to interrupt life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias during cardiac arrest. Recommendations on the use of precordial thump vary, and the 2020 American Heart Association guidelines for cardiopulmonary resuscitation do not recommend this technique unless very specific criteria are fulfilled.

destinations.label: Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation → Basic life support (BLS)

n3a7Q4.title: Windowing
n3a7Q4.description: The manipulation of a CT image's grayscale to highlight specific structures. Involves mapping a range of voxel values to specific Hounsfield units (HU) ranges. Windows are defined by the window level (i.e., the midpoint of an image's HU range) and the window width (the HU range within an image).

K3aUj4.title: Hyperdensity
K3aUj4.description:
An area of tissue with higher density and, accordingly, higher x-ray attenuation than normal or surrounding tissue 
Hyperdense tissue appears brighter because increased x-ray absorption by the tissue decreases the amount of x-rays that pass the tissue and expose the detector.

63ajj4.title: Hypodensity
63ajj4.description:
An area of tissue with lower density and, accordingly, lower x-ray attenuation than normal or surrounding tissue.
Hypodense tissue appears darker because decreased x-ray absorption by the tissue increases the amount of x-rays that pass through the tissue and expose the detector.

q3aCj4.title: Hyperintensity
q3aCj4.description: A radiologic descriptor for tissue that has higher signal intensity and, therefore, appears brighter than surrounding or normal tissue.

I3aYP4.title: Hypointensity
I3aYP4.description: A radiologic descriptor for tissue that has lower signal intensity and, therefore, appears darker than surrounding or normal tissue.

r3afP4.title: Isointensity
r3afP4.description: Signal intensity and tissue brightness are the same as those of surrounding or normal tissue.

H3aKP4.title: T1 weighting
H3aKP4.description: An MRI sequence that uses short time to echo (TE) and repetition time (TR) to produce images in which the contrast and brightness are primarily determined by the rate at which excited protons return to equilibrium. As a result, fat is typically bright, and fluid (e.g., CSF) is generally dark.

G3aBP4.title: T2 weighting
G3aBP4.description: An MRI sequence produced by using long time to echo and repetition time. Image determined by the rate of transverse relaxation (spin-spin relaxation), i.e., differences in decay of proton spin from the transverse plane (toward the main longitudinal magnetic vector). On T2-weighted images of the brain, CSF is bright and gray matter is a lighter gray color than white matter.

t3aX44.title: Triple-phase bone scan
t3aX44.description: A radionuclide scan that uses technetium-99m to evaluate for bone disorders. Images are captured during three phases performed over several hours. If uptake occurs in all three phases, there is active inflammation in the bone (e.g., acute fracture, osteomyelitis, metastases). If uptake occurs only in the first two phases, this suggests soft tissue inflammation.

83aO44.title: Bethanechol
83aO44.description: A direct, nonselective agonist of muscarinic receptors with no nicotinic activity. Often used to treat urinary retention and overflow incontinence.

u3ap44.title: Carbachol
u3ap44.description: A cholinomimetic drug that binds to muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Used to constrict the pupil and relieve intraocular pressure in patients with open-angle glaucoma.

E3a844.title: Direct parasympathomimetics
E3a844.description: A group of agents that bind directly to muscarinic or nicotinic ACh receptors, which causes cholinergic effects including bradycardia, increased intestinal peristalsis and bladder contraction, bronchoconstriction and increased bronchial secretions, miosis, and sweating. Examples include bethanechol (used to treat ileus and urinary retention) and carbachol (used to reduce intraocular pressure).

D3a1k4.title: Indirect parasympathomimetics
D3a1k4.description: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase and thus the breakdown of endogenous acetylcholine, which prolongs the action of the neurotransmitter in the neural junction. Commonly used to treat Alzheimer disease, postoperative ileus, urinary retention, and myasthenia gravis, but certain agents are used as pesticides (e.g., organophosphates) or chemical weapons (e.g., sarin)

w3ahk4.title: Neostigmine
w3ahk4.description: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prevents the breakdown of acetylcholine, which leads to accumulation in the synaptic cleft. Used to relieve symptoms of myasthenia gravis, treat colonic pseudo-obstruction and non-obstructive urinary retention, and reverse the effect of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.

93aNk4.title: Physostigmine
93aNk4.description: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prevents the breakdown of acetylcholine, which leads to accumulation in the synaptic cleft. Used to treat severe anticholinergic toxicity.

C3aqk4.title: Pilocarpine
C3aqk4.description: Cholinergic agonist that primarily acts on M3 muscarinic receptors. Primarily used for glaucoma and Sjögren syndrome. Causes pupillary constriction and ciliary muscle contraction (beneficial in glaucoma) and increases tear, sweat, and saliva production (beneficial in Sjögren syndrome).

x3aEk4.title: Pyridostigmine
x3aEk4.description: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prevents the breakdown of acetylcholine, which leads to accumulation in the synaptic cleft. Used to relieve symptoms of myasthenia gravis and reverse the effect of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.

B3azk4.title: Atropine
B3azk4.description: An anticholinergic agent that competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Used to treat acute symptomatic bradycardia or AV block, decrease salivation (e.g., in surgery), reverse neuromuscular blockade, and reverse organophosphate poisoning.

_3a5O4.title: Ipratropium bromide
_3a5O4.description: An anti-muscarinic agent commonly used to treat COPD and bronchial asthma.

z3arO4.title: Oxybutynin
z3arO4.description: A competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors that functions as an antispasmodic agent for the bladder. Used to treat overactive bladder, including urgency urinary incontinence.

destinations.label: Overactive bladder and urgency urinary incontinence → Treatment

-3aDO4.title: Tiotropium bromide
-3aDO4.description: An antimuscarinic agent commonly used to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Acts by inhibiting type 3 muscarinic (M3) receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, which results in bronchodilation.

ZRaZl4.title: Tolterodine
ZRaZl4.description: A competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors that functions as an antispasmodic agent for the bladder. Used to treat overactive bladder, including urgency urinary incontinence.

destinations.label: Overactive bladder and urgency urinary incontinence → Treatment

XRa9l4.title: Anticholinergic syndrome
XRa9l4.description: A term used to refer to signs and symptoms resulting from the toxic effects of anticholinergic agents (e.g., atropine, scopolamine), which inhibit the normal interaction of acetylcholine at the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. These include hyperthermia, tachycardia, delirium, mydriasis, hot and dry skin, ileus, and urinary retention.

gRaFm4.title: Formoterol
gRaFm4.description: A long-acting, selective β2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Has a minimal effect on heart rate. Often used in oral inhalant formulation, in combination with budesonide, for the treatment of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

hRac54.title: Salbutamol
hRac54.description: A short-acting beta-2 agonist that causes relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle. Used as a bronchodilator.

3RaS54.title: Salmeterol
3RaS54.description: A long-acting β2 adrenergic agonist used to treat COPD and moderate/severe chronic asthma.

RRal54.title: Terbutaline
RRal54.description: A β2-adrenergic agonist used as a short-acting drug to relax bronchial smooth muscle in patients with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Can also be used as a tocolytic agent to delay preterm labor for up to 48 hours.

jRa_54.title: Dopamine
jRa_54.description: A catecholamine with several functions. Functions as a neurotransmitter in the brain and a local chemical messenger elsewhere in the body (e.g., increases natriuresis in the kidney and inhibits the secretion of prolactin by the anterior pituitary upon release by the hypothalamus). Used in the treatment of hypotension and shock.

PRaWM4.title: Dobutamine
PRaWM4.description: A synthetic catecholamine with a strong affinity for adrenergic β1 receptors, and weak β2 and α1 activity. Used as a direct-acting inotropic agent for the treatment of decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock.

NRa-M4.title: Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity
NRa-M4.description: A property of some β-blockers that is characterized by the ability to bind to and stimulate the β-adrenergic receptor (agonistic effect) while competitively inhibiting the binding of epinephrine and norepinephrine to these (antagonistic effect). Examples include acebutolol, carteolol, and alprenolol.

5Rain4.title: Metoprolol
5Rain4.description: A selective β1-receptor blocker. Various uses, including treatment of hypertension, angina pectoris, and atrial fibrillation.

MRaMn4.title: Atenolol
MRaMn4.description: A beta-blocker that selectively antagonizes B1 receptors. Used to treat hypertension, angina pectoris, and, after myocardial infarction, to prevent future infarction and improve overall survival. Also used for rate control for atrial fibrillation. Adverse effects include hypotension, bradycardia, depression, insomnia, dizziness, bronchospasm, and sexual dysfunction.

nRa7n4.title: Bisoprolol
nRa7n4.description: A cardioselective beta blocker (β1 selective) without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.

LRawn4.title: Nebivolol
LRawn4.description: A cardioselective beta blocker (β1 selective) with beta-3 agonistic activity. Release of nitric oxide due to beta-3 agonism leads to vasodilation.

oRa0L4.title: Nonselective beta blockers
oRa0L4.description: A group of beta blockers that block β receptors in multiple tissues (not just β1 receptors in the heart). As a result, they can cause bronchoconstriction, peripheral vasoconstriction, and metabolic imbalances (e.g., hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia) in addition to cardiac effects.

6RajL4.title: Propranolol
6RajL4.description: A nonselective beta blocker. Effects include decreased heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Indications include atrial fibrillation, essential tremor, and migraine prophylaxis.

pRaLL4.title: Carvedilol
pRaLL4.description: A nonselective α- and β-antagonist used to treat heart failure and variceal bleeding

JRasL4.title: Sotalol
JRasL4.description: A nonselective beta blocker used as an antiarrhythmic. Has potent class II (beta blocker) and class III (potassium channel blocker) antiarrhythmic properties. A major adverse effect is an increased risk of developing torsades de pointes.

qRaCL4.title: Desflurane
qRaCL4.description: A highly fluorinated inhaled anesthetic agent with myocardial depressant effects. The exact mechanism of action is not well understood, but it is thought to disrupt neuronal transmission in the brain by interfering with the lipid matrix of the neuronal membrane. Adverse effects include postoperative nausea, malignant hyperthermia, and agitation (especially in pediatric patients).

IRaYo4.title: Isoflurane
IRaYo4.description: An inhaled anesthetic agent. Mechanism is unknown, but it is thought to alter neuronal ion channels. Causes respiratory and myocardial depression. Malignant hyperthermia is a significant, though rare, adverse effect.

rRafo4.title: Nitrous oxide
rRafo4.description: A weak inhalational anesthetic that may be self-administered for labor analgesia or procedural sedation, or given in combination with a more potent anesthetic (e.g., sevoflurane) during general anesthesia. Also used recreationally. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and dizziness.

7Ra4o4.title: Sevoflurane
7Ra4o4.description: An inhaled anesthetic agent. Mechanism is unknown, but it is thought to alter neuronal ion channels. Causes respiratory and myocardial depression. Most significant adverse effect, though rare, is malignant hyperthermia.

HRaKo4.title: Blood-gas partition coefficient
HRaKo4.description: The ratio of anesthetic concentrations in the blood and alveolar space when partial pressures in the two compartments are equal. Higher blood-gas partition coefficients of an inhalational anesthetic correspond to higher solubility in the blood.

sRato4.title: Brain-blood partition coefficient
sRato4.description: The ratio of anesthetic concentration between the brain and the blood when partial pressures remain constant. The higher the brain-blood partition coefficient, the higher the solubility of a given substance in brain tissue.

GRaBo4.title: Barbiturates
GRaBo4.description: A group of sedative drugs that act by binding GABA-A receptors and increasing the duration that they remain open when activated. Has significant potential for addiction and can cause respiratory and circulatory depression as well as potent cytochrome P450 induction.

tRaXK4.title: Etomidate
tRaXK4.description: A rapid-onset anesthetic with hypnotic effects that acts on GABA receptors in the reticular formation. Used for the induction of general anesthesia. Has milder cardiovascular effects compared to other intravenous anesthetics.

FRagK4.title: Ketamine
FRagK4.description: A rapidly acting dissociative anesthetic that is typically used to sedate patients prior to rapid sequence intubation or as an emergency anesthetic for polytrauma patients with risk of hypotension. Antagonizes NMDA receptors and increases blood pressure, cerebral blood flow, temperature, and pain tolerance. Adverse effects include confusion, hallucinations, ataxia, and nightmares.

ERa8K4.title: Propofol infusion syndrome
ERa8K4.description: Condition that can develop from high doses or prolonged administration of propofol. Characterized by severe metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and/or cardiac failure (often fatal). Elevated triglyceride levels are an early sign.

vRaAK4.title: Thiopental
vRaAK4.description: A barbiturate that is administered intravenously for the induction of general anesthesia or short surgical procedures. Increases the duration of time that GABA-A receptors are open.

wRah64.title: Depolarizing muscle relaxants
wRah64.description: A drug that acts as an agonist at neuromuscular junction acetylcholine receptors, which results in nerve cell depolarization that leads to sustained cell excitation. Results in nerve endplate resistance to further activation by acetylcholine, which paralyses the muscle. A commonly used depolarizing agent is succinylcholine.

media.title: Mechanism of action: depolarizing muscle relaxants

9RaN64.title: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular junction blockers
9RaN64.description: A group of drugs that act as competitive antagonists of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, which inhibits channel opening at the neuromuscular junction and thus prevents the formation of end-plate potentials and blocks skeletal muscles from depolarizing.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

CRaq64.title: Mivacurium
CRaq64.description: A short-acting, nondepolarizing neuromuscular junction blocker. Competitively antagonizes ACh at the motor junction, preventing depolarization. Adverse effects include flushing and histamine release (e.g., bronchospasm, hives).

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

xRaE64.title: Rocuronium
xRaE64.description: An intermediate-acting, nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. Often used for rapid sequence intubation when the use of succinylcholine is contraindicated. Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor junction, which prevents depolarization and causes paralysis.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

BRaz64.title: Atracurium
BRaz64.description: An intermediate-acting, nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor junction, which prevents depolarization and causes paralysis. Can cause histamine release with subsequent hypotension and flushing.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

yRadp4.title: Cisatracurium
yRadp4.description: An intermediate-acting, nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant and isomer of atracurium. Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor junction, which prevents depolarization and causes paralysis. Unlike atracurium, cisatracurium does not cause histamine release.

_Ra5p4.title: Vecuronium
_Ra5p4.description: An intermediate-acting, nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor junction, which prevents depolarization and causes paralysis. Has a slower onset of action compared to rocuronium.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

zRarp4.title: Pancuronium
zRarp4.description: A long-acting, nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor junction, which prevents depolarization and causes paralysis. Has a slow onset of action. Common adverse effects include tachycardia and postoperative weakness.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nondepolarizing muscle relaxants

-RaDp4.title: Succinylcholine
-RaDp4.description: A short-acting drug that acts similarly to acetylcholine. Produces depolarization of the motor endplate, which leads to flaccid skeletal muscle paralysis. Adverse effects include malignant hyperthermia and hyperkalemia.

media.title: Mechanism of action: depolarizing muscle relaxants

aiaQJ4.title: Neuromuscular monitoring
aiaQJ4.description: A technique to assess neuromuscular blockade in patients receiving anesthesia. Four successive electric stimuli are administered along the ulnar nerve; the number of twitches of the adductor pollicis muscle are counted. Zero twitches indicates profound block; 1–2 twitches indicate partial block.

YianJ4.title: Amide group anesthetics
YianJ4.description: A group of local anesthetics that is metabolized in the liver. Includes lidocaine, ropivacaine, and bupivacaine.

biaHJ4.title: Bupivacaine
biaHJ4.description: A long-acting amide type local anesthetic agent. Acts by reversibly blocking the sodium channels of nerve fibers, thereby inhibiting the conduction of nerve impulses.

Xia9J4.title: Ester group anesthetics
Xia9J4.description: A group of local anesthetics that is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase. Includes procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, and chloroprocaine.

ciaaq4.title: Etidocaine
ciaaq4.description: A long-acting amide-type local anesthetic agent that acts by reversibly blocking the sodium channels of nerve fibers and thereby inhibiting the conduction of nerve impulses.

1ia2q4.title: Lidocaine
1ia2q4.description: A local anesthetic that acts by inhibiting fast voltage-gated sodium channels in the cell membrane of neurons. It also blocks the sodium channels in cardiac cells when administered intravenously and is therefore used as an antiarrhythmic drug (class Ib) to treat ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

WiaPq4.title: Mepivacaine
WiaPq4.description: A local amide type anesthetic agent with intermediate duration of action. Acts by reversibly blocking the sodium channels of nerve fibers, thereby inhibiting the conduction of nerve impulses. Cannot be used for spinal anesthesia!

eiaxq4.title: Ropivacaine
eiaxq4.description: A long-acting amide type local anesthetic agent. Acts by reversibly blocking the sodium channels of nerve fibers, thereby inhibiting the conduction of nerve impulses.

UiabI4.title: Tetracaine
UiabI4.description: An ester local anesthetic agent used topically to numb the skin and mucous membranes. Most commonly used for ophthalmic procedures.

2iaTI4.title: Midazolam
2iaTI4.description: A short-acting, sedative-hypnotic benzodiazepine with anxiolytic and amnestic properties.

fiakI4.title: Triazolam
fiakI4.description: A benzodiazepine derivative primarily used for short-term management of insomnia.

Tia6I4.title: Oxazepam
Tia6I4.description: A short-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine that binds to allosteric sites on GABA-A receptors to increase chloride flux. Used to treat sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, anxiety disorders, and alcohol withdrawal.

giaFI4.title: Temazepam
giaFI4.description: An intermediate-acting benzodiazepine derivate that binds to allosteric sites on GABA-A receptors to increase chloride flux. Commonly used as a hypnotic for patients with increased sleep latency and difficulty maintaining sleep. Due to minimal first-pass metabolism, it can be used to treat alcohol withdrawal in patients with liver disease.

3iaSr4.title: Lorazepam
3iaSr4.description: A long-acting benzodiazepine used to treat patients in status epilepticus and to help manage anxiety, panic, or stress disorders. Also used for muscle relaxation and in patients with acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome.

Rialr4.title: Diazepam
Rialr4.description: A long-acting benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety and alcohol withdrawal.

iiaJr4.title: Clonazepam
iiaJr4.description: A long-acting benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety and panic attacks, as well as seizures.

jia_r4.title: Chlordiazepoxide
jia_r4.description: A long-acting benzodiazepine that binds at the GABA receptor. Uses include treatment of alcohol withdrawal and short-term relief of anxiety.

miaVH4.title: Zolpidem
miaVH4.description: A benzodiazepine-like agent that functions as a short-acting GABA-A receptor agonist. It is mainly used to treat sleep disorders.

MiaMH4.title: Zaleplon
MiaMH4.description: A benzodiazepine-like drug that functions as a short-acting GABA-A receptor agonist. Mainly used to treat sleep disorders.

nia7H4.title: Celecoxib
nia7H4.description: A selective COX-2 inhibitor with analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects. Used in the treatment of acute pain, rheumatoid arthritis, and nonrheumatoid joint pain. In comparison to nonselective COX-2 inhibitors, these agents have no antiplatelet effect and minimal gastrointestinal adverse effects.

oia0s4.title: Diclofenac
oia0s4.description: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that reduces pain, fever, and inflammation. Inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2).

piaLs4.title: Ibuprofen
piaLs4.description: Ibuprofen, a propanoic acid derivative, is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that is used to treat fever, pain, and/or inflammation.

Jiass4.title: Indomethacin
Jiass4.description: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that blocks both COX-1 and 2 receptors. Used to reduce pain, inflammation, and fever. Also used as a tocolytic agent (inhibits contractions mediated by prostaglandins).

IiaYG4.title: Naproxen
IiaYG4.description: An orally administered, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that nonselectively blocks COX-1 and 2. Used to reduce pain, inflammation, and fever.

riafG4.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
riafG4.description: A class of drugs that reduce pain, fever, and inflammation through the inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Examples include aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, ketorolac, piroxicam, and naproxen.

Fiagt4.title: Selective COX-2 inhibitors
Fiagt4.description: A group of NSAIDs that only block COX-2 (without affecting COX-1). Commonly used for analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in patients with a history of gastrointestinal complaints because they are less likely than other NSAIDs to cause gastrointestinal adverse effects.

uiapt4.title: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
uiapt4.description: A condition characterized by a combination of bronchial asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with polyposis, and hypersensitivity to aspirin or other cyclooxygenase-1 inhibitors.

CiaqF4.title: Tramadol
CiaqF4.description: A weak opioid agonist that also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.

AiaR84.title: Oxycodone
AiaR84.description: An opioid analgesic commonly used to treat severe pain.

ZQaZu4.title: Buprenorphine
ZQaZu4.description: A semisynthetic partial agonist of μ-opioid receptors with high receptor affinity. Used for pain management and treatment of opioid dependence. When used to treat opioid use disorder, buprenorphine is administered sublingually, typically in combination with naloxone.

0Qaeu4.title: (Relative) analgesic potency
0Qaeu4.description: A ratio to compare the analgesic potency of a drug in relation to morphine. For example, if a drug has a relative potency of 85, 0.1 mg of the drug will have the same analgesic effect as 8.5 mg of morphine, when both substances are administered via the same route.

aQaQu4.title: Fentanyl
aQaQu4.description: A potent opioid with rapid onset of action and significant CNS penetration. Used for analgesia in anesthesiology and in patch form for the treatment of acute and/or chronic pain.

YQanu4.title: Remifentanil
YQanu4.description: A potent short-acting opioid analgesic used for pain management during anesthesia and in the intensive care setting. Adverse effects include respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypotension, and skeletal muscle rigidity.

cQaaE4.title: Loperamide
cQaaE4.description: An opioid receptor agonist that acts mainly on intestinal μ-receptors and is used as an antidiarrheal drug. It increases intestinal transit time by inhibiting intestinal peristalsis, intestinal fluid secretion, and increasing sphincter tone. Unlike other opioids, loperamide cannot pass the blood-brain barrier and, therefore, does not enter the CNS.

1Qa2E4.title: Opioid overdose
1Qa2E4.description: The toxic effects of exogenous opioids (e.g., oxycodone, morphine, heroin). Clinical features include miosis, a reduced level of consciousness, and potentially fatal respiratory depression.

dQaoE4.title: Naloxone
dQaoE4.description: A competitive opioid receptor antagonist with high binding affinity to the mu (μ) opioid receptor. Used to reverse opioid overdose. It has a relatively short duration of action, which can lead to renewed effect of opioids.

VQaGE4.title: Naltrexone
VQaGE4.description: An opioid receptor antagonist used primarily in the management of opioid or alcohol dependence.

eQaxE4.title: First-generation antipsychotics
eQaxE4.description: A group of D2 antagonistic drugs used to treat psychotic illnesses such as acute psychosis, schizophrenia, and bipolar mania. Compared to second-generation antipsychotics, these drugs are associated with a higher incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms and hyperprolactinemia. Examples include chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and haloperidol.

UQabv4.title: High-potency antipsychotics
UQabv4.description: A group of drugs indicated for the treatment of delusions, illusions, and hallucinations (e.g., in schizophrenia). Extrapyramidal adverse effects are more pronounced than in less potent antipsychotics. Common agents include haloperidol, fluphenazine, and flupentixol.

2QaTv4.title: Haloperidol
2QaTv4.description: A high-potency typical antipsychotic that acts as an antagonist at dopamine (D2) receptors. It has strong antipsychotic effects even in relatively low doses but is associated with significant risk of extrapyramidal syndrome.

SQayv4.title: Fluphenazine
SQayv4.description: A first-generation (typical), high-potency antipsychotic agent that works through dopamine blockade. Indications include psychosis, acute mania, and agitation. Adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms, such as dystonia, akathisia, bradykinesia, and tardive dyskinesia.

iQaJD4.title: Chlorpromazine
iQaJD4.description: A low-potency antipsychotic that acts as an antagonist at dopamine (D2) receptors. It is used primarily for schizophrenia but can be used to treat bipolar disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and nausea. Adverse effects include extrapyramidal and anticholinergic symptoms.

QQauD4.title: Low-potency antipsychotics
QQauD4.description: A group of drugs such as promethazine that are used to treat psychosis (e.g., from schizophrenia). Primarily have a sedative effective via antidopaminergic, antihistaminergic, and anticholinergic action.

kQamw4.title: Second-generation antipsychotics
kQamw4.description: A class of medications that act through postsynaptic blockade of dopamine D₂ receptors. They also act on 5-HT₂, α-adrenergic, and H₁ receptors. Commonly used to treat psychosis but also used as chemical sedatives. Less likely to cause extrapyramidal adverse effects than typical antipsychotics, but more likely to cause metabolic disturbances (e.g., weight gain, hyperglycemia). Examples include olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, and aripiprazole.

OQaIw4.title: Clozapine
OQaIw4.description: An atypical antipsychotic mainly used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia that has a decreased risk of extrapyramidal symptoms compared to typical antipsychotics. Its most dangerous adverse effect is life-threatening agranulocytosis; as a result, frequent blood testing is required after initiating treatment.

lQavw4.title: Olanzapine
lQavw4.description: An atypical antipsychotic used primarily as first-line treatment for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Adverse effects include metabolic syndrome, hyperglycemia (diabetes mellitus), hypercholesterolemia, weight gain, asymptomatic increase of liver enzymes, anticholinergic symptoms, and orthostatic hypotension.

NQa-w4.title: Risperidone
NQa-w4.description: An atypical antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, aggression in children with autism disorder, and tics in people with Tourette syndrome. A specific adverse effect associated with risperidone is hyperprolactinemia, possibly leading to gynecomastia, lactation, irregular menses, and infertility.

mQaV94.title: Quetiapine
mQaV94.description: A second-generation antipsychotic used to treat psychotic illnesses (e.g., schizophrenia) that has sedative and anxiolytic properties. Antagonizes D2 receptors less than typical antipsychotics, which leads to a decreased risk of extrapyramidal adverse effects. Associated with a smaller increase in prolactin levels compared to first-generation antipsychotics.

MQaM94.title: Ziprasidone
MQaM94.description: A second-generation antipsychotic used to treat patients with schizophrenia, delusional disorder, acute agitation, and acute mania. Adverse effects include sleepiness and prolongation of the QT interval.

nQa794.title: Aripiprazole
nQa794.description: An atypical antipsychotic drug that is a partial dopamine agonist.

LQaw94.title: Extrapyramidal syndrome
LQaw94.description: A collection of movement disorders that are typically seen due to disruption of pathways in the basal ganglia. Symptoms include bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia, athetosis, chorea, ballismus, akathisia, tics, and tremors.

media.title: Timeline of extrapyramidal symptoms induced by antipsychotics

JQasC4.title: Dyskinesia
JQasC4.description: A disorder characterized by involuntary muscle movements, such as jerking, twitching or tics, which impair voluntary movement. Commonly seen as an adverse effect of treatment with levodopa or antipsychotics.

destinations.label: Medication for Parkinson disease → Adverse effects

IQaYx4.title: Tardive dyskinesia
IQaYx4.description: A movement disorder with a range of manifestations. Most commonly causes dyskinetic, involuntary movements of the mouth and tongue; limbs, face, and respiratory muscles can also be affected. Caused by prolonged exposure to dopamine receptor antagonists such as antipsychotics and antiemetics.

HQaKx4.title: Akathisia
HQaKx4.description: A movement disorder characterized by restlessness (e.g., an inability to sit or stand still and a constant urge to move). Affected people typically fidget, pace, and rock on their feet. Common causes include adverse effects of antipsychotic medication and drug withdrawal.

sQatx4.title: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
sQatx4.description: A rare life-threatening adverse drug event that manifests with high fever, altered mental status, muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. Typically associated with antipsychotic medications (e.g., haloperidol) and medications that block central D2 dopamine receptors (e.g., metoclopramide).

8QaOB4.title: Tricyclic antidepressants
8QaOB4.description: A class of medications that inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake from the synaptic cleft. Commonly used to treat psychiatric diseases including major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. Cause significant anticholinergic adverse effects. Many drug names in this class end in –ipramine or –triptyline (e.g., imipramine, amitriptyline).

wQahy4.title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
wQahy4.description: A class of drugs that increase synaptic serotonin by selectively inhibiting serotonin reuptake. Used to treat a variety of conditions, including depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, SIADH, and sexual dysfunction (e.g., anorgasmia, decreased libido).

BQazy4.title: Citalopram
BQazy4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) commonly used to treat depression, general anxiety disorder, and other psychiatric disorders.

yQadA4.title: Escitalopram
yQadA4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used for the treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. Adverse effects include decreased libido and anorgasmia.

AQaRA4.title: Sertraline
AQaRA4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) commonly used to treat major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and other psychiatric disorders.

_Qa5A4.title: Fluvoxamine
_Qa5A4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Adverse effects include nausea, somnolence, and insomnia.

zQarA4.title: Fluoxetine
zQarA4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that is used in the treatment of depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorders, premenstrual syndrome, and somatoform disorders.

-QaDA4.title: Paroxetine
-QaDA4.description: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that is used in the treatment of depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorders, and premenstrual syndrome. Adverse effects include drowsiness, nausea, serotonin syndrome, and sexual dysfunction. Sexual dysfunction (e.g., delay of ejaculation) is sometimes a desired effect of paroxetine for patients with premature ejaculation.

ZjaZ_4.title: Selective serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor
ZjaZ_4.description: A class of drugs that inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake from the synaptic cleft. Usually used to treat depression, anxiety, OCD, ADHD, and chronic pain. Adverse effects include elevated blood pressure (likely secondary to elevated norepinephrine), stimulant effects (e.g., agitation), and sedation.

bjaH_4.title: Venlafaxine
bjaH_4.description: A selective serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) commonly used to treat depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, PTSD, and peripheral neuropathy. Adverse effects include elevated blood pressure, stimulant effects (e.g., anxiety), and sedation. Discontinuation syndrome symptoms are more prominent than for other antidepressants due to venlafaxine's short half-life.

Xja9_4.title: Duloxetine
Xja9_4.description: A selective serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) used in major depressive disorder, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, generalized anxiety disorder, chronic pain, and off-label in stress urinary incontinence in women. Adverse effects include headaches, nausea, dizziness, sexual dysfunction, serotonin syndrome, and hypertension.

ejaxz4.title: Atomoxetine
ejaxz4.description: A selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI) that increases the concentration of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft. Used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

fjak-4.title: Bupropion
fjak-4.description: An atypical antidepressant used for both major depressive disorder and as a smoking cessation aid. It works by inhibiting reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine. The most severe adverse effect is a decreased seizure threshold.

Tja6-4.title: Mirtazapine
Tja6-4.description: An atypical antidepressant that increases synaptic serotonin and norepinephrine by antagonizing presynaptic α-2-receptors and postsynaptic 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors. Primarily used as a second-line treatment for major depressive disorder. Adverse effects include sedation, dry mouth, and weight gain.

gjaF-4.title: MAO inhibitor
gjaF-4.description: A class of drugs that inhibits monoamine oxidase, an enzyme that breaks down monoamine neurotransmitters such as serotonin and norepinephrine. Usually used to treat atypical depression and Parkinson disease. The most common adverse effects include hypertensive crisis (with ingestion of tyramine-rich foods), serotonin syndrome, and CNS stimulation.

hjacZk.title: Tranylcypromine
hjacZk.description: A monoamine oxidase inhibitor antidepressant used in the management of treatment-resistant depression. Adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, and tremor.

3jaSZk.title: Melatonin
3jaSZk.description: A hormone produced from tryptophan in the pineal gland. Has an important role in circadian rhythms. Darkness causes norepinephrine release onto pinealocytes, resulting in melatonin secretion and increased sleep drive. Melatonin preparations can be prescribed for insomnia, shift work, and jet lag.

RjalZk.title: St. John's wort
RjalZk.description: An herbal medicine used as a supplement for mental health conditions (depression in particular). Induces the cytochrome-P450 system.

ijaJZk.title: Serotonin syndrome
ijaJZk.description: A potentially life-threatening condition caused by serotonergic overactivity due to the therapeutic use of serotonergic drugs, accidental or intentional overdose, or drug interactions. Clinical features include the classic triad of neuromuscular excitability, which can lead to hyperthermia; autonomic dysfunction; and altered mental status. Severe serotonin syndrome can cause rhabdomyolysis, seizures, and death.

4ja30k.title: Valproic acid
4ja30k.description: An anticonvulsant that inhibits GABA transaminase and sodium channels. Used to treat bipolar disorder, epilepsy, and to prevent migraine and cluster headaches.

OjaI0k.title: Carbamazepine
OjaI0k.description: An antiepileptic drug that inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels in the brain, which reduces the excitability of neurons. Also used as a first-line treatment for neuropathic pain (e.g., trigeminal neuralgia), and for treating acute manic episodes in patients with bipolar disorder.

ljav0k.title: Ethosuximide
ljav0k.description: An antiepileptic medication that reduces excitability in the brain by blocking thalamic T-type calcium channels. Primarily used to treat absence seizures.

Nja-0k.title: Phenytoin
Nja-0k.description: An antiepileptic drug that inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels in the brain, which reduces the excitability of neurons. Used primarily for tonic-clonic and focal seizure prophylaxis. Can also be used as a second-line drug to treat status epilepticus. Adverse effects include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, gingival hyperplasia, hypertrichosis, and fetal hydantoin syndrome.

mjaVak.title: Lamotrigine
mjaVak.description: An antiepileptic drug that is used for seizure prophylaxis in patients with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, focal (partial) seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. It reduces the excitability of neurons by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release in the brain. Because of its broad spectrum of action (e.g., also inhibits serotonin reuptake), it is also an effective mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder.

5jaiak.title: Levetiracetam
5jaiak.description: An antiepileptic drug that is currently licensed for adjunctive seizure prophylaxis in patients > 16 years old with myoclonic seizures, focal seizures, and/or generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The mechanism of levetiracetam is not well understood, but it is believed to alter synaptic vesicle binding and indirectly alter GABA activity.

MjaMak.title: Gabapentin
MjaMak.description: An anticonvulsant used to treat focal seizure disorders, restless legs syndrome, and neuropathic pain. It works via Inhibition of high voltage-activated Ca2+ channels.

nja7ak.title: Pregabalin
nja7ak.description: An anticonvulsive medication that is an antagonist of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. It is used for the treatment of fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, post-herpetic neuralgia, and seizures. It also has many off-label uses (e.g., generalized anxiety disorder, restless leg syndrome).

Ljawak.title: Vigabatrin
Ljawak.description: An antiepileptic medication that reduces excitability in the brain by inhibiting the catabolism of GABA. Primarily used to treat infantile spasms and refractory complex partial seizures. Vigabatrin is teratogenic and can cause neural tube defects.

oja0Yk.title: Topiramate
oja0Yk.description: A drug used to treat seizures and for migraine prophylaxis. Mechanism of action is not fully understood but is thought to involve blockage of neuronal voltage-dependent sodium channels, enhancement of GABA-A activity, and antagonism of AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors.

KjaUYk.title: L-DOPA
KjaUYk.description: A precursor amino acid that is metabolized to the neurotransmitter dopamine by decarboxylation in the presynaptic neuron. Used in the treatment of Parkinson disease, restless legs syndrome, and dystonia. Usually given in combination with the DOPA-decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa to prevent decarboxylation to dopamine outside of the CNS. Adverse effects include nausea, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, and dyskinesia.

JjasYk.title: Carbidopa
JjasYk.description: A decarboxylase inhibitor that is given in combination with the dopamine precursors levodopa to prevent its decarboxylation to dopamine peripherally, thereby increasing availability in the brain and preventing side-effects of increased peripheral dopamine levels (nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension).

IjaYbk.title: Dopamine receptor agonists
IjaYbk.description: A class of drugs that activate dopamine D₁ and/or D₂ receptors. Used to treat Parkinson disease, prolactinoma, and restless legs syndrome. Further subdivided into ergot and nonergot dopamine agonists. Adverse effects include nausea, drowsiness, orthostatic hypotension, confusion, hallucinations, impulse control disorders, and compulsive drug use (dopamine dysregulation syndrome).

rjafbk.title: Nonergot dopamine agonist
rjafbk.description: A type of dopamine agonist that, unlike ergot dopamine agonists, is not derived from alkaloid compounds produced by the ergot fungus and is not associated with pulmonary, peritoneal, and cardiac fibrosis. Agents include pramipexole, ropinirole, and rotigotine.

7ja4bk.title: Ropinirole
7ja4bk.description: A non-ergot dopamine receptor agonist used to treat Parkinson disease and restless leg syndrome. Adverse effects include hypotension, nausea, and impulse control disorders.

HjaKbk.title: Pramipexole
HjaKbk.description: A nonergot dopamine D2 receptor agonist used for the treatment of Parkinson disease and restless legs syndrome. Adverse effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, and sedation. Some patients develop impulse control disorders with compulsive gambling or hypersexuality.

sjatbk.title: Apomorphine
sjatbk.description: A parenterally administered dopamine agonist, with a greater effect on D2 receptors. Indicated for akinetic episodes in advanced Parkinson disease.

GjaBbk.title: Rotigotine
GjaBbk.description: A non-ergot dopamine receptor agonist used to treat Parkinson disease and restless leg syndrome. Adverse effects include hypotension, nausea, and impulse control disorders.

FjagXk.title: Ergot dopamine agonist
FjagXk.description: A type of dopamine agonist derived from alkaloid compounds produced by the ergot fungus. Ergot dopamine agonists are associated with rare but severe adverse effects (e.g., pulmonary, peritoneal, and cardiac fibrosis). Agents include bromocriptine, pergolide, and cabergoline.

8jaOXk.title: Bromocriptine
8jaOXk.description: An ergot derivative dopamine D2 receptor agonist. Indications include hyperprolactinemia, Parkinson disease, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Adverse effects include nausea and impulse control disorder.

vjaAXk.title: Cabergoline
vjaAXk.description: Ergot derivative that is a potent dopamine agonist on D2 receptors. Mainly used to treat prolactinoma.

Dja1ck.title: Catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors
Dja1ck.description: A group of drugs that are used in conjunction with levodopa to treat Parkinson disease. Inhibition of COMT reduces catabolism of levodopa, which increases drug availability, prolongs its action, and reduces motor fluctuations. Examples include entacapone and tolcapone.

wjahck.title: Entacapone
wjahck.description: Used in conjunction with levodopa to treat Parkinson disease. It reversibly and selectively inhibits peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), reducing the catabolism of levodopa.

9jaNck.title: Tolcapone
9jaNck.description: A drug used to treat Parkinson disease that reversibly and selectively inhibits peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), which reduces the catabolism of levodopa. Can cause hepatotoxicity.

xjaEck.title: Monoamine oxidase B inhibitors
xjaEck.description: A group of drugs that inhibit the mitochondrial MAO-B enzyme, which results in decreased dopamine metabolism in the brain. Examples include rasagiline, safinamide, and selegiline.

Bjazck.title: Selegiline
Bjazck.description: At lower doses a selective MAO-B inhibitor used in the treatment of Parkinson disease by reducing catabolism of dopamine. At higher concentrations (delivered transdermally) also inhibits MAO-A and can be used to treat major depressive disorder.

yjad1k.title: Rasagiline
yjad1k.description: A selective monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitor that decreases dopamine catabolism in the brain, which prolongs the effect of dopamine and reduces the symptoms of Parkinson disease. Also prevents free radical damage caused by oxidative metabolism of dopamine.

_ja51k.title: End-of-dose akinesia
_ja51k.description: A phenomenon that appears in patients with Parkinson disease after long-term levodopa use and that manifests with the reemergence of symptoms, typically toward the end-of-dose period. While the exact mechanism is unknown, progression of disease and levodopa neurotoxicity are believed to be contributing factors.

destinations.label: Medication for Parkinson disease → Adverse effects

bPaHWk.title: Akinetic crisis
bPaHWk.description: A condition caused by severe dopamine deficiency (e.g., after discontinuation of L-DOPA therapy in a patient with Parkinson disease). Characterized by inability to move, incomprehensible speech, and possibly hyperthermia. Complications include dehydration, deep vein thrombosis, and pneumonia.

destinations.label: Medication for Parkinson disease → Adverse effects

WPaPdk.title: Simvastatin
WPaPdk.description: An HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor used to treat hypercholesterolemia. Has a relatively short half-life and thus is ideally administered in the evening (when endogenous synthesis of cholesterol peaks).

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

ePaxdk.title: Atorvastatin
ePaxdk.description: A statin, a lipid-lowering drug that inhibits the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. Its primary effect is to lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol.

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

UPabVk.title: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
UPabVk.description: A class of calcium channel blockers that cause systemic vasodilation. Commonly used in antihypertensive therapy. In contrast to non-dihydropyridines, they have minimal myocardial depressant activity. Adverse effects include peripheral edema, headaches, dizziness, facial flushing, reflex tachycardia, and gingival hyperplasia. Agents include nifedipine, nicardipine, and amlodipine.

TPa6Vk.title: Nitrendipine
TPa6Vk.description: A medium-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a half-life of 8-12 hours commonly used in the management of hypertension, angina and supraventricular arrhythmias. Adverse effects include headaches, peripheral edema, and reflex tachycardia.

gPaFVk.title: Lercanidipine
gPaFVk.description: A medium-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a half-life of 8-12 hours commonly used in the management of hypertension, angina and supraventricular arrhythmias. Adverse effects include headaches, peripheral edema, and reflex tachycardia.

SPayVk.title: Amlodipine
SPayVk.description: A long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a half-life > 24 hours commonly used in the management of hypertension, angina and supraventricular arrhythmias. Adverse effects include headaches, peripheral edema (especially compared to other dihydropyridine agents), and reflex tachycardia.

3PaSek.title: Diltiazem
3PaSek.description: A nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker and class IV antiarrhythmic agent.

iPaJek.title: Verapamil
iPaJek.description: A nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocking agent primarily used for its myocardial depressive effects (e.g., to treat supraventricular tachycardia). Has vasodilating effects and is also used in migraine prophylaxis.

jPa_ek.title: Enalapril
jPa_ek.description: An ACE inhibitor that, like other agents in this class, prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Used to treat hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, myocardial infarction, and as a nephroprotective medication in patients with diabetes mellitus.

PPaWUk.title: Lisinopril
PPaWUk.description: An ACE inhibitor that, like other agents in this class, prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Used to treat hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, myocardial infarction, and as a nephroprotective medication in patients with diabetes mellitus.

4Pa3Uk.title: Ramipril
4Pa3Uk.description: An ACE inhibitor that, like other agents in this class, prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Used to treat hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, myocardial infarction, and as a nephroprotective medication in patients with diabetes mellitus.

kPamUk.title: Captopril
kPamUk.description: An ACE inhibitor that, like other agents in this class, prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Used to treat hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, myocardial infarction, and as a nephroprotective medication in patients with diabetes mellitus.

OPaIUk.title: Valsartan
OPaIUk.description: An angiotensin-receptor blocker used as second-line treatment for the management of hypertension if angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated. Like other agents in this class, functions by inhibiting blocking AT1 receptors, decreasing the binding of angiotensin II. This decreases vasoconstriction, which lowers the blood pressure. Also leads to decreased secretion of aldosterone, causing decreased reabsorption of Na+ and water, which also lowers blood pressure.

media.title: Mechanism of action: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors

lPavUk.title: Candesartan
lPavUk.description: An angiotensin-receptor blocker used as second-line treatment for the management of hypertension if angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated. Like other agents in this class, functions by inhibiting blocking AT1 receptors, decreasing the binding of angiotensin II. This decreases vasoconstriction, which lowers the blood pressure. Also leads to decreased secretion of aldosterone, causing decreased reabsorption of Na+ and water, which also lowers blood pressure.

NPa-Uk.title: Losartan
NPa-Uk.description: An angiotensin-receptor blocker used as second-line treatment for the management of hypertension if angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated. Like other agents in this class, functions by inhibiting blocking AT1 receptors, decreasing the binding of angiotensin II. This decreases vasoconstriction, which lowers the blood pressure. Also leads to decreased secretion of aldosterone, causing decreased reabsorption of Na+ and water, which also lowers blood pressure.

mPaV2k.title: Aliskiren
mPaV2k.description: A direct renin inhibitor that decreases RAAS activity and lowers blood pressure by diminishing the effects of angiotensin II and aldosterone. Used to treat arterial hypertension if both ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers are not tolerated.

5Pai2k.title: ACE inhibitors
5Pai2k.description: A group of antihypertensive drugs that inhibit the enzyme responsible for the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Other uses include slowing the progress of chronic kidney disease, delaying the onset of nephropathy in patients with diabetes mellitus, and treatment of left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Agents include lisinopril, enalapril, and captopril.

media.title: Mechanism of action: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors

MPaM2k.title: Angiotensin receptor blockers
MPaM2k.description: A group of drugs that blocks AT1 receptors, which decreases the binding of angiotensin II. This decreases vasoconstriction, which lowers the blood pressure. Also leads to decreased secretion of aldosterone, which causes decreased reabsorption of Na+ and water and lowers blood pressure. Agents include valsartan, irbesartan, losartan, and candesartan. Used if angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated.

KPaUfk.title: Cardiac glycoside poisoning
KPaUfk.description: A toxicity of digoxin caused by overdose, hypokalemia, renal failure, volume depletion, and/or use of certain other drugs (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone, or quinidine). Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, gastrointestinal pain, anorexia, and blurred vision with a yellow tint (xanthopsia).

pPaLfk.title: Digoxin immune Fab
pPaLfk.description: A mixture of antigen-binding fragments (fab regions) derived from animals immunized against digoxin. Used to treat cardiac glycoside toxicity. Fab fragments bind free toxins to form complexes that are excreted in urine. Decreased serum concentrations of digoxin also promote its release from cardiac myocyte receptors.

JPasfk.title: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor
JPasfk.description: An agent that inhibits phosphodiesterase type 5 in vascular smooth muscle. PDE-5 normally breaks down cGMP. Inhibition of PDE-5 therefore leads to increased cGMP and subsequent vasodilation. Commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

media.title: Mechanism of action: nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors

IPaYTk.title: Sildenafil
IPaYTk.description: A phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

7Pa4Tk.title: Tadalafil
7Pa4Tk.description: A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor; commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction, mild BPH, and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Contraindicated in patients taking nitrates due to a high risk of profound hypotension. May cause orthostatic hypotension in patients taking alpha-adrenergic antagonists (e.g., for BPH).

HPaKTk.title: Vardenafil
HPaKTk.description: A phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor used to treat erectile dysfunction. Adverse effects include flushing, nasal congestion, and dyspepsia.

tPaXgk.title: Roflumilast
tPaXgk.description: A selective phosphodiesterase type 4 inhibitor. Roflumilast is used to improve lung function and prevent exacerbations in patients with severe cases of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

uPapgk.title: Milrinone
uPapgk.description: A phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor with positive inotropic and vasodilatory effects. Commonly used in perioperative and critical care settings as an intravenous infusion for hemodynamic support and in the treatment of heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.

vPaAgk.title: ADP receptor inhibitor​s
vPaAgk.description: A group of drugs that irreversibly inhibit platelet aggregation by preventing the ADP-mediated formation of the GpIIb/IIIa receptor complex.

media.title: Mechanism of action: drugs acting against primary hemostasis

DPa1Sk.title: Clopidogrel
DPa1Sk.description: A P2Y12 receptor antagonist that blocks platelet aggregation. It is used in the treatment of acute coronary syndrome and peripheral arterial disease as well as in the prevention of ischemic stroke.

wPahSk.title: Prasugrel
wPahSk.description: A P2Y12 receptor antagonist that blocks platelet aggregation. It is used in the treatment of acute coronary syndrome.

9PaNSk.title: Ticagrelor
9PaNSk.description: A P2Y12 receptor antagonist that blocks platelet aggregation. Sometimes used in  dual antiplatelet therapy in combination with aspirin.

xPaESk.title: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors
xPaESk.description: A group of drugs that blocks fibrinogen binding to platelets, which prevents proper platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Examples include abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban.

media.title: Mechanism of action: drugs acting against primary hemostasis

BPazSk.title: Abciximab
BPazSk.description: A monoclonal antibody against glycoprotein receptor IIb/IIIa. Prevents platelet aggregation. Adverse effects include acute profound thrombocytopenia and hemorrhage.

yPadhk.title: Tirofiban
yPadhk.description: An intravenously administered nonpeptide drug that directly inhibits glycoprotein receptor IIb/IIIa. It prevents platelet aggregation.

APaRhk.title: Eptifibatide
APaRhk.description: An intravenously administered cyclic peptide that directly inhibits glycoprotein receptor IIb/IIIa. It prevents platelet aggregation.

-PaDhk.title: Reye syndrome
-PaDhk.description: A rare but potentially life-threatening condition in children < 19 years that generally develops after treating a viral illness (e.g., influenza, varicella) with salicylates like aspirin. The viral infection alters the metabolism of salicylates and leads to accumulation of metabolites in the liver, which causes hepatic mitochondrial injury that prevents hepatic ATP production. The result is hepatic failure (hyperammonemia, metabolic acidosis, and hepatic steatosis) that manifests with acute hepatic encephalopathy.

14a2Rk.title: Argatroban
14a2Rk.description: A parenteral anticoagulant that directly inhibits thrombin independently of antithrombin.

V4aGRk.title: Danaparoid
V4aGRk.description: A low molecular weight heparinoid administered subcutaneously or intravenously for the treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism. It inhibits thrombin generation by potentiating antithrombin-mediated inactivation of factor Xa.

U4abik.title: Enoxaparin
U4abik.description: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) that is administered via subcutaneous injection and is primarily used to prevent and treat deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism following surgery. The antidote is protamine sulfate.

24aTik.title: Fondaparinux
24aTik.description: A synthetic heparin administered subcutaneously for the treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism. It binds to antithrombin III, thereby potentiating antithrombin's inhibition of factor Xa.

h4acQk.title: Low molecular weight heparin
h4acQk.description: A therapeutic fraction of heparin that has a lower average molecular weight, a higher bioavailability, fewer adverse effects, and a more precise and predictable anticoagulant effect than unfractionated heparin.

34aSQk.title: Protamine sulfate
34aSQk.description: An intravenously administered medication used to reverse the effects of heparin (e.g., in heparin overdose). It is a cationic peptide and forms a stable ion pair with heparin or low molecular weight heparin, which does not provide any anticoagulant activity.

i4aJQk.title: Unfractionated heparin
i4aJQk.description: A mixture of sulfated mucopolysaccharides of various sizes (5,000–40,000 daltons), which acts as an anticoagulant by indirectly inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa. UFH has a fast onset of action and must be administered parenterally. aPTT (activated thromboplastin time) must be monitored in patients who are on UFH.

P4aWjk.title: Nonimmune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia
P4aWjk.description: A mild, transient drop in platelet count that can occur within 5 days of heparin exposure. Mediated by heparin-induced platelet aggregation. Not associated with thrombosis. Formerly known as HIT type 1.

44a3jk.title: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
44a3jk.description: An immune-mediated prothrombotic disorder  (formerly called “type 2 HIT”) characterized by sudden thrombocytopenia (usually > 50% from baseline) during treatment with heparin. Typically occurs within 5–10 days of heparin initiation and leads to thromboembolic complications.

m4aVPk.title: Warfarin
m4aVPk.description: A vitamin K antagonist that inhibits hepatic epoxide reductase, thereby blocking synthesis (recycling) of the active, reduced form of vit. K. Without reduced vit. K, γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues cannot occur, which reduces the production of active coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as anticoagulatory proteins C and S. Typically administered in patients with artificial heart valves, increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and/or valvular A-fib.

M4aMPk.title: Dabigatran
M4aMPk.description: A direct oral thrombin inhibitor that may be used for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or prophylaxis for thromboembolism.

n4a7Pk.title: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitors
n4a7Pk.description: Drugs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) that have an anticoagulatory effect via direct inhibition of factor Xa. Indications include prophylaxis and treatment of venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism and non-valvular atrial fibrillation.

L4awPk.title: Apixaban
L4awPk.description: An orally administered anticoagulant that directly inhibits factor Xa. Used for the treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolic events. Adverse effects include bleeding and thrombocytopenia.

o4a04k.title: Rivaroxaban
o4a04k.description: An orally administered anticoagulant that directly and selectively inhibits factor Xa.

K4aU4k.title: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis
K4aU4k.description: Skin necrosis caused by paradoxical coagulation due to an early warfarin drug effect occurring within 3–5 days after initiating therapy.

q4aC4k.title: Hydrochlorothiazide
q4aC4k.description: A thiazide diuretic that inhibits Na+ and Cl- resorption in the distal convoluted tubule. Used to treat hypertension, chronic edema, and renal diabetes insipidus. Also used to prevent calcium kidney stones.

H4aKkk.title: Bumetanide
H4aKkk.description: A loop diuretic that blocks Na+-K+-2Cl--cotransporters in the ascending loop of Henle. Also stimulates prostaglandin release. Used to treat edema (e.g., from heart failure, hepatic disease, and renal disease).

t4aXOk.title: Furosemide
t4aXOk.description: A sulfonamide-derived loop diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride resorption by competitively inhibiting the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

84aOOk.title: Torsemide
84aOOk.description: A sulfonamide loop diuretic that inhibits the resorption of Na+, K+, and Cl- in the thick ascending loop of Henle.

u4apOk.title: Forced diuresis
u4apOk.description: Massive diuresis aimed at forced renal elimination of (toxic) substances. Involves IV administration of large amounts of fluids in combination with loop diuretics.

w4ahlk.title: Aldosterone receptor antagonists
w4ahlk.description: A group of drugs that act on the distal convoluted tubules and inhibit the effects of aldosterone. Results in decreased Na⁺ reabsorption (and thus decreased H₂O retention) and inhibited H⁺ and K⁺ excretion. Can be steroidal (examples include spironolactone and eplerenone) or nonsteroidal (examples include finerenone and esaxerenone).

94aNlk.title: Eplerenone
94aNlk.description: An aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor antagonist that can be used as a potassium-sparing diuretic (antihypertensive) and in the treatment of hyperaldosteronism. Eplerenone has a low affinity for progesterone and androgen receptors and thus has fewer antiandrogenic adverse effects (e.g., gynecomastia) than spironolactone.

C4aqlk.title: Spironolactone
C4aqlk.description: An aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor antagonist that can be used as a potassium-sparing diuretic (antihypertensive), an anti-androgen, or in the treatment of hyperaldosteronism.

B4azlk.title: Triamterene
B4azlk.description: A potassium-sparing diuretic that acts by direct inhibition of the epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct leading to reduced Na+ reabsorption and reduced K+ secretion as well as increased diuresis.

y4adNk.title: Amiloride
y4adNk.description: A potassium-sparing diuretic that directly inhibits epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. Causes reduced sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Adverse effects include hyperkalemia and gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).

A4aRNk.title: Antihistamine
A4aRNk.description: A drug that reversiby blocks histamine receptors. Drugs that inhibit H1 receptors are typically used to treat allergic reactions. Drugs that inhibit H2 receptors are used to suppress gastric acid secretion.

_4a5Nk.title: Azelastine
_4a5Nk.description: An H1 antihistaminic drug typically used as a nasal spray to treat allergic and nonallergic rhinitis. Also used as ophthalmic drops to symptomatically treat allergic conjunctivitis.

z4arNk.title: Cetirizine
z4arNk.description: A second generation anti-histamine that selectively targets the H1 receptor. It is used to treat allergic rhinitis, urticaria, angioedema, anaphylactic reactions, pruritus, and allergic conjunctivitis.

ZkaZmk.title: Clemastine
ZkaZmk.description: A first-generation antihistaminic drug used in the management of allergic rhinitis and urticaria.

0kaemk.title: Dimetindene
0kaemk.description: A first-generation H₁ receptor antagonist used to treat symptoms of allergic conditions and pruritus.

akaQmk.title: Fexofenadine
akaQmk.description: A second-generation H1-blocking antihistamine used to treat allergies and as an adjunct in cases of anaphylactic shock. Similarly efficient to first-generation antihistamines, but has fewer sedating and anticholinergic adverse effects.

Ykanmk.title: H1-antihistamine
Ykanmk.description: A class of drugs that competitively inhibits histamine binding at the H1 receptor. Commonly used to treat the symptoms of allergic reactions. First-generation H1 blockers can also inhibit muscarinic receptors and cross the blood-brain barrier. Second-generation H1 blockers selectively block H1 receptors and do not cross the blood-brain barrier.

bkaHmk.title: H₂ receptor blocker
bkaHmk.description: A group of drugs that decrease acid production in the stomach by blocking H₂ histamine receptors. Effective at suppressing nocturnal acid secretions; less effective at suppressing postprandial acid secretions. Also used to relieve symptoms of acute allergic reactions.

Xka9mk.title: Loratadine
Xka9mk.description: A second-generation H1 antihistamine. Similar to other agents in its class, it has fewer effects on the central nervous system (and thus is less sedating) compared to first-generation H1 antihistamines. Used as an antiallergic agent.

ckaa5k.title: Promethazine
ckaa5k.description: A first-generation antihistamine and a low-potency antipsychotic agent. Has nominal anti-α-adrenergic and local anesthetic action as well as a strong sedative action and anticholinergic adverse effects. Primarily used as an antiemetic, sedative, and antiallergic agent.

1ka25k.title: Ranitidine
1ka25k.description: An H2 receptor inhibitor that suppresses gastric acid secretion.
