Previously used to treat various conditions that cause or are exacerbated by excess acid production (e.g., peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease). Removed from the market by the FDA in 2020 following the repeated detection of the potentially carcinogenic substance N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA).

WkaP5k.title: Alkylating agents
WkaP5k.description: A class of antiproliferative drugs that alkylates and, thus, damages DNA. Used as chemotherapeutic agents and immunosuppressants. Examples include nitrogen mustards (e.g., chlorambucil, melphalan), oxazaphosphorines (e.g., cyclophosphamide), and busulfan.

VkaG5k.title: Oxazaphosphorines
VkaG5k.description: A type of alkylating chemotherapeutic agent that induces cross-linking at guanine. Examples include cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide. Used to treat solid tumors, leukemia, and lymphomas. Adverse effects include myelosuppression and hemorrhagic cystitis.

ekax5k.title: Cyclophosphamide
ekax5k.description: An alkylating agent used to treat many solid tumors, leukemias, lymphomas, and multiple myeloma and as an immunosuppressant to treat autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) and severe nephrotic syndrome. Adverse effects include myelosuppression, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), and hemorrhagic cystitis (risk reduced with prophylactic administration of mesna and aggressive hydration).

UkabMk.title: Ifosfamide
UkabMk.description: An alkylating agent used to treat a variety of solid tumors (especially testicular, gynecological and lung cancers), leukemias, and lymphomas. Adverse effects include myelosuppression, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), and hemorrhagic cystitis (risk reduced with prophylactic administration of mesna and aggressive hydration).

2kaTMk.title: Nitrogen mustards
2kaTMk.description: A group of nonspecific DNA alkylating agents used to treat various cancers, including ovarian cancer, melanoma, and cutaneous T-cell lymphomas. Examples include chlorambucil, melphalan, and topical mechlorethamine gel.

fkakMk.title: Busulfan
fkakMk.description: An alkylating chemotherapeutic agent of the alkyl sulfonate class. Often used in bone marrow ablation prior to transplantation for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Common adverse effects include severe myelosuppression, electrolyte imbalance, hyperpigmentation, cardiac, pulmonary, and hepatic toxicity.

Tka6Mk.title: Chlorambucil
Tka6Mk.description: An alkylating chemotherapeutic agent of the nitrogen mustard class typically used in the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Hodgkin lymphoma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Common adverse effects include myelosuppression, oral ulcers, and pulmonary fibrosis.

gkaFMk.title: Melphalan
gkaFMk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent (alkylating agent, nitrogen mustard) typically used in the treatment of multiple myeloma and ovarian cancer. Adverse effects include fatigue, myelosuppression, hypokalemia, and peripheral edema.

hkacnk.title: Temozolomide
hkacnk.description: An alkylating chemotherapeutic agent used to treat anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma multiforme. Common adverse effects include myelosuppression and neurotoxicity.

ikaJnk.title: Platinum-based agents
ikaJnk.description: A group of chemotherapeutic agents that functions by cross-linking between DNA strands, thus decreasing DNA replication. Agents include cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin. Used to treat urothelial cell, lung, ovarian, testicular, and bladder cancer. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and ototoxicity.

Qkaunk.title: Cisplatin
Qkaunk.description: A first-generation, platinum-based, alkylating agent that prevents replication of tumor cells by causing intrastrand links within DNA. Used to treat bladder, ovarian, and particularly testicular cancer. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and ototoxicity.

jka_nk.title: Carboplatin
jka_nk.description: A first-generation, platinum-based alkylating agent that prevents replication of tumor cells by causing intrastrand links within DNA. Used to treat several types of cancer, including ovarian and lung cancer. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity (reduced risk with prophylactic administration of amifostine), peripheral neuropathy, and ototoxicity.

PkaWLk.title: Oxaliplatin
PkaWLk.description: A third-generation, platinum-based, alkylating agent that prevents replication of tumor cells by causing intrastrand links within DNA. Frequently used to treat colorectal cancer. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity (reduced risk with prophylactic administration of amifostine), peripheral neuropathy, ototoxicity.

4ka3Lk.title: Topoisomerase inhibitors
4ka3Lk.description: A group of chemotherapeutic agents that block topoisomerases (e.g., topoisomerase I and II) and, therefore, interrupt DNA unwinding.

kkamLk.title: Anthracyclines
kkamLk.description: A group of chemotherapeutic drugs including doxorubicin, daunorubicin, and idarubicin. Anthracyclines have multiple mechanisms of action including the inhibition of topoisomerase II, the inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis by intercalation with DNA, DNA strand excision, and generation of free radicals. They are used to treat several types of cancer, including leukemias, lymphomas, breast, ovarian, and bone cancer (e.g., osteosarcoma). Adverse effects include cardiotoxicity and dilated cardiomyopathy, which can be limited with dexrazoxane, an iron chelating agent.

OkaILk.title: Doxorubicin
OkaILk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent from the class of anthracycline antibiotics. Used to treat cancers, including sarcomas and hematologic malignancies. Has multiple mechanisms of actions, including inhibition of topoisomerase II, inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis by intercalation with DNA, DNA strand excision, and generation of free radicals. Adverse effects include myelosuppression and cardiotoxicity.

lkavLk.title: Daunorubicin
lkavLk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent from the anthracycline antibiotics class. Used to treat acute lymphocytic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia. Adverse effects include dose-dependent cardiotoxicity (reduced with administration of dexrazoxane), myelosuppression, and alopecia.

Nka-Lk.title: Idarubicin
Nka-Lk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent from the anthracycline antibiotic class used for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Adverse effects include dose-dependent cardiotoxicity (which can be reduced with dexrazoxane), myelosuppression, and alopecia.

mkaVok.title: Irinotecan
mkaVok.description: A chemotherapeutic agent that inhibits topoisomerase I, leading to ssDNA breaks and prevention of strand reannealing. Often used in the treatment of colon cancer. Adverse effects include myelosuppression and diarrhea.

5kaiok.title: Topotecan
5kaiok.description: A chemotherapeutic agent that inhibits topoisomerase I and prevents DNA unwinding and replication. Often used in the treatment of cervical, ovarian, and small cell lung cancer. Adverse effects include myelosuppression and diarrhea.

oka0Kk.title: Vinca alkaloids
oka0Kk.description: A group of chemotherapeutic agents that functions by binding β-tubulin and inhibiting polymerization into microtubules to prevent mitotic spindle formation, thus arresting the cell cycle in M-phase. Agents include vincristine and vinblastine. Used to treat many solid tumors, leukemias, and Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

6kajKk.title: Vinblastine
6kajKk.description: A vinca alkaloid chemotherapeutic agent that inhibits microtubule formation in the mitotic spindle. Used to treat lymphomas, testicular cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Causes myelosuppression.

pkaLKk.title: Taxanes
pkaLKk.description: A group of chemotherapeutic agents that stabilizes polymerized microtubules of the mitotic spindle to stop mitosis (mitotic inhibitors) and thereby the process of cell division. Agents include paclitaxel and docetaxel. Commonly used in the treatment of ovarian, breast, prostate, lung, head and neck, and gastric cancer. Adverse effects include peripheral neuropathy, interstitial pneumonitis, myelosuppression, cardiotoxicity, alopecia, and skin changes.

JkasKk.title: Docetaxel
JkasKk.description: A taxane chemotherapeutic agent that stabilizes polymerized microtubules of the mitotic spindle to stop mitosis. Commonly used to treat breast, gastric, head and neck, non-small cell lung, and prostate cancer. Adverse effects include neurotoxicity, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, fluid retention, alopecia, and skin reactions (especially nail changes).

qkaCKk.title: Paclitaxel
qkaCKk.description: A taxane chemotherapeutic agent that stabilizes polymerized microtubules of the mitotic spindle to stop mitosis. It is commonly used to treat Kaposi sarcoma, ovarian, breast, and non-small cell lung cancer. Adverse effects include flushing, peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression, and alopecia.

IkaY6k.title: Antimetabolites
IkaY6k.description: A class of drugs commonly used as chemotherapeutic agents and antibiotics to interfere with cell division. They have a wide range of mechanisms of action, but typically impair DNA replication machinery by altering or destroying the deoxynucleotides needed for DNA replication. Drugs include azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, cytarabine, methotrexate, and 5-fluorouracil. Can induce myelosuppression.

rkaf6k.title: Antifolates
rkaf6k.description: A class of antimetabolites that blocks the activity of folic acid, resulting in inhibition of cell division, DNA and RNA synthesis and repair, and protein synthesis. The main mechanism of action of antifolates is the inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Medications from this class include methotrexate and pemetrexed, both of which are used as chemotherapeutic and immunosuppressant agents.

HkaK6k.title: Pemetrexed
HkaK6k.description: An antifolate that inhibits thymidylate synthase, dihydrofolate reductase, and other enzymes involved in folate metabolism. Primarily used as a chemotherapeutic agent to treat non-small cell lung cancer and pleural mesothelioma. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, desquamation, and anemia.

skat6k.title: Pyrimidine analogues
skat6k.description: A class of antineoplastic agents that mimic the structure of metabolic pyrimidine nucleosides and inhibit enzymes involved in DNA synthesis through competitive antagonism. Examples include 5-fluorouracil, cytarabine, and gemcitabine.

tkaXpk.title: 5-Fluorouracil
tkaXpk.description: A cytostatic/cytotoxic antimetabolite in the subgroup of pyrimidine antagonists. Acts mainly through inhibition of thymidylate synthase to block synthesis of thymidine, thus halting DNA replication and promoting cell death. Also inhibits protein synthesis.

8kaOpk.title: Gemcitabine
8kaOpk.description: Gemcitabine is a cytostatic/cytotoxic antimetabolite in the subgroup of pyrimidine antagonists. When incorporated into DNA in place of cytidine, it arrests DNA replication and thus causes cell death.

ukappk.title: Capecitabine
ukappk.description: An antineoplastic drug that works by inhibiting thymidylate synthase. Typically used to treat advanced breast, colorectal, and gastric cancer. It is a prodrug of 5-fluorouracil.

vkaApk.title: Fludarabine
vkaApk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Fludarabine is a purine analog that acts by inhibiting DNA synthesis in normal and cancerous cells. Common adverse effects include myelosuppression and neurotoxicity.

Dka1Jk.title: Ribonucleotide reductase inhibitors
Dka1Jk.description: A group of drugs that block the formation of deoxyribonucleotides, thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis. Examples include hydroxyurea, fludarabine, cladribine, and gemcitabine.

wkahJk.title: Hydroxyurea
wkahJk.description: An antineoplastic drug used to treat both neoplastic (e.g., myeloproliferative neoplasms, squamous head and neck cancers) and non-neoplastic conditions (e.g., sickle cell anemia, psoriasis). Antineoplastic effects result from the inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase, which inhibits DNA replication and causes cell cycle arrest during the S phase. Beneficial effects in sickle cell disease result from increased nitric oxide levels and cGMP signaling, which increase fetal hemoglobin levels, decrease the frequency of sickle cell crises, and decrease the need for blood transfusions.

9kaNJk.title: Bleomycin
9kaNJk.description: A metal-chelating, glycopeptide antibiotic that has a cytotoxic effect on nondividing tumor cells by causing fragmentation of DNA chains. Used to treat lymphomas, germ cell tumors, head and neck cancers, and squamous cell carcinoma. Adverse effects include fever, hypersensitivity reactions, skin changes, and severe pulmonary fibrosis.

CkaqJk.title: Actinomycin D
CkaqJk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent (antibiotic) that intercalates into DNA and prevents DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis. Used to treat several tumors of childhood, including Wilms tumor, Ewing sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Adverse effects include myelosuppression and dermatologic toxicity.

xkaEJk.title: Mitomycin
xkaEJk.description: A chemotherapeutic agent (antibiotic) that alkylates DNA and inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis. Used to treat gastric and pancreatic cancer. Adverse effects include fever, myelosuppression, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

BkazJk.title: L-asparaginase
BkazJk.description: An enzyme that breaks down the amino acid L-asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia, reducing the source of asparagine for leukemic cells and inhibiting protein synthesis in tumor cells. Mostly used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Common adverse effects include allergic reactions, hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, pancreatitis, and blood clotting problems.

AkaRqk.title: Mesna
AkaRqk.description: A drug used to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis in patients receiving chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide. Functions by inactivating the toxic metabolite acrolein.

-kaDqk.title: Relative glucocorticoid potency
-kaDqk.description: The potency of a steroid (in terms of its anti-inflammatory effects) compared with hydrocortisone. Hydrocortisone is the synthetic equivalent of physiologic cortisol and, by definition, has a glucocorticoid potency of 1. The relative glucocorticoid potency can be used to calculate the dosages required when switching from one steroid to another.

ZOaZIk.title: Hydrocortisone
ZOaZIk.description: A short-acting, low-potency glucocorticoid with some mineralocorticoid activity available in IV, IM, oral or topical forms. It has wide range of indications, including adrenal insufficiency, COPD/asthma, and allergies.

aOaQIk.title: Prednisolone
aOaQIk.description: A synthetic high-potency oral glucocorticoid with similar properties and uses to those of prednisone. Prednisolone is the active metabolite of prednisone; prednisone undergoes hepatic conversion to prednisolone to become biologically active.

YOanIk.title: Prednisone
YOanIk.description: A synthetic oral glucocorticoid that has an intermediate duration of action (12–36 hours) and an anti-inflammatory potential that is 4 times greater than that of cortisol.

bOaHIk.title: Dexamethasone
bOaHIk.description: A glucocorticoid that has anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant properties. Used to treat many conditions, including rheumatological disease, allergies, asthma/COPD, and adrenal insufficiency. Due to its antiedematous effects, it is also used in patients with increased intracranial pressure.

XOa9Ik.title: Betamethasone
XOa9Ik.description: A very potent corticosteroid with long duration of action that can be administered topically or systemically. It is used for several medical indications, including rheumatologic disorders (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, arthritis), dermatologic diseases (e.g., bullous pemphigoid), allergies, antenatal fetal lung maturation, ulcerative colitis, and temporal arteritis. Adverse effects include systemic changes (e.g., Cushing syndrome) and local reactions (e.g., skin thinning, hyperpigmentation).

WOaPrk.title: Methylprednisolone
WOaPrk.description: A synthetic corticosteroid that has an intermediate duration of action (30-36 hr if given PO and 7 days with IV administration) and an anti-inflammatory potential that is 5 times greater than that of cortisol.

dOaork.title: Budesonide
dOaork.description: A synthetic steroid used to treat several inflammatory conditions such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, and Crohn disease.

VOaGrk.title: Fluticasone
VOaGrk.description: A synthetic glucocorticoid used as a topical anti-inflammatory or an inhaled corticosteroid (for mild/moderate/severe persistent asthma).

eOaxrk.title: Triamcinolone
eOaxrk.description: A synthetic corticosteroid that can be administered orally, intravenously, intralesionally, topically, or by inhalation. Used to treat skin conditions (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), immune-mediated diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, ulcerative colitis, alopecia areata), and asthma.

UOab7k.title: Penicillin
UOab7k.description: A group of beta-lactam antibiotics that includes penicillin V and penicillin G and benzathine penicillin.

2OaT7k.title: Penicillin G
2OaT7k.description: A parenterally administered classical penicillin that is typically used to treat infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis, Treponema, or certain gram-positive bacteria (e.g., S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae, Actinomyces).

fOak7k.title: Penicillin V
fOak7k.description: A beta-lactam antibiotic that is used to treat various infections, including streptococcal pharyngitis, rheumatic fever, scarlet fever, and erysipelas.

gOaF7k.title: Anti-staphylococcal penicillins
gOaF7k.description: A group of penicillin derivatives with β-lactamase resistance due to a bulky side chain that prevents bacterial beta-lactamase from breaking down the beta-lactam ring. Used primarily to treat gram-positive aerobes, especially S. aureus (but not MRSA). Includes nafcillin, dicloxacillin, oxacillin, and methicillin (no longer used).

SOay7k.title: Oxacillin
SOay7k.description: An antistaphylococcal penicillin that is effective against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus but not methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

3OaSHk.title: Aminopenicillins
3OaSHk.description: A group of beta-lactam containing antibiotics with a wider spectrum of activity than penicillin (i.e., coverage of some gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria). Includes amoxicillin and ampicillin. Often combined with beta-lactamase inhibitors (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, ampicillin-sulbactam) to prevent degradation.

ROalHk.title: Amoxicillin
ROalHk.description: An aminopenicillin antibiotic that is bactericidal for many gram-positive bacteria and gram-negative bacteria. Commonly used to treat acute otitis media and acute group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis.

iOaJHk.title: Ampicillin
iOaJHk.description: An aminopenicillin antibiotic with bactericidal activity against gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus spp., Enterococcus spp., Listeria monocytogenes) and some gram-negative bacteria (e.g., H. influenzae, P. mirabilis, E. coli, H. pylori, Shigella spp.).

jOa_Hk.title: Piperacillin
jOa_Hk.description: An ureidopenicillin antibiotic that is effective against gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria. Often given in combination with tazobactam, a β-lactamase inhibitor.

4Oa3sk.title: Clavulanate
4Oa3sk.description: A β-lactamase inhibitor used in combination with β-lactam antibiotics (particularly amoxicillin) to prevent bacteria from inactivating the antibiotic.

destinations.label: Overview of antibiotic therapy → Beta-lactam antibiotics

kOamsk.title: Sulbactam
kOamsk.description: A β-lactamase inhibitor used in combination with β-lactam antibiotics (particularly ampicillin) to prevent bacteria from inactivating the antibiotic.

destinations.label: Overview of antibiotic therapy → Beta-lactam antibiotics

OOaIsk.title: Carbapenems
OOaIsk.description: A class of broad-spectrum, β-lactam antibiotics that are resistant to β-lactamase. Effective against gram-positive and gram-negative aerobes and anaerobes. Administered intravenously due to poor enteric absorption. Examples include imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem, and doripenem.

NOa-sk.title: Meropenem
NOa-sk.description: A carbapenem antibiotic that is considered a treatment of last resort for severe gram-positive and gram-negative infections because of its significant adverse effects (e.g., seizures, rash, gastrointestinal discomfort).

mOaVGk.title: Ertapenem
mOaVGk.description: A carbapenem antibiotic that has a broad spectrum of action against many gram-positive and gram-negative species of bacteria. Indications include community-acquired pneumonia, severe cases of skin infections, and complicated UTI. It is not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA and should not be used when these pathogens are suspected.

5OaiGk.title: Macrolides
5OaiGk.description: A group of bacteriostatic antibiotics that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by blocking peptidyl transferase at the ribosomal 50S subunit. Includes erythromycin, azithromycin, and clarithromycin. Used for the treatment of atypical pneumonia, upper respiratory infections, STIs caused by Chlamydia, Streptococcal infections in patients allergic to penicillin, Bordetella pertussis, and Neisseria. Adverse effects include GI discomfort, QT interval prolongation, acute cholestatic hepatitis, exanthem, and eosinophilia.

MOaMGk.title: Erythromycin
MOaMGk.description: A macrolide antibiotic active against gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria. Acts by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis after binding to the 50S subunit of the ribosome. Used for treatment of respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital tract, skin, and soft tissue infections.

nOa7Gk.title: Azithromycin
nOa7Gk.description: A macrolide antibiotic that is typically used to treat pneumonia, gram-positive infections (especially in patients who cannot tolerate penicillin), and some sexually transmitted diseases (e.g., chlamydial infections).

oOa0tk.title: Clarithromycin
oOa0tk.description: An orally administered macrolide antibiotic that has a broad spectrum of action against many gram-positive and gram-negative species of bacteria.

media.title: Mechanisms of action of antibiotics on the bacterial ribosome

6Oajtk.title: Doxycycline
6Oajtk.description: A broad-spectrum bacteriostatic tetracycline antibiotic. Used for a variety of infections (e.g., to treat sexually transmitted infections or respiratory infections or as prophylaxis for malaria).

pOaLtk.title: Tetracyclines
pOaLtk.description: A group of antibiotics that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by blocking aminoacyl-tRNA from binding to the ribosome acceptor site. Used to treat Borrelia, Mycoplasma, Rickettsia, and Chlamydia infections. Also used to treat acne vulgaris. Adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and discoloration of teeth.

JOastk.title: Aminoglycosides
JOastk.description: A group of bactericidal antibiotics that target gram-negative aerobes and some anaerobic bacilli by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis and damaging the bacterial cell wall. Primarily used to treat infection with pseudomonas, enterobacter, acinetobacter, and mycobacteria (tuberculosis). Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, oto- and vestibulotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade.

media.title: Mechanisms of action of antibiotics on the bacterial ribosome

qOaCtk.title: Gentamicin
qOaCtk.description: An aminoglycoside antibiotic that has potent activity against gram-negative infections (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa). It also has activity against some gram-positive and atypical organisms.

IOaYFk.title: Tobramycin
IOaYFk.description: An aminoglycoside antibiotic that is effective against gram-negative infections, including Pseudomonas.

rOafFk.title: Streptomycin
rOafFk.description: An aminoglycoside used to treat Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, and mycobacterial infections. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, vestibulotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade.

HOaKFk.title: Clindamycin
HOaKFk.description: A bacteriostatic lincosamide antibiotic that is effective against anaerobic bacteria and certain gram-positive organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

GOaBFk.title: Vancomycin
GOaBFk.description: A glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by forming a complex with murein. Effective against gram-positive bacteria only (including MRSA, S. epidermidis, enterococci, and Clostridioides difficile).

FOag8k.title: Nitroimidazole
FOag8k.description: A group of bactericidal antibiotics that create free radicals within the cell, which leads to DNA-strand break. Includes metronidazole, nimorazole, and tinidazole. Effective against a number of protozoa (e.g., Giardia, E. histolytica, Trichomonas) and anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Clostridioides difficile). Adverse effects include disulfiram-like reaction when consumed with alcohol (flushing, tachycardia, hypotension) and metallic taste.

uOap8k.title: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
uOap8k.description: A combination antibiotic comprised of a sulfonamide (sulfamethoxazole) and a dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitor (trimethoprim) that functions by inhibiting folate synthesis. Has a broad spectrum of activity against many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

destinations.label: Overview of antibiotic therapy → Sulfonamides and diaminopyrimidine

vOaA8k.title: Fosfomycin
vOaA8k.description: A bactericidal antibiotic that interferes with cell wall synthesis. Has broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Mainly used to treat urinary tract infections.

wOahuk.title: Linezolid
wOahuk.description: An antibiotic commonly used to treat infection caused by gram-positive bacteria resistant to other antibiotics, e.g., methicillin-resistant staphylococci and vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

9OaNuk.title: Daptomycin
9OaNuk.description: A lipopeptide antibiotic only effective against gram-positive bacteria. Binds to the bacterial cell membrane and causes rapid depolarization, which inhibits synthesis of DNA, RNA, and protein. Active against enterococci, staphylococci (including MRSA), streptococci, and corynebacteria.

COaquk.title: Tigecycline
COaquk.description: A bacteriostatic, broad-spectrum antibiotic that binds to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, which blocks peptidyl transferase and inhibits protein synthesis. Used to treat anaerobic, gram-positive, gram-negative, and multidrug-resistant organisms (e.g., MRSA, VRE).

xOaEuk.title: Vancomycin flushing reaction
xOaEuk.description: An anaphylactoid reaction caused by rapid infusion of vancomycin that leads to nonspecific mast cell degranulation with subsequent histamine-mediated skin flushing, hypotension, and dyspnea. Can be prevented by slowing the rate of infusion and possibly pretreating with antihistamines.

yOadEk.title: Empiric antibiotic therapy
yOadEk.description: The use of antibiotics against the most probable causative organism(s) before the resistance pattern and/or specific causative organism have been identified.

destinations.label: Overview of antibiotic therapy → Additional considerations

ZlaZvk.title: First generation cephalosporins
ZlaZvk.description: A class of cephalosporin antibiotics that includes cephalexin and cefazolin. Active against gram-positive bacteria and some gram-negative bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis, E. coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Ineffective against Enterococcus, Listeria, MRSA, Pseudomonas, and atypical bacteria.

alaQvk.title: Cefazolin
alaQvk.description: A first-generation cephalosporin administered intravenously and intramuscularly. Active against many gram-positive bacteria and some gram-negative bacteria, such as Proteus, E. coli, and Klebsiella.

Ylanvk.title: Second generation cephalosporins
Ylanvk.description: A class of cephalosporin antibiotics that includes cefaclor, cefuroxime, cefoxitin, and cefotetan. Active against many gram-negative bacteria but less active against gram-positive bacteria when compared to first-generation cephalosporins. Ineffective against Enterococcus, Listeria, MRSA, Pseudomonas, and atypical bacteria.

Xla9vk.title: Cefuroxime
Xla9vk.description: A second-generation cephalosporin with intravenous and oral formulations. Active against gram-positive cocci, H. influenza, Enterobacter, Neisseria, Proteus mirabilis, E. coli, Klebsiella, and Serratia.

1la2Dk.title: Third generation cephalosporins
1la2Dk.description: A class of cephalosporin antibiotics that includes ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, and others. Active against many gram-negative bacteria but are less active against gram-positive bacteria than first-generation cephalosporins. Ineffective against Enterococcus, Listeria, and MRSA; has variable activity against Pseudomonas.

dlaoDk.title: Cefotaxime
dlaoDk.description: An intravenously administered third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic. Used to treat some gram-positive and severe gram-negative infections that are resistant to other beta-lactam antibiotics.

VlaGDk.title: Cefixime
VlaGDk.description: An oral third-generation cephalosporin used to treat uncomplicated urinary tract infections and exacerbations of chronic bronchitis.

elaxDk.title: Ceftazidime
elaxDk.description: An intravenously administered, third generation cephalosporin antibiotic. Indications include severe Gram-negative infections that are resistant to other beta-lactams. Also has activity against Pseudomonas.

Ulabwk.title: Ceftriaxone
Ulabwk.description: A third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic with good CNS penetration. Used to treat some gram-positive and severe gram-negative infections (e.g., with Neisseria meningitidis) that are resistant to other beta-lactam antibiotics.

flakwk.title: Ciprofloxacin
flakwk.description: A fluoroquinolone broad-spectrum antibiotic that covers both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria and is commonly used to treat gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections. Contraindications include patients younger than 18 years of age, pregnancy, and QT prolongation.

Tla6wk.title: Ofloxacin
Tla6wk.description: A fluoroquinolone broad-spectrum antibiotic that covers both gram-positive (e.g., S. aureus, S. pneumoniae) and gram-negative bacteria (e.g., E. coli, H. influenzae, P. aeruginosa). Used systemically for pneumonia, bronchitis, UTIs, and PID and topically for bacterial keratitis.

glaFwk.title: Levofloxacin
glaFwk.description: A 3rd-generation fluoroquinolone that has excellent activity against most strains of bacterial pathogens responsible for gastrointestinal, respiratory, and urinary tract infections, including gram-negative, gram-positive, and atypical bacteria. Acts by inhibiting gyrase enzymes, preventing bacterial DNA from winding and unwinding.

Slaywk.title: Moxifloxacin
Slaywk.description: A fourth-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic. The spectrum of coverage includes gram-negative rods (though not health care-acquired species such as Pseudomonas), atypical bacteria, some gram-positive organisms (notably S. pneumoniae), and some anaerobes. Commonly used to treat community-acquired pneumonia, sinusitis, skin/soft tissue infections, bacterial conjunctivitis, and intraabdominal infections.

hlac9k.title: Aprepitant
hlac9k.description: A neurokinin receptor antagonist used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea. Adverse effects include fatigue and hiccups.

3laS9k.title: Dimenhydrinate
3laS9k.description: An H1-receptor antagonist in the GI tract, blood vessels, and respiratory tract with central anticholinergic activity. Used in motion sickness, nausea, vomiting, and vertigo. Adverse effects include drowsiness, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, reduced bowel sounds, and urinary retention. Its antidote is physostigmine.

Rlal9k.title: Diphenhydramine
Rlal9k.description: A first-generation, H1-blocking antihistamine used to treat pruritus, allergies, and nausea. The most common adverse effect is sedation, though at high doses, anticholinergic adverse effects may arise.

ilaJ9k.title: Domperidone
ilaJ9k.description: A dopamine antagonist with antiemetic properties that is commonly used for GI motility disorders (gastroparesis/gastritis) and nausea/vomiting adverse effects from dopaminergic antiparkinsonian drugs.

Qlau9k.title: Dopamine antagonist
Qlau9k.description: A type of drug that blocks dopamine receptors, most commonly D2, and has antipsychotic, antiemetic, and sedative effects. Most relevant adverse effects are extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g., dyskinesia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia). Dopamine antagonists are classified as mildly, moderately, and highly antipsychotic. Agents include haloperidol, flupentixol, promazine, and melperone.

PlaWCk.title: Meclizine
PlaWCk.description: A first-generation, nonselective, H1 antagonist with strong anticholinergic properties. Used to prevent and treat motion sickness. Also safe to use for nausea in pregnancy.

4la3Ck.title: Metoclopramide
4la3Ck.description: A dopamine-2 receptor and serotonin receptor antagonist. Commonly used as an antiemetic and to promote gastrointestinal motility in patients with gastroparesis. Adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g., dystonia), likely secondary to dopamine antagonism.

klamCk.title: Neurokinin receptor antagonists
klamCk.description: A group of drugs that block neurokinin receptors in the solitary nucleus and inhibit substance P-induced vomiting. Used to treat chemotherapy-induced emesis, especially delayed emesis. Adverse effects include fatigue and hiccups. Examples include aprepitant, fosaprepitant, and rolapitant.

OlaICk.title: Ondansetron
OlaICk.description: An 5-HT₃ serotonin receptor antagonist that is used as an antiemetic to treat severe nausea and/or vomiting.

llavCk.title: Prokinetic agents
llavCk.description: Medications used to increase gastric contractions, intestinal motility, and decrease sphincter tone. Most common mechanism of action is via dopamine receptor antagonism on smooth muscle cells. Used to treat conditions such as gastroparesis, hyperemesis gravidarum, and GERD. Examples include metoclopramide and domperidone.

mlaVxk.title: Scopolamine
mlaVxk.description: A nonselective muscarinic antagonist that inhibits intestinal tract vagal nerve signaling and acts on the area postrema to produce an antiemetic effect. Used in the treatment of motion sickness and vestibular-induced nausea and vomiting.

5laixk.title: Serotonin receptor antagonists
5laixk.description: A group of drugs that inhibit serotonin (5-HT) receptors. Examples include 5-HT3 receptor antagonists such as the antiemetics ondansetron, granisetron, and palonosetron, and the 5-HT2A receptor antagonist cyproheptadine, which is used to treat moderate-to-severe serotonin syndrome.

tlaXAk.title: Carbimazole
tlaXAk.description: A prodrug of the antithyroid drug methimazole. Once metabolized to methimazole, it inhibits thyroid peroxidase to decrease thyroid hormone synthesis. Adverse effects include a pruritic rash, agranulocytosis, and teratogenicity.

ulapAk.title: Propylthiouracil
ulapAk.description:
An antithyroid drug that works by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase enzyme, resulting in a decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis. Additionally, it inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Indications include hyperthyroidism,
thyroid storm, and radioactive iodine therapy (in which case it is administered prior to it).

Ela8Ak.title: Methimazole
Ela8Ak.description: An antithyroid drug of the thioamide group. Inhibits thyroid peroxidase to decrease thyroid hormone synthesis. Adverse effects include a pruritic rash, agranulocytosis, and teratogenicity.

Dla1_k.title: Oral contraceptive pill
Dla1_k.description: An oral method of birth control. Most forms contain estrogen and progesterone, which act on the pituitary to suppress FSH and LH secretion, thereby preventing ovulation. Adverse effects include headache, hypertension, and venous thromboembolism.

Claq_k.title: Contraceptive implant
Claq_k.description: A progestin-releasing, subdermal implant that suppresses FSH and LH secretion, thereby preventing ovulation. Results in cervical mucus thickening, a decrease in tubal motility, and endometrial changes.

AlaRzk.title: Progestin-only contraceptive pills
AlaRzk.description: A type of short-acting, reversible oral contraceptive that contains low doses of norethindrone. Used when estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated or in conditions such as endometriosis (due to its atrophic effect on the endometrium).

_la5zk.title: Vaginal ring
_la5zk.description: A hormonal contraceptive that contains estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) and progestin (etonogestrel). It prevents conception by suppressing ovulation, thickening cervical mucus, thinning the endometrium, and decreasing tubal motility. The ring is worn inside the vagina for 3 weeks, then removed for 1 week to allow for withdrawal bleeding before inserting a new ring. If suppression of menstruation is desired, a ring is inserted every 3 weeks, foregoing the withdrawal week.

zlarzk.title: Contraceptive patch
zlarzk.description: A hormonal contraceptive that contains estrogen and progestin, which suppresses FSH and LH secretion, thereby preventing ovulation. Results in cervical mucus thickening, a decrease in tubal motility, and endometrial changes. The patch is replaced weekly.

0Nae-k.title: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome
0Nae-k.description: A collection of physiological and immune-mediated reactions to an infectious or noninfectious insult (e.g., an acute inflammatory process, trauma). SIRS is diagnosed if ≥ 2 of the following 4 criteria are fulfilled: 1) temperature > 38ºC or < 36ºC; 2) heart rate > 90 beats/min; 3) respiratory rate > 20 breaths/min or PaCO₂ < 32 mm Hg; 4) white blood cell count > 12,000 cells/mm³, < 4000 cells/mm³, and/or > 10% band cells.

YNan-k.title: Sepsis
YNan-k.description: The presence of life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated immune response to infection. Organ dysfunction due to sepsis is commonly defined as an increase in the sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score of ≥ 2.

bNaH-k.title: Urosepsis
bNaH-k.description: A potentially life-threatening syndrome of organ dysfunction secondary to a dysregulated host response to a urinary tract infection. SIRS criteria are often present.

eNaxZO.title: Procalcitonin
eNaxZO.description: Peptide precursor of calcitonin, a hormone involved in calcium homeostasis. Procalcitonin is also an acute phase reactant and is used as a biomarker for the diagnosis of sepsis, severe sepsis, and septic shock.

2NaT0O.title: Antigenic drift
2NaT0O.description: A minor genetic change from random point mutation that occurs as viruses replicate and evolve. Often results in changes in antigenic structure (e.g., hemagglutinin and neuraminidase in influenza virus) that cause epidemics.

gNaF0O.title: Antigenic shift
gNaF0O.description: An abrupt, major change in a viral genome caused by exchange of genetic segments (reassortment) when two subtypes of a virus infect the same cell. Can increase the potential of a virus to cause pandemics, particularly if human pathogenic and animal pathogenic viruses exchange genetic information.

hNacaO.title: Arrhythmogenic syncope
hNacaO.description: Syncope due to cerebral hypoperfusion that results from the heart's inability to meet increased oxygen demand. May be the first sign of heart disease. Causes include ventricular tachycardia, AV block, sick sinus syndrome, Afib, and Adams-Stokes syndrome, among others.

iNaJaO.title: Cardiac syncope
iNaJaO.description: A loss of consciousness due to the heart's inability to meet an increased oxygen demand (e.g., during exertion), leading to reduced cerebral perfusion. Can also manifest as a secondary hypoxic seizure. Common causes include arrhythmia and structural heart disease (e.g., aortic stenosis).

jNa_aO.title: Carotid sinus syndrome
jNa_aO.description: A type of recurrent reflex syncope that primarily occurs in patients > 50 years of age with carotid sinus hypersensitivity when pressure is applied to the carotid sinus. This pressure triggers an exaggerated parasympathetic response that results in an excessive decrease in systolic blood pressure and/or a cardiac pause, resulting in syncope.

PNaWYO.title: Vasovagal syncope
PNaWYO.description: A type of syncope associated with activation of the vagus nerve and a subsequent parasympathetically-mediated decrease in cardiac output, which culminates in a transient loss of consciousness.

NNa-YO.title: Postural hypotension
NNa-YO.description: A 20 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure or 10 mm Hg drop in diastolic blood pressure that occurs within 3 minutes after rising from a supine or seated position. May be asymptomatic, cause presyncope, or syncope. There are a number of predisposing factors, including hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction, medications (e.g., antihypertensives), and aging (causing decreased baroreceptor sensitivity).

5NaibO.title: Postural tachycardia syndrome
5NaibO.description: An uncommon autonomic condition characterized by an abnormal increase in the resting heart rate by ≥30 beats per minute within 10 minutes of moving from a supine to an upright position (or an absolute heart rate of >120 beats per minute in the standing position). Usually associated with symptoms of orthostatic intolerance (e.g., light-headedness, dizziness, presyncope, sweating).

KNaUXO.title: Vasovagal response
KNaUXO.description: A hemodynamic response to a trigger (e.g., stress) of the vagus nerve, resulting in a decrease in sympathetic nervous tone simultaneous with parasympathetic nervous tone increase. Increased parasympathetic activity results in a drop in heart rate, blood pressure, and heart contractility. Can lead to fainting (vasovagal syncope).

6NajXO.title: Convulsive syncope
6NajXO.description: Common form of syncope in which loss of consciousness is accompanied by myoclonic movements and seizures (due to reduced midbrain perfusion).

pNaLXO.title: Presyncope
pNaLXO.description: A sensation of imminent loss of consciousness.

INaYcO.title: Tilt table test
INaYcO.description: A procedure that is used to determine if vasovagal or orthostatic syncope is present. The patient is strapped onto a tilt table in a supine position for 15 minutes and then raised passively to an angle of around 70°. Normally, the patient's heart rate increases while the blood pressure barely changes. The test is positive if the patient develops hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg) and bradycardia (vasovagal) or slow progressive hypotension (orthostatic) with presyncope or syncope.

tNaX1O.title: Chagas disease
tNaX1O.description: A tropical infectious disease caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, which is typically transmitted by triatomine bugs ("kissing bugs"). Endemic to Central and South America. Manifestations include fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, cardiomyopathy, gastrointestinal disease.

8NaO1O.title: Chagoma
8NaO1O.description: A localized inflammatory swelling that can develop at the site of a bite by insects in the Reduviidae family (kissing bugs), which are vectors for Trypanosoma cruzi infection.

uNap1O.title: Trypanosomal chancre
uNap1O.description: The localized, primary lesion of a trypanosomal infection. Typically manifests as a red, painful, indurated, nodular swelling 2–5 cm in size that develops at the bite site within 2 weeks of the bite.

xNaEWO.title: Hemodialysis
xNaEWO.description: A type of renal replacement therapy that uses diffusion and a small degree of ultrafiltration to remove solutes and excess water from the patient's blood. Indications include the following conditions after unsuccessful medical management: acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia), ingestion of certain substances, fluid overload, and uremic symptoms.

destinations.label: Renal replacement therapy → Hemodialysis and hemofiltration

yNaddO.title: Peritoneal dialysis
yNaddO.description: A type of intracorporeal renal replacement therapy that uses diffusion to remove solutes and excess water from the patient's blood. Utilizes the patient's own peritoneal membrane as a semipermeable membrane.

ANaRdO.title: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
ANaRdO.description: A syndrome seen in patients initiating dialysis characterized by headache, blurred vision, and altered mental status that is secondary to cerebral edema from osmotic shifts.

destinations.label: Renal replacement therapy → Hemodialysis and hemofiltration

0maeVO.title: Cystic medial necrosis
0maeVO.description: A degeneration of large blood vessels such as the aorta. Histopathologic findings include loss, thinning, disorganization, and fragmentation of elastic fibers, accumulation of mucoid extracellular matrix, and loss of smooth muscle nuclei.

destinations.label: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome → Pathology

YmanVO.title: DeBakey classification
YmanVO.description: A system of classification of thoracic aortic dissection. A type I DeBakey dissection begins in the ascending aorta and extends to the descending aorta. A type II DeBakey dissection is restricted to the ascending aorta. A type IIIa DeBakey dissection begins in the region of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery and is restricted to the supradiaphragmatic portion of the descending aorta. A type IIIb DeBakey dissection begins in the thoracic descending aorta and extends to the abdominal portion of the descending aorta.

WmaPeO.title: Abdominal thrusts
WmaPeO.description: A basic first-aid maneuver designed to dislodge a foreign body (FB) in the upper airway by increasing intrathoracic pressure. Standing behind the patient, place one fist in the patient's epigastric area and the other hand on top of the fist. Administer abdominal thrusts with sharp inward and upward movements. Repeat until the FB is dislodged.

emaxeO.title: Mobitz I second-degree atrioventricular block
emaxeO.description: A type of second-degree atrioventricular block characterized by progressive prolongation of the PR interval that culminates in a P wave that is not followed by a QRS complex (i.e., a dropped beat).

UmabUO.title: Left posterior fascicular block
UmabUO.description: A conduction abnormality within the His-Purkinje system that manifests with right axis deviation on ECG in the absence of right ventricular hypertrophy or any other attributable cause for right axis deviation. Usually occurs in combination with a right bundle branch block as a bifascicular block. Less common than left anterior fascicular blocks.

2maTUO.title: Left anterior fascicular block
2maTUO.description: A conduction abnormality within the His-Purkinje system that manifests with marked left axis deviation on ECG. Isolated LAFB can occur as a benign consequence of aging or can be caused by coronary artery disease, valvular disease, hypertension, or cardiomyopathies.

fmakUO.title: Sinoatrial exit block
fmakUO.description: The failure of sinoatrial node transitional cells to transmit the electrical depolarization to the surrounding atrial tissue. Classified similarly to AV blocks (e.g., first-, second-, third-degree), but conduction is blocked to the atria rather than the ventricle. Only second-degree SA exit blocks can be diagnosed from a 12-lead ECG (e.g., intermittent dropped P wave); third-degree SA exit blocks are indistinguishable from sinus arrest on ECG and require electrophysiological studies (EPS). First-degree SA exit blocks are not visible on ECG and can only be diagnosed on EPS.

gmaFUO.title: Distal esophageal spasm
gmaFUO.description: An esophageal motility disorder that is characterized by repetitive, uncoordinated, nonprogressive contraction waves of the distal esophagus. This condition was previously known as diffuse esophageal spasm. The typical presentation includes dysphagia, regurgitation, and squeezing retrosternal chest pain during meals.

SmayUO.title: Hypertensive peristalsis
SmayUO.description: An esophageal motility disorder characterized by smooth muscle contractions of excessive amplitude and duration in a normal peristaltic pattern. Typically manifests with dysphagia and retrosternal chest pain.

Qmau2O.title: Esophageal motility disorders
Qmau2O.description: A group of esophageal disorders that result in weak/absent peristalsis and/or abnormal esophageal contractions (e.g., premature, spastic, vigorous, repetitive). Causes include primary esophageal disorders (e.g., achalasia, nutcracker esophagus) and systemic illness (e.g., tumors, compression, Chagas disease, or systemic sclerosis).

jma_2O.title: Pulmonary hypertension
jma_2O.description: A state of chronically elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mm Hg (normal: 10–14 mm Hg) at rest with increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Grouped into 5 different subtypes (WHO group 1-5) based on underlying etiology.

destinations.label: Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale → Definitions

media.title: ECG in pulmonary hypertension secondary to an atrial septal defect

PmaWfO.title: Cor pulmonale
PmaWfO.description: Altered structure (hypertrophy, dilation) or impaired functioning of the right ventricle caused by a primary disorder of the respiratory system (e.g., COPD, cystic fibrosis, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary embolism). The primary respiratory disorder causes acute/chronic pulmonary hypertension, which in turn causes acute/chronic right heart failure.

destinations.label: Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale → Cor pulmonale

4ma3fO.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
4ma3fO.description: A type of pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group 1) that is characterized by proliferative vasculopathy, resulting in increased pulmonary arterial pressure at rest. By definition, it is not caused by another underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease (left heart failure, COPD, etc). Can have various causes, including connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, HIV, and/or drugs/toxins, or it may be idiopathic.

destinations.label: Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale → Etiology
Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale → Definitions

OmaIfO.title: Infertility
OmaIfO.description: An inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected sexual intercourse in female individuals < 35 years of age and after 6 months in those ≥ 35 years of age, or the need for medical intervention (including assisted reproductive technology) to achieve pregnancy.

Nma-fO.title: Primary infertility
Nma-fO.description: Inability to conceive in female individuals who have never been pregnant or in male individuals who have never successfully conceived with a partner.

mmaVTO.title: Secondary infertility
mmaVTO.description: Inability to conceive despite 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse in female individuals < 35 years of age or 6 months of regular, unprotected intercourse in female individuals > 35 years of age who have previously conceived, and/or in male individuals who have previously successfully conceived with a partner.

nma7TO.title: Erectile dysfunction
nma7TO.description: A persistent or recurrent inability to acquire or maintain an erection of sufficient rigidity or duration for sexual performance. Causes vary and can be vascular, neurological, endocrinologic, psychological, or drug-related.

6majgO.title: Female infertility
6majgO.description: The inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of unprotected sexual intercourse or therapeutic donor insemination in women < 35 years of age and after 6 months in those ≥ 35 years of age.

ImaYSO.title: Male infertility
ImaYSO.description: The inability to achieve pregnancy in a fertile female partner after one year. Causes include genetic abnormalities, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, varicocele, and certain medications.

rmafSO.title: Vasectomy
rmafSO.description: An surgical procedure that involves cutting the vas deferens to achieve permanent sterilization. Often performed under local anesthesia as an outpatient procedure.

7ma4SO.title: Kallmann syndrome
7ma4SO.description: A rare genetic condition characterized by anosmia (an inability to smell) and decreased production of GnRH from the hypothalamus, leading to delayed or absent puberty.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Kallmann syndrome

tmaXhO.title: Clomiphene citrate challenge test
tmaXhO.description: A test used to evaluate for diminished ovarian reserve (DOR) in women with unexplained infertility. Involves measuring serum FSH concentration on day 3 of the menstrual cycle, giving clomiphene citrate on days 5-9, and retesting serum FSH concentration on day 10. Increased serum FSH concentrations after clomiphene citrate administration suggest DOR.

umaphO.title: Hysterosalpingography
umaphO.description: A radiologic procedure in which contrast dye is injected into the cervical canal and serial x-rays are obtained in order to evaluate the uterine cavity and morphology/patency of the fallopian tubes.

Ema8hO.title: Postcoital test
Ema8hO.description: Examination of the cervical mucus 8–12 hours after sexual intercourse to evaluate the quality of cervical mucus and the ability of sperm to survive in it. The postcoital test is performed during the pre-ovulatory period (day 12–13 of the menstrual cycle) for the evaluation of infertility. The presence of at least 10 progressively motile sperms per high power field indicates a normal result. Due to its poor predictive value, this test is no longer recommended.

9maN3O.title: Assisted reproductive technology
9maN3O.description: Infertility treatments involving the in vitro handling of human embryos, or of oocytes together with sperm. Includes in vitro fertilization, intracytoplasmic sperm injection, and gamete donation.

xmaE3O.title: In vitro fertilization
xmaE3O.description: A form of assisted reproductive technology in which ovulation induction is used to stimulate multiple oocytes, and fertilization occurs extracorporeally. One or more embryos are then transferred into the uterus.

zmarRO.title: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
zmarRO.description: A serious complication of ovulation induction or ovarian stimulation characterized by ovarian enlargement, ascites, and hypovolemia. Caused by extravasation of fluid into the interstitial space due to increased capillary permeability. Most commonly occurs following hCG administration.

media.title: Transvaginal ultrasonography in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (1/2)
Transvaginal ultrasonography in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (2/2)

b5aHiO.title: Mast cell stabilizers
b5aHiO.description: A group of drugs that inhibits mast cell degranulation and thus prevents the release of inflammatory mediators (e.g., histamine, leukotrienes). Previously used to treat asthma by preventing bronchospasm. Associated with minimal adverse effects, but low treatment efficacy.

c5aaQO.title: Enterocele
c5aaQO.description: Herniation of a peritoneum-lined sac, containing a portion of the small bowel, into the rectovaginal space. Commonly seen in postmenopausal women, esp. in those who are multiparous or who have undergone a pelvic surgery (e.g., hysterectomy). Small enteroceles are usually asymptomatic. Large enteroceles can cause pelvic pain, difficulty defecating, or a feeling of incomplete stool evacuation.

15a2QO.title: Rectocele
15a2QO.description: A herniation (bulging) of the anterior wall of the rectum into the posterior wall of the vagina. Patients may be asymptomatic or can present with difficult bowel movements, a sensation of fullness in the vagina, and/or pain during sex. Diagnosis is typically made with vaginal examination (i.e., speculum and bimanual examination) and with digital rectal examination as the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver.

d5aoQO.title: Cystocele
d5aoQO.description: A pelvic organ prolapse characterized by protrusion of the bladder behind the anterior vaginal wall and into the vaginal introitus. Typically causes urinary hesitancy and a sensation of vaginal fullness.

V5aGQO.title: Cyclosporine A
V5aGQO.description: A calcineurin inhibitor used as an immunosuppressant for patients who receive organ transplantation. Also used in the treatment of immune-mediated conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis.

U5abjO.title: Tacrolimus
U5abjO.description: An immunosuppressive agent that acts by inhibiting calcineurin and thus decreasing activation of T cells. Indications for systemic administration include prevention of organ rejection after allogeneic transplantation and ulcerative colitis. Indications for topical administration include immune-mediated disorders, such as atopic dermatitis and cutaneous graft versus host disease.

f5akjO.title: Rapamycin
f5akjO.description: An mTOR inhibitor used as part of immunosuppression therapy for rejection prophylaxis after organ transplantation. Also used in some drug-eluting stents to reduce the rate of restenosis.

T5a6jO.title: Mycophenolate mofetil
T5a6jO.description: A drug that exerts a cytostatic effect on both B and T cells by inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme that is responsible for guanosine synthesis. Most commonly used to prevent graft rejection in renal transplant recipients.

g5aFjO.title: Azathioprine
g5aFjO.description: A prodrug to 6-mercaptopurine, an antimetabolite (purine analog) that impairs cell replication. It is mainly used as an immunosuppressant for autoimmune diseases, renal transplantation, and inflammatory bowel disease.

h5acPO.title: Methotrexate
h5acPO.description: A drug that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and AICAR transformylase. Primarily used as an antineoplastic agent, immunosuppressant agent, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drug. Common adverse effects include myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, nephrotoxicity, and mucositis.

35aSPO.title: Biopharmaceuticals
35aSPO.description: A group of recombinant proteins (often antibodies) that are engineered to interfere with specific immunological processes. Most commonly used in the treatment of autoimmune diseases and malignancies. Examples include infliximab and rituximab.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

i5aJPO.title: Infliximab
i5aJPO.description: An anti-human tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) monoclonal antibody. TNF-α activation normally results in pro-inflammatory cytokine production (IL-1, IL-6). Infliximab acts as an immunosuppressant by preventing TNF-α and leukocyte activation. It is used in refractory chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, and psoriatic arthritis.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

Q5auPO.title: Adalimumab
Q5auPO.description: An anti-TNF-alpha inhibitor indicated for refractory-therapy of chronic inflammatory systemic diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis (considered a biologic DMARD).

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

j5a_PO.title: Etanercept
j5a_PO.description: A fusion protein that binds to and inhibits tumor necrosis factor. Used in treatment-refractory chronic inflammatory systemic diseases, e.g., rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

P5aW4O.title: Rituximab
P5aW4O.description: A monoclonal antibody against the CD20 antigen, which is found on the surface of B cells. Activates complement-dependent B-cell cytotoxicity. Also binds to Fc receptors and activates antibody-dependent cellular toxicity. Used to treat non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and many autoimmune diseases (e.g., bullous pemphigoid, rheumatoid arthritis).

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

45a34O.title: Alemtuzumab
45a34O.description: A humanized monoclonal antibody against CD52, an antigen present on mature lymphocytes. Used in the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and relapsed forms of multiple sclerosis.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

k5am4O.title: Natalizumab
k5am4O.description: An antibody against α4-integrin that decreases lymphocyte invasion of the CNS. May be used in the long-term management of relapsing-remitting MS and secondary progressive MS

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

O5aI4O.title: Omalizumab
O5aI4O.description: A monoclonal antibody that binds to free IgE. Used to treat refractory allergic asthma.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

N5a-4O.title: Basiliximab
N5a-4O.description: A monoclonal antibody that blocks the IL-2 receptor. Used as part of an immunosuppressive regimen, particularly for patients who have undergone kidney transplantation. Adverse effects include edema, hypertension, and tremor.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

m5aVkO.title: Daclizumab
m5aVkO.description: Daclizumab is a biologic recombinant protein that intervenes in immunological processes. It was formerly used for the prevention of kidney transplant rejection but is used solely for relapsing multiple sclerosis today.

destinations.label: Immunosuppressants → Biological agents used in immunotherapy

55aikO.title: Gingival hyperplasia
55aikO.description: Increased size of the gingiva. Often caused by a drug reaction to phenytoin, calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine, verapamil), or cyclosporine. Spontaneous regression usually occurs after cessation of the agent. Other causes include gingival inflammation, leukemia, and hereditary gingival fibromatosis.

K5aUOO.title: Relaxation atelectasis
K5aUOO.description: A form of nonobstructive atelectasis caused by loss of negative pressure between the parietal and visceral pleura. Causes include pneumothorax and pleural effusion.

65ajOO.title: Compression atelectasis
65ajOO.description: A form of nonobstructive atelectasis caused by a space-occupying lesion that compresses the lung. Causes can be extrapulmonary (e.g., pleural tumor, chest wall mass lesion, hepatosplenomegaly, massive ascites, large intra-abdominal tumors, or surgical manipiulation) or intrapulmonary (e.g., lung cancer).

p5aLOO.title: Cicatrization atelectasis
p5aLOO.description: A form of nonobstructive atelectasis caused by parenchymal scarring due to chronic destructive lung conditions. Causes include tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and fibrosis secondary to radiation therapy.

J5asOO.title: Obstructive atelectasis
J5asOO.description: A subtype of atelectasis caused by airway obstruction (e.g., by a foreign body, mucus plug, malignancy).

r5aflO.title: Clasp knife phenomenon
r5aflO.description: An initial resistance to passive movement due to increased muscle tone, which is then followed by a sudden decrease in resistance.

75a4lO.title: Baclofen
75a4lO.description: A GABA receptor agonist with central nervous system depressant activity. Commonly used as a muscle relaxant to treat spasticity.

G5aBlO.title: Bisacodyl
G5aBlO.description: A stimulant laxative used to treat constipation.

u5apNO.title: Psyllium
u5apNO.description: A bulk-forming laxative used in the treatment of constipation. Also used to regulate bowel movements in, e.g., anal fissure or chronic diarrhea.

v5aANO.title: Lactulose
v5aANO.description: A nonabsorbable disaccharide sugar used to treat constipation and hepatic encephalopathy. As it passes through the lumen of the GI tract, it pulls in water that softens stool and is broken down by bacteria into acidic compounds, which trap ammonia and prevent it from entering the bloodstream.

w5ahmO.title: Laxatives
w5ahmO.description: A group of substances that enhance intestinal evacuation and defecation via different mechanisms. Types include stimulant, hyperosmotic, bulk-forming, and stool-softening laxatives. Uses include treatment of constipation and bowel cleansing before diagnostic procedures.

B5azmO.title: Magnesium sulfate
B5azmO.description: A substance that is used intravenously to prevent convulsions in patients with pre-eclampsia or acute nephritis, to provide neuroprotection for premature infants (given to mother before birth), as a tocolytic agent, to treat torsades de pointes syndrome, and to correct hypomagnesemia. Magnesium sulfate is also used as a component of hygroscopic dressings, and orally as a laxative.

-5aD5O.title: Polyethylene glycol
-5aD5O.description: A well-tolerated osmotic laxative used in the treatment of constipation. Commonly used to prepare the bowel before intestinal surgery or colonoscopy. Can be misused for rapid weight loss by patients with eating disorders.

ZMaZMO.title: Castor oil
ZMaZMO.description: A stimulant laxative derived from vegetable oil. Used to treat constipation and to cleanse the bowel before an examination and/or surgery.

3MaSoO.title: Duplex ultrasonography
3MaSoO.description: A noninvasive imaging modality that combines ultrasound imaging of vessels with Doppler assessment of blood flow. An arterial duplex scan can be used to identify the site and severity of arterial occlusion in peripheral arterial disease as well as to diagnose aneurysms. Venous duplex scan is the test of choice to identify the patency of deep veins (e.g., in suspected DVT) and to identify venous reflux and the site of incompetent valves in chronic venous insufficiency.

media.title: Cavernous transformation of the portal vein

QMauoO.title: Color duplex ultrasonography
QMauoO.description: An ultrasound technique that utilizes the Doppler effect to visualize blood flow, typically within blood vessels. By convention, flow toward the transducer appears as a red signal and flow away from the transducer as a blue signal. The color brightness reflects the flow rates (i.e., the brighter the color, the faster the flow rate).

NMa-KO.title: Endoscopic ultrasound
NMa-KO.description: An invasive imaging technique that combines ultrasonography and endoscopy. The endoscope aids visualization of the gastrointestinal mucosa as well as any intraluminal mass. Ultrasonography is used to assess the depth of invasion of gastrointestinal tumors and delineates extraluminal structures (e.g., pancreas, lymph nodes) that are not easily seen on other imaging modalities.

mMaV6O.title: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound
mMaV6O.description: An ultrasound technique in which gas microbubbles are used as a contrast agent. May be used in the assessment of focal liver lesions and for echocardiography, with the contrast agent administered intravenously to visualize vasculature and blood flow.

wMahIO.title: ALARA principle
wMahIO.description: The avoidance of unnecessary radiation or acoustic exposure by minimizing exposure time and/or power to "As Low As Reasonably Achievable" and maximizing distance and shielding between the individual and the radiation source.

_Ma5rO.title: Positron emission tomography scan
_Ma5rO.description: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses a radiotracer to provide information about blood flow and/or metabolic processes in the body. The most common radiotracer used is fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG).

-MaDrO.title: Lassa fever
-MaDrO.description: A viral hemorrhagic fever caused by Lassa virus. Most cases are mild and cause fever, malaise, and headache. Can cause pharyngitis, cough, retrosternal chest pain, and severe bleeding. Deafness is a common complication.

0nae7O.title: Ebola virus disease
0nae7O.description: A severe infection caused by Ebola virus. Typically manifests with sudden onset flu-like symptoms (e.g., fever, headache, myalgia), vomiting, and diarrhea. Progressive disease often results in hemorrhage, shock, and multiorgan failure.

anaQ7O.title: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever
anaQ7O.description: A zoonotic disease caused by the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Manifestations include sudden-onset fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, sore throat, conjunctivitis, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Can cause hemorrhage.

Ynan7O.title: Rift valley fever
Ynan7O.description: A vector-borne infection caused by the Rift Valley fever virus. It causes fever, malaise, headache, muscle pains, and abnormal liver enzymes. It can occasionally progress to hemorrhagic fever and/or meningoencephalitis.

destinations.label: Miscellaneous mosquito-borne diseases → Mosquito-borne Bunyavirus diseases

cnaaHO.title: Chikungunya fever
cnaaHO.description: A mosquito-borne tropical disease that causes fever and polyarthralgia. Onset of symptoms occurs within 2 weeks of infection. Treatment is supportive and patients usually make a full recovery.

destinations.label: Miscellaneous mosquito-borne diseases → Mosquito-borne Togavirus diseases

WnaPHO.title: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
WnaPHO.description: An illness caused by hantavirus infection. Classically manifests with fever, hemorrhage, hypotension, and acute kidney injury (AKI) with proteinuria and hematuria. Mediated by increased vascular permeability and damage to the vascular endothelium and kidneys due to cytokine release.

enaxHO.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome
enaxHO.description: A severe form of hantavirus infection that initially manifests with fatigue, fever, and myalgias that is later followed by coughing, shortness of breath, and dyspnea.

fnaksO.title: Primary headaches
fnaksO.description: A headache that is not the result of another medical condition. Examples include migraines, tension-type headaches, and cluster headaches.

media.title: Differential diagnoses of primary headaches fact sheet

RnalGO.title: Lymphogranuloma venereum
RnalGO.description: A sexually transmitted disease caused by L1–3 serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis. Patients initially develop a small, painless papule in the genital region that may ulcerate but will heal and disappear within one week. 2–4 weeks after the initial lesion, patients present with painful, suppurative, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, chills, and/or myalgia.

inaJGO.title: Chlamydia psittaci
inaJGO.description: An obligate intracellular bacterium that causes psittacosis. Birds are the primary reservoir. Infection spreads via inhalation of organisms from dried bird feces.

QnauGO.title: Psittacosis
QnauGO.description: A zoonotic disease caused by Chlamydophila psittaci that typically manifests with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, headache, sweats, myalgias) and respiratory symptoms (e.g., cough, dyspnea).

4na3tO.title: Chlamydia trachomatis
4na3tO.description: A pleomorphic, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium. There are various serotypes: Serotypes A–C mainly affect the eyes and cause trachoma; infection with serotypes D–K can result in genitourinary infections (e.g., vaginitis, PID, urethritis), conjunctivitis, and infant pneumonia; serotypes L1–L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum.

lnavtO.title: Aflatoxin
lnavtO.description: A toxin and carcinogen that is produced by Aspergillus flavus. Aspergillus flavus can grow on improperly stored food such as nuts, pistachios, rice, and corn. Acute ingestion can result in acute liver failure. Chronic ingestion increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Nna-tO.title: Histamine fish poisoning
Nna-tO.description: A foodborne illness caused by ingestion of histidine-rich fish that has spoiled or been inadequately refrigerated. Histidine is converted to histamine by bacteria at warm temperatures. Typically manifests with flushing, urticaria, nausea, edema, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps within minutes to hours after ingestion.

MnaMFO.title: Staphylococcal food poisoning
MnaMFO.description: A condition caused by ingestion of food contaminated with heat-stable Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxins (most commonly inadequately refrigerated foods). Typically manifests with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea after an incubation period of 1-8 hours. Symptoms usually resolve after 24-48 hours.

nna7FO.title: Botulism
nna7FO.description: An acute paralytic disorder caused by botulinum neurotoxin, a neurotoxic protein produced by Clostridium botulinum. Typically manifests with cranial nerve palsies, neuromuscular weakness or paralysis, and autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

LnawFO.title: Foodborne botulism
LnawFO.description: A condition caused by the ingestion of botulism neurotoxins (e.g., from improperly canned foods). Classically manifests with descending flaccid paralysis 12-36 hours after ingestion.

KnaU8O.title: Botulinum neurotoxin
KnaU8O.description: A neurotoxic protein produced by Clostridium botulinum that causes botulism. Blocks the release of acetylcholine from the neuromuscular junction by cleaving SNARE proteins involved in vesicle fusion, which leads to flaccid muscle paralysis. May be used therapeutically to treat muscle spasms, focal dystonia, and facial wrinkles.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

pnaL8O.title: Gingivostomatitis
pnaL8O.description: An inflammation of the gums and mouth that is caused by certain viruses (e.g., herpes simplex virus 1, coxsackievirus), certain bacteria, or poor oral hygiene. Possible symptoms include the abrupt onset of high fever, gingivitis, vesicular lesions (of the oral mucosa, tongue, and lips), tender lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms.

destinations.label: Herpes simplex virus infections → Oral herpes

Jnas8O.title: Aphthous stomatitis
Jnas8O.description: A condition of benign, noncontagious, painful ulcers of the oral mucosa. Typically occur sporadically but can be triggered by viral infections and local trauma. Recurrent aphthous ulcers may be a sign of an underlying condition (e.g., Behçet disease, Crohn disease, celiac disease, vitamin B12 deficiency).

media.title: Aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa

InaYuO.title: Eczema herpeticum
InaYuO.description: An acute skin infection that is most commonly caused by HSV-1 and HSV-2 and primarily occurs in patients with pre-existing skin conditions (classically atopic dermatitis). Patients present with fever, malaise, and disseminated, painful, vesicular lesions. Complications include bacterial superinfection and systemic viral dissemination.

destinations.label: Herpes simplex virus infections → Cutaneous herpes

rnafuO.title: Alpha herpes viruses
rnafuO.description: A subfamily of viruses in the Herpesviridae family. They have a fast replication cycle, a broad host range, and persist in ganglion cells. Includes herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2 and varicella zoster virus.

7na4uO.title: Beta herpes viruses
7na4uO.description: A subfamily of viruses in the Herpesviridae family. They have a slow replication cycle, a limited host range, and persist in granulocytes and lymphocytes. Includes cytomegalovirus and human herpesviruses 6 and 7.

HnaKuO.title: Gamma herpes viruses
HnaKuO.description: A subfamily of viruses in the Herpesviridae family. They have oncogenic potential, a very restricted host range, and persist in B lymphocytes. Includes Epstein-Barr virus and Kaposi sarcoma-associated virus (HHV-8).

tnaXEO.title: Herpes simplex virus 1
tnaXEO.description: An extremely common, highly contagious member of the herpesvirus family that primarily causes labial herpes, herpetic whitlow, herpetic gingivostomatitis, and, less commonly, genital herpes.

unapEO.title: Herpes simplex virus 2
unapEO.description: A common, highly contagious member of the herpesvirus family that primarily causes genital herpes and rarely labial herpes and herpetic whitlow.

Dna1vO.title: Varicella zoster virus
Dna1vO.description: A DNA virus that belongs to the family of human herpesviruses. Transmitted via respiratory secretions. The primary infection manifests as chickenpox (varicella); reactivation leads to shingles (zoster).

CnaqvO.title: Epstein-Barr virus
CnaqvO.description: A double-stranded, enveloped DNA virus that causes mononucleosis. Most adults are carriers of the virus. Infection is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, primary central nervous system lymphoma, gastric cancer, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

ynadDO.title: Cytomegalovirus
ynadDO.description: A double-stranded DNA virus that is spread by secretions (saliva, urine, blood, etc.). Infection with CMV is usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts (sometimes causing heterophile-negative mononucleosis) but may cause severe disease in immunocompromised patients (e.g., those with AIDS) and severe congenital malformations (TORCH pathogen). Cells with a characteristic owl-eye appearance are visible on biopsy.

-naDDO.title: HHV-6
-naDDO.description: A virus in the Herpesviridae family that causes roseola (exanthema subitum). Roseola is thought to be acquired as a droplet infection.

ZLaZwO.title: HHV-7
ZLaZwO.description: A virus in the Herpesviridae family transmitted in saliva. A less common cause of roseola (exanthema subitum) compared to HHV-6.

aLaQwO.title: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated virus
aLaQwO.description: A double-stranded DNA herpesvirus primarily associated with primary effusion lymphoma and Kaposi sarcoma in patients who are HIV-positive. Transmitted orally or sexually.

media.title: Intraoral Kaposi sarcoma of the palate

XLa9wO.title: Herpes labialis
XLa9wO.description: A reactivation of HSV-1 (or less commonly HSV-2) virus after a period of dormancy within the ganglia of the trigeminal nerve. Characterized by a prodrome of paresthesia, burning/stabbing pain in the dermatomal distribution of the mandibular/maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, followed by numerous vesicles that have a tendency to ulcerate.

destinations.label: Herpes simplex virus infections → Oral herpes

1La29O.title: Tinea capitis
1La29O.description: A dermatophyte infection of the scalp that mainly affects children. Appears as round, pruritic, scaly plaques with alopecia in affected areas. Lymphadenopathy may also be present. Treated with systemic antifungals (e.g., griseofulvin, terbinafine).

eLax9O.title: Tinea corporis
eLax9O.description: A dermatophyte infection that affects a body area other than the feet, scalp, nails, or groin. Manifests with erythematous, round, pruritic plaques with central clearing and raised borders (ringworm appearance).

ULabCO.title: Tinea pedis
ULabCO.description: A dermatophyte infection that involves the sole of the foot and/or interdigital spaces of the toes. Predisposing factors include closed, tight footwear and the use of public showers.

fLakCO.title: Onychomycosis
fLakCO.description: A fungal infection of the nail that results in nail thickening, discoloration, and separation from the nail bed. Most commonly caused by dermatophytes (tinea unguium). Yeasts (e.g., Candida albicans) and nondermatophyte molds (e.g., Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp.) can also cause onychomycosis.

media.title: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) of both big toe nails

hLacxO.title: Toxocariasis
hLacxO.description: A zoonosis that is caused by the nematodes Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati. Typically acquired by ingesting Toxocara eggs, which are shed in the feces of infected cats and dogs. Can manifest with acute or chronic endophthalmitis (ocular toxocariasis) and/or visceral larva migrans (visceral toxocariasis).

QLauxO.title: Enterobiasis
