QLauxO.description: A helminthic infection with Enterobius vermicularis that primarily affects children 5–10 years of age. Transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Clinical features include intense anal pruritus (especially at night when the female pinworms deposit eggs on the perianal skin), vulvovaginitis, and, occasionally, symptoms of intestinal infection (e.g., nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain).

jLa_xO.title: Ascariasis
jLa_xO.description: An infection caused by Ascaris lumbricoides nematodes. Most common helminth infection worldwide; typically affects children in tropical and developing countries. Has a fecal-oral mode of transmission. Symptoms of early infection include dry cough, blood-tinged sputum, and wheezing (Löffler syndrome). Late symptoms include anorexia, abdominal discomfort or blockage, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

PLaWBO.title: Trichinellosis
PLaWBO.description: An infection caused by Trichinella species (typically T. spiralis). Transmitted via ingestion of encysted larvae in undercooked meat (especially pork). Infection can be subclinical or manifest with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. In severe infections, larvae disseminate into the skeletal muscle and cause fever, pain, weakness, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.

OLaIBO.title: Hookworm infection
OLaIBO.description: The most common parasitic infection globally. Typically causes iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss from parasite consumption of blood from the gastrointestinal tract. Transmitted via cutaneous penetration (e.g., from walking barefoot).

mLaVyO.title: Diphyllobothrium latum infection
mLaVyO.description: An infection caused by Dibothriocephalus species, most commonly Dibothriocephalus latus. Transmitted via consumption of raw or undercooked fish. Patients are typically asymptomatic, but chronic infection can cause megaloblastic anemia because the parasite competes with the host for vitamin B12.

LLawyO.title: Cysticercosis
LLawyO.description: A parasitic infection typically acquired by ingesting T. solium eggs in undercooked pork. Symptoms result from the presence of larvae (cysticerci) in various organs such as the muscles, brain, and skin.

KLaUAO.title: Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli
KLaUAO.description: A subset of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC). Transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Infection with EHEC (particularly serotype O157:H7) can cause bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome, most commonly in children.

destinations.label: Diarrheagenic E. coli → Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC)

7La4_O.title: EIEC
7La4_O.description: A gram-negative rod that can cause traveler's diarrhea and typically presents with watery or bloody stools.

destinations.label: Diarrheagenic E. coli → Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC)

GLaB_O.title: Traveler's diarrhea
GLaB_O.description: An infectious diarrhea caused by a variety of bacterial, viral, and parasitic organisms. Typically acquired during travel to resource-limited regions, most commonly through ingestion of contaminated food or water. Causative pathogens include enterotoxigenic E. coli (most common), enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Entamoeba histolytica, Norovirus, and Rotavirus.

FLagzO.title: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
FLagzO.description: A gram-negative rod that produces heat-labile as well as heat-stable enterotoxins. The bacteria is common in Asia, Africa, and Latin America and the most frequent cause of traveler's diarrhea. Symptoms last 3–4 days and patients usually only require supportive treatment.

destinations.label: Diarrheagenic E. coli → Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)

8LaOzO.title: α-amanitin
8LaOzO.description: A toxin produced by Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom) that inhibits RNA polymerase II, which prevents RNA translocation.

uLapzO.title: Amanita phalloides
uLapzO.description: A mushroom species produces a potent toxin, α-amanitin, that inhibits RNA polymerase II. Ingestion of the mushrooms produces GI symptoms followed by acute hepatic failure that can be fatal.

ELa8zO.title: Phalloidin
ELa8zO.description: A toxin produced by Amanita phalloides that stabilizes actin filaments and prevents their depolymerization.

DLa1-O.title: Silibinin
DLa1-O.description: An antidote for acute Amanita phalloides poisoning that is derived from milk thistle. Widely used in Europe and South America but not currently FDA-approved for use in the US.

BLaz-O.title: Atropa belladonna
BLaz-O.description: A plant with toxic berries and leaves that contain antimuscarinic compounds such as atropine. Ingestion causes anticholinergic syndrome.

yLadZl.title: Organophosphate
yLadZl.description: A chemical compound that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase and causes activation of the parasympathetic nervous system. The active ingredient in many pesticides and nerve agents. Clinical features of organophosphate poisoning include increased salivation, diarrhea, bronchospasm, lacrimation, tremor, and paralysis.

zLarZl.title: Cyanide
zLarZl.description: A compound that blocks the electron transport chain and thus decreases oxidative phosphorylation. Features of toxicity include breath that smells like bitter almonds, altered mental status (e.g., confusion, agitation, coma), and elevated anion gap metabolic lactic acidosis.

2oaTYl.title: Hospital-acquired pneumonia
2oaTYl.description: An episode of pneumonia that develops > 48 hours after a patient is admitted to a hospital without evidence of disease at the time of admission.

Toa6Yl.title: Nosocomial urinary tract infection
Toa6Yl.description: A urinary tract infection acquired within a health care institution or as a complication of patient management (e.g., from indwelling catheter use).

goaFYl.title: Surgical site infection
goaFYl.description: A hospital-acquired infection that arises at the site of surgical intervention within 30 days of a surgical procedure or within 90 days in the case of breast surgery, herniorrhaphy, cardiac surgery, vascular bypass surgery, craniotomy, ventricular shunt surgery, joint replacement surgery, or open fracture reduction.

hoacbl.title: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci
hoacbl.description: Bacterial strains of the genus Enterococcus that are resistant to the antibiotic vancomycin (e.g., E. faecalis, E. faecium).

destinations.label: Multidrug-resistant organism infections → Common gram-positive bacteria

3oaSbl.title: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
3oaSbl.description: An isolate of Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to certain beta-lactam antibiotics as a result of a penicillin-binding protein (PBP).

destinations.label: Multidrug-resistant organism infections → Common gram-positive bacteria

ioaJbl.title: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing bacteria
ioaJbl.description: A group of bacteria that produce β-lactamases, thus inactivating penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenem resistance may be seen in rare cases of additional genes or genetic mutations. Common pathogens include gram-negative bacteria (e.g., Klebsiella and Escherichia coli).

destinations.label: Multidrug-resistant organism infections → Common gram-negative bacteria

joa_bl.title: Multi-drug resistant gram-negative bacteria
joa_bl.description: A gram-negative bacterial isolate that demonstrates resistance to at least three of the four main antibiotic classes, which consist of broadband penicillins, cephalosporins (groups 3 and 4), carbapenems, and fluoroquinolones.

PoaWXl.title: Multi-drug resistant organism
PoaWXl.description: An organism that is resistant to one or more agent in three or more antimicrobial categories (e.g., vancomycin-resistant enterococci, extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing organisms).

koamXl.title: Large vessel vasculitis
koamXl.description: A systemic vasculitis that predominantly affects large vessels (i.e., the aorta, its main branches, and any vessel that is not located within an organ). Examples of large vessel vasculitis include giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, and aortitis associated with certain rheumatic disorders. Clinical features suggestive of large vessel involvement include limb claudication, asymmetric blood pressure readings, and absence of peripheral pulses, and/or bruits.

OoaIXl.title: Takayasu arteritis
OoaIXl.description: A large vessel vasculitis that mainly involves the aorta and its major branches. Predominantly affects women < 50 years of age. Manifests with fever, malaise, and weight loss. Typical clinical features include absent or decreased peripheral pulses, bruits, and limb claudication.

Noa-Xl.title: Polyarteritis nodosa
Noa-Xl.description: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis that predominantly affects medium-sized vessels (i.e., the main visceral arteries and their branches) resulting in tissue ischemia, The arterioles, venules, and capillaries are usually spared. Most commonly involves the skin, peripheral nervous system, muscles, joints, GI tract, and kidneys.

MoaMcl.title: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
MoaMcl.description: A necrotizing, granulomatous small vessel vasculitis that commonly manifests with pulmonary (e.g., asthma, allergic rhinitis) and skin (e.g., purpura or tender nodules) involvement. Can affect the intestines (e.g., bleeding, ischemia, perforation), heart (e.g., pericarditis), and/or kidneys (e.g., focal segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis). Associated with peripheral eosinophilia, increased IgE levels, p-ANCA positivity.

noa7cl.title: Microscopic polyangiitis
noa7cl.description: A necrotizing small vessel vasculitis that typically presents with renal (e.g, hypertension, glomerulonephritis), pulmonary (e.g., alveolar hemorrhage), and skin (e.g., palpable purpura) involvement. Similar to granulomatosis with polyangiitis but without granulomas and the nasopharynx is not involved.

Loawcl.title: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Loawcl.description: A small- or, less frequently, medium-vessel vasculitis that can occur in patients with cryoglobulinemia. Damage is caused by cryoglobulin precipitation in the microcirculation and immune complex-mediated inflammation. Typically manifests with cutaneous lesions (e.g., purpura, livedo reticularis), arthralgia, myalgia, and renal involvement.

ooa01l.title: Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis
ooa01l.description: A small-vessel vasculitis that is limited to the skin. Often idiopathic, but may be caused by infections (e.g., HIV, HCV), other vasculitides (e.g., eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis), and certain drugs (e.g., propylthiouracil, hydralazine, allopurinol). Manifests as tender, symmetrically distributed palpable purpura, mainly on the lower extremities. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a characteristic histopathology finding.

KoaU1l.title: Behcet disease
KoaU1l.description: An immune-mediated vasculitis that can involve blood vessels of all sizes (i.e., small, medium, and large) and may affect both the arterial and venous vessels. It commonly presents as oral and genital ulceration and uveitis.

media.title: Aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa

qoaC1l.title: Reactive thrombocytosis
qoaC1l.description: A transient elevation in platelet count caused by an underlying condition (e.g., systemic infection, inflammation, malignancy, splenectomy).

7oa4Wl.title: Hypereosinophilic syndrome
7oa4Wl.description: A group of rare conditions characterized by persistent elevations in absolute eosinophil count ≥ 1500/mm3 in peripheral circulation with eosinophil tissue infiltration and resultant end-organ damage (most commonly to the skin, lungs, heart, gastrointestinal tract, and/or nervous system).

soatWl.title: Myelofibrosis
soatWl.description: Myeloproliferative neoplasm leading to bone marrow insufficiency, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and splenomegaly. Primary myelofibrosis occurs spontaneously, while secondary myelofibrosis occurs as a result of disease progression in patients previously diagnosed with another myeloproliferative neoplasm (e.g., polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia).

GoaBWl.title: Hypersplenism
GoaBWl.description: A condition characterized by one or more cytopenia (e.g., anemia, thrombocytopenia) caused by the pooling, sequestration, and premature destruction of blood cells in an enlarged spleen. May be seen in splenic enlargement resulting from any cause (e.g., portal hypertension, infection, autoimmune disease).

8oaOdl.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
8oaOdl.description: A rare, acquired blood disease caused by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells lacking CD55 and CD59. Commonly associated with bone marrow failure syndromes, e.g., aplastic anemia and MDS. In RBCs, absence of CD55 and CD59 increases susceptibility to destruction by complement and subsequent hemolysis. Can manifest with Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria, jaundice, pancytopenia, and/or thromboembolism.

Eoa8dl.title: Hemoglobinopathies
Eoa8dl.description: A group of disorders characterized by hemoglobin that has an abnormal structure. Examples include sickle cell disease, thalassemias, and hemoglobin C disease.

woahVl.title: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
woahVl.description: An intravascular and extravascular hemolytic anemia typically caused by IgM or IgG antibodies. Associated with Mycoplasma infection, Epstein-Barr virus infection, autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus), and malignancies (e.g., non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).

AoaRel.title: Warm agglutinin hemolytic anemia
AoaRel.description: An autoimmune hemolytic anemia caused by circulating IgG antibodies against red blood cells that are active at  ≥ 37°C.

destinations.label: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Warm agglutinin hemolytic anemia

_oa5el.title: Laboratory findings of hemolysis
_oa5el.description: A collection of serum and urine laboratory findings that can include ↑ reticulocyte count, ↑ indirect bilirubin concentration, ↑ LDH concentration, ↓ haptoglobin, hemoglobinuria, ↑ urobilinogen, and schistocytes on peripheral blood smear.

zoarel.title: Haptoglobin
zoarel.description: A plasma glycoprotein that binds to free hemoglobin, resulting in its clearance. Hemolysis (especially intravascular hemolysis) results in decreased concentrations of free, circulating haptoglobin.

-oaDel.title: Coombs test
-oaDel.description: An agglutination test that is used either to detect hemolytic antibodies and/or complement proteins that are already bound to erythrocytes (direct Coombs test) or unbound anti-erythrocyte antibodies in serum (indirect Coombs test).

ZKaZUl.title: Hormone
ZKaZUl.description: A diverse group of endogenous messengers that are produced in glands or by single cells. Hormones are responsible for signal transduction and influence the function and metabolic rate of other organs and cells. Examples include testosterone, estrogen, aldosterone, and antidiuretic hormone.

bKaHUl.title: Hypothalamus
bKaHUl.description: The region of the forebrain below the thalamus that secretes substances that influence pituitary and other gland function. Involved in the control of body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and other homeostatic processes.

media.title: Anatomical illustration of the thalamus and hypothalamus

1Ka22l.title: Pituitary gland
1Ka22l.description: An endocrine gland located in the sella turcica in the middle cranial fossa. Divided into the anterior pituitary gland (adenohypophyis) and the posterior pituitary gland (neurohypophysis). The anterior pituitary gland is responsible for the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), growth hormone (GH), melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) and prolactin. The posterior pituitary gland is responsible for the release of antiduiretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin.

destinations.label: General endocrinology → Hypothalamus and pituitary gland

media.title: Hormonal feedback control of the neurohypophysial hormones

WKaP2l.title: Anterior pituitary gland
WKaP2l.description: The ventral part of the pituitary gland that develops from oral ectoderm. Produces tropic hormones (ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH) and nontropic hormones (GH, MSH, prolactin).

destinations.label: General endocrinology → Hypothalamus and pituitary gland

VKaG2l.title: Posterior pituitary gland
VKaG2l.description: A collection of axonal projections from the hypothalamus that secrete oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

destinations.label: General endocrinology → Hypothalamus and pituitary gland

media.title: Functional anatomy of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis

fKakfl.title: Corticotropin-releasing hormone
fKakfl.description: A hypothalamic peptide hormone in the hypothalamo-hypophyseal-adrenal axis that primarily regulates glucocorticoid homeostasis. CRH stimulates secretion of ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) in the anterior pituitary, which stimulates secretion of glucocorticoids and androgens in the adrenal cortex.

hKacTl.title: Adrenocorticotropic hormone
hKacTl.description: A polypeptide hormone of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that is physiologically produced by the anterior pituitary gland. ACTH stimulates the secretion of glucocorticoids and androgens in the adrenal cortex.

media.title: Hormonal feedback control of the adrenal hormones

3KaSTl.title: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone
3KaSTl.description: Signaling substance produced by the hypothalamus that stimulates the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH;thyrotropin) from the anterior lobule of the pituitary gland.

jKa_Tl.title: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
jKa_Tl.description: A hormone synthesized in the pituitary gland that stimulates the release of T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine, tetraiodothyronine) in the thyroid gland.

PKaWgl.title: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone
PKaWgl.description: A peptide hormone synthesized and released from gonadotropic neurons in the hypothalamus. Pulsatile secretion stimulates the release of LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary.

NKa-gl.title: Follicle-stimulating hormone
NKa-gl.description: A polypeptide hormone that is synthesized and secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. Functions together with luteinizing hormone in the reproductive system. Stimulates the maturation of germ cells in both men and women.

mKaVSl.title: Growth hormone-releasing hormone
mKaVSl.description: A peptide hormone produced in the hypothalamus that acts on the anterior pituitary to stimulate secretion of growth hormone (GH). Release of GHRH and, therefore, GH are pulsatile.

oKa0hl.title: Growth hormone
oKa0hl.description: A peptide hormone secreted from the pituitary gland that stimulates the growth of linear bone, skeletal muscle, and organs. Also stimulates erythropoietin, which increases red blood cell mass. A recombinant form is used as a prescription drug to treat pediatric growth disorders and adult growth hormone deficiency.

pKaLhl.title: Somatostatin
pKaLhl.description: A peptide hormone produced in the hypothalamus and some parts of the digestive system such as pancreatic δ cells. Inhibits the release of growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Reduces secretion of gastrointestinal hormones, glucagon, and insulin.

destinations.label: Gastrointestinal tract → Secretory and regulatory products of the gastrointestinal tract

media.title: Hormonal feedback control of nontropic hormones

rKaf3l.title: Melanocyte-stimulating hormone
rKaf3l.description: A peptide hormone that stimulates the production and release of melanin by melanocytes in skin and hair. Also involved in appetite regulation. Produced from proopiomelanocortin in the anterior and intermediate lobe of the pituitary gland.

HKaK3l.title: Prolactin
HKaK3l.description: A non-tropic hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It primarily regulates the growth and differentiation of breast tissue during pregnancy and lactation. In excess, prolactin can cause galactorrhea, decreased libido, inhibition of ovulation and spermatogenesis, and amenorrhea.

tKaXRl.title: Vasopressin (hormone)
tKaXRl.description: A posterior pituitary hormone that regulates blood pressure, fluid balance, and sodium balance by causing the sensation of thirst, increased water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts, and peripheral arteriolar constriction. Arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) is released in response to ≥ 1% increase in serum osmolality (primary stimulus) or > 10% extracellular fluid volume contraction (secondary stimulus).

vKaARl.title: Oxytocin
vKaARl.description: A hypothalamic hormone released from the posterior pituitary. Stimulates uterine contractions and milk expression. Exogenous oxytocin can be used to induce labor, strengthen uterine contractions during labor, contract uterine muscle after delivery of the placenta, and control postpartum hemorrhage.

DKa1il.title: Adrenal cortex
DKa1il.description: The outer layer of adrenal gland. Contains the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis, which produce mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and androgens respectively.

media.title: Transition zone of the adrenal cortex to the adrenal medulla

wKahil.title: Aldosterone
wKahil.description: A steroid hormone that increases renal reabsorption of water and sodium, as well as the secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. A decrease in renal perfusion causes activation of the renin-angiotensin system, which in turn causes secretion of aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex.

media.title: Action of aldosterone on renal tubular epithelial cells

9KaNil.title: Angiotensin I
9KaNil.description: A peptide that is part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system. Cleaved from angiotensinogen. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) then converts angiotensin I to hormonally active angiotensin II.

CKaqil.title: Angiotensin II
CKaqil.description: A peptide hormone that helps maintain blood pressure and blood volume. Effects include aldosterone secretion, peripheral vasoconstriction, and constriction of the efferent arterioles of the kidneys. Generated from Angiotensin I by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lungs.

zKarQl.title: Dehydroepiandrosterone
zKarQl.description: An intermediate male sex steroid hormone produced in the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex. On reaching the target cell, it serves as a precursor to testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, or estrogen.

-KaDQl.title: Cortisol
-KaDQl.description: A steroid hormone that is produced in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. Most important effects include glucose formation (via stimulation of gluconeogenesis), immunosuppression, increased insulin resistance, blood pressure elevation, and inhibition of bone formation.

Y6anjl.title: Renin
Y6anjl.description: An enzyme that is secreted by renal juxtaglomerular cells in response to low renal blood pressure, beta-1 adrenergic receptor activation, and NaCl deficiency to secure a stable glomerular filtration rate. By hydrolyzing angiotensinogen to angiotensin 1, renin activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

b6aHjl.title: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
b6aHjl.description: A hormonal system that regulates arterial blood pressure and sodium concentration through secretion of renin in response to renal hypoperfusion. Increased renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II both acts as a vasocontrictor and increases secretion of aldosterone, which increases renal reabsorption of sodium and water.

destinations.label: Physiology of the kidney → Renal blood flow

c6aaPl.title: Thyroid gland
c6aaPl.description: An endocrine gland located inferior to the larynx and anterior to the trachea. Secretes thyroid hormones, which regulate body metabolism and growth, and calcitonin, which lowers serum calcium and phosphate through inhibition of osteoclasts.

destinations.label: Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands → Thyroid gland

media.title: Surface anatomy of the thyroid gland

16a2Pl.title: Thyroid hormones
16a2Pl.description: The two hormones (T3 and T4) secreted by the thyroid gland. T3 is a biologically active thyroid hormone that binds nuclear receptors with significantly higher affinity than T4. Helps regulate energy metabolism, neuronal and skeletal development, and catecholamine sensitivity.

destinations.label: Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands →  Function

d6aoPl.title: Thyroxine
d6aoPl.description: A tyrosine-based inactive thyroid prohormone that contains iodine. After secretion it primarily circulates in blood, where it is converted to active triiodothyronine (T₃), which has a diverse range of functions that help regulate energy metabolism, neuronal and skeletal development, and catecholamine sensitivity.

destinations.label: Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands →  Function

V6aGPl.title: Triiodothyronine
V6aGPl.description: A tyrosine-based thyroid hormone that contains iodine. Secreted by the thyroid gland along with thyroxine (T₄), but most of it is converted from the inactive thyroid prohormone (T₄) by a deiodinase enzyme in the blood. Helps regulate energy metabolism, neuronal and skeletal development, and catecholamine sensitivity.

destinations.label: Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands →  Function

U6ab4l.title: Testosterone
U6ab4l.description: A steroid hormone that is mainly produced by Leydig cells of the testes. Essential for the male reproductive system and the development of secondary sexual characteristics.

26aT4l.title: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
26aT4l.description: A collection of endocrine neoplasias caused by an alteration in menin protein expression. Characterized by primary hyperparathyroidism, often in association with endocrine pancreatic tumors and/or pituitary adenomas.

f6ak4l.title: MEN 2
f6ak4l.description: A syndrome caused by mutations of the RET proto-oncogene. Has two subtypes: MEN 2A and MEN 2B.

T6a64l.title: MEN 2A
T6a64l.description: A syndrome caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. Manifestations include medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism.

g6aF4l.title: Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B
g6aF4l.description: An autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, multiple mucosal neuromas, and intestinal ganglioneuromas. Caused a single amino acid substitution in the proto-oncogene RET. Often associated with a marfanoid habitus and other skeletal abnormalities. Symptoms and signs reflect the glandular abnormalities present.

R6alkl.title: Urinalysis
R6alkl.description: A set of tests performed on a sample of urine to screen for disorders of the urinary tract (e.g., urinary tract infection, nephrolithiasis, nephropathy), as well as systemic disorders (e.g., diabetes mellitus, ketoacidosis, phenylketonuria). Urine is examined visually (e.g., color and transparency), microscopically (e.g., presence of RBCs, WBCs, casts, crystals, bacteria), and chemically (e.g., pH, protein, glucose, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, β-hCG).

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Urinalysis

P6aWOl.title: Hyaline casts
P6aWOl.description: A type of urinary cast that consists of a mucoprotein matrix of Tamm-Horsfall proteins. Hyaline casts originate from the thick ascending loop of Henle and appear on microscopy as homogeneous and transparent. They are a nonspecific finding that can be found in healthy individuals but may also be seen with dehydration (e.g., pre-renal AKI).

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Urinalysis

46a3Ol.title: Renal tubular epithelial cell casts
46a3Ol.description: A finding on urine microscopy. Composed of desquamated renal tubular epithelial cells. Etiologies include acute tubular necrosis (ATN), acute interstitial nephritis, and proliferative glomerulonephritis.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Urinalysis

k6amOl.title: White blood cell casts
k6amOl.description: A collection of casts composed of white blood cells in a tubular mucoprotein matrix. Identified on urine microscopy by a sharply demarcated cellular outline and central nucleus. Most often associated with pyelonephritis.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Urinalysis

l6avOl.title: Creatinine clearance
l6avOl.description: The rate at which creatinine is removed from the blood by the kidneys. Often used to estimate glomerular filtration rate because creatinine is freely filtered and secreted only in very small amounts.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Renal function test

N6a-Ol.title: Cockcroft-Gault equation
N6a-Ol.description: An equation used to estimate creatinine clearance: CCr (mL/min) = ((140 – age) x lean body weight (kg)) / (72 x serum creatinine (mg/dL)). For women, the result should be multiplied by 0.85.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Renal function test

n6a7ll.title: Thin basement membrane disease
n6a7ll.description: A genetic nephropathy caused by abnormalities of type IV collagen and thinning of the glomerular basement membrane. Causes episodes of intermittent gross hematuria and flank pain, often triggered by upper respiratory tract infections or exercise. Kidney biopsy is required for diagnosis. Often no treatment required; patients with proteinuria should be treated with ACE inhibitors to slow progression.

L6awll.title: Alport syndrome
L6awll.description: A genetic disorder characterized by glomerulonephritis, often in combination with sensorineural hearing loss and, in some cases, eye abnormalities. Caused by a genetic defect of type IV collagen. Most commonly inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern.

K6aUNl.title: IgA nephropathy
K6aUNl.description: The most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Most frequently affects male individuals in the second to third decades of life. Clinical manifestations include gross hematuria, flank pain, and sometimes proteinuria, are often triggered by upper respiratory tract or gastrointestinal infections, and may be episodic.

D6a1Ml.title: Target cells
D6a1Ml.description: A type of pathologic red blood cell with a bullseye appearance due to an overabundance of membrane. Etiologies include asplenia, liver disease, and thalassemia.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Erythrocyte morphology

0paeLl.title: Howell-Jolly bodies
0paeLl.description: A collection of basophilic remnants of DNA found in circulating immature RBCs that are normally removed by the spleen. Their presence is greatly increased in patients with decreased splenic function or asplenia.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Erythrocyte morphology

bpaHLl.title: Deoxyhemoglobin
bpaHLl.description: A hemoglobin molecule without oxygen bound to heme. Has a lower light absorption spectrum than oxyhemoglobin that results in a dark red-purple appearance.

destinations.label: Erythrocyte morphology and hemoglobin → Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

dpaool.title: Biloma
dpaool.description: A localized collection of bile that forms as a result of biliary tree disruption (e.g., from iatrogenic injury during cholecystectomy).

destinations.label: Benign liver tumors and hepatic cysts → Differential diagnoses

epaxol.title: Focal nodular hyperplasia
epaxol.description: A benign, indolent tumor of the liver that is most commonly seen in women of reproductive age. Typically asymptomatic but can cause nonspecific upper abdominal symptoms when large. Typically appears on imaging as a solitary intraparenchymal mass < 5 cm in size, with or without a central scar. Histopathologic features include benign hepatocytes arranged in nodules separated by fibrous septa that contain aberrant blood vessels.

destinations.label: Benign liver tumors and hepatic cysts → Benign liver tumors

UpabKl.title: Hepatocellular adenoma
UpabKl.description: A rare benign liver tumor associated with increased levels of estrogen, usually affecting women aged 20–40 on oral contraceptive pills. They may also be associated with anabolic steroids, glycogen storage disorders, or iron overload disorders. Usually asymptomatic and are found incidentally on imaging. Bleeding is a possible complication.

destinations.label: Benign liver tumors and hepatic cysts → Benign liver tumors

fpakKl.title: Hepatic hemangioma
fpakKl.description: The most common benign liver tumor. Composed of endothelium-lined blood-filled sinuses. More common in women between 30-50 years. Mostly asymptomatic but large hepatic hemangiomas may cause nonspecific symptoms (e.g., abdominal discomfort, early satiety, nausea).

destinations.label: Benign liver tumors and hepatic cysts → Benign liver tumors

gpaFKl.title: Hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor
gpaFKl.description: A rare hepatic lesion that typically develops as a well-circumscribed, encapsulated inflammatory mass. Associated with other inflammatory conditions (e.g., sclerosing cholangitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, autoimmune diseases).

destinations.label: Benign liver tumors and hepatic cysts → Differential diagnoses

hpac6l.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
hpac6l.description: A pathologic condition of the heart muscle characterized by decreased compliance and stiffening of atrium and ventricle walls resulting in diastolic dysfunction. Most common causes are amyloidosis and myocardial fibrosis after cardiac surgery or radiation. Systolic ejection fraction is commonly preserved.

kpampl.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
kpampl.description: A condition of acute, stress-induced, reversible dysfunction and apical ballooning of the left ventricle. Symptoms resemble those of acute coronary syndrome but often resolve spontaneously.

lpavpl.title: Carbon monoxide
lpavpl.description: A colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas that has high affinity to hemoglobin. Exposure (e.g., from house fires, wood-burning stoves, motor vehicle exhaust) leads to the formation of carboxyhemoglobin and can cause acute CO poisoning.

MpaMJl.title: Skin grafting
MpaMJl.description: The transplantation of viable skin from one area of the body to another, usually to treat areas of extensive skin loss following burns, necrotizing fasciitis, or trauma.

destinations.label: Wound treatment → Plastic and reconstructive surgery

npa7Jl.title: Full-thickness skin graft
npa7Jl.description: A skin graft used for permanent wound coverage, comprised of the epidermis and the entire dermis.

destinations.label: Wound treatment → Plastic and reconstructive surgery

LpawJl.title: Split-thickness skin graft
LpawJl.description: A skin graft used for permanent wound coverage, comprised of the entire epidermis and an altered dermal layer that has been split by a dermatome blade to enable greater surface coverage.

destinations.label: Wound treatment → Plastic and reconstructive surgery

ppaLql.title: Lymphangitis
ppaLql.description: An inflammation of the lymphatic channels. Etiologies include infectious causes (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes infection) and noninfectious causes (e.g., neoplastic lymphangitis).

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Nonpurulent SSTIs

Jpasql.title: Carbuncle
Jpasql.description: A coalescence of multiple inflamed follicles (i.e., a coalescence of furuncles) with drainage of pus. Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Purulent SSTIs

qpaCql.title: Ecthyma
qpaCql.description: Ulcerative impetigo that extends into the dermis. Presents as a coin-sized, superficial ulcer, with a 'punched-out' appearance.

rpafIl.title: Furuncle
rpafIl.description: A well-demarcated, firm, painful, purulent nodule that can develop after folliculitis. Extension into surrounding tissue can cause abscess and/or cellulitis.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Purulent SSTIs

7pa4Il.title: Folliculitis
7pa4Il.description: A localized inflammation of the hair follicle or sebaceous glands that is primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Characterized by erythema, tender papules, and/or pustules at the site of hair follicles.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Purulent SSTIs

HpaKIl.title: Cellulitis
HpaKIl.description: A rapidly spreading local infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue caused most commonly by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Commonly appears in areas with broken skin (e.g., due to trauma or another infection).

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Nonpurulent SSTIs

GpaBIl.title: Skin abscess
GpaBIl.description: An accumulation of white-yellow pus predominantly consisting of proteins and neutrophils in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue. Most commonly caused by S. aureus.

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Purulent SSTIs

tpaXrl.title: Rib fracture
tpaXrl.description: A partial or complete break in a rib bone. Clinical features include pain on inspiration, respiratory distress, tachypnea, shallow breathing, crepitus, focal chest wall tenderness, and chest wall deformity.

upaprl.title: Diaphragmatic injury
upaprl.description: A penetrating or blunt thoracoabdominal injury in which the continuity of the diaphragm is compromised (e.g., via a tear, perforation, or rupture). Abdominal contents can herniate through the resulting defect into the thorax causing an acquired diaphragmatic hernia.

vpaArl.title: Phrenic nerve paralysis
vpaArl.description: A condition caused by trauma or compression of the phrenic nerve. Unilateral paralysis can be asymptomatic or present with dyspnea; bilateral paralysis causes severe dyspnea. Treatments involves airway management and possible implantation of a diaphragmatic pacemaker.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

Dpa17l.title: Myocardial contusion
Dpa17l.description: A cardiac injury secondary to blunt thoracic trauma, which causes myocardial dysfunction with a wide range of clinical effects including chest pain, hypotension, arrhythmias, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and cardiogenic shock.

wpah7l.title: Aortic rupture
wpah7l.description: A breakage of the aorta, most commonly caused by spontaneous rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Can also be caused by blunt trauma to the chest. Typically manifests with rapidly progressive hemorrhagic shock (e.g., tachycardia, hypotension) and tearing pain.

media.title: Nontraumatic rupture of the thoracic aorta

9paN7l.title: Tracheobronchial injury
9paN7l.description: A tear in the tracheobronchial tree as a result of a high-energy impact or a penetrating chest wall injury. The most common site of the tear is within 2 cm of the carina. Patients present with hemoptysis, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and possibly a pneumothorax.

Cpaq7l.title: Pneumomediastinum
Cpaq7l.description: The presence of air in the mediastinum. Can be spontaneous or traumatic. Due to injury to an air-filled organ in the mediastinum (e.g., tracheobronchial tree, esophagus).

media.title: Traumatic pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum with subcutaneous emphysema

Bpaz7l.title: Pulmonary contusion
Bpaz7l.description: Edema and blood collecting in the alveolar spaces as a result of blunt chest trauma, which induces capillary damage and leads to impairment of lung function.

zparHl.title: Epigastric hernia
zparHl.description: The protrusion of intraabdominal contents through the linea alba, between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus.

YJansl.title: Umbilical hernias
YJansl.description: A congenital or acquired abdominal wall defect with protrusion of a sac (possibly containing intestines) at the umbilicus. In children, umbilical hernias often spontaneously close without intervention by 4-5 years of age; older patients may require surgery for resolution.

bJaHsl.title: Incisional hernia
bJaHsl.description: A herniation of intraabdominal contents through an abdominal wall defect created during a previous abdominal surgery.

cJaaGl.title: Diastasis recti
cJaaGl.description: A > 2 cm separation of the left and right rectus abdominis muscles, which can lead to the protrusion of abdominal organs. Results from increased intraabdominal pressure (e.g., due to pregnancy). Considered a benign condition that usually resolves over time but may require surgery for complications or cosmetic reasons.

1Ja2Gl.title: Richter's hernia
1Ja2Gl.description: A type of hernia in which only the antimesenteric portion of the intestinal wall is trapped by the abdominal wall defect, leading to ischemia without bowel obstruction. Most commonly seen in femoral hernias, but may also occur at surgical port sites following laparoscopic surgery.

WJaPGl.title: Spigelian hernia
WJaPGl.description: A rare type of hernia that arises in the ventral abdominal wall along the semilunar line, typically below the level of the umbilicus. Has a high risk of complications (e.g., incarceration, strangulation).

dJaoGl.title: Essential tremor
dJaoGl.description: Isolated bilateral postural tremor of the upper limbs in the absence of other neurological signs (e.g., dystonia, ataxia, or parkinsonism). Frequency typically ranges from 4 to 12 Hz. May be accompanied by tremors of the head, neck, voice, and/or lower limbs. Worsens with voluntary movements (e.g., reaching for a glass), stress, fatigue, and caffeine, and improves with alcohol consumption.

eJaxGl.title: Holmes tremor
eJaxGl.description: A low-frequency, large-amplitude tremor that is present at rest and worsens when performing an action or maintaining certain postures. Causes include stroke, traumatic brain injury, and CNS infections.

2JaTtl.title: Flapping tremor
2JaTtl.description: An irregular, high-amplitude tremor of the hand that occurs when the arm is outstretched and the wrist and fingers are dorsiflexed. Most commonly a sign of encephalopathy, e.g., due to liver failure, uremia, or hypercapnia.

SJaytl.title: Resting tremor
SJaytl.description: Tremor that occurs when a body part is not voluntarily activated. Most commonly apparent in the upper limbs and hands; may also affect the chin, lips, and/or trunk. Worsens with emotional stress and is reduced with target-directed movement. Most common in Parkinson disease.

hJacFl.title: Action tremor
hJacFl.description: A tremor that occurs during voluntary contraction of skeletal muscle. Subtypes include postural, isometric, and kinetic tremors.

3JaSFl.title: Postural tremor
3JaSFl.description: Tremor that appears when the body part is held in a fixed position against gravity.

RJalFl.title: Intention tremor
RJalFl.description: A coarse hand tremor with a frequency of < 5 Hz that worsens with goal-directed movements. Most commonly due to cerebellar pathology; causes include stroke, tumor, drugs (e.g., lithium), alcohol, and multiple sclerosis.

jJa_Fl.title: Multiple system atrophy
jJa_Fl.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the abnormal deposition of α-synuclein, primarily in glial cells. Common features include severe autonomic dysfunction, parkinsonism (classified as MSA-P if predominant), and cerebellar ataxia (classified as MSA-C if predominant).

NJa-8l.title: Pure autonomic failure
NJa-8l.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the abnormal deposition of α-synuclein aggregates primarily in the peripheral autonomic nervous system. Manifests as severe autonomic dysfunction without other neurological features (e.g., those seen in multiple system atrophy). Treatment is symptomatic and emphasizes managing blood pressure fluctuations.

5Jaiul.title: Corticobasal degeneration
5Jaiul.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the abnormal deposition of tau protein. Leads to asymmetric degeneration, primarily in the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia. Common features include asymmetric motor abnormalities (e.g., rigidity, dystonia, alien limb phenomenon) and cognitive impairment.

MJaMul.title: Dementia with Lewy bodies
MJaMul.description: A neurodegenerative form of Lewy body dementia characterized by the abnormal deposition of Lewy bodies containing α-synuclein in cerebral neurons. Common features include fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder.

destinations.label: Parkinson-plus syndromes → Dementia with Lewy bodies

LJawul.title: Progressive supranuclear palsy
LJawul.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the abnormal deposition of tau protein, causing brain atrophy and neuronal loss. Common features include recurrent falls due to postural instability and vertical gaze palsy.

oJa0El.title: Temporal lobe epilepsy
oJa0El.description: Recurrent, unprovoked seizures that originate from the medial or lateral temporal lobe. Usually accompanied by olfactory or gustatory hallucinations.

destinations.label: Focal seizures and syndromes → Focal seizures with structural or metabolic cause

media.title: Anterior temporal spikes and sharp waves

pJaLEl.title: Postictal paralysis
pJaLEl.description: Postictal weakness or paralysis of the involved limb or facial muscles following a seizure. Thought to result from exhaustion of the primary motor cortex. May last up to 36 hours.

HJaKvl.title: Childhood absence epilepsy
HJaKvl.description: The most common childhood epilepsy syndrome. Characterized by multiple, daily absence seizures in children between the ages of 2–12 years (peak incidence: 5–6 years). Typical episodes involve the child appearing to be daydreaming (eyes open/fluttering, staring off into space) for several seconds at a time, multiple times per day.

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndromes

GJaBvl.title: Juvenile absence epilepsy
GJaBvl.description: An epilepsy syndrome characterized by infrequent absence seizures with onset of seizures between 8–20 years (peak incidence: 9–13 years). 75% of patients also develop generalized tonic-clonic seizures that occur upon waking up. Unlike childhood absence epilepsy which resolves during adulthood, most patients with juvenile absence epilepsy require seizure prophylaxis for life.

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndromes

tJaXDl.title: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
tJaXDl.description: A genetic epilepsy syndrome characterized by recurrent myoclonic seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and absence seizures. The onset of seizures occurs between the ages of 8 and 25, and seizures characteristically occur immediately after waking up or following sleep deprivation.

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndromes

wJahwl.title: West syndrome
wJahwl.description: A condition of epileptic spasms with an onset within the first year of life. Typically accompanied by a global developmental delay. Common causes include structural brain anomalies (e.g., tuberous sclerosis), Down syndrome, and certain genetic defects (e.g., ARX, CDKL5 mutations).

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Symptomatic or cryptogenic generalized epilepsy syndromes

CJaqwl.title: Hypsarrhythmia
CJaqwl.description: A pathological EEG pattern consisting of generalized, irregular, slow waveforms interspersed with multifocal polymorphic spikes. Indicates West syndrome (infantile spasms).

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Symptomatic or cryptogenic generalized epilepsy syndromes

xJaEwl.title: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
xJaEwl.description: An epilepsy syndrome characterized by tonic seizures that typically occur during sleep. Atypical absence seizures and atonic seizures may also occur. Most often caused by structural abnormalities of the brain, and less commonly (30%) by de novo genetic mutations.

destinations.label: Generalized epilepsy in childhood → Symptomatic or cryptogenic generalized epilepsy syndromes

yJad9l.title: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy
yJad9l.description: A group of rare seizure disorders characterized by severe, progressive, multifocal seizures leading to cognitive decline and, eventually, death.

AJaR9l.title: Brown-Séquard syndrome
AJaR9l.description: A syndrome involving hemisection of the spinal cord. Common causes include penetrating trauma and demyelinating diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis). Presents with ipsilateral loss of proprioception, tactile discrimination, and vibration sense due to dorsal column damage, ipsilateral flaccid paralysis due to corticospinal tract damage, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to spinothalamic tract damage.

destinations.label: Incomplete spinal cord syndromes → Brown-Séquard syndrome

0qaeCl.title: Dissociated sensory loss
0qaeCl.description: Impairment of either pain and temperature sensation (carried by the spinothalamic tracts) or light touch and proprioception (carried by the dorsal columns), but not both. Suggestive of a lesion of the brain stem or spinal cord involving only one sensory tract, e.g., incomplete spinal cord injury.

YqanCl.title: Epicritic sensation
YqanCl.description: A type of sensation that can discriminate between small degrees of change. Signals are transmitted through the posterior column (posterior funiculus consisting of gracile and cuneate fasciculi). Includes fine touch, vibration, and pressure.

destinations.label: Spinal cord tracts and reflexes → Spinal cord tracts

bqaHCl.title: Proprioception
bqaHCl.description: A sense of the position and movement of one's own body in space. Skeletal muscles and tendons as well as fibrous joint capsules possess proprioceptors that send information to the CNS via the posterior column (posterior funiculus consisting of gracile and cuneate fasciculi) and spinocerebellar tract.

Xqa9Cl.title: Protopathic sensation
Xqa9Cl.description: A type of sensation that responds to gross sensory stimuli. Signals are transmitted through the anterior and lateral spinothalamic tracts. Includes temperature extremes, pain, and crude touch.

destinations.label: Spinal cord tracts and reflexes → Spinal cord tracts

1qa2xl.title: Kugelberg-Welander disease
1qa2xl.description: A mild form of spinal muscular atrophy that may present during late childhood or adolescence with variable degrees of limb weakness. Unlike other severe forms of spinal muscular atrophy, patients are often able to walk without support and have a near normal life expectancy.

WqaPxl.title: Progressive muscular atrophy
WqaPxl.description: A nonhereditary, adult-onset, progressive lower motor neuron disorder. Clinical features include muscle wasting and weakness. Some patients develop amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, presenting with upper motor neuron signs later in the clinical course.

dqaoxl.title: Werdnig-Hoffmann disease
dqaoxl.description: The most severe type of spinal muscular atrophies. Affected children present at 0–6 months of age with severe muscle weakness and hypotonia of proximal muscles (mostly of the lower extremities). Additional features include severe bulbar palsy with inability to swallow, respiratory failure, atrophy and fasciculations in the tongue, and a weak cry and cough.

fqakBl.title: Lateral rectus palsy
fqakBl.description: A weakness of the lateral rectus muscles of the eye due to paralysis of the abducens nerve (CN VI). Manifests with convergent (medial) strabismus with an inability to abduct the eye. Horizontal diplopia can also be present.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Abducens nerve palsy (VI)

SqayBl.title: Vagus nerve lesion
SqayBl.description: A dysfunction of the vagus nerve that manifests with dysfunction in several organ systems. Etiologies include diabetic neuropathy, trauma, and inflammation. Manifestations include flaccid paralysis of the soft palate, dysphagia, vocal cord paralysis, and gastroparesis.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Vagus nerve palsy (X)

hqacyl.title: Accessory nerve lesion
hqacyl.description: A cranial nerve palsy that causes paresis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (which results in weakness turning the head toward the contralateral side) and trapezius muscle (which causes weakness during elevation of the ipsilateral shoulder). Can be caused by surgery in the lateral cervical region (e.g., resection of cervical lymph nodes).

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Accessory nerve palsy (XI)

PqaWAl.title: Olfactory nerve
PqaWAl.description: A sensory cranial nerve that transmits information related to smell. The only cranial nerve without thalamic relay to the cortex.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

kqamAl.title: Optic nerve
kqamAl.description: A sensory cranial nerve responsible for sight. Exits the skull through the optic canal. Responsible for the afferent portion of the pupillary reflex.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

lqavAl.title: Oculomotor nerve
lqavAl.description: A cranial nerve that consists of inner somatic fibers, which innervate 4 of the 6 extraocular muscles (superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique), as well as the levator palpebrae superioris and superficial parasympathetic fibers (which innervate the ciliary muscle and the pupillary sphincter).

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

mqaV_l.title: Trochlear nerve
mqaV_l.description: A motor cranial nerve that serves solely to innervate the superior oblique muscle. It arises from the trochlear nucleus in the midbrain. It has the longest intracranial course out of all of the cranial nerves and is the only one to exit from the posterior surface of the brainstem.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

MqaM_l.title: Trigeminal nerve
MqaM_l.description: A sensorimotor cranial nerve that originates in the pons. Divides into three branches: the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular branches. Main sensory supply to the face, scalp, sinuses, oral cavity, and meninges. The mandibular branch also provides motor supply to the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, pterygoids), tensor tympani, tensor veli palati, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of the digastric. Also provides parasympathetic supply to the salivary glands, lacrimal glands, and nasal mucosa.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

media.title: Trigeminal nerve branches and areas of sensory innervation

Lqaw_l.title: Abducens nerve
Lqaw_l.description: A pure motor nerve that innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Arises from the abducens nucleus in the pons and exits the brain at the junction between the pons and the medulla. Passes through the cavernous sinus.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

KqaUzl.title: Facial nerve
KqaUzl.description: A cranial nerve that provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands. Carries afferents from taste receptors of the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and somatic receptors from the anterior auditory canal and pinna.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

media.title: Course and branches of the facial nerve (VII)

pqaLzl.title: Vestibulocochlear nerve
pqaLzl.description: A purely sensory cranial nerve comprised of two functional divisions: the cochlear nerve and vestibular nerve. The cochlear nerve transmits auditory stimuli from the cochlea to the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei. The vestibular nerve transmits kinesthetic stimuli from the semicircular canals and otoliths to the vestibular nucleus.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

qqaCzl.title: Nervus glossopharyngeus
qqaCzl.description: A nerve that provides general sensation afferents from the pharynx, tonsils, middle ear, and posterior 1/3 of the tongue; taste afferents from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue; visceral afferents from the carotid body; parasympathetic efferents to the parotid gland; and motor efferents to the stylopharyngeus. Contributes to the pharyngeal plexus and supplies the carotid sinus.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

rqaf-l.title: Vagus nerve
rqaf-l.description: A nerve of the parasympathetic autonomic nervous system. Responsible for smooth muscle contraction within the digestive tract. Regulates heart rate and blood pressure. Also carries afferent fibers that promote vomiting and efferent motor fibers that innervate the larynx and pharynx muscles.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

HqaK-l.title: Accessory nerve
HqaK-l.description: A cranial nerve that innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, thus controlling rotation of the head and shrugging of the shoulders. It is the only cranial nerve with neurons in the spinal cord.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

media.title: Brainstem and origin of cranial nerves II-XII

GqaB-l.title: Hypoglossal nerve
GqaB-l.description: A pure motor cranial nerve that innervates the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Cranial nerve types and functions

vqaAZN.title: Oculomotor nerve lesion
vqaAZN.description: A nerve palsy with manifestations that depend on whether the inner somatic fibers or the superficial parasympathetic fibers are affected. Involvement of the inner somatic fibers manifests as ptosis (paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris) and a down-and-out-gaze (paralysis of 4 extraocular muscles). Involvement of the superficial parasympathetic fibers manifests as dilated pupil and loss of accommodation.

destinations.label: Cranial nerve palsies → Oculomotor nerve palsy (III)

Dqa10N.title: Alkaptonuria
Dqa10N.description: A rare, autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism caused by deficient activity of homogentisic acid dioxygenase. Clinical features include ochronosis, calcification of the heart valves, nephrolithiasis, arthritis, and urine that turns dark brown/black when left standing or alkalinized.

wqah0N.title: Ochronosis
wqah0N.description: A collection of clinical features characterized by bluish-brown discoloration of cartilage, tendons, skin, and sclera. Most commonly associated with alkaptonuria, wherein ochronosis ultimately results in arthritis and degenerative changes in the vertebral column.

9qaN0N.title: Homocystinuria
9qaN0N.description: A group of hereditary diseases characterized by defects in homocysteine metabolism, resulting in inferonasal (down and in) lens dislocation, thrombosis, elongated bones, epilepsy, and intellectual disability. Caused by cystathionine synthase deficiency, methionine synthase deficiency, or decreased affinity of cystathionine synthase for pyridoxal phosphate.

Cqaq0N.title: Phenylketonuria
Cqaq0N.description: A congenital disorder characterized by the accumulation of phenylalanine in the central nervous system. Can be caused by a defect of phenylalanine hydroxylase (classic PKU) or deficiency in tetrahydrobiopterin (malignant PKU). Causes psychomotor retardation, seizures, a musty odor, and pale skin/hair (from lack of melanin production).

media.title: Classic phenylketonuria vs. tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency (malignant PKU)

Bqaz0N.title: MCAD deficiency
Bqaz0N.description: A disease characterized by a defect in the breakdown of medium-chain fatty acids, which renders fatty acids an unusable alternative energy source in case of carbohydrate deficiency. Can result in hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, and lethargy in fasting states.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Fatty acid metabolism disorders

AqaRaN.title: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
AqaRaN.description: A progressive ophthalmologic disorder characterized by the inability to move the eyebrows and eyes. Most commonly develops in individuals with mitochondrial myopathies.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Mitochondrial myopathies

_qa5aN.title: Kearns-Sayre syndrome
_qa5aN.description: A mitochondrial myopathy whose symptoms manifest before the age of 20 and include ocular problems (progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy), cerebellar ataxia, and heart block.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Mitochondrial myopathies

zqaraN.title: MELAS syndrome
zqaraN.description: Inherited myopathy caused by mutations of mitochondrial DNA. MELAS stands for "Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes”. Tonic-clonic seizures and dementia due to encephalopathy may also be present.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Mitochondrial myopathies

-qaDaN.title: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers
-qaDaN.description: An inherited myopathy typically caused by point mutations of mitochondrial DNA. Clinical features include myoclonic jerks, generalized seizures, cerebellar ataxia, and dementia.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Mitochondrial myopathies

ZIaZYN.title: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
ZIaZYN.description: An X-linked deficit of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) that leads to a systemic buildup of uric acid. Causes choreoathetotic movement, cognitive delay, delayed growth and puberty, self-mutilating behavior, and gouty arthritis.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Purine salvage deficiencies

0IaeYN.title: α1-antitrypsin deficiency
0IaeYN.description: A genetic condition characterized by reduced levels or activity of the protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin. Clinical manifestations may include COPD, emphysema, and cirrhosis.

aIaQYN.title: α1-antitrypsin
aIaQYN.description: An enzyme that inhibits proteases such as neutrophil elastase, preventing the breakdown of alveolar cells. AAT mutations can cause AAT deficiency, which clinically manifests in the lungs (e.g., with COPD, emphysema) and, in some cases, the liver (e.g., with cirrhosis, hepatitis).

XIa9YN.title: Axillary nerve injury
XIa9YN.description: An injury most commonly caused by trauma (e.g., anterior shoulder dislocation, fractures involving the surgical neck of the humerus) or iatrogenic damage (e.g., rotator cuff surgery, osteosynthesis of humeral fractures). Manifests with impaired abduction and external rotation of the arm and sensory deficit of skin overlying the deltoid.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

media.title: Clinical features of axillary nerve injury

cIaabN.title: Femoral nerve injury
cIaabN.description: Injury to the femoral nerve usually caused by trauma, pressure (e.g., psoas hematoma, aortic aneurysm), surgery, or femoral line placement. Results in sensory deficits over the anteromedial lower leg and motor deficits with hip flexion and knee extension.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

1Ia2bN.title: Saphenous nerve
1Ia2bN.description: A purely sensory nerve of the lower extremity that arises from the femoral nerve. Carries sensory information from the medial leg and proximal medial foot.

destinations.label: Neurovasculature of the lower limbs → Nerves
The leg, ankle, and foot → Innervation

media.title: Innervation of the lower extremity (ventral view)

WIaPbN.title: Meralgia paresthetica
WIaPbN.description: An injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve that results in pain and paresthesias of the outer thigh.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

VIaGbN.title: Obturator nerve injury
VIaGbN.description: Injury to the obturator nerve usually caused by trauma (e.g., pelvic ring fracture) or, less commonly, obturator hernias. Results in sensory deficit of the skin over the medial thigh and paralysis of hip adductors.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

eIaxbN.title: Sciatic nerve injury
eIaxbN.description: A type of peripheral nerve injury usually caused by direct trauma, hip dislocation, total hip arthroplasty, or misplaced gluteal injections. Common signs include a sensory deficit over the lower leg and foot (except the medial malleolus and medial foot, as these are innervated by the saphenous nerve) in addition to hamstring muscle weakness.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

UIabXN.title: Tibial nerve injury
UIabXN.description: A type of peripheral nerve dysfunction usually caused by tibial fracture or tarsal tunnel syndrome. Common signs include a sensory deficit over the sole of foot and impaired plantar flexion.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

2IaTXN.title: Common peroneal nerve injury
2IaTXN.description: Commonly caused by fracture of the fibular head, external compression (i.e., from obstetric stirrups or a tight-fitting cast) or forceful knee flexion during vaginal delivery. Classified as either superficial and deep peroneal nerve injury: Superficial peroneal nerve injury affects sensation in the back of the feet and toes as well as the lateral surface of the legs. It also affects pronation of the foot. Deep peroneal nerve injury affects sensation in the area between the first and second toes. It affects movement of the foot and toe extensors as well, causing a foot drop and high-stepping gait.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the lower body

TIa6XN.title: High-stepping gait
TIa6XN.description: A gait abnormality characterized by compensatory high lifting of the leg to prevent dragging of the foot (due to foot drop from weakness of dorsiflexion). Etiologies of unilateral high-stepping gait include injury to the deep peroneal nerve and L5 radiculopathy. Etiologies of bilateral high-stepping gait include amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy (e.g., from uncontrolled diabetes).

hIaccN.title: Neuropraxia
hIaccN.description: The mildest form of peripheral nerve injury, characterized by a temporary loss of motor or sensory function. Blunt injury, compression or stretching of a peripheral nerve causes focal demyelination (due to ischemia/edema), leading to a transient nerve conduction block. The axon and its coverings (endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium) remain intact. Complete recovery usually occurs within 12 weeks.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Types of nerve damage

iIaJcN.title: Wallerian degeneration
iIaJcN.description: A process that occurs in response to a proximal axonal or neuronal cell body injury; it is characterized by the degeneration of the distal segment of the transected nerve fiber and axonal retraction proximally.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Types of nerve damage

QIaucN.title: Neurorrhaphy
QIaucN.description: A surgical nerve repair in which the ends of a transsected nerve are sutured either directly or using nerve grafts.

PIaW1N.title: Phrenic nerves
PIaW1N.description: A pair of sensorimotor nerves that arise from the ventral rami of C3, C4, and C5 bilaterally. Each phrenic nerve provides motor supply to the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm and sensory supply to the diaphragm (pleural and peritoneal surfaces), pericardium, and the mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura.

destinations.label: Head and neck region → Vasculature and innervation

4Ia31N.title: Suprascapular nerve injury
4Ia31N.description: A peripheral nerve injury that causes impaired function of the infraspinatus and supraspinatus muscles, which manifests with limited adduction, abduction, and external rotation of the arm and shoulder instability. Most commonly occurs due to trauma (e.g. fractured scapula) and compression (e.g. bony ossification of the overlying superior transverse scapular ligament).

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

kIam1N.title: Long thoracic nerve injury
kIam1N.description: A peripheral nerve injury that presents with impaired serratus anterior function (i.e., medial winging of the scapula with impaired abduction of the arm beyond 90°). Most commonly occurs as a consequence of trauma.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

OIaI1N.title: Thoracodorsal nerve injury
OIaI1N.description: A peripheral nerve injury that presents with impaired latissimus dorsi function (i.e., limited shoulder retraction, impaired adduction and internal rotation of the arm) and teres major function (i.e., limited internal rotation and adduction of the arm). Most commonly occurs due to surgical injury (e.g., after axillary lymph node dissection).

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

lIav1N.title: Spastic bladder
lIav1N.description: A bladder dysfunction caused by neurological damage (e.g., spinal injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis). Results in uncoordinated bladder contraction against a closed urinary sphincter (detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia). Manifests with an overactive bladder (e.g., frequent urination with a sudden urge to urinate, urine leakage, nocturia) as well as urinary retention.

mIaVWN.title: Hypospadia
mIaVWN.description: A common congenital malformation in which the urethral meatus is incorrectly positioned (either along the penile shaft or on the scrotum or perineum). Caused by failure of urethral folds and foreskin to fuse on the ventral side of the penis. May be associated with inguinal hernias and cryptorchidism. Proximal hypospadias may also occur along with bifid scrotum and penoscrotal transposition (proximal hypospadias).

destinations.label: Abnormalities of the male urethra and webbed penis → Hypospadias

nIa7WN.title: Posterior urethral valves
nIa7WN.description: A developmental condition in which membranous folds within the urethra obstruct the outflow of urine. Common complications include vesicoureteral reflux, recurrent UTIs, and bladder dysfunction. Treatment is ablation of the obstruction. A common cause of Potter sequence.

destinations.label: Abnormalities of the male urethra and webbed penis → Posterior urethral valves

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

LIawWN.title: Bladder exstrophy
LIawWN.description: An embryological defect in which the bladder and urethra herniate through a defect in the ventral abdominal wall. Causes incontinence, genital abnormalities, and pubic bone diastasis. Complications include UTIs, vesicoureteral reflux, hip dysplasia, vaginal and rectal prolapse.

destinations.label: Congenital visceral malformations → Other complex abdominal wall defects

media.title: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT)

JIasdN.title: Cryptorchidism
JIasdN.description: A common congenital anomaly characterized by a failure of one or both testicles to descend into the scrotum. Undescended tests are usually palpable in the abdominal or inguinal region.

7Ia4VN.title: Azoospermia
7Ia4VN.description: The absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate. Associated with exogenous testosterone use, which inhibits the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. Can also result from obstruction of the ejaculatory duct (e.g., in men with cystic fibrosis).

EIa8eN.title: Glomerular proteinuria
EIa8eN.description: Increased urinary protein excretion (> 150 mg/day) caused by glomerular damage that increases the permeability of the filtration barrier, allowing medium and large proteins to pass into the urine (e.g., in minimal change disease or IgA nephropathy).

vIaAeN.title: Severely increased albuminuria
vIaAeN.description: A persistently elevated urine albumin excretion rate > 300 mg/day or an albumin-to-creatinine ratio > 300 mg/g or > 30 mg/mmol.

DIa1UN.title: Moderately increased albuminuria
DIa1UN.description: A persistently elevated urine albumin excretion rate of 30-300 mg/day (20-200 mcg/min) or a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30-300 mg/g (3-30 mg/mmol).

wIahUN.title: Post-renal proteinuria
wIahUN.description: Category of proteinuria that results from deposition of protein in the urine at any part of the urinary tract distal to the renal pelvis.

9IaNUN.title: Overflow proteinuria
9IaNUN.description: Increased urinary protein excretion due to excessive production of low molecular weight proteins that exceeds reabsorption capacity of the tubules. Associated with light chains or Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma, hemoglobinuria in hemolysis, and myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis.

yIad2N.title: Benign proteinuria
yIad2N.description: Isolated proteinuria (< 3.5 g/day) that mostly affects younger individuals. Resolves spontaneously and does not require treatment.

AIaR2N.title: Functional proteinuria
AIaR2N.description: A benign etiology of mild proteinuria, especially in children. It often results from physiologic stressors, such as cold temperature exposure, fever, or intense exercise. Follow-up urine dipstick demonstrating no protein and normal urinary protein/creatinine ratio confirms the diagnosis. No treatment is required.

zIar2N.title: Orthostatic proteinuria
zIar2N.description: A type of benign proteinuria characterized by increased protein excretion only in the upright position. Typically presents with isolated proteinuria during the day and normal protein excretion at night when the individual is in a recumbent position. Renal function is usually not impaired. Commonly occurs in obese adolescents and does not require any treatment.

draoTN.title: Latex allergy
draoTN.description: A type I or type IV hypersensitivity to latex-based products (e.g., exam gloves, condoms). Affects 8-12% of health care workers in the US. Causes allergic contact dermatitis and anaphylactic reactions in severe cases.

eraxTN.title: Femoral anteversion angle
eraxTN.description: An angle formed by the main axis of the femoral neck and the transverse axis of both femoral condyles of the distal femur.

Tra6gN.title: Caput-collum-diaphyseal angle
Tra6gN.description: An angle measured between the longitudinal femoral neck and shaft axis on an AP x-ray. Used to assess hip morphology. The normal range of the angle is generally considered 120-135° (150° in newborns, 125° in adults).

SraygN.title: Coxa vara
SraygN.description: A decreased femoral neck-shaft angle, typically < 120°, associated with an ossification defect of the metaphysis and abnormal development of the femoral physis. Clinical features include abductor muscle weakness, limb length discrepancy, and Trendelenburg gait.

hracSN.title: Coxa valga
hracSN.description: A deformity of the femur due to an increased femoral neck and shaft angle (> 140°). Clinical features include groin pain due to long periods of weight-bearing and limited hip abduction.

3raSSN.title: Femoral anteversion
3raSSN.description: A forward rotation of the femoral neck in relation to the femoral condyles due to an increased femoral anteversion angle.

RralSN.title: Femoral retroversion
RralSN.description: A backward rotation of the femoral neck in relation to the femoral condyles due to a decreased femoral anteversion angle.

iraJSN.title: Anterior cruciate ligament injury
iraJSN.description: A ligamentous knee injury typically caused by sudden deceleration and/or change of direction that involves rotating and/or valgus stress of the knee. Manifestations include an audible pop followed by knee swelling (e.g., hemarthrosis), pain, and instability.

destinations.label: Knee ligament injuries → Anterior cruciate ligament injury

QrauSN.title: Unhappy triad
QrauSN.description: An injury to three major structural components of the knee: the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial collateral ligament, and the medial meniscus. Results in a tender medial joint line, poor knee extension, and instability. Usually caused by lateral force to the knee.

destinations.label: Knee ligament injuries → Anterior cruciate ligament injury

jra_SN.title: Anterior drawer test
jra_SN.description: A physical exam test that assesses anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) integrity. The patient is to lie down in the supine position and flex the knee to 90°. The foot of the knee being tested is fixed in place by the examiner and the patient is asked to relax. The proximal end of the tibia is then pulled anteriorly. A firm endpoint along with the absence of anterior tibial movement implies that the ACL is intact. If there is a lax endpoint (especially in comparison to the contralateral leg), the test is positive, suggestive of ACL injury.

destinations.label: Knee ligament injuries → Anterior cruciate ligament injury

PraWhN.title: Lachman test
PraWhN.description: A physical examination maneuver used to test for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. The patient lies supine and flexes the knee by 20–30° with the heel of the foot resting on the examining table. The examiner stabilizes the femur and moves the proximal tibia anteriorly. Normally, there is resistance to forward translation of the tibia. A soft end point and increased anterior translation compared with the contralateral leg indicate an ACL tear.

destinations.label: Knee ligament injuries → Anterior cruciate ligament injury

4ra3hN.title: Pivot shift test
4ra3hN.description: A physical examination maneuver that assesses anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) integrity. With the patient supine and the knee completely extended, the examiner slowly flexes the knee while applying valgus stress and internally rotating the tibia. If the ACL is torn, the tibial plateau jerks backward at 30° of knee flexion.

destinations.label: Knee ligament injuries → Anterior cruciate ligament injury

kramhN.title: Talipes equinovarus
kramhN.description: A complex foot deformity that consists of 5 fixed deformities: equinus foot position (i.e., plantar flexion), varus position (i.e., supination of the calcaneus), adduction of the forefoot, inversion of the forefoot, and pes cavus (i.e., high arch). Most commonly congenital but can be acquired in rare cases (e.g., secondary to neurological conditions or trauma).

Nra-hN.title: Haglund exostosis
Nra-hN.description: A calcaneal spur localized at the posterior aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the Achilles tendon. Can cause heel pain.

5rai3N.title: Metatarsalgia
5rai3N.description: A condition characterized by pain and inflammation of a metatarsal head due to repetitive, high-intensity physical activity. Associated with overpronation and/or collapse of the transverse arch of the foot. Pain typically improves with rest.

MraM3N.title: Morton neuroma
MraM3N.description: A benign forefoot tumor formed by the thickening of the epineural and perineural tissue surrounding a plantar digital nerve, possibly due to chronic pressure. Manifests with burning pain and numbness, most commonly between the third and fourth metatarsal.

6rajRN.title: Acquired flat foot
6rajRN.description: An acquired flexible foot deformity characterized by the complete collapse of the longitudinal arch, usually due to posterior tibialis tendon insufficiency. Manifests as a flat or convex plantar surface of the foot.

praLRN.title: Congenital rigid pes planus
praLRN.description: A congenital foot deformity characterized by a fixed vertical talus position and luxation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

rrafiN.title: Silfverskjöld test
