rrafiN.description: A physical examination maneuver used to detect isolated gastrocnemius contracture. While the patient is seated or lying supine, the foot is held in an inverted position and dorsiflexed while the knee is bent and while straight. The degree of dorsiflexion is measured.

sratiN.title: Pes cavus
sratiN.description: A foot deformity characterized by a congenital or acquired high arch of the foot that does not flatten with weight bearing.

destinations.label: Foot deformities → Pes cavus (high arch, carvovarus foot, high instep, talipes cavus)

vraAQN.title: Hallux valgus
vraAQN.description: An anatomic deformity of the great toe (the hallux) in which the metatarsal is oriented medially whereas the phalanges are pointed laterally. The resulting bump on the medial side of the hallux can cause painful arthritis, especially with shoes. Colloquially known as a bunion.

9raNjN.title: Hammer toe
9raNjN.description: The hyperextension of the metatarsophalangeal joints due to atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the foot. Hammer toe is a sign of motor neuropathy but can also develop after trauma or arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis). Neurological causes include chronic diabetes mellitus, Friedrich ataxia, and acute intermittent porphyria.

destinations.label: Toe deformities → Other toe deformities (hallux varus, hammer toe, and claw toe)

BrazjN.title: Osteoclastoma
BrazjN.description: A primary bone tumor that affects the subchondral regions of long bones (usually around the knee or distal end of the radius) or the sacrococcygeal region. Occurs in individuals aged 20–40 years. The tumor is benign but can be locally aggressive.

destinations.label: Benign bone tumors → Giant-cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma)

AraRPN.title: Chondroblastoma
AraRPN.description: A rare, benign tumor of cartilage precursor cells that arises in the epiphyses of long bones and affects patients younger than 20 years of age. May present with pain and swelling over the affected bone.

zrarPN.title: Enchondroma
zrarPN.description: A benign intramedullary cartilaginous neoplasm that typically occurs in patients 10–40 years of age. Most commonly seen in the phalanges. Appears on x-ray as a well-defined osteolytic lesion. A calcified chondroid matrix may be present, but a periosteal reaction is usually absent.

media.title: Enchondroma of the fifth metacarpal of the left hand

a7aQ4N.title: Ossifying fibroma
a7aQ4N.description: A rare, benign lesion that affects the cortex of the tibia and/or fibula at the diaphysis and typically occurs during early childhood. Within the lesion, normal bone fails to form and is replaced by fibrous tissue. X-ray shows a lytic lesion within the cortex. The lesion may result in anterior bowing of the lower limb or pathological fractures, but smaller lesions usually regress by adulthood.

destinations.label: Benign bone tumors → Ossifying fibroma (osteofibrous dysplasia)

b7aH4N.title: Osteoid osteoma
b7aH4N.description: A benign bone tumor in the cortex of the diaphysis of long bones that typically occurs in patients 10–30 years of age. May be painful, and pain is characteristically relieved by aspirin. X-ray typically shows a small lytic nidus surrounded by a dense sclerotic reaction.

destinations.label: Benign bone tumors → Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma

X7a94N.title: Osteoblastoma
X7a94N.description: A benign bone tumor that most commonly develops in the vertebrae of children and young adults (peak incidence of 10–20 years of age). Typically manifests with progressive pain that is unresponsive to NSAID therapy. X-ray usually shows a bony mass with a radiolucent core.

destinations.label: Benign bone tumors → Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma

W7aPkN.title: Osteochondroma
W7aPkN.description: The most common primary benign bone tumor. It appears on an x-ray as a bony protrusion with a cartilaginous cap and either a broad base (sessile) or narrow base (pedunculated). The tumor arises from the growth plate during periods of rapid bone growth (late childhood and adolescence) but is left behind on the metaphysis as the bone grows in length. Usually asymptomatic but may occasionally cause pain due to pressure on soft tissue structures.

d7aokN.title: Bone metastases
d7aokN.description: Secondary malignant tumors of the bone, most commonly due to metastasis of breast, lung, or prostate primary malignancies. Often asymptomatic but may manifest with bone pain, local deformity, and/or pathological fractures.

V7aGkN.title: Periosteal reactions
V7aGkN.description: A destruction of bone by a malignant or inflammatory process that leads to reactive periosteal bone synthesis. The formation of new bone with subsequent thickening of the cortical bone improves bone stability. However, rapid destructive or irritative processes prevent normal cortical regeneration. Periosteal reactions can also occur as a result of trauma or insufficient perfusion.

media.title: Periosteal reactions in malignant bone tumors

T7a6ON.title: Sunburst appearance
T7a6ON.description: A type of periosteal reaction caused by tumor extension and formation of periosteal spicules, which give the appearance of a sunburst. Associated with osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and osteoblastic metastases.

g7aFON.title: Codman triangle
g7aFON.description: A type of aggressive periosteal reaction in which a ridge of subperiosteal new bone is raised by an underlying tumor. Most commonly seen in patients with an osteosarcoma.

h7aclN.title: Osteosarcoma
h7aclN.description: A malignant bone-forming tumor that arises from bone mesenchymal tissue and typically occurs in the metaphysis of long bones. Characterized by rapid growth and cortical destruction as well as a florid periosteal reaction with a sunburst pattern on x-ray. Usually arises in individuals before the age of 30 years, but a small subset of cases occur in elderly patients.

37aSlN.title: Ewing sarcoma
37aSlN.description: A malignant bone tumor that arises from neuroectodermal tissue. Peak incidence is between 10 and 15 years of age. Typically occurs in flat bones (e.g., ilium, scapula) or in the diaphysis of long bones.

R7allN.title: Chondrosarcoma
R7allN.description: A heterogeneous group of malignant tumors that arise from cartilaginous tissue and typically occur in patients > 50 years old. Usually occur in the pelvis, ribs, and metaphyses of long bones.

i7aJlN.title: Chordoma
i7aJlN.description: A rare, slowly growing, malignant bone tumor that arises from notochordal remnants, typically in patients older than 50 years. The most common sites are the sacrococcygeal region, the clivus and base of the skull, and the vertebral body. Although they are malignant, chordomas do not usually metastasize

G7aBMN.title: D-penicillamine
G7aBMN.description: A metal-chelating agent that facilitates the renal excretion of heavy metals by forming water-soluble compounds. Used in the treatment of copper, gold, and mercury poisoning. Also used as an antifibrotic in patients with systemic sclerosis. Rarely used to treat rheumatoid arthritis in patients who do not respond to other therapies.

F7agnN.title: Arsenic poisoning
F7agnN.description: A heavy metal found in contaminated groundwater, pesticides, and as an occupational exposure. Acute ingestion, injection, or inhalation causes severe abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, arrhythmias, and a garlic-like odor on the breath. Chronic exposure can cause lung cancer, squamous cell carcinoma, hepatic angiosarcomas, and peripheral polyneuropathy.

E7a8nN.title: Organic mercury poisoning
E7a8nN.description: Poisoning caused by acute, subacute, or chronic exposure to organic mercury compounds (e.g., methylmercury) found in industrial chemicals or environmental contaminants. Manifestations include neurological symptoms (e.g., ataxia, polyneuropathy, blindness, deafness) and, in cases of fetal exposure, teratogenesis. Minamata disease refers to the syndrome caused by ingestion of methylmercury-contaminated seafood.

YHanKN.title: Phosphine
YHanKN.description: A colorless and odorless gas that is commonly used as a fumigant in pest control. Phosphine gas poisoning can lead to respiratory symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, chest pain, acute respiratory distress syndrome), neurologic symptoms (e.g., tremor, paresthesia), and cardiac shock.

bHaHKN.title: Radon
bHaHKN.description: A radioactive, odorless, and colorless gas that is a byproduct of uranium, thorium, and radium decay. Can be found in groundwater and soil. Exposure is associated with lung cancer.

XHa9KN.title: Hydrogen sulfide
XHa9KN.description: A gaseous compound that can be found in the household (e.g., cleaning products), industrial setting (e.g., food processing), and the natural environment (e.g., swamps, hot springs, volcanoes) settings. Hydrogen sulfide intoxication can lead to several adverse effects, such as irritation of the mucous membranes, pulmonary edema, and seizures.

1Ha26N.title: Fluoride
1Ha26N.description: An inorganic compound required for proper mineralization of bones and teeth. Deficiency causes dental caries. Excess causes fluorosis (mottled teeth, joint stiffness).

dHao6N.title: Fluorosis
dHao6N.description: A condition caused by excessive intake of fluoride, typically due to very high levels in drinking water. Dental fluorosis is characterized by mottling and opaque, white staining of teeth. Skeletal fluorosis manifests with joint pain and stiffness caused by mineralization of ligaments, cartilage, and periarticular muscles.

VHaG6N.title: Chronic toxic encephalopathy
VHaG6N.description: A condition of cerebral, cerebellar, and/or brain stem atrophy induced by chronic exposure to organic solvents and/or heavy metals. Characterized by altered mental status and behavioral changes.

gHaFpN.title: Toluene
gHaFpN.description: A chemical compound found in paint thinners sometimes used as a recreational inhalant. Overdose can cause CNS depression, altered mental status, and long-term cognitive impairment.

iHaJJN.title: Ketone
iHaJJN.description: An acidic biochemical compound synthesized in hepatocytes from fatty acids. Produced during periods of starvation, alcohol consumption, and inadequately treated type 1 diabetes. Includes acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate, which can be metabolized by most extrahepatic tissue (e.g., brain, muscle, heart), and acetone, which cannot be metabolized and is exhaled.

destinations.label: Lipids and their metabolism → Ketone body metabolism

media.title: Absorption, metabolism, and synthesis of fatty acids

4Ha3qN.title: Volatile organic compounds
4Ha3qN.description: An organic compound (i.e., one containing carbon-hydrogen bonds) that has high vapor pressure at room temperature. Household items that emit VOCs include paints, cleaning supplies, pesticides, office equipment, and glues.

NHa-qN.title: Methanol
NHa-qN.description: An alcohol used as an antifreeze and solvent. Ingestion (e.g., as a substitute for ethanol) causes altered mental status, hallucinations, seizures, dyspnea, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and blindness due to enzymatic breakdown into the toxic metabolite formats (e.g., formic acid).

nHa7IN.title: Vinyl chloride
nHa7IN.description: A colorless compound that is used in the wood and plastic making industry to make polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Long-term exposure to this compound has been associated with higher prevalence of hepatocellular carcinoma and hepatic angiosarcoma.

oHa0rN.title: Trichloroethene
oHa0rN.description: A volatile liquid that is used to manufacture refrigerants and as a degreasing solvent for metal. Household items that may contain TCE include cleaning wipes and other cleaning products (e.g., carpet cleaner). Prolonged exposure is known to cause cancer in humans (group 1 carcinogen), especially kidney cancer.

sHat7N.title: Anthracosis
sHat7N.description: A type of pneumoconiosis seen in city inhabitants and coal miners due to the chronic inhalation of carbon dust and sooty air. Typically milder than other types of pneumoconiosis and is usually asymptomatic. Primarily affects the upper lobes of the lungs.

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Overview of pneumoconioses

GHaB7N.title: Berylliosis
GHaB7N.description: A rare pneumoconiosis caused by occupational exposure to beryllium, an alkaline earth metal used in alloys (e.g., in the aerospace and manufacturing industries). Usually affects the upper lobes of the lungs.

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Overview of pneumoconioses

uHapHN.title: Byssinosis
uHapHN.description: A pneumoconiosis caused by exposure to nonsynthetic textile dust, such as from cotton, flax, jute, hemp, and sisal. Clinical features include dyspnea, cough, chest tightness, and wheezing.

destinations.label: Interstitial lung diseases → Overview of pneumoconioses

DHa1sN.title: Isocyanate
DHa1sN.description: A chemical used in the production of foams, fibers, and coatings (e.g., varnishes, paint). Inhalation can result in non-IgE-mediated allergic asthma.

wHahsN.title: Two-by-two table
wHahsN.description: A graphical representation of relationships between categorical variables, from which formulas for measures of association (e.g., relative risk, odds ratio), measures of diagnostic accuracy (e.g., sensitivity, specificity), and statistical tests (e.g., Chi-square test, Fisher exact test) can be derived.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Measures of association

CHaqsN.title: Specificity
CHaqsN.description: Most commonly used in the context of epidemiology to refer to the proportion of people without a condition who test negative. A test with a high specificity can be used for confirmatory purposes. The formula for calculating specificity is: True Negatives/(True Negatives + False Positives).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

xHaEsN.title: Positive predictive value
xHaEsN.description: The likelihood that an individual with a positive test result has the condition that is being tested. PPV has a direct relationship with the condition's prevalence and the pretest probability. The formula for calculating PPV is: True Positives/(True Positives + False Positives).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

yHadGN.title: Negative predictive value
yHadGN.description: The likelihood that an individual with a negative test result does not have the condition that is being tested. NPV has an inverse relationship with the condition's prevalence and the pretest probability. The formula for calculating NPV is: True Negatives/(True Negatives + False Negatives).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

_Ha5GN.title: Reliability (epidemiology)
_Ha5GN.description: The reproducibility of test results from the same sample under comparable conditions. A test with a high precision will have minimal random error and a small standard deviation.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Precision and validity

zHarGN.title: Validity
zHarGN.description: The correspondence between a test's results and what the test was developed to measure. A test with high validity/accuracy will have minimal systematic error. For diagnostic tests, accuracy is influenced by the sensitivity and specificity of the test as well as the prevalence of the condition that the test is designed for. Mathematically, accuracy = (true positives + true negatives)/(true positives + false positives + true negatives + false negatives) or the area under the receiver operator curve.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Precision and validity

0saetN.title: Confidence interval
0saetN.description: A range of values associated with an estimate that is thought to contain the true population value with a given level of confidence (most commonly 95%). It is calculated using the standard deviation and the sample size. The specific equation used to calculate confidence intervals depends on the sampling technique and probability distribution used in the study.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Confidence interval

bsaHtN.title: Null hypothesis
bsaHtN.description: The assumption that there is no association between two measured variables (e.g., the exposure and the outcome) or no significant difference between two studied populations other than what would be expected from sampling or experimental error. Statistical tests of significance are designed to assess the strength of the evidence (e.g., experimental data) against the null hypothesis.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Hypothesis testing and probability

Xsa9tN.title: Alternative hypothesis
Xsa9tN.description: The rival statement to the null hypothesis that attributes the association between measured variables (or differences between studied populations) to the existence of a real relationship between the variables (or true effect) as opposed to what may be expected from sampling or experimental error.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Hypothesis testing and probability

csaaFN.title: T-test
csaaFN.description: A statistical test that compares the means of two sets of data to establish whether they are significantly different from one another. E.g., comparing the blood pressure means between men and women. In a paired t-test, data is derived from study subjects who have been measured at two points in time (e.g., before and after a treatment), while in an unpaired t-test, two different groups are sampled at the same time.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Statistical tests

VsaGFN.title: Relative risk
VsaGFN.description: The ratio of the probability of an outcome occurring in an exposed group to the probability of the outcome occurring in an unexposed group. Used as a measure of association in cohort studies and randomized controlled trials. A relative risk > 1.0 indicates a positive association or increased risk; a relative risk < 1.0 indicates a decreased risk or a protective effect.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of association strength

esaxFN.title: Absolute risk reduction
esaxFN.description: The difference in risk attributable to an exposure as compared to non-exposure (i.e., ARR = risk in non-exposed group – risk in exposed group).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of population impact

Usab8N.title: Relative risk reduction
Usab8N.description: An epidemiological measure of risk that refers to the proportion of decreased risk due to an intervention compared to the control group. Calculated by subtracting the relative risk from 1 (i.e., 1 - RR).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of population impact

2saT8N.title: Number needed to treat
2saT8N.description: An epidemiological measure of risk that refers to the number of individuals that must be treated in a particular time period for one person to benefit from treatment (i.e., not develop disease or injury). Calculated by taking the inverse of the absolute risk reduction (i.e., 1/ARR).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of population impact

Tsa68N.title: Number needed to screen
Tsa68N.description: An epidemiological measure of risk that refers to the number of individuals who need to be screened in a particular time period in order to detect a single case of a disease. Calculated by taking the inverse of the absolute risk reduction (i.e., 1/ARR).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of population impact

gsaF8N.title: Number needed to harm
gsaF8N.description: An epidemiological measure of risk that refers to the number of individuals who need to be exposed to a certain risk factor before one person develops disease or injury. Calculated by taking the inverse of the attributable risk (i.e., 1/AR).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of population impact

Ssay8N.title: Odds
Ssay8N.description: The probability of an event occurring divided by the probability of this event not occurring. (Probability of disease) / (Probability of nondisease) = (Probability of disease) / (1 - Probability of disease).

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of association strength

hsacuN.title: Odds ratio
hsacuN.description:
A relative measure of association between an exposure and an event/outcome. Calculated as the odds of 
an event/outcome occurring in the presence of a particular exposure divided by the odds of the event/outcome occurring in the absence of exposure. Typically used in case-control studies.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Estimates of association strength

jsa_uN.title: Clinical significance (epidemiology)
jsa_uN.description:
A significant change in a patient's clinical condition that may or may not be the result of an intervention. 
High clinical significance signifies the intervention's greater impact on patient outcomes or measures.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Statistical tests

lsavEN.title: Confounding
lsavEN.description: A type of systematic error in which a third variable that has not been factored into the study (the confounder) has an association with both the dependent variable (outcome) as well as the independent variable (e.g., exposure to a risk factor). The confounder can suggest a causal association of the outcome with the independent variable, when, in fact, there is none.

destinations.label: Epidemiology → Random errors, bias, and confounding

Nsa-EN.title: Bias
Nsa-EN.description: A statistical error due to faulty design, conduct, or analysis of a study that distorts the statistical findings.  Commonly divided into selection types of bias and observational types of bias.

destinations.label: Epidemiology → Random errors, bias, and confounding

5saivN.title: Healthy worker effect
5saivN.description: A type of sampling bias that occurs when individuals from the working population are preferentially included in a trial. The working population is healthier (on average) than the general population. Limits the external validity of the results of a trial.

destinations.label: Epidemiology → Random errors, bias, and confounding

MsaMvN.title: Information bias
MsaMvN.description: A systematic error caused by inconsistencies in measurement and/or classification between sample groups. Can be caused by human error (e.g., the observer-expectancy effect) or instrument error (e.g., instrument malfunction). Commonly occurs when there are discrepancies in the accuracy of information collected between case and control groups or exposed and unexposed groups.

destinations.label: Epidemiology → Random errors, bias, and confounding

nsa7vN.title: Lead-time bias
nsa7vN.description: A type of bias in studies of screening tests in which survival time is overestimated because of early diagnosis through screening rather than reflecting an actual delay in mortality.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

LsawvN.title: Length-time bias
LsawvN.description: A type of bias in studies of screening tests. Describes a situation in which survival time is overestimated because a larger proportion of slowly progressive cases is detected. Screen tests have a higher probability of detecting slowly progressive cases, which have a longer asymptomatic phase and better prognosis, compared to rapidly progressive cases.

destinations.label: Interpreting medical evidence → Evaluation of screening or diagnostic tests

KsaUDN.title: Cross-sectional study
KsaUDN.description: A type of observational, descriptive study that assesses the point prevalence of exposure and/or prevalence of outcome (e.g., disease) using data from individuals (e.g., assessed in a survey). Can show association but not causality.

6sajDN.title: Cohort study
6sajDN.description: A type of observational, analytical study in which a group of people with and without exposure (e.g., to a risk factor, a preexisting condition) is monitored over time (i.e., longitudinal study) to determine whether the exposure is associated with the outcome of interest (e.g., a disease). Can be prospective or retrospective (through review of medical records). Cohort studies allow for the calculation of the relative risk between exposure and outcome.

psaLDN.title: Observational studies
psaLDN.description: A study design in which the investigator does not apply an intervention to study participants. Particularly useful for studying outcomes when there are ethical concerns about applying the exposure (e.g., the association between radiation exposure and incidence of cancer).

IsaYwN.title: Randomized controlled trials
IsaYwN.description: An type of experimental study that determines the effect of a specific intervention. Patients are randomly allocated as treatment or control subjects for a new intervention/treatment, monitored, and subsequently evaluated for the outcome of interest. Considered the gold standard for a clinical trial.

rsafwN.title: Randomization
rsafwN.description: The act of randomly assigning study participants to treatment and control groups in order to reduce selection bias and confounding bias in clinical trials.

7sa4wN.title: Blinding
7sa4wN.description: The practice of not informing an individual or group about which study participants are part of the control group and which are part of the treatment group in order to reduce bias.

HsaKwN.title: Single-blind study
HsaKwN.description: A type of blinding in a randomized controlled trial in which the study participants do not know who is in the control group and who is in the treatment group, but the study investigators and data analysts are aware of which participants are assigned to which group.

ssatwN.title: Double-blind study
ssatwN.description: A type of blinding in a randomized controlled trial in which the researchers and study participants do not know who is in the control group and who is in the treatment group.

GsaBwN.title: Intention-to-treat analysis
GsaBwN.description: A method of statistical analysis in which the initial randomized treatment groups are compared regardless of the treatment they eventually receive, i.e., regardless of medication nonadherence or refusal of allocated treatment. This method preserves the balance between the two groups created by randomization and reduces selection bias.

tsaX9N.title: Case-control study
tsaX9N.description: A type of observational, analytical study that retrospectively compares the exposure status of individuals with the outcome (cases) to the exposure status of individuals without the outcome (controls). Case-control studies can determine the odds ratio between these groups of people.

Esa89N.title: Morbidity
Esa89N.description: In epidemiology: the number of individuals in a population with a disease at a specific point in time or time interval (i.e., disease frequency). More broadly, refers to the negative health effects, excluding death, associated with a medical condition in a population.

destinations.label: Population health → Measures of disease frequency

vsaA9N.title: Incidence rate
vsaA9N.description: The number of new cases of disease per unit of person-time. Reflects the rate at which the new cases are developing (e.g., 1 case per 100 person-years). Calculated by dividing the number of new cases of disease by the total time the population was at risk. The incidence rate takes into account persons lost to follow-up and attributes some risk of disease to them for the time they are not followed.

destinations.label: Population health → Measures of disease frequency

Dsa1CN.title: Prevalence
Dsa1CN.description: The proportion of a population that has a condition at a specified point in time (point prevalence) or during a specified time period (period prevalence).

destinations.label: Population health → Measures of disease frequency

9saNCN.title: Case fatality rate
9saNCN.description: The proportion of cases of a specific illness that result in death within a specific time period. Calculated as the number of deaths from a specific illness divided by the number of cases with the same specific illness, which is then multiplied by a conversion factor.

destinations.label: Population health → Measures of disease frequency

ysadxN.title: Survival analysis
ysadxN.description: A study used to identify the expected period of time for a particular outcome to manifest. Examples include 5-year survival rates, risk factor exposure to disease onset, and birth to onset of disease.

zsarxN.title: Kaplan-Meier analysis
zsarxN.description: A method of survival analysis that allows the probability of an event occurring over time to be estimated, even when patients are lost to follow-up or are studied for different lengths of time. The probability of an event occurring is calculated for each time interval as the number of patients still without the event having occurred divided by the number of patients at risk. Used to evaluate recovery rates, probability of death, or the effectiveness of treatment.

YGanBN.title: Prevention paradox
YGanBN.description: The phenomenon whereby a preventive measure benefiting a population as a whole offers little benefit to each individual member of the population (e.g., even without measles immunization, only a relatively small proportion of the population would contract the disease).

cGaayN.title: Primary prevention
cGaayN.description: Measures to prevent the onset of disease. Aims to decrease disease incidence and, subsequently, prevalence. Includes lifestyle modifications (e.g., healthy diet, smoking cessation, regular exercise), vaccinations, and health legislation (e.g., seat belt laws, food safety standards).

WGaPyN.title: Secondary prevention
WGaPyN.description: Actions aimed at detecting early-stage disease in asymptomatic patients, allowing for early intervention, which increases the chance of treatment success. Screening is an important example of secondary prevention.

2GaTAN.title: Tertiary prevention
2GaTAN.description: A type of prevention that focuses on optimizing the care of patients with an established disease to improve functionality and prevent complications and relapse (e.g., blood pressure management in hypertension to reduce the risk of a cardiovascular event).

itaJWm.title: Otitis media chronica mesotympanalis
itaJWm.description: Chronic inflammation of the middle ear and mastoid cavity that is associated with conductive hearing loss and recurrent otorrhea through a defect in the tympanic membrane.

QtauWm.title: Tympanosclerosis
QtauWm.description: A condition caused by the calcification of tissues in the middle ear and tympanic membrane most commonly due to recurrent otitis media.

jta_Wm.title: Otitis media with effusion
jta_Wm.description: The presence of mucoid or serous effusion in the tympanic cavity with no signs of acute infection. More common in children than adults and usually occurs after an episode of acute otitis media, during a viral upper respiratory tract infection, or in individuals with eustachian tube dysfunction. Usually self-limited.

4ta3dm.title: Chronic otitis media with effusion
4ta3dm.description: Otitis media with effusion that persists for ≥ 3 months.

ttaX2m.title: Nasal septal hematoma
ttaX2m.description: A collection of blood around the nasal septal bone or cartilage with intact nasal mucosa. It is a serious complication of nasal or facial trauma and associated with a high risk of infection.

Ftag2m.title: Glossitis rhombica mediana
Ftag2m.description: Uncommon, benign condition that appears as a rhomboid-shaped, reddish midline lesion on the middle or back of the dorsum of the tongue. The area is devoid of filiform papillae. Although its etiology is unclear, the condition is often associated with Candida. Affected individuals may report mild discomfort or a burning sensation. No treatment is necessary because the lesion typically regresses.

8taO2m.title: Lingua geographica
8taO2m.description: Benign, recurrent inflammation of the tongue. Loss of filiform papillae results in irregular red patches with surrounding white borders, giving the tongue a map-like appearance. Associated with psoriasis and reactive arthritis. Affected individuals may report mild discomfort or a burning sensation. No treatment is necessary because the lesions typically regress.

utap2m.title: Lingua plicata
utap2m.description: A common tongue condition found in 20–30% of the population and consisting of one or more deep grooves in the dorsum of the tongue. It is associated with Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome, psoriasis, and Trisomy 21. No treatment is necessary unless debris trapped in fissures leads to inflammation, in which case it may be necessary to rinse or brush the area.

vtaA2m.title: Strawberry tongue
vtaA2m.description: A bright red tongue with papillary hyperplasia that typically occurs in scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome, Kawasaki disease, MIS-C, and drug hypersensitivity reactions.

9taNfm.title: Reinke edema
9taNfm.description: A benign buildup of fluid in the superficial lamina propria of the true vocal cords (also known as Reinke's space). Caused by chronic inflammation and irritation secondary to smoking. Patients present with a low-pitched, rough voice. Bilateral swelling of the true vocal cords is visible on laryngoscopy. Treatment includes smoking cessation and voice therapy.

Btazfm.title: Laryngeal papillomatosis
Btazfm.description: A benign tumor of the laryngeal epithelium caused by HPV infection of the throat. Presents with voice changes (e.g., hoarseness) and, in more severe cases, airway obstruction.

AtaRTm.title: Branchial cleft cyst
AtaRTm.description: A congenital neck mass that arise if the embryological second branchial cleft or cervical sinus fail to completely obliterate. Typically presents as a painless mass lateral to midline, usually anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which does not move with swallowing. Treatment involves surgical excision.

destinations.label: Congenital neck masses → Branchial cleft cyst

ztarTm.title: Sialadenosis
ztarTm.description: A recurrent, noninflammatory swelling of the salivary glands that is typically painless. Risk factors include diabetes, nutritional disorders, liver disease, and metabolic syndrome.

destinations.label: Diseases of the salivary glands → Sialadenosis

0Faegm.title: Sialolithiasis
0Faegm.description: The formation of concrements (stones) in the salivary ducts or parenchyma of the glands, most commonly in the submandibular duct. Patients usually present with pain and swelling in the affected gland, typically right before and during eating. More often affects men.

destinations.label: Diseases of the salivary glands → Sialolithiasis

YFangm.title: Ranula
YFangm.description: A retention cyst (mucocele) that arises in the sublingual gland. Presents as a translucent, blue swelling below the tongue. Large ranulas can cause problems swallowing and speaking.

destinations.label: Diseases of the salivary glands → Ranula

dFaoSm.title: Pleomorphic adenoma
dFaoSm.description: A benign mixed (epithelial, myoepithelial, and stromal components) tumor of the salivary glands that most commonly occurs in the parotid gland, followed by the other major salivary glands and the palate.

destinations.label: Diseases of the salivary glands → Benign tumors

media.title: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland

UFabhm.title: Warthin tumor
UFabhm.description: A benign salivary gland tumor that primarily affects the parotid gland. Risk factors for development include smoking and male sex. Typically manifests with painless unilateral swelling of the affected gland.

destinations.label: Diseases of the salivary glands → Benign tumors

jFa_3m.title: Dyslexia
jFa_3m.description: A type of specific learning disorder characterized by difficulties with word recognition, decoding, and spelling.

kFamRm.title: Agrammatism
kFamRm.description: A language impairment that is characterized by the omission or incorrect use of grammatical elements in speech or writing and seen in neurological conditions such as nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia.

oFa0Qm.title: Childhood-onset fluency disorder
oFa0Qm.description: A communication disorder characterized by disturbances in the normal fluency of speech, with onset in early childhood. Manifestations include sound and syllable repetition, broken words, and prolongation of consonants and vowels.

pFaLQm.title: Expressive language delay
pFaLQm.description: A language disorder characterized by the inability to formulate language (e.g., spoken, written, signed language). Can result in word-finding difficulty, omission of words within sentences, and use of incorrect tenses.

JFasQm.title: Receptive language delay
JFasQm.description: A language disorder characterized by the inability to understand and process language (e.g., spoken, written, signed language) received from others. Can result in impairments in paying attention, following directions, and recalling information.

qFaCQm.title: Landau-Kleffner syndrome
qFaCQm.description: A rare childhood disorder characterized by recurrent seizures and loss of language comprehension and verbal expression. Typically manifests between 3–7 years of age.

HFaKjm.title: Hematoxylin-eosin staining
HFaKjm.description: A commonly used histologic stain. Hematoxylin binds to basophilic substances (e.g., DNA/RNA in nucleus) and stains them blue/violet. Eosin binds to acidophilic substances (e.g., intracytoplasmatic proteins, mitochondria, collagen) and stains them in shades of red.

EFa8Pm.title: Periodic acid-Schiff
EFa8Pm.description: A staining method for detecting sugars within tissues. Used to help detect a variety of diseases (e.g., glycogen storage disease, renal disease) and certain pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium avium, pathogenic fungi).

media.title: PAS-positive foam cells in Whipple's disease

DFa14m.title: Prussian blue staining
DFa14m.description: A stain used to evaluate for the presence of iron in tissue samples.

9FaN4m.title: Congo red
9FaN4m.description: A chemical dye used to stain amyloid deposits (e.g., in amyloidosis, medullary thyroid carcinoma).

BFaz4m.title: Punch biopsy
BFaz4m.description: Procedure in which a cone-shaped core of tissue is removed, with the wide base of the cone corresponding to the skin surface and the point of the cone corresponding to the biopsy base; often used for diagnostic biopsies or removing small skin lesions.

_Fa5km.title: Cytology
_Fa5km.description: The study of cellular morphology. Cells are collected (e.g., from swabs, sputum, aspiration) and examined with microscopic techniques. Often used to evaluate for malignancy.

-FaDkm.title: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy
-FaDkm.description: A procedure in which a thin, hollow needle is used to collect a sample of cells from a mass or lesion for analysis. Less invasive than an incisional or excisional surgical biopsy.

a8aQOm.title: Flow cytometry
a8aQOm.description: A diagnostic test in which fluorescent-labeled antibodies against a target antigen (e.g., cellular biomarker) are exposed to a sample of cells. A specific laser wavelength is then passed through the labeled sample to detect the degree of fluorescence, indicating target antigen levels.

destinations.label: Pathology techniques → Special methods in pathology and molecular biology

media.title: Flow cytometry scatter plot of B and T cells in infectious mononucleosis

Y8anOm.title: Electron microscopy
Y8anOm.description: A type of microscopy that uses a beam of electrons to achieve higher magnification than is possible with light microscopy.

destinations.label: Pathology techniques → Special methods in pathology and molecular biology

X8a9Om.title: Immunohistochemistry
X8a9Om.description: The identification of specific antigens in a histological specimen using antibodies that are tagged with an indicator (e.g., enzymes, radioactive molecules, or fluorescent dyes).

destinations.label: Pathology techniques → Special methods in pathology and molecular biology

18a2lm.title: Dysplasia
18a2lm.description: A disordered growth of epithelium characterized by abnormally frequent mitotic figures and loss of cell orientation and uniformity (size, shape). Can progress to irreversible malignancy but reversible if not all epithelial layers are affected (known as carcinoma in situ).

W8aPlm.title: Hyperplasia
W8aPlm.description: An increase in the amount of organic tissue due to an increase in cell number.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular adaptation

d8aolm.title: Hypertrophy
d8aolm.description: An increase in the amount of organic tissue due to an increase in cell size.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular adaptation

e8axlm.title: Labile cell
e8axlm.description: A cell type that divides rapidly with a short G1 phase and never enters the G0 phase. Especially sensitive to chemotherapy due to their rapid and continuous division. Examples include epithelial cells of the skin and gastrointestinal tract, hematopoietic tissue, and germ cells.

destinations.label: The cell cycle → Cell cycle regulation

j8a_mm.title: Apoptosis
j8a_mm.description: A process of programmed cell death. Characterized by destruction of cellular contents with an intact cell membrane and minimal inflammation.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Apoptosis

P8aW5m.title: Fibrinoid necrosis
P8aW5m.description: The necrosis of small blood vessels caused by autoimmune diseases or malignant hypertension. Deposits of immune complexes, complement, fibrin, and other plasma proteins result in a bright pink and amorphous (fibrinoid) appearance on hematoxylin-eosin staining.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

48a35m.title: Coagulative necrosis
48a35m.description: A type of necrosis caused by tissue ischemia, which denatures proteolytic enzymes. Occurs in most tissues except the brain. Histopathologic examination shows preserved, anuclear, eosinophilic cellular architecture.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

k8am5m.title: Liquefactive necrosis
k8am5m.description: A type of necrosis characterized by partial or complete dissolution of dead tissue and transformation into a liquid, viscous mass. Caused by neutrophilic release of lysosomal enzymes that digest tissue. Characterized histologically by macrophages and cellular debris (early) followed by cystic spaces (late). Seen in bacterial abscesses and brain infarcts.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

O8aI5m.title: Necrosis
O8aI5m.description: An irreversible tissue injury that results in cellular death and inflammation. Typically caused by cellular swelling and damage (oncosis) due to tissue ischemia. In contrast to apoptosis, necrosis involves rupture of the cellular membrane and is generally not considered physiologic.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Necrosis

N8a-5m.title: Councilman body
N8a-5m.description: An eosinophilic remnant of apoptotic hepatocytes seen on liver biopsy. Associated with yellow fever and viral hepatitis.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular inclusions

m8aVMm.title: Hyaline
m8aVMm.description: An intracellular or extracellular eosinophilic protein deposition that appears pink on H&E staining (and red on Van Gieson stain). Intracellular hyaline can accumulate in hepatocytes and neurons. Extracellular hyaline can accumulate in arterial walls or as amyloid in individuals with Alzheimer disease.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular inclusions

58aiMm.title: Hyalinization
58aiMm.description: The replacement of normal tissue by nonspecific proteins that have an eosinophilic, homogeneous, translucent appearance on hematoxylin and eosin staining.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular inclusions

n8a7Mm.title: Mallory bodies
n8a7Mm.description: A histopathologic finding characterized by inclusion bodies within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes. Consist of intermediate filaments and appear pink on H&E stain. Associated with alcoholic liver disease.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular inclusions

68ajnm.title: Schaumann bodies
68ajnm.description: A type of cellular inclusion body associated with granulomatous diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, Crohn disease, berylliosis). Consists of intracytoplasmic calcium, iron, and protein with laminar stratification.

destinations.label: Cellular changes and adaptive responses → Cellular inclusions

u8apom.title: Generalized anxiety disorder
u8apom.description: An anxiety disorder characterized by excessive and persistent anxiety for ≥ 6 months. Symptoms can be triggered in various situations, with or without an identifiable stressor, and cause significant social or occupational dysfunction.

v8aAom.title: Panic disorder
v8aAom.description: An anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks in addition to a ≥ 1-month period of persistent worry about experiencing additional attacks or their consequences, and/or maladaptive behavior to avoid further episodes.

B8azKm.title: Agoraphobia
B8azKm.description: An inordinate fear or anxiety of being in situations that are perceived as difficult to escape from and/or situations in which it might be difficult to seek help. Symptoms must occur over a period of ≥ 6 months in ≥ 2 of the following situations: 1) when using public transportation, 2) when in open spaces, 3) when in enclosed places, 4) when in line or a crowd, 5) when outside of the home alone.

y8ad6m.title: Social anxiety disorder
y8ad6m.description: An anxiety disorder characterized by intense and disproportionate fear and/or anxiety of social situations in which the individual may be scrutinized or judged (e.g., meeting new people, parties, eating in public). Typically accompanied by multiple physical symptoms, e.g., blushing, palpitations, sweating.

A8aR6m.title: Specific phobia
A8aR6m.description: A type of anxiety disorder in which patients have a persistent and intense fear of specific situations or objects (phobic stimulus). Patients develop symptoms of anxiety during encounters with the phobic stimulus.

_8a56m.title: Acute stress disorder
_8a56m.description: A psychiatric disorder triggered by a personally experienced or witnessed traumatic event. Symptoms last between 3 days and 1 month and include intrusive thoughts, avoidance of reminders of traumatic events, negative cognition or mood (e.g., depression), and altered reactivity and arousal (e.g., irritability, sleep disturbances).

destinations.label: Acute and posttraumatic stress disorders → Summary

cuaaJm.title: Dissociative amnesia
cuaaJm.description: A type of memory impairment that affects autobiographical memory (knowledge of the self) and is often associated with a traumatic or stressful event. Can be localized (i.e., of a single event or time period), selective (i.e., of a specific aspect of an event), or generalized (i.e., of life history and identity). Patients typically recover, although in some cases memory loss is not reversible.

WuaPJm.title: Dissociative fugue
WuaPJm.description: A dissociative disorder characterized by wandering or purposeful travel that the affected individual has no recollection of. It is associated with generalized dissociative amnesia.

duaoJm.title: Dissociative identity disorder
duaoJm.description: A form of dissociative disorder that results in the formation of one or more alternate personalities. The patient's main personality may or may not be conscious of the actions of the emergent personalities. Patients may present with large gaps in memory and deficits in their consciousness, awareness, and perception that can interfere with functioning in their day to day life.

euaxJm.title: Dissociative anesthesia
euaxJm.description: A pharmacologically induced cataleptic state characterized by profound amnesia and analgesia. Protective airway reflexes, spontaneous respiration, and cardiovascular stability are usually maintained. Dissociative anesthetics include ketamine and nitrous oxide.

Tua6qm.title: Ganser syndrome
Tua6qm.description: A syndrome in which patients give approximate answers (i.e., answers that are incorrect but demonstrate some understanding of the question). For example, a patient may answer "December" when asked what month comes after August. This etiology of this syndrome is unknown; it is not listed in the DSM-5.

3uaSIm.title: Battered child syndrome
3uaSIm.description: A clinical condition in young children who have received serious physical abuse, often caused by a parent or caretaker. It is characterized by multiple non-accidental injuries showing different states of healing in a child, resulting from long-term physical violence.

iuaJIm.title: Shaken baby syndrome
iuaJIm.description: A form of physical abuse in which a child is violently shaken, leading to head trauma due to rotational shearing forces. These forces tear bridging veins, leading to subdural hematoma, and cause diffuse axonal damage. Symptoms include irritability, lethargy, retinal hemorrhages, and tense or bulging fontanelles. Often associated with other injuries indicative of child abuse, such as rib fractures.

destinations.label: Child maltreatment → Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome)

media.title: Retinal findings in shaken baby syndrome

PuaWrm.title: Illness anxiety disorder
PuaWrm.description: A persistent preoccupation with having or developing a serious illness for ≥ 6 months. Somatic symptoms are usually absent or mild, but patients display a long-term obsession with their health and/or the possibility of developing a disease.

destinations.label: Somatic symptom and related disorders → Illness anxiety disorder

kuamrm.title: Neurocirculatory asthenia
kuamrm.description: A syndrome considered to be a form of anxiety disorder. Symptoms typically manifest after mild exertion and include palpitations, shortness of breath, subjective discomfort, dizziness, sweating, and tremulousness.

5uai7m.title: Paranoid personality disorder
5uai7m.description: A cluster A personality disorder that is characterized by excessive distrust and suspicion of others. Individuals perceive even insignificant incidents as directed against them. Onset is typically in early adulthood.

nua77m.title: Schizoid personality disorder
nua77m.description: A cluster A personality disorder characterized by detachment from interpersonal relationships and restricted expression of emotions in interpersonal settings. Patients do not enjoy or have close relationships, tend to choose solitary activities, and appear indifferent to praise/criticism of others. The symptoms usually begin during adolescence.

oua0Hm.title: Antisocial personality disorder
oua0Hm.description: A cluster B personality disorder that is characterized by a lack of empathy and remorse. Affected individuals are manipulative, impulsive, and break laws and rules for their own gain. The patient must be ≥ 18 years old and must have met the criteria for conduct disorder before age 15. In addition, ≥ 3 following diagnostic criteria have to be present: history of unlawful acts, history of deceiving or manipulating others, history of aggression or assaults, disregard for safety, impulsivity, failure to sustain work or other obligations, and lack of remorse.

6uajHm.title: Histrionic personality disorder
6uajHm.description: A cluster B personality disorder characterized by theatrical affect and behavior that others may perceive as shallow and exaggerating. Patients have patterns of excessive emotionality, sexual inappropriateness, and attention-seeking behavior (e.g., using physical appearance to draw attention to self). Speech is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail.

JuasHm.title: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
JuasHm.description: A cluster C personality disorder characterized by egosyntonic perfectionism, unwillingness to delegate work, inflexibility, and obsession with work, productivity, rules, and rigid routines. Obsession often occurs at the expense of occupational success (e.g., missing deadlines), social relationships (e.g., excluding social activities to complete tasks), and pleasurable activities (e.g., not taking a vacation). In contrast to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are not present.

ruafsm.title: Avoidant personality disorder
ruafsm.description: A cluster C personality disorder characterized by an overall feeling of inadequacy, an intense fear of rejection, and avoidance of situations that may result in rejection (e.g., interpersonal relationships). Such patients actually wish to be with others but are timid and easily hurt by other people's remarks. The symptoms usually begin during adolescence.

7ua4sm.title: Dependent personality disorder
7ua4sm.description: A cluster C personality disorder characterized by a pervasive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behavior (e.g., difficulty making decisions independently, feeling a need to have others assume responsibility over own life, lack of self-confidence; feeling of helplessness when alone; urgently seeking out a new relationship if previous relationship is ended).  The symptoms usually begin during adolescence.

GuaBsm.title: Cluster A
GuaBsm.description: A group of personality disorders characterized by odd and eccentric behavior. Includes paranoid personality disorder, schizoid personality disorder, and schizotypal personality disorder.

9uaNtm.title: Cannabinoids
9uaNtm.description: A category of exogenous bioactive substances that act primarily on cannabinoid receptors.  May be derived from the cannabis plant or synthesized.

xuaEtm.title: Cocaine use disorder
xuaEtm.description: A problematic pattern of cocaine use that causes clinically significant impairment or distress. Features include tolerance, withdrawal, craving, excess time and activity obtaining or using cocaine, and disruption of social or occupational activities due to cocaine use.

destinations.label: Substance-related and addictive disorders → Stimulant-related disorders

Buaztm.title: Amphetamines
Buaztm.description: A drug (and class of drugs) that act as sympathomimetics. They function by promoting the release of catecholamines (primarily dopamine and norepinephrine) from presynaptic nerve terminals, increasing time in the synapse by competitively inhibiting reuptake, and inhibiting monoamine oxidase. Sometimes used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness (e.g., narcolepsy) or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Rarely first-line drugs because of the high risk of dependence and abuse.

ZEaZ8m.title: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate
ZEaZ8m.description: A direct agonist of GABA receptors. Intoxication typically causes lightheadedness, loss of consciousness, and can induce amnesia for the time of intoxication.

0Eae8m.title: Date rape drug
0Eae8m.description: A substance that can be used to incapacitate a victim, impairing the ability to make decisions and provide consent and thereby making them vulnerable to sexual assault. Examples include alcohol, psychoactive drugs (e.g., MDMA), and CNS depressants (e.g., GHB, ketamine).

aEaQ8m.title: Kanner's syndrome
aEaQ8m.description: A condition previously established in the DSM-IV and now considered an autism spectrum disorder in the DSM-V. Typically characterized by impaired language competence, communication skills, and emotional response. Patients with this condition often also have repetitive, stereotyped movements, fixation and attachment to certain objects, and are uncomfortable with changes to their typical environment.

cEaaum.title: Asperger syndrome
cEaaum.description: The term "Asperger syndrome" was historically used for a condition that is now considered an autism spectrum disorder. This term is not used within AMBOSS. Hans Asperger was an Austrian pediatrician who cooperated with Nazi policies of eugenics, forced sterilization, and mass murder.

VEaGum.title: Childhood disintegrative disorder
VEaGum.description: A condition previously established in the DSM-IV and now considered an autism spectrum disorder in the DSM-V. Typically characterized by normal language and cognitive development followed by a loss of these acquired skills within the course of a few months.

2EaTEm.title: Nocturnal enuresis
2EaTEm.description: Bedwetting that occurs at least twice weekly, for ≥ 3 months, in patients ≥ 5 years old (or equivalent developmental age).

fEakEm.title: Enuresis
fEakEm.description: The repeated elimination of urine during sleep in an individual with a developmental age ≥ 5 years. Monosymptomatic enuresis is characterized by nighttime wetting only, while nonmonosymptomatic enuresis manifests with additional daytime urinary symptoms (e.g., daytime incontinence, urinary urgency, difficulty voiding). In primary enuresis, nocturnal dryness has never been achieved. In secondary enuresis, symptom onset occurs after ≥ 6 months of nocturnal dryness.

TEa6Em.title: Encopresis
TEa6Em.description: A disorder primarily seen in children that is characterized by recurrent defecation in inappropriate places (e.g., into clothes, on the floor). May be involuntary or intentional. Diagnostic criteria include age > 4 years, frequency of > 3 months, and at least 1 episode per month.

SEayEm.title: Pica
SEayEm.description: An eating disorder characterized by the ingestion of nonnutritive substances (e.g., hair, paint, plaster, cloth) in individuals for whom this is neither developmentally appropriate nor part of a culturally normative practice. Causes include nutritional deficiencies (e.g., iron deficiency anemia), intellectual developmental disorder, and pregnancy.

hEacvm.title: Stereotypic movement disorder
hEacvm.description: A neurodevelopmental condition characterized by repetitive, purposeless movements that interfere with daily functioning and may cause self-injury.

3EaSvm.title: Tic
3EaSvm.description: Sudden and rapid movements or vocalizations that are intermittent, nonrhythmic, and without any recognizable purpose. Usually involuntary but may be temporarily controlled. An urge or sensation preceding the tic is relieved by its onset (premonitory urge). Exacerbating factors include fatigue and excitement.

iEaJvm.title: Tourette syndrome
iEaJvm.description: A neurobehavioral disorder characterized by motor and vocal tics that manifest in childhood. Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common.

PEaWDm.title: Hemifacial spasm
PEaWDm.description: A condition characterized by involuntary contactions of the muscles on one side of the face. Manifestations include eyelid twitching and pulling of the mouth to one side. Most commonly caused by compression of the facial nerve by a blood vessel.

4Ea3Dm.title: Sleep hygiene
4Ea3Dm.description: A set of practices and habits that promote good nighttime sleep. Includes getting regular aerobic exercise and avoiding naps during the day, avoiding stimulants (e.g., caffeine, nicotine), bright lights, and electronic screens before bedtime, establishing a bedtime routine, and maintaining a regular sleep schedule involving 7-8 hours of sleep per night.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Insomnia disorder

kEamDm.title: Nightmare disorder
kEamDm.description: An REM sleep arousal disorder characterized by recurrent frightening dreams during the second half of the sleep cycle, which the patient remembers upon waking.

mEaVwm.title: Insomnia disorder
mEaVwm.description: The most common sleep-wake disorder. Characterized by difficulty initiating sleep, frequent awakening, awakening too early in the morning, and/or fatigue after waking. Diagnosed if symptoms occur ≥ 3 days/week for ≥ 3 months, cause functional impairment and/or distress, occur despite having adequate time to sleep, and occur in the absence of an underlying psychiatric disorder or substance use.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Insomnia disorder

MEaMwm.title: Parasomnias
MEaMwm.description: A group of disorders characterized by abnormal movements, behavior, emotions, and/or perceptions that occur during specific sleep stages (e.g., REM or NREM sleep) or during sleep-wake transitions. Parasomnias are most common in young children (pre-schoolers). NREM-associated parasomnias include sleep terror disorder and sleep walking. REM-associated parasomnias include nightmares and sleep paralysis.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Classification of sleep disorders

nEa7wm.title: Sleep terror disorder
nEa7wm.description: A non-REM sleep arousal disorder characterized by episodes of apparent nightmares, during which patients will show signs of stress (including tachycardia or diaphoresis), are difficult to rouse, and do not recall what they dreamed after awakening.

oEa09m.title: Somnambulism
oEa09m.description: A parasomnia characterized by ambulating while in a state of sleep.

-EaDym.title: Autopsy
-EaDym.description: The postmortem examination of a body to determine the cause of death, which typically involves the dissection of the body. There are two types of autopsies: clinical autopsies, which can be requested by patients, surrogates, or next of kin regardless of the manner of death; and forensic autopsies, which are part of a medicolegal death investigation in unexplained or unnatural deaths and are performed at the request of the local death investigation office.

ZvaZAm.title: Clinical autopsy
ZvaZAm.description: An autopsy that is performed at the behest of the patient, patient's surrogate decision-maker, or patient's next-of-kin to determine the cause(s) of death or to confirm a diagnosis that could not have been confirmed before death.

avaQAm.title: Forensic autopsy
avaQAm.description: An autopsy requested by a death investigation authority (such as a coroner or medical examiner) or law enforcement. Although specific criteria differ by state, common indications include unwitnessed deaths, unexplained deaths (e.g., SIDS, sudden death), deaths in custody, deaths occurring during a medical procedure or within 24 hours of hospital admission; and deaths suspected to involve suicide, homicide, manslaughter, accidental overdose, accidental trauma, or malpractice.

KvaUa5.title: Dashboard injury
KvaUa5.description: An injury caused by sudden, posteriorly directed force to the proximal tibia while the knee is in flexion (e.g., from the dashboard of a car during a motor vehicle collision). Most commonly causes posterior cruciate ligament tear, hip dislocation, and fractures of the patella and femoral neck.

Dva1X5.title: External suffocation
Dva1X5.description: A type of asphyxia caused by oxygen deprivation due to obstruction of the nose and mouth.

WDaPW5.title: Bruise
WDaPW5.description: An injury associated with localized ischemia, edema, and/or mass effect due to the rupture of blood vessels, usually as a result of direct trauma without penetrating injury. Can occur in soft tissue (e.g., skin, muscle, brain), bone, and internal organs.

dDaoW5.title: Coma blisters
dDaoW5.description: Tense, subepidermal bullae that develop over pressure points in patients who are comatose. May be preceded by erythematous patches or plaques.

VDaGW5.title: Frostbite
VDaGW5.description: A severe localized tissue injury due to freezing. Damage occurs by direct cold-induced cell death as well as delayed inflammation from reperfusion injury. Electrolyte flux can also occur if intracellular ice crystals form.

TDa6d5.title: Electric shock
TDa6d5.description: An injury sustained when electrical current enters the body, passes through tissues, and exits the body. Can cause thermal injury because the electric current converts to heat. Other effects include tetanic muscle contraction, arrhythmia, and acute compartment syndrome.

destinations.label: Environmental pathology → Electrical and lightning injuries

hDacV5.title: Lichtenberg figure
hDacV5.description: A skin lesion characterized by branching, fern- or feather-like patterns. Pathognomonic for lightning injury. Typically fade within hours of onset.

destinations.label: Environmental pathology → Electrical and lightning injuries

jDa_V5.title: Factitious disorder imposed on another
jDa_V5.description: A psychiatric condition in which an individual intentionally falsifies manifestations of disease in another individual (e.g., their child or elderly dependent) for primary gain. Associated with a history of maternal abuse and personality disorders.

destinations.label: Somatic symptom and related disorders → Factitious disorders

mDaVU5.title: Apgar score
mDaVU5.description: A scoring system used to gauge the clinical status of newborn infants at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Includes: Appearance (skin color), Pulse, Grimace (reflex irritability upon tactile stimulation), Activity (muscle tone, movement), and Respirations. An Apgar score ≥ 7 is considered reassuring.

destinations.label: The newborn infant → Postdelivery care and Apgar score

nDa7U5.title: Biotinidase deficiency
nDa7U5.description: An inherited metabolic disorder that leads to biotin deficiency. Manifestations include neurologic abnormalities (e.g., seizures, delayed development), dermatitis, and hypotonia.

KDaU25.title: Isovaleric acidemia
KDaU25.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of isovaleryl-CoA carboxylase, which converts isovaleryl-CoA (a product of leucine catabolism) to methylcrotonyl-CoA. Usually manifests in infancy with vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, failure to thrive, seizures, anion gap metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, ketotic hypoglycemia, and urinary excretion of isovaleric acid.

6Daj25.title: Long-chain hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
6Daj25.description: A condition in which a deficiency in long-chain fatty acid oxidation causes a buildup of toxic fatty acid intermediates. Manifests with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, increased urinary 3-hydroxycarboxylic acids, liver dysfunction, skeletal myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and cardiomyopathy.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of metabolism → Fatty acid metabolism disorders

qDaC25.title: Preterm birth
qDaC25.description: A live birth between 20 weeks' and 37 weeks' gestation. Subcategories include extremely preterm (< 28 weeks), very preterm (28 to < 32 weeks), and moderate to late preterm (32 to < 37 weeks). Associated with a higher risk for severe complications, such as neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, cardiovascular disease (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus, hypotonia), retinopathy of prematurity, necrotizing enterocolitis, periventricular leukomalacia, intracranial hemorrhage, anemia, infection, and sepsis.

7Da4f5.title: Large-for-gestational-age infant
7Da4f5.description: An infant with a birth weight > 90th percentile for its gestational age.

HDaKf5.title: Small-for-gestational-age infant
HDaKf5.description: An infant with a birth weight < 10th percentile for gestational age.

GDaBf5.title: Perinatal period
GDaBf5.description: A time period that precedes and follows birth. The World Health Organization defines the beginning of the perinatal period at 22 completed weeks (154 days) of gestation and the end at seven completed days after birth.

tDaXT5.title: Full term infant
tDaXT5.description: A live birth that occurs between 39 0/7 weeks and 40 6/7 weeks of gestation.

vDaAT5.title: Denver Developmental Screening Test
vDaAT5.description: A standardized test that assesses the development of children between 0–6 years. The test is broken down into for categories: personal-social, fine motor-adaptive, language, gross motor. Less frequently used today as it does not include socioemotional development.

wDahg5.title: Moro reflex
wDahg5.description: A primitive reflex elicited by loud noises and sudden movements (e.g., holding an infant in the supine position while supporting the head, then allowing the head to suddenly fall back). In response, the infant abducts and extends the arms, opens the hands, then adducts the arms and flexes the elbows. Typically persists until 3–6 months of age. A bilaterally absent Moro reflex indicates brain injury (e.g., birth asphyxia, intracranial hemorrhage). A unilaterally absent Moro reflex indicates ipsilateral brachial plexus injury or ipsilateral clavicle fracture.

destinations.label: Child development and milestones → Primitive reflexes

2waTR5.title: Achondroplasia
2waTR5.description: A common cause of short stature caused by mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene. Associated with abnormalities of the spinal curvature, varus or valgus knee deformities, and an increased risk for ear infections.

SwayR5.title: Osteogenesis imperfecta
SwayR5.description: A genetic disorder characterized by defective synthesis of type 1 collagen, which is important in bone formation. Patients present with signs that are sometimes mistaken for child abuse (e.g., easy bruising, predisposition to bony fractures). Additional clinical features include blue sclerae, joint laxity, hearing loss, and brittle, opalescent teeth.

destinations.label: Skeletal dysplasias → Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease)

media.title: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) fact sheet

hwaci5.title: Familial short stature
hwaci5.description: Inherited, nonpathological short stature. Individuals with familial short stature have a normal birth history and gestational weight as well as a bone age that is consistent with the individual's age. The onset of puberty is not delayed.

destinations.label: Short stature → Genetic causes of short stature

Rwali5.title: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Rwali5.description: A benign, nonpathological variant of growth and pubertal development in which children grow at a normal rate but have a delayed skeletal maturation, delayed growth spurt, and delayed onset of puberty. Normal adult height is expected.

destinations.label: Short stature → Genetic causes of short stature

4wa3Q5.title: Noonan syndrome
4wa3Q5.description: A rare genetic condition due to a mutation in the PTPN11 gene on chromosome 12. Clinical features include short stature, webbed neck, chest deformities, facial anomalies (hypertelorism and downslanting eyes), and cardiac defects (particularly pulmonary valve stenosis).

kwamQ5.title: Cerebral gigantism
kwamQ5.description: A condition caused by haploinsufficiency of the NSD1 gene, which encodes a histone methyltransferase involved in histone modification and chromatin remodeling. Characterized by increased head circumference, scoliosis, advanced bone age, hypotonia, and delays in gross motor, fine motor, and intellectual development.

lwavQ5.title: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
lwavQ5.description: A congenital overgrowth syndrome in which affected infants are larger than normal. Other commonly associated features include macroglossia, abdominal wall defects (e.g., omphalocele), recurrent neonatal hypoglycemia, and an increased risk of neoplasia during childhood (e.g., Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma).

5waij5.title: Pituitary gigantism
5waij5.description: A disorder characterized by abnormal linear growth secondary to excess growth hormone (GH) during childhood, when the epiphyseal growth plates are still open. Most commonly caused by a GH-secreting anterior pituitary adenoma.

nwa7j5.title: 47,XXX syndrome
nwa7j5.description: A syndrome caused by an additional X chromosome in females. Manifests with tall stature, delayed motor development, learning disabilities, and menstrual abnormalities. The majority of triple X women are never diagnosed.

Lwawj5.title: XYY syndrome
Lwawj5.description: A chromosomal disorder, in which males have an extra Y chromosome. Affected patients are usually very tall and often have learning disabilities. Former notions that individuals with  XYY syndrome are more aggressive and at increased risk of committing crimes have been disproven.

KwaUP5.title: Congenital toxoplasmosis
KwaUP5.description: Neonatal toxoplasmosis infection as a result of intrauterine transmission. Usually asymptomatic but may present with low birth weight, premature delivery, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae/purpura, chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and/or diffuse intracranial calcifications.

qwaCP5.title: Triad of congenital rubella syndrome
qwaCP5.description: A constellation of birth defects resulting from intrauterine rubella infection during the first trimester. Classical triad of defects: sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and/or cardiac defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus).

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital rubella infection

media.title: Congenital rubella infection TORCH fact sheet

IwaY45.title: Congenital rubella infection
IwaY45.description: A neonatal rubella infection as a result of intrauterine transmission during the first trimester. Classic triad of defects is sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and cardiac defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus). Additional features include low birth weight, purpura/petechiae, a blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, osteitis, microcephaly, and other ocular manifestations (e.g., salt and pepper retinopathy, microphthalmos, congenital glaucoma).

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital rubella infection

media.title: Congenital rubella infection TORCH fact sheet

rwaf45.title: Congenital syphilis
rwaf45.description: A neonatal T. pallidum infection as a result of intrauterine transmission or contact with an active syphilitic lesion during delivery. Most remain asymptomatic at birth, while 10–30% present with hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, a mucocutaneous rash, persistent rhinitis (snuffles), hemolytic anemia, hydrops fetalis, and/or osteitis. Late manifestations include dental abnormalities, sensorineural deafness, and interstitial keratitis (Hutchinson triad).

media.title: Hutchinson's Teeth resulting from congenital syphilis

Fwagk5.title: Hutchinson triad
Fwagk5.description: A constellation of birth defects typical of late congenital syphilis that includes interstitial keratitis, sensorineural hearing loss (due to damage to cranial nerve VIII), and Hutchinson teeth (notched incisors).

uwapk5.title: Congenital listeriosis
uwapk5.description: Neonatal infection with Listeria monocytogenes. Significant risk factors include maternal exposure to unpasteurized dairy. Intrauterine infection causes early-onset severe systemic infection with respiratory distress syndrome and skin lesions (granulomatosis infantiseptica). Peripartum infection causes meningitis/encephalitis at ~ 3 weeks of age.

vwaAk5.title: Congenital CMV infection
vwaAk5.description: Newborn CMV infection due to intrauterine transmission. Usually asymptomatic, but 10% present with jaundice due to liver dysfunction, petechiae/purpura due to thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, hearing loss, low birth weight, premature birth, and/or periventricular calcification on an MRI. Most common congenital infection in the US affecting ~ 1% of all live births.

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital CMV infection

Dwa1O5.title: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection
Dwa1O5.description: A severe vesicular eruption of the skin, eyes, or mouth (SEM disease) in newborns caused by vertical transmission of HSV, typically during vaginal delivery in a mother with active genital herpes. Complications such as meningoencephalitis and/or disseminated disease (causing sepsis and affecting visceral organs) are common.

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital herpes simplex virus infection

wwahO5.title: Congenital varicella syndrome
wwahO5.description: Neonatal varicella-zoster infection as a result of intrauterine transmission during the first and second trimester. Results in low birth weight, cicatricial scarring along dermatomes, limb atrophy, ocular defects (e.g., chorioretinitis, cataracts, microphthalmus), and/or neurological abnormalities (e.g., cortical atrophy, seizures, neurogenic bladder). Rare condition in the US because of maternal immunity due to vaccination, or prior exposure to the virus.

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital varicella infection

CwaqO5.title: Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy
CwaqO5.description: Neonatal parvovirus B19 infection as result of intrauterine transmission. Most often asymptomatic but some infections result in aplastic anemia and fetal hydrops. Less common features include hepatosplenomegaly, blueberry muffin rash, as well radiolucent metaphyseal lesions. Intrauterine demise occurs in ~ 10% of cases, most often during the 1st or 2nd trimester.

destinations.label: Congenital TORCH infections → Congenital parvovirus B19 infection

xwaEO5.title: Fetal alcohol syndrome
xwaEO5.description: A condition caused by maternal alcohol use during pregnancy that is characterized by facial dysmorphisms, growth deficiency, and neurocognitive deficits. Associated birth defects such as ventricular septal defect, aplastic/horseshoe kidneys, hearing loss, and joint abnormalities are also common.

destinations.label: Teratogenesis → Risks of substance use during pregnancy

media.title: Clinical findings in fetal alcohol syndrome

-waDl5.title: Phocomelia
-waDl5.description: A teratogenic limb defect caused by maternal use of thalidomide or from genetic inheritance. Hands or feet are attached to the shoulder or hip due to absence of the proximal portion of the limb.

c9aam5.title: Syndactyly
c9aam5.description: A fusion of two or more fingers or toes. The most common congenital malformation of the limbs.

19a2m5.title: Klinefelter syndrome
19a2m5.description: A genetic condition in which a male inherits one (~ 80%) or more additional X chromosomes (e.g., 47, XXY or 48, XXXY), causing decreased serum testosterone. Typical presentations include a tall/slender frame, sparse pubic hair, decreased muscle bulk, infertility, and gynecomastia.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Klinefelter syndrome

d9aom5.title: Trisomy 18
d9aom5.description: A congenital disease in which there is a third copy of chromosome 18 (trisomy 18). Characterized by prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched fists with flexion contractures of the fingers, rocker bottom feet, and organ malformations (congenital heart defects, horseshoe kidneys). Constitutes the second most common trisomy in liveborn children.

e9axm5.title: Rocker-bottom feet
e9axm5.description: A convex deformity of the plantar side of the foot. May be congenital (characteristic finding in infants with trisomy 18 and trisomy 13) or acquired (most commonly seen in patients with neuropathic arthropathy).

29aT55.title: Trisomy 13
29aT55.description: A disease caused by trisomy of chromosome 13. The least common and most severe chromosomal trisomy (~ 1:10,000 live births). The most characteristic clinical features include microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, polydactyly, and congenital heart defects.

T9a655.title: Triploidy
T9a655.description: A type of numerical chromosomal aberration characterized by the presence of three sets of chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes (two sets of 23 chromosomes), while triploids have 69 chromosomes.

g9aF55.title: Trisomy
