g9aF55.description: A type of numerical chromosomal aberration characterized by the presence of a triplicate instead of a duplicate number of a particular chromosome or part of a chromosome.

S9ay55.title: Webbed neck
S9ay55.description: A physical finding characterized by skin folds along the side of the neck between the mastoid process and the acromion. Almost exclusively observed in patients with Turner syndrome.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Turner syndrome

39aSM5.title: Streak gonads
39aSM5.description: A consequence of gonadal dysgenesis characterized by gonads that have been replaced by connective tissue. Most commonly associated with Turner syndrome.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Turner syndrome

R9alM5.title: Swyer syndrome
R9alM5.description: A disorder of sexual development caused by a defect in the SRY gene on chromosome Y, that results in impaired testicular development. Female external genitalia, a vagina, and uterus are present, but menarche and breast development do not occur because patients lack functioning ovaries.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis

i9aJM5.title: Turner syndrome
i9aJM5.description: A chromosomal abnormality with karyotype 45,XO. Occurs in approximately 1:2500 births. Patients are phenotypically female and have short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and gonadal dysgenesis. Turner syndrome is associated with many additional abnormalities, including infertility, coarctation of the aorta, horseshoe kidney, and osteoporosis.

destinations.label: Differences (disorders) of sex development → Turner syndrome

P9aWn5.title: Fragile X syndrome
P9aWn5.description: An X-linked dominant disease caused by trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 (fragile X mental retardation 1) gene. Causes intellectual disability, delayed language development, long facies, large ears, macroorchidism, mitral valve prolapse, and hyperactivity.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Fragile X syndrome

O9aIn5.title: Zellweger syndrome
O9aIn5.description: An autosomal recessive defect in peroxisome formation that prevents catabolism of elevated long-chain fatty acids, thereby leading to their accumulation. Notable for neonatal seizures, hypotonia, malformation of the face and head, hepatomegaly, polycystic kidney disease, retinal dystrophy and sensorineural hearing loss.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome)

l9avn5.title: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
l9avn5.description: A congenital disorder caused by microdeletion on the long arm of chromosome 22. The clinical presentation is variable and includes features such as congenital heart defects, craniofacial abnormalities, and/or defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, resulting in hypoplastic thymus and parathyroids.

destinations.label: Congenital immunodeficiency disorders → Congenital T-cell immunodeficiencies

media.title: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) fact sheet

N9a-n5.title: CATCH-22
N9a-n5.description: Acronym for the clinical features present in DiGeorge syndrome: cardiac anomalies, anomalous face, thymus aplasia/hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, chromosome 22 (location of mutation).

destinations.label: Congenital immunodeficiency disorders → Congenital T-cell immunodeficiencies

m9aVL5.title: Rett syndrome
m9aVL5.description:
A rare neurodevelopmental disorder that is almost exclusively seen in girls. Manifestations typically appear between the ages of 6 and 18 months. Affected individuals initially develop normally but then have milestone regression in all domains (motor, language, and cognitive abilities). Other features include growth failure (especially in relation to head circumference) and characteristic hand movements (e.g., rubbing, wringing) and vocal grunting.

The term "Rett syndrome" is named after Andreas Rett, an Austrian neurologist and member of the Nazi Party whose work used research data from individuals murdered by the Nazi regime. Although we refrain from eponyms whenever possible, there is no accepted replacement term at this time.

59aiL5.title: Williams syndrome
59aiL5.description: An autosomal dominant disease caused by a deletion in the elastin gene on chromosome 7. Typical features include mental retardation and facial features such as a broad forehead, wide mouth, full cheeks and lips, and a long, smooth philtrum (aka "elfin" facies). Among the cardiac malformations associated with Williams syndrome, supravalvular aortic stenosis is the most common.

M9aML5.title: Cri-du-chat syndrome
M9aML5.description: A rare genetic disease caused by a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5. Affected children present with a variety of syndromes including intellectual and developmental disability and skull/face malformations. The most characteristic feature is a high-pitched, cat-like cry.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Cri-du-chat syndrome (cat cry syndrome)

media.title: Cri-du-chat syndrome (Cat cry syndrome) fact sheet

L9awL5.title: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome
L9awL5.description: Autosomal recessive disease with cholesterol shortage due to deficient 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase. Symptoms are extremely variable but may include short stature, dysmorphic facial features (ptosis, epicanthal folds, microcephaly, micrognathia), intellectual disability, internal organ malformations, toe syndactyly and single palmar crease.

K9aUo5.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
K9aUo5.description: A congenital (x-linked recessive) immunodeficiency that is characterized by the classic triad of eczema, thrombocytopenic purpura, and recurrent opportunistic infections. Caused by a mutation in the WAS gene, which results in impaired signaling to actin cytoskeleton reorganization and therefore impaired T-cell function and thrombocytopenia.

destinations.label: Congenital immunodeficiency disorders → Congenital mixed immunodeficiencies

p9aLo5.title: Prader-Willi syndrome
p9aLo5.description: A genetic syndrome caused by microdeletion of the paternal gene copy at 15q11-q13. The condition is characterized by muscular hypotonia during infancy, genital hypoplasia, short stature, and hyperphagia, which often results in morbid obesity.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome

J9aso5.title: Angelman syndrome
J9aso5.description: A genetic syndrome caused by a microdeletion of the 15q11-q13 region on the maternal copy of chromosome 15. Children present with developmental delays, intellectual disability, epileptic seizures, ataxia, and a happy demeanor with frequent, uncontrollable laughter.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome

q9aCo5.title: Pierre Robin syndrome
q9aCo5.description: A set of abnormalities causing possible intellectual disability as well as fetal oral and maxillofacial malformations, including cleft palate, glossoptosis, and mandibular retrognathia or micrognathia.

destinations.label: Rare inherited syndromes → Pierre Robin sequence (Pierre Robin syndrome)

r9afK5.title: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism
r9afK5.description: An autosomal dominant condition that mimics PHP type 1a but without end-organ resistance to PTH. Patients present with features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy but do not have laboratory findings of pseudohypoparathyroidism (i.e., no hypocalcemia, normal PTH).

H9aKK5.title: Congenital torticollis
H9aKK5.description: A postural deformity of the neck (i.e., heat tilt and/or neck rotation) that develops prenatally or perinatally. Causes may be muscular (congenital muscular torticollis) or nonmuscular (e.g., bony abnormalities, birth trauma).

t9aX65.title: Upper brachial plexus palsy
t9aX65.description: An injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus that typically affects the suprascapular, musculocutaneous, and axillary nerves. Manifests with an adducted, extended, pronated, and medially rotated arm (waiter's tip position). Most commonly occurs secondary to shoulder dystocia.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

media.title: Waiter's tip deformity in Erb palsy
Brachial plexus injuries: Erb palsy and Klumpke palsy

89aO65.title: Lower brachial plexus palsy
89aO65.description: A paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles (i.e., lumbricals, interossei, thenar eminence, and hypothenar muscles) and often forearm muscles (i.e., flexors of the wrist and fingers; sometimes also the pronators) due to injury of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, which is formed by the C8 and T1 nerve roots. Can manifest with a "claw hand" deformity. Etiologies include hyperabduction of the arm (e.g., birth trauma, an attempt to break a fall from a height by grabbing a support), cervical rib, and Pancoast tumor.

destinations.label: Peripheral nerve injuries → Nerve injuries in the upper body

media.title: Brachial plexus injuries: Erb palsy and Klumpke palsy

v9aA65.title: Caput succedaneum
v9aA65.description: A scalp swelling that is formed in the neonate by the stagnation of fluid within the layers of the scalp. Caused by prolonged engagement of the head in the birth canal, which restricts venous drainage of the scalp. A caput succedaneum is not limited by suture lines and usually disappears spontaneously within 24 hours of birth.

destinations.label: Birth traumas → Neonatal soft tissue injuries

w9ahp5.title: Cephalohematoma
w9ahp5.description: A subperiosteal hematoma of the skull that develops in neonates 12–24 hours after birth, usually as a result of ruptured subperiosteal vessels. The swelling is limited by the suture lines of the skull. Risk factors include use of forceps and vacuum-assisted delivery.

destinations.label: Birth traumas → Neonatal soft tissue injuries

C9aqp5.title: Subgaleal hemorrhage
C9aqp5.description: Bleeding between the periosteum of the skull and the aponeurosis that may extend across the suture lines. Most commonly a birth trauma that occurs during vacuum or forceps delivery when shearing forces cause injury to the emissary veins. It is associated with a high risk of significant hemorrhage and hemorrhagic shock.

destinations.label: Birth traumas → Neonatal soft tissue injuries

z9arJ5.title: Left-to-right shunt
z9arJ5.description: A cardiac defect that causes oxygenated blood from the lungs to be shunted back into the pulmonary circulation. Leads to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular pressure overload, which causes right-sided heart hypertrophy and eventually heart failure without cyanosis. Etiologies include septal defects and a patent ductus arteriosus. If untreated, can progress to a right-to-left shunt due to worsening pulmonary hypertension.

-9aDJ5.title: Eisenmenger syndrome
-9aDJ5.description: A complication of acyanotic heart disease in which the shunt direction reverses and cyanotic heart disease develops. Over time, increased pulmonary flow from left-to-right shunting causes pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy. When right ventricular pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure, right-to-left shunting occurs, resulting in cyanosis.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Eisenmenger syndrome

media.title: Cardiac hemodynamics in patent ductus arteriosus
Cardiac hemodynamics in ventricular septal defect

ZCaZq5.title: Ventricular septal defect
ZCaZq5.description: An abnormal communication between the left and right ventricle that results in left-to-right shunting of blood flow. It is the most common congenital heart defect. Manifests as a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur best appreciated at the left sternal border.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

media.title: Cardiac hemodynamics in ventricular septal defect

0Caeq5.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
0Caeq5.description: The most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease. Characterized by four particular abnormalities: right ventricular outflow obstruction due to pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, a ventricular septal defect (VSD), and an overriding aorta (above the VSD).

destinations.label: Cyanotic congenital heart defects → Tetralogy of Fallot

media.title: Boot-shaped heart in tetralogy of Fallot

aCaQq5.title: Transposition of the great vessels
aCaQq5.description: A cyanotic congenital heart defect in which the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle.

destinations.label: Cyanotic congenital heart defects → Transposition of the great vessels (TGV)

XCa9q5.title: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
XCa9q5.description: A rare, congenital, cyanotic heart defect characterized by underdevelopment of the left-sided structures of the heart. Can involve the left ventricle, mitral valve, aortic valve, aortic root, and aortic arch. Associated with DiGeorge syndrome, Turner syndrome, Jacobsen syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18.

destinations.label: Cyanotic congenital heart defects → Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)

1Ca2I5.title: Cyanotic congenital heart defects
1Ca2I5.description: A congenital heart defect in which deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the systemic circulation, which causes cyanosis.

VCaGI5.title: Patent ductus arteriosus
VCaGI5.description: The incomplete closure of the ductus arteriosus postnatally. Results in a left-to-right shunt that causes a loud, continuous murmur. Associated with heart failure in infancy, Eisenmenger syndrome, and infective endocarditis. More common in premature infants and those with congenital infections.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

media.title: Cardiac hemodynamics in patent ductus arteriosus

eCaxI5.title: Coarctation of the aorta
eCaxI5.description: A congenital heart defect that involves narrowing of the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery or, less commonly, narrowing of the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta. Manifestations often include upper extremity hypertension and weak femoral pulses. Frequently associated with other congenital heart defects (e.g., bicuspid aortic valve, VSD, PDA) and Turner syndrome.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Coarctation of the aorta

fCakr5.title: Pulmonary valve stenosis
fCakr5.description: A valvular heart disease characterized by obstruction of blood outflow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary arteries during systole.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Pulmonary valve stenosis

3CaS75.title: Ostium primum atrial septal defect
3CaS75.description: An atrial septal defect caused by incomplete fusion of the septum primum and the endocardial cushion. It is the second most common type of atrial septal defect. Often associated with mitral valve abnormalities.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Atrial septal defect (ASD)

jCa_75.title: Atrial septal defect
jCa_75.description: A congenital defect in the atrial wall resulting from impaired growth or excessive resorption of the atrial septum. Leads to a low-pressure, low-volume, left-to-right shunt, which is commonly asymptomatic until adulthood.

destinations.label: Acyanotic congenital heart defects → Atrial septal defect (ASD)

PCaWH5.title: Double aortic arch
PCaWH5.description: A congenital anomaly of the aortic arch in which the left and right pharyngeal arteries persist postnatally, forming a ring structure around the trachea and esophagus. Typically presents with compressive symptoms of the trachea (e.g., dyspnea/stridor) and/or esophagus (e.g., difficulty swallowing, regurgitation of food).

OCaIH5.title: Ebstein anomaly
OCaIH5.description: A congenital heart defect characterized by caudal displacement of a tricuspid valve leaflet that results in atrialization of the right ventricle, tricuspid regurgitation, and right atrial enlargement. Classically associated with fetal lithium exposure. The age of presentation and severity of symptoms vary. Some patients may develop cyanosis due to mixing of blood via an atrial septal defect.

destinations.label: Cyanotic congenital heart defects → Ebstein anomaly

lCavH5.title: Tricuspid atresia
lCavH5.description: A cyanotic congenital heart defect characterized by hypoplasia or agenesis of the tricuspid valve, that results in blockage of blood flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle. 100% of cases are associated with ASD, 95% of cases are associated with VSD, and 75% of cases are associated with pulmonary outflow obstruction. Requires surgical repair soon after birth.

destinations.label: Cyanotic congenital heart defects → Tricuspid valve atresia

NCa-H5.title: Anal atresia
NCa-H5.description: A sporadically occurring malformation of the rectum with absence of an anal opening due to failure of the anal membrane to canalize during embryonic development.

mCaVs5.title: Omphalocele
mCaVs5.description: Congenital visceral malformation in which organs herniate at the midline abdominal wall through the umbilicus into a hernial sac. Associated with trisomies, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and other genetic disorders.

media.title: Visual mnemonic for omphalocele and gastroschisis
Congenital malformations of the anterior abdominal wall

LCaws5.title: Gastroschisis
LCaws5.description: A congenital visceral malformation with paraumbilical herniation of the intestine through the abdominal wall, most commonly on the right side. The herniated organs are not covered by a sac. Seen especially in premature infants and associated with bowel abnormalities (e.g., atresia, malrotation, or stenosis from vascular compromise). Extra-gastrointestinal comorbidities are uncommon (unlike in omphalocele).

media.title: Visual mnemonic for omphalocele and gastroschisis
Congenital malformations of the anterior abdominal wall

KCaUG5.title: Alagille syndrome
KCaUG5.description: A genetic disorder characterized by aplasia or hypoplasia of the intrahepatic biliary tree. Alagille syndrome, which is typically caused by mutation of the JAG1 gene on chromosome 20, presents with cholestatic jaundice, congenital heart defects, butterfly vertebrae, facial dysmorphism, and a posterior embryotoxon.

destinations.label: Congenital visceral malformations → Biliary tract malformations

6CajG5.title: Biliary atresia
6CajG5.description: A rare neonatal condition characterized by progressive fibrosis and obliteration of the extrahepatic biliary tree that leads to cholestasis, jaundice, acholic stools, and dark urine. This condition often progresses to liver failure requiring transplantation.

destinations.label: Congenital visceral malformations → Biliary tract malformations

pCaLG5.title: Coxsackie A
pCaLG5.description: A group of RNA nonpolio enteroviruses that are part of the Picornaviridae family. Infection with group A coxsackieviruses is the most common cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina.

JCasG5.title: Hand, foot, and mouth disease
JCasG5.description: A highly contagious seasonal infection most commonly caused by group A coxsackieviruses. Typically manifests with fever; painful oral and pharyngeal lesions; and a cutaneous macular, papular and vesicular rash on the hands and feet. Most commonly affects children < 5 years of age.

destinations.label: Coxsackievirus infections → Hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina

qCaCG5.title: Coxsackie B
qCaCG5.description: A group of RNA nonpolio enteroviruses that are part of the Picornaviridae family. Group B coxsackievirus infections more commonly cause epidemic pleurodynia, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, and pericarditis than group A.

ICaYt5.title: Pleurodynia
ICaYt5.description: An acute illness characterized by fever or flu-like symptoms and painful spasms of the chest and upper abdomen due to irritation of the pleura and muscles. Caused by group B coxsackieviruses. Most common in older children and young adults.

7Ca4t5.title: Overwhelming postsplenectomy infection
7Ca4t5.description: Fulminant sepsis that develops in asplenic individuals as a result of infection by encapsulated organisms (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae). The risk of OPSI is highest among children under the age of 6 years. Patients initially have flu-like symptoms (e.g., fever, malaise), but rapidly deteriorate within hours.

sCatt5.title: Papule
sCatt5.description: A small, palpable skin lesion < 1 cm in size.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Primary skin lesions

tCaXF5.title: Vesicle (dermatology)
tCaXF5.description: A cutaneous, fluid-filled blister < 1 cm in diameter.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Primary skin lesions

FCagF5.title: Bulla
FCagF5.description: A dermatological bulla is a fluid-filled cutaneous vesicle over 0.5-1.0 cm in diameter. A pulmonary bulla is an air-filled cavity that replaces normal lung tissue in emphysematous disease (e.g., COPD).

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Primary skin lesions

8CaOF5.title: Urticaria
8CaOF5.description: An inflammatory skin disorder characterized by hives (wheals) with or without angioedema. Often caused by an allergic reaction, e.g., to latex or medication, but can occur without a known trigger.

uCapF5.title: Pustule
uCapF5.description: A small, pus-containing blister < 1 cm in size.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Primary skin lesions

9CaN85.title: Erosion
9CaN85.description: A morphologic descriptor used to describe several types of lesions. In dermatology, refers to a loss of a portion of or all of the epidermis (with an intact basement membrane). In gastroenterology, refers to a superficial mucosal lesion with intact muscularis mucosae. In dentistry, refers to a loss of tooth enamel.

BCaz85.title: Purpura
BCaz85.description: A purple-red, nonblanchable cutaneous or mucosal lesion that typically measures 0.2–1 cm in size. Results from the extravasation of blood into skin or mucous membranes. Can be palpable or flat. Palpable purpura are caused by vasculitis of small vessels or infectious emboli while flat purpura are typically the result of a noninflammatory process (e.g., bleeding diathesis, increased venous pressure, increased capillary fragility).

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

yCadu5.title: Petechiae
yCadu5.description: A cutaneous finding of nonblanchable, nonpalpable, red, pinpoint macules caused by capillary inflammation and hemorrhage (e.g., in patients with thrombocytopenia).

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

_Ca5u5.title: Ecchymosis
_Ca5u5.description: A flat, red-purple bruise > 5 mm in size. Caused by extravasation of nearby blood vessels.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

zCaru5.title: Hematoma
zCaru5.description: A collection caused by bleeding into subcutaneous tissue, muscle, organ tissue, or a cavity.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

-CaDu5.title: Exanthem
-CaDu5.description: An extended, uniform rash that can be localized or generalized. Often used to refer to cutaneous manifestations of viral conditions.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

ZxaZE5.title: Enanthem
ZxaZE5.description: A dermatologic finding that is confined to the mucous membranes (e.g., Koplik spots in the oral mucosa).

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

0xaeE5.title: Eczema
0xaeE5.description: A morphologic description for skin lesions characterized by scaly, pruritic papules, papulovesicles, and plaques that are frequently inflamed. Can be applied to multiple diseases, e.g., atopic, irritant, or contact dermatitis.

destinations.label: Principles of dermatology → Complex skin lesions

exaxv5.title: Epidermis
exaxv5.description: The superficial layer of the skin, consisting (from superficial to deep) of the stratum corneum, the stratum lucidum (found only on palms and soles of the feet), the stratum granulosum, the stratum spinosum, and the stratum basale. Primary cell type is the keratinocyte. Other resident cells including melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

UxabD5.title: Stratum corneum
UxabD5.description: The outermost layer of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Consists of terminally-differentiated, anucleate, dead, keratin-filled cells (keratinocytes). Serves as a barrier to water loss, trauma, and infection.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

2xaTD5.title: Stratum lucidum
2xaTD5.description: A thin, translucent layer of the epidermis located between the stratum corneum and the stratum granulosum on the skin of the palms and soles.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

Txa6D5.title: Stratum spinosum
Txa6D5.description: A layer of the epidermis located between the stratum granulosum and the stratum basale. Named for the spine-like appearance of abundant desmosomes.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

gxaFD5.title: Stratum basale
gxaFD5.description: The deepest layer of the epidermis. Situated on the basement membrane of the dermal-epidermal junction. Contains melanocytes and the epidermal stem cells that divide and migrate into the upper layers of the epidermis, where they differentiate into other cell types.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

SxayD5.title: Dermal-epidermal junction
SxayD5.description: The area of tissue (basement membrane) joining the epidermis and dermis of the skin. Neighboring attachments include hemodesmosomes (attaching keratinocytes of the epidermis to the basement membrane) and collagen fibrils (attaching the papillary dermis to the basement membrane).

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

Qxauw5.title: Dermis
Qxauw5.description: A layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissue. Consists of the papillary dermis and reticular dermis. Provides structural integrity to the skin and contains blood vessels, lymphatic channels for regulation of fluid resorption, and nerves.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

jxa_w5.title: Papillary dermis
jxa_w5.description: The upper level of the dermis that is directly beneath the stratum basale. Consists of fine, loosely arranged collagen fibers. Supplies the epidermis with nutrients and regulates temperature with its extensive vascular system. Also contains nerve endings (Meissner corpuscles and free nerve endings) and immune cells (mast cells and macrophages).

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

4xa395.title: Reticular dermis
4xa395.description: The layer of skin below the papillary dermis. Consists of thick, densely packed fibers that provide the structure and elastic fibers that lend the skin elasticity. Supports other skin components (e.g., hair follicles, receptor cells, glands, and blood and lymphatic vessels).

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

OxaI95.title: Subcutaneous tissue
OxaI95.description: The layer of connective tissue below the dermis. This layer consists primarily of adipose tissue that protects underlying structures from cold and trauma and contains superficial blood vessels as well as mechanoreceptors.

destinations.label: Skin and skin appendage → Structure of the skin

nxa7C5.title: Pediculosis capitis
nxa7C5.description: An infestation of Pediculus humanus capitis, spread through direct head-to-head contact or shared hair accessories, bedding, clothing, or towels. Nymphs and/or adult lice are typically detected on the scalp and/or hair. Most commonly affects children. May be asymptomatic or manifest with pruritus.

destinations.label: Lice infestation → Pediculosis capitis (head lice infestation)

oxa0x5.title: Pubic lice infestation
oxa0x5.description: An infestation of Pthirus pubis, spread through sexual contact or shared bedding, clothing, or towels. Most common in teenagers and young adults. Manifests with pruritus, excoriation, and visible lice and/or nits in pubic hair and/or other areas with coarse hair (e.g., axilla, perianal region, eyelashes).

destinations.label: Lice infestation → Pediculosis pubis (pubic lice infestation)

qxaCx5.title: Body lice infestation
qxaCx5.description: An infestation of Pediculus humanus corporis, spread through direct contact with infested skin or sharing bedding or clothing. Most common in individuals living in crowded, unsanitary conditions. Manifests with pruritus, erythematous macules and papules, and excoriations.

destinations.label: Lice infestation → Pediculosis corporis (body lice infestation)

7xa4B5.title: Polymorphous light eruption
7xa4B5.description: A photodermatosis caused by a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction to prolonged exposure to sunlight (esp. in the spring and summer) following a period of little exposure. Skin lesions vary, but are usually pruritic and often include erythema, plaques, papules, and/or vesicles. PMLE usually resolves spontaneously if sun exposure is avoided but tends to recur (usually at the same sites) upon subsequent exposure to the sun. Also erroneously known as "sun poisoning" or "sun allergy."

txaXy5.title: Phytophotodermatitis
txaXy5.description: A plant-induced phototoxic reaction that results in a rash, often resembling a stripe-like or reticular pattern. Additional manifestations at the site of contact may include erythema, pruritus, blistering, and a burning sensation.

Dxa1A5.title: Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dxa1A5.description: An autoimmune blistering disease caused by autoantibodies against epidermal transglutaminase. Considered a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease. Manifests with intensely pruritic grouped papules and vesicles, typically on extensor surfaces. Lesions often erode due to scratching and heal with pigmentation changes.

wxahA5.title: Pemphigus vulgaris
wxahA5.description: An autoimmune blistering disease caused by autoantibodies against desmoglein. Manifests with painful mucosal and/or cutaneous lesions that rupture easily. May be life-threatening without adequate treatment.

9xaNA5.title: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
9xaNA5.description: An acquired autoimmune blistering disease characterized by the development of subepidermal tense vesicles and bullae as a result of autoantibodies against type VII collagen. Can affect mucous membranes. Most commonly occurs in older adults. Characterized by a linear pattern of immunoglobulin G on direct immunofluorescence.

CxaqA5.title: Bullous pemphigoid
CxaqA5.description: A chronic autoimmune blistering disease that primarily affects older adults. Caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes. Manifests with tense vesicles and bullae and moderate to intense pruritus. Lesions commonly appear on the trunk and flexural surfaces and usually heal without scarring

yxad_5.title: Nikolsky sign
yxad_5.description: The sloughing of epidermis when lateral pressure is applied to the skin. Suggests detachment of the epidermis from the dermis. Characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and certain forms of epidermolysis bullosa.

_xa5_5.title: Tzanck test
_xa5_5.description: A cytodiagnostic tool used to diagnose autoimmune bullous diseases and herpes virus infections when the clinical diagnosis is not apparent. A vesicle is deroofed, the base of the vesicle is scraped, and the scraping is put on a glass slide stained with either Giemsa or Papanicolaou stains. Tzanck cells are multinucleated giant cells seen in pemphigus vulgaris, HSV infection, chickenpox/shingles, and CMV infection; they are characteristically absent in bullous pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis.

YBanz5.title: Malignant acanthosis nigricans
YBanz5.description: A paraneoplastic syndrome associated with visceral adenocarcinomas, especially gastric adenocarcinomas. Manifests with verrucous or papulous, hyperpigmented, pruritic skin lesions with rapid growth. Mainly affects the neck, genital area, and axillae.

bBaHz5.title: Benign acanthosis nigricans
bBaHz5.description: A dermatological condition characterized by hyperkeratotic, velvety patches or plaques in intertriginous areas and/or the back of the neck. Commonly associated with metabolic conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovary syndrome, Cushing syndrome) and the use of certain medications (e.g., glucocorticoids, oral contraceptives).

cBaa-5.title: Necrolytic migratory erythema
cBaa-5.description: A cutaneous paraneoplastic skin finding that is typically associated with glucagonoma. Erythema necroticans migrans is characterized by multiple, centrifugally spreading erythematous lesions, especially, on the face, perineum, buttocks, and lower extremities. After 1-2 weeks, these lesions develop into painful, crusty, and pruritic patches. Central clearing leaves indurated, bronze-colored areas in the center and blistering and scaling at the borders. The lesions tend to resolve spontaneously and reappear in different locations shortly after.

1Ba2-5.title: Erythema gyratum repens
1Ba2-5.description: A dermatologic finding characterized by concentric rings of rapidly migrating erythematous and pruritic plaques. Most cases are associated with internal malignancy (most often bronchogenic carcinoma).

WBaP-5.title: Anti-Hu associated encephalitis
WBaP-5.description: A rare paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis that typically manifests with rapid onset symptoms of autonomic neuropathy (e.g. sensory deficits, lower extremity pain, cerebellar symptoms, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction). Symptoms often emerge before the discovery of a primary tumor. The most common associated primary tumor is small cell lung carcinoma.

VBaG-5.title: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
VBaG-5.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome caused by autoantibodies against antigens in the cerbellum (e.g., Yo antigens of Purkinje cells, Tr antigens, Hu antigens). The most common causes of PCD are small cell lung cancer, gynecologic cancer and lymphoma.

2BaTZM.title: Porphyria cutanea tarda
2BaTZM.description: A condition caused by defective uroporphyrinogen-III decarboxylase (UROD) which leads to the accumulation of uroporphyrinogen in the skin and chronic photosensitivity with blistering and hyperpigmentation. Can be acquired (type I) or inherited (autosomal dominant; type II).

fBakZM.title: Acute intermittent porphyria
fBakZM.description: An inherited metabolic disorder caused by deficient enzymes in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Characterized by attacks of severe abdominal pain, constipation, tachycardia, and neuropsychiatric abnormalities that are typically triggered by certain drugs or infections.

gBaFZM.title: Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome
gBaFZM.description: A rare, inherited neurocutaneous syndrome that typically manifests during childhood or adolescence. Manifestations include a fissured tongue, recurrent facial nerve palsy, and facial and lip edema (granulomatous cheilitis).

hBac0M.title: Seborrheic keratosis
hBac0M.description: A benign growth of immature keratinocytes. Most frequently located on the trunk, upper extremities, face, and scalp. Most common benign skin tumor in adults > 30 years of age. Appear as single or multiple soft papules or plaques with a greasy, wax-like, and "stuck-on" appearance.

RBal0M.title: Keloid
RBal0M.description: A scar that extends beyond the original margins of a wound. Consists of disorganized collagen (types I and III)  and is usually seen 3-12 months after injury. Recurrence after resection is common.

iBaJ0M.title: Lipoma
iBaJ0M.description: A benign tumor composed of adipocytes that presents as a painless, mobile, rubbery nodule. The most common type are superficial subcutaneous lipomas, presenting as soft subcutaneous lumps of fat tissue.

jBa_0M.title: Pyogenic granuloma
jBa_0M.description: A benign, vascular lesion that typically appears as a bright red polypoid or pedunculated nodule. They can occur anywhere on the body, often develop after minor trauma, and tend to bleed easily. Pyogenic granulomas are neither pyogenic nor granulomatous.

destinations.label: Benign skin tumors → Vascular skin tumors

PBaWaM.title: Dermatofibroma
PBaWaM.description: A benign, slowly-growing, skin-colored or hyperpigmented dermal growth, most commonly found on the lower extremities.  Pinching the lesion typically produces a central dimple. Typically asymptomatic, but may be pruritic or tender.

4Ba3aM.title: Dimple sign
4Ba3aM.description: A dermatologic finding characterized by central dimpling of a skin lesion upon pinching of the surrounding skin. Most commonly associated with dermatofibromas.

lBavaM.title: Nevus
lBavaM.description: A congenital or acquired benign neoplasm of the skin. Classified as either an epidermal nevus or melanocytic nevus (mole).

5BaiYM.title: Congenital dermal melanocytosis
5BaiYM.description: A congenital, benign, blue-gray patch caused by melanocytes entrapped in the dermis. Typically fades by adulthood. Most commonly seen on the lower back of individuals of Asian and African descent. Sometimes mistaken for child abuse because it can resemble bruising.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

oBa0bM.title: Epidermal nevus
oBa0bM.description: A cutaneous hamartoma caused by excessive proliferation of the epidermis and/or adnexa that manifests at birth or during early childhood. Lesions in combination with extracutaneous symptoms (e.g., cardiac, neurologic) suggest an epidermal nevus syndrome (e.g., Becker nevus syndrome, Schimmelpenning syndrome).

pBaLbM.title: Speckled lentiginous nevus
pBaLbM.description: A benign subtype of congenital melanocytic nevus that manifests as a light café-au-lait spot at birth or during infancy. Over months to years, the lesion can grow, manifesting as a flat, hairless, irregular oval macule or patch (1-20 cm in diameter) with small, elevated black dots (1–3 mm in diameter) throughout.

rBafXM.title: Nevus sebaceous
rBafXM.description: A type of epidermal nevus caused by hyperplasia of the epidermis and adnexa. Most commonly manifests on the scalp as a single, hairless plaque. Lesions in combination with extracutaneous abnormalities (e.g., CNS, ocular, musculoskeletal) may indicate an epidermal nevus syndrome.

7Ba4XM.title: Atypical nevus
7Ba4XM.description: A benign melanocytic nevus that resembles melanoma but does not change in size, shape, or color. Predominantly seen on sun-exposed areas (e.g., trunk, back) in individuals with light skin but can occur in individuals with dark skin, most commonly on non-sun-exposed areas. A risk factor for developing melanoma, especially in individuals with familial syndromes (e.g., FAMMM).

sBatXM.title: Congenital melanocytic nevus
sBatXM.description: A congenital skin lesion caused by the proliferation of melanocytes. Typically appears as a light brown or black, well-circumscribed macule or patch, possibly with increased hair growth. Giant melanocytic nevi (> 20 cm) can undergo malignant transformation into melanomas.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

tBaXcM.title: Giant congenital melanocytic nevus
tBaXcM.description: A congenital melanocytic nevus > 20 cm in size. Can undergo malignant transformation into melanoma.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

FBagcM.title: Cutaneous warts
FBagcM.description: A group of hyperkeratotic cutaneous conditions caused by human papillomaviruses. Includes common warts, flat warts, and plantar warts.

uBapcM.title: Hypertrophic scars
uBapcM.description: Excess fibroblast proliferation in response to penetrating trauma. Results in increased collagen production (primarily type III collagen) with parallel organization. Does not grow beyond the boundaries of the original lesion, as opposed to keloid formation. Regresses spontaneously.

wBah1M.title: Bowen disease
wBah1M.description: A precancerous skin lesion that manifests as an erythematous and scaly plaque with irregularly shaped and sharply defined borders. May progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

destinations.label: Precancerous skin lesions → Bowen disease and Erythroplasia of Queyrat

BBaz1M.title: Leukoplakia
BBaz1M.description: Precancerous hyperkeratosis and dysplasia of the epithelium and mucous membranes most commonly located in the oral cavity. Risk factors include tobacco and alcohol consumption. Clinically manifests as persistent white plaques that usually cannot be scraped off. May develop into squamous cell carcinoma.

yBadWM.title: Androgenetic alopecia
yBadWM.description: A condition of hair loss caused by the effect of dihydrotestosterone on the the hair follicle, resulting in a characteristic pattern of balding (bitemporal scalp in men and vertex and frontal scalp in women). Can be caused by increased sensitivity of androgen receptors in the hair follicle (hereditary or idiopathic) or by conditions that result in hyperandrogenism (e.g., polycystic ovarian disease, anabolic steroid use).

-BaDWM.title: Alopecia areata
-BaDWM.description: An autoimmune condition characterized by smooth, rounded patches of hair loss without scarring, itching, or inflammation.

cyaaVM.title: Brocq pseudopelade
cyaaVM.description: A rare type of progressive, scarring alopecia that leads to irregular areas of irreversible hair loss.

eyaxVM.title: Gynecomastia
eyaxVM.description: A benign proliferation of mammary tissue in male individuals due to increased estrogen and/or decreased testosterone levels. Can be physiological (e.g., at puberty, old age), pathological (e.g., from hyperestrogenic states such as cirrhosis or as a drug adverse effect), or idiopathic.

destinations.label: Overview of common breast conditions → Disorders of breast development

2yaTeM.title: Polymastia
2yaTeM.description: The presence of mammary tissue beyond the normal bilateral breasts, most commonly manifesting as accessory areola and nipple tissue (polythelia). May also include accessory glandular tissue.

destinations.label: Overview of common breast conditions → Disorders of breast development

fyakeM.title: Polythelia
fyakeM.description: The presence of an accessory (additional) nipple, which most commonly forms along the mammary ridge.

destinations.label: Overview of common breast conditions → Disorders of breast development

Tya6eM.title: Anteflexion
Tya6eM.description: Forward bending and/or displacement of a body structure.

gyaFeM.title: Anteverted
gyaFeM.description: An anatomical descriptor for anterior tilting of a body part (e.g., the uterus).

destinations.label: Anatomical terms → Anatomical terms of motion

hyacUM.title: Bicornuate uterus
hyacUM.description: A type of uterine malformation characterized by failure of the upper part of the uterus to fuse, resulting in two "horns" separated by a septum. It may appear heart-shaped. It is associated with adverse reproductive outcomes such as recurrent pregnancy loss, preterm birth, and malpresentation.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the uterus

3yaSUM.title: Didelphic uterus
3yaSUM.description: A congenital anomaly of the uterus that occurs due to a complete lack of Müllerian duct fusion. Characterized by a double uterus and two separate cervices. Doubling of the vagina can occur as well. Pregnancy is still possible.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the uterus

iyaJUM.title: Septate uterus
iyaJUM.description: A uterine anomaly characterized by persistent septa between the two Müllerian ducts after their fusion.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the uterus

PyaW2M.title: Imperforate hymen
PyaW2M.description: A congenital defect in which the hymen does not have an opening. Caused by failure of the central cells of the Müllerian eminence to disintegrate. Causes cryptomenorrhea (backup of menstrual blood) at puberty. Typically manifests as primary amenorrhea with periodic lower abdominal pain.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the vulva and vagina

4ya32M.title: Labial fusion
4ya32M.description: A condition of partial or complete adhesion of the labia minora that typically affects young girls up to 4 years of age. These adhesions form as a result of superficial labial injuries caused by perineal inflammation (e.g., urinary tract infection, diaper dermatitis, diarrhea). Usually asymptomatic but can cause recurrent urinary tract infections if the external urethral opening is obstructed.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the vulva and vagina

kyam2M.title: Vaginal atresia
kyam2M.description: A condition in which the vagina is abnormally closed or absent. Can be asymptomatic before puberty and manifest with primary amenorrhea, infertility, and/or dyspareunia. Etiologies include vaginal obstruction (e.g., from an imperforate hymen) and vaginal agenesis (e.g., from Müllerian agenesis).

Nya-2M.title: Müllerian agenesis
Nya-2M.description: A rare, congenital defect in which the Müllerian ducts fail to fuse, which results in an atretic uterus, cervix, and upper-third of the vagina. Patients usually present during puberty with primary amenorrhea but have normal secondary sexual characteristics.

destinations.label: Anomalies of the female genital tract → Anomalies of the uterus

myaVfM.title: Pearl index
myaVfM.description: A measure of contraceptive efficacy. Defined as the number of unintended pregnancies in 100 women per year with perfect use of the method of contraception.

5yaifM.title: Intrauterine device
5yaifM.description: A long-term, reversible form of contraception in which a small, T-shaped device is inserted into a woman's uterus to prevent pregnancy. In the United States, options include the nonhormonal copper IUD or a progestin IUD. These long-term birth control devices may be left in place for 3-12 years, depending on the type and the brand.

MyaMfM.title: Basal body temperature method
MyaMfM.description: A fertility awareness-based contraceptive method in which the fertility period is estimated by evaluating the rise in basal body temperature that typically occurs with ovulation.

nya7fM.title: Billings ovulation method
nya7fM.description: A fertility awareness-based contraceptive method in which the fertility period is estimated by evaluating the abundance and consistency of cervical mucus throughout the menstrual cycle.

oya0TM.title: Herpes genitalis
oya0TM.description: A sexually transmitted disease usually caused by HSV2 (may also be caused by HSV1). Patients typically present with painful ulcerative vesicles and fever. Dysuria and/or tender lymphadenopathy may also be present.

destinations.label: Herpes simplex virus infections → Genital herpes

qyaCTM.title: Pelvic inflammatory disease
qyaCTM.description: A bacterial infection that spreads beyond the cervix to any part of the upper female reproductive tract. Pelvic inflammatory disease can affect the uterus (endometritis), fallopian tubes (salpingitis, pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess), ovaries (oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess), and surrounding tissue (parametritis, pelvic peritonitis).

media.title: Chlamydia trachomatis in McCoy cell culture

IyaYgM.title: Endometritis
IyaYgM.description: An acute or chronic inflammation of the endometrium. Acute endometritis in nonpregnant individuals is one of the manifestations of pelvic inflammatory disease and is often accompanied by other inflammatory conditions of the female genital tract (e.g., salpingitis). Chronic endometritis can be due to infections (e.g., chlamydia), intrauterine growths (e.g., leiomyoma, polyps), and radiation therapy.

destinations.label: Pelvic pain → Gynecologic and obstetric causes

ryafgM.title: Salpingitis
ryafgM.description: A form of pelvic inflammatory disease in which the fallopian tubes become inflamed. Short-term complications include pyosalpinx and/or tubo-ovarian abscess. A common long-term complication is tubal infertility resulting from tubal ciliary damage and/or tubal obstruction.

tyaXSM.title: Bacterial vaginosis
tyaXSM.description: The most common vaginal infection, typically caused by Gardnerella vaginalis. Often asymptomatic but can produce gray or milky vaginal discharge with a fishy odor. Characterized by clue cells on wet mount microscopy, vaginal pH > 4.5, and a positive whiff test.

FyagSM.title: Trichomoniasis
FyagSM.description: A sexually transmitted infection of the vulva and vagina that is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, an anaerobic, motile protozoan with flagella. Presents with foul-smelling, frothy, yellow-green, discharge as well as vulvovaginal pruritus, a burning sensation, dyspareunia, dysuria, and a “strawberry” cervix (erythematous cervical mucosa with petechiae).

uyapSM.title: Vulvovaginal candidiasis
uyapSM.description: A vaginal infection with Candida yeast. Risk factors include pregnancy, immunodeficiency, and history of antimicrobial treatment, all of which facilitate overgrowth of C. albicans. Manifestations include odorless, white, crumbly, and sticky vaginal discharge (cottage cheese-like), erythema of the vulva and vagina, vaginal burning, pruritus, dysuria, and dyspareunia.

wyahhM.title: Nonpuerperal mastitis
wyahhM.description: Mastitis that is not associated with lactation. May affect the subareolar ducts (periductal mastitis) or peripheral breast parenchyma. Risk factors include smoking, trauma, diabetes mellitus, and immunosuppression.

9yaNhM.title: Fibrocystic changes of the breast
9yaNhM.description: A nonspecific term that includes a heterogeneous spectrum of breast conditions that commonly affect women between 20 and 50 years of age. Characterized by the formation of fibrotic and/or cystic tissue and often presents with cyclic pain associated with menses, and clear/white nipple discharge.

AyaR3M.title: Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin test
AyaR3M.description: A urine or serum test that is used to detect pregnancy through the identification of the β-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin. It is also a component of some prenatal genetic tests. Positive results may also be seen in patients with gestational trophoblastic disease.

zyar3M.title: Naegele's rule
zyar3M.description: A method of estimating the date of delivery (due date) for a pregnancy. Calculated as the first day of the last menstrual period + 7 days + 1 year - 3 months. Can be inaccurate if the patient has irregular menstrual cycles.

0AaeRM.title: Placenta
0AaeRM.description: An organ that connects the developing fetus to the uterine wall. Functions include exchange of nutrients, blood gases, metabolites, and other substances between mother and fetus as well as endocrine activity.

destinations.label: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac → The placenta

aAaQRM.title: Placentation
aAaQRM.description: The development of the placenta, which facilitates hemotrophic nutrition and the transfer of hormones, respiratory gases, and fluids from maternal tissue to the embryo. The embryonic portion of the placenta is derived from cells of the trophoblast. The maternal portion is derived from the decidua basalis.

destinations.label: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac → Development of uteroplacental circulation

YAanRM.title: Amniotic sac
YAanRM.description: A fluid-filled sac that contains a developing fetus. Consists of the amniotic membrane and amniotic fluid.

destinations.label: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac → Amnion and amniotic cavity

media.title: Development of the yolk sac and amniotic cavity

cAaaiM.title: Umbilical cord prolapse
cAaaiM.description: Presentation of the umbilical cord ahead of the presenting body part of the fetus with prolapse into the cervix or vagina. Compression of the cord can cause life-threatening fetal hypoxemia and bradycardia.

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Umbilical cord complications

fAakQM.title: Embryopathies
fAakQM.description: A group of congenital anomalies of individual organs or organ systems caused by disruption of embryogenesis. Most commonly occur due to maternal diseases (e.g., diabetic embryopathy) or drug intake (e.g., warfarin embryopathy).

TAa6QM.title: Fetopathies
TAa6QM.description: A group of congenital conditions caused by abnormal fetogenesis. Etiologies include maternal viral infections and exposure to toxins. Fetopathies typically result in milder anatomic abnormalities compared to conditions of abnormal organogenesis. They often cause functional disruption (e.g., learning and behavioral problems).

iAaJjM.title: Amniotic membrane
iAaJjM.description: A membrane that lines the inside of the amniotic cavity. Consists of a layer of cuboidal epithelial cells and an underlying layer of fibrous tissue. Derived from epiblast cells.

destinations.label: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac → Amnion and amniotic cavity

media.title: Development of the yolk sac and amniotic cavity

jAa_jM.title: Oligohydramnios
jAa_jM.description: Lower amniotic fluid volume than expected for gestational age. Measured on ultrasound as < 2 cm of fluid in the deepest vertical pocket or an amniotic fluid index < 5 cm. Often discovered incidentally during routine prenatal care. May be isolated or associated with maternal (e.g., uteroplacental insufficiency, hypertensive pregnancy disorders) or fetal (e.g., renal agenesis, aneuploidy) causes.

PAaWPM.title: Polyhydramnios
PAaWPM.description: Greater amniotic fluid volume than expected for gestational age. Measured on ultrasound as ≥ 8 cm of fluid in the deepest vertical pocket or an amniotic fluid index ≥ 24 cm. Often discovered incidentally during routine prenatal ultrasound. May be idiopathic or caused by maternal (e.g., diabetes, rhesus incompatibility) or fetal factors (e.g., conditions that impair swallowing or increase urine output).

4Aa3PM.title: Amniotic fluid
4Aa3PM.description: The protective fluid within the amniotic sac that cushions the fetus. Facilitates fetal movement, reduces the risk of injury from the external environment, prevents adherence of the fetus to the amnion, and serves as a transport medium for nutrients and metabolites.

destinations.label: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac → Amnion and amniotic cavity

OAaIPM.title: Induction of labor
OAaIPM.description: An obstetric procedure used to induce active labor that involves stimulating the cervix (cervical ripening) and causing uterine contractions. Pharmacologic (e.g., prostaglandins, oxytocin) and/or mechanical (balloon and osmotic dilators) methods may be used.

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Induction of labor

lAavPM.title: Bishop score
lAavPM.description: A scoring system used to evaluate the potential for successful elective labor induction. Components include cervical dilation (the extent of opening of the cervical os), cervical effacement (the degree of thinning of the cervix), fetal station (position of the fetal head in relation to the ischial spines), cervical position (e.g., posterior, middle, or anterior), and cervical consistency (e.g., firm, medium, or soft).

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Induction of labor

mAaV4M.title: Rupture of membranes
mAaV4M.description: The rupture of the amniotic sac followed by the release of the amniotic fluid. Typically occurs spontaneously at the onset of labor. Can also be delayed, occur prematurely, or be induced iatrogenically.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Normal spontaneous labor

oAa0kM.title: Prelabor rupture of membranes
oAa0kM.description: The rupture of amniotic membranes before the onset of uterine contractions. Common risk factors include ascending infection and cigarette smoking. Complications include chorioamnionitis, placental abruption, and umbilical cord prolapse.

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Abnormal rupture of membranes

pAaLkM.title: Delayed rupture of membranes
pAaLkM.description: Rupture of membranes that occurs during, rather than before, fetal expulsion, after cervical dilation and effacement.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Normal spontaneous labor

rAafOM.title: Lochia
rAafOM.description: A postpartum vaginal discharge comprising, e.g., cervical mucus, blood, and other uterine secretions from the site of placental detachment. Appearance depends on the amount of time elapsed since delivery: initially bloodred, then a watery brown-red, then yellow-white.

7Aa4OM.title: Postpartum endometritis
7Aa4OM.description: Infection of the uterine lining following delivery. Risk factors include retention of products of conception, cesarean delivery, and prolonged labor. Usually polymicrobial.

sAatOM.title: Ectropion
sAatOM.description: An outward turning of the eyelid, which can increase the exposure of the ocular surface and mucous membrane of the inner eyelid to the environment. Occurs as a result of chronic inflammation (e.g., from blepharitis).

tAaXlM.title: Entropion
tAaXlM.description: An inward turning of the eyelid, which can cause irritation from eyelashes rubbing against the ocular surface. Occurs as a result of chronic inflammation (e.g., from blepharitis).

uAaplM.title: Ptosis
uAaplM.description: A drooping or falling of a body part. Most commonly used in reference to the upper eyelid, which can obstruct normal vision if it droops.

vAaAlM.title: Lagophthalmos
vAaAlM.description: The inability to close the eyelids completely. Caused by facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, severe exophthalmos, or certain skin disorders (e.g., ichthyosis).

wAahNM.title: Blepharitis
wAahNM.description: Chronic/recurrent inflammation of the eyelid margins. Most commonly due to a staphylococcal infection. Characterized by redness, swelling, crusty scaling and/or oily deposits on the eyelid margins and eyelashes.

CAaqNM.title: Chalazion
CAaqNM.description: A focal lipogranulomatous swelling of the meibomian gland, a lipid-secreting gland of the eyelid. Presents as a chronic, slow-growing nodule on the eyelid that is often better seen on eversion of the eyelid.

destinations.label: Inflammation of the eyelids → Hordeolum and chalazion

BAazNM.title: Hordeolum
BAazNM.description: A common, acute inflammation of the sweat or sebaceous glands around eyelash follicles. Usually caused by a staphylococcal infection. Manifests as a painful or tender, erythematous, pus-filled mass with eyelid edema. Spontaneous rupture with purulent drainage can occur.

destinations.label: Inflammation of the eyelids → Hordeolum and chalazion

Z_aZ5M.title: Benign lymphoepithelial lesion
Z_aZ5M.description: A condition characterized by bilateral painless swelling of the lacrimal glands as well as the parotid and/or submandibular glands.

destinations.label: Diseases of the lacrimal apparatus → Dacryoadenitis

0_ae5M.title: Inflammation of the lacrimal sac
0_ae5M.description: Acute or chronic infection resulting in inflammation of the lacrimal sac. S. aureus, Pneumococcus, and Pseudomonas are the most common pathogens.

destinations.label: Diseases of the lacrimal apparatus → Dacryocystitis

a_aQ5M.title: Dacryocystorhinostomy
a_aQ5M.description: A surgical procedure in which a direct connection is created between the lacrimal sac and the nose to allow for unimpeded drainage of tears. DCR can be performed either through a skin incision or endoscopically through the nose. Indicated in patients with dacryostenosis and dacryocystitis, which is often a complication of dacryostenosis.

destinations.label: Diseases of the lacrimal apparatus → Dacryostenosis

X_a95M.title: Congenital dacryostenosis
X_a95M.description: A condition characterized by congenital obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD) either due to atresia of the distal third of the NLD (incomplete patency) or the presence of a mucus membrane fold within the duct. Typically causes persistent watering of the eyes (epiphora).

destinations.label: Diseases of the lacrimal apparatus → Dacryostenosis

1_a2MM.title: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis
1_a2MM.description: A highly contagious and self-limiting type of conjunctivitis that is accompanied by keratitis and most commonly caused by adenovirus. Manifestations include conjunctival erythema, pruritus, edema, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Symptoms typically start in one eye and rapidly become bilateral. Management consists of supportive therapy (e.g., artificial tears, cold compresses).

e_axMM.title: Neisserial conjunctivitis
e_axMM.description: A severe type of infectious conjunctivitis most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and characterized by a sudden onset of purulent discharge, rapidly worsening eye pain, and changes in vision. May involve the cornea (e.g., ulcer, perforation).

f_aknM.title: Chlamydial conjunctivitis
f_aknM.description: An infection of the conjunctiva caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The two forms are granular conjunctivitis (trachoma), caused by C. trachomatis serotypes A-C, and inclusion conjunctivitis (paratrachoma), caused by serotypes D-K.

S_aynM.title: Inclusion conjunctivitis
S_aynM.description: A form of bacterial conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D–K and characterized by mucopurulent discharge and papillary hypertrophy. Can be spread to the eyes from a preexisting genital infection (from the genitals to the hands to the eyes) or transmitted perinatally or via contaminated swimming pools.

h_acLM.title: Neonatal conjunctivitis
h_acLM.description: An inflammation of the conjunctiva in neonates aged < 4 weeks. Etiologies include bacterial infection (e.g., from Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis), viral infection (e.g., from herpes simplex virus), and chemical exposure (e.g., silver nitrate).

3_aSLM.title: Trachoma
3_aSLM.description: A chronic keratoconjunctivitis caused by recurrent Chlamydia trachomatis infection that may result in blindness. Infection results in an active phase of conjunctivitis and a cicatricial phase characterized by conjunctival scarring.

R_alLM.title: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid
R_alLM.description: A chronic autoimmune disorder of the conjunctiva that is a subset of benign mucous membrane pemphigoid. Causes inflammation and subepithelial blistering and, in severe cases, can lead to scarring and blindness.

i_aJLM.title: Allergic conjunctivitis
i_aJLM.description: A type of noninfectious conjunctivitis typically due to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity (type I) to specific allergens (e.g., cat dander). Manifests with itching, excessive tearing, sneezing, foreign body sensation, and, potentially, ptosis. May be associated with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

P_aWoM.title: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis
P_aWoM.description: A severe type of allergic conjunctivitis caused by environmental allergens (e.g., a dry, hot climate) and associated with atopy, especially in children. Manifests with recurrent bilateral inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea, severe itching, tearing, and photophobia.

k_amoM.title: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
k_amoM.description: A type of noninfectious conjunctivitis caused by underproduction, increased evaporation, or changes in the composition of lacrimal fluid. Symptoms include conjunctival injection, itching, dry eyes, blurred vision, and entropion or ectropion. Associated with irritants (e.g., contact lenses, tobacco smoke) or systemic autoimmune conditions (e.g., Sjogren syndrome).

M_aMKM.title: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
M_aMKM.description: A collection of blood between the conjunctiva and the sclera. Usually appears as a focal, red region on the surface of the eye as a result of ocular trauma. Typically asymptomatic.

L_awKM.title: Limbal dermoid
L_awKM.description: A congenital, benign tumor in the region of the corneal limbus.

destinations.label: Noninfectious conjunctival conditions → Tumors of the conjunctiva

I_aYpM.title: Acanthamoeba keratitis
I_aYpM.description: A rare, potentially sight-threatening infection of the cornea caused by the parasite Acanthamoeba. Primarily occurs in contact lens wearers. Patients present with pain, photophobia, tearing, and decreased vision. In later stages, slit lamp examination may show a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate.

7_a4pM.title: Herpes simplex keratitis
7_a4pM.description: Primary or reactivated infection of the cornea with herpes simplex virus. Presents with eye pain, blurred vision, and watery discharge. A branching pattern of inflammation seen on fluorescein staining is characteristic. Prompt treatment with topical ganciclovir is required to prevent severe visual impairment. Glucocorticoids are contraindicated as they can exacerbate infection.

G_aBpM.title: Interstitial keratitis
G_aBpM.description: A condition of corneal inflammation between the epithelial and endothelial layers of the stroma. Typically due to syphilis infection but also seen in HSV infection, Lyme disease, and tuberculosis. Can cause eye pain, blurry vision, and photophobia.

u_apJM.title: Herpes zoster keratitis
u_apJM.description: Infection due to reactivation of herpes zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation may occur due to stress, sunlight exposure, or impaired immunity.

E_a8JM.title: Bacterial keratitis
E_a8JM.description: A bacterial infection of the cornea most commonly caused by S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and P. aeruginosa. Risk factors for infection include contact lens use, lacrimal duct stenosis, and eye injury/surgery. Manifests with pain, excessive tearing, redness, blurry vision, and a purulent discharge. Can cause corneal scarring and permanent vision loss if not treated adequately.

v_aAJM.title: Hypopyon
v_aAJM.description: A sedimentation of leukocytes at the bottom of the anterior chamber of the eye secondary to an inflammatory process (e.g., bacterial/fungal keratitis, uveitis, endophthalmitis). Indicates a potentially sight-threatening condition that requires prompt assessment and treatment.

C_aqqM.title: Neurotrophic keratopathy
C_aqqM.description: Chronic degenerative corneal disease caused by a lesion of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (sensory nerve of the cornea and the lacrimal gland). Results in loss of corneal sensation, decreased lacrimation, increased breakdown of epithelium, and impaired corneal healing. Presents with decreased visual acuity, dry eye, and the absence of eye pain.

x_aEqM.title: Photokeratitis
x_aEqM.description: A condition caused by exposure of the eyes to UV radiation, leading to inflammation and damage of the cornea. Manifestations include pain, photophobia, and foreign body sensation.

__a5IM.title: Scleromalacia perforans
__a5IM.description: A necrotizing type of anterior scleritis that is painless and therefore often detected in its later stages. Complications include astigmatism, cataract, uveitis, and glaucoma, which can result in visual loss and, rarely, rupture of the globe. Most frequent type of scleritis associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

z_arIM.title: Aphakia
z_arIM.description: Absence of the lens of the eye.

azaQrM.title: Uveitis
azaQrM.description: An inflammation of the uvea. Can be caused by infectious (e.g., syphilis, tuberculosis) and noninfectious conditions (e.g., systemic disease, drug-induced, trauma). Classified according to the location of the affected structures: anterior, intermediate, and posterior. Panuveitis is inflammation that involves all structures of the uvea.

czaa7M.title: Anterior uveitis
czaa7M.description: A condition of inflammation of the anterior uveal tract. Manifestations include eye pain, redness, photophobia, and leukocytes in the anterior chamber of the eye.

1za27M.title: Intermediate uveitis
1za27M.description: A type of uveitis that affects the vitreous body (vitritis), pars plana (pars planitis), and peripheral retina. Manifests similarly to posterior uveitis with painless visual disturbance (i.e., floaters or blurry vision).

UzabHM.title: Iridodialysis
UzabHM.description: The separation of the iris from the ciliary body.

destinations.label: Diseases of the uvea → Rare conditions

SzayHM.title: Adie tonic pupil
SzayHM.description: Dilated tonic pupil that shows sluggish response to light with accomodation intact (light-near dissociation). Due to postganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor damage.

destinations.label: Physiology and abnormalities of the pupil → Other pupillary defects

3zaSsM.title: Argyll Robertson pupil
3zaSsM.description: Bilateral miosis and light-near dissociation as a result of a dorsal midbrain lesion, which selectively damages the fibers that control the pupillary reflex but spares the more ventral fibres that control the accommodation reflex. Common causes include syphilis and diabetes mellitus.

4za3GM.title: Posterior vitreous detachment
4za3GM.description: Detachment of the posterior vitreous cortex from the internal limiting membrane of the retina.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Posterior vitreous detachment

lzavGM.title: Vitreous hemorrhage
lzavGM.description: Bleeding into the vitreous chamber, which most often occurs from the retinal vessels. Important risk factors include trauma, posterior vitreous detachment, diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, blood dyscrasias (e.g., polycythemia, leukemia, sickle cell disease), and intraocular neoplasms.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Vitreous hemorrhage

Nza-GM.title: Vitrectomy
Nza-GM.description: A surgical procedure used to remove vitreous humor from the eye. Common indications include retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, and severe endophthalmitis.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Vitreous hemorrhage

5zaitM.title: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous
5zaitM.description: A congenital ocular disease that is due to the failure of both the embryonic primary vitreous and hyaloid vascular system to regress during gestation. Manifests with leukocoria and, if uncorrected, amblyopia.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous

oza0FM.title: Degenerative retinoschisis
oza0FM.description: Splitting of internal retina layers; typically occurs in elderly individuals and is usually asymptomatic.

IzaY8M.title: Central serous retinopathy
IzaY8M.description: An exudative retinal detachment that is limited to the macular region. Idiopathic, self-limited, and recurrent. Mostly affects men aged 20–45 years and may occur spontaneously or be triggered by stress, hypertension, or systemic steroid therapy. Patients present with micropsia, metamorphopsia, scotomas, or sudden painless loss of vision.

destinations.label: Diseases of the retina → Degenerative diseases of the retina

rzaf8M.title: Retinoschisis
rzaf8M.description: Splitting of the internal layers of the retina. May mimic retinal detachment on examination. There are two types: (1) the degenerative type, which is more common and usually asymptomatic and (2) the juvenile type, which is less common and can cause significant visual loss.

HzaK8M.title: Retinal periphlebitis
HzaK8M.description: A type of retinal vasculitis characterized by periphlebitis, vascular occlusion, and retinal neovascularization.

destinations.label: Diseases of the retina → Other retinal disorders

szat8M.title: Chloroquine maculopathy
szat8M.description: A type of toxic retinopathy caused by chronic chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine use. Clinical features include decreased visual acuity and impaired color perception.

tzaXuM.title: Bull's eye maculopathy
tzaXuM.description: A funduscopic finding consisting of annular changes to the retinal pigment epithelium with hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation.

uzapuM.title: Retinitis pigmentosa
uzapuM.description: Progressive hereditary dystrophy of the retina or of the photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium. Presents with visual changes (e.g., night blindness, tunnel vision). Similar symptoms may complicate phenothiazine or chloroquine therapy (i.e., pseudoretinitis pigmentosa).

destinations.label: Diseases of the retina → Dystrophic retinal diseases

CzaqEM.title: Coats disease
CzaqEM.description: A retinal disease characterized by retinal telangiectasias and exudative retinal detachment. Occurs during the first decade of life, predominantly in males, and usually affects only one eye.

destinations.label: Diseases of the retina → Vascular diseases of the retina

BzazEM.title: Retinopathy of prematurity
BzazEM.description: Disease of the retina with abnormal vessel proliferations that affects preterm, low-weight infants and leads to hemorrhages, fibrosis, and, in severe cases, retinal detachment presenting as leukocoria.

destinations.label: Diseases of the retina → Vascular diseases of the retina

media.title: Plus disease of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)

_za5vM.title: Leukocoria
_za5vM.description: Abnormal white reflection from the pupil (instead of the normal red-eye reflex). Though most commonly associated with retinoblastomas, it can also be seen in cataracts, retinal detachment, and Coats disease.

T-a69M.title: Papillitis
T-a69M.description: An inflammation of the optic disc characterized by a poorly-defined papilla, hyperemia, and hemorrhage at the border of the papilla on ophthalmoscopy. Etiologies include optic neuritis and anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.

g-aF9M.title: Retrobulbar neuritis
g-aF9M.description: A form of optic neuritis characterized by inflammation of the optic nerve behind the eyeball. Patients present with impaired vision, color blindness, mild pain that is worse with eye movement, and mostly normal findings on ophthalmoscopy. Most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.

destinations.label: Disorders of the visual pathway → Optic neuritis

h-acCM.title: Bitemporal hemianopsia
h-acCM.description: A condition characterized by a bilateral loss of vision in the outer (temporal) halves of the visual field. Usually associated with compression of the optic chiasm by adjacent structures such as the pituitary gland or blood vessels.

destinations.label: Disorders of the visual pathway → Scotoma and anopia

j-a_CM.title: Emmetropia
j-a_CM.description: A physiologic state of vision without refractive error in which rays of light entering the eye are focused on the retina. Results in 20/20 vision.

O-aIxM.title: Myopia
O-aIxM.description: A refractive error in which light rays entering the eye are focused anterior to the retina. Nearby objects appear in focus, while objects in the distance appear blurry. Onset is typically in childhood or adolescence.

m-aVBM.title: Hyperopia
m-aVBM.description: A refractive error in which light rays entering the eye are focused posterior to the retina. Nearby objects appear blurry, while objects in the distance appear in focus.

5-aiBM.title: Refractive surgery
5-aiBM.description: Surgical correction of refractive errors such as myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism. Options include keratorefractive surgery (in which the cornea is reshaped) and placement of intraocular lenses.

M-aMBM.title: Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis
M-aMBM.description: The most commonly performed refractive surgery, in which the cornea is reshaped using a laser. Indicated for the correction of myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism.

n-a7BM.title: Keratectomy
n-a7BM.description: The surgical removal of a corneal layer and reshaping of the cornea, usually using a laser (i.e., photorefractive keratectomy).

p-aLyM.title: Astigmatism
p-aLyM.description: A condition in which abnormal curvature of the cornea leads to two or more focal points, causing blurred vision at all distances.

I-aYAM.title: Presbyopia
I-aYAM.description: An age-related decrease in the power of accommodation of the eye caused by decreased elasticity of the crystalline lens and increased weakness of the ciliary muscles. Typically leads to the inability to focus on nearby objects.

H-aKAM.title: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
H-aKAM.description: A gaze abnormality localized to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) of the brainstem. Characterized by impaired horizontal eye movements with weak adduction of the affected eye and abduction nystagmus of the unaffected eye. Most cases (70%) are due to multiple sclerosis or stroke.

destinations.label: Ocular motility disorders and strabismus → Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)

s-atAM.title: Concomitant strabismus
s-atAM.description: A type of strabismus in which the deviation of the eyes (i.e., the angle between the visual axes of both eyes) remains constant in all directions of gaze.

destinations.label: Ocular motility disorders and strabismus → Concomitant strabismus

G-aBAM.title: Amblyopia
G-aBAM.description: A vision impairment of one eye (also called "lazy eye"), due to abnormal communication between the eye and the brain. May develop as a result of uncorrected strabismus, cataract, or refractive errors.

destinations.label: Ocular motility disorders and strabismus → Concomitant strabismus

E-a8_M.title: Occlusion treatment
E-a8_M.description: A treatment option for strabismus. Covering of the good eye results in training of the weaker eye and may prevent visual impairment.

destinations.label: Ocular motility disorders and strabismus → Concomitant strabismus

C-aqzM.title: Paralytic strabismus
C-aqzM.description: A type of strabismus that occurs as result of weakness or paralysis of one or more extraocular muscles.

destinations.label: Ocular motility disorders and strabismus → Paralytic strabismus

B-azzM.title: Commotio retinae
B-azzM.description: The development of retinal edema following blunt closed globe injury. Can cause decreased visual acuity.

destinations.label: Traumatic eye injuries → Closed globe contusion

y-ad-M.title: Hyphema
y-ad-M.description: A condition of grossly visible blood in the anterior chamber of the eye. Can have associated eye pain, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, and anisocoria. Etiologies include trauma and bleeding disorders.

A-aR-M.title: Blowout fracture
A-aR-M.description: A fracture of one or more walls of the orbit without a fracture of the orbital rim. Typically caused by blunt trauma to the eye. Clinical features include periorbital pain, edema, and/or ecchymosis; enophthalmos or proptosis; and restricted ocular movement.

z-ar-M.title: Sympathetic ophthalmia
z-ar-M.description: A bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs as a complication of unilateral penetrating injury (and rarely after ocular surgery). An autoimmune reaction is triggered by retinal antigens within the injured eye, which results in inflammation in both eyes. Manifests days to years after the initial injury with bilateral pain and photophobia; blindness can occur.

destinations.label: Traumatic eye injuries → Open globe injuries

0ZYeZn.title: Duty to protect
0ZYeZn.description: A health care professional's responsibility to safeguard a patient or others from serious and/or imminent physical harm or death. This obligation may entail warning a potential victim or initiating involuntary commitment of the patient. Most jurisdictions have established "Duty to Protect" laws, which provide the legal framework for such professional actions.

destinations.label: Ethics of communicating medical information → Confidentiality

bZYHZn.title: Therapeutic privilege
