bZYHZn.description: An exception to full disclosure in which the physician is allowed to withhold relevant health information from the patient if withholding it is in the patient's best interest (e.g., if disclosing it would pose serious psychological harm).

destinations.label: Ethics of communicating medical information → Disclosure

3ZYSYn.title: Legal competence
3ZYSYn.description: A legal determination that is made by a court of law that describes an individual's global decision-making ability (e.g., financial, legal, and health care decisions). Adults are assumed to be competent unless they have been officially declared incompetent via a legal process. In contrast, minors are not deemed competent unless they have been legally emancipated (e.g., via marriage, military service, or another official emancipation process).

destinations.label: Capacity, competence, and consent → Legal competence

jZY_Yn.title: Obligation to treat
jZY_Yn.description: In a medical emergency, a physician is legally obliged to treat a patient if failing to provide treatment would immediately endanger the patient's life.

destinations.label: Principles of medical law and ethics → Medical ethics

MZYMXn.title: Band keratopathy
MZYMXn.description: A type of corneal degeneration that involves the appearance of a band-shaped area of calcification across the central cornea. Most commonly caused by chronic eye infections or increased serum calcium and/or phosphate. Symptoms include decreased visual acuity, foreign body sensation in the eye, and photophobia.

destinations.label: Corneal disorders → Corneal degeneration, dystrophy, and deposits

nZY7Xn.title: Fuchs dystrophy
nZY7Xn.description: A inherited disease that predisposes to progressive loss of corneal endothelial cells, which results in an imbalance of water and electrolytes in the corneal epithelium. Manifestations include corneal edema, opacification, and bullous epithelial detachment.

destinations.label: Corneal disorders → Corneal degeneration, dystrophy, and deposits

oZY0cn.title: Arcus lipoides
oZY0cn.description: A yellow or gray discoloration of the corneal margin caused by deposits of fat and cholesterol or by hyalinosis of corneal stroma. Frequently occurs in the elderly but can also present in younger individuals with lipid disorders.

destinations.label: Corneal disorders → Corneal degeneration, dystrophy, and deposits

6ZYjcn.title: Kayser-Fleischer rings
6ZYjcn.description: An ophthalmologic finding characterized by green-brown, 1–2 mm rings in the periphery of the iris. Caused by copper accumulation in the Descemet membrane of the cornea. The rings can be seen on slit-lamp examination and are characteristic for Wilson disease (occur in 98% of patients who also have neurologic symptoms).

qZYCcn.title: Corneal erosion
qZYCcn.description: A detachment of the corneal epithelium from the tissue layers below, including the basement membrane and Bowman membrane. Risk factors for development include corneal dystrophy, corneal ulceration, and corneal abrasion. Manifestations include foreign body sensation, eye pain, tearing, and blurry vision.

IZYY1n.title: Keratoplasty
IZYY1n.description: The replacement of diseased cornea with cornea harvested from a recently deceased donor. Perforating keratoplasty (replacement of the complete cornea) is indicated when both anterior and posterior layers of the cornea are damaged. Lamellar keratoplasty (replacement of only the anterior or posterior corneal layers) is indicated when only the anterior or posterior layer of the cornea is damaged.

7ZY41n.title: Keratoconus
7ZY41n.description: Noninflammatory corneal condition in which the cornea becomes thinner than normal and develops a conic shape, bulging outward at the center.

destinations.label: Corneal disorders → Curvature anomalies of the cornea

HZYK1n.title: Keratoglobus
HZYK1n.description: A noninflammatory corneal condition in which the cornea becomes thinner than normal and develops a globular shape, bulging outward at the center.

destinations.label: Corneal disorders → Curvature anomalies of the cornea

GZYB1n.title: Occiput posterior position
GZYB1n.description: A type of malposition in which the fetal occiput faces the posterior maternal pelvis.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

uZYpWn.title: Breech presentation
uZYpWn.description: A fetal presentation in which the buttocks or the feet lie closest to the cervix. Factors such as prematurity, polyhydramnios, and placenta previa are commonly associated with breech presentation. Breech presentation in a term gestation is generally managed with a trial of external cephalic version (transabdominal rotation of the fetus to a cephalic presentation) and vaginal delivery. Cesarean section is done if ECV is unsuccessful or contraindicated (e.g., in active labor, fetal distress) to avoid possible complications of breech presentation, such as cord prolapse, fetal hypoxic injury, and birth trauma.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

vZYAWn.title: Frank breech
vZYAWn.description: A type of malpresentation in which the fetus is in a buttock-presenting position with the hips flexed and knees extended.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

media.title: Types of breech presentation: Frank breech

DZY1dn.title: Complete breech
DZY1dn.description: A type of malpresentation in which the fetus is in a buttock-presenting position with the hips and knees flexed and the feet near the buttocks.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

media.title: Types of breech presentation: complete breech

wZYhdn.title: Single footling breech
wZYhdn.description: A type of malpresentation in which the fetus presents with a foot from an extended leg, while the other hip and knee are flexed.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

media.title: Types of breech presentation: Single Footling breech

9ZYNdn.title: Double footling breech
9ZYNdn.description: A type of malpresentation in which the fetus presents with two feet and both hips and knees extended.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

media.title: Types of breech presentation: Double Footling breech

CZYqdn.title: Transverse lie
CZYqdn.description: A type of malpresentation in which the fetal long axis is perpendicular to the uterine long axis.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Orientation in utero

BZYzdn.title: Mauriceau maneuver
BZYzdn.description: An emergency maneuver used in obstetrics for the management of vaginal breech delivery. External suprapubic pressure is applied while flexing the fetal neck to rotate the fetus and allow for delivery of the head.

10Y2Un.title: Shoulder dystocia
10Y2Un.description: An obstetric emergency in which the anterior shoulder of the infant cannot pass below the pubic symphysis after delivery of the head. Various obstetrical maneuvers may be tried (e.g., McRoberts, Zavanelli) to deliver the infant and avoid fetal demise from umbilical cord compression. Risk factors include maternal diabetes and fetal macrosomia. Brachial plexus injury is a potential complication.

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Shoulder dystocia

V0YGUn.title: McRoberts maneuver
V0YGUn.description: An obstetric maneuver used as a first-line step in the management of shoulder dystocia. The patient lies in supine position with the buttocks on the edge of the table. The clinicians then abduct, externally rotate, and hyperflex the maternal hips to the symphysis pubis to move anteriorly and release the impacted fetal shoulder.

destinations.label: Abnormal labor and delivery → Shoulder dystocia

media.title: McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver) in shoulder dystocia

U0Yb2n.title: Bartter syndrome
U0Yb2n.description: A syndrome caused by a group of rare genetic disorders. Affects chloride reabsorption in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Patients present during early infancy with severe polyuria, hypotension, weakness, failure to thrive, metabolic alkalosis, and hypokalemia. Antenatal history of polyhydramnios may be present.

20YT2n.title: Fanconi syndrome
20YT2n.description: A rare renal tubular disorder characterized by a generalized defect in reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules. Causes increased excretion of glucose, phosphate, amino acids, bicarbonate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, and water. Can be hereditary (e.g., as part of inherited disorders like Wilson disease) or acquired (e.g., from drug toxicity, multiple myeloma, amyloidosis).

destinations.label: Renal tubular disorders → Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2)

f0Yk2n.title: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets
f0Yk2n.description: Hypophosphatemic rickets that is caused by a hereditary overactivity of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). The most common cause (80% of cases) of hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets is an X-linked dominant mutation in the PHEX gene, which is responsible for down-regulating FGF23 activity (X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets). Less commonly, hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation that makes FGF23 resistant to proteolysis, or by an autosomal recessive mutation that increases FGF23 production.

destinations.label: Renal tubular disorders → X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets

T0Y62n.title: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets
T0Y62n.description: The most common form of hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets. Caused by a dominant mutation of the PHEX gene on the X chromosome, which results in decreased deactivation of FGF23 and, subsequently, decreased reabsorption of phosphate at the proximal convoluted tubule. Typically manifests in early childhood with failure to thrive, bone pain, enthesopathy, and skeletal and dental deformities.

destinations.label: Renal tubular disorders → X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets

S0Yy2n.title: Renal tubular acidosis
S0Yy2n.description: A normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis in the presence of normal or almost normal renal function. The various types of RTA include proximal tubular bicarbonate wasting (type II), distal tubular acid secretion (type I), very rarely carbonic anhydrase deficiency (type III), and aldosterone deficiency/resistance (type IV). Renal tubular acidosis arises as a result of defects in the tubular transport of HCO3- and/or H+. Most forms of RTA are asymptomatic although, rarely, life-threatening electrolyte imbalances can occur.

destinations.label: Renal tubular disorders → Renal tubular acidosis (RTA)

h0Ycfn.title: Bag-mask ventilation
h0Ycfn.description: A method of manually providing ventilation to patients with severe respiratory distress or apnea. A mask is held in place over the face and breaths are delivered by squeezing a self-inflating bag attached to the mask. The equipment can be attached to oxygen and used with airway adjuncts such as an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway.

O0YITn.title: Red flags for a difficult airway
O0YITn.description: A collection of conditions that predispose to difficulties in ventilation, laryngoscopy, and/or endotracheal intubation. Examples include airway obstruction (e.g., from angioedema, masses, foreign bodies), altered anatomy (e.g., from congenital, acquired, or iatrogenic causes), trauma/burns, obesity, reduced mouth opening, and decreased neck mobility.

l0YvTn.title: Mallampati score
l0YvTn.description: A score that is used to assess the visibility of oropharyngeal structures in upright patients with open mouths and fully protruding tongues. Used primarily to predict difficult conditions for tracheal intubation (with difficulty scored on a scale of 1-4). Occasionally used in the risk stratification of patients with obstructive sleep apnea.

q0YCSn.title: Laryngotracheal stenosis
q0YCSn.description: An abnormal narrowing of the larynx (i.e., supraglottis, glottis, subglottis) or trachea. Commonly manifests with stridor, which may be inspiratory (supraglottic or glottic stenosis) or biphasic (glottic, subglottic, tracheal stenosis); hypoxia; and respiratory distress.

I0YYhn.title: Tracheomalacia
I0YYhn.description: An abnormal collapsing of the walls of the trachea. It can arise due to a primary issue of the cartilage or from an external source (vascular rings, masses, etc). Symptoms are similar to those of airway obstruction and include (expiratory) stridor and wheezing.

r0Yfhn.title: Bronchospasm
r0Yfhn.description: A constriction of the smooth airway muscles that causes severe hypoxia and hypotension if left untreated. Risk factors include smoking, obstructive airway disease (e.g., asthma, COPD), and viral upper respiratory tract infection. May also occur as a result of general anesthesia and mechanical ventilation.

70Y4hn.title: Intubation
70Y4hn.description: A procedure in which a tube is placed into the trachea through the mouth (orotracheal) or nose (nasotracheal) to maintain a patent airway. Used perioperatively for anesthetized patients and has various indications in emergency medicine, including acute respiratory failure, poor oxygenation or ventilation, and risk of airway compromise.

G0YBhn.title: Capnography
G0YBhn.description: A noninvasive method of continuously measuring the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in exhaled gases. Detector applications include nasal cannula, endotracheal tube, and transcutaneous detectors. Used to monitor respiratory status (e.g., in patients with decreased respiratory drive, to confirm ETT tube placement after intubation) and to assess response after cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

80YO3n.title: Continuous positive airway pressure
80YO3n.description: A form of noninvasive ventilation that uses positive air pressure to keep airways open. It is used in the treatment of a variety of conditions, including severe pneumonia, COPD, obstructive sleep apnea, and acute congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema.

u0Yp3n.title: PEEP
u0Yp3n.description: The maintenance of positive pressure within the alveoli at the end of expiration.

_0Y5in.title: TIVA
_0Y5in.description: A technique for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia using IV drugs alone, without inhalational agents. Propofol is usually the anesthetic agent of choice, mainly because it is associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting compared to other IV anesthetic agents.

YaYnQn.title: Laryngeal mask airway
YaYnQn.description: A method of ventilation using a supraglottic airway device. Can be used for difficult airways after a failed intubation, as an alternative to intubation in cardiac arrest patients, or as an alternative to bag-valve-mask ventilation prior to intubation.

XaY9Qn.title: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan
XaY9Qn.description: A nuclear medicine examination that uses Tc-99m pertechnetate (a radioactive tracer) to visualize various structures in the body. Examples of studies that use this technique include bone scintigraphy, myocardial perfusion imaging, and the Meckel scan.

1aY2jn.title: Immunohistochemical marker
1aY2jn.description: A cell-surface antigen that can be detected via histopathologic examination of tissue. Used to categorize cell types based on expressed markers (e.g., CD20 as a marker for B cells).

WaYPjn.title: Vimentin
WaYPjn.description: An intermediate filament expressed in the cytoskeleton of mesenchymal cells. Used as a marker for mesenchymal tumors (e.g. sarcoma, mesothelioma).

daYojn.title: Desmin
daYojn.description: A muscle-specific protein that comprises intermediate filaments. Desmin staining is used to histologically identify neoplastic cells that arise from muscle.

eaYxjn.title: CD20
eaYxjn.description: An antigen that is present on the B-cell surface during all stages development with the exception of the first (early pro-B cells) and last stages (plasmablasts/plasma cells). CD20 is commonly used as a tumor marker to identify hematological malignancies of B cell lineage. Monoclonal antibodies against CD20 (e.g., rituximab) can be used against these tumors.

UaYbPn.title: CD3
UaYbPn.description: An immunohistochemical marker used to identify T lymphocytes.

2aYTPn.title: CD8
2aYTPn.description: A surface protein found on cytotoxic T cells. Acts as a coreceptor to the T cell receptor when communicating with antigen-presenting cells. CD8 specifically binds to MHC class I molecules expressed on antigen-presenting cells.

faYkPn.title: CD4
faYkPn.description: A surface protein found on T helper cells. Acts as a coreceptor to the T cell receptor when communicating with antigen-presenting cells. CD4 specifically binds to MHC class II molecules expressed on antigen-presenting cells. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) specifically infects CD4+ lymphocytes.

TaY6Pn.title: Alpha-fetoprotein
TaY6Pn.description: A globulin normally produced by fetal endodermal tissues with unclear function (possibly similar to albumin). AFP levels can be used for prenatal testing and as a tumor marker for some germ cell and liver tumors.

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

haYc4n.title: CA 15-3
haYc4n.description: A serum marker used to monitor response to treatment and tumor recurrence in breast cancer.

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

RaYl4n.title: CA 19-9
RaYl4n.description: A carbohydrate antigen used as a tumor marker for pancreatic (elevated in 70% of cases), hepatobiliary, gastric, colorectal, and endometrial carcinomas. May also be elevated in benign conditions, such as liver cirrhosis, cholestasis, and lung abnormalities (e.g., pneumonia, cystic fibrosis).

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

iaYJ4n.title: Carcinoma antigen 125
iaYJ4n.description: A protein that is secreted by epithelial cells and elevated in the majority of individuals with epithelial ovarian or fallopian tube cancer. CA 125 is commonly used as a biomarker for ovarian cancer detection, but it is neither sensitive nor specific. Levels may be elevated in other malignancies (e.g., breast, lung, and endometrial cancer) and in various physiological states and disease processes (e.g., menstruation, pregnancy, endometriosis, heart failure).

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

jaY_4n.title: Carcinoembryonic antigen
jaY_4n.description: Very nonspecific tumor marker which is elevated in most adenocarcinomas.

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

4aY3kn.title: Chromogranin A
4aY3kn.description: A secretory protein produced by neuroendocrine cells. Used as a biomarker for neuroendocrine neoplasms (e.g., pheochromocytoma, small cell lung carcinoma).

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

OaYIkn.title: Neuron specific enolase
OaYIkn.description: An isoform of phosphopyruvate hydratase (a glycolytic enzyme) found in neurons and neuroendocrine cells. Used as a biomarker of neuronal damage (e.g., anoxic-ischemic encephalopathy) and of tumors of neuroendocrine origin (e.g., small cell lung carcinoma).

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

laYvkn.title: Placental alkaline phosphatase
laYvkn.description: A molecule primarily expressed in placental and endometrial tissue. Can be used as a tumor marker for germ cell tumors and ovarian adenocarcinoma.

NaY-kn.title: S-100 protein
NaY-kn.description: A cytoplasmic protein that is used as a tumor marker on immunohistochemical staining, particularly for cells derived from neural crest. Associated with malignant melanoma, schwannomas, neurofibromas, peripheral neural sheath tumors, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

destinations.label: Tumor markers → Common tumor markers in peripheral blood

oaY0ln.title: Sputum
oaY0ln.description: A collection of mucus expectorated from the respiratory tract that consists of water, cells (e.g., leukocytes, sloughed tracheobronchial epithelial cells), particles, proteins (e.g., glycoproteins, IgA, albumin, fibrinogen), and microorganisms.

KaYUln.title: Dyspnea
KaYUln.description: A sensation of breathing discomfort or shortness of breath.

7aY4Nn.title: Stridor
7aY4Nn.description: A pathological high-pitched breath sound produced by airflow through a partially obstructed airway. May occur during inspiration and/or expiration.

media.title: Barking cough, inspiratory stridor und chest retractions in viral croup | External video

GaYBNn.title: Lung percussion
GaYBNn.description: A part of the pulmonary examination. Hyperextends your nondominant middle finger and place the distal interphalangeal joint over the lung fields. Strike the joint with the other middle finger and evaluate the elicited sound. Pathologic findings include hyperresonance (e.g., in pneumothorax) and dullness (e.g., in pleural effusion, consolidation).

vaYAmn.title: Bronchial breathing
vaYAmn.description: A physiological breath sound characterized by loud and high-pitched sounds auscultated through part of inspiration and all of expiration, best heard over the sternum.

waYh5n.title: Auscultation of the lungs
waYh5n.description: The use of a stethoscope to examine the lungs. Typically performed with the patient sitting upright with auscultation posteriorly, anteriorly, and laterally. Used to assess the quality of breath sounds of the upper, middle, and lower lung fields. Pathological findings include absent breath sounds, crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi.

xaYE5n.title: Airway resistance
xaYE5n.description: The resistance to airflow from the mouth to the alveoli during inspiration and expiration.

AaYRMn.title: Peak expiratory flow
AaYRMn.description: The maximum airflow rate attained during forced expiration, which can be measured by a peak flow meter or during formal spirometry. Decreased in patients with obstructive lung disease. Typically correlates with FEV₁ as a marker of airway obstruction. Accuracy decreases with low airflow.

_aY5Mn.title: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second
_aY5Mn.description: The maximum volume of air that can be expired in the first second of forced expiration after maximal inspiration.

-aYDMn.title: Inspiratory vital capacity
-aYDMn.description: The maximum volume of air that can be inspired after maximal expiration (during slow respiratory maneuvers).

0YYenn.title: Forced vital capacity
0YYenn.description: The maximum volume of air that can be forcefully expired after maximal inspiration. Depends on race, height, age, and sex; it is approximately 4.5–5 L in healthy young adults.

aYYQnn.title: FEV1/FVC
aYYQnn.description: The ratio of FEV₁ (maximum volume of air that can be forcefully expired within 1 second after maximal inspiration) to forced vital capacity. FEV₁/FVC ratio is decreased (< LLN) in obstructive lung disease. In restrictive lung diseases, FEV₁/FVC ratio may be normal or increased (> ULN).

YYYnnn.title: Forced expiratory flow rate
YYYnnn.description: Average airflow rates observed during forced expiration when 75%, 50%, and 25% of the vital capacity remains in the lungs. For example, FEF75 refers to the average airflow rate observed when 75% of the vital capacity is left in the lungs or, in other words, when 25% of the vital capacity has been expired. These three values (FEF75, FEF50, and FEF25) can be used to localize obstructions.

bYYHnn.title: Spirometry
bYYHnn.description: A test in which the volume and flow rate of air is measured as a patient breathes normally (measuring vital capacity), inhales deeply (measuring forced vital capacity), and forcefully exhales (measuring forced expiratory volume).

cYYaLn.title: Restrictive lung diseases
cYYaLn.description: A group of lung conditions characterized by an impaired ability of the lungs to expand. Causes include disorders that affect the lung parenchyma (e.g., interstitial lung disease, pneumonia, pulmonary edema), pleura, and pleural cavity, deformities of the thorax, and respiratory muscle weakness. Typically causes ↓ vital capacity, ↓ total lung capacity, normal/↓ FEV1 (due to ↓ in vital capacity), and a normal or ↑ FEV1:FVC ratio.

WYYPLn.title: Diffusing capacity
WYYPLn.description: A measure of gas exchange from the alveoli to erythrocytes in the pulmonary capillaries. Used to assess the ability of the lungs to transport gas via diffusion across the air-blood barrier. To determine diffusion capacity, patients inhale a predefined amount of carbon monoxide (CO), and then the exhaled CO is measured to determine the difference between inhaled and exhaled CO.

destinations.label: Pulmonary function testing → Single-breath diffusing capacity

VYYGLn.title: Obstructive lung diseases
VYYGLn.description: A group of lung diseases associated with increased resistance to airflow. Examples include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchial asthma, and bronchiectasis. Patients with obstructive lung disease have decreased FEV₁, an FEV₁/FVC ratio < LLN (or < 0.7), decreased vital capacity, increased residual volume (due to air trapping), and normal or increased total lung capacity.

UYYbon.title: Air trapping
UYYbon.description: The retention of excess gas in the lungs due to airway obstruction and/or changes in lung compliance (e.g., due to emphysema). Results in hyperresonance on percussion of the lung fields.

2YYTon.title: Post-bronchodilator test
2YYTon.description: An assessment of airflow after bronchodilator (e.g., albuterol) administration. A positive response is defined as an increase in FEV₁ and/or FVC of ≥ 12% of the predicted value and ≥ 200 mL after inhalation of the bronchodilator; usually indicates asthma but may also be the result of a reversible component of airway obstruction in COPD.

destinations.label: Pulmonary function testing → Specialized testing in obstructive lung disease

TYY6on.title: Methacholine provocation test
TYY6on.description: A test that is used to assess for bronchial hyperresponsiveness. The patient is given gradually increasing doses of methacholine (a potent bronchoconstrictor), and spirometry measurements are taken after each dose. Spirometry shows a reduction in FEV at lower doses in individuals with bronchial hyperresponsiveness than in those without. May be used to help rule out asthma when initial spirometry is equivocal, or if symptoms and/or response to therapy are atypical.

destinations.label: Pulmonary function testing → Specialized testing in obstructive lung disease

3YYSKn.title: Total lung capacity
3YYSKn.description: The volume of air in the lungs after maximal inhalation; approximately 6-6.5 L in a healthy adult. Can be calculated as the sum of all lung volumes (i.e., tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, residual volume).

RYYlKn.title: Vital capacity
RYYlKn.description: The change in lung volume between maximum inspiration and maximum expiration; approximately 4.5-5 L in a healthy adult. Vital capacity is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume.

iYYJKn.title: Residual volume
iYYJKn.description: The volume of air that remains in the lungs after forced maximal exhalation. Normally 1–1.5 liters.

QYYuKn.title: Tidal volume
QYYuKn.description: The volume of air that is inhaled during a normal breath at rest. Normally ∼ 500 mL or 7 mL/kg.

PYYW6n.title: Inspiratory reserve volume
PYYW6n.description: The maximum volume of air that can still be forcibly inhaled following the inhalation of a normal tidal volume. Normally 3–3.5 liters.

4YY36n.title: Inspiratory reserve capacity
4YY36n.description: The maximum volume of air that can be inhaled after the exhalation of a normal tidal volume (i.e., the sum of inspiratory reserve volume and tidal volume). Normally 3.5–4 liters.

kYYm6n.title: Expiratory reserve volume
kYYm6n.description: The maximum volume of air that can still be forcibly exhaled after the exhalation of a normal tidal volume. Normally ~1.5 liters.

media.title: Measurement of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)

OYYI6n.title: Expiratory capacity
OYYI6n.description: The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the inspiration of a normal tidal volume (i.e., the sum of expiratory reserve volume and tidal volume). Normally ~ 2 liters.

lYYv6n.title: Functional residual capacity
lYYv6n.description: The volume of air that remains in the lungs after the exhalation of a normal tidal volume (i.e., the sum of residual volume and expiratory reserve volume). Normally 2.5–3 liters.

MYYMpn.title: Extractable nuclear antigen antibodies
MYYMpn.description: A group of autoantibodies directed against various extractable nuclear antigens (e.g., ribonucleoprotein complexes, double-stranded DNA). Includes anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-Sm, and anti-RNP. Antigen-specific antinuclear antibodies may be found in patients with autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren syndrome, and polymyositis.

destinations.label: Autoantibodies in rheumatic diseases → Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs)

nYY7pn.title: Antinuclear antibody
nYY7pn.description: A group of autoantibodies directed against various nuclear antigens (e.g., DNA, RNA, histones, acidic nuclear proteins) and complexes of these molecular elements. ANAs can be positive in patients with several autoimmune (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, polymyositis) and infectious diseases (e.g., tuberculosis) but can also be present in healthy individuals.

destinations.label: Autoantibodies in rheumatic diseases → Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs)

LYYwpn.title: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
LYYwpn.description: A group of antibodies against specific cytoplasmic proteins in neutrophils and lysosomal proteins in monocytes. Typically found in either cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) or perinuclear (p-ANCA) patterns in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (e.g., eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis) but may also be found in patients with other conditions such as ulcerative colitis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

destinations.label: Autoantibodies in rheumatic diseases → Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs)

oYY0Jn.title: Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody
oYY0Jn.description: A type of ANCA primarily directed against serine proteinase 3. Visualized as diffuse cytoplasmic staining pattern on immunofluorescence. Levels are typically increased in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, but may also be present in patients with other vasculitides or infective endocarditis.

destinations.label: Autoantibodies in rheumatic diseases → Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs)

media.title: Cytoplasmic pattern of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA)

KYYUJn.title: p-ANCA
KYYUJn.description: A type of ANCA directed most often against myeloperoxidase granules (present in the perinuclear region of cytoplasm). Visualized as perinuclear cytoplasmic staining on immunofluorescence. p-ANCA levels are typically increased in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (especially eosinophilic polyangiitis with granulomatosis and microscopic polyangiitis); may also be found in patients with other conditions such as ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis.

destinations.label: Autoantibodies in rheumatic diseases → Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs)

rYYfqn.title: Resection arthroplasty
rYYfqn.description: A surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is partially or completed removed to preserve as much function as possible.

7YY4qn.title: Salter osteotomy
7YY4qn.description: A surgical technique that involves complete transection and repositioning of the iliac bone for better coverage of the femoral head. Frequently used to correct bone misalignment in children ages 2-10 with hip dysplasia.

sYYtqn.title: Nonunion
sYYtqn.description: A failure of bone healing caused by nonunion of long bone fragments (e.g., due to insufficient immobilization). Results in the creation of a false joint (pseudarthrosis) due to the nonunion.

GYYBqn.title: Amputations
GYYBqn.description: The loss or removal of a limb or appendage. Traumatic amputations result from injury; surgical amputations can be performed as a life-saving treatment.

tYYXIn.title: Rotationplasty
tYYXIn.description: A surgical procedure that involves the resection of a femoral lesion (e.g., malignancy) with reattachment of the lower leg, rotated 180°, to the proximal thigh. Allows the ankle joint to function as a knee joint with subsequent attachment of a prosthesis.

uYYpIn.title: Internal fixation
uYYpIn.description: The placement of rods, nails, plates, and/or screws within the body to immobilize and stabilize the site of a fracture and/or dislocation.

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → Internal fixation

media.title: Internal fixation of a vertebral fracture
Open reduction-internal fixation of Weber B ankle fracture  (2/2)
Open reduction-internal fixation of Weber B ankle fracture (1/2)

vYYAIn.title: Lag screw fixation
vYYAIn.description: A surgical method that internally stabilizes a fracture by using a screw to align bone fragments. When the screw is tightened, the fragment farthest from the screw head is moved closer to the fragment in which the head is embedded. This provides the maximal direct fracture stabilization, as compared to bone plates which indirectly stabilize the fracture by exerting force on the bone cortex.

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → Internal fixation

media.title: Cancellous lag screw osteosynthesis of femoral neck fracture

DYY1rn.title: Intramedullary nails
DYY1rn.description: A metal rod that is inserted into the medullary cavity of a bone to internally fix fractures.

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → Internal fixation

media.title: Intramedullary nail fixation of femoral shaft fracture

9YYNrn.title: Tension-band wiring
9YYNrn.description: An internal fixation technique that converts distraction forces into compression forces. Typically done with two Kirschner wires and a tension band applied in a figure eight loop across the fracture.

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → Internal fixation

CYYqrn.title: Kirschner wire
CYYqrn.description: Stainless steel wires used in orthopedic surgery to fixate bone fragments. Used particularly in fractures of smaller bones and in pediatric patients.

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → Internal fixation

media.title: Kirschner wire (K-wire) fixation of distal radius fracture

yYYd7n.title: External fixation
yYYd7n.description: A method of immobilizing and stabilizing a fracture using pins and/or screws that are secured outside of the skin. Typically used when managing unstable polytrauma victims in whom more critical interventions are prioritized (e.g., patients with vascular injury or severe open fractures).

destinations.label: Trauma and orthopedic surgery → External fixation

media.title: External fixation of a comminuted fracture of the tibia

zYYr7n.title: Arthroplasty
zYYr7n.description: A surgical procedure performed to reconstruct or replace a dysfunctional joint. Both total arthroplasty or partial arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty) are performed using an endoprosthesis.

dbYosn.title: Volkmann's ischemic contracture
dbYosn.description: A permanent shortening of the forearm muscles, which results in a claw-like deformity of the fingers, hand, and wrist. Caused by atrophy of the flexors of the hand and fingers when casts are too tight or blood vessels or nerves have been damaged during fracture or repositioning of the bones.

fbYkGn.title: Pancreaticoduodenectomy
fbYkGn.description: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) involves resection of the pancreatic head, distal stomach, duodenum, gallbladder, common bile duct, lymphadenectomy, and reconstruction, most commonly by enteroenterostomy or Roux-en-Y anastomosis. It is indicated for pancreatic head carcinoma and is the most commonly performed procedure to remove pancreatic tumors.

destinations.label: Pancreatic and hepatic surgery → Pancreatic surgery

SbYyGn.title: Pringle maneuver
SbYyGn.description: A surgical maneuver in which the hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the hepatic artery and portal vein) is temporarily clamped in order to reduce vascular inflow to the liver or control liver hemorrhage. The occlusion is released every 30–45 minutes to minimize risk of hepatic artery/portal vein thrombosis and ischemic injury to the liver.

destinations.label: Pancreatic and hepatic surgery → Hepatic surgery

PbYWFn.title: Genu varum
PbYWFn.description: A misalignment of the lower extremity characterized by outward curving of the leg at the knees, resulting in separation of the knees when the ankles are close together. The degree of misalignment can be measured using the hip-knee-ankle angle on radiography. May be a physiological finding in children ≤ 2 years of age. Pathological causes include rickets, osteoarthritis, and injury.

destinations.label: Angular deformities of the lower extremities → Overview

mbYV8n.title: Examination of the spine
mbYV8n.description: A part of the physical examination that involves assessment of the back and spine. Note any skin abnormalities and assess the curvature of the spine, gait abnormalities, and range of motion (flexion to ~ 75° is normal; extension to ~ 20° is normal). Palpate the spine and note any swelling, tenderness, or protrusions. Test the sacroiliac joints by placing each thumb beneath the patient's posterior superior iliac spines, then asking the patient to lift their knees sequentially. Pain during this maneuver can indicate sacroiliac strain or arthritis.

BbYzDn.title: Colposcopy
BbYzDn.description: An examination of the cervix, vagina, and vulva using a colposcope.

media.title: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion of the cervix (HSIL)
Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) of the cervix
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) of the cervix
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) of the cervix

ybYdwn.title: Nabothian cysts
ybYdwn.description: A benign cyst that can form on the surface of the cervix when squamous epithelium grows over glandular columnar epithelium. Typically asymptomatic but can cause pain or a feeling of vaginal fullness. Treatment involves ablation with electrocautery.

_bY5wn.title: Cervical polyps
_bY5wn.description: A small, benign growth of hyperplastic endocervical epithelium that may be asymptomatic or cause spontaneous or postcoital vaginal bleeding. More common in multiparous perimenopausal or postmenopausal individuals. Treatment is often unnecessary, but ablation may be performed for persistent symptoms.

-bYDwn.title: Endocervical curettage
-bYDwn.description: A gynecological procedure used to obtain a specimen to evaluate for cervical dysplasia. An endocervical curette is placed into the external cervix and samples are taken.

0XYe9n.title: Transvaginal ultrasound
0XYe9n.description: A procedure in which an ultrasonography probe is inserted into the vagina to visualize pelvic structures, including the vagina, uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and bladder. Typically performed with the patient in the lithotomy position.

bXYH9n.title: Nuchal translucency
bXYH9n.description: The ultrasound assessment of the fluid-filled area in the posterior fetal neck. Measurement of this space may be used for prenatal genetic screening. A NT ≥ 3 mm or > 99th percentile for a specified crown-rump length measurement is associated with fetal aneuploidies (e.g., Down syndrome) and congenital anomalies.

media.title: Increased nuchal translucency in Down syndrome

cXYaCn.title: Quad screen test
cXYaCn.description: A prenatal screening test performed at 15–22 weeks' gestation that includes the measurement of β-HCG, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), estriol, and inhibin A in the maternal serum. Decreased levels of free estriol and AFP suggest numerical abnormalities of the fetal chromosomes. β-HCG is also elevated in trisomy 21 and decreased in trisomy 18. In cases with an increased risk (based on maternal age, lab results, and ultrasound), amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling are recommended for chromosome analysis.

1XY2Cn.title: Amniocentesis
1XY2Cn.description: A prenatal diagnostic procedure in which amniotic fluid is extracted under sonographic guidance via transabdominal puncture. It is optimally performed from 15 weeks' of gestation onwards. Indications include evaluation for possible chromosomal abnormalities or fetal infections. Possible complications include miscarriage, premature rupture of the membranes, and infection.

WXYPCn.title: Chorionic villus sampling
WXYPCn.description: The transcervical or transabdominal removal of chorionic tissue under sonographic guidance for diagnosing potential genetic abnormalities in early pregnancy. Performed for definitive testing between 10–13 weeks of gestation.

hXYcBn.title: Fetal heart rate
hXYcBn.description: The number of fetal heart contractions per minute (beats per minute, bpm). Normal fetal heart rate is between 110-160 bpm and can be measured via cardiotocography (CTG). A reassuring fetal heart rate pattern on CTG exhibits moderate baseline variability with ≥ 2 accelerations but no decelerations in a 20 minute period.

destinations.label: Normal labor and delivery → Intrapartum fetal monitoring

kXYmyn.title: Crown-rump length
kXYmyn.description: The length of the embryo or fetus from the top of its head (vertex) to the coccyx or bottom of the torso as measured by ultrasonography. CRL is the most accurate measurement of gestational age during the first trimester. Gestational age is estimated using the formula: CRL (in mm) + 42.

OXYIyn.title: Biparietal diameter
OXYIyn.description: The largest transverse diameter of the head as measured between the two parietal prominences. During pregnancy, fetal biparietal diameter can be measured ultrasonographically in a transverse plane of the head at the level of the thalami and cavum septum pellucidum. Fetal biparietal diameter gives the most reliable estimate of gestational age between 14 and 20 weeks. By term, the biparietal diameter measures 9.5 cm on average; a large biparietal diameter can increase the risk of obstructed labor. Gestational age is estimated using the formula: 44.2 + (BPD in mm x 2).

media.title: Fetal biometry: biparietal diameter and head circumference

5XYiAn.title: Psychodynamic psychotherapy
5XYiAn.description: A type of psychotherapy that uncovers unconscious patterns of childhood experiences, previous relationships, past conflicts, and desires with the goal of improving an individual's current situation and everyday functioning. Most effective in patients with anxiety disorders (e.g., phobias) and depressive disorders. Usually weekly sessions for 6 months to years.

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Psychodynamic psychotherapy

LXYwAn.title: Regression (psychiatry)
LXYwAn.description: An immature defense mechanism characterized by an attempt to return to a child-like state in order to avoid particular situations or stress associated with the present level of development (e.g., a previously toilet-trained child begins to wet the bed again after the birth of a new sibling).

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Defense mechanisms

IXYYzn.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy
IXYYzn.description: A type of psychological therapy that involves identifying and modifying maladaptive thought patterns, emotional responses, and behaviors. Used in the treatment of many psychiatric disorders (e.g., major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and eating disorders).

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)

DXY1ZL.title: Systemic desensitization
DXY1ZL.description: A behavioral therapy technique that pairs relaxation techniques with increasing exposure to an anxiety- or fear-provoking stimulus. A relaxation response gradually replaces the fear response. Used to treat multiple disorders, including phobias.

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Behavioral therapy

AXYR0L.title: Aversion therapy
AXYR0L.description: A technique in behavioral therapy in which an unwanted behavior is repeatedly paired with a nonrewarding stimulus. Used to treat addictions and paraphilias. For example, an unpleasant tasting nail polish can be used in aversion therapy to discourage nail biting)

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Behavioral therapy

acYQaL.title: Biofeedback
acYQaL.description: A patient-guided treatment that teaches an individual to control biological signals (e.g., muscle tension, pain, body temperature, brain waves, and other bodily functions and processes) through relaxation, visualization, and other cognitive control techniques. Used in patients with chronic pain, IBS, epilepsy, several psychiatric disorders, headaches, high blood pressure, and urinary incontinence.

destinations.label: Psychotherapy and defense mechanisms → Behavioral therapy

bcYHaL.title: Primary survey
bcYHaL.description: An approach to the initial evaluation of critically ill or injured patients, performed in sequence: Airway (assess patency by having the patient speak and/or inspecting the mouth and larynx), Breathing (check respiratory rate and effort, perform pulse oximetry, and auscultate the chest), Circulation (evaluate heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral perfusion; palpate pulses), Disability (assess mental status and pupils), and Exposure (check temperature, inspect skin, and remove inciting agents; in trauma, undress to assess for occult injuries and spinal or rectal findings).

destinations.label: Management of trauma patients → Primary survey

WcYPYL.title: Polytrauma
WcYPYL.description: A combination of severe injuries occurring in more than one anatomical region that are associated with systemic physiological disturbances.

UcYbbL.title: Speech audiometry
UcYbbL.description: A procedure in which increasingly loud words are played via a speaker to a patient, who then repeats the words. The speech reception threshold is determined by the sound intensity level at which a patient can correctly repeat 50% of words.

gcYFbL.title: Audiogram
gcYFbL.description: A graphic plot generated from pure tone audiometry. The plot is an auditory threshold curve for air and bone conduction, which represents the degree of hearing loss for individual frequencies.

4cY3cL.title: Otoacoustic emissions
4cY3cL.description: The sound emissions that originate from the cochlea, which arise spontaneously or in response to acoustic stimulation. The emissions can be measured in the auditory canal to assess cochlear function (e.g., for newborn hearing screening).

NcY-cL.title: Stapedius muscle
NcY-cL.description: The smallest skeletal muscle in the body. Originates from the pyramidal walls of the middle ear and inserts onto the neck of the stapes. Innervated by the nerve to stapedius, a branch of the facial nerve. Dampens transmission of loud noises to the inner ear. Stapedius weakness (e.g., due to Bell palsy) can cause hyperacusis.

5cYi1L.title: Tuning fork test
5cYi1L.description: A type of test used to assess hearing loss. The Weber test evaluates for asymmetric hearing loss (lateralization). The Rinne test evaluates air conduction and bone conduction in the examined ear to assess for the presence of conductive hearing loss.

destinations.label: Head and neck examination → Examination of the ears

ncY71L.title: Rinne test
ncY71L.description: A test that assesses for conductive hearing loss. A vibrating tuning fork is placed on the mastoid process. When the patient no longer hears the tone, the fork is immediately placed over the outer ipsilateral ear. A patient with normal conductive hearing will hear the tuning fork again once it is held over the ear because air conduction is greater than bone conduction (positive Rinne test). This finding also occurs in sensorineural hearing loss, in which bone and air conduction are equally diminished. If the patient does not hear a sound again, the test is negative, which indicates that the patient has conductive hearing loss.

destinations.label: Head and neck examination → Examination of the ears

media.title: Weber and Rinne Test - Clinical Examination

LcYw1L.title: Weber test
LcYw1L.description: A test that assesses for hearing loss by analysis of sound conduction. A vibrating tuning fork is placed on the middle of the forehead. A patient with normal hearing or symmetric hearing loss will hear the sound equally in both ears; lateralization indicates asymmetric hearing loss. Sound lateralizes to the affected ear in patients with conductive hearing loss and to the healthy ear in patients with sensorineural hearing loss.

destinations.label: Head and neck examination → Examination of the ears

media.title: Weber and Rinne Test - Clinical Examination
Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests

KcYUWL.title: Sensorineural hearing loss
KcYUWL.description: A hearing loss caused by acquired or congenital lesions in the cochlea, cranial nerve VIII, or central auditory pathways. Etiologies of acquired sensorineural hearing loss include presbycusis, ototoxicity, Ménière disease, acoustic neuroma, noise-induced hearing loss, trauma, inner ear infections, and systemic diseases (e.g., diabetic otopathy, autoimmune disorders).

pcYLWL.title: Conductive hearing loss
pcYLWL.description: A condition of hearing loss caused by impaired or interrupted conduction of sound through the outer ear, tympanic membrane, or middle ear. Etiologies include cerumen buildup, perforation or retraction of the tympanic membrane, otitis media, barotrauma, and otosclerosis.

7cY4dL.title: Pharmacokinetics
7cY4dL.description: The properties of a drug that relate to how it moves through the body (e.g., liberation, absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination).

scYtdL.title: Amphiphilic
scYtdL.description: A chemical compound with both hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties.

FcYgVL.title: Biotransformation
FcYgVL.description: A process that takes place primarily in the liver and affects both endogenous and exogenous substances. Serves as a mechanism of detoxification by altering a drug's chemical structure to facilitate elimination. Can be divided into phase I and phase II reactions.

8cYOVL.title: Bioavailability
8cYOVL.description: The ratio of a given drug that reaches systemic circulation. In reference to oral drugs, bioavailability is dependent on the first-pass effect (in the liver) and individual absorption rates. Intravenously administered drugs have a bioavailability of 1.

media.title: Area under the curve of bioavailability graphs

EcY8VL.title: First pass effect
EcY8VL.description: A process in which an agent that is absorbed by the gastrointestinal mucosa (usually orally administered drugs) undergoes metabolism by the liver before it enters the systemic circulation. Decreases bioavailability of the drug.

vcYAVL.title: Half-life
vcYAVL.description: The time it takes for half of the initial plasma concentration of a drug to be eliminated. After four half-lives, more than 90% of the drug has been eliminated. Half-life is typically reported as the half-life of the terminal elimination phase of a drug; however, this may not accurately predict accumulation or the duration of action of drugs with atypical kinetics (e.g., those with a high volume of distribution).

CcYqeL.title: First order kinetics
CcYqeL.description: A chemical property of a drug in which the rate of drug metabolism (or elimination) is directly proportional to the plasma concentration of the drug (e.g., there is a constant fraction of drug being eliminated per unit of time).

media.title: Drug kinetics (zero order and first order)

xcYEeL.title: Zero order kinetics
xcYEeL.description: A chemical property of a drug in which metabolism (or elimination) remains constant and is independent of the concentration of the drug (e.g., concentration decreases linearly with time).

media.title: Drug kinetics (zero order and first order)

ycYdUL.title: Lipophilic
ycYdUL.description: A descriptor for chemical compounds that can dissolve in nonpolar solvents such as lipids. Lipophilic compounds can diffuse across the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane to enter cells and freely cross the blood-brain barrier.

AcYRUL.title: Phase I reaction
AcYRUL.description: A pharmacokinetic term for the first phase of drug metabolism (which occurs mostly in the liver), e.g., oxidation or hydrolysis.

_cY5UL.title: Phase II reactions
_cY5UL.description: A biochemical reaction in the liver that combines drugs or products of metabolism with another (most commonly hydrophilic) molecule. Conjugation reactions are also called phase II biotransformation reactions. Conjugation reactions can detoxify substances and/or enable them to be excreted by the kidney or in bile. An important example of a conjugation reaction is the conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid to form water-soluble, direct bilirubin.

-cYDUL.title: Renal elimination
-cYDUL.description: The net effect of glomerular filtration, renal tubular reabsorption, and active renal tubular secretion. Renal excretion rate = Filtration rate – Reabsorption rate + Secretion rate.

01Ye2L.title: Volume of distribution
01Ye2L.description: The volume of water that would contain the total amount of the substance within the body at a concentration equal to that present in plasma. Reflects the tendency of a drug to be distributed in body tissue rather than plasma. Drugs that are restricted to the intravascular compartment tend to have a low volume of distribution (< 0.2 L). Vd = total drug amount / drug concentration seen in plasma.

a1YQ2L.title: Pharmacodynamics
a1YQ2L.description: The properties of a drug that relate to the body's therapeutic response (e.g., drug affinity to specific receptors, drug activity, dose-response relationship). Can be simplified as "what the drug does to the body."

Y1Yn2L.title: Dose-response relationship
Y1Yn2L.description: The relationship between the dose of a drug or substance and the measured response. Typically plotted on a graph where the X axis is the drug dose and the Y axis is the measured response.

X1Y92L.title: Drug potency
X1Y92L.description: The dose of a drug required to produce a pharmacologic response of a specified intensity. It is dependent on affinity but not efficacy. Commonly measured by the half maximal effective concentration (EC50) of a drug.

11Y2fL.title: Lethal dose
11Y2fL.description: The dose of an agent that is lethal in 50% of the test population as determined through animal experiments.

d1YofL.title: Tachyphylaxis
d1YofL.description: A rapid, diminished response to consecutive doses of a drug due to depletion of endogenous mediators.

21YTTL.title: CYP2C19
21YTTL.description: An enzyme of the hepatic cytochrome P450 2C system that metabolizes drugs including antidepressants, proton pump inhibitors, clopidogrel, and indomethacin.

destinations.label: Fundamentals of pharmacology → Drug interactions and the cytochrome P450 system

R1YlgL.title: Cytochrome-P450 system
R1YlgL.description: A superfamily of heme-containing, primarily oxidative enzymes that take part in phase 1 reactions. Responsible for a large amount of drug/toxin breakdown. Alterations in CYP-activity (e.g., due to drug interactions) can cause severe shifts in drug half-life and may lead to supra- or subtherapeutic drug levels.

destinations.label: Fundamentals of pharmacology → Drug interactions and the cytochrome P450 system

i1YJgL.title: Atypical pseudocholinesterase
i1YJgL.description: An abnormal form of pseudocholinesterase that has a much lower affinity for succinylcholine. Patients with atypical pseudocholinesterase break down succinylcholine slowly and thus have prolonged duration of muscle relaxation during anesthesia.

j1Y_gL.title: N-acetyltransferase polymorphism
j1Y_gL.description: Genetic polymorphisms that can cause decreased activity of hepatic N-acetyltransferase. Negative acetylator status may lead to impaired metabolism of certain drugs, e.g., isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, dapsone, and sulfasalazine.

k1YmSL.title: Clonidine
k1YmSL.description: An alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used to treat hypertension, ADHD, and neuropathic pain. Adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, sedation, and rebound hypertension (if the drug is abruptly discontinued).

O1YISL.title: α-Methyldopa
O1YISL.description: An alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that can be used to treat hypertensive disorders during pregnancy.

N1Y-SL.title: Urapidil
N1Y-SL.description: A selective alpha-1 blocker used in the preoperative management of pheochromocytoma to prevent uncontrolled catecholamine secretion during surgery, which can result in hypertension and cardiac failure.

51YihL.title: Reserpine
51YihL.description: An antipsychotic and antihypertensive drug that inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), which results in the depletion of norepinephrine and dopamine. Not available in the United States.

M1YMhL.title: Tizanidine
M1YMhL.description: An alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used in the treatment of muscle spasticity, particularly in patients with multiple sclerosis or spinal cord disease. Adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, sedation, dry mouth, and bradycardia.

L1YwhL.title: Referred pain
L1YwhL.description: A pain that is perceived at a location other than that of the causative stimulus.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Subtypes and variants

p1YL3L.title: Kehr sign
p1YL3L.description: A referred pain to the left shoulder as a result of irritation of the left hemidiaphragm. Occurs because both left phrenic nerve, which innervates the left hemidiaphragm, and the left supraclavicular nerves, which innervate the skin over the shoulder, have common cranial nerve roots (C3 and C4). Most common cause is splenic injury.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Subtypes and variants

r1YfRL.title: International association for the study of pain
r1YfRL.description: A nongovernmental international organization that provides information about the prevention and treatment of pain. Promotes research and education with the goal to improve pain relief on a global scale.

s1YtRL.title: Nociception
s1YtRL.description: The sensation of pain in response to mechanical, thermal, and/or chemical stimuli. Sensed by somatic sensory receptors called nociceptors.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Classification of pain

F1YgiL.title: Neuropathic pain
F1YgiL.description: Pain arising as a direct result of a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory system. Typically a burning type of pain that radiates along the area innervated by the affected nerve.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Classification of pain

81YOiL.title: Hyperalgesia
81YOiL.description: An increased sensitivity to pain. May be caused by nerve damage due to inflammation or injury, or by changes to the nociception pathways due to the long-term use of certain drugs, e.g., opioids.

u1YpiL.title: Hypoalgesia
u1YpiL.description: A diminished sensitivity to painful stimuli.

y1YdjL.title: WHO analgesic ladder
y1YdjL.description: A 3-step algorithm for the management of acute and chronic pain that recommends giving nonopioid analgesics only for mild pain (step 1); nonopioid analgesics and mild opioids in moderate pain (step 2); and nonopioid analgesics, mild opioids, and strong opioids in severe pain (step 3).  A modification of the WHO analgesic algorithm recommends interventional procedures (e.g., nerve blocks) for unrelenting pain (step 4).

A1YRjL.title: Adjuvant analgesics
A1YRjL.description: Pharmacological therapies with a primary function other than pain relief that can have an analgesic effect in selected circumstances. Examples include antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and antispasmodic medications.

0WYePL.title: Phantom limb pain
0WYePL.description: The sensation of pain in an amputated limb. Results from nociceptive structures becoming sensitized on a peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal level, leading to an excessive stimulation of glutamate-gated NMDA receptors. Can arise from the illusion of the phantom limb being fixed in a painful position.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Subtypes and variants

bWYHPL.title: Mirror therapy
bWYHPL.description: An analgesic therapy used in the management of phantom limb pain and complex regional pain syndrome. The healthy limb is reflected in a mirror to make it appear in the place of the other limb. When the patient moves the healthy limb, the mirror creates the illusion that both limbs are moving freely without pain. This may help retrain neural perception pathways and reduce chronic pain.

destinations.label: Principles of pain management → Subtypes and variants

XWY9PL.title: Colestipol
XWY9PL.description: A bile acid resin used as a lipid-lowering agent. Increases fecal loss of bile acid-bound LDL cholesterol.

destinations.label: Second-line lipid-lowering agents → Bile acid resins

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

cWYa4L.title: Cholestyramine
cWYa4L.description: A synthetic polymeric resin that binds bile acid and prevents its reabsorption in the gastrointestinal tract, which lowers plasma LDL cholesterol levels. It is also used to treat bile acid diarrhea and cholestasis-associated pruritus; but the mechanism behind pruritus relief is not fully understood.

destinations.label: Second-line lipid-lowering agents → Bile acid resins

WWYP4L.title: Fibric acid derivatives
WWYP4L.description: A group of lipid-lowering agents used as second-line treatment for dyslipidemia. The mechanism of action involves the activation of PPARα, which results in a more rapid degradation of LDL and triglycerides. Fibrates are the most effective drug for reducing triglyceride levels.

destinations.label: Second-line lipid-lowering agents → Fibrates (fibric acid derivatives)

VWYG4L.title: Fenofibrate
VWYG4L.description: A fibric acid derivative that primarily functions to lower triglycerides, though mild decreases in LDL and mild increases in HDL are also possible. It functions via activation of lipoprotein lipase, leading to increased triglyceride elimination.

destinations.label: Second-line lipid-lowering agents → Fibrates (fibric acid derivatives)

media.title: Overview of lipid metabolism and lipid-lowering agents

UWYbkL.title: Gemfibrozil
UWYbkL.description: A fibrate lipid-lowering agent that primarily decreases serum triglyceride concentrations. Also decreases serum VLDL and increases serum HDL cholesterol concentrations.

destinations.label: Second-line lipid-lowering agents → Fibrates (fibric acid derivatives)

2WYTkL.title: Nicotinic acid
2WYTkL.description: A water-soluble vitamin that is synthesized from tryptophan. It is used to synthesize NAD, which is used in redox reaction. Niacin can be used as a lipid-lowering agent because it decreases hepatic VLDL synthesis and inhibits the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue. Deficiency of niacin causes pellagra (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia), while niacin toxicity causes podagra (hyperuricemia), flushing, and hyperglycemia.

gWYFkL.title: Ezetimibe
gWYFkL.description: A cholesterol absorption inhibitor that leads to a marked reduction in LDL cholesterol. Can be given as a monotherapy if statins are contraindicated or not tolerated, or in combination with statins to augment their lipid-lowering effect.

hWYcOL.title: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
hWYcOL.description: A class of diuretics that inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron leading to ↑ H⁺ reabsorption and inhibition of Na⁺/H⁺ exchange, causing ↑ NaHCO₃ diuresis and ↑ HCO₃⁻ elimination. These drugs also decrease aqueous humor production in the eye and decreased CSF production. Common indications include acute glaucoma and idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Adverse effects include hyperammonemia with paresthesias and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

3WYSOL.title: Acetazolamide
3WYSOL.description: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor commonly used to treat acute glaucoma, altitude illness, metabolic alkalosis, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

RWYlOL.title: Osmotic diuretics
RWYlOL.description: A group of agents that increase the osmotic gradient within vessels and tubules to pull water in. Used to treat elevated intracranial and intraocular pressures.

QWYuOL.title: Mannitol
QWYuOL.description: A 6-carbon sugar that establishes an osmotic gradient. Primarily used to lower intracranial pressure by osmotically driving water from inside the brain tissue into the intravascular space, which is then diuresed by the kidneys. Can also be used to lower intraocular pressure and eliminate some toxins.

PWYWlL.title: Amphotericin B
PWYWlL.description: An antifungal drug that disrupts fungal cell membranes by reacting with ergosterol. Administered intravenously, intrathecally, or via bladder irrigation. Used to treat severe fungal infections, (e.g., disseminated candidiasis or aspergillosis, fungal meningitis, fungal cystitis). Can cause severe toxicity, including arrhythmias due to QT prolongation, nephrotoxicity (most common adverse effect), electrolyte abnormalities, and hearing loss.

4WY3lL.title: Nystatin
4WY3lL.description: A broad-spectrum polyene antifungal used in the treatment of vaginal candidiasis, diaper rash, and oropharyngeal candidiasis. Adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, stomach pain, contact dermatitis, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Only available in topical and oral form (due to high toxicity if administered systemically).

kWYmlL.title: Clotrimazole
kWYmlL.description: An imidazole antifungal commonly used for fungal and yeast infections, including tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, tinea versicolor, oropharyngeal candidiasis, and vaginal candidiasis.

OWYIlL.title: Ketoconazole
OWYIlL.description: An antifungal agent used topically to prevent and treat fungal skin infections, including tinea and seborrheic dermatitis. Also inhibits cortisol synthesis and can be used systemically to treat Cushing syndrome. Adverse effects of oral administration include hepatotoxicity, headache, and sedation.

media.title: Drugs influencing the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal-axis

NWY-lL.title: Triazole derivatives
NWY-lL.description: A group of antifungal agents with a broad spectrum of activity. They inhibit fungal cytochrome P450, which decreases fungal synthesis of ergosterol from lanosterol, resulting in fungal cell death. Includes fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole.

5WYiNL.title: Fluconazole
5WYiNL.description: A triazole-derived antifungal agent that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis, which is necessary for cytoplasmic membrane formation. Commonly used to treat cutaneous and systemic fungal infections caused by Candida, Cryptococcus, or dermatophytes.

MWYMNL.title: Voriconazole
MWYMNL.description: An azole antifungal agent that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis and is mainly used for invasive aspergillosis and disseminated candidiasis. Besides hepatotoxicity, which is seen in all azole derivatives, voriconazole is associated with hallucinations and visual disturbances.

nWY7NL.title: Itraconazole
nWY7NL.description: An oral azole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis and is effective in dermatophytosis (e.g., onychomycosis), oropharyngeal/esophageal candidiasis, histoplasmosis, and other fungal infections.

KWYUmL.title: Terbinafine
KWYUmL.description: An antifungal commonly used for superficial dermatophyte infections (tinea), especially of the nails (onychomycosis) or hair (tinea capitis and tinea favus). Available orally and as a topical treatment. Adverse effects include alterations in taste, gastrointestinal upset, hepatotoxicity, and headaches.

6WYjmL.title: Acyclovir
6WYjmL.description: A guanosine analog and antiviral drug primarily used to treat herpes virus infections (e.g., herpes zoster, HSV encephalitis). Only affects actively replicating viruses and has no effect on latent infections.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against herpes viruses

pWYLmL.title: Valacyclovir
pWYLmL.description: An oral antiviral agent that is a prodrug of acyclovir with a great bioavailability. Used to treat severe herpetic infections (e.g., shingles or herpes simplex).

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against herpes viruses

JWYsmL.title: Ganciclovir
JWYsmL.description: A guanosine analog used to treat herpetic infections, especially cytomegalovirus. It is activated by viral and cellular kinases and is incorporated into viral DNA, leading to the termination of DNA synthesis.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against herpes viruses

qWYCmL.title: Foscarnet
qWYCmL.description: A viral DNA/RNA polymerase and HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitor used to treat acyclovir-resistant HSV infections and as a second line treatment for CMV retinitis in patients who are immunocompromised.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against herpes viruses

7WY45L.title: Tenofovir
7WY45L.description: An analog of adenosine-5-monophosphate that functions as a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRI). Tenofovir is used to treat chronic hepatitis B infection in patients > 12 years of age and those with HIV-1 infection.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C
Human immunodeficiency virus infection → Antiretroviral therapy

media.title: HIV replication and mechanism of action of antiretroviral drugs

HWYK5L.title: Adefovir
HWYK5L.description: A nucleotide analog reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI) used to treat chronic hepatitis B virus infection in patients with active viral replication. Available as a prodrug (adefovir dipivoxil).

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

sWYt5L.title: Lamivudine
sWYt5L.description: A nucleoside analog and inhibitor of reverse transcriptase used as an antiviral medication in the treatment of patients with hepatitis B and HIV infection. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), fever, and headache.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C
Human immunodeficiency virus infection → Antiretroviral therapy

GWYB5L.title: Entecavir
GWYB5L.description: A nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor. Entecavir is used to treat chronic hepatitis B infection in patients older than 2 years.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

media.title: HIV replication and mechanism of action of antiretroviral drugs

tWYXML.title: Telbivudine
tWYXML.description: A nucleoside analog and inhibitor of reverse transcriptase. Used as an antiviral medication in the treatment of adult and adolescent patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection who have active viral replication. Adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, myopathy, and peripheral neuropathy.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

FWYgML.title: Ribavirin
FWYgML.description: Antiviral drug that is used to treat hepatitis C, RSV infection, and viral hemorrhagic fever (e.g., Lassa fever, Hantavirus infection). It is a nucleoside analog that can act on both RNA and DNA viruses. For hepatitis C, it is always used in combination with other medications such as simeprevir or PEG-interferon-α. Adverse effects include nausea, irritability, hemolytic anemia, and severe teratogenicity.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

EWY8ML.title: Amantadine
EWY8ML.description: A drug that acts as a weak NMDA receptor antagonist and a dopamine agonist. Used to treat Parkinson disease and drug-induced parkinsonism. Previously used for prophylaxis and treatment of influenza, but this is no longer recommended because of widespread antiviral resistance.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against influenza viruses

vWYAML.title: Oseltamivir
vWYAML.description: A neuraminidase inhibitor used in the prophylaxis and treatment of influenza A and B. Inhibits viral budding and prevents dissemination of the virus into the bloodstream.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against influenza viruses

DWY1nL.title: Neuraminidase inhibitor
DWY1nL.description: An antiviral agent that inhibits viral budding and prevents viral dissemination into the bloodstream. They are used for prophylaxis and treatment of influenza A and B. Examples include oseltamivir and zanamivir.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against influenza viruses

9WYNnL.title: Downbeat nystagmus
9WYNnL.description: A variant of vertical nystagmus in which the eyes beat toward the chin. May be associated with a torsional nystagmus component in patients with anterior canal BPPV on performing the Dix-Hallpike maneuver. Downbeat nystagmus can be seen in anterior canal BPPV, as well as in patients with brainstem and cerebellar lesions.

yWYdLL.title: Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV13)
yWYdLL.description: An inactivated conjugate vaccine that protects against 13 subtypes of S. pneumoniae. No longer available in the US since April 2024.

YdYnoL.title: Active immunization
YdYnoL.description: The process of acquiring active immunity by vaccination.

XdY9oL.title: Live attenuated vaccines
XdY9oL.description: A group of vaccines containing a modified virus or bacterium that are no longer pathogenic but are able to replicate within the host's body. These vaccines trigger a humoral and cellular immune response that usually provides lifelong immunity. Contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromised patients because of the risk of reverting to virulent forms. Examples include vaccines against mumps-measles-rubella, varicella, zoster, rotavirus, yellow fever, influenza (intranasal), typhoid (oral), smallpox, and adenovirus.

WdYPKL.title: Inactivated vaccination
WdYPKL.description: A type of vaccination in which a bacteria or virus is inactivated (via heat or chemicals) before it is administered to induce an immune response. Examples include vaccines for polio (Salk vaccine), hepatitis A, rabies, and cholera.

VdYGKL.title: Polysaccharide conjugate vaccine
VdYGKL.description: A type of vaccine in which a weakly immunogenic antigen (usually a polysaccharide) is chemically linked to a strongly immunogenic antigen (usually a protein). This combination dramatically increases the immune response to the polysaccharide, especially in infants and toddlers, in whom the polysaccharide alone would not produce sufficient immunization. Examples of polysaccharide vaccines are: Haemophilus influenzae B, meningococcal, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines

UdYb6L.title: Passive vaccination
UdYb6L.description: A form of vaccination in which antibodies are directly provided (either by injection or from mother to fetus through the placenta) conferring temporary immunity until the antibodies degrade.

SdYy6L.title: Chloracne
SdYy6L.description: A skin condition caused by exposure to halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (especially dioxins and polychlorinated biphenyls). Characterized by acneiform eruptions of pustules, cysts, and comedones, mostly behind the ears and on the cheeks.

RdYlpL.title: Polychlorinated biphenyl
RdYlpL.description: A polychlorinated chemical that was widely used as a coolant, plasticizer, and sealant before it was officially banned in the US in 1979. Ingestion or inhalation can cause skin hyperpigmentation, liver cancer, kidney damage, and delayed growth.

idYJpL.title: Polychlorinated dibenzodioxins
idYJpL.description: A group of polyhalogenated organic compounds derived from dibenzo-p-dioxins. Mostly found as byproducts in the manufacture of other chemicals (e.g., PCBs, pesticides) or as a result of combustion processes (e.g., burning of waste). Short-term exposure causes chloracne. Classified as probable human carcinogens.

jdY_pL.title: Presbycusis
jdY_pL.description: An age-related type of sensorineural hearing loss that occurs due to progressive irreversible damage to hair cells of the organ of Corti. Usually manifests with high-frequency, bilateral hearing loss

PdYWJL.title: Patulous eustachian tube
PdYWJL.description: A condition characterized by a chronically patent (open) eustachian tube. Etiology is frequently unknown but can be caused by severe weight loss, mucosal scarring and/or atrophy from chronic inflammation, and sustained contraction of the tensor veli palatini (e.g., from stress or anxiety). Associated with autophony and aerophony.

4dY3JL.title: Autophony
4dY3JL.description: The abnormally loud hearing of one's own voice. Can be caused by patulous eustachian tube.

kdYmJL.title: Decompression sickness
kdYmJL.description: A condition caused by the formation of inert gas bubbles within tissues and blood as a result of a rapid decline in ambient barometric pressure (e.g., due to rapid ascent after diving). Manifests as either type 1 (involving the muscles, joints, and skin) or type 2 decompression sickness (involving other organ systems such as the CNS, lungs, and ears). Decompression illness encompasses both types of decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism.

mdYVqL.title: Temporomandibular joint disorder
mdYVqL.description: A syndrome of pain and dysfunction of the temporomandibular joint and muscles of mastication. Etiology is multifactorial and includes joint trauma as well as behavioral, environmental, and cognitive factors.

6dYjIL.title: Cerumen
6dYjIL.description: Secretions of the apocrine glands in the external auditory canal.

JdYsIL.title: Barotitis media
JdYsIL.description: A mechanical injury to structures of the inner and/or middle ear as a result of unsuccessful equalization of the pressure between the ambient environment and air-filled structures. Middle ear barotrauma is caused by retraction, bulging, or rupture of the tympanic membrane. Inner ear barotrauma is caused by rupture of the oval and/or round windows and related cochleovestibular apparatus damage. The most common causes of ear barotrauma are flying and diving.

IdYYrL.title: External auditory canal atresia
IdYYrL.description: An absent or stenotic external auditory canal. Frequently results in conductive hearing loss in the ipsilateral ear. Can be congenital or acquired (e.g., following a motor vehicle accident).

destinations.label: Miscellaneous ear, nose, and throat disorders → External auditory canal atresia

rdYfrL.title: Renal scintigraphy
rdYfrL.description: A diagnostic procedure in which radioisotopes are used to assess the anatomy and function of the kidneys. In static renal scintigraphy, a radiotracer that is retained by the renal cortex is used (e.g, Tc-99 DTPA), while a radiotracer that is almost completely excreted in urine is used for dynamic renal scintigraphy (e.g., Tc-99 MAG3, Tc-99 DPTA).

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

7dY4rL.title: DMSA scan
7dY4rL.description: A diagnostic test in which a radiotracer that is retained by the renal cortex (e.g., Tc-99 labeled dimercaptosuccinic acid or Tc-DMSA) is used to assess renal function as well as the degree of structural damage to the renal cortex. DMSA is used because it is retained by the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule.

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

8dYO7L.title: Retrograde urethrogram
