8dYO7L.description: A diagnostic test in which a contrast agent is injected into the urethra to evaluate for urethral injuries and disorders via x-ray.

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

DdY1HL.title: Urodynamic studies
DdY1HL.description: A group of tests to assess function of the urinary tract and to identify sites of obstruction. Includes cystometry (evaluates bladder function during filling, storage, and voiding), uroflowmetry (evaluates rate of urine flow), and urethral tests (evaluate intrinsic sphincter function). Indicated in the diagnostic workup of lower urinary tract dysfunction and for the planning of surgical treatment.

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Urodynamic studies

9dYNHL.title: Voiding cystourethrography
9dYNHL.description: A fluoroscopic imaging study that visualizes the bladder and urethra during filling and voiding to detect vesicoureteral reflux and abnormalities of the urinary tract. The bladder is catheterized and filled with a radiocontrast and the urinary tract is visualized via fluoroscopy during the filling phase and as the patient voids.

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

AdYRsL.title: Intravenous urography
AdYRsL.description: A diagnostic procedure that involves intravenous contrast agent and x-rays to provide images of the genitourinary tract. Especially useful for assessing the upper urinary tract.

destinations.label: Diagnostic investigations and procedures in urology → Imaging techniques

_dY5sL.title: Q fever
_dY5sL.description: A zoonotic disease caused by Coxiella burnetii. Transmitted by inhalation of aerosols from the secretions of livestock or ingestion of raw milk produced by infected animals. Cattle, sheep, and goats are the primary reservoir. Symptoms of acute presentation include flulike symptoms, atypical pneumonia, and hepatitis. Chronic disease is uncommon but can cause culture-negative endocarditis. Typical diagnostic evaluation uses immunofluorescence assay. First-line therapy is doxycycline.

-dYDsL.title: Coxiella burnetii
-dYDsL.description: A gram-negative intracellular organism that causes Q fever. Transmitted by inhalation of aerosols from the secretions of livestock or ingestion of raw milk produced by infected animals. Primary reservoir includes cattle, sheep, and goats. Can survive in harsh environments in an endospore form.

ZVYZGL.title: Typhus
ZVYZGL.description: An umbrella term for three zoonotic diseases caused by bacteria in the family Rickettsiaceae. Common clinical features include fever, headache, and a rash. Untreated disease can manifest with altered mental status. Not to be confused with typhoid fever, which is caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi.

0VYeGL.title: Rickettsia prowazekii
0VYeGL.description: A small, gram-negative, obligate, intracellular coccobacillus that causes epidemic typhus. Spreads via contact with infected body lice.

YVYnGL.title: Plague
YVYnGL.description: An acute febrile, infectious, highly fatal disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is transmitted by fleas. There are three major forms of the disease: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic, with bubonic being the most common form. Bubonic plague presents with sudden onset of fever, headache, myalgias, chills, and painful swollen lymph nodes (buboes). It may progress to sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis if left untreated.

destinations.label: Louse- and flea-borne diseases → Flea-borne diseases

media.title: Axillary lymph node swelling due to plague

bVYHGL.title: Granuloma inguinale
bVYHGL.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Causes painless genital nodules that eventually ulcerate to form large, beefy-red lesions that bleed easily. Regional lymph nodes are spared.

cVYatL.title: Popliteal cyst
cVYatL.description: A collection of synovial fluid in the popliteal fossa between the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle and the semimembranosus muscle. Most commonly asymptomatic. Risk factors include a history of inflammatory, degenerative, or traumatic intra-articular changes in the knee joint.

3VYS8L.title: Splinter hemorrhage
3VYS8L.description: A thin, linear collection of blood that accumulates under the nail plate due to rupture of nail bed capillaries. Etiologies include trauma, nail psoriasis, infective endocarditis.

QVYu8L.title: Olecranon bursitis
QVYu8L.description: Inflammation of the olecranon bursa that is caused by acute trauma to the elbow joint, chronic irritation (e.g., leaning on the elbows for a prolonged period of time, repetitive elbow flexion-extension, gout crystals), systemic inflammatory process (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis), or abrasions to the skin overlying the olecranon bursa. Patients typically present with a swelling on the posterior surface of the elbow. If infected, the skin over the swollen bursa may become warm and tender.

jVY_8L.title: Prepatellar bursitis
jVY_8L.description: A condition of inflammation of the synovial bursa between the skin and patella. Often caused by chronic strain to the knee joint secondary to prolonged kneeling or repeated trauma to the area.

PVYWuL.title: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
PVYWuL.description: Lateral hip pain caused by a tendinopathy of the gluteus medius or minimus. Previously known as trochanteric bursitis, but this term is now considered a misnomer because the involvement of the trochanteric bursa is only an associated finding.

destinations.label: Collection of orthopedic conditions → Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

4VY3uL.title: Bursitis
4VY3uL.description: Inflammation of a bursa (the synovial fluid-filled sacs in the musculoskeletal system, lined by synovial membrane, which act to reduce friction when muscles and tendons pass over bones). Presents with acute joint pain, redness, tenderness, and limited mobility. Usually caused by trauma (e.g., overuse or a fall) and is self-limited.

NVY-uL.title: Biphasic fever
NVY-uL.description: A fever that breaks and returns once more.

destinations.label: Fever → Differential diagnoses by fever characteristics

LVYwEL.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
LVYwEL.description: A test that measures the distance erythrocytes fall after one hour in a vertical tube of anticoagulated blood. Can be elevated in many conditions such as infection, inflammation, and malignancy.

JVYsvL.title: Inflammatory markers
JVYsvL.description: A set of biomarkers whose plasma concentration increases (positive markers) or decreases (negative markers) in response to an ongoing inflammatory process. Positive inflammatory markers include C-reactive protein (CRP), leukocytes, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Negative inflammatory markers include transferrin, albumin, and antithrombin.

IVYYDL.title: C-reactive protein
IVYYDL.description: An acute phase reactant involved in the opsonization of pathogens with a half-life of 24 hours. It is a highly sensitive marker for inflammation but is not specific to any disease or organ. Increases about 6–12 hours after the inflammatory process begins.

sVYtDL.title: Negative acute phase reactants
sVYtDL.description: Proteins that decrease during acute inflammation. These include albumin, transferrin, antithrombin, transthyretin, transcortin, and retinol-binding protein.

wVYh9L.title: Familial Mediterranean fever
wVYh9L.description: An autosomal-recessive autoinflammatory disorder that is especially prevalent in the Middle East (e.g., Syria, Jordan, Turkey, Israel). It is characterized by recurrent episodes of fever and severe abdominal pain, and sometimes accompanied by monoarthritis and skin manifestations.

CVYq9L.title: Neutropenic fever
CVYq9L.description: An oncological emergency commonly caused by myelosuppressive chemotherapy. Defined as a temperature ≥ 38°C (100.4°F) for ≥ 1 hour or ≥ 38.3°C (101°F) once in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count < 500/mm3. Increases the risk for sepsis, septic shock, hospitalization, and delayed chemotherapy.

xVYE9L.title: Fever of unknown origin
xVYE9L.description: A temperature of > 38.3°C recorded on multiple occasions that lasts for > 3 weeks with no clear etiology despite appropriate diagnostics on 3 outpatient visits, 3 days in the hospital, or 1 week of invasive ambulatory investigation.

BVYz9L.title: Classic signs of inflammation
BVYz9L.description: A collection of clinical signs that characterize acute inflammation: rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain), and functio laesa (loss of function).

destinations.label: Skin and soft tissue infections → Overview
Local inflammatory responses → Classic signs of inflammation

yVYdCL.title: Diapedesis
yVYdCL.description: The transmigration of leukocytes across endothelial barriers during the process of extravasation. Can occur paracellularly or transcellularly.

destinations.label: Local inflammatory responses → Chemotaxis and leukocyte extravasation

ZeYZxL.title: Foster-Kennedy syndrome
ZeYZxL.description: A clinical syndrome of ipsilateral atrophy of the optic nerve (due to nerve compression), contralateral papilledema (due to elevated ICP), and anosmia. Usually caused by frontal lobe tumors, most commonly meningiomas.

aeYQxL.title: Cavernous sinus syndrome
aeYQxL.description: A condition caused by compression of the cranial nerves that pass through the cavernous sinus (i.e., III, IV, V1, V2, and VI). Symptoms include ophthalmoplegia, chemosis, proptosis, sensory loss on the forehead and cheek (trigeminal area), and Horner syndrome. Conditions that involve the area within or around the cavernous sinus can cause CSS (e.g., cavernous sinus thrombosis, carotid-cavernous fistula, cerebral metastases).

destinations.label: Skull base syndromes → Cavernous sinus syndrome

2eYTyL.title: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy
2eYTyL.description: A severe neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive lower extremity paralysis and blindness. Thousands of cases were linked to oral administration of the antiparasitic drug clioquinol in Japan in the 1960s.

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON)

feYkyL.title: Kleine-Levin syndrome
feYkyL.description: A rare neurologic disease characterized by binge eating, hypersomnia, and hypersexuality. It occurs mainly in adolescent males. While exact etiology is unknown, viral infections may be contributory.

TeY6yL.title: Kuru
TeY6yL.description: A rapidly lethal prion infection. Like other prion disorders, characterized by neuronal loss, gliosis, and spongiform degeneration of the brain gray matter. Historically acquired through ritualistic cannibalism practiced by some tribes in Papua New Guinea. Clinical features include cerebellar ataxia, muscle tremors, and pathological laughter. Treatment is supportive.

geYFyL.title: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
geYFyL.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease in which arylsulfatase A deficiency leads to a buildup of cerebroside sulfate, causing central and peripheral demyelination. Symptoms include hypotonia, developmental delay or regression, ataxia, seizures, choledocholithiasis, and optic nerve atrophy. There is no cure, and death usually occurs 5 (infantile onset) to 20 (juvenile onset) years after diagnosis.

SeYyyL.title: Adrenoleukodystrophy
SeYyyL.description: A rare X-linked neurological disease usually seen in young males. An impaired peroxisomal ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein leads to an accumulation of very long chain fatty acids in the adrenal glands, testes, and white matter. Symptoms include adrenal insufficiency, cognitive impairment, and progressive vision, hearing, and motor deterioration.

heYcAL.title: Central core disease
heYcAL.description: A rare, congenital myopathy that manifests with proximal muscle weakness, kyphoscoliosis, hip dysplasia, and developmental delay.

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → Central core disease

3eYSAL.title: Chronic posthypoxic myoclonus
3eYSAL.description: A syndrome characterized by multifocal myoclonus following hypoxic brain injury (e.g., due to cardiac arrest).

keYm_L.title: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome
keYm_L.description: A syndrome of unknown etiology that is characterized by unilateral periorbital headache and palsy of one or more oculomotor nerves.

leYv_L.title: Periodic limb movement disorder
leYv_L.description: A condition characterized by frequent, involuntary flexion and extension of the toes and ankles (and sometimes the knee and hip) during sleep.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Periodic limb movement disorder

5eYizL.title: Vertical gaze palsy
5eYizL.description: A conjugate, bilateral, limitation of the eye movements in upgaze and/or downgaze. Caused by damage of cranial nerves and/superior colliculi in the midbrain (e.g., due to tumors, multiple sclerosis, encephalitis, or infarction). Associated with hydrocephalus, ataxia, mydriasis, poor pupillary constriction to light but intact constriction with accommodation.

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → Vertical gaze palsy

MeYMzL.title: Elsberg syndrome
MeYMzL.description: An infectious syndrome characterized by bilateral lumbosacral radiculitis and myelitis of the lower spinal cord. Caused by reactivation or, less commonly, primary herpes simplex virus 2 infection.

neY7zL.title: Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome
neY7zL.description: A rare, fatal, transmissible spongiform encephalopathy characterized by dysarthria, cerebellar ataxia, and progressive dementia. Most commonly caused by a mutation of codon 102 (proline to leucine) of the prion protein gene. This mutation leads to the formation and accumulation of pathologic prion protein.

LeYwzL.title: HTLV-1 associated myelopathy
LeYwzL.description: A rare, slowly progressive, chronic neurologic disease that is associated with human T-cell lymphotropic virus, type 1 (HTLV-1). Can cause symptoms that resemble multiple sclerosis and/or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Additional manifestations include arthritis, uveitis, alveolitis, and polymyositis.

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → HTLV-1 associated myelopathy

oeY0-L.title: Fabry disease
oeY0-L.description: A rare, x-linked, lysosomal storage disease caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, which leads to the cellular accumulation of ceramide trihexoside. Patients usually present during childhood with distal limb pain, anhidrosis, angiokeratomas, and corneal clouding. Later in the course, patients can develop cardiovascular disease and nephropathy (the most common cause of death). Treatment is enzyme replacement therapy with alpha-galactosidase A.

KeYU-L.title: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 1
KeYU-L.description: An inherited neurologic disorder in which iron accumulates in the brain (particularly in the basal ganglia). Manifestations include tremors, dystonia, dementia, and pyramidal tract signs (e.g., Babinski sign).

destinations.label: Rare neurological diseases → Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 1

6eYj-L.title: Oculogyric crisis
6eYj-L.description: An episode of spasmodic upward movement of the eyes that typically lasts for several minutes. Most commonly associated with the use of first-generation antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol).

peYL-L.title: Krabbe disease
peYL-L.description: Rare autosomal recessive disease caused by a deficiency in lysosomal galactocerebrosidase that leads to progressive neurodegeneration due to intracellular accumulation of toxic myelin breakdown products. Symptoms include developmental delay, peripheral neuropathy, visual impairment, and hypertonia. Patients usually die around the age of 2 years.

qeYC-L.title: Niemann-Pick disease
qeYC-L.description: A rare, autosomal recessive disease caused by a deficiency in sphingomyelinase that leads to progressive neurodegeneration due to intracellular accumulation of sphingomyelin. Symptoms include developmental delay, cherry-red spots on macula, and hepatosplenomegaly.

IeYYZo.title: Tay-Sachs disease
IeYYZo.description: Rare autosomal recessive disease caused by a deficiency in beta-hexosaminidase A. Leads to progressive neurodegeneration due to intracellular accumulation of GM2 gangliosides. Symptoms include developmental delay, "cherry-red" spot on macula, seizures, and hearing impairment. Patients usually die around the age of 4. More prevalent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

reYfZo.title: Gaucher disease
reYfZo.description: An autosomal recessive disease caused by a deficiency in β-glucocerebrosidase that leads to intracellular accumulation of glucocerebroside in the brain, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Causes hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration, osteoporosis, and aseptic necrosis of the femur. The most common lysosomal lipid storage disease.

FeYg0o.title: Biceps reflex
FeYg0o.description: A tendon reflex elicited by striking the bicepts tendon, which causes flexion at the elbow joint. The nerve root for this tendon reflex is C5-C6.

weYhao.title: Triceps reflex
weYhao.description: A tendon reflex elicited by striking the triceps tendon while the forearm hands loosely at a right angle, which causes extension at the elbow joint. The nerve root for this tendon reflex is C7-C8.

AeYRYo.title: Posterior tibial reflex
AeYRYo.description: A lower limb reflex mediated by L5. The reflex is positive if foot inversion occurs when tapping the tibialis posterior muscle with a reflex hammer, either just above or below the medial malleolus.

zeYrYo.title: Ankle reflex
zeYrYo.description: A deep tendon reflex mediated by the S1 and S2 nerve roots. With the ankle of the patient relaxed, the examiner strikes the Achilles tendon, resulting in brisk plantar flexion of the foot.

YUYnbo.title: Cremasteric reflex
YUYnbo.description: A physiologic reflex characterized by cremaster muscle contraction with subsequent elevation of the testicle and scrotum in response to stroking of the ipsilateral inner thigh.

bUYHbo.title: Anocutaneous reflex
bUYHbo.description: An S3-S5 nerve root reflex characterized by contraction of the external anal sphincter in response to stroking of the skin around the anus. Absence of this reflex suggests nerve damage.

XUY9bo.title: Bulbocavernosus reflex
XUY9bo.description: Reflex contraction of the external anal sphincter in response to stretching of the bulbocavernosus muscle. The bulbocavernosus can be stretched by squeezing the the glans penis or by pulling on the Foley catheter. The reflex is controlled by spinal levels S2–S4. The return of the bulbocavernosus reflex in a patient with spinal cord injury heralds the end of spinal shock and indicates that the patient will be able to retain some degree of fecal and urinary continence. However, damage to the conus medullaris or the cauda equina result in permanent loss of this reflex.

cUYaXo.title: Primitive reflexes
cUYaXo.description: A set of reflexes that are present at birth and generated at the brainstem or spinal cord level. Typically resolve over time as inhibitory pathways to the subcortical motor areas develop but can re-emerge later in life with CNS lesions (frontal release signs).

destinations.label: Child development and milestones → Primitive reflexes

WUYPXo.title: Corticospinal tract signs
WUYPXo.description: A primitive reflex (e.g., Babinski sign, Gordon sign, Oppenheim sign) that is normal in healthy infants but indicates damage to the pyramidal tract in adults.

dUYoXo.title: Babinski sign
dUYoXo.description: A physical examination finding elicited by stroking the sole of the foot with a blunt, narrow tool (e.g., handle of a reflex hammer) from the lateral heel up to the base of the small toe, then medially across the bases of the toes, following a "J" path. A normal response to the stimulus in adults is plantarflexion of all toes; a pathologic response is extension of the hallux with abduction of all toes and indicates corticospinal tract damage. A positive Babinski sign (hallux extension) is normal up to the age of approx. 2 years.

destinations.label: Child development and milestones → Primitive reflexes

media.title: Babinski Reflex in Infants - Clinical Examination

2UYTco.title: Clonus
2UYTco.description: A series of rapid, rhythmic, involuntary muscular contractions.

QUYu1o.title: Peripheral paresis
QUYu1o.description: The inability of voluntary movement in combination with reduced muscle tone (weakness). Usually due to lower motor neuron damage.

4UY3Wo.title: Central paresis
4UY3Wo.description: A condition characterized by the inability of voluntary movement in combination with increased muscle tone, spasticity, clonus, weakness, and tendon reflex activity.

lUYvWo.title: Neglect syndrome
lUYvWo.description: An inability to respond to unilateral stimuli due to a brain lesion (not due to a primary motor or sensory lesion).

destinations.label: Overview of stroke → Stroke symptoms by affected vessel

NUY-Wo.title: Amnesia
NUY-Wo.description: The partial or complete loss of memory as a result of trauma, disease, or iatrogenic. Inability to form new memories is referred to as anterograde amnesia while the inability to recall previously formed memories is referred to as retrograde amnesia.

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Sensorium and cognition

mUYVdo.title: Aphasia
mUYVdo.description: An inability to comprehend and/or formulate language due to damage to specific brain regions.

KUYUVo.title: Anomic aphasia
KUYUVo.description: A form of expressive aphasia in which the patient has word-finding difficulties, particularly with regard to nouns and verbs. Patients may be able to accurately describe a place, event, person, or action, but have trouble naming them. Caused by damage to the parietal or temporal lobes due to trauma, ischemia, or hemorrhage, or tumor.

pUYLVo.title: Apraxia
pUYLVo.description: The inability to perform coordinated, purposeful, and/or learned movements when asked even though the request is understood (e.g., combing one's hair, putting on shoes and socks).

destinations.label: Mental status examination → Appearance and behavior

IUYYeo.title: Agnosia
IUYYeo.description: An inability to process sensory information that results in a failure to recognize and identify objects, persons, and/or sounds. Can be seen in patients with right posterior cerebral artery strokes.

HUYKeo.title: Muscle power grading
HUYKeo.description: A subjective scoring system used to assess muscle activity ranging from 0 to 5. A score of 0 corresponds to no contraction (paralysis); 1 corresponds to trace contraction; 2 corresponds to movement but not against gravity (e.g., lateral movement); 3 corresponds to active movement against gravity; 4 corresponds to active movement against gravity and resistance; 5 corresponds to normal power.

FUYgUo.title: Pronator drift test
FUYgUo.description: A neurological test to assess motor neuron function. The patient stands with outstretched arms and closes their eyes for 30 seconds. The pronator test is positive if there is asymmetric pronation and drifting movement of the arms. Cerebellar lesions typically cause pronation and upward drift; upper motor neuron lesions typically cause pronation and downward drift.

uUYpUo.title: Meningismus
uUYpUo.description: A collection of symptoms and signs associated with meningeal irritation (e.g., due to subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis). Includes nuchal rigidity, headache, and photophobia.

DUY12o.title: Romberg test
DUY12o.description: A test for assessing sensory ataxia. The patient is asked to stand with both feet together, raise their arms, and close their eyes. The test is positive if closing the eyes impairs coordination (e.g., the patient starts swaying), which is indicative of sensory ataxia. The test is negative if closing the eyes does not affect the patient's balance.

BUYz2o.title: Trendelenburg's sign
BUYz2o.description: A physical examination finding exhibited when a patient stands on one leg and the pelvis tilts downward toward the contralateral side. Caused by ipsilateral neurological weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus due to malfunction of the ipsilateral superior gluteal nerve.

_UY5fo.title: Examination of cranial nerves
_UY5fo.description: A part of the neurological examination. Evaluate visual acuity and visual fields (CN II), extraocular movements (CNs III, IV, VI), facial sensation and muscle strength (CN V), facial movements (CN VII), audition (CN VIII), elevation of the soft palate and the uvula (CNs IX, X), trapezius and sternocleidomastoid contraction strength (CN XI), and movement of the tongue. (CN XII). Olfactory examination (CN I) is generally omitted unless relevant to the patient's complaint.

-UYDfo.title: Corneal reflex
-UYDfo.description: A brainstem reflex elicited by touching the cornea with a foreign object. In a positive test, both eyelids blink. The reflex is mediated by the afferent sensory pathways of CN V1 and the efferent motor pathway of CN VII. If the reflex is present, it indicates functioning of the pons.

02YeTo.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma
02YeTo.description: A low-grade astrocytoma. It is the most common primary brain tumor of childhood.

a2YQTo.title: Optic glioma
a2YQTo.description: A glial tumor of the optic pathway, usually a grade I pilocytic astrocytoma. May cause visual impairment or impaired eye movements and is associated with neurofibromatosis type I in approx. 30% of cases.

b2YHTo.title: Glioblastoma multiforme
b2YHTo.description: A highly malignant brain tumor (grade IV astrocytoma) and the most common primary nervous system cancer. Typically develops in the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres. Can cross the midline (butterfly glioma).

12Y2go.title: Ependymoma
12Y2go.description: A brain tumor that arises from the modified ependymal cells that line the walls of the cerebral ventricles and central canal of the spine. Intracranial ependymomas typically are more common among children; spinal ependymomas are more common among adults 15–40 years of age.

d2Yogo.title: Craniopharyngioma
d2Yogo.description: A suprasellar tumor that arises from a remnant of Rathke's pouch. There are two histological variants: adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas, which typically occur among children, and papillary craniopharyngiomas, which occur almost exclusively among adults. Craniopharyngiomas present with headache, bitemporal hemianopsia, and endocrine abnormalities (e.g., hyperprolactinemia, hypopituitarism).

media.title: Tumor at the base of the skull

V2YGgo.title: Medulloblastoma
V2YGgo.description: The most common malignant brain tumor among children. Typically arises in the cerebellar vermis. Peak incidence is during the first decade of life. Aggressive and prone to local and disseminated metastasis.

e2Yxgo.title: Oligodendroglioma
e2Yxgo.description: A primary CNS tumor that arises from oligodendrocytes, a type of glial cell in the central nervous system. May be benign or malignant, depending on the tumor grade.

22YTSo.title: Gliomas
22YTSo.description: A group of tumors that arise from glial cells in the CNS. Includes oligodendrogliomas, astrocytomas, and ependymomas.

T2Y6So.title: Graves ophthalmopathy
T2Y6So.description: An autoimmune condition that affects retro-orbital tissue, resulting in a set of characteristic ocular and orbital features in patients with Graves disease. Manifests with bilateral exophthalmos, lid retraction, disturbances in ocular motility (causing diplopia), and conjunctival hyperemia. Can occur with predominance of symptoms in one eye.

i2YJho.title: Orbital cellulitis
i2YJho.description: An infection of the orbital contents posterior to the orbital septum, including the fat and extraocular muscles. Although most commonly bacterial in origin (Staphylococci and Streptococci), viral pathogens can also cause orbital cellulitis.

Q2Yuho.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma
Q2Yuho.description: A rare, malignant, mesenchymal tumor of primitive muscle cells that primarily occurs in the orbital cavity but can also arise in the head, neck, or genital regions. Most commonly affects children in the first decade of life.

P2YW3o.title: Immune deficiency
P2YW3o.description: A state of reduced activation and/or efficacy of the immune system. Etiologies include congenital immunodeficiency disorders, AIDS, asplenia (including functional asplenia), diabetes mellitus, chronic alcoholism, certain neoplasms (e.g., lymphoma), treatment with certain drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, chemotherapeutic agents), and radiation therapy.

42Y33o.title: Innate immunity
42Y33o.description: A nonspecific immune response that includes physical barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, and complement. Unlike the adaptive immune system, it does not provide permanent immunity against pathogens.

media.title: Animation: Innate and Adaptive Immunity (full version)

m2YVRo.title: Lysozyme
m2YVRo.description: An enzyme produced by neutrophils, granulocytes, and macrophages that can lyse linkages in peptidoglycans (e.g., the cell wall of gram-positive bacteria). Plays important antibacterial functions in mucosal barriers (e.g., digestive tract).

52YiRo.title: Lactoferrin
52YiRo.description: An iron-binding protein produced by neutrophils and found in secretory fluids and mucosal barriers that inhibits microbial growth.

M2YMRo.title: Human leukocyte antigen
M2YMRo.description: A gene complex on chromosome 6p21 that encodes the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins. HLA is involved in recognizing foreign antigens and initiating an immune response to infectious diseases and cancerous cells. It also plays a role in graft rejection and autoimmune diseases.

K2YUio.title: Major histocompatibility complex class I
K2YUio.description: A transmembrane protein expressed by all nucleated cells and platelets. Composed of a long and short chain associated beta-2 microglobulin. Binds endogenously synthesized antigens (e.g., viral and cytosolic proteins) to present to CD8+ T cells.

p2YLio.title: Major histocompatibility complex class II
p2YLio.description: A transmembrane protein expressed on antigen-presenting cells (e.g., macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells). Composed of alpha and beta chains associated with an invariant chain. Bind exogenously-synthesized antigens to present to CD4+ T cells.

media.title: Antigen Presentation: MHC Class I vs. MHC Class II

J2Ysio.title: Complement system
J2Ysio.description: A group of proteins that circulate in the blood as inactive precursors. After stimulation by antibody complexes (classical pathway) or by pathogens (alternative pathway), complement proteases activate other complement precursors, which leads to a cascade of reactions that enhances the function of antibodies and phagocytes.

q2YCio.title: Proinflammatory cytokines
q2YCio.description: A group of immunomodulatory proteins that are released in response to a trigger (e.g., infection, injury, ischemia). Includes interleukins 1, 6, 8, 12, and 18 as well as IFN-γ. Result in fever, inflammation, tissue destruction, and release of anti-inflammatory cytokines.

I2YYQo.title: Interferon alpha
I2YYQo.description: An antiviral and immunomodulatory glycoprotein used to treat chronic viral infections (e.g., HBV, HCV, HHV8, HPV) and neoplastic conditions (e.g., myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms). Antiviral effects result from the inhibition of viral protein synthesis, breakdown of viral RNA, and increased expression of MHC class I molecules. Antineoplastic effects result from the inhibition of hematopoietic progenitor cells (e.g., megakaryocytes) in addition to the increased production and presentation of tumor antigens to the immune system.

destinations.label: Antiviral agents → Antivirals against hepatitis B and C
Cytokines and eicosanoids → Interferons and tumor necrosis factor family

t2YXjo.title: Interferon beta
t2YXjo.description: An immunomodulatory glycoprotein that is used in disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis.

destinations.label: Cytokines and eicosanoids → Interferons and tumor necrosis factor family

D2Y1Po.title: Interferon gamma
D2Y1Po.description: A cell signaling protein that mediates macrophage activity and expression of MHC molecules. Plays an important role in innate and adaptive immunity against viral, bacterial, and protozoal infections.

destinations.label: Cytokines and eicosanoids → Interferons and tumor necrosis factor family

C2YqPo.title: Cachectin
C2YqPo.description: A cytokine produced predominantly by macrophages that plays a key role in systemic inflammation, apoptosis, and immunity. TNF-α primarily acts as an upregulator of the immune response. It induces fever and increases the production of acute phase reactants and other pro-inflammatory cytokines. It also enhances the cytotoxic effects of leukocytes and the expression of endothelial adhesion molecules.

destinations.label: Cytokines and eicosanoids → Interferons and tumor necrosis factor family

x2YEPo.title: Interleukins
x2YEPo.description: A class of secreted proteins that mediate intercellular communication in order to regulate various cellular functions, especially the immune response. For example, interleukin-1 is proinflammatory while interleukin-2 exhibits stimulates production of acute phase proteins.

B2YzPo.title: Interleukin 1
B2YzPo.description: An interleukin released after immune system contact with lipopolysaccharides (e.g., the wall of gram-negative bacteria). Causes fever and acute inflammation, including chemokine secretion to recruit white blood cells. Induces vasodilation and promotes the adhesion and diapedesis of inflammatory cells by activating endothelium. Dysregulation of IL‑1 in cartilage leads to damage and osteoarthritis, as IL-1 activates osteoclasts.

afYQko.title: Arachidonic acid derivatives
afYQko.description: A group of pro-inflammatory products derived from arachidonic acid that includes leukotrienes, prostacyclins, prostaglandins, and thromboxane.

YfYnko.title: Adaptive immune system
YfYnko.description: A part of the immune system mediated by antigen-specific cells. Adaptive immunity generally takes effect several days after initial pathogen recognition by the innate immune system. Unlike the innate immune system, the adaptive immune system mounts a more specific and effective immune response and can form memory in order to respond more quickly to reinfection by a previously encountered pathogen.

1fY2Oo.title: Immunoglobulins
1fY2Oo.description: A group of proteins produced by B lymphocytes that contribute to the humoral immune response. The different types of immunoglobulins include IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE, and IgD.

UfYblo.title: Balanced translocation
UfYblo.description: A structural chromosomal aberration in which chromosome segments are exchanged equally, with no subsequent loss or gain of genetic material in the cell.

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Types of mutations

2fYTlo.title: Unbalanced translocation
2fYTlo.description: A structural chromosomal aberration in which chromosome segments are exchanged unequally, which results in a loss or gain of genetic material in the cell.

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Types of mutations

ffYklo.title: Chromosomal instability
ffYklo.description: Gain or loss of chromosome parts or whole chromosomes caused by acquired or inherited genetic mutations, most commonly related to DNA repair. Associated with colorectal cancer, Fanconi anemia, and ataxia telangiectasia.

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Types of mutations

TfY6lo.title: Compound heterozygosity
TfY6lo.description: Alteration of a gene due to two differently mutated alleles. Can cause a loss-of-function mutation of the affected gene, despite the mutation not being homozygous.

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Fundamental concepts of genetics

gfYFlo.title: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
gfYFlo.description: A principle that states that genetic variation in a population remains constant under a set of a idealized assumptions (including random mating and no migration, mutation, or selection). Although these assumptions rarely hold in reality, the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is often used to estimate allele frequencies. Given two allele frequencies, p and q, p+q = 1 and (p+q)2 = p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1.

destinations.label: Basics of human genetics → Population genetics

hfYcNo.title: Fluorescence in situ hybridization
hfYcNo.description: A molecular cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescent DNA probes to identify the presence or absence of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes.

RfYlNo.title: Polymerase chain reaction
RfYlNo.description: A method of DNA amplification used for various diagnostic and research purposes. It requires 4 components: a DNA template containing a target sequence, DNA polymerase to synthesize the new DNA, primers that are complementary to the target sequence, and nucleotides as DNA building blocks. It takes place in 3 phases: denaturation of the double helix, primer hybridization, and elongation and amplification of the target region.

ifYJNo.title: Kleptomania
ifYJNo.description: A recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value. Individuals with kleptomania experience an internal tension before committing the theft and relief at the time of committing the theft. Afterwards, they often feel guilty and fear consequences.

destinations.label: Impulse and conduct disorders → Other impulse and conduct disorders

4fY3mo.title: Pyromania
4fY3mo.description: A conduct and impulse-control disorder characterized by the impulse to start fires. Affected individuals typically experience internal tension before setting a fire and relief after committing or witnessing it.

destinations.label: Impulse and conduct disorders → Other impulse and conduct disorders

kfYmmo.title: Trichotillomania
kfYmmo.description: A condition characterized by recurrent, uncontrollable hair pulling, resulting in patchy hair loss, often followed by a feeling of relief/gratification once the hair is pulled. Associated with stress. Patients often have an underlying psychiatric disorder.

OfYImo.title: Conduct disorder
OfYImo.description: A disruptive, impulse-control, and conduct disorder characterized by disruptive behavior that interferes with the basic rights of others and/or age-appropriate social norms. Diagnostic criteria include a pattern of disruptive behaviors (e.g., aggression toward people and animals, destruction of property, serious rule violations) for over 12 months and impairment in functioning; if the individual is over 18 years of age, diagnosis is made only if the criteria for antisocial personality disorder are not met.

destinations.label: Impulse and conduct disorders → Conduct disorder

NfY-mo.title: Separation anxiety disorder
NfY-mo.description: A disorder characterized by excessive anxiety and fear of separation from major attachment figures or home that causes clinically significant distress and impairs functioning. By DSM-5 criteria, symptoms must be present for over 4 weeks and the patient must be under 18 years old. Anxiety associated with separation anxiety disorder differs from normal separation anxiety in its intensity, persistence (beyond the age-appropriate range), and effect on the social and academic life of the individual.

nfY75o.title: Reactive attachment disorder
nfY75o.description: A psychiatric disorder of childhood and adolescence with an onset before the age of 5 years characterized by a consistent pattern of inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behavior that is not the result of an autism spectrum disorder. Reactive attachment disorder is usually the result of neglect from the primary caregivers or a limited opportunity to form selective attachments caused by a repeated change of primary caregivers.

destinations.label: Trauma- and stressor-related disorders → Reactive attachment disorder

JfYsMo.title: Swinging-flashlight test
JfYsMo.description: A physical examination technique to identify afferent defects in the retina or optic nerve. While the patient fixates on a point in the distance, swing a light back and forth from one eye to the other and observe the size of the pupils. Normally, both the illuminated pupil and the nonilluminated pupil constrict. If the optic nerve of one eye is damaged, both pupils dilate when the affected eye is lit.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Pupillary examination

qfYCMo.title: Relative afferent pupillary defect
qfYCMo.description: The presence of a unilateral afferent pupillary defect. If a flashlight is swung back and forth between the two eyes (swinging flashlight test), the eye with the afferent pupillary defect appears to dilate in response to illumination. This happens because the pupil constricts in response to illumination of the contralateral eye (an intact indirect pupillary reflex) but fails to constrict with illumination of the affected eye (impaired direct pupillary reflex). This phenomenon does not occur with bilateral afferent pupillary defects.

destinations.label: Physiology and abnormalities of the pupil → Afferent pupillary defect

7fY4no.title: Confrontation visual field examination
7fY4no.description: A part of the eye examination that can be conducted with or without instrumentation. For confrontation visual field testing, the examiner covers one of the patient's eyes and asks the patient to look straight ahead and count how many fingers the examiner holds up in each of the four quadrants. Failure to detect this stimulus from a given direction indicates a visual field defect.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Visual field examination

sfYtno.title: Kinetic perimetry
sfYtno.description: An ophthalmological examination used to determine visual field defects by using moving light targets to find the edge of the individual's visual field.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Visual field examination

GfYBno.title: Tear film break-up time
GfYBno.description: A study to evaluate tear film stability. During slit-lamp examination, a fluorescein dye is applied to stain the tear film. After 2 minutes, the time between the patient's last blink and the appearance of a random dry spot on the cornea is measured. This is performed three times and the average value is recorded. Tear film break-up time is decreased in patients with keratoconjunctivitis sicca.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Slit lamp biomicroscopy examination

8fYOLo.title: Cover-uncover test
8fYOLo.description: A test used to detect latent strabismus (heterophoria). One eye is covered for a few seconds and observed for refixation movements after being uncovered. Refixation movement indicates latent strabismus.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Cover tests

vfYALo.title: Optical coherence tomography
vfYALo.description: A noninvasive imaging modality that uses light rays (interferometry) to obtain high-resolution, cross-sectional images. It can be used to image various parts of the body, e.g., the retina, gastrointestinal epithelium, coronary arteries.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Retinal examination

media.title: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of the macula

wfYhoo.title: Electrooculography
wfYhoo.description: An electrophysiological test that measures eye movement by detecting voltage differences between two electrodes placed on the face (either superior and inferior to the eye or medial and lateral to the eye).

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Retinal examination

9fYNoo.title: Schirmer's test
9fYNoo.description: A study used to evaluate tear production. It is commonly used in patients with suspected Sjogren syndrome. A piece of filter paper is placed in the patient's lower eyelid and the amount of tear fluid absorbed by the strip is measured. Normal wetting is > 15 mm after 5 minutes; a value of < 5 mm fulfills one of the classification criteria for Sjogren syndrome.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Schirmer test

BfYzoo.title: Landolt ring
BfYzoo.description: An ophthalmological chart used to evaluate visual acuity. Displays several rows of a ring with a gap, that resembles the letter “C” in different sizes and rotations.The patient, from a predetermined distance from the chart (in the US typically 20 feet or 6 meters), covers one eye and consecutively reads the rows of letters out loud beginning with the smallest row they can read. The patient points or states in which direction the gap in the ring or C is pointing (up, down, left, or right).

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Visual acuity

AfYRKo.title: Electroretinogram
AfYRKo.description: An ophthalmologic test that uses electrodes to measure the electrical activity generated by the retina in response to light stimuli.

destinations.label: Examination of the eye → Retinal examination

zfYrKo.title: Thyroglobulin antibodies
zfYrKo.description: Antibodies against thyroglobulin, a thyroid hormone precursor protein found in the thyroid gland. Elevated levels are often found in Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease, although they may also be found in euthyroid individuals.

-fYDKo.title: Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
-fYDKo.description: A group of antibodies directed against the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, which plays an important role in thyroid hormone production. Elevated antibody levels are seen in > 90% of patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, but may also be present in Graves disease, Hashimoto encephalopathy, and in healthy individuals.

ZTYZ6o.title: TSH receptor antibody
ZTYZ6o.description: An autoantibody against the TSH receptor. Includes TSH-stimulating, TSH-blocking, and TSH-neutral antibodies. Elevated in most individuals with Graves disease and in some individuals with silent thyroiditis or Hashimoto thyroiditis.

XTY96o.title: Bronchoalveolar lavage
XTY96o.description: A minimally invasive technique that is performed during flexible bronchoscopy in order to evaluate the immunologic, inflammatory, and infectious processes at the level of the alveoli in diffuse lung disease. Differential cell counts, microbiologic studies, and cytology of the BAL specimen help to diagnose various diseases.

cTYapo.title: Thoracentesis
cTYapo.description: A procedure performed to drain an accumulation of pleural fluid (pleural effusion) by inserting a needle into the pleural cavity. Ultrasonography is used to determine the location and size of the pleural effusion. Indications include drainage for symptom relief (e.g., dyspnea) and fluid analysis for diagnosis of the underlying cause (e.g., infection, malignancy).

3TYSqo.title: Adjuvant treatment
3TYSqo.description: A therapy that is provided after the initial treatment, usually to prevent additional tumor formation. For example, chemotherapy that is provided after tumor removal.

destinations.label: Principles of cancer care → Overview of cancer care

ETY8so.title: Angiokeratoma
ETY8so.description: A benign ectasia of the superficial dermal blood vessels with overlying hyperkeratosis of the epidermis. Specific features vary by subtype.

destinations.label: Benign skin tumors → Vascular skin tumors

vTYAso.title: SAPHO syndrome
vTYAso.description: A rare rheumatologic condition that manifests with synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis.

destinations.label: Collection of dermatological disorders → SAPHO syndrome

DTY1Go.title: Epidermoid cyst
DTY1Go.description: A common, slow-growing, benign cutaneous cyst formed by implantation of epithelium within the dermis. Cysts are skin-colored with a central black punctum and contain keratinaceous material. Usually asymptomatic but can rupture and become infected. Often incorrectly referred to as a sebaceous cyst.

9TYNGo.title: Sebaceous cyst
9TYNGo.description: A benign lesion containing sebum due to a blocked sebaceous gland. Sometimes inaccurately used to refer to epidermoid cysts, which do not arise from sebaceous glands and do not contain sebum. Typically asymptomatic but can become inflamed. Treatment options include intralesional steroids and surgical excision.

CTYqGo.title: Cat scratch disease
CTYqGo.description: An infectious disease caused by Bartonella henselae, transmitted via scratching, biting, and/or exposure to saliva, primarily by cats. Most commonly manifests as localized disease with ≥ 1 erythematous, nontender papule and/or pustule at the cutaneous site of inoculation, followed by painful proximal lymphadenopathy. Disseminated disease is rare, but bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis are more common in immunocompromised individuals.

xTYEGo.title: Miliaria
xTYEGo.description: A transient, papular exanthem caused by blockage of eccrine sweat glands. Typically occurs following exposure to heat and most commonly manifests on the head, neck, and upper trunk.

zTYrto.title: Nummular dermatitis
zTYrto.description: A chronic, inflammatory skin condition characterized by multiple coin-shaped, well-demarcated, pruritic, erythematous plaques that typically manifest on the extremities.

0gYeFo.title: Clavus
0gYeFo.description: A small circumscribed skin lesion characterized by hypertrophy of the stratum corneum and a central cone-shaped keratin core. Caused by repetitive mechanical pressure or irritation.

XgY9Fo.title: Darier sign
XgY9Fo.description: The development of localized erythema and urticaria due to the release of mast cell mediators following mechanical irritation (e.g., rubbing, scratching) of the skin or skin lesions that are rich in mast cells. Associated with mastocytosis.

cgYa8o.title: Mastocytosis
cgYa8o.description: A group of rare disorders characterized by abnormal mast cell proliferation and accumulation in tissues. Includes cutaneous mastocytosis, which is limited to the skin, and systemic mastocytosis, which affects organs such as the bone marrow, GI tract, and/or bone, with or without skin involvement.

fgYkuo.title: Rhesus positive
fgYkuo.description: Indicates the presence of the Rhesus antigen on the surface of erythrocytes. The Rhesus antigen is the most common erythrocyte antigen, present in ∼ 85% of the general population. The D subtype of Rhesus antigen is the most clinically relevant and responsible for hemolytic anemia of the newborn in Rh incompatibility between mother and fetus.

hgYcEo.title: Fresh frozen plasma
hgYcEo.description: A blood product containing all coagulation factors, which may be administered for treatment of severe coagulopathy associated with warfarin, liver failure, and/or vitamin K deficiency, and in combination with other blood products for massive hemorrhage.

igYJEo.title: Platelet transfusion
igYJEo.description: The administration of a concentrate of platelets to increase the platelet count in a patient with severe thrombocytopenia. Indicated if the platelet count is below 10,000 mm³ or in the case of massive bleeding to prevent spontaneous bleeding and in cases of massive blood loss. One platelet transfusion increases the platelet count by approx. 20–40/nL.

QgYuEo.title: Prothrombin complex concentrate
QgYuEo.description: A blood product used to treat severe coagulopathy or bleeding associated with some forms of anticoagulant use and/or vitamin K deficiency. Composed of inactivated clotting factors and protein C and S (PCC containing activated factors is known as activated PCC [aPCC]).

PgYWvo.title: Antithrombin III
PgYWvo.description: An enzyme important for inhibiting the coagulation cascade. It functions as a non-vitamin K-dependent protease that cleaves factors IIa, IXa, Xa. Both heparin and low molecular weight heparins (e.g., enoxaparin) function by potentiating the activity of this enzyme. Antithrombin III deficiency can be genetic or acquired (e.g., nephrotic syndrome) and results in a hypercoagulable state.

NgY-vo.title: Fluid resuscitation
NgY-vo.description: A procedure in which intravascular fluid loss (e.g., due to hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea) is replenished via parenteral or oral routes.

MgYMDo.title: Hydroxyethyl starch
MgYMDo.description: A colloidal solution that contains derivatives of amylopectin. Used for intravenous volume repletion in the acute management of hemorrhagic hypovolemia.

destinations.label: Intravenous fluid therapy → Types of parenteral fluids

ngY7Do.title: Colloidal solutions
ngY7Do.description: A group of solutions containing high molecular weight substances (e.g., fresh frozen plasma, albumin solution). These molecules stay in the intravascular compartment, generating oncotic pressure to draw in fluid and increase intravascular volume. More effective at volume expansion than crystalloid solutions but less often used due to cost and adverse effects (e.g., anaphylactoid reactions).

destinations.label: Intravenous fluid therapy → Types of parenteral fluids

ogY0wo.title: Crystalloid solutions
ogY0wo.description: A group of solutions containing water-soluble molecules (e.g., saline, dextrose solution). These solutions increase intravascular volume and are commonly used for fluid resuscitation and maintenance fluid therapy.

destinations.label: Intravenous fluid therapy → Types of parenteral fluids

pgYLwo.title: Enteral nutrition
pgYLwo.description: A method of nutrition delivery via a tube inserted through the mouth, nose, or percutaneously through the abdominal wall (e.g., percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) into the gastrointestinal tract (i.e., the stomach, duodenum, or jejunum).

JgYswo.title: Parenteral feeding
JgYswo.description: The intravenous administration of nutrition through a peripheral or central vein, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract. May be used for patients requiring specialized nutrition support if enteral nutrition is contraindicated or insufficient to meet metabolic needs.

rgYf9o.title: Omphalitis
rgYf9o.description: A bacterial infection of the umbilical cord stump. Common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Clostridium tetani (in low-income countries). Manifests with periumbilical redness, tenderness, swelling, fluctuance, and purulent discharge. Complications include sepsis and necrotizing fasciitis.

7gY49o.title: Intra-amniotic infection
7gY49o.description: Confirmed microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity causing infection and inflammation of the placenta, fetus, fetal membranes, and/or endometrial decidua. Most commonly caused by ascending cervicovaginal bacteria (e.g., Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis). May lead to maternal complications (e.g., dysfunctional labor, sepsis) and/or neonatal complications (e.g., neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy, fetal death).

sgYt9o.title: Interleukin-8
sgYt9o.description: A cytokine produced by macrophages. Major functions include phagocytosis and inducing chemotaxis of neutrophils and other granulocytes.

tgYXCo.title: Lymphedema
tgYXCo.description: The abnormal accumulation of lymph in the interstitium due to compromised lymphatic vessels or lymph nodes. Primary lymphedema is idiopathic and results from congenital abnormalities in lymphatic vessels, while secondary lymphedema is caused by damage to the lymphatic system, e.g., due to tumors, surgery, or radiation therapy.

FgYgCo.title: Lymphatic filariasis
FgYgCo.description: A roundworm infection typically caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and transmitted via mosquito bites. Characterized by lymphatic obstruction by the worms and/or immune-mediated destruction of lymphatic capillaries. Causes fever, painful lymphadenopathy, and progressive swelling of the region drained by the obstructed lymphatics (often the lower extremities) that can progress to elephantiasis. Also a common cause of hydrocele in endemic regions (e.g., Brazil, India, Cambodia).

EgY8Co.title: Crigler-Najjar syndrome
EgY8Co.description: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by absence (type I) or reduced activity (type II) of the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. This disease disrupts the liver's ability to conjugate bilirubin, resulting in severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Without treatment, Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is incompatible with life because it causes kernicterus.

9gYNxo.title: Gilbert's syndrome
9gYNxo.description: Inherited metabolic disease in which the intrahepatic conjugation of bilirubin and glucuronic acid is impaired. Often presents as mild jaundice during times of stress (e.g. sickness, overexertion, dehydration, etc.) and causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Most cases are asymptomatic or mild and do not require treatment.

xgYExo.title: Dubin-Johnson syndrome
xgYExo.description: A rare autosomal recessive disorder of bilirubin excretion. Results in the inability to excrete bilirubin glucuronides from hepatocytes into bile canaliculi due to the absence of a biliary transport protein. This mild condition typically only manifests as occasional scleral icterus. Impaired hepatic excretion of adrenaline metabolites leads to a darkly pigmented ("black") liver.

ygYdBo.title: Rotor syndrome
ygYdBo.description: A relatively benign, autosomal recessive condition causing direct hyperbilirubinemia. It is caused by a mutation in the hepatic transport proteins OATP 1B1 and 1B3, which leads to impaired hepatic secretion of conjugated bilirubin.

_gY5Bo.title: Scintillating scotoma
_gY5Bo.description: A migraine aura typically characterized by an arch-shaped area of decreased vision that starts centrally and shifts peripherally.

destinations.label: Disorders of the visual pathway → Scotoma and anopia

XSY9yo.title: Floater
XSY9yo.description: A collection of deposits in the vitreous body of the retina perceived as spots or strings drifting through the visual field. Easier to see against bright lighting and tend to move away when gazed at directly. Common and typically result from normal degenerative changes in the vitreous body from the natural aging process. A sudden increase in floaters, especially if accompanied by light flashes and vision loss, can indicate a serious condition, such as vitreous hemorrhage, an eye tumor, or retinal detachment.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Floaters

cSYaAo.title: Photopsia
cSYaAo.description: A sudden and brief perception of bright flashes of light that often start in one area of the visual field. It usually is unilateral and occurs in the dark or with closed eyes. Most often caused by vitreous tissue pulling on the retina due to shrinkage or liquefaction of the vitreous body. Other causes include posterior vitreous detachment, retinal detachment, age-related macular degeneration, migraine aura, optic neuritis, occipital lobe infarction, and hallucinations.

destinations.label: Diseases of the vitreous body → Posterior vitreous detachment

WSYPAo.title: Thelarche
WSYPAo.description: Onset of breast development. Usually the first visible secondary sexual characteristic in girls.

VSYGAo.title: Menarche
VSYGAo.description: The first occurrence of menstrual bleeding. Mean age is 13 years; typically occurs 2 years after the onset of puberty.

USYb_o.title: Precocious puberty
USYb_o.description: The appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys. Classified as central precocious puberty, caused by early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, or peripheral precocious puberty, caused by sex hormone production that is not driven by secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone.

2SYT_o.title: Central precocious puberty
2SYT_o.description: Premature appearance of secondary sexual characteristics (before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys) caused by early gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion and activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Can be idiopathic or due to CNS lesions.

TSY6_o.title: Peripheral precocious puberty
TSY6_o.description: Early development of secondary sexual characteristics caused by increased exposure to or production of sex hormones, independent of gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion. Etiologies include granulosa cell tumors, Leydig cell tumors, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and McCune-Albright syndrome.

gSYF_o.title: Leydig cell tumor
gSYF_o.description: A neoplasm of the Leydig cells of the gonads, most often seen in young boys or middle-aged men. Overproduction of testosterone results in precocious puberty (young boys) or masculinization (young girls). Tumors in older men may produce excessive estrogens, leading to gynecomastia and infertility.

SSYy_o.title: Delayed puberty
SSYy_o.description: A delay in the development of secondary sex characteristics. In female individuals, this is defined as absent breast development by 13 years of age; in male individuals, as a lack of testicular growth by 14 years of age. Most commonly due to constitutional growth delay but can also be caused by malnutrition, chronic disease, and hypogonadism.

hSYczo.title: Type 1 glycogen storage disease
hSYczo.description: A type of glycogen storage disorder caused by the deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase (type a disease) or glucose 6-phosphate translocase (type b disease). Patients typically present in the neonatal period with massive hepatomegaly and a protuberant abdomen, puffy cheeks, and a rounded face, and biochemical abnormalities such as severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Glycogen storage disorders (GSD)

RSYlzo.title: Type 2 glycogen storage disease
RSYlzo.description: A type of glycogen storage disease caused by lysosomal acid maltase deficiency. Presents with myopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, macroglossia, and, in infants, a failure to thrive. The clinical phenotype varies depending on whether the onset of symptoms occurs in infancy, childhood, or early adulthood.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Glycogen storage disorders (GSD)

iSYJzo.title: Fructose intolerance
iSYJzo.description: An autosomal recessive disorder of fructose metabolism caused by aldolase B deficiency, which results in the accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate. Patients present with severe hypoglycemia, vomiting, jaundice, bleeding manifestations, hepatomegaly, and/or a failure to thrive.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Disorders of fructose metabolism

QSYuzo.title: Galactokinase
QSYuzo.description: The enzyme responsible for the first step in galactose metabolism, the conversion of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate. This reaction requires the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP.

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Galactosemia

jSY_zo.title: Galactosemia
jSY_zo.description: A group of autosomal recessive disorders of galactose metabolism. Includes Type I (classic galactosemia, caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency), Type II (caused by galactokinase deficiency) and Type III (caused by UDP-galactose-4-epimerase deficiency).

destinations.label: Inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism → Galactosemia

PSYW-o.title: Uterine atony
PSYW-o.description:
Failure of the uterus to effectively contract after delivery, which can lead to severe bleeding from the myometrial vessels and is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Patients present with abnormal vaginal bleeding
and a soft and enlarged uterus. Risk factors are related to overdistention of the uterus and include multiparity, post-term pregnancy, instrumental delivery, fetal macrosomia, or a prolonged or rapid and forceful birth.

4SY3-o.title: Credé's maneuver
4SY3-o.description: A technique used in obstetrics to aid the expulsion of the placenta after childbirth. Fundal pressure is applied by placing one hand on the uterine fundus and squeezing it between the thumb and other fingers to help placental separation and delivery. If not performed correctly, pain, hemorrhage and inversion of the uterus can occur. Sometimes also used to void urine from the bladder in patients with chronic urinary retention (e.g., due to paralysis) by applying suprapubic pressure.

NSY--o.title: Placenta accreta
NSY--o.description: A rare disorder in which the placenta is directly adherent to the myometrium (without penetrating) instead of the decidua basalis. Results in delayed separation and/or placental retention as well as postpartum hemorrhage. The most important risk factors for placenta accreta are a previous C-section and placenta previa.

oSY00K.title: Velamentous cord insertion
oSY00K.description: An abnormally located insertion of the umbilical cord in the chorioamniotic membranes. The fetal blood vessels travel without the protective Wharton jelly from the insertion of the umbilical cord to their entry site in the placenta.

KSYU0K.title: Campylobacter enterocolitis
KSYU0K.description: A bacterial infection caused by Campylobacter jejuni. The most common cause of bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis. Associated with inflammatory bloody diarrhea (in 50% of cases), high fever, and severe abdominal pain that can manifest as pseudoappendicitis or colitis.

JSYs0K.title: Shigellosis
JSYs0K.description: Bacterial infection with Shigella causing profuse inflammatory, mucoid-bloody diarrhea, high fever, and tenesmus. Transmitted fecal-orally in areas with poor sanitation, or through unpasteurized milk products, contaminated water, or unwashed raw vegetables. Complications include toxic megacolon, reactive arthritis, and hemolytic-uremic syndrome caused by the Shiga toxin.

ISYYaK.title: Salmonellosis
ISYYaK.description: A bacterial infection caused by Salmonella enteritidis and nontyphoidal salmonella. The second-most common cause of bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis. Associated with watery-bloody diarrhea, fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and severe vomiting.

rSYfaK.title: Cholera
rSYfaK.description: An infectious disease caused by Vibrio cholerae which usually leads to moderate diarrhea, low grade fever, and vomiting. In some cases, profuse diarrhea ("rice water stools") can occur and rapid fluid replacement is required. Treatment is largely symptomatic and antibiotics are only given in severely ill cases.

7SY4aK.title: Yersiniosis
7SY4aK.description: A bacterial gastroenteritis caused by Yersinia enterocolitica, which is transmitted primarily via contaminated unpasteurized milk products or undercooked pork. Manifestations include subacute abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea that can be bloody, and pseudoappendicitis.

HSYKaK.title: Pseudoappendicitis
HSYKaK.description: A condition that presents with signs and symptoms classically associated with appendicitis (e.g., right lower quadrant pain, fever, vomiting, leukocytosis). Caused by mesenteric lymphadenitis, typically as a complication of Yersinia infection. Management involves antibiotic therapy to eradicate the underlying infection.

GSYBaK.title: Epidermophyton
GSYBaK.description: A genus of fungi that infects keratinized tissue and causes dermatophyte infections (e.g., tinea pedis).

tSYXYK.title: Trichophyton
tSYXYK.description: A genus of fungi that infects keratinized tissue. The most common cause of dermatophyte infections (e.g., tinea pedis).

ESY8YK.title: Candida
ESY8YK.description: A type of yeast (fungus) that appears almost universally in low numbers on healthy skin and mucosa as a commensal organism. Can cause a skin and mucosal infection (candidiasis). In immunocompetent individuals, usually causes minor localized infections, including thrush (affecting the oral cavity), vulvovaginitis, and infections of intertriginous areas of skin (e.g., the axillae or gluteal folds). More widespread and systemic infections may occur in immunocompromised individuals.

DSY1bK.title: Cryptococcus neoformans
DSY1bK.description: An encapsulated yeast found in soil and pigeon droppings. Causes cryptococcosis, cryptococcal meningitis, and cryptococcal encephalitis after inhalation and hematogenous dissemination. Grows on Sabouraud agar. Can also be detected with India ink stains and mucicarmine stains.

destinations.label: Overview of fungal infections → Opportunistic fungal infections

wSYhbK.title: Malassezia furfur
wSYhbK.description: A species of yeast that is naturally present on human skin. Can cause tinea versicolor if overgrowth occurs in individuals with factors predisposing to infection (e.g., immunosuppression, excessive sweating).

xSYEbK.title: Aspergillus
xSYEbK.description: A genus of fungi found ubiquitously in the environment. Transmitted via airborne exposure to mold spores. Risk factors for infection include destructive pulmonary pathology (e.g., COPD) and immunosuppression. Can cause invasive aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and aspergilloma.

media.title: Aspergilloma (fungus ball) within right upper lobe cavity
Pulmonary aspergillosis with air crescent sign

ySYdXK.title: Hyphae
ySYdXK.description: A collection of branching, filamentous structures found on microscopic analysis of fungal infections (e.g., dermatophyte infections).

-SYDXK.title: Secretory diarrhea
-SYDXK.description: A type of diarrhea characterized by active secretion of water into the intestinal lumen, which is induced by inhibition or activation of enzymes of the intestinal mucosa. Causes include infections (cholera, ETEC), tumors (gastrinoma, VIPoma), malabsorption disorders (fat or bile compounds), and medications (colchicine).

ZhYZcK.title: Inflammatory diarrhea
ZhYZcK.description: Diarrhea characterized by mucus in the stool due to destruction of the enteric mucosa by an invasive pathogen or due to chronic inflammatory bowel disorder. Other findings can include fever, bloody stools, and leukocytes in stool.

0hYecK.title: Functional diarrhea
0hYecK.description: The chronic or continuous passage of loose or watery stools with no associated abdominal pain and no known underlying anatomical or biochemical cause. It is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after ruling out organic causes and other functional disorders of chronic diarrhea (including IBS-D).

ahYQcK.title: Osmotic diarrhea
ahYQcK.description: Diarrhea caused by osmotic pull of ingested substances that is characterized by watery stools. Causes include lactose intolerance and osmotic laxatives such as lactulose, mannitol, or sorbitol.

chYa1K.title: Melanosis coli
chYa1K.description: A benign hyperpigmentation of colonic epithelial cells associated with chronic use of anthraquinone laxative or, less commonly, chronic colitis. Colonoscopy shows dark brown pigmentation of the colon, interspersed with pale patches reflecting lymph follicles ("alligator/snake skin" appearance). Biopsy reveals lipofuscin-laden macrophages.

3hYSdK.title: Perseveration
3hYSdK.description: The inappropriate repetition or persistence of behavior, speech, or sounds secondary to cognitive impairment (e.g. frontal lobe damage), speech and language processing disorders (e.g. developmental delay), and/or anterograde amnesia.

N3Y-iK.title: Pulsus paradoxus
N3Y-iK.description: A physical examination finding in which there is an exaggerated decrease (> 10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during inspiration. Classically associated with cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis, but can also be seen in noncardiac conditions (e.g., massive pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, obstructive sleep apnea, obstructive lung disease).

m3YVQK.title: Pulse deficit
m3YVQK.description: The difference between the heart rate (measured using cardiac auscultation) and the peripheral pulse rate (obtained by palpating the radial artery for 1 minute). A pulse deficit > 10/min can be caused by atrial fibrillation. A pulse deficit < 10/min can be caused by premature ventricular contractions.

53YiQK.title: Pulsus alternans
53YiQK.description: A physical finding characterized by alternating strong and weak pulses (with a regular pulse rhythm) caused by alterations in cardiac output. Associated with left ventricular failure and cardiac tamponade.

n3Y7QK.title: Auscultation of the heart
n3Y7QK.description: The use of a stethoscope to examine the heart. Typically performed with the patient supine with slight elevation of the torso. Used to assess the location, timing, and quality of heart sounds and murmurs. Techniques to best hear specific sounds include auscultating at specific anatomical locations, using the stethoscope bell for low frequency sounds and the diaphragm for high frequency sounds, positioning the patient (e.g., leaning forward, lying in the left lateral position), and having the patient perform specific maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva, inspiration).

media.title: Anatomical locations and auscultatory sites for heart valves

J3YsjK.title: Heart sounds
J3YsjK.description: A noise produced during the cardiac cycle that can be observed through cardiac auscultation. Usual heart sounds include S1 and S2, which are produced by valve closure. Additional heart sounds that suggest pathology include gallops (S3, S4), clicks, knocks, murmurs, rubs, and snaps.

media.title: Anatomical locations and auscultatory sites for heart valves

q3YCjK.title: Heart murmurs
q3YCjK.description: An auscultatory finding of sounds that can be heard between normal heartbeats. Occur when there are turbulences in blood that flows through the heart. Can be normal (e.g., due to exercise) but can also indicate cardiac pathologies such as valvular disorders.

media.title: Anatomical locations and auscultatory sites for heart valves

I3YYPK.title: First heart sound
I3YYPK.description: The sound created by the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves. Marks the transition from diastole to systole. Best heard over the apex.

r3YfPK.title: 2nd heart sound
r3YfPK.description: A heart sound that marks the transition from systole to diastole with the closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves. Consists of two components: the louder A2 (closure of the aortic valve) and softer P2 (closure of the pulmonary valve). Best heard in the 2nd right parasternal ICS (A2) and 2nd left parasternal ICS (P2).

73Y4PK.title: 3rd heart sound
73Y4PK.description: The finding of an extra heart sound on cardiac auscultation that occurs during early diastole, as the ventricle is filling. An S3 gallop is due to a sudden deceleration of blood flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. Can be normal variant in young, healthy individuals, but can be also associated with congestive heart failure, dilated cardiomyopathy, and/or volume overload. The S3 sound is associated with a galloping rhythm, similar to the cadence of the word "Kentucky". Best heard with the bell of the stethoscope over the apex.

media.title: S3 Heart Sound (S3 Gallop) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 9

s3YtPK.title: Echocardiogram
s3YtPK.description: An ultrasound examination performed to assess the structure and function of the heart. Can be transthoracic (noninvasive) or transesophageal (via endoscopy).

G3YBPK.title: Peritonsillar abscess
G3YBPK.description: Most common deep neck infection, especially seen in adolescents and young adults. Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common causative agent. Peritonsillar abscess forms in the area between the palatine tonsil and its capsule that presents with unilateral sore throat, odynophagia, tender lymphadenopathy, and possible trismus. If the abscess progresses, it can involve the surrounding muscles or, rarely, the carotid sheath

t3YX4K.title: Parapharyngeal abscess
t3YX4K.description: An abscess of the parapharyngeal space that most commonly occurs in children < 5 years of age. Manifestations include trismus, induration and edema inferior to the angle of the mandible (when involving the anterior space), medial displacement of the lateral pharyngeal wall and tonsil (when involving the posterior space), respiratory distress, and limited cervical neck extension. Can cause life-threatening airway obstruction and sepsis.

83YO4K.title: Retropharyngeal abscess
83YO4K.description: An abscess in the retropharyngeal space that most commonly develops in children < 5 years of age. Typically a polymicrobial infection secondary to local penetrating trauma or spread of oral, upper respiratory tract, or other deep infections of the neck (e.g., from nasopharynx, sinuses, adenoids). Clinical features include tonsillitis, neck asymmetry with unilateral swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall, and torticollis.

YRYnlK.title: Selective IgA deficiency
YRYnlK.description: The most common primary immunodeficiency syndrome. Patients have an isolated deficiency of IgA, with normal serum levels of IgG and IgM. Clinical manifestations are highly variable and range from asymptomatic to recurrent sinopulmonary (mostly caused by encapsulated bacteria, e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and GI infections (e.g., due to Giardia lamblia), as secretory IgA antibodies are a crucial part of mucosal defense.

destinations.label: Congenital immunodeficiency disorders → Congenital B-cell immunodeficiencies

gRYFmK.title: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
gRYFmK.description: A relatively common, benign, self-limited skin condition that most commonly develops within the first week of life and appears as small, red macules and papules that progress to pustules with surrounding erythema. The rash is located predominantly on the trunk and proximal extremities; the palms of hands and soles of feet are usually spared.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

SRYymK.title: Milia neonatorum
SRYymK.description: A neonatal condition characterized by the presence of small, white papules on the face and occasionally on the trunk caused by the buildup of keratin and sebaceous secretions. Typically self-limited and does not result in scarring.

destinations.label: Overview of neonatal conditions → Neonatal skin lesions

hRYc5K.title: Bruton agammaglobulinemia
hRYc5K.description: An X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency syndrome caused by a mutation in the B-cell tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which results in arrested B cell development and agammaglobulinema. Patients present with recurrent bacterial infections typically after 6 months of age. Lymphoid hypoplasia may be present on physical examination.

destinations.label: Congenital immunodeficiency disorders → Congenital B-cell immunodeficiencies

jRY_5K.title: Intracavernous injection
jRY_5K.description: The injection of smooth muscle relaxants directly into the corpus cavernosum to induce vasodilation. Used to treat erectile dysfunction. Common agents include alprostadil alone or in combination with papaverine.

PRYWMK.title: Penile prosthesis
PRYWMK.description: A surgical implant used in the management of erectile dysfunction when medical therapy and other nonsurgical treatments fail.

kRYmMK.title: Premature ejaculation
kRYmMK.description: A sexual disorder characterized by ejaculation that occurs within ∼ 1 minute of penetration and before the patient wishes to ejaculate.

destinations.label: Sexual dysfunction and paraphilic disorders → Sexual dysfunction

ORYIMK.title: Hydrocephalus
ORYIMK.description: Increased amount of cerebrospinal fluid in the cranial cavity as a result of increased production and/or decreased outflow of CSF.

media.title: Manifestations of increased intracranial pressure in infants

lRYvMK.title: Communicating hydrocephalus
lRYvMK.description: Excessive intracranial CSF with full communication between the ventricles and the subarachnoid space (where CSF is resorbed). It can be caused by impaired CSF resorption (most often), impaired venous drainage (occasionally), or CSF overproduction (rarely).
