Typically presents with signs of intracranial hypertension (e.g., headache, vomiting, papilledema).

NRY-MK.title: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo
NRY-MK.description: A reduction of brain parenchyma volume caused by cerebral atrophy or malformation that results in relatively increased size of the ventricles and subarachnoid space. Usually asymptomatic and seen in older adults secondary to age-related brain atrophy but can also be caused by pathological brain degeneration (e.g., Alzheimer disease). Not a true hydrocephalus; intracranial pressure and flow of cerebrospinal fluid are normal.

5RYinK.title: Non-communicating hydrocephalus
5RYinK.description: A condition of excessive intracranial cerebrospinal fluid due to obstruction of flow. Can be congenital (e.g., Dandy-Walker malformation) or acquired due to a brain tumor, fibrosis (e.g., after intracranial hemorrhage), or inflammation (e.g., after meningitis).

HRYKoK.title: Gamekeeper's thumb
HRYKoK.description: An injury to the ulnar collateral ligament, often caused by sudden hyperextension and abduction of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint of the thumb. Typically presents with pain, swelling, and laxity of the thumb MCP joint and weak pinch grip. Treatment includes splinting and surgical repair.

sRYtoK.title: Quadriceps tendon rupture
sRYtoK.description: A disruption of the extensor mechanism of the knee proximal to the patella that is usually the result of a sudden contraction of the quadriceps muscle on a flexed knee, e.g., during a fall. The rupture may be partial or complete.

GRYBoK.title: Patellar tendon rupture
GRYBoK.description: A disruption of the extensor mechanism of the knee distal to the patella that is usually a result of direct trauma.  The rupture may be partial or complete.

CRYq6K.title: RICE protocol
CRYq6K.description: A protocol that was previously used in the acute management of sports injuries, consisting of rest (ceasing athletic activity), ice (cooling for 20-30 minutes, then a break, then more cooling), compression (elastic bandage), and elevation (of the extremities above the level of the heart). It has been modified to the POLICE principle where protection (e.g., with a cast or brace) and optimal loading of the injured area is recommended over immobilization.

destinations.label: Sports injuries → Initial management of sports injuries

EiY8tK.title: Acute transplant rejection
EiY8tK.description: A rejection of transplanted tissue that occurs within 6 months after transplantation (usually within days to weeks) and causes ~ 50% of post-transplant organ dysfunction. Due to allorecognition (T-lymphocyte-induced cell-mediated and/or humoral immunity). Manifests with fever, edema, graft pain, and organ dysfunction.

BiYzFK.title: Chronic rejection
BiYzFK.description: A rejection of transplanted tissue that occurs > 6 months after transplantation (usually after a few years) and causes about half of all post-transplant organ dysfunction. Typically manifests with slow, progressive loss of organ function. Caused by a poorly understood mechanism that involves irreversible intimal fibrosis and obstruction of vessels.

yiYd8K.title: Crossmatching (transplantation)
yiYd8K.description: The process of examining recipient serum for preformed antibodies against donor T and B cells in order to estimate the risk of transplant rejection.

0QYeuK.title: Graft-versus-tumor effect
0QYeuK.description: A possible sequela of allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in which donor T cells attack malignant cells, thus decreasing the risk of relapse.

XQY9uK.title: Hyperacute rejection
XQY9uK.description: A rejection of transplanted tissue that occurs within 48 hours after transplantation (usually within minutes to hours). Typically manifests with intraoperative swelling of the graft as soon as perfusion is restored. It is due to preformed cytotoxic antibodies against class I HLA molecules that trigger the activation of the complement system, leading to thrombosis and graft ischemia.

3QYSDK.title: Liver transplantation
3QYSDK.description: The transplantation of a liver from a deceased or living donor. Indicated in patients with end-stage liver disease, including fulminant hepatic failure, decompensated cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Complications include vascular complications, biliary leak, graft rejection, and post-transplant infection.

RQYlDK.title: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
RQYlDK.description: The transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells, which arise from peripheral blood, bone marrow transplant, or umbilical cord blood. There are two types of stem cell transplantation: autologous (removal of the patient's own hematopoietic stem cells) and allogenous (transfer of hematopoietic stem cells from a sibling or donor).

QQYuDK.title: Acute graft-versus-host disease
QQYuDK.description: A complication of bone marrow transplant in which donor T lymphocytes react with the recipient's organs < 100 days after transplantation. Presentations include a pruritic maculopapular rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and hepatic dysfunction. Treatments include immunosuppressants, such as cyclosporine and corticosteroids (topical and systemic).

jQY_DK.title: Allogeneic HCT
jQY_DK.description: The donation of stem cells that are taken from an individual who is genetically similar but not identical to the recipient.

PQYWwK.title: Autologous stem cell transplantation
PQYWwK.description: Removal and storage of a patient's own hematopoietic stem cells, which are retransfused back to the patient after high-dose myeloablative chemotherapy.

4QY3wK.title: Bone marrow transplant
4QY3wK.description: A type of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation using bone marrow aspirate, typically from the posterior superior iliac spine. Associated with a low risk of graft-vs-host disease.

OQYIwK.title: Graft-versus-host disease
OQYIwK.description: A transplantation-associated immunologic reaction that occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes in the graft recognize the recipient (host) as foreign, resulting in a systemic inflammatory reaction. Typically affects the skin (rash), gastrointestinal tract (nausea, diarrhea), and the liver (elevated liver enzymes). Primarily occurs in allogenous hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation recipients.

nQY79K.title: Cord factor
nQY79K.description: A cell wall component and virulence factor of M. tuberculosis that stimulates the release of TNF-α and induces granuloma formation by activating macrophages.

LQYw9K.title: Mycobacterium leprae
LQYw9K.description: An obligate intracellular, acid-fast bacillus that causes lepromatous leprosy and tuberculoid leprosy. Thought to be transmitted via respiratory droplet and/or close contact with fomites, infected soil, and infected individuals. Reservoirs include humans and armadillos.

oQY0CK.title: Nontuberculous mycobacteria
oQY0CK.description: A type of mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis and M. leprae. These opportunistic pathogens can cause several conditions, including cervical lymphadenitis (M. scrofulaceum), fish tank granuloma (M. marinum), and M. avium complex infection (M. avium and M. intracellulare).

6QYjCK.title: Mycoplasma
6QYjCK.description: A type of bacteria characterized by the lack of a cell wall, making them resistant to antibiotics that target cell-wall synthesis. Common subspecies that cause infections in humans are Mycoplasma pneumoniae (atypical pneumonia) and Mycoplasma hominis (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease).

pQYLCK.title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
pQYLCK.description: A species of bacteria that causes atypical pneumonia and tracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients. Lacks a cell wall.

JQYsCK.title: Ureaplasma urealyticum
JQYsCK.description: A urease-positive bacterial species of the Mycoplasmataceae family. Lacks a cell well. Part of the normal genital flora of sexually-active adults. Colonization of the urinary tract can result in cystitis and increase the risk of developing struvite renal calculi.

HQYKxK.title: Catalase-positive organisms
HQYKxK.description: A group of organisms that produce catalase, an enzyme that degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen before neutrophils can convert it via myeloperoxidase into microbicidal products. Cause recurrent infections in patients with chronic granulomatous disease. Species include Nocardia, Pseudomonas, Listeria, Aspergillus, Candida, E. coli, Staphylococcus, Serratia, B. cepacia, and H. pylori.

sQYtxK.title: Staphylococcus aureus
sQYtxK.description: A gram-positive and coagulase-positive coccus that causes many localized infections (e.g., folliculitis, cervical lymphadenopathy), food poisoning, and also severe organ infections in the setting of bacteremia (e.g., endocarditis, osteomyelitis).

GQYBxK.title: Staphylococcus epidermidis
GQYBxK.description: A gram-positive, coagulase-negative coccus that is part of the normal skin flora. Its ability to form biofilms makes it an especially common pathogen in infections associated with foreign bodies (e.g., contaminated peripheral lines, prosthetic joints). Urease-positive and novobiocin-sensitive.

tQYXBK.title: Staphylococcus saprophyticus
tQYXBK.description: A coagulase-negative, gram-positive bacterium that is part of the normal flora of the female genital tract and perineum. It is a common cause of cystitis, especially in sexually active women.

FQYgBK.title: Streptococcus
FQYgBK.description: A genus of gram-positive bacteria known for their characteristic chainlike growth due to the cell division occurring along a single axis. Can cause endocarditis, meningitis, bacterial pink eye, and necrotizing fasciitis. Members are classified by the way in which they oxidize iron from heme (alpha- or beta-hemolytic).

8QYOBK.title: Lancefield group
8QYOBK.description: A classification system for catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci (e.g., Streptococci) that distinguishes between different groups based on the presence of different carbohydrates in the bacterial cell wall that facilitate agglutination.

uQYpBK.title: Streptococcus pneumoniae
uQYpBK.description: A gram-positive, capsulated diplococcus. One of the prime causes of community-acquired pneumonia and meningitis. S. pneumoniae is α-hemolytic and catalase-negative.

vQYABK.title: Viridans streptococci
vQYABK.description: A group of gram-positive, aerobic, alpha-hemolytic streptococci that are normally commensals of the oral cavity but may be introducted into blood following dental procedures. Members of the viridans group of streptococci include S. sanguinis, S. mutans, S. salivarius, S. mitis, and S. anginosus. Viridans streptococci cause subacute bacterial endocarditis, especially in patients with an underlying valvular heart disease.

wQYhyK.title: Group A Streptococcus
wQYhyK.description: A group of gram-positive cocci that express the Lancefield group A carbohydrate. Infection with group A Streptococcus (GAS) can cause a variety of illnesses, including tonsillitis, impetigo, cellulitis, and toxic shock syndrome. The term GAS is often used synonymously with Streptococcus pyogenes, the most common type of GAS, but the group also includes Streptococcus dysgalactiae and some strains of Streptococcus anginosus.

9QYNyK.title: Group B Streptococcus
9QYNyK.description: A gram-positive coccus that is part of the normal flora of the human GI and genital tracts. Frequently causes neonatal meningitis, sepsis, and pneumonia.

xQYEyK.title: Peptostreptococcus
xQYEyK.description: A genus of gram-positive anaerobic cocci found in the oral cavity.

BQYzyK.title: Enterococcus
BQYzyK.description: A genus of gram-positive, gamma-hemolytic cocci that includes E. faecium and E. faecalis. Part of the natural flora of the gastrointestinal tract. Can grow in bile and 6.5% NaCl. Can cause urinary tract infections, biliary tract infections, and endocarditis (especially after genitourinary or gastrointestinal interventions).

_QY5AK.title: Neisseria
_QY5AK.description: A genus of gram-negative diplococci. Includes N. gonorrhoeae (which causes gonorrhea), and N. meningitidis (which causes meningitis and meningococcemia).

zQYrAK.title: Neisseria meningitidis
zQYrAK.description: A gram-negative diplococcus that is a common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis.

0jYe_K.title: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
0jYe_K.description: A gram-negative, aerobic, facultative intracellular diplococcus that is typically transmitted via sexual contact. Common cause of genitourinary infections, neonatal conjunctivitis, and septic arthritis.

bjYH_K.title: Clostridia
bjYH_K.description: A genus of gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacteria. The most clinically-significant species include: C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis), C. perfringens (gas gangrene, food poisoning), C. tetani (tetanus), and C. botulinum (botulism).

XjY9_K.title: Clostridioides difficile
XjY9_K.description: A gram-positive, rod-shaped, obligate anaerobe bacillus that is commonly involved in antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Toxigenic strains are highly contagious and form environmentally resistant spores that are capable of withstanding heat and acid. Nontoxigenic strains may be present in asymptomatic individuals. Formerly known as Clostridium difficile.

cjYazK.title: Clostridium perfringens
cjYazK.description: A gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus that is ubiquitous in soil. Can cause food poisoning and life-threatening gas gangrene.

1jY2zK.title: Clostridium tetani
1jY2zK.description: A gram-positive, obligately anaerobic, spore-forming rod. Produces neurotoxins which cause tetanus. C. tetani is ubiquitous (especially animal feces and soil), and infection occurs via wound entry, especially wounds with poor blood supply which creates an anaerobic environment.

WjYPzK.title: Tetanospasmin
WjYPzK.description: A neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani. The toxin undergoes retrograde axonal transport back to the CNS, binds inhibitory neurotransmitters, and causes the tonic-clonic spasms and autonomic instability seen in tetanus.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

djYozK.title: Clostridium botulinum
djYozK.description: A gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium that forms heat-resistant endospores and produces the neurotoxin botulinum toxin. C botulinum exposure can cause foodborne botulism (ingestion of preformed toxin), infant botulism (ingestion of spores), and wound botulism (wound contamination).

VjYGzK.title: Listeria
VjYGzK.description: A genus of gram-positive, non-spore-forming bacilli. The most clinically relevant species is Listeria monocytogenes.

ejYxzK.title: Listeria monocytogenes
ejYxzK.description: A gram-positive bacillus. Does not typically cause disease in immunocompetent patients. Can cause invasive disease (e.g., sepsis and meningitis) in immunocompromised and older patients.

UjYb-K.title: Corynebacterium
UjYb-K.description: Gram-positive, club-shaped bacteria. C. diphtheriae causes diphtheria and is usually transmitted via respiratory droplets. Other species of Corynebacteria are part of the resident flora of the skin, respiratory tract, conjunctiva and urinary tract.

2jYT-K.title: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
2jYT-K.description: A gram-positive rod that causes diphtheria due to an exotoxin (diphtheria toxin). Causes pseudomembranous pharyngitis with lymphedema, myocarditis, and cardiac arrhythmias.

TjY6-K.title: Bacillus anthracis
TjY6-K.description: A spore-forming, gram-positive rod. Produces anthrax toxin (a multicomponent virulence factor comprised of edema factor, lethal factor, and protective antigen). Unlike other bacteria, has a poly-D glutamate capsule. Causes cutaneous anthrax and pulmonary anthrax.

gjYF-K.title: Bacillus cereus
gjYF-K.description: A gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium that causes food poisoning. Infection usually occurs when spores are warmed and allowed to germinate, as is classically the case with reheated rice. Produces heat-stable and labile toxins that cause diarrhea and vomiting.

SjYy-K.title: Actinomyces
SjYy-K.description:
A genus of gram-positive, non-acid fast, anaerobic bacteria that form branching filaments. Forms characteristic yellow sulfur granules in tissue. Natural bacteria of the oral cavity and the intestine. Can cause oral abscesses.
Includes Actinomyces spp., Streptomyces spp., and Nocardia spp.

hjYcZ6.title: Actinomyces israelii
hjYcZ6.description: A gram-positive, anaerobic, rod-shaped, filamentous bacteria that exists as part of the normal oral flora. Pathogenic only in the setting of mucosal damage (e.g., oral surgery) or immunosuppression (e.g., from severe diabetes, chemotherapy).

3jYSZ6.title: Nocardiosis
3jYSZ6.description: A rare infection caused by Nocardia (such as N. asteroides and N. brasiliensis), a genus of aerobic, gram-positive bacteria that appear as filamentous branching rods on microscopy. Typically seen in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g., post-transplant patients). Manifests either as pulmonary (virulent form of pneumonia), cutaneous (cellulitis or purulent erythematous nodules), or disseminated disease.

ijYJZ6.title: Haemophilus
ijYJZ6.description: A genus of gram-negative coccobacilli. The most clinically-relevant species are H. influenzae (which causes epiglottitis, otitis media, and meningitis), H. parainfluenzae (which causes HACEK endocarditis), and H. ducreyi (which causes chancroid).

QjYuZ6.title: Haemophilus influenzae
QjYuZ6.description: A gram-negative coccobacillus that colonizes the respiratory tract. Nontypeable strains cause mucosal infections (e.g., otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia). The type b strain can cause more severe infections (e.g., meningitis, epiglottitis), but the incidence of these infections has decreased with routine vaccination.

jjY_Z6.title: Haemophilus ducreyi
jjY_Z6.description: A gram-negative coccobacillus that causes the sexually transmitted disease chancroid.

PjYW06.title: Brucella
PjYW06.description: A small, nonmotile, facultative intracellular, gram-negative coccobacillus that causes brucellosis. Includes Brucella melitensis (transmitted by goats and sheep), Brucella abortus (transmitted by cattle) and Brucella suis (transmitted by pigs).

ljYv06.title: Bordetella pertussis
ljYv06.description: A gram-negative coccobacillus that causes a highly contagious acute respiratory illness characterized by a paroxysmal cough ("whooping cough").

5jYia6.title: Enterobacteriaceae
5jYia6.description: A family of the order Enterobacterales. Includes Klebsiella, Escherichia, Enterobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella.

MjYMa6.title: Yersinia
MjYMa6.description: A gram-negative, lactose-nonfermenting, oxidase-negative rod. Y. enterocolitica is transmitted from pet feces or contaminated milk and causes acute diarrhea or pseudoappendicitis (yersiniosis). Y. pestis is transmitted by fleas and causes plague.

njY7a6.title: Yersinia pestis
njY7a6.description: A bacterial species that causes the bubonic plague (the Black Death). Prairie dogs, squirrels, and rodents are the reservoir of this bacteria. Can be transmitted by flea bites.

LjYwa6.title: Yersinia enterocolitica
LjYwa6.description: Gram-negative, rod-shaped, pleomorphic bacterium of the Enterobacteriaceae family that is transmitted through ingestion of raw pork, unpasteurized milk products, contaminated water, or contact with infected animals (e.g., dogs, pigs, rodents), and their feces. Causes yersiniosis with inflammatory diarrhea, fever, and pseudoappendicitis.

KjYUY6.title: Shigella
KjYUY6.description: A genus of gastric acid-resistant gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Shigella dysenteriae) that invade via M cells of intestinal Peyer patches and produce Shiga toxin, which can cause bloody diarrhea (shigellosis).

pjYLY6.title: Shigella flexneri
pjYLY6.description: A gram-negative rod that produces Shiga toxin, which leads to bloody diarrhea and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome. Compared to S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri produces less toxin and causes less severe symptoms.

JjYsY6.title: Shigella dysenteriae
JjYsY6.description: A gram-negative rod that produces Shiga toxin, which leads to bloody diarrhea and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome.

qjYCY6.title: Salmonella
qjYCY6.description: A group of facultative intracellular, rod-shaped, non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-negative, gram-negative bacteria that belong to the Enterobacteriaceae family. Produces endotoxin and can disseminate hematogenously. Common sources include reptiles (e.g., turtles) and raw meat, poultry, and eggs. Causes typhoid and paratyphoid fever, gastroenteritis, osteomyelitis (in patients with sickle cell disease), and reactive arthritis.

IjYYb6.title: Salmonella enterica
IjYYb6.description: A group of rod-shaped, flagellated, facultative anaerobic, Gram-negative bacteria that are members of the genus Salmonella. Common cause of food poisoning and gastroenteritis after consumption of raw eggs or poultry. Salmonella serogroups that belong to the salmonella enterica subspecies include Salmonella Typhi, Salmonella Enteritidis, and Salmonella Paratyphi.

rjYfb6.title: Salmonella enterica serotype Enteritidis
rjYfb6.description: A serotype of of Salmonella enterica that causes gastroenteritis. Less commonly can cause bacteremia and systemic illness. Most commonly transmitted via consumption of poultry, eggs, and egg products.

GjYBb6.title: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi
GjYBb6.description: Rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria that is transmitted by person-to-person contact or fecal-orally. Causes typhoid fever (enteric fever).

FjYgX6.title: Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphi
FjYgX6.description: A typhoidal serotype of Salmonella enterica that may cause local gastroenteritis or a mild form of typhoid fever. Usually clinically and pathologically indistinguishable from S. enterica serotype Typhi.

ujYpX6.title: Klebsiella
ujYpX6.description: A genus of gram-negative rods that form mucoid colonies due to their abundant polysaccharide capsules. Part of the intestinal flora. Can cause dark red, currant-jelly sputum in cases of aspiration pneumonia.

EjY8X6.title: Klebsiella pneumoniae
EjY8X6.description: A gram-negative, rod-shaped bacillus that is a common cause of nosocomial pneumonia and urinary tract infections.

vjYAX6.title: Escherichia coli
vjYAX6.description: A gram-negative bacillus that is part of the normal colonic flora but may cause, e.g., diarrhea, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, neonatal meningitis, and septicemia.

BjYzc6.title: Proteus
BjYzc6.description: A genus of urease-positive, nonlactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, sulfur-reducing, gram-negative bacilli. Part of the normal gastrointestinal flora. Species include Proteus mirabilis and Proteus vulgaris, which can cause urinary tract infections.

yjYd16.title: Proteus vulgaris
yjYd16.description: A gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic rod that belongs to the family of Enterobacteriaceae. Produces urease. Causes urinary tract infections, kidney stones (struvite stones), and respiratory tract infections.

AjYR16.title: Proteus mirabilis
AjYR16.description: A gram-negative, urease-positive, rod-shaped bacterium that is part of the natural flora of the gastrointestinal tract. Can cause urinary tract infections and lead to the development of kidney stones (struvite stones).

_jY516.title: Helicobacter pylori
_jY516.description: A gram-negative, microaerophilic, spiral-shaped bacterium that typically infects the stomach. A common cause of peptic ulcer disease and chronic gastritis.

zjYr16.title: Legionella
zjYr16.description: A genus of gram-negative bacteria that is present in freshwater environments and poses a health risk when found in water systems. Can be visualized with a silver stain and cultured in buffered charcoal yeast extract agar. Can cause Legionnaires' disease, which can be life-threatening, and Pontiac fever, which has more mild symptoms.

-jYD16.title: Legionella pneumophila
-jYD16.description: A gram-negative, flagellated bacterium that causes Legionnaires' disease and Pontiac fever.

0PYeW6.title: Bartonella henselae
0PYeW6.description: A gram-negative, aerobic, rod-shaped bacterium that causes cat scratch disease. Can also cause bacillary angiomatosis (cutaneous nodules formed of capillaries) and peliosis hepatis (formation of vascular cavities in the liver).

aPYQW6.title: Bartonella quintana
aPYQW6.description: A small, gram-negative, facultative intracellular rod. Causes trench fever, bacteremia, endocarditis, and bacillary angiomatosis. Humans are the reservoir (with lice as the vector).

bPYHW6.title: Bartonellosis
bPYHW6.description: A group of zoonotic and/or vector-borne infections caused by gram-negative intracellular facultative bacteria belonging to the genus Bartonella. Infections include cat scratch disease, bacillary angiomatosis, trench fever, Carrión disease, and peliosis hepatis.

XPY9W6.title: Carrión disease
XPY9W6.description: A vector-borne illness endemic to South America that is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis. Usually transmitted via sandfly species (Phlebotomus verrucarum or Lutzomyia verrucarum). Course of disease is biphasic, involving an acute phase (Oroya fever) and a chronic phase (Peruvian warts).

cPYad6.title: Oroya fever
cPYad6.description: The acute phase of Carrion disease. Usually manifests ~ 60 days after exposure with severe bacteremia and acute hemolytic anemia due to splenic elimination of infected erythrocytes. Other symptoms include fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, tachycardia, and hepatomegaly.

1PY2d6.title: Verruga peruana
1PY2d6.description: The chronic phase of Carrion disease, caused by Bartonella bacilliformis infection. Manifests with hemangioma-like nodules of the skin, usually on the head and extremities, which can persist for weeks to months.

WPYPd6.title: Campylobacter
WPYPd6.description: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive, comma-shaped bacillus that can grow at 42° Celsius. Transmission is fecal-oral or through ingestion of undercooked, contaminated meat or unpasteurized milk. Infection causes bloody diarrhea. Associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

dPYod6.title: Campylobacter jejuni
dPYod6.description: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive, comma-shaped bacillus that can grow at 42° Celsius. Transmission is fecal-oral or through ingestion of undercooked, contaminated meat or unpasteurized milk. Infection causes bloody diarrhea. Associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

VPYGd6.title: Pseudomonas
VPYGd6.description: A gram-negative capsulated bacillus responsible for opportunistic and nosocomial infections (e.g., pneumonia, urinary tract infections), especially in individuals who are immunocompromised. Pseudomonas are oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenters, and grow blue-green colonies on culture.

ePYxd6.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
ePYxd6.description: A gram-negative rod that grows in water and humid conditions (e.g., hot tubs, lakes, or contaminated contact lens solution). Causes nosocomial infections (e.g., urinary tract infections or pneumonia), pneumonia in adult patients with cystic fibrosis, external otitis ("swimmer's ear"), and endocarditis in intravenous drug users.

fPYkV6.title: Vibrio cholerae
fPYkV6.description: Gram-negative bacteria that produce the cholera toxin leading to increased Cl− secretion in the gut and subsequent hypersecretion of water into the intestinal lumen. Transmitted fecal-orally via ingestion of contaminated water and seafood. Causes only moderate diarrhea or follows an asymptomatic course in > 90% of cases. Clinical findings of severe infection include low-grade fever, vomiting, and profuse 'rice-water' diarrhea. May be complicated by severe dehydration and pneumonia in children.

TPY6V6.title: Fusobacteriaceae
TPY6V6.description: A genus of anaerobic, gram-negative rods that commonly colonizes the oropharynx. Can cause pharyngitis, dental infections, deep neck space infections, and aspiration pneumonia. Species include F. necrophorum and F. nucleatum.

gPYFV6.title: Bacteroides
gPYFV6.description: A genus of gram-negative, anaerobic bacilli that do not form spores. Represents ~ 90% of the fecal flora. Some species can be pathogenic (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis).

SPYyV6.title: Spirochetes
SPYyV6.description: A group of spiral-shaped bacteria. Includes Borrelia, Leptospira, and Treponema.

hPYce6.title: Treponema pallidum
hPYce6.description: A gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacteria belonging to the Spirochete family that causes syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection.

RPYle6.title: Borrelia burgdorferi
RPYle6.description: A spirochete (a corkscrew-shaped bacterium) that causes Lyme disease.

QPYue6.title: Hospice care
QPYue6.description: A type of palliative care specifically given to patients who have an estimated life expectancy < 6 months and have made the decision to stop curative or life-sustaining treatment in order to maximize quality of life.

4PY3U6.title: Total pain
4PY3U6.description: The combination of physical, social, spiritual, psychological, and emotional pain in a patient. Total pain describes the multifactorial nature of pain and emphasizes the need for a multidimensional approach to adequately address a patient's pain.

kPYmU6.title: Mixed pain
kPYmU6.description: The simultaneous or concurrent presence of nociceptive, neuropathic, and/or nociplastic pain in one area of the body.

OPYIU6.title: Emotional pain
OPYIU6.description: A term used to describe both mental suffering and the impact of emotions on the experience of pain. In the latter context, it may contribute more to a decreased quality of life than the pain caused by actual or potential tissue damage.

mPYV26.title: SPIKES protocol
mPYV26.description: An evidence-based protocol for delivering serious news. It includes the following steps: 1. creating an appropriate SETTING; 2. addressing the patient's PERCEPTION of his/her situation; 3. seeking the patient's INVITATION; 4. giving KNOWLEDGE to the patient regarding diagnosis and prognosis; 5. addressing the patient's EMOTIONS; 6. providing a management STRATEGY and SUMMARY of what had been discussed so far.

destinations.label: Grief and end-of-life counseling → End-of-life counseling

MPYM26.title: Living will
MPYM26.description: A legal document that provides personal preferences and instructions regarding future medical care. Takes effect when an indvidual is terminally ill without chance of recovery. Typically includes preferences regarding end-of-life care (e.g., cardiopulmonary resuscitation, mechanical ventilation) but can also establish other specific preferences (e.g., regarding chemotherapy or tube feedings). It is a type of written advance health care directive.

destinations.label: Capacity, competence, and consent → Decision-making capacity

LPYw26.title: Physician aid-in-dying
LPYw26.description: The physician-facilitated process of providing a terminally-ill patient, at their explicit request, with a medication, intervention, and/or information that will allow for the patient to hasten or end their own life (e.g., a physician prescribes the patient benzodiazepines and informs the patient of the lethal dose, with the knowledge that the patient may use this information to end their own life). Preferred terminology is controversial and varies.

6PYjf6.title: Euthanasia
6PYjf6.description: The administration of a lethal medication, such as sedatives or paralytics, to intentionally bring about the end of the patient's life. Only performed at the explicit request of the patient and requires the full process of informed consent. Not currently legal in the United States.

wPYhS6.title: Symbiosis
wPYhS6.description: A long-term biological interaction between two organisms of different species. Subtypes include mutualism, parasitism, and commensalism.

9PYNS6.title: Commensalism
9PYNS6.description: A relationship between a symbiont (commensal) and its host in which the symbiont benefits from the relationship and the host derives neither benefit nor harm.

xPYES6.title: Ectoparasite
xPYES6.description: A parasite that lives on the host's skin, skin appendages, or mucous membranes exposed to the external environment. Examples include fleas, ticks, and lice.

BPYzS6.title: Endoparasite
BPYzS6.description: A parasite that lives inside the host's body. Examples include helminths and protozoa.

APYRh6.title: Antihelminthics
APYRh6.description: A group of drugs used to treat helminth infections (e.g., individual treatment of symptomatic infection, mass drug administration to decrease endemic prevalence). Examples include ivermectin, albendazole, triclabendazole, praziquantel, and diethylcarbamazine.

_PY5h6.title: Praziquantel
_PY5h6.description: An anthelmintic drug used in the treatment of schistosomiasis as well as Taenia spp. (e.g., intestinal taeniasis and neurocysticercosis) and Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) infestations. Causes muscle spasms in worms and alters their surface morphology, thereby facilitating recognition by the immune system and leading to their death. The worms are then either digested completely or passed in the stool.

zPYrh6.title: Albendazole
zPYrh6.description: An orally administered, broad-spectrum antihelminthic drug that is used to treat echinococcosis, cysticercosis, pinworm infection (enterobiasis), hookworm infection (ancylostomiasis, necatoriasis), ascariasis, trichuriasis, and strongyloidiasis. Mechanism of action: inhibition of microtubule synthesis.

-PYDh6.title: Mebendazole
-PYDh6.description: An orally administered, broad-spectrum antihelminthic drug that inhibits the microtubule synthesis and is used to treat nematode infestations, including roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, threadworm, pinworm, and the intestinal form of trichinosis.

04Ye36.title: Permethrin
04Ye36.description: A substance toxic to parasites, insects, fleas, mites, and flies. Used to treat head lice and scabies infections. It can also be used prophylactically (as a spray for clothing and bedding) to prevent bites.

a4YQ36.title: Dimeticone
a4YQ36.description: A silicone-based compound used to treat pediculosis capitis. Interferes with the ability of lice to regulate water (e.g., penetrates the respiratory system, thereby causing suffocation). Also used as a skin barrier cream.

b4YH36.title: Cestoda
b4YH36.description: A class of the flatworm phylum. Infection occurs via ingestion of larvae from raw freshwater fish or dog feces and can cause gastrointestinal and/or systemic infections.

14Y2R6.title: Taenia saginata
14Y2R6.description: A tapeworm transmitted by the ingestion of larvae (cysticerci) in raw or undercooked beef. Can cause intestinal taeniasis.

W4YPR6.title: Taenia solium
W4YPR6.description: A tapeworm contracted by ingestion of undercooked pork. Ingestion of larvae (aka cysticerci) can cause intestinal taeniasis; ingestion of eggs from feces of humans with intestinal taeniasis can cause cysticercosis. Migration to the brain causes neurocysticercosis.

media.title: Head of a pork tapeworm (Taenia solium)

d4YoR6.title: Echinococcus
d4YoR6.description: A genus of tapeworms that causes echinococcosis. Echinococcus granulosus causes cystic echinococcosis; Echinococcus multilocularis causes alveolar echinococcosis.

media.title: Life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus (dog tapeworm)

V4YGR6.title: Echinococcus granulosus
V4YGR6.description: A tapeworm that causes hydatid cysts in the liver. Transmitted via ingestion of food contaminated with dog feces.

media.title: Life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus (dog tapeworm)

f4Yki6.title: Diphyllobothrium latum
f4Yki6.description: A type of tapeworm that is usually contracted via consumption of raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Larvae develop into adult tapeworms in the small intestine. Formerly known as Diphyllobothrium latum.

g4YFi6.title: Nematodes
g4YFi6.description: A class of worms that includes pinworms, giant roundworms, and hookworms. Can cause intestinal, skin, and systemic infections.

i4YJQ6.title: Ascaris lumbricoides
i4YJQ6.description: A type of intestinal nematode. Infection with Ascaria larvae is acquired by ingestion of Ascaria eggs. The eggs hatch into larvae, which burrow through the intestinal wall and migrate to the lungs. Re-expectorated larvae migrate back to the intestines and mature into adult form.

Q4YuQ6.title: Toxocara
Q4YuQ6.description: A genus of the family Toxocaridae, a group of parasitic round worms, that includes the species T. canis and T. cati.

j4Y_Q6.title: Toxocara canis
j4Y_Q6.description: A nematode parasite that causes toxocariasis in humans. Transmitted through ingestion of embryonated eggs (passed in dog feces) or tissue that contains encysted larvae. Dogs are its definitive host.

P4YWj6.title: Toxocara cati
P4YWj6.description: A nematode parasite that causes toxocariasis in humans. Transmitted through ingestion of embryonated eggs (passed in cat feces) or tissue that contains encysted larvae. Dogs are its definitive host.

44Y3j6.title: Hookworms
44Y3j6.description: A group of parasitic nematodes that uses hook-like mouthparts to attach to the intestinal wall and consume blood. Includes Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. Transmitted via cutaneous penetration (e.g., from walking barefoot).

k4Ymj6.title: Ancylostoma duodenale
k4Ymj6.description: A common hookworm that is transmitted through cutaneous penetration by larvae. Causes cutaneous larva migrans (a pruritic, serpiginous rash) and, in some cases, anemia by consuming blood from the gastrointestinal tract.

O4YIj6.title: Trichinella spiralis
O4YIj6.description: A nematode parasite (roundworm) of the Trichinella genus that causes trichinosis and is transmitted through consumption of undercooked meat of wild or farm animals (esp. pork) or less likely fecal-orally. Its larvae migrate from the intestine to the striated muscles, where they encyst and cause severe myositis and myalgia.

l4Yvj6.title: Enterobius vermicularis
l4Yvj6.description: A helminth from the nematode phylum (roundworms) that most commonly infects children (via the fecal-oral route), causing perianal pruritus.

54YiP6.title: Wuchereria bancrofti
54YiP6.description: A roundworm that is transmitted by mosquitoes and causes elephantiasis. Endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, India, and parts of Latin America.

M4YMP6.title: Trematodes
M4YMP6.description: A class of parasitic worms that includes Schistosoma species.

n4Y7P6.title: Schistosoma
n4Y7P6.description: A trematode (fluke) that causes schistosomiasis. Freshwater snails serve as the intermediate host and release the infectious version of the parasite (cercariae) into the water, where it comes into human contact and penetrates the skin. Includes S. mansoni, S. japonicum, and S. haematobium.

media.title: Geographic distribution of schistosomiasis (risk of transmission)

L4YwP6.title: Arthropods
L4YwP6.description: A phylum of the animal kingdom that includes spiders, mites, and insects. Viruses transmitted via arthropods include West Nile virus, dengue virus, and chikungunya virus. Arthropod bites can also cause a pruritic rash.

J4Ys46.title: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
J4Ys46.description: A potentially fatal tickborne disease caused by the bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii. Symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, conjunctivitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and a blanching macular rash (90% of cases) that begins on the wrists and ankles and spreads to the trunk, palms, and soles.

destinations.label: Tick-borne diseases → Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF)

I4YYk6.title: Louse
I4YYk6.description: A wingless insect and obligate ectoparasite that lives on warm-blooded hosts. Examples include Pediculus humanus capitis, Pediculus humanus corporis, and Pthirus pubis.

media.title: Developmental stages of the body louse

D4Y1l6.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
D4Y1l6.description: A flagellated protozoa that can cause sexually transmitted infections such as vaginitis or urethritis.

B4Yzl6.title: Leishmania donovani
B4Yzl6.description: An intracellular protozoan that causes leishmaniasis (visceral or cutaneous). Transmitted by infected phlebotomine sand flies.

_4Y5N6.title: Trypanosoma brucei
_4Y5N6.description: A protozoa transmitted by the bite of the Tsetse fly. Infection causes African sleeping sickness.

media.title: Life cycle of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and rhodesiense

z4YrN6.title: Trypanosoma cruzi
z4YrN6.description: A parasitic microorganism responsible for Chagas disease. Endemic to Central and South America. Reduviid bugs serve as the vector.

-4YDN6.title: Sporozoa
-4YDN6.description: An outdated taxonomic protozoan phylum that contains many single-celled, parasitic, spore-forming organisms. Includes Plasmodium species. The majority of species previously classified under Sporozoa are now classified under the phylum Apicomplexa.

ZkYZm6.title: Toxoplasma gondii
ZkYZm6.description: An obligate intracellular parasite that causes toxoplasmosis in humans. Transmitted primarily via contaminated cat feces and consumption of raw meat or unpasteurized milk products.

0kYem6.title: Plasmodium
0kYem6.description: An eukaryotic parasite that is transmitted to humans through the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito and causes malaria. Species include Plasmodium vivax, ovale, malariae, and falciparum.

akYQm6.title: Plasmodium falciparum
akYQm6.description: A protozoan (eukaryotic) parasite of the Plasmodiidae family that is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito, which is present in many tropical and subtropical regions and may cause severe falciparum malaria. By invading and destroying RBCs, P. falciparum causes microinfarctions that lead to significant organ dysfunction. P. falciparum presents with a trophozoite ring form within RBCs. Carriers of sickle‑cell mutation have a partial resistance against P. falciparum.

media.title: Microgametocyte and macrogametocyte of Plasmodium falciparum

bkYHm6.title: Plasmodium vivax
bkYHm6.description: A protozoan that is the most common cause of malaria outside of West Africa. Causes tertian malaria with characteristic fevers at 48-hour intervals.

media.title: Tertian malaria: immature trophozoite in Plasmodium vivax infection

ckYa56.title: Plasmodium ovale
ckYa56.description: A protozoan (eukaryotic) parasite of the Plasmodiidae family that is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito, which occurs in many tropical and subtropical regions. After an incubation period of 7-42 days, P. ovale causes tertian malaria with periodic fever spikes every 48 hrs. Following the presumably successful treatment of tertian malaria, some Plasmodium ovale forms (hypnozoites) may persist within the liver and cause reinfection after lying dormant for months or even years.

media.title: Erythrocytes with and without Schüffner's stippling in Plasmodium ovale infection

UkYbM6.title: Cryptosporidium parvum
UkYbM6.description: An intracellular parasite that can cause self-limited diarrhea in individuals who are immunocompetent. Can cause chronic, severe gastrointestinal illness in individuals who are immunocompromised. Transmitted via the fecal-oral route (e.g., food handlers, contaminated water, oral-anal sexual contact).

destinations.label: Food poisoning → Overview of foodborne diseases

TkY6M6.title: Entamoeba histolytica
TkY6M6.description: An anaerobic protozoan that is usually transmitted via the fecal-oral route (e.g., via contaminated drinking water). Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Causes amebiasis that may either present with intestinal manifestations, such as dysentery (i.e., loose stools with mucus and bright red blood, painful defecation, tenesmus, abdominal pain, cramps, weight loss, and anorexia) or extraintestinal manifestations (most often amebic liver abscess).

gkYFM6.title: Entamoeba dispar
gkYFM6.description: A nonpathogenic protozoan that is morphologically similar to Entamoeba histolytica.

SkYyM6.title: Protozoa
SkYyM6.description: A single-celled eukaryotic organism. Protozoal parasites are further categorized as amebae, flagellates, ciliates, and sporozoa.

QkYun6.title: Adenovirus
QkYun6.description: A non-enveloped virus with a linear, double-stranded DNA structure and icosahedral nucleocapsid. Transmitted via contaminated water or via the fecal-oral route. Causes pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, pneumonia, hemorrhagic cystitis, gastroenteritis, myocarditis, and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

4kY3L6.title: Human papillomavirus
4kY3L6.description: A group of > 150 viruses that commonly cause skin diseases, including anogenital warts (e.g., condylomata acuminata), common warts (verruca vulgaris), and oral warts. Also implicated in the pathogenesis of some types of cancer (e.g., cervical cancer, oropharyngeal cancer).

5kYio6.title: Polyomaviridae
5kYio6.description: A family of non-enveloped, double-stranded, circular DNA viruses that most commonly affect immunosuppressed (HIV and transplant) patients. Two common members include JC virus (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) and BK virus (nephropathy and/or hemorrhagic cystitis).

MkYMo6.title: JC virus
MkYMo6.description: A type of human polyomavirus that causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in patients with immunodeficiency (AIDS, immunosuppression after transplant).

media.title: JC virus in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

nkY7o6.title: BK virus
nkY7o6.description: A non-enveloped, double-stranded circular DNA virus of the polyomavirus family that infects the urothelium. BK virus infection is widespread but asymptomatic in the general population. Reactivation of the virus in immunosuppressed patients (especially transplant recipients) can cause polyomavirus-associated nephropathy and/or or polyomavirus-associated hemorrhagic cystitis. The name is derived from the initials of the first kidney transplant patient from which the virus was isolated.

okY0K6.title: Parvoviridae
okY0K6.description: A family of non-enveloped viruses with a linear, single-stranded DNA structure. Includes parvovirus B19.

6kYjK6.title: Parvovirus B19
6kYjK6.description: The smallest known DNA virus. It is nonenveloped with a linear, single-stranded genome. Mainly transmitted by droplets in humans and commonly affects children. Causes erythema infectiosum, also known as fifth disease.

qkYCK6.title: Respiratory syncytial virus
qkYCK6.description: An enveloped, negative-strand RNA virus of the Pneumoviridae family. Infection typically occurs during fall and winter. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets or through contact with contaminated surfaces. Manifestations include fever, cough, rhinorrhea, wheezing, and difficulty breathing. Commonly causes lower respiratory tract infections in young children and older adults.

HkYK66.title: Measles virus
HkYK66.description: Single-stranded RNA virus, member of the Paramyxoviridae family and the etiological agent of measles.

8kYOp6.title: Paramyxoviridae
8kYOp6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a nonsegmented, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes parainfluenza virus,  measles virus, and mumps virus.

ukYpp6.title: Parainfluenza virus
ukYpp6.description: A group of RNA viruses of the Paramyxoviridae family. Contracted via droplet and contact transmission, typically in spring and summer. Has 4 serotypes. Type 1 is the most common causative organism of laryngotracheobronchitis (croup). Type 3 causes bronchiolitis. Other serotypes cause less severe respiratory tract infections.

9kYNJ6.title: Hepatitis C virus
9kYNJ6.description: An enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded, bloodborne RNA virus that is hepatotropic and transmitted primarily through parenteral exposure to blood.

BkYzJ6.title: Flaviviridae
BkYzJ6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes hepatitis C virus, yellow fever virus, dengue fever virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, and Zika virus.

ykYdq6.title: Arbovirus
ykYdq6.description: A virus that is transmitted by an arthropod vector (e.g., ticks, mosquitoes). Examples include Dengue virus and West Nile virus.

_kY5q6.title: Tick-borne encephalitis virus
_kY5q6.description: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) is a member of the Flavivirus family. Transmission occurs via bites from Ixodes species. It causes tick-borne encephalitis, a viral infection of the CNS that results in meningism (neck stiffness, headache, and fever) as well as signs of encephalitis (altered sensorium and motor abnormalities).

media.title: Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) fact sheet and prevalence map

0OYeI6.title: Dengue virus
0OYeI6.description: An enveloped, single-stranded RNA, positive-strand virus of the family Flaviviridae transmitted by mosquitoes (especially Aedes aegypti). Widely distributed throughout the tropics and subtropics. An infection may cause self-limited Dengue fever or life-threatening Dengue hemorrhagic fever or Dengue shock syndrome. There are four Dengue virus serotypes (DENV 1–4). Cross-protective immunity is only weak and transient.

YOYnI6.title: Orthomyxoviridae
YOYnI6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a negative-sense, single-stranded, 8-segmented RNA structure. Includes influenza virus A and B.

XOY9I6.title: Influenza virus
XOY9I6.description: A group of RNA viruses of the Orthomyxoviridae family. Transmission is predominantly airborne, typically in winter. Serotypes A and B are virulent in humans and are the causative agents for the annual flu epidemic.

dOYor6.title: Influenzavirus B
dOYor6.description: A single-stranded RNA virus of the family Orhtomyxoviruses that can cause influenza. Influenza B virus is less common than influenza A virus, and infections have a significantly milder course. Less likely to cause epidemics because it cannot undergo genetic shift.

2OYT76.title: Rhabdoviridae
2OYT76.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a linear, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes rabies virus and the vesicular stomatitis virus.

SOYy76.title: Coronavirus
SOYy76.description: A family of enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with a helical nucleocapsid and characteristic crown-like appearance on electron microscopy. Transmitted via direct contact or aerosol droplets. Most commonly causes upper respiratory infections but can also cause gastroenteritis, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS). Please search SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19 for more info on this specific coronavirus and the disease it causes.

3OYSH6.title: Severe acute respiratory syndrome
3OYSH6.description: Unusual respiratory viral disease, which is characterized by fever, headaches, malaise, and myalgias. This episode usually lasts three to seven days, and is followed by a respiratory phase that presents with nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and possible infiltrates on chest x-ray. SARS is also associated with an elevated LDH and depressed total lymphocytes.

POYWs6.title: Hantavirus
POYWs6.description: A single-stranded, enveloped, RNA virus belonging to the order Bunyavirales. Rodents are the main reservoir for hantavirus. Transmission occurs primarily via inhalation of aerosolized particles excreted in rodent urine and rodent bites. Infection is associated with two acute syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).

kOYms6.title: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus
kOYms6.description: An enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus of the family Nairoviridae. Reservoir include livestock and wild animals. Widely distributed in Africa, the Middle East, Southeastern Europe, and Western and Central Asia. Transmission occurs via ticks and contact to bodily fluids of infected individuals. Infection can cause Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever.

lOYvs6.title: Arenaviridae
lOYvs6.description: An encapsulated RNA virus with a helical capsid. Contains circular RNA subunits of both positive-sense ssRNA and negative-sense ssRNA. Causes lymphocytic choriomeningitis and Lassa fever, although most infections manifest with mild, flu-like symptoms.

MOYMG6.title: Togaviridae
MOYMG6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes rubella virus, Western and Eastern equine encephalitis viruses, and chikungunya virus.

nOY7G6.title: Rubella virus
nOY7G6.description: A positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus in the Matonavirus family. Humans are the only natural host of the virus, which can be spread via droplet, contact, or transplacental transmission. Infection causes rubella.

oOY0t6.title: Filoviridae
oOY0t6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a linear, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes Ebola virus and Marburg virus.

6OYjt6.title: Ebolavirus
6OYjt6.description: A negative-sense, single-stranded virus of the Filoviridae family. Causes acute viral hemorrhage and multiorgan failure, resulting in a high mortality rate. Transmitted through contact with infected body fluids.

qOYCt6.title: Picornaviridae
qOYCt6.description: A family of non-enveloped viruses with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes poliovirus, echovirus, rhinovirus, coxsackievirus (A and B), and hepatitis A virus.

rOYfF6.title: Enterovirus
rOYfF6.description: A genus of positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, including poliovirus, Coxsackie A and B, and rhinovirus. These viruses are spread via the fecal-oral route and can cause several different infectious diseases.

HOYKF6.title: Coxsackievirus
HOYKF6.description: A nonenveloped virus with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA and an icosahedral capsid. Belongs to the Enterovirus genus and the Picornaviridae family.

GOYBF6.title: Echovirus
GOYBF6.description: A picornavirus that causes several conditions, including conjunctivitis, myocarditis, meningitis, hepatitis, and severe neonatal diarrhea.

FOYg86.title: Poliovirus
FOYg86.description: A non-enveloped virus with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA and an icosahedral capsid. It belongs to the Enterovirus genus and the Picornaviridae family. It is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and causes acute flaccid parlaysis (poliomyelitis).

uOYp86.title: Hepatitis A virus
uOYp86.description: A non-enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA enterovirus of the Picornavirus family that is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Causes an acute viral hepatitis after an incubation period of 2-6 weeks.

DOY1u6.title: Rhinovirus
DOY1u6.description: A member of the group of Picornaviridae viruses responsible for the common cold and other upper respiratory infections.

yOYdE6.title: Rotavirus
yOYdE6.description: A non-enveloped, double-stranded RNA reovirus that is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Rotavirus is a frequent cause of viral gastroenteritis in infants and young children.

-OYDE6.title: Hepeviridae
-OYDE6.description: A family of non-enveloped viruses with a linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes hepatitis E virus.

ZlYZv6.title: Hepatitis E virus
ZlYZv6.description: A non-enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus that is hepatotropic and spread feco-orally. It causes acute viral hepatitis and is associated with a higher risk of fulminant hepatic failure during pregnancy.

destinations.label: Overview of viral hepatitides → Hepatitis E

YlYnv6.title: Caliciviridae
YlYnv6.description: A family of non-enveloped viruses with a linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA structure. Includes Lagovirus, Nebovirus, Sapovirus, Vesivirus, and Norovirus.

blYHv6.title: Norovirus
blYHv6.description: A highly virulent, non‑enveloped positive-sense, single-stranded RNA calicivirus ((+)ssRNA virus), which is the most common cause of adult gastroenteritis and foodborne illness. Transmission occurs via the fecal‑oral route through contaminated food or water, person‑to‑person contact, via airborne droplets, and contact with contaminated surfaces.

WlYPD6.title: Deltaviridae
WlYPD6.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genome. Hepatitis D virus belongs to this family.

TlY6w6.title: Hepatitis B virus
TlY6w6.description: An enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the Hepadnavirus that can be transmitted sexually, parenterally, or perinatally and causes acute or chronic hepatitis. Prophylactic immunization with a recombinant vaccine is recommended for all age groups.

hlYc96.title: Poxviridae
hlYc96.description: A family of enveloped viruses with a linear, double-stranded DNA structure. Includes smallpox virus, cowpox virus, and molluscum contagiosum virus.

3lYS96.title: Smallpox
3lYS96.description: An enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus with a morphologically complex nucleocapsid that is member of the Poxviridae family. Variola is the causative agent of smallpox, a highly infectious disease globally eradicated by 1980 through widespread immunization programs. It is transmitted by respiratory shedding and is clinically characterized by fever, rash, headache, backache, and malaise.

OlYIC6.title: Tinetti test
OlYIC6.description: A test to assess an individual's balance and gait, typically used in older adults. The balance test assesses the ability to sit, stand upright, and turn 360°. The gait test assesses the ability to walk at normal speed, turn around, and walk back.

destinations.label: Basics of hematology → Red cell line: erythrocytes

8lYOA6.title: Mean corpuscular volume
8lYOA6.description: The average volume of a red blood cell. Normal values are 80–100 fL. Depending on the MCV, anemias can be classified as either microcytic (< 80 fL), normocytic (80–100 fL), or macrocytic (> 100 fL).

ElY8A6.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin
ElY8A6.description: The average mass of hemoglobin in a red blood cell (typically 25.4–34.6 pg). Can be decreased due to thalassemia or iron deficiency.

DlY1_6.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
DlY1_6.description: Mean hemoglobin concentration of all RBCs; calculated as hemoglobin/hematocrit. Increased, e.g., in spherocytosis and potentially decreased in iron deficiency and thalassemia.

ylYdz6.title: Leukocytosis
ylYdz6.description: An increase of the total number of white blood cells (> 11,000/mm³ in adults). Can be further classified according to the fraction of white blood cells that is increased (e.g., lymphocytosis, neutrophilia, eosinophilia).

fNYk0p.title: Th17 cells
fNYk0p.description: A subset of T helper cells that secretes IL-17 and plays an important role in neutrophil and macrophage recruitment to the site of infection.

destinations.label: Adaptive immune system → T cells (T lymphocytes)

HNYKcp.title: Prion
HNYKcp.description: A misfolded protein that has an increase in beta-sheet structure and induces a conformational change of normal cellular prion proteins (PrPc). Intracerebral accumulation of prions leads to plaque formation that causes neural cell death and progression to spongiform encephalopathy.

8NYO1p.title: Probability of an independent event
8NYO1p.description: The likelihood that an event that is not dependent on or influenced by preceding events will occur.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Hypothesis testing and probability

uNYp1p.title: Conditional probability
uNYp1p.description: The probability that an event (A) occurs given that another event (B) has occurred. Expressed as P(A|B), which is equal to P(A and B) divided by P(B).

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Hypothesis testing and probability

wNYhWp.title: Independent variable
wNYhWp.description: A variable that is not dependent on other variables and can thus be manipulated by the researcher for the purpose of a study. E.g., dose of a drug that is changed in a clinical trial for the drug in order to determine its adverse effect profile. In contrast, the dependent variable is only measured but not changed.

9NYNWp.title: Dependent variable
9NYNWp.description: A variable with a value that depends on another variable and therefore cannot be manipulated by the researcher. E.g., the frequency of adverse effects in a clinical trial for a drug is the dependent variable and is only measured but not changed. The frequency of adverse effects depends on the dose and type of the drug, which can be changed by the researcher (independent variable).

xNYEWp.title: Bimodal distribution
xNYEWp.description: A statistical distribution with two peaks, indicating two subgroups within a study population. For example, the incidence rate of Hodgkin lymphoma has a peak at 25–30 years and at 50–70 years.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Distribution and graphical representation of data

BNYzWp.title: Normal distribution
BNYzWp.description: A symmetrical distribution of values in a bell-shaped curve. The curve reflects the frequency with which the values of a variable are obtained or observed, with the highest frequency occurring in the middle (mean value) and gradually tapering toward the extremes.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Distribution and graphical representation of data

ZmYZVp.title: Ordinal scale
ZmYZVp.description: A type of variable scale that places values in categories that have a meaningful order but do not necessarily have even spacing between each category. For example, sizes can be described as small, medium, and large and have a smaller step between small and medium than between medium and large.

dmYoep.title: Histogram
dmYoep.description: A graphical method to represent data. Involves grouping a continuous variable into distinct intervals that are plotted on the x-axis.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Distribution and graphical representation of data

UmYbUp.title: Measures of central tendency
UmYbUp.description: A collection of measures that reflect the center point or value of a dataset, around which most values in a distribution will fall. Includes mean, median, and mode.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Measures of central tendency and outliers

3mYS2p.title: Measures of dispersion
3mYS2p.description: The statistical measures of the degree of distribution or variability in a data set. They include range, standard deviation, variance, standard error, confidence intervals, and coefficient of variation.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Measures of dispersion

RmYl2p.title: Interquartile range
RmYl2p.description: The range from the second to the third quartile. Calculated by establishing the difference between the 75th and 25th percentile. Less influenced by extreme data values (outliers).

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Measures of dispersion

imYJ2p.title: Variance (statistics)
imYJ2p.description: The average of the squared differences of values in a data set from the mean value. The variance allows interpretation of how far a set of data is spread out. A variance of zero means that there is no variability in the values. Largely different numbers in a set of data lead to a large variance.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Measures of dispersion

QmYu2p.title: Standard deviation
QmYu2p.description: The average distance of a set of values from the mean value. The SD is equal to the square root of the average of the squared deviations from the mean (i.e., square root of the variance). In a normal distribution, one standard deviation above and below the mean includes about 68% of the sample, 2 SDs include 95%, and 3 SDs 99.7%.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Measures of dispersion

OmYIfp.title: Pearson correlation coefficient
OmYIfp.description: A statistical measure of the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables expressed on a scatter plot. It ranges anywhere from -1 to +1, where -1 represents a perfectly negative linear relationship and +1 represents a perfectly positive linear relationship.

destinations.label: Statistical analysis of data → Statistical tests

mmYVTp.title: Liver function tests
mmYVTp.description: A group of laboratory tests that serve as parameters of hepatocellular damage, cholestasis, and hepatic synthesis. Most commonly refers to a panel that includes alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), bilirubin (direct and indirect), total protein, and albumin. Can also include γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT).

MmYMTp.title: Transaminases
MmYMTp.description: Enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, e.g., alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), which are used clinically as parameters of hepatocellular injury.

nmY7Tp.title: Alanine aminotransferase
nmY7Tp.description: An enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism that catalyzes the transfer of an alpha-amino group between glutamate and alanine. Primarily found in hepatocytes; thus, serum concentrations are used to monitor for hepatocellular damage.

destinations.label: Amino acids →  Biochemical reactions of amino acid metabolism

LmYwTp.title: Aspartate aminotransferase
LmYwTp.description: An enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism that catalyzes the transfer of an alpha-amino group between glutamate and aspartate. This enzyme is found in many cells (e.g., liver,  heart, kidney). AST levels are most commonly used to monitor hepatocellular damage.

destinations.label: Amino acids →  Biochemical reactions of amino acid metabolism

omY0gp.title: Glutamate dehydrogenase
omY0gp.description: An enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia. An enzyme immunoassay for GDH is used as a screening test for C. difficile infection.

6mYjgp.title: Parameters of cholestasis
6mYjgp.description: The laboratory values that indicate that bile cannot flow from the liver to the duodenum: ↑ ALP, ↑ GGT, ↑ total and ↑ direct bilirubin.

pmYLgp.title: γ-Glutamyl transpeptidase
pmYLgp.description: A membrane-bound enzyme of glutathione metabolism and amino acid transport. The most sensitive parameter for diseases of the liver and/or biliary tract. However, it is not very specific, as it is found in many tissues.

rmYfSp.title: Alkaline phosphatase
rmYfSp.description: A group of enzymes found throughout the body but produced predominantly in the liver, bones, placenta, and small intestine. Common causes of elevated serum ALP include cholestasis, bone disease (e.g., bone metastases, Paget's disease, hyperparathyroidism), and pregnancy. The normal reference range is 20–70 U/L.

HmYKSp.title: Bilirubin
HmYKSp.description: A hemoglobin breakdown product and parameter of cholestasis. Serum total bilirubin consists of unconjugated bilirubin and conjugated bilirubin.

GmYBSp.title: Albumin
GmYBSp.description: A protein whose functions include maintenance of colloid osmotic pressure and transportation of enzymes and degradation products. Produced exclusively by the liver and comprises the majority of total plasma proteins (~60%). Levels decrease with decreased hepatic synthesis, urinary protein loss, and malnutrition.

tmYXhp.title: Cholinesterase
tmYXhp.description: A family of enzymes that catalyze the breakdown of choline esters (e.g., acetylcholine, succinylcholine). Includes acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase.

EmY8hp.title: Creatinine
EmY8hp.description: Creatinine is a breakdown product of the creatine phosphate found in muscles. Since it is produced at a base rate and its renal excretion rate is relatively physiologically constant, serum creatinine levels are used as a measure of renal function.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Renal function test

9mYN3p.title: Cystatin C
9mYN3p.description: An enzyme that inhibits cysteine proteinases. Found in most nucleated cells. Used as a marker of kidney function and is more reliable than creatinine in assessing close-to-normal GFR and thus mild renal impairment.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Renal function test

xmYE3p.title: Urea
xmYE3p.description: A nitrogenous compound produced in the liver as a product of protein catabolism. Excreted primarily in the urine. Freely filtered by the glomerulus. Normal serum urea concentration is 7–18 mg/dL; levels are elevated in patients with kidney dysfunction.

BmYz3p.title: Uric acid
BmYz3p.description: A byproduct of the breakdown of purine bases. Excess amounts can trigger gout and uric acid nephropathy. Elevated serum concentrations are found in patients with renal excretion disorders, conditions that cause increased cell death (e.g., tumor lysis syndrome), and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

destinations.label: Diagnostic evaluation of the kidney and urinary tract → Renal function test

_mY5Rp.title: Amylase
_mY5Rp.description: A group of enzymes present in the pancreas and salivary glands that facilitate the breakdown of dietary starch. Elevated serum levels are most commonly associated with acute pancreatitis or parotitis. Normal range: 25–125 U/L.

zmYrRp.title: Elastase
zmYrRp.description: A protease enzyme that breaks down elastin. Usually inhibited by α1-antitrypsin. Produced by the pancreas to digest protein and measured as a marker of exocrine pancreatic function. Excessive activity caused loss of elastic fibers in the lung, increase compliance (as in emphysema). Also produced by bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas) and destroys host tissues.

-mYDRp.title: Electrolyte
-mYDRp.description: ̄A solvent that contains dissolved cations and anions. Normal body function requires the appropriate concentrations of the following serum electrolytes: sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), chloride (Cl⁻), bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), and phosphate (H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻).

Z5YZip.title: Chloride
Z5YZip.description: The main anion found in the extracellular space. Changes in serum chloride concentrations typically reflect changes in serum sodium concentrations. Involved in water balance, maintaining osmotic pressure, and acid-base balance

05Yeip.title: Magnesium
05Yeip.description: An essential element. As an electrolyte (Mg⁺²), it functions as one of the main intracellular cations and is an important cofactor for several enzymes and transporters (e.g., related to glucose and lipid metabolism, neuromuscular function, energy transfer and storage, and bone development). Magnesium balance is closely interlinked with calcium and potassium homeostasis.

a5YQip.title: Phosphate
a5YQip.description: The biologically active form of phosphorus. 85% of the body's phosphate is contained in bone and teeth. Most of the remaining 15% is contained in the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes or complexed with adenosine or guanosine to make energy-storing molecules (e.g., ATP, GTP). Phosphate moieties typically exist as anions at physiologic pH.

c5YaQp.title: Ferritin
c5YaQp.description: A protein complex responsible for iron storage. Also an acute phase reactant that increases in response to systemic inflammation. Serum ferritin is the parameter of choice for determining iron deficiency (decreased ferritin) and iron overload (increased ferritin).

15Y2Qp.title: Transferrin
15Y2Qp.description: An iron-carrier protein that binds to and transports Fe3+ from iron-laden cells (e.g., intestinal mucosal cells, macrophages) to the rest of the body via the bloodstream. Transferrin is synthesized in the liver.

25YTjp.title: Lipoprotein
25YTjp.description: A molecule composed of lipids and proteins. Plasma lipoproteins such as ultra low- (ULDL), very low- (VLDL), low- (LDL), intermediate- (IDL), and high-density lipoproteins (HDL) are synthesized in the liver and small intestine. They are responsible for transporting lipids (e.g., cholesterol, triglycerides, phospholipids).

destinations.label: Lipids and their metabolism → Lipid transport

T5Y6jp.title: Lipoprotein(a)
T5Y6jp.description: A low-density lipoprotein that is bonded with apolipoprotein A. Increased levels have been associated with elevated ASCVD risk.

l5Yv4p.title: Hyperlipidemia
l5Yv4p.description: A condition of elevated serum concentrations of both triglycerides (> 150 mg/dL) and cholesterol (> 200 mg/dL). Causes include genetic predisposition, a diet high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and other conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism). Contributes to the development of atherosclerosis.

55Yikp.title: Biuret test
55Yikp.description: A laboratory test used to measure serum protein levels. Uses a reagent that contains copper ions that bind to peptide bonds, inducing a purple color change in the sample. Total protein concentration is determined by measuring the sample's light absorption.

destinations.label: Protein analysis → Basics of protein analysis

p5YLOp.title: Serum protein electrophoresis
p5YLOp.description: A test that measures the amount of protein (e.g., albumin, globulins) in the blood. Blood is collected and serum is separated out and placed on a medium. Electrical current is then used to separate the serum proteins by their charge, size, and shape. Used to diagnose multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, amyloidosis, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and Castleman disease.

media.title: Normal finding in serum protein electrophoresis

J5YsOp.title: Prokaryotes
J5YsOp.description: A group of single-celled organisms that lack membrane-bound organelles (e.g., nucleus, mitochondria).

75Y4lp.title: Ribosome
75Y4lp.description: A complex of RNA and associated proteins present in all living cells that carries out protein synthesis (translation). Can be present freely in the cytoplasm or membrane-bound (e.g., in the rough endoplasmic reticulum)

s5Ytlp.title: Transduction (genetics)
s5Ytlp.description: A process of virally-mediated transfer and integration of genetic material into a cell. Further categorized into generalized and specialized transduction.

G5YBlp.title: Virulence factor
G5YBlp.description: A molecule produced by a pathogen that promotes infection (e.g., by facilitating evasion of the host immune response). Examples include Protein A and pertussis toxin, which impair phagocytosis.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

t5YXNp.title: Pseudomonas exotoxin A
t5YXNp.description: A bacterial AB toxin produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa that inactivates elongation factor (EF-2), thus impairing protein synthesis and causing host cell death. Thought to be responsible for the ulcerative lesions of ecthyma gangrenosum.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

F5YgNp.title: Enterotoxins
F5YgNp.description: An exotoxin produced by certain bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus (enterotoxin B), Clostridioides difficile, Clostridium perfringens, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, and Shigella dysenteriae. Primarily targets intestinal mucosa and causes diarrhea and vomiting.

E5Y8Np.title: Neurotoxins
E5Y8Np.description: A substance that can injure or impair the function of the nervous system (e.g., by damaging neurons, axons, or glia). Examples include ethanol, nitric oxide, botulinum toxin, tetanus toxin, mercury, and lead.

v5YANp.title: Coagulase
v5YANp.description: Enzyme that converts fibrinogen into fibrin. It is produced by Staphylococcus aureus and can aid in distinguishing it from other staphylococci strains.

D5Y1mp.title: Flagella
D5Y1mp.description: A slender, whip-like appendage that facilitates cell movement.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

w5Yhmp.title: Peritrichous flagella
w5Yhmp.description: An arrangement of flagella at multiple points around certain bacteria (e.g., E. coli), which facilitates cell movement.

destinations.label: General bacteriology → Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

x5YEmp.title: Spore former
x5YEmp.description: An organism that forms a round, thick-walled, heat- and desiccation-resistant microscopic reproductive unit (spore) as a part of its life cycle. Includes some gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Bacillus anthracis, Clostridioides difficile, Clostridium tetani), some protozoa (e.g., Cryptosporidium, Isosporum, Microsporidium), and most fungi.

-5YD5p.title: Gram staining
-5YD5p.description: A standard microbiological laboratory test used to test for bacteria. Based on the cell wall characteristics of bacteria, they stain blue/purple (gram positive) or pink/red (gram negative), although some bacteria do not Gram stain well due to unique cell wall characteristics (e.g., Mycobacteria) or cannot be seen because they are intracellular (e.g., Chlamydia).

bMYHMp.title: Microaerophile
bMYHMp.description: A type of bacterium that requires low levels of oxygen for respiration. Typically cannot survive at normal environmental levels of oxygen due to oxidative stress.

XMY9Mp.title: Alpha hemolysis
XMY9Mp.description: A characteristic of certain bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae and Viridans streptococci) to partially break down hemoglobin when grown on blood agar medium; can be identified by the greenish discoloration the bacteria cause when grown on blood agar. Used as a classification system in microbiology.

eMYxnp.title: Beta hemolysis
eMYxnp.description: The ability of certain pathogens (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae) to completely break down hemoglobin. Identified by complete discoloration surrounding colonies growing on blood agar.

gMYFLp.title: Gamma hemolysis
gMYFLp.description: A distinguishing characteristic of certain bacteria (e.g., Peptostreptococcus species, Enterococci) that are unable to break down hemoglobin when grown on blood agar medium.

6MYjpp.title: Pack years
6MYjpp.description: The number of cigarette packs (20 cigarettes) that a person smokes per day multiplied by the number of years of cigarette consumption, e.g., (1 pack/day) x (10 years smoking history) = 10 pack years. This figure is used to quantify a person's lifetime exposure to tobacco.

destinations.label: Tobacco product use and smoking cessation → Prevention

rMYfJp.title: Electromyography
rMYfJp.description: A diagnostic procedure in which the muscle activity in response to neural stimulation is measured to detect dysfunction at the level of the neuromuscular junction, the muscle, or the corresponding nerve. It involves inserting a needle electrode into a muscle to record electrical activity.

7MY4Jp.title: Nerve conduction study
7MY4Jp.description: An analysis of a muscle's electrical activity in response to stimulation of its supplying nerve. Measured parameters include conduction velocity, amplitude of the nerve impulse, distal motor latency (time between stimulation of the nerve and muscular contraction), and F-wave latency. Indications include assessment of polyneuropathy (e.g., due to diabetes mellitus, vitamin B12 deficiency) or entrapment neuropathy (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome).

8MYOqp.title: Berger effect
8MYOqp.description: A physiological phenomenon in which EEG alpha wave activity decreases when a person opens his/her eyes or concentrates (transition into beta waves).

uMYpqp.title: EEG beta wave
uMYpqp.description: Waves with the highest frequency (12.5–30 Hz) and the lowest amplitude of all waves measured on EEG. Beta waves are seen during the wakeful state and during REM sleep.

destinations.label: Sleep and sleep disorders → Sleep physiology

vMYAqp.title: Electroencephalography
vMYAqp.description: A method for recording the electrical activity of the brain (e.g., to evaluate for seizure activity). Routine EEG is noninvasive, with the electrodes placed on the scalp.
